docs.title: Question
docs.text: What does Scripture explicitly say about the nature and composition of human beings (biblical anthropology)? Focus on nephesh (soul), ruach (spirit), neshamah (breath), the creation of man, whether humans ARE souls or HAVE souls, and what happens at death.

docs.title: Nephesh chayyah applied to sea creatures before humans
docs.text:
And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl [that] may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven. And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that [it was] good.

Context: Fifth day of creation. Animals receive the same designation (nephesh chayyah) that will later be applied to the man in Gen 2:7.

Notes: The Hebrew 'nephesh chayyah' (living creature/soul) is first applied to animals, not humans. This establishes that nephesh is not an exclusively human property.

docs.title: Nephesh chayyah applied to land animals
docs.text:
And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so. And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that [it was] good.

Context: Sixth day of creation, before man is created. Land animals are also nephesh chayyah.

Notes: Same terminology (nephesh chayyah) used for land animals as will be used for man in Gen 2:7.

docs.title: Creation of man in the image of God — tselem and demuth
docs.text:
And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. So God created man in his [own] image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

Context: Sixth day of creation. God uses 1cp cohortative (na'aseh) — 'let us make.' Two terms: tselem (image) and demuth (likeness). Dominion mandate immediately follows.

Notes: na'aseh (Qal.Impf.1p of asah) — 1cp cohortative. tselem (Noun.ms.Abs.+1up) in 'our image'; demuth (Noun.fs.Abs.+1up) 'after our likeness.' The image of God distinguishes humans from animals who are also nephesh chayyah. See grammar reference: cohortative-1cp-divine-speech.md.

docs.title: FOUNDATIONAL creation text — dust + neshamah = nephesh chayyah
docs.text:
And the LORD God formed man [of] the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

Context: The detailed creation account. Three-part formula: (1) yatsar — God FORMED man from dust (aphar) of the ground (adamah), (2) naphach — God BREATHED (blew) into his nostrils the neshamah of chayyim, (3) wayehi — man BECAME a nephesh chayyah.

Notes: wayehi (Verb.Qal.Wayq.3ms of hayah) — transformation verb 'became,' not 'received.' Man did not receive a soul; the entire entity IS the nephesh chayyah. The breath is neshamah (not ruach) — the specific, rarest term. nephesh (Noun.fs.Abs) + chayyah (Adj.fs.Abs) — same compound applied to animals in 1:20-24. See word studies: H5315-nephesh, H5397-nshamah, H2416-chay, H1961-hayah.

docs.title: Mot tamut — death penalty for disobedience
docs.text:
But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.

Context: God's command to Adam in the garden, before the Fall. The mot tamut construction (infinitive absolute + imperfect) is the same used for judicial death penalties throughout the Pentateuch.

Notes: mot (Verb.Qal.InfAbs of muwth) + tamut (Verb.Qal.Impf.2ms of muwth) — emphatic 'dying you shall die' / 'you shall surely die.' See grammar reference: infinitive-absolute-intensification.md. Same construction in Exo 21:12 for capital punishment.

docs.title: Tree of life in the garden — conditional immortality
docs.text:
And out of the ground made the LORD God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.

Context: The tree of life was accessible before the Fall, implying that continued life was conditional on access to this tree.

Notes: The presence of the tree of life suggests that immortality was not inherent but dependent on the tree. This is confirmed in Gen 3:22-24 where access is barred.

docs.title: Animals formed from the same ground as man
docs.text:
And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought [them] unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that [was] the name thereof.

Context: Same verb yatsar (to form) and same material (adamah/ground) used for animals as for man in Gen 2:7.

Notes: Animals share the same material origin as humans. The distinguishing factor is not the substance but the image of God (Gen 1:26-27) and the direct divine breathing of neshamah (Gen 2:7).

docs.title: Dust returns to dust — reversal of creation
docs.text:
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou [art], and unto dust shalt thou return.

Context: God's judgment on Adam after the Fall. Death is described as a reversal of the creation process — returning to the ground/dust from which man was taken.

Notes: The reversal language directly mirrors Gen 2:7. Man came from dust (aphar) and returns to dust. No mention of a surviving component.

docs.title: Tree of life barred — most direct statement humans are not inherently immortal
docs.text:
And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever: Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken. So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

Context: After the Fall. God explicitly bars access to the tree of life to PREVENT man from living forever — which would be unnecessary if man had an inherently immortal soul.

Notes: 'Lest he... eat, and live for ever' — this is the most direct statement in Scripture that humans are not inherently immortal. The mechanism for eternal life (the tree) had to be removed to ensure death would result. Cherubim and flaming sword guard the way.

docs.title: Rachel's nephesh departing at death
docs.text:
And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin.

Context: Rachel's death during childbirth. Her nephesh 'goes out' (yatsa) at the moment of death.

Notes: Nephesh departing = death occurring. The text does not describe where the nephesh goes or what state it enters. Compare with 1 Kgs 17:21-22 where Elijah prays for the nephesh to return.

docs.title: Nephesh meth — dead soul/body (nephesh used for corpse)
docs.text:
Neither shall he go in to any dead body, nor defile himself for his father, or for his mother;

Context: Priestly regulations. The Hebrew is nephesh meth — literally 'a dead nephesh/soul.' Nephesh here refers to a corpse.

Notes: nephesh meth (construct chain) — 'dead soul.' This usage demolishes any claim that nephesh inherently means an immortal entity. A nephesh can be dead. See also Num 6:6.

docs.title: Nephesh meth — dead body/soul (Nazirite regulations)
docs.text:
All the days that he separateth [himself] unto the LORD he shall come at no dead body.

Context: Nazirite vow regulations. Same term nephesh meth as Lev 21:11.

Notes: Confirms nephesh meth usage for a corpse/dead body. Nephesh can die and refer to dead entities.

docs.title: The soul (nephesh) that sins shall die
docs.text:
Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

Context: God declares His ownership of all souls and the principle of individual accountability. The nephesh that sins — it (hi') shall die (tamut).

Notes: hannephesh hachote't hi' tamut — 'the soul (nephesh, fs) the sinning-one (Qal.Ptcp.fs) she (PersPron.3fs) shall-die (Qal.Impf.3fs).' Death is predicated of the nephesh itself. If nephesh were inherently immortal, this statement would be self-contradictory.

docs.title: The soul (nephesh) that sins, it shall die — repeated
docs.text:
The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

Context: Restatement of the principle from v.4 with expansion on individual accountability.

Notes: Identical formula repeated for emphasis. Individual accountability and the mortality of the nephesh.

docs.title: Elijah's prayer for the nephesh to return — nephesh can depart and return
docs.text:
And he stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried unto the LORD, and said, O LORD my God, I pray thee, let this child's soul come into him again. And the LORD heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.

Context: Elijah raises the widow's son from death. The nephesh 'comes back' (shub) into the child.

Notes: The nephesh departed at death (as with Rachel in Gen 35:18) and returned when life was restored. This is consistent with nephesh as the living being — when the animating force departs, the nephesh ceases; when it returns, the nephesh revives.

docs.title: Ruach chayyim — breath/spirit of life in all creatures
docs.text:
And, behold, I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh, wherein [is] the breath of life, from under heaven; [and] every thing that [is] in the earth shall die.

Context: God announces the flood. All flesh with ruach chayyim (spirit/breath of life) will die — humans and animals share this ruach.

Notes: Ruach chayyim is shared by all flesh — not exclusively human. This parallels Ecc 3:19 where man and beast have 'one breath.'

docs.title: Neshamah-ruach-chayyim triple compound — all three terms together
docs.text:
All in whose nostrils [was] the breath of life, of all that [was] in the dry [land], died.

Context: The flood kills everything on dry land. The Hebrew contains the remarkable triple compound: nishmat-ruach-chayyim (breath of the spirit of life).

Notes: nishmat (Noun.fs.Cst of neshamah) ruach (Noun.s.Abs) chayyim (Noun.mp.Abs) — all three anthropological terms in a single construct chain. This is the only verse that combines neshamah, ruach, and chayyim together. Applied to ALL creatures that died in the flood, not just humans.

docs.title: Ruach of God made me, neshamah of the Almighty gives life
docs.text:
The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.

Context: Elihu's speech. He affirms that both ruach and neshamah are divine gifts that give life.

Notes: Ruach and neshamah in synonymous parallelism. Both attributed to God as source. Human life is entirely dependent on the divine gift of breath/spirit.

docs.title: If God gathers ruach and neshamah, all flesh perishes
docs.text:
If he set his heart upon man, [if] he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath; All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust.

Context: Elihu continues. If God were to recall His ruach and neshamah from all living things, all flesh would die and return to dust.

Notes: rucho (Noun.s.Abs.+3ms — his spirit/wind) and nishmato (Noun.fs.Abs.+3ms — his breath). If God gathers these back, 'all flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust' — echoing Gen 3:19 and Ecc 12:7. Life is sustained only by continued divine bestowal.

docs.title: God takes away ruach — they die; sends forth ruach — they are created
docs.text:
Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust. Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth.

Context: A creation psalm celebrating God's sustaining providence. The pattern: God's ruach given = life; God's ruach withdrawn = death and return to dust.

Notes: The same ruach that creates life, when withdrawn, causes death. This is applied universally to all creatures. The pattern reinforces the creation-death reversal theme of Gen 2:7 / Ecc 12:7.

docs.title: In death there is no remembrance of God
docs.text:
For in death [there is] no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?

Context: David's prayer in distress. He appeals to God for deliverance because in death (maveth) and the grave (sheol), there is no remembrance or thanksgiving.

Notes: Explicit statement: no remembrance of God in death. The dead cannot praise or thank God. Consistent with Psa 115:17 and Psa 88:10-12.

docs.title: The dead praise not the LORD
docs.text:
The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence.

Context: Contrasting the living who praise God with the dead who are in silence.

Notes: dumah — silence. Death is characterized by silence, not conscious activity. 'Neither any that go down into silence' — comprehensive negation.

docs.title: Ruach departs, returns to earth, thoughts perish — comprehensive death description
docs.text:
Praise ye the LORD. Praise the LORD, O my soul. While I live will I praise the LORD: I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being. Put not your trust in princes, [nor] in the son of man, in whom [there is] no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

Context: A psalm of praise. Verses 3-4 warn against trusting in mortal humans. When the ruach departs, the person returns to the ground, and their thoughts (eshtonotav) perish that very day.

Notes: tetse' (Qal.Impf.3fs of yatsa' — 'goes out') rucho (his spirit/breath); yashub (Qal.Impf.3ms of shub — 'returns') to his adamah (ground); abdu (Qal.Perf.3p of abad — 'perish') eshtonotav (his thoughts). Three things happen at death: (1) spirit goes out, (2) body returns to ground, (3) thoughts perish. The thoughts perishing is particularly significant — consciousness ceases.

docs.title: Dead know nothing, forgotten in the grave
docs.text:
Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise [and] praise thee? Selah. Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? [or] thy faithfulness in destruction? Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

Context: Heman the Ezrahite's lament. Series of rhetorical questions expecting negative answers about the state of the dead.

Notes: The land of forgetfulness (erets neshiyyah) — a powerful image for the unconsciousness of death. No wonders, no praise, no declaration, no knowledge in sheol.

docs.title: Man and beast have one ruach — shared breath/spirit
docs.text:
For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all [is] vanity. All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again. Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth?

Context: The Preacher reflects on mortality. Man and beast share the same fate (miqreh echad) and the same breath (ruach echad).

Notes: ruach echad lakol — 'one breath/spirit for all.' mikreh (Noun.ms.Abs — accident/fate) echad (one) — the same fate befalls both. All come from dust, all return to dust (v.20). v.21 asks rhetorically whether the ruach of man goes up and the ruach of beast goes down — the question implies uncertainty, not affirmation.

docs.title: The dead know nothing — explicit statement of unconsciousness
docs.text:
For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any [thing] that is done under the sun.

Context: The Preacher on death. Direct, unqualified statement: the dead know nothing. All emotions and engagement with the world have perished.

Notes: hammetim einam yod'im me'umah — 'the dead know not anything.' Their love, hatred, envy have all perished (avdah). They have no more portion forever in anything done under the sun.

docs.title: No work, device, knowledge, wisdom in sheol
docs.text:
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do [it] with thy might; for [there is] no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.

Context: Exhortation to act now because sheol offers no opportunity. Four-fold negation of activity in death.

Notes: 'ein ma'aseh, wecheshbon, wada'at, wechokmah bishe'ol — no work, no device/planning, no knowledge, no wisdom in sheol. Comprehensive negation of all cognitive and volitional activity after death.

docs.title: Dust returns to earth, spirit returns to God — reversal of Gen 2:7
docs.text:
Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

Context: The conclusion of the Preacher's meditation on aging and death (Ecc 12:1-7). A precise reversal of the creation formula in Gen 2:7.

Notes: weyashob (Qal.Impf.3ms of shub — return) he'aphar (the dust) al-ha'arets (upon the earth) keshehayyah (as it was); weharuach (and the spirit/breath) tashub (Qal.Impf.3fs of shub — return) el-ha'elohim (to God) asher netanah (who gave it, Qal.Perf.3ms+3fs). The ruach returns to the God who gave it — this is the reversal of Gen 2:7 where God breathed neshamah into man. The ruach returns to its source, not to a conscious intermediate state. Compare Psa 104:29-30.

docs.title: Those who sleep in the dust shall awake — death as sleep, resurrection
docs.text:
And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame [and] everlasting contempt.

Context: Daniel's vision of the end times. The dead are described as sleeping in the dust (aphar) — the same dust language as Gen 2:7 and 3:19.

Notes: yeshene admat-aphar — 'sleepers of the ground of dust.' Uses 'sleep' (yashen) for the state of death and 'dust' (aphar) connecting to Gen 2:7 and 3:19. Resurrection, not conscious intermediate existence, is the biblical hope.

docs.title: God ALONE has immortality — exclusive divine attribute
docs.text:
Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom [be] honour and power everlasting. Amen.

Context: Paul's doxology about God. The word monos (alone/only) combined with echon (having, present active participle) athanasian (immortality) is an unambiguous exclusion of all others from possessing immortality inherently.

  • ὁ (G3588) — T-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • μόνος (G3441) — A-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • ἔχων (G2192) — V-PAP-NSM — Pres Act Ptcp Nom Sg M
  • ἀθανασίαν, (G110) — N-ASF — Acc Sg F
  • φῶς (G5457) — N-ASN — Acc Sg N
  • οἰκῶν (G3611) — V-PAP-NSM — Pres Act Ptcp Nom Sg M
  • ἀπρόσιτον, (G676) — A-ASN — Acc Sg N
  • ὃν (G3739) — R-ASM — Acc Sg M
  • εἶδεν (G3708) — V-2AAI-3S — Aor Act Ind Sg thirdPers
  • οὐδεὶς (G3762) — A-NSM-N — Nom Sg M
  • ἀνθρώπων (G444) — N-GPM — Gen Pl M
  • οὐδὲ (G3761) — CONJ-N — ἰδεῖν ὁράω G3708 [V-2AAN] Aor Act Inf
  • δύναται· (G1410) — V-PNI-3S — Pres M/P Ind Sg thirdPers
  • τιμὴ (G5092) — N-NSF — Nom Sg F
  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — κράτος κράτος G2904 [N-NSN] Nom Sg N
  • αἰώνιον· (G166) — A-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • ἀμήν. (G281) — HEB —

Notes: ho monos echon athanasian — 'the only one having immortality.' monos (A-NSM, G3441) — alone, only. echon (V-PAP-NSM of echo, G2192) — present active participle, ongoing possession. athanasian (N-ASF, G110) — immortality/deathlessness. Alpha-privative: a- + thanatos = un-death. If God ALONE has immortality, no created being — human souls included — possesses it inherently.

docs.title: Sown corruptible, raised incorruptible — resurrection transformation
docs.text:
So also [is] the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam [was made] a quickening spirit. Howbeit that [was] not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual. The first man [is] of the earth, earthy: the second man [is] the Lord from heaven. As [is] the earthy, such [are] they also that are earthy: and as [is] the heavenly, such [are] they also that are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.

Context: Paul's resurrection chapter. Four contrasts: corruption/incorruption, dishonour/glory, weakness/power, natural/spiritual. Then the Adam-Christ typology: first Adam = living psyche (Gen 2:7 quoted); last Adam = life-giving pneuma.

Notes: v.45 quotes Gen 2:7 (LXX) — 'the first man Adam became (egeneto) a living soul (psychen zosan).' The last Adam became a life-giving spirit (pneuma zoopoioun). The first man is ek ges choikos (of the earth, earthy); the second man is from heaven. The present state (natural body, corruption, mortality) must be TRANSFORMED, not escaped.

docs.title: Mortal must put on immortality — future acquisition, not present possession
docs.text:
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal [must] put on immortality. So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

Context: The climax of the resurrection argument. Immortality (athanasia) is something mortals PUT ON at the resurrection, not something they presently possess.

  • δεῖ (G1163) — V-PAI-3S — Pres Act Ind Sg thirdPers
  • γὰρ (G1063) — CONJ — τὸ ὁ G3588 [T-NSN] Nom Sg N
  • φθαρτὸν (G5349) — A-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • τοῦτο (G3778) — D-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • ἐνδύσασθαι (G1746) — V-AMN — Aor Mid Inf
  • ἀφθαρσίαν (G861) — N-ASF — Acc Sg F
  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — τὸ ὁ G3588 [T-NSN] Nom Sg N
  • θνητὸν (G2349) — A-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • ἀθανασίαν. (G110) — N-ASF — Acc Sg F

Notes: dei (V-PAI-3S, G1163 — 'it is necessary') + endysasthai (V-AMN of endyo, G1746 — aorist middle infinitive, 'to put on/clothe oneself'). Two pairs: to phtharton / aphtharsian (corruptible / incorruption); to thneton / athanasian (mortal / immortality). athanasian (N-ASF, G110) — accusative, object of 'put on.' thneton (A-NSN, G2349) — mortal, nominative substantival. 'Must put on' — immortality is NOT presently possessed. It must be acquired at the resurrection event.

docs.title: Seek for immortality — immortality must be sought, not inherent
docs.text:
To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life:

Context: Paul's discussion of judgment according to works. Those who seek (zeteo) immortality (aphtharsia) receive eternal life.

Notes: Immortality (aphtharsia, G861) is something to seek — not something inherently possessed. If humans had immortal souls, seeking immortality would be nonsensical.

docs.title: Incorruptible God vs. corruptible man — aphthartos/phthartos contrast
docs.text:
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.

Context: Paul's indictment of humanity. The incorruptible (aphthartos) God is contrasted with corruptible (phthartos) man.

Notes: aphthartos (G862) — incorruptible, applied to God. phthartos — corruptible, applied to man. Direct contrast: God is incorruptible; man is corruptible.

docs.title: Tree of life barred lest man live forever
docs.text:
And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever: Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken. So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

Context: Post-Fall. God prevents man from accessing the tree of life.

Notes: pen-yishlach yado ... wachai le'olam — 'lest he ... and live forever.' The tree of life was the mechanism for immortality. Barring access ensures man will die. If man had an inherently immortal soul, this action would be pointless.

docs.title: Eternal life is in the Son — conditional on relationship with Christ
docs.text:
And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; [and] he that hath not the Son of God hath not life.

Context: John's summary statement on eternal life. Life is IN the Son and conditional on having the Son.

Notes: zoen aionion — eternal life. 'This life is in his Son' — not inherent in the human person. 'He that hath not the Son of God hath not life' — explicit binary: no Son = no life.

docs.title: Spirit, soul, and body — tripartite listing; bipartite vs tripartite debate
docs.text:
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and [I pray God] your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Context: Paul's closing prayer for the Thessalonians. Lists pneuma, psyche, and soma connected by kai...kai...kai.

  • Αὐτὸς (G846) — P-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • δὲ (G1161) — CONJ — ὁ ὁ G3588 [T-NSM] Nom Sg M
  • Θεὸς (G2316) — N-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • τῆς (G3588) — T-GSF — Gen Sg F
  • εἰρήνης (G1515) — N-GSF — Gen Sg F
  • ἁγιάσαι (G37) — V-AAO-3S — Aor Act Opt Sg thirdPers
  • ὑμᾶς (G4771) — P-2AP — Acc Pl

Notes: holokeron hymon to pneuma (N-NSN, G4151) kai he psyche (N-NSF, G5590) kai to soma (N-NSN, G4983) — 'your whole spirit and soul and body.' hagiasai (V-AAO-3S of hagiazo — aorist active optative) — 'may he sanctify.' holoteles (A-APM, G3651) — 'completely/wholly.' The triple kai...kai...kai does not necessarily imply three ontologically distinct parts. Compare Deu 6:5 (heart, soul, might) which no one reads as three separate components. The emphasis is on WHOLENESS (holoteles, holokeron) — the entire person preserved blameless.

docs.title: Dividing asunder soul and spirit — distinction or parallelism?
docs.text:
For the word of God [is] quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and [is] a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

Context: The power and penetrating nature of God's word. The 'dividing of soul and spirit' parallels the 'dividing of joints and marrow.'

  • Ζῶν (G2198) — V-PAP-NSM — Pres Act Ptcp Nom Sg M
  • γὰρ (G1063) — CONJ — ὁ ὁ G3588 [T-NSM] Nom Sg M
  • λόγος (G3056) — N-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • τοῦ (G3588) — T-GSM — Gen Sg M
  • Θεοῦ (G2316) — N-GSM — Gen Sg M
  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — ἐνεργὴς ἐνεργής G1756 [A-NSM] Nom Sg M
  • ὑπὲρ (G5228) — PREP — πᾶσαν πᾶς G3956 [A-ASF] Acc Sg F
  • μάχαιραν (G3162) — N-ASF — Acc Sg F
  • δίστομον (G1366) — A-ASF — Acc Sg F
  • ἄχρι (G891) — ADV — μερισμοῦ μερισμός G3311 [N-GSM] Gen Sg M

Notes: merismos (N-GSM, G3311) — division/separation. psyches (N-GSF, G5590) kai pneumatos (N-GSN, G4151) — 'of soul and spirit.' harmon (N-GPM, G719) te kai myelon (N-GPM, G3452) — 'of joints and marrow.' The parallel structure soul/spirit :: joints/marrow suggests the point is God's penetrating discernment into the deepest parts of human existence, NOT a teaching that soul and spirit are two separable entities. Joints and marrow are not two separate body parts but intimately connected tissues.

docs.title: Earthly tabernacle dissolved; absent from body present with Lord — debated
docs.text:
For we know that if our earthly house of [this] tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked. For we that are in [this] tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing [is] God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit. Therefore [we are] always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord: (For we walk by faith, not by sight:) We are confident, [I say], and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.

Context: Paul's discussion of the hope beyond this mortal life. Key: v.4 clarifies Paul's desire — NOT to be 'unclothed' (disembodied) but to be 'clothed upon' (resurrection body), that mortality might be swallowed up of life.

Notes: v.4 is determinative: ou thelomen ekdysasthai all' ependysasthai — 'we do not want to be unclothed but to be clothed upon.' Paul's hope is not disembodiment but resurrection. 'Absent from the body, present with the Lord' (v.8) must be read in this context — Paul's horizon is the resurrection, which he connects to 'the coming of our Lord' in 1 Thess 4:13-17.

docs.title: Desire to depart and be with Christ — debated intermediate state text
docs.text:
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:

Context: Paul writing from prison. He expresses desire to depart and be with Christ. The same letter (Phil 3:11, 20-21) has Paul hoping for the resurrection.

Notes: analysa (V-AAN of analyo) — 'to depart.' syn Christo einai (to be with Christ). Paul does not specify timing or mechanism. From the dead person's perspective, the next conscious moment after death IS being with Christ at the resurrection. The same letter has Paul hoping for the resurrection of the dead (3:11) and the transformation of our bodies (3:20-21).

docs.title: God can destroy both soul and body in gehenna
docs.text:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: Jesus teaching the twelve about fear. Man can kill the body but not the psyche; God can destroy (apollymi) both psyche and soma in gehenna.

  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — μὴ μή G3361 [PRT-N]
  • φοβεῖσθε (G5399) — V-PNM-2P — Pres M/P Impv Pl secondPers
  • ἀπὸ (G575) — PREP — τῶν ὁ G3588 [T-GPM] Gen Pl M
  • ἀποκτεννόντων (G615) — V-PAP-GPM — Pres Act Ptcp Gen Pl M

Both psyche AND soma can be destroyed by God. This does NOT teach the immortality of the soul — it teaches God's power over the whole person, beyond what human persecutors can do.

docs.title: Body without spirit (pneuma) is dead — spirit as animating principle
docs.text:
For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.

Context: James's argument that faith without works is dead. The analogy: body without pneuma = dead.

Notes: to soma choris pneumatos nekron estin — 'the body without spirit is dead.' pneuma here is the animating principle/breath. When the spirit departs, the body is dead. This is consistent with the OT pattern (Psa 146:4; Ecc 12:7).

docs.title: The dead in Christ shall rise — resurrection as the hope
docs.text:
But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him. For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive [and] remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep. For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:

Context: Paul's primary teaching on the Christian hope for the dead. He calls the dead 'asleep' (koimao) and comforts believers with the RESURRECTION, not with the idea that the dead are already with Christ.

Notes: Paul's comfort for grieving believers is resurrection at Christ's coming, not a conscious intermediate state. The dead are described as 'asleep' (koimomenon, v.13). 'The dead in Christ shall rise first' (v.16) — the event that reunites believers with Christ.

docs.title: David is NOT ascended into the heavens — denial of conscious intermediate state
docs.text:
For David is not ascended into the heavens: but he saith himself, The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand,

Context: Peter's Pentecost sermon. He explicitly states that David — a man after God's own heart — has NOT ascended to heaven, though he died centuries earlier.

Notes: ou gar Dauid anebe eis tous ouranous — 'for David did not ascend into the heavens.' This is a direct denial that the righteous dead go to heaven at death. David is still in his tomb (v.29) — not in heaven.

docs.title: Valley of dry bones — ruach breathed into dead, they live
docs.text:
The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which [was] full of bones, And caused me to pass by them round about: and, behold, [there were] very many in the open valley; and, lo, [they were] very dry. And he said unto me, Son of man, can these bones live? And I answered, O Lord GOD, thou knowest. Again he said unto me, Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live: And I will lay sinews upon you, and will bring up flesh upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and ye shall live; and ye shall know that I [am] the LORD. So I prophesied as I was commanded: and as I prophesied, there was a noise, and behold a shaking, and the bones came together, bone to his bone. And when I beheld, lo, the sinews and the flesh came up upon them, and the skin covered them above: but [there was] no breath in them. Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army. Then he said unto me, Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel: behold, they say, Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost: we are cut off for our parts. Therefore prophesy and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, O my people, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, and bring you into the land of Israel. And ye shall know that I [am] the LORD, when I have opened your graves, O my people, and brought you up out of your graves, And shall put my spirit in you, and ye shall live, and I shall place you in your own land: then shall ye know that I the LORD have spoken [it], and performed [it], saith the LORD.

Context: Ezekiel's vision. The re-creation of dead bodies parallels the original creation: formation of physical body (bones, sinews, flesh, skin) + ruach = life. Without ruach, the bodies remained dead (v.8).

Notes: v.8: 'but there was no breath (ruach) in them' — the physical body without ruach is dead. v.9-10: ruach enters and they live. v.14: 'I will put my spirit (ruach) in you, and ye shall live.' This vision recapitulates Gen 2:7: body + divine breath = living being. It functions as a reversal of death and a promise of resurrection.

docs.title: In the likeness (demuth) of God — creation reiterated
docs.text:
This [is] the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made he him; Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created.

Context: The genealogy of Adam. The image/likeness language of Gen 1:26-27 is repeated.

Notes: bidmut elohim — 'in the likeness of God.' The image persists through generations. Called their name 'Adam' (human) — both male and female.

docs.title: In the image of God made he man — image reaffirmed after the flood
docs.text:
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.

Context: Noahic covenant. The image of God in man is the basis for the prohibition against murder — even after the Fall.

Notes: betselem elohim asah et-ha'adam — 'in the image of God made he man.' The image of God persists after the Fall and after the Flood. It is the basis for human dignity and the capital prohibition.

docs.title: What is man? Made a little lower than the angels — human place in creation
docs.text:
What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him? For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour. Thou madest him to have dominion over the works of thy hands; thou hast put all [things] under his feet:

Context: David's reflection on human dignity despite human smallness. Man is 'a little lower than the angels' (or 'than God' — me'at me'elohim) with dominion over creation.

Notes: me'at me'elohim — 'a little lower than elohim' (God or angels). This connects back to Gen 1:26-28 — the dominion mandate. Man is crowned with glory (kabod) and honor (hadar).

docs.title: Man is the image and glory of God — image language in NT
docs.text:
For a man indeed ought not to cover [his] head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man.

Context: Paul's discussion of head coverings. Man is called 'the image (eikon) and glory (doxa) of God.'

Notes: eikon (G1504) kai doxa (G1391) theou — man IS the image of God (present tense). The image persists after the Fall, in the NT era.

docs.title: Men made after the similitude (homoiosis) of God
docs.text:
Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God.

Context: James on the tongue. People are made 'after the similitude (homoiosis) of God' — the reason cursing people is contradictory to blessing God.

Notes: kath' homoiosin theou gegonotas — 'after the likeness of God having been made' (perfect passive participle). The image of God remains the basis for human dignity.

docs.title: Renewed in knowledge after the image of the creator
docs.text:
And have put on the new [man], which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him:

Context: Paul on the new life in Christ. The 'new man' is being renewed according to the image (eikon) of the creator.

Notes: kat' eikona tou ktisantos auton — 'according to the image of the one who created him.' The image of God is being restored in believers through renewal.

docs.title: God made man upright — original state of creation
docs.text:
Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.

Context: The Preacher's finding about human nature. God made man yashar (upright/straight), but humanity went astray.

Notes: asah ha'elohim et-ha'adam yashar — God made man upright. The original creation was good; the corruption came from human choices.

docs.title: Guard your heart — leb as the executive center
docs.text:
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it [are] the issues of life.

Context: Wisdom instruction. The heart (leb) is the executive center from which the issues of life flow.

Notes: mikol-mishmar netsor libbekha — 'above all guarding, guard your heart.' ki-mimmenu tots'ot chayyim — 'for from it are the outgoings of life.' The heart is the central anthropological term in Hebrew wisdom — the directing center of the whole person.

docs.title: Flesh and spirit contrast — moral/qualitative, not ontological
docs.text:
Now the Egyptians [are] men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together.

Context: Isaiah's warning against trusting Egypt. The flesh/spirit contrast is about weakness vs. power, not two parts of a human being.

Notes: adam welo' el — 'man and not God.' basar welo' ruach — 'flesh and not spirit.' This is the foundational OT flesh-spirit contrast, and it is clearly moral/qualitative (human weakness vs. divine power), NOT ontological (body vs. soul).

docs.title: Works of the flesh — include non-bodily sins
docs.text:
Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are [these]; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told [you] in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.

Context: Paul's flesh-spirit contrast in the context of Christian living. The 'works of the flesh' include hatred, jealousy, envy, seditions — clearly not bodily sins.

Notes: ta erga tes sarkos — 'the works of the flesh.' The list includes idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, strife, heresies, envyings — these are not physical/bodily sins. This confirms that sarx in Paul's ethical usage means the sinful orientation, not the physical body.

docs.title: Carnally minded vs. spiritually minded — moral orientation, not body parts
docs.text:
For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit. For to be carnally minded [is] death; but to be spiritually minded [is] life and peace. Because the carnal mind [is] enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.

Context: Paul's discussion of life in the Spirit vs. life in the flesh. 'Carnally minded' (to phronema tes sarkos) is a mindset, not the physical body.

Notes: to phronema tes sarkos — 'the mind-set of the flesh.' This is an orientation of the whole person toward self rather than God. The flesh-spirit contrast in Paul is moral/volitional, not ontological.

docs.title: Souls under the altar cry out — apocalyptic genre, personification
docs.text:
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth? And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they [were], should be fulfilled.

Context: Fifth seal in John's apocalyptic vision. Souls (psychai) of martyrs are seen under the altar crying for justice. Apocalyptic genre.

Notes: This is apocalyptic literature with extensive symbolism. Parallel to Gen 4:10 where Abel's blood 'cries from the ground' — personification of shed blood/life demanding justice. The souls are specifically 'under the altar' — the place where sacrificial blood was poured (Lev 4:7). This is the blood of the martyrs personified as crying for vindication.

docs.title: Every living soul (psyche) in the sea died — psyche applied to sea creatures
docs.text:
And the second angel poured out his vial upon the sea; and it became as the blood of a dead [man]: and every living soul died in the sea.

Context: The second bowl judgment. Psyche (soul) is applied to sea creatures — the same term used for human souls.

Notes: pasa psyche zosa apethanen — 'every living soul died.' Psyche is applied to sea creatures, mirroring the OT usage of nephesh chayyah for animals (Gen 1:20-21). If psyche here means 'immortal soul,' then sea creatures have immortal souls too.

docs.title: Death and hades cast into the lake of fire — the second death
docs.text:
And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Context: After the final judgment. Death (thanatos) and hades (G86) themselves are destroyed in the lake of fire. This IS the second death.

Notes: thanatos kai hades — death and hades personified and destroyed. The second death (ho thanatos ho deuteros) uses the same word thanatos — death. The lake of fire is identified AS the second death, not as something distinct from death.

docs.title: Soul and spirit in poetic parallelism — synonymous, not distinct components
docs.text:
And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.

Context: Mary's Magnificat. Psyche and pneuma in synonymous parallelism.

Notes: he psyche mou / to pneuma mou — 'my soul / my spirit.' These are in synonymous Hebrew-style parallelism (A says X, B says the same in different words). This argues against reading them as two ontologically distinct components.

docs.title: Soul and spirit in OT poetic parallelism
docs.text:
With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early: for when thy judgments [are] in the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness.

Context: Isaiah's song. Nephesh and ruach in synonymous parallelism — desiring/seeking God.

Notes: benaphshi — 'with my soul (nephesh)' / ruach beqirbi — 'with my spirit (ruach) within me.' Soul and spirit function as synonymous terms for the whole inner person longing for God.

docs.title: OT faithful died NOT having received the promises
docs.text:
And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.

Context: The conclusion of the faith chapter. All the OT heroes of faith died without receiving what was promised — they are not yet 'made perfect.'

Notes: ouk ekomisanto ten epangelian — 'did not receive the promise.' hina me choris hemon teleiothosin — 'that apart from us they should not be made perfect.' The OT faithful are waiting — they have NOT yet received their reward. This contradicts the idea of immediate heavenly reward at death.

docs.title: Heart, soul, might — the Shema, not three ontological parts
docs.text:
And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.

Context: The Shema — the foundational command of Israel. Three terms (leb, nephesh, me'od) describe the totality of devotion, not three separate parts of a person.

Notes: leb (heart) + nephesh (soul/being) + me'od (might/muchness). No one reads this as three ontological components. It means 'with your whole self.' This is the background for 1 Thess 5:23.

docs.title: Through one man sin entered, and death through sin — origin of death
docs.text:
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:

Context: Paul's Adam-Christ typology. Death entered through sin — it was not part of the original creation.

Notes: di' henos anthropou he hamartia eis ton kosmon eiselthen, kai dia tes hamartias ho thanatos — 'through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death.' Death is a consequence of sin, not an inherent feature of human existence.

docs.title: Wages of sin is death, gift of God is eternal life — death-life binary
docs.text:
For the wages of sin [is] death; but the gift of God [is] eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Context: Paul's summary of the sin-death and grace-life contrast.

Notes: ta opsonia tes hamartias thanatos — 'the wages of sin is death.' to charisma tou theou zoe aionios — 'the gift of God is eternal life.' Death and eternal life are presented as an exhaustive binary. Death is the consequence; eternal life is the gift. No third option (eternal conscious torment) appears in this formulation.

docs.title: Mortal man compared to houses of clay — human insignificance and mortality
docs.text:
Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? Behold, he put no trust in his servants; and his angels he charged with folly: How much less [in] them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation [is] in the dust, [which] are crushed before the moth?

Context: Eliphaz's first speech. Humans are described as dwelling in 'houses of clay' with their 'foundation in the dust' — fragile, mortal beings.

Notes: enosh (mortal man) — distinct from adam (man generically). 'Houses of clay' (batey-chomer) — the body as a clay house with foundation in dust (aphar). Crushed before a moth — extreme fragility. Affirms human mortality and material composition.

docs.title: Into thy hand I commit my ruach — spirit entrusted to God
docs.text:
Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth.

Context: David's prayer of trust. He commits his ruach (spirit) into God's hand. Quoted by Jesus on the cross (Luke 23:46).

Notes: beyad'kha afqid ruchi — 'into your hand I deposit my spirit.' The same words Jesus spoke on the cross (Luke 23:46, pneuma). Committing the spirit to God at death is consistent with Ecc 12:7 — the spirit returns to God who gave it.

docs.title: Ruach departs, returns to earth, thoughts perish — death sequence
docs.text:
His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

Context: Warning against trusting in mortal humans. When the ruach departs, the person returns to the ground and thoughts cease that very day.

Notes: tetse' rucho (his spirit goes out) yashub le'admato (he returns to his ground) bayom hahu abdu eshtonotav (in that very day his thoughts perish). Three events at death: (1) spirit departs, (2) body returns to ground, (3) thoughts perish. Consciousness ceases at death — 'in that very day.'

docs.title: Thy dead shall live — resurrection hope in OT
docs.text:
Thy dead [men] shall live, [together with] my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew [is as] the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead.

Context: Isaiah's apocalypse (chapters 24-27). A promise of resurrection: the dead shall live, those dwelling in dust shall awake.

Notes: yichyu metekha — 'your dead shall live.' haqitsu weranenu shokne aphar — 'awake and sing, dwellers of dust.' The 'dust' language connects to Gen 2:7 and 3:19. Resurrection is from the dust, not from a conscious intermediate state.

docs.title: Today you will be with me in paradise — debated intermediate-state text
docs.text:
And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.

Context: Jesus on the cross, speaking to the penitent thief. Commonly cited for conscious intermediate state.

Notes: semeron met' emou ese en to paradeiso — 'today with me you will be in paradise.' Key issue: Jesus was NOT in paradise that day — John 20:17 has Jesus saying on Sunday morning 'I am not yet ascended to my Father.' The comma placement in the KJV ('I say unto thee, To day') is an editorial choice. Greek has no punctuation. The statement may be 'I say unto thee today, thou shalt be with me in paradise' — emphasizing the certainty of the promise, not the timing of its fulfillment.

docs.title: Lazarus sleeps — Jesus calls death sleep
docs.text:
These things said he: and after that he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep. Then said his disciples, Lord, if he sleep, he shall do well. Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they thought that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep. Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead.

Context: Jesus speaking about Lazarus's death. He calls death 'sleep' (koimao), then clarifies 'plainly' that Lazarus is dead.

Notes: Lazaros ho philos hemon kekoimetai — 'Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep.' Jesus uses koimao (to sleep) for death, then clarifies with apethanen (he died). This is significant because Jesus knew exactly what death was and chose to call it sleep.

docs.title: God gives to all life, breath (pnoe), and all things — divine sustaining
docs.text:
Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things;

Context: Paul's Areopagus speech in Athens. God is the source and sustainer of all life and breath (pnoe).

Notes: didous pasi zoen kai pnoen kai ta panta — 'giving to all life and breath and all things.' Pnoe (G4157) — breath, the NT equivalent of neshamah via LXX. God is the ongoing source of life and breath for all creatures. Life is not self-sustaining but continually dependent on God.

docs.title: By man came death, by man came resurrection — Adam-Christ typology
docs.text:
For since by man [came] death, by man [came] also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.

Context: Paul's Adam-Christ typology in the resurrection chapter. Death came through Adam; resurrection comes through Christ.

Notes: di' anthropou thanatos / di' anthropou anastasis nekron — 'through man death / through man resurrection of the dead.' en to Adam pantes apothneskousin / en to Christo pantes zoopoiethesontai — 'in Adam all die / in Christ all shall be made alive.' Death is universal through Adam; life is through Christ. The answer to death is resurrection, not an immortal soul.

docs.title: Made a little lower than the angels — NT citation of Psa 8
docs.text:
Thou madest him a little lower than the angels; thou crownedst him with glory and honour, and didst set him over the works of thy hands: Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing [that is] not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him.

Context: The author of Hebrews quoting Psalm 8:4-6. Applied to both humanity's original dignity and Christ's incarnation.

Notes: elatosas auton brachy ti par' angelous — 'you made him a little lower than the angels.' The LXX translates elohim as angelous (angels). The passage establishes humanity's place: lower than angels but crowned with glory, given dominion. 'But now we see not yet all things put under him' — the present reality is not yet the eschatological fulfillment.

docs.title: LORD forms the spirit (ruach) of man within him — spirit as divine gift
docs.text:
The burden of the word of the LORD for Israel, saith the LORD, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him.

Context: Zechariah's oracle. God is described as the one who forms (yotser) the ruach of man within him — the spirit is a divine creation.

Notes: weyotser ruach-adam beqirbo — 'and forming the spirit of man within him.' The verb yotser (Qal.Ptcp of yatsar — the same verb as Gen 2:7 for 'formed') presents the spirit as something God actively creates within each person. The spirit is not self-generated but divinely bestowed.

docs.title: Spirit (neshamah) of man is the lamp of the LORD — neshamah as divine connection
docs.text:
The spirit of man [is] the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly.

Context: A wisdom proverb. The neshamah of man serves as God's lamp — a means by which God searches the inner person.

Notes: ner YHWH nishmat adam — 'the lamp of the LORD is the neshamah of man.' chofes kol-chadrey-baten — 'searching all the chambers of the belly/inner parts.' The neshamah here functions as God's instrument of searching within the person — connecting the divine breath of Gen 2:7 to ongoing divine access to human consciousness.

docs.title: God gives neshamah to the people and ruach to those who walk on earth
docs.text:
Thus saith God the LORD, he that created the heavens, and stretched them out; he that spread forth the earth, and that which cometh out of it; he that giveth breath unto the people upon it, and spirit to them that walk therein:

Context: God introduces His servant. Described as creator of heavens and earth, and giver of neshamah and ruach to all people.

Notes: noten neshamah la'am aleha weruach laholkhim bah — 'giving breath (neshamah) to the people upon it and spirit (ruach) to those walking in it.' Both neshamah and ruach in one verse, both presented as divine gifts to humanity. Parallels Job 33:4 and Gen 2:7.

docs.title: First Adam living soul (psyche), last Adam quickening spirit (pneuma)
docs.text:
And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam [was made] a quickening spirit.

Context: Paul quotes Gen 2:7 (LXX) and draws the Adam-Christ contrast. The first Adam became a living psyche; the last Adam became a life-giving pneuma.

Notes: egeneto ho protos anthropos Adam eis psychen zosan — 'the first man Adam became a living soul' (quoting Gen 2:7 LXX). ho eschatos Adam eis pneuma zoopoioun — 'the last Adam a life-giving spirit.' The verb egeneto (became, from ginomai G1096) matches wayehi in Gen 2:7. Adam became a living psyche — he did not receive one. Christ, as the last Adam, is the source of life (zoopoioun, from zoopoieo G2227).

docs.title: There is a spirit (ruach) in man, the neshamah of the Almighty gives understanding
docs.text:
But [there is] a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.

Context: Elihu's speech. He attributes understanding not to age but to the ruach and neshamah from God.

Notes: aken ruach-hi' be'enosh — 'but it is a spirit in man.' wenishmat shaddai tebinem — 'and the breath/inspiration of the Almighty gives them understanding.' Both ruach and neshamah appear, with neshamah specifically as the source of understanding/wisdom. This is the illumination function of neshamah (see H5397 word study, semantic category 4).

docs.title: Right to the tree of life — eschatological access restored
docs.text:
Blessed [are] they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.

Context: Near the end of Revelation. Access to the tree of life is restored for the redeemed — bookending Gen 3:22-24 where access was barred.

Notes: hina estai he exousia auton epi to xylon tes zoes — 'that their authority/right may be upon the tree of life.' The tree of life reappears (cf. Gen 2:9, 3:22-24). What was barred after the Fall is restored in the new creation. Immortality through the tree of life — conditional on obedience and relationship, not inherent.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: What does Scripture explicitly say about the nature and composition of human beings (biblical anthropology)? Focus on nephesh (soul), ruach (spirit), neshamah (breath), the creation of man, whether humans ARE souls or HAVE souls, and what happens at death.

docs.title: Genesis 1:20-21 — Nephesh chayyah applied to sea creatures
docs.text: Context: Fifth day of creation. God commands the waters to bring forth living creatures. Direct statement: Sea creatures are designated nephesh chayyah — the same compound term that will be applied to the man in Genesis 2:7. Original language: Nephesh chayyah (H5315 + H2416) — "living soul" or "living creature." The KJV translates it here as "the moving creature that hath life." The same Hebrew phrase receives different English translations depending on whether the subject is human or animal, but the Hebrew is identical. Cross-references: Gen 1:24-25 applies the same term to land animals. Gen 2:7 applies it to man. Rev 16:3 applies psyche (G5590, the LXX equivalent of nephesh) to sea creatures. Relationship to other evidence: This establishes that nephesh is not an exclusively human attribute. Animals are nephesh chayyah before humans receive that designation.

docs.title: Genesis 1:24-25 — Nephesh chayyah applied to land animals
docs.text: Context: Sixth day, before man's creation. Land animals are also nephesh chayyah. Direct statement: Land animals receive the identical term (nephesh chayyah) that man will receive in Gen 2:7. Original language: Same compound: nephesh chayyah (H5315 + H2416). Cross-references: Gen 1:20-21 (sea creatures), Gen 2:7 (man), Gen 2:19 (animals formed from same ground). Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces the point from 1:20-21. Whatever nephesh chayyah means, it applies equally to animals and humans. The distinguishing feature between humans and animals must be something else — the image of God (1:26-27).

docs.title: Genesis 1:26-27 — Creation of man in the image of God
docs.text: Context: Sixth day. God says "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." The 1cp cohortative na'aseh signals a deliberate divine act distinct from the commands for other creatures. Direct statement: Man is created in the tselem (H6754, image) and demuth (H1823, likeness) of God. Dominion over creation immediately follows. Original language: na'aseh (Qal.Impf.1p of asah) — cohortative "let us make." tselem (Noun.ms.Abs+1up) — "our image." demuth (Noun.fs.Abs+1up) — "our likeness." See grammar reference on cohortative-1cp-divine-speech. Cross-references: Gen 5:1-2 reiterates the likeness language. Gen 9:6 grounds the prohibition against murder in the image of God — indicating the image persists after the Fall. 1 Cor 11:7 says man IS the image and glory of God (present tense). Jas 3:9 says men are made after the homoiosis (similitude) of God. Relationship to other evidence: Since animals are also nephesh chayyah, what makes humans unique is the image of God, not the possession of a soul. The image is connected to dominion (1:28) and persists after the Fall (9:6), after the Flood (9:6), and into the NT era (1 Cor 11:7; Jas 3:9; Col 3:10).

docs.title: Genesis 2:7 — FOUNDATIONAL: Dust + Neshamah = Nephesh Chayyah
docs.text: Context: The detailed creation account. This verse contains the three-part formula defining human composition. Direct statement: God formed (yatsar) man from the dust (aphar, H6083) of the ground (adamah, H127), breathed (naphach, H5301) into his nostrils the neshamah (H5397) of chayyim (H2416), and man became (wayehi) a nephesh chayyah (H5315 + H2416). Original language: The Hebrew parsing is critical. wayehi (Verb.Qal.Wayq.3ms of hayah, H1961) — "became." This is a transformation verb. Man did not receive a soul; the composite entity — dust animated by divine breath — IS the living soul. The word study for hayah (H1961) documents this as one of 4,280 occurrences, with the "becoming" sense well-attested. The neshamah breathed in is specifically neshamah (H5397), not ruach (H7307). The word study for neshamah shows only 25 OT occurrences, making this the rarest of the three key anthropological terms. The construct nishmat chayyim ("breath of life") uses the construct state (see grammar reference on construct-state). Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:45 quotes the LXX of Gen 2:7: "The first man Adam was made a living soul" (egeneto... eis psychen zosan). Paul preserves the "became" verb. Gen 2:19 uses the same verb yatsar and same material (adamah) for animals. Ecc 12:7 reverses this formula: dust returns to earth, spirit returns to God. Isa 42:5 echoes the creation language: God gives neshamah to the people and ruach to those who walk on earth. Relationship to other evidence: This is the foundational text for biblical anthropology. Every other passage about human nature, death, and resurrection relates back to this formula. The verb "became" settles the "are vs. have" question at the textual level: man IS a nephesh, not a possessor of one.

docs.title: Genesis 2:9 — Tree of life in the garden
docs.text: Context: The tree of life is introduced as present in the garden, accessible before the Fall. Direct statement: The tree of life was in the midst of the garden alongside the tree of knowledge of good and evil. Cross-references: Gen 3:22-24 bars access after the Fall. Rev 22:14 restores access eschatologically. Relationship to other evidence: The presence of the tree of life implies that continued life required access to it — immortality was not inherent but conditional on the tree. This is confirmed explicitly in Gen 3:22.

docs.title: Genesis 2:17 — Mot tamut: the death penalty
docs.text: Context: God's command to Adam before the Fall. Direct statement: "In the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die." Original language: mot (Verb.Qal.InfAbs of muwth, H4191) + tamut (Verb.Qal.Impf.2ms of muwth) — the infinitive absolute intensification construction (see grammar reference on infinitive-absolute-intensification). This same construction appears in Exo 21:12 and other judicial death penalty texts where it invariably means actual death. Cross-references: Gen 3:19 (dust returns to dust — the death takes effect). Gen 5:5 (Adam died at 930 years). Rom 5:12 (death entered through one man's sin). Relationship to other evidence: The mot tamut construction links Adam's penalty to the same vocabulary used for capital punishment throughout the Torah. The penalty is death — actual cessation of life, not metaphorical "separation."

docs.title: Genesis 2:19 — Animals formed from the same ground
docs.text: Context: God forms animals from the ground and brings them to Adam. Direct statement: Animals were formed (yatsar) from the ground (adamah) — the same verb and material as Gen 2:7 for man. Original language: Same verb yatsar (H3335) as Gen 2:7. Relationship to other evidence: Humans and animals share material origin. The distinguishing factor is not substance but the image of God (1:26-27) and the direct divine breathing of neshamah (2:7).

docs.title: Genesis 3:19 — Dust returns to dust
docs.text: Context: God's judgment on Adam after the Fall. Direct statement: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Original language: The reversal language mirrors Gen 2:7. Man came from aphar (dust) and returns to aphar. Cross-references: Ecc 12:7 completes the reversal: dust to earth, spirit to God. Ecc 3:20 — all go to one place, all are of dust, all return to dust. Relationship to other evidence: No surviving component is mentioned. The statement "dust thou art" identifies man's fundamental nature — not as an immortal soul temporarily housed in dust, but as dust that was animated and will return to its original state.

docs.title: Genesis 3:22-24 — Tree of life barred
docs.text: Context: After the Fall. God explicitly prevents man from eating from the tree of life. Direct statement: "Lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever" — God drove man out and placed cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way. Original language: wachai le'olam — "and live forever." The verb chayah (H2421) with le'olam indicates that "living forever" depended on the tree. Cross-references: Gen 2:9 (tree of life in the garden). Rev 22:14 (right to the tree of life restored). Relationship to other evidence: This is the most direct statement that humans are not inherently immortal. If man already had an immortal soul, barring access to the tree of life would be pointless. The action presupposes that without the tree, man will die completely.

docs.title: Genesis 5:1-2 — Likeness of God reiterated
docs.text: Context: The genealogy of Adam. The creation language is repeated. Direct statement: "In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made he him." Original language: bidmut elohim — "in the likeness of God." Relationship to other evidence: The image/likeness persists through generations. Both male and female are included.

docs.title: Genesis 6:17 — Ruach chayyim in all creatures
docs.text: Context: God announces the flood. All flesh with ruach chayyim will perish. Direct statement: All flesh "wherein is the breath of life" (ruach chayyim) will die. Original language: ruach chayyim — "spirit/breath of life." Cross-references: Ecc 3:19 — man and beast have "one breath" (ruach echad). Relationship to other evidence: Ruach chayyim is shared by all flesh — not exclusively human. This parallels the nephesh chayyah shared terminology.

docs.title: Genesis 7:22 — The triple compound: neshamah-ruach-chayyim
docs.text: Context: The flood kills everything on dry land. Direct statement: "All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died." Original language: nishmat (Noun.fs.Cst of neshamah) ruach (Noun.s.Abs) chayyim (Noun.mp.Abs) — "breath of spirit of life." This is the only verse combining all three anthropological terms in a single construct chain. The Hebrew parsing confirms the triple compound. Cross-references: Gen 2:7 (neshamah of chayyim), Gen 6:17 (ruach chayyim). Relationship to other evidence: Applied to ALL creatures that died in the flood, not just humans. This confirms that neshamah, like ruach, is shared between humans and animals in the context of the life-breath.

docs.title: Genesis 9:6 — Image of God reaffirmed after the flood
docs.text: Context: The Noahic covenant. Direct statement: "In the image of God made he man" — the basis for the prohibition against murder. Original language: betselem elohim — "in the image of God." Relationship to other evidence: The image persists after the Fall and after the Flood. It remains the basis for human dignity.

docs.title: Genesis 35:18 — Rachel's nephesh departing
docs.text: Context: Rachel dies during childbirth. Direct statement: "As her soul was in departing, (for she died)." Original language: The nephesh "goes out" (yatsa) at the moment of death. Cross-references: 1 Kgs 17:21-22 — Elijah prays for the nephesh to return, and it does. Relationship to other evidence: Nephesh departing = death occurring. The text does not describe where the nephesh goes or what state it enters. The parenthetical "(for she died)" equates the nephesh departing with the event of death itself.

docs.title: Leviticus 21:11 — Nephesh meth: dead soul/body
docs.text: Context: Priestly regulations about contact with the dead. Direct statement: The priest "shall not go in to any dead body." Original language: The Hebrew is nephesh meth — literally "a dead nephesh/soul." The construct chain links nephesh directly with meth (dead). Cross-references: Num 6:6 — same term. Relationship to other evidence: If nephesh meant "immortal soul," the phrase nephesh meth ("dead soul") would be self-contradictory. The fact that nephesh can be dead confirms it means the whole being or person, not an immortal component.

docs.title: Numbers 6:6 — Nephesh meth in Nazirite regulations
docs.text: Context: Nazirite vow regulations. Direct statement: "He shall come at no dead body." Original language: nephesh meth — identical construct to Lev 21:11. Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the nephesh meth usage. A nephesh can die and refer to a dead entity.

docs.title: Ezekiel 18:4 — The nephesh that sins shall die
docs.text: Context: God declares ownership of all souls and the principle of individual accountability. Direct statement: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die." Original language: hannephesh hachote't (the sinning nephesh, Qal.Ptcp.fs) hi' (she) tamut (Qal.Impf.3fs of muwth — shall die). Death is predicated of the nephesh itself. Cross-references: Ezek 18:20 repeats this. Rom 6:23 — "the wages of sin is death." Relationship to other evidence: If nephesh were inherently immortal, this statement would be self-contradictory. The text predicates death of the very entity identified as nephesh.

docs.title: Ezekiel 18:20 — Repeated: the nephesh that sins dies
docs.text: Context: Restatement of v.4 with expansion on individual accountability. Direct statement: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die." Relationship to other evidence: The repetition underscores the point. Individual accountability and the mortality of the nephesh.

docs.title: 1 Kings 17:21-22 — Nephesh departs and returns
docs.text: Context: Elijah raises the widow's son. Direct statement: Elijah prays "let this child's soul come into him again," and "the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived." Original language: The nephesh departs at death and returns when life is restored. Cross-references: Gen 35:18 — Rachel's nephesh departing. Relationship to other evidence: This is consistent with nephesh as the living being: when the animating principle departs, the nephesh ceases; when it returns, the nephesh revives. The text does not describe where the nephesh was during the interval or attribute consciousness to it.

docs.title: Job 4:17-19 — Mortal man in houses of clay
docs.text: Context: Eliphaz's first speech about human insignificance. Direct statement: "Shall mortal man be more just than God?" Humans dwell in "houses of clay" with "foundation in the dust." Original language: enosh (mortal man) — a term emphasizing human frailty. "Houses of clay" (batey-chomer) describes the body. "Crushed before the moth" — extreme fragility. Relationship to other evidence: Affirms human mortality and material composition. The body-as-clay metaphor connects to Gen 2:7 (formed from dust).

docs.title: Job 32:8 — Ruach and neshamah give understanding
docs.text: Context: Elihu's speech attributing understanding to divine breath. Direct statement: "There is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding." Original language: ruach (H7307) in man; neshamah (H5397) of the Almighty gives understanding. Both terms in one verse. Cross-references: Job 33:4 — "The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life." Pro 20:27 — neshamah as the lamp of the LORD. Relationship to other evidence: Ruach and neshamah appear in synonymous parallelism, both attributed to God. The neshamah here functions as the source of understanding — the illumination function of neshamah (semantic category 4 in the H5397 word study).

docs.title: Job 33:4 — Ruach and neshamah give life
docs.text: Context: Elihu affirms his own creation by divine breath. Direct statement: "The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life." Original language: Ruach (H7307) of God made him; neshamah (H5397) of Shaddai gave him life. Relationship to other evidence: Both ruach and neshamah are divine gifts that give life. Human life is entirely dependent on what God gives.

docs.title: Job 34:14-15 — If God gathers ruach and neshamah, all perish
docs.text: Context: Elihu on God's sustaining power. Direct statement: "If he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath; all flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust." Original language: rucho (his spirit) and nishmato (his breath, from neshamah). Both terms with 3ms suffix — "his spirit and his breath." If God gathers these back, the result: all flesh perishes, man returns to dust. Cross-references: Gen 3:19 (dust returns to dust), Ecc 12:7 (spirit returns to God), Psa 104:29-30 (God withdraws breath, they die). Relationship to other evidence: Life is sustained only by continued divine bestowal. The moment God withdraws the life-breath, death occurs and the body returns to dust. This is the creation formula in reverse.

docs.title: Psalm 6:5 — No remembrance in death
docs.text: Context: David's prayer in distress, appealing for deliverance. Direct statement: "In death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?" Original language: No remembrance of God in death (maveth, H4194). The dead cannot praise or thank. Cross-references: Psa 115:17, Psa 88:10-12, Ecc 9:5. Relationship to other evidence: One of a cluster of explicit statements across Psalms and Ecclesiastes describing the dead as unconscious. The consistent testimony of multiple OT authors.

docs.title: Psalm 31:5 — Into thy hand I commit my ruach
docs.text: Context: David's prayer of trust. Direct statement: "Into thine hand I commit my spirit." Original language: beyad'kha afqid ruchi — "into your hand I deposit my spirit." Cross-references: Luke 23:46 — Jesus quotes this on the cross. Ecc 12:7 — spirit returns to God. Relationship to other evidence: Committing the spirit to God at death is consistent with Ecc 12:7. The spirit returns to God who gave it — the life-force entrusted back to its source.

docs.title: Psalm 88:10-12 — The land of forgetfulness
docs.text: Context: Heman the Ezrahite's lament. Rhetorical questions expecting negative answers. Direct statement: "Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?" Original language: erets neshiyyah — "land of forgetfulness." No wonders, no praise, no declaration, no knowledge in sheol. Relationship to other evidence: Expands the testimony of Psa 6:5 and Psa 115:17. Death is darkness, silence, forgetfulness.

docs.title: Psalm 104:29-30 — God gives and withdraws ruach
docs.text: Context: A creation psalm celebrating divine providence. Direct statement: "Thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust. Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created." Original language: The same ruach creates and sustains. Withdrawal = death and return to dust. Sending forth = creation/renewal. Cross-references: Gen 2:7, Ecc 12:7, Job 34:14-15. Relationship to other evidence: Applied universally to all creatures. The pattern: God's ruach given = life; God's ruach withdrawn = death and return to dust. This reinforces the creation-death reversal theme.

docs.title: Psalm 115:17 — The dead praise not the LORD
docs.text: Context: Contrasting the living with the dead. Direct statement: "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence." Original language: dumah — "silence." Death is characterized by silence. Relationship to other evidence: Consistent with Psa 6:5, Psa 88:10-12, Ecc 9:5.

docs.title: Psalm 146:4 — Ruach departs, thoughts perish
docs.text: Context: Warning against trusting mortals. Direct statement: "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish." Original language: tetse' (Qal.Impf.3fs of yatsa') rucho (his spirit) — spirit goes out. yashub (Qal.Impf.3ms of shub) le'admato (to his ground) — returns to earth. abdu (Qal.Perf.3p of abad) eshtonotav (his thoughts) — thoughts perish. Three events at death: (1) spirit departs, (2) body returns to ground, (3) thoughts perish. Cross-references: Ecc 12:7 (dust to earth, spirit to God), Gen 3:19 (dust returns to dust). Relationship to other evidence: The thoughts perishing is significant. Consciousness ceases at death — "in that very day." This is among the most explicit statements about the state of the dead.

docs.title: Psalm 8:4-6 — Made a little lower than the angels
docs.text: Context: David's meditation on human dignity despite human smallness. Direct statement: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Man is made "a little lower than the angels" with dominion over creation. Original language: me'at me'elohim — "a little lower than elohim" (God or angels). Crowned with glory (kabod) and honor (hadar). Cross-references: Heb 2:7-8 quotes this passage. Gen 1:26-28 — the dominion mandate.
