Relationship to other evidence: Connects the image of God to the dominion mandate. Man's place: lower than heavenly beings but crowned with glory and given authority over creation.

docs.title: Proverbs 4:23 — Guard your heart
docs.text: Context: Wisdom instruction. Direct statement: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." Original language: mikol-mishmar netsor libbekha — "above all guarding, guard your heart (leb, H3820)." The heart is the executive center from which the issues (tots'ot) of life flow. Relationship to other evidence: The leb word study (H3820) documents 654 occurrences — the most frequent anthropological term. What modern Western thought assigns to "soul" or "mind," Hebrew assigns to "heart."

docs.title: Proverbs 20:27 — Neshamah as the lamp of the LORD
docs.text: Context: A wisdom proverb. Direct statement: "The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly." Original language: ner YHWH nishmat adam — "the lamp of the LORD is the neshamah of man." chofes kol-chadrey-baten — "searching all chambers of the belly/inner parts." Relationship to other evidence: The neshamah here functions as God's instrument within the person — connecting the divine breath of Gen 2:7 to ongoing divine access. This is the illumination function of neshamah (semantic category 4 in the H5397 word study).

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 3:19-21 — Man and beast have one ruach
docs.text: Context: The Preacher reflects on mortality. Direct statement: "They have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast." All come from dust, all return to dust. Original language: ruach echad lakol — "one breath/spirit for all." mikreh echad — "one fate." v.21 asks rhetorically whether the ruach of man goes up and the ruach of beast goes down — the question implies uncertainty, not affirmation. Cross-references: Gen 6:17, Gen 7:22 (ruach/neshamah shared by all creatures). Relationship to other evidence: Humans and animals share the same animating breath. The distinction between humans and animals is not in having different kinds of ruach but in bearing the image of God.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 7:29 — God made man upright
docs.text: Context: The Preacher's finding about human nature. Direct statement: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions." Original language: asah ha'elohim et-ha'adam yashar — "God made man upright/straight." Relationship to other evidence: The original creation was good. Corruption came from human choices, not from inherent nature.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 9:5-6 — The dead know nothing
docs.text: Context: The Preacher on death. Direct statement: "The dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished." Original language: hammetim einam yod'im me'umah — "the dead know not anything." Their love, hatred, envy have all avdah (perished). They have no more portion forever in anything done "under the sun." Cross-references: Ecc 9:10, Psa 146:4, Psa 6:5, Psa 115:17. Relationship to other evidence: One of the most direct statements about the state of the dead. The negation is comprehensive: no knowledge, no reward, no memory, no emotion, no participation.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 9:10 — No work, knowledge, or wisdom in sheol
docs.text: Context: Exhortation to act now because death offers no opportunity. Direct statement: "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest." Original language: Four-fold negation: 'ein ma'aseh, wecheshbon, wada'at, wechokmah bishe'ol — no work, no planning, no knowledge, no wisdom in sheol (H7585). Relationship to other evidence: The comprehensive negation of all cognitive and volitional activity after death. This verse describes sheol — the destination of all the dead.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 12:7 — Dust to earth, spirit to God
docs.text: Context: The conclusion of the Preacher's meditation on aging and death. Direct statement: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." Original language: weyashob (Qal.Impf.3ms of shub) he'aphar (the dust) al-ha'arets (upon the earth) keshehayyah (as it was). weharuach (the spirit) tashub (Qal.Impf.3fs of shub) el-ha'elohim (to God) asher netanah (who gave it). The Hebrew parsing shows a precise reversal of Gen 2:7: what was formed from dust returns to dust; what was breathed in returns to the God who breathed it. Cross-references: Gen 2:7 (creation formula), Gen 3:19 (dust returns to dust), Psa 104:29-30 (God withdraws breath), Psa 146:4 (thoughts perish when spirit departs). Relationship to other evidence: The ruach returns to the God who gave it. The text does not say the ruach goes to heaven as a conscious entity. Combined with Psa 146:4 (thoughts perish that very day) and Ecc 9:5 (the dead know nothing), the spirit returning to God is the life-force returning to its source, not a conscious person going to a destination.

docs.title: Daniel 12:2 — Those who sleep in dust awake
docs.text: Context: Daniel's vision of the end times. Direct statement: "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." Original language: yeshene admat-aphar — "sleepers of the ground of dust." The "dust" (aphar) language connects to Gen 2:7 and 3:19. Death is called "sleep" (yashen). Cross-references: Isa 26:19 (those dwelling in dust shall awake). Gen 3:19 (dust returns to dust). 1 Thess 4:16 (dead in Christ rise). Relationship to other evidence: Resurrection — not conscious intermediate existence — is the biblical hope. The dead sleep in dust until they are awakened.

docs.title: Isaiah 26:9 — Soul and spirit in OT parallelism
docs.text: Context: Isaiah's song. Direct statement: "With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early." Original language: benaphshi (with my nephesh) / ruach beqirbi (with my ruach within me). Soul and spirit function as synonymous terms for the whole inner person. Cross-references: Luke 1:46-47 (psyche and pneuma in identical parallelism). Relationship to other evidence: The synonymous parallelism argues against treating nephesh and ruach (or psyche and pneuma) as two ontologically distinct substances.

docs.title: Isaiah 26:19 — Resurrection hope
docs.text: Context: Isaiah's apocalypse. Direct statement: "Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust." Original language: yichyu metekha — "your dead shall live." haqitsu weranenu shokne aphar — "awake and sing, dwellers of dust." The "dust" language connects to Gen 2:7 and 3:19. Relationship to other evidence: Resurrection is from the dust, not from a conscious intermediate state.

docs.title: Isaiah 31:3 — Flesh-spirit contrast is moral, not ontological
docs.text: Context: Isaiah's warning against trusting Egypt. Direct statement: "The Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit." Original language: adam welo' el — "man and not God." basar (H1320) welo' ruach (H7307) — "flesh and not spirit." Cross-references: Gal 5:19-21 (works of the flesh include non-bodily sins). Rom 8:5-8 (carnally minded vs. spiritually minded). Relationship to other evidence: This is the foundational OT flesh-spirit contrast. It is about human weakness vs. divine power — a qualitative/moral distinction, not an ontological one about two parts of the human being.

docs.title: Isaiah 42:5 — God gives neshamah and ruach
docs.text: Context: God introduces His servant. Direct statement: God "giveth breath unto the people upon it, and spirit to them that walk therein." Original language: noten neshamah (H5397) la'am aleha weruach (H7307) laholkhim bah — giving neshamah to the people and ruach to those walking on earth. Both terms presented as divine gifts. Cross-references: Gen 2:7, Job 33:4, Job 34:14-15. Relationship to other evidence: Parallels the creation language. God is the continuous giver of life-breath to all humanity.

docs.title: Zechariah 12:1 — God forms the ruach of man
docs.text: Context: Zechariah's oracle. Direct statement: The LORD "formeth the spirit of man within him." Original language: weyotser (Qal.Ptcp of yatsar, H3335) ruach-adam beqirbo — "forming the spirit of man within him." The verb yotser is the same used in Gen 2:7 for "formed." Relationship to other evidence: The spirit is not self-generated but divinely bestowed and formed. The use of yatsar (the Gen 2:7 creation verb) presents this as an ongoing creative act.

docs.title: Matthew 10:28 — God can destroy soul and body
docs.text: Context: Jesus teaching the twelve about fear. Direct statement: "Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." Original language: apokteinonton to soma (killing the body, G4983) / ten de psychen me dynamenon apokteinai (not able to kill the psyche, G5590). ton dynamenon kai psychen kai soma apolesai en geenne (the one able to destroy both psyche and soma in gehenna, G1067). The verb apollymi (G622) means to destroy utterly. Cross-references: Ezek 18:4 (the nephesh that sins dies). Luke 12:5 (fear him who, after killing, has power to cast into gehenna). Relationship to other evidence: This verse does NOT teach the immortality of the soul. It teaches God's power over the whole person beyond what human persecutors can do. Man can kill the body; God can destroy both soul AND body. The psyche is destructible by God.

docs.title: Luke 1:46-47 — Soul and spirit in NT parallelism
docs.text: Context: Mary's Magnificat. Direct statement: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." Original language: he psyche mou (my soul, G5590) / to pneuma mou (my spirit, G4151). Hebrew-style synonymous parallelism. Cross-references: Isa 26:9 (nephesh and ruach in identical parallelism). Relationship to other evidence: Soul and spirit function as interchangeable terms for the whole inner person, not as two distinct ontological components. This is directly relevant to the bipartite/tripartite question.

docs.title: Acts 2:34 — David is NOT in heaven
docs.text: Context: Peter's Pentecost sermon. Direct statement: "David is not ascended into the heavens." Original language: ou gar Dauid anebe eis tous ouranous — "for David did not ascend into the heavens." Cross-references: Acts 2:29 (David is in his tomb). Heb 11:39-40 (OT faithful have not yet received the promise). Relationship to other evidence: A direct denial that the righteous dead are in heaven. David — a man after God's own heart — died centuries before Peter's sermon and had NOT ascended to heaven.

docs.title: Acts 17:25 — God gives life and breath (pnoe)
docs.text: Context: Paul's Areopagus speech. Direct statement: God "giveth to all life, and breath, and all things." Original language: didous pasi zoen (G2222) kai pnoen (G4157) kai ta panta — giving to all life and breath and all things. Pnoe (G4157) is the NT equivalent of neshamah via the LXX bridge (14 co-occurrences). Cross-references: Gen 2:7, Isa 42:5. Relationship to other evidence: God is the ongoing source and sustainer of all life and breath. Life is not self-sustaining but continuously dependent on God.

docs.title: Romans 1:23 — Incorruptible God vs. corruptible man
docs.text: Context: Paul's indictment of humanity. Direct statement: They "changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man." Original language: aphthartos (G862) — incorruptible, applied to God. phthartos — corruptible, applied to man. Cross-references: 1 Tim 1:17 (God is immortal/incorruptible). Relationship to other evidence: Direct contrast: God is incorruptible; man is corruptible. No suggestion that humans have an incorruptible component.

docs.title: Romans 2:7 — Immortality must be sought
docs.text: Context: Paul on judgment according to works. Direct statement: "To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life." Original language: Immortality (aphtharsia, G861) is something to seek (zeteo). The word study for G861 documents 8 occurrences. Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:53-54 (put on immortality). 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has it). Relationship to other evidence: Seeking immortality would be nonsensical if humans already possessed it inherently.

docs.title: Romans 5:12 — Death entered through sin
docs.text: Context: Paul's Adam-Christ typology. Direct statement: "By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." Original language: thanatos (G2288) entered through hamartia (sin). Cross-references: Gen 2:17 (death penalty), 1 Cor 15:21-22 (by man came death, by man came resurrection). Relationship to other evidence: Death is a consequence of sin, not an inherent feature of human existence. Death was not part of the original creation.

docs.title: Romans 6:23 — Wages of sin is death
docs.text: Context: Paul's summary of the sin-death and grace-life contrast. Direct statement: "The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Original language: ta opsonia tes hamartias thanatos (G2288) / to charisma tou theou zoe aionios (G2222). Cross-references: Gen 2:17, Ezek 18:4. Relationship to other evidence: Death and eternal life are presented as an exhaustive binary. Death is the consequence; eternal life is the gift. No third option appears in this formulation.

docs.title: Romans 7:22 — The inner man
docs.text: Context: Paul's struggle between the flesh and the spirit. Direct statement: "I delight in the law of God after the inward man." Cross-references: Eph 3:16 ("strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man"). The Nave's entry for SPIRIT cross-references this as "the inner man." Relationship to other evidence: The "inner man" corresponds to the OT concept of "heart" (leb) — the directing center of the whole person — rather than to a separable soul.

docs.title: Romans 8:5-8 — Carnally minded vs. spiritually minded
docs.text: Context: Paul's flesh-Spirit contrast. Direct statement: "To be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace." Original language: to phronema tes sarkos (G4561) — "the mindset of the flesh." This is an orientation of the whole person, not the physical body. Cross-references: Isa 31:3 (foundational flesh-spirit contrast), Gal 5:19-21 (works of the flesh include non-bodily sins). Relationship to other evidence: The flesh-spirit contrast in Paul is moral and volitional, not ontological. Being "in the flesh" means being oriented toward self rather than God.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 11:7 — Man IS the image of God
docs.text: Context: Paul on head coverings. Direct statement: Man "is the image and glory of God." Original language: eikon (G1504) kai doxa (G1391) theou — present tense: man IS the image of God. Cross-references: Gen 1:26-27, Gen 9:6, Jas 3:9, Col 3:10. Relationship to other evidence: The image of God persists into the NT era. Man IS — not "was" — the image of God.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 — By man came death, by man came resurrection
docs.text: Context: Adam-Christ typology in the resurrection chapter. Direct statement: "By man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. In Adam all die, in Christ shall all be made alive." Original language: di' anthropou thanatos (G2288) / di' anthropou anastasis nekron. Relationship to other evidence: Death is universal through Adam; life is through Christ. The answer to death is resurrection, not an immortal soul.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:42-49 — Sown corruptible, raised incorruptible
docs.text: Context: Paul's resurrection chapter. Four contrasts and the Adam-Christ typology. Direct statement: Sown in corruption/raised in incorruption; sown in dishonour/raised in glory; sown in weakness/raised in power; sown a natural body/raised a spiritual body. The first Adam became a living psyche (quoting Gen 2:7 LXX); the last Adam became a life-giving pneuma. The first man is earthy (choikos, G5517); the second man is from heaven. Original language: egeneto (G1096, "became") ho protos anthropos Adam eis psychen zosan (G5590) — quoting Gen 2:7 LXX. ho eschatos Adam eis pneuma zoopoioun (G2227) — "life-giving spirit." Cross-references: Gen 2:7, Gen 3:19, Phil 3:20-21. Relationship to other evidence: The present state (natural body, corruption, mortality) must be TRANSFORMED, not escaped. Paul's hope is resurrection and transformation, not the release of an immortal soul.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:45 — First Adam living soul, last Adam life-giving spirit
docs.text: Context: Paul's Adam-Christ contrast. Direct statement: "The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit." Original language: egeneto (from ginomai, G1096) preserves the "became" verb from Gen 2:7 (hayah, H1961). Adam BECAME a living psyche; he did not receive one. Christ, as the last Adam, is the source of life (zoopoioun, from zoopoieo, G2227). Cross-references: Gen 2:7 (direct quotation via LXX). Relationship to other evidence: Paul quotes and interprets Gen 2:7 in a way that preserves the holistic anthropology: Adam became a living soul.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 — Mortal must put on immortality
docs.text: Context: The climax of the resurrection argument. Direct statement: "This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." Original language: dei (G1163, "it is necessary") + endysasthai (G1746, aorist middle infinitive, "to put on/clothe oneself"). Two pairs: to phtharton / aphtharsian (G861, corruptible / incorruption); to thneton (G2349) / athanasian (G110, mortal / immortality). The word study for G110 documents only 3 NT occurrences. The word study for G2349 documents 6 occurrences. Cross-references: 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has immortality). Rom 2:7 (seek immortality). Relationship to other evidence: Immortality is NOT presently possessed. It must be acquired at the resurrection event. The clothing metaphor ("put on") indicates transformation, not revelation of something already there.

docs.title: 1 Timothy 6:16 — God ALONE has immortality
docs.text: Context: Paul's doxology about God. Direct statement: God "only hath immortality." Original language: ho monos (G3441, alone/only) echon (G2192, present active participle — ongoing possession) athanasian (G110, immortality). Alpha-privative: a- + thanatos = deathlessness. The word study for G110 documents only 3 occurrences. Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:53-54 (mortals put on immortality at resurrection). Rom 1:23 (God is incorruptible, man is corruptible). Relationship to other evidence: The monos (alone/only) is an unambiguous exclusion. If God ALONE has immortality, no created being — including human souls — possesses it inherently.

docs.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:23 — Spirit, soul, and body
docs.text: Context: Paul's closing prayer for the Thessalonians. Direct statement: "Your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." Original language: holokeron (G3648, whole/complete) hymon to pneuma (G4151, spirit) kai he psyche (G5590, soul) kai to soma (G4983, body). The verb hagiasai (G37, V-AAO-3S, aorist active optative) — "may he sanctify." holoteles (G3651, completely/wholly). The triple kai...kai...kai links the three terms. Cross-references: Deu 6:5 (heart, soul, might — three terms that no one reads as three ontological components). Matt 22:37 (heart, soul, mind). Luke 1:46-47 and Isa 26:9 (soul and spirit in synonymous parallelism). Relationship to other evidence: The emphasis is on WHOLENESS (holoteles, holokeron) — the entire person preserved blameless. The triple listing does not necessarily imply three ontologically distinct parts, just as Deu 6:5's "heart, soul, might" does not. The stress falls on completeness of sanctification, not on anatomical enumeration.

docs.title: Hebrews 4:12 — Dividing soul and spirit
docs.text: Context: The power of God's word. Direct statement: "Piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow." Original language: merismos (G3311, division) psyches (G5590, of soul) kai pneumatos (G4151, and spirit). harmon (G719, of joints) te kai myelon (G3452, and marrow). The parallel structure is: soul/spirit :: joints/marrow. Cross-references: 1 Thess 5:23. Relationship to other evidence: The parallel with joints/marrow is instructive. Joints and marrow are not two separate body parts but intimately connected tissues. The point is God's penetrating discernment into the deepest parts of human existence, NOT a teaching that soul and spirit are two physically separable entities. The verse is about the power of God's word, not about human composition.

docs.title: 2 Corinthians 5:1-8 — Absent from body, present with Lord
docs.text: Context: Paul's discussion of the hope beyond mortality. Direct statement: v.4 is determinative: Paul does NOT want to be "unclothed" (disembodied) but "clothed upon" (the resurrection body), "that mortality might be swallowed up of life." v.8: "willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord." Original language: ou thelomen ekdysasthai all' ependysasthai — "we do not want to be unclothed but to be clothed upon." Cross-references: Phil 3:11, 20-21 (Paul's hope is resurrection). 1 Thess 4:16-17 (the dead in Christ rise at his coming). Relationship to other evidence: Paul's explicit preference is for the resurrection body, not disembodiment. "Absent from the body, present with the Lord" must be read in the context of Paul's horizon — the resurrection at Christ's coming. From the dead person's perspective (with no consciousness in between — Ecc 9:5; Psa 146:4), the next conscious moment after death IS being with Christ at the resurrection.

docs.title: Philippians 1:23 — Desire to depart and be with Christ
docs.text: Context: Paul writing from prison. Direct statement: "Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better." Original language: analysa (aorist active infinitive of analyo) — "to depart." syn Christo einai — "to be with Christ." Paul does not specify timing or mechanism. Cross-references: Phil 3:11 (hoping for the resurrection), Phil 3:20-21 (citizenship in heaven, from whence we look for the Saviour who will transform our bodies). Relationship to other evidence: The same letter has Paul hoping for the resurrection (3:11) and the transformation of bodies at Christ's return (3:20-21). From Paul's perspective, departing and being with Christ are a single expectation because there is no conscious interval between death and resurrection.

docs.title: Luke 23:43 — Today in paradise
docs.text: Context: Jesus on the cross, speaking to the penitent thief. Direct statement: "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." Original language: semeron met' emou ese en to paradeiso — "today with me you will be in paradise." Cross-references: John 20:17 — on Sunday morning (two days later) Jesus says "I am not yet ascended to my Father." Jesus was NOT in paradise on Friday. Relationship to other evidence: Greek has no punctuation. The comma placement ("I say unto thee, To day...") is editorial. Given that Jesus was not in paradise that day (John 20:17), the statement is better understood as "I say unto thee today, thou shalt be with me in paradise" — affirming the certainty of the promise, not its timing.

docs.title: John 11:11-14 — Jesus calls death sleep
docs.text: Context: Jesus speaking about Lazarus. Direct statement: "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep." Then: "Lazarus is dead." Original language: kekoimetai (from koimao, to sleep) — Jesus uses "sleep" for death. apethanen (from apothnesko, G599) — then clarifies "plainly" that Lazarus is dead. Cross-references: Dan 12:2 (sleepers in the dust), 1 Thess 4:14 (asleep in Jesus), Acts 7:60 (Stephen fell asleep). Relationship to other evidence: Jesus, who knew exactly what death was, chose to call it sleep. This is consistent with the OT description of the dead as unconscious.

docs.title: Galatians 5:19-21 — Works of the flesh include non-bodily sins
docs.text: Context: Paul's flesh-Spirit contrast. Direct statement: The "works of the flesh" include "hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, envyings" — clearly not physical/bodily sins. Original language: ta erga tes sarkos (G4561) — "the works of the flesh." Relationship to other evidence: Confirms that sarx in Paul's ethical usage means the sinful orientation of the whole person, not the physical body. The flesh-spirit contrast is moral, not ontological.

docs.title: John 3:6 — Born of flesh vs. born of Spirit
docs.text: Context: Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus. Direct statement: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." Relationship to other evidence: This is about spiritual origin and orientation, not about two parts of the human being. Being "born of the Spirit" is about regeneration, not about having a spirit-component.

docs.title: John 6:63 — The flesh profits nothing
docs.text: Context: Jesus' discourse on the bread of life. Direct statement: "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing." Relationship to other evidence: Consistent with the moral/qualitative flesh-spirit contrast (Isa 31:3). The flesh (human capacity apart from God) profits nothing; the spirit (divine power) gives life.

docs.title: Genesis 6:3 — My spirit shall not always strive with man
docs.text: Context: Pre-flood judgment. Direct statement: "My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh." Original language: basar (H1320, flesh) — man's nature is identified as "flesh." Relationship to other evidence: "He also is flesh" describes the human condition — mortal, material, limited.

docs.title: James 2:26 — Body without spirit is dead
docs.text: Context: James's analogy about faith and works. Direct statement: "As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also." Original language: to soma choris pneumatos (G4151) nekron estin — "the body without spirit is dead." Cross-references: Psa 146:4 (spirit goes out, they die). Ecc 12:7 (spirit returns to God). Relationship to other evidence: Pneuma here is the animating principle. When the spirit departs, the body is dead. This is consistent with the OT pattern and confirms the creation formula in reverse.

docs.title: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-16 — The dead in Christ shall rise
docs.text: Context: Paul's primary teaching on the Christian hope. Direct statement: The dead are "asleep" (koimao). Comfort for the grieving is the RESURRECTION: "the dead in Christ shall rise first." Original language: koimomenon (G2837, present middle/passive participle — those sleeping). Cross-references: Dan 12:2, John 11:11, 1 Cor 15:51. Relationship to other evidence: Paul's comfort for those who have lost loved ones is resurrection at Christ's coming, not a conscious intermediate state. The dead are described as sleeping, and they RISE — they are not called down from heaven.

docs.title: Hebrews 11:39-40 — OT faithful not yet rewarded
docs.text: Context: The conclusion of the faith chapter. Direct statement: All the OT heroes of faith "received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect." Original language: ouk ekomisanto ten epangelian — "did not receive the promise." hina me choris hemon teleiothosin — "that apart from us they should not be made perfect." Cross-references: Acts 2:34 (David not in heaven). Relationship to other evidence: The OT faithful are waiting. They have NOT yet received their reward. This contradicts the idea of immediate heavenly reward at death.

docs.title: Ezekiel 37:1-14 — Valley of dry bones
docs.text: Context: Ezekiel's vision of national restoration. Direct statement: The re-creation of dead bodies parallels the original creation: physical body formed (bones, sinews, flesh, skin) + ruach = life. v.8: "but there was no breath (ruach) in them" — the physical body without ruach is dead. v.9-10: ruach enters and they live. v.14: "I will put my spirit (ruach) in you, and ye shall live." Cross-references: Gen 2:7 (creation formula: body + breath = living being). Relationship to other evidence: This vision recapitulates Gen 2:7: body + divine breath = living being. It confirms the holistic anthropology — physical form alone is not life; the animating breath is required.

docs.title: Revelation 6:9-11 — Souls under the altar
docs.text: Context: Fifth seal in John's apocalyptic vision. Direct statement: Psychai (souls) of martyrs are under the altar crying "How long, O Lord?" Original language: Apocalyptic genre with extensive symbolism. Cross-references: Gen 4:10 (Abel's blood "cries from the ground" — personification of shed blood). Relationship to other evidence: The souls are under the altar — the place where sacrificial blood was poured (Lev 4:7). This is apocalyptic imagery: the blood/life of the martyrs personified as crying for justice, just as Abel's blood "cried" from the ground. The genre is apocalyptic, and the passage parallels other personification passages, not didactic teaching about the state of the dead.

docs.title: Revelation 16:3 — Psyche applied to sea creatures
docs.text: Context: The second bowl judgment. Direct statement: "Every living soul died in the sea." Original language: pasa psyche zosa apethanen — "every living soul/creature died." Cross-references: Gen 1:20-21 (nephesh chayyah applied to sea creatures). Relationship to other evidence: Psyche applied to sea creatures mirrors nephesh chayyah for animals in the OT. If psyche means "immortal soul," then sea creatures have immortal souls. The usage confirms that psyche, like nephesh, means "living creature/being."

docs.title: Revelation 20:14 — Death and hades cast into the lake of fire
docs.text: Context: After the final judgment. Direct statement: "Death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death." Original language: thanatos (G2288) kai hades (G86). ho thanatos ho deuteros — "the second death." Same word thanatos used for both death and the second death. Cross-references: Rev 21:8 (the second death identified as the lake of fire). 1 Cor 15:26 (last enemy destroyed is death). Relationship to other evidence: Death and hades are themselves destroyed. The second death uses the same vocabulary as physical death (thanatos). Hades is temporary, not eternal — it is destroyed at the end.

docs.title: Revelation 22:14 — Right to the tree of life restored
docs.text: Context: Near the end of Revelation. Direct statement: "Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life." Cross-references: Gen 2:9 (tree of life in the garden), Gen 3:22-24 (access barred after the Fall). Relationship to other evidence: What was barred after the Fall is restored in the new creation. The tree of life reappears — immortality through the tree remains conditional on relationship with God, not inherent.

docs.title: 1 John 5:11-12 — Eternal life is in the Son
docs.text: Context: John's summary on eternal life. Direct statement: "God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life." Original language: zoen aionion (eternal life, G2222). Binary: has the Son = has life; lacks the Son = lacks life. Cross-references: Rom 6:23 (gift of God is eternal life). John 3:16 (whosoever believes shall not perish but have everlasting life). Relationship to other evidence: Eternal life is IN the Son, not inherent in the person. "He that hath not the Son of God hath not life" — an explicit denial that life is possessed independently of Christ.

docs.title: Colossians 3:10 — Renewed after the image of the creator
docs.text: Context: Paul on the new life in Christ. Direct statement: "Have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him." Original language: kat' eikona (G1504) tou ktisantos auton — "according to the image of the one who created him." Relationship to other evidence: The image of God is being restored in believers through renewal. The image is not static but involves ongoing transformation.

docs.title: James 3:9 — Men made after the similitude of God
docs.text: Context: James on the tongue. Direct statement: People are "made after the similitude of God." Original language: kath' homoiosin theou gegonotas — "after the likeness of God having been made" (perfect passive participle). Relationship to other evidence: The image of God remains the basis for human dignity in the NT era.

docs.title: Hebrews 2:7-8 — Made a little lower than the angels (NT)
docs.text: Context: Hebrews quoting Psalm 8:4-6. Direct statement: "Thou madest him a little lower than the angels; thou crownedst him with glory and honour." Original language: elatosas auton brachy ti par' angelous — the LXX translates elohim as angelous. Cross-references: Psa 8:4-6 (OT source). Gen 1:26-28 (dominion mandate). Relationship to other evidence: Establishes humanity's place: lower than angels but crowned with glory and given dominion. Applied both to humanity generally and to Christ's incarnation.

docs.title: Deuteronomy 6:5 — The Shema
docs.text: Context: The foundational command of Israel. Direct statement: "Thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." Original language: leb (H3820) + nephesh (H5315) + me'od ("might/muchness"). Cross-references: Matt 22:37 (Jesus quotes this with heart, soul, mind). 1 Thess 5:23 (spirit, soul, body). Relationship to other evidence: Three terms describe the totality of devotion, not three ontological components. No one reads the Shema as enumerating three separable parts of the human being. This is the background for understanding 1 Thess 5:23.

docs.title: Ephesians 3:16 — Strengthened in the inner man
docs.text: Context: Paul's prayer for the Ephesians. Direct statement: "That he would grant you... to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man." Cross-references: Rom 7:22 ("I delight in the law of God after the inward man"). Relationship to other evidence: The "inner man" language corresponds to the OT concept of "heart" (leb) — the directing center of the whole person — rather than to a separable soul.

docs.title: Deuteronomy 6:5 / Matthew 22:37 — Heart, soul, mind/might
docs.text: Context: The greatest commandment, cited by Jesus. Direct statement: Matthew adds "mind" (dianoia) alongside "heart, soul, strength." Mark 12:30 has four terms: heart, soul, mind, strength. Relationship to other evidence: The varying number of terms (three in Deu 6:5, four in Mark 12:30) confirms that the listing is about totality of devotion, not precise enumeration of human parts.

docs.title: 1 Samuel 16:7 — God looks on the heart
docs.text: Context: God's instruction to Samuel when choosing David. Direct statement: "Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Original language: leb (H3820) — the heart as the true seat of the person, accessible to God. Relationship to other evidence: The heart is where God evaluates the person. This reinforces leb/kardia as the central anthropological concept in Hebrew thought.

docs.title: Psalm 51:10 — Create in me a clean heart
docs.text: Context: David's prayer of repentance. Direct statement: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." Original language: leb (H3820) in parallelism with ruach (H7307). Heart and spirit as parallel terms for the inner person. Relationship to other evidence: Heart and spirit function as overlapping terms for the inner person — similar to the nephesh/ruach parallelism in Isa 26:9.

docs.title: Jeremiah 17:9-10 — The heart is deceitful
docs.text: Context: Jeremiah on human nature. Direct statement: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the LORD search the heart." Original language: leb (H3820). The heart is the site of moral condition and the object of divine searching. Relationship to other evidence: The heart as the moral center of the person, known fully only to God.

docs.title: Ezekiel 36:26 — A new heart
docs.text: Context: God's promise of restoration. Direct statement: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you." Original language: leb (H3820) and ruach (H7307) in parallelism. Heart and spirit are renewed together. Relationship to other evidence: The renewal of the whole inner person is described through heart and spirit — parallel terms, not distinct ontological substances.

docs.title: Romans 10:10 — Heart as the site of faith
docs.text: Context: Paul on salvation. Direct statement: "With the heart man believeth unto righteousness." Original language: kardia (G2588) — the NT continuation of leb. Relationship to other evidence: What Greek philosophy assigns to "soul" or "intellect," the biblical authors assign to "heart."

docs.title: 1. The Creation Formula and Its Reversal
docs.text: Gen 2:7 establishes the formula: dust + divine breath = living being. Multiple passages describe death as the reversal: dust returns to earth (Gen 3:19; Ecc 12:7), breath/spirit returns to God (Ecc 12:7; Psa 104:29), thoughts perish (Psa 146:4), knowledge ceases (Ecc 9:5). This creation-reversal pattern is the single most consistent framework for understanding biblical anthropology.

docs.title: 2. Shared Terminology Between Humans and Animals
docs.text: Nephesh chayyah is applied to sea creatures (Gen 1:20-21), land animals (Gen 1:24-25), and humans (Gen 2:7). Ruach chayyim is shared by all flesh (Gen 6:17; Gen 7:22). Man and beast have "one breath" (Ecc 3:19). The triple compound neshamah-ruach-chayyim is applied to all creatures (Gen 7:22). Whatever soul, spirit, and breath mean, they are not exclusively human.

docs.title: 3. The Image of God as the Distinguishing Factor
docs.text: Since animals share nephesh, ruach, and material origin (adamah) with humans, the distinguishing factor is the image of God (tselem + demuth, Gen 1:26-27). The image persists after the Fall (Gen 9:6), through the OT, and into the NT (1 Cor 11:7; Jas 3:9; Col 3:10). It is connected to dominion (Gen 1:28; Psa 8:5-6), moral capacity (Ecc 7:29), and relationship with God.

docs.title: 4. Mortality as the Human Condition
docs.text: The immortality vocabulary (athanasia, aphtharsia, aphthartos) is applied exclusively to God as a present possession and to believers as a future acquisition. Thnetos (mortal) is applied to human bodies. The tree of life was barred to prevent man from living forever. Immortality must be sought (Rom 2:7), put on (1 Cor 15:53-54). God alone has it (1 Tim 6:16).

docs.title: 5. Comprehensive Unconsciousness in Death
docs.text: Multiple OT authors across at least three books (Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Job) describe the dead as lacking knowledge (Ecc 9:5), thoughts (Psa 146:4), praise (Psa 115:17), remembrance (Psa 6:5), work, device, wisdom (Ecc 9:10). This is corroborated by the "sleep" metaphor used by seven or more biblical authors.

docs.title: 6. Soul and Spirit in Parallelism, Not Contrast
docs.text: Isa 26:9 and Luke 1:46-47 use nephesh/psyche and ruach/pneuma in synonymous parallelism. The Shema (Deu 6:5) uses heart, soul, might — not as three parts but as total devotion. Heb 4:12 pairs soul/spirit with joints/marrow — an analogy about God's penetrating discernment, not an anatomy lesson.

docs.title: 7. The Flesh-Spirit Contrast Is Moral, Not Ontological
docs.text: The foundational text (Isa 31:3) sets flesh vs. spirit as human weakness vs. divine power. Paul's "works of the flesh" include non-bodily sins (Gal 5:19-21). "Carnally minded" is a moral orientation (Rom 8:5-8). The contrast is not between two parts of the human being but between two orientations of the whole person.

docs.title: Nephesh (H5315) — 788 Occurrences
docs.text: The word study documents 788 tokens across 31 books with 214 unique KJV translations. This extraordinary semantic breadth prevents equating nephesh with the Greek philosophical "immortal soul." Nephesh means the whole person (Gen 2:7), life at risk (Job 2:4), desire (Deu 14:26), reflexive self (Amos 6:8), and even a corpse (Lev 21:11; Num 6:6, nephesh meth). The LXX maps nephesh to psyche 599 times (87%).

docs.title: Psyche (G5590) — 104 Occurrences
docs.text: The NT equivalent of nephesh, with 104 occurrences. Applied to sea creatures (Rev 16:3), confirming continuity with nephesh chayyah. Both can be destroyed by God (Matt 10:28). The Thayer lexicon calls pneuma "the rational and immortal soul," but this imports a Greek-philosophical assumption Scripture does not support.

docs.title: Ruach (H7307) — 434 Occurrences
docs.text: Three major categories: spirit (~50%), wind (~15%), breath (~3%). Ruach is the animating principle shared by humans and animals (Ecc 3:19). It returns to God at death (Ecc 12:7). Ruach is NEVER used for corpses (unlike nephesh), confirming it is the animating force while nephesh is the whole being. The LXX maps ruach to pneuma 235 times (~90%).

docs.title: Neshamah (H5397) — 25 Occurrences
docs.text: The rarest of the three key terms, specifically used in Gen 2:7 for what God breathed into man. The LXX maps neshamah to pnoe (G4157, physical breath) 14 times — preserving the concrete breath-of-life nuance rather than translating it as pneuma (spirit). Key uses: creation (Gen 2:7), illumination/understanding (Job 32:8; Pro 20:27), divine judgment (Job 4:9), and universal life (Isa 42:5; Gen 7:22).

docs.title: Athanasia (G110) — 3 Occurrences
docs.text: Only 3 NT occurrences: God alone has it (1 Tim 6:16), mortals put it on at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53, 54). Alpha-privative: a- + thanatos = deathlessness. The word's extreme rarity and exclusive assignment to God (as present possession) or believers (as future acquisition) is the most direct lexical evidence against inherent human immortality.

docs.title: Leb (H3820) — 654 Occurrences
docs.text: The most frequent anthropological term. What modern Western thought assigns to "soul" or "mind," Hebrew assigns to "heart." The heart is the executive center encompassing thought (1 Kgs 3:9), will (Gen 8:21), emotion (Gen 6:6), moral condition (Gen 6:5), and devotion (Deu 6:5). The LXX maps leb to kardia 436 times.

docs.title: Gen 2:7 → 1 Cor 15:45
docs.text: Paul directly quotes Gen 2:7 (via LXX): "The first man Adam was made (egeneto) a living soul (psychen zosan)." The verb "became" is preserved. The NT confirms the OT's holistic anthropology.

docs.title: Gen 2:7 → Ecc 12:7
docs.text: Creation and reversal: dust + breath = living being (Gen 2:7). At death: dust → earth, spirit → God (Ecc 12:7). The two passages are structural mirrors.

docs.title: Ecc 12:7 → Psa 146:4
docs.text: The spirit returns to God (Ecc 12:7); that day thoughts perish (Psa 146:4). Combined, these teach that the spirit's return is not a conscious journey to heaven but the withdrawal of the animating life-force.

docs.title: Gen 2:7 → Ezek 37:5-10
docs.text: Ezekiel's dry bones vision recapitulates creation: physical body + ruach = living beings. v.8: "but there was no breath in them" — body without breath is dead. v.10: breath enters, they live.

docs.title: OT Death Descriptions → NT Sleep Metaphor
docs.text: Seven or more biblical authors call death "sleep": Moses (Deu 31:16), Job (14:12), Jeremiah (51:39), Daniel (12:2), Jesus (John 11:11), Stephen via Luke (Acts 7:60), Paul (1 Cor 15:6, 18, 51; 1 Thess 4:14). The cross-testament consistency is remarkable.

docs.title: Gen 3:22-24 → Rev 22:14
docs.text: The tree of life barred after the Fall is restored eschatologically. Conditional immortality frames the entire biblical narrative from Genesis to Revelation.

docs.title: 2 Corinthians 5:1-8 — "Absent from body, present with Lord"
docs.text: This passage is commonly cited for a conscious intermediate state. The complicating element is v.8: Paul seems to expect immediate presence with the Lord upon departing the body. However, v.4 is determinative: Paul explicitly says he does NOT want to be "unclothed" (disembodied) but "clothed upon" (the resurrection body). His horizon is the resurrection, not disembodiment. The passage supports resurrection hope, not the immortality of the soul.

docs.title: Philippians 1:23 — "Depart and be with Christ"
docs.text: Paul expresses desire to depart and be with Christ as "far better." The same letter has Paul hoping for the resurrection (3:11) and the transformation of bodies at Christ's return (3:20-21). Paul treats departing-and-being-with-Christ as a single expectation, consistent with no conscious interval between death and resurrection.

docs.title: Luke 23:43 — "Today you will be with me in paradise"
docs.text: The complicating factor: Jesus tells the thief he will be in paradise "today." But Jesus was NOT in paradise that day — John 20:17 has him saying on Sunday morning "I am not yet ascended to my Father." Since Greek has no punctuation, the comma is editorial. The statement "I say unto thee today, thou shalt be with me in paradise" fits the known facts: Jesus was not in paradise on Friday.

docs.title: Revelation 6:9-11 — Souls under the altar
docs.text: Psychai of martyrs cry out from under the altar. The genre is apocalyptic, with extensive symbolism. The parallel with Gen 4:10 (Abel's blood "cries from the ground") shows this is personification of shed blood/life demanding justice, not a literal scene of conscious dead people.

docs.title: 1 Kings 17:21-22 / Genesis 35:18 — Nephesh departing and returning
docs.text: These passages describe the nephesh "going out" at death and "coming back" at resurrection. The complicating element is that nephesh appears to be something that moves. However, the texts do not describe where the nephesh goes during the interval, do not attribute consciousness to it, and are consistent with nephesh as "life" that departs and returns rather than a conscious entity that travels.

docs.title: Matthew 10:28 — "Kill the body, not the soul"
docs.text: The distinction between killing the body and not being able to kill the psyche might suggest the soul survives bodily death. However, the verse's conclusion is that God can DESTROY both soul and body in gehenna. The psyche is destructible. The point is about the scope of God's power over the whole person, not about an immortal component.

docs.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:23 — "Spirit, soul, and body"
docs.text: The three-term listing might suggest a tripartite human nature. However, the emphasis falls on "wholly" (holoteles) and "whole" (holokeron) — completeness, not enumeration. Deu 6:5 uses three terms (heart, soul, might) without implying three ontological parts. Mark 12:30 uses four terms. The number varies because the point is totality, not anatomy.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The evidence from all verse categories points in a consistent direction. The creation formula of Gen 2:7 establishes that man BECAME a living soul — the composite entity of dust + breath IS the nephesh, not a possessor of one. The same terminology (nephesh chayyah, ruach chayyim) applies to animals. What distinguishes humans from animals is the image of God, not the possession of soul or spirit.

Death reverses the creation formula: dust returns to earth, spirit returns to God, thoughts perish, the dead know nothing. Multiple authors across both testaments describe death as unconsciousness and call it "sleep." The biblical hope for the dead is resurrection, not disembodied survival.

Immortality vocabulary is applied exclusively to God as a present possession and to believers as a future acquisition at the resurrection. The tree of life narrative (Gen 2:9 → 3:22-24 → Rev 22:14) frames the entire biblical story as one of conditional immortality.

The flesh-spirit contrast throughout both testaments is moral and qualitative, not ontological. Soul and spirit appear in synonymous parallelism, not as distinct substances. The heart (leb/kardia) is the most frequent anthropological term, functioning as the executive center of the whole person.

Passages commonly cited for a conscious intermediate state each have genre, grammatical, or contextual qualifications that prevent them from overriding the consistent testimony of didactic texts.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: What does Scripture explicitly say about the nature and composition of human beings (biblical anthropology)? Focus on nephesh (soul), ruach (spirit), neshamah (breath), the creation of man, whether humans ARE souls or HAVE souls, and what happens at death.

docs.title: H5315 — nephesh
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5315-nephesh.md

Occurrences: 788

Feminine noun from H5314 (naphash, to breathe). 682 unique verses, 788 tokens, across 31 books. 214 unique KJV translations — the broadest translation range of any Hebrew word. Primarily rendered 'soul' (64%), 'life' (14%), 'person' (4%), 'creature' (1%), 'body/dead body' (1%). First occurrence Gen 1:20 for sea creatures — applied to animals before humans. Used for the whole person (Gen 2:7), life at risk (Job 2:4), desire/appetite (Deu 14:26), reflexive pronoun 'self' (Amos 6:8), and corpses (Num 6:6, nephesh meth). Key: man BECAME a nephesh (Gen 2:7), not received one. Nephesh can die (Ezek 18:4), be destroyed (Matt 10:28 via psyche), and depart at death (Gen 35:18). LXX maps to psyche G5590 599 times (87%).

Semantic categories: breathing creature, whole person, life at risk, desire/appetite, self/reflexive, corpse/dead body

Key verses: Gen 1:20, Gen 2:7, Gen 35:18, Lev 21:11, Num 6:6, Ezek 18:4, Deu 14:26

Relevance: The central Hebrew anthropological term. Its extraordinary semantic breadth (214 translations) proves it cannot be equated with the Greek philosophical 'immortal soul.' Man BECAME a nephesh — the holistic, integrated being is the nephesh.

docs.title: H7307 — ruach
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7307-ruach.md

Occurrences: 434

Feminine noun. 434 OT occurrences. Translated 'spirit' (54%), 'wind' (21%), 'breath' (8%). Six semantic categories: Spirit of God, wind, breath/life-force, human spirit/disposition, spirit beings, vanity. Key anthropological uses: ruach as the life-force God gives and takes back (Job 34:14-15, Psa 104:29-30), ruach shared by humans AND animals (Ecc 3:19 — ruach echad), ruach returning to God at death (Ecc 12:7). Ruach is NEVER used for corpses (unlike nephesh), suggesting it is the animating principle while nephesh is the whole being. LXX maps to pneuma G4151 235 times (~90%).

Semantic categories: Spirit of God, wind, breath/life-force, human disposition, spirit beings, vanity/futility

Key verses: Gen 1:2, Gen 6:17, Ecc 3:19, Ecc 12:7, Psa 104:29-30, Psa 146:4, Job 34:14-15

Relevance: The breath/spirit that animates all living things. Shared by humans and animals. Returns to God at death — not a conscious entity going to heaven, but the life-force returning to its source.

docs.title: H5397 — neshamah
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5397-nshamah.md

Occurrences: 25

Feminine noun from H5395 (nasham, to blow away). Only 24 unique verses (25 tokens) across 10 books — the rarest of the three key anthropological terms. Translated 'breath' (42%), 'breathe/breatheth' (21%), 'blast' (12.5%), 'spirit' (8%), 'inspiration' (4%). Five semantic categories: breath of life at creation (Gen 2:7), divine blast in judgment (Job 4:9), total annihilation formula (Deu 20:16), human inner life/illumination (Pro 20:27, Job 32:8), every living being (Psa 150:6). Specifically the word used in Gen 2:7 for what God breathed into man (not ruach). LXX maps primarily to pnoe G4157 (14x, PMI 9.36), preserving its physical-breath nuance.

Semantic categories: breath of life, divine blast, total annihilation, illumination/understanding, every living being

Key verses: Gen 2:7, Gen 7:22, Job 32:8, Job 33:4, Pro 20:27, Isa 42:5, Psa 150:6

Relevance: The rarest and most specific of the three key terms. Used exclusively for the divine breath that gives life. Its presence in Gen 2:7 distinguishes that creation act. Job dominates with 7 of 24 occurrences. The LXX maps it to pnoe (physical breath) rather than pneuma (spirit), preserving its concrete breath-of-life nuance.

docs.title: G5590 — psyche
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5590-psyche.md

Occurrences: 104

Feminine noun from psycho (to breathe). 105 NT occurrences (87 in KJV translation DB). Translated 'soul/souls' (60%), 'life/lives' (33%), 'mind' (2%), 'heart' (2%). Five semantic categories: inner self/emotions (Matt 26:38), physical life (Matt 16:25), person/individual for counting (Acts 2:41), living creature (Rev 16:3), mind/will (Eph 6:6). LXX renders nephesh as psyche 599 times — direct semantic parallel. Derives from breathing root, describing what a creature IS when alive. Can be destroyed by God (Matt 10:28). Applied to sea creatures (Rev 16:3).

Semantic categories: inner self, physical life, person/individual, living creature, mind/will

Key verses: Matt 10:28, Matt 16:25, Acts 2:41, Rev 16:3, 1 Thess 5:23

Relevance: NT equivalent of nephesh. The note on the Thayer lexicon definition is important — it calls pneuma 'the rational and immortal soul,' but that imports a Greek-philosophical assumption Scripture does not support.

docs.title: G4151 — pneuma
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4151-pneuma.md

Occurrences: 385

Neuter noun from pneo (to blow, breathe). 385 NT occurrences (342 indexed). Translated 'Spirit/spirit' (62%), 'Ghost' (25%), 'spirits' (8%). Seven semantic categories: Holy Spirit (dominant ~50%), evil spirits (~8%), human spirit/disposition (~35%), life-force/animating breath, disembodied spirits, wind/breath (rare), figurative. LXX renders ruach as pneuma 235 times (~90%). Key anthropological uses: 'the body without the spirit is dead' (Jas 2:26), 'yielded up the ghost' (Matt 27:50), spirit listed alongside soul and body (1 Thess 5:23).

Semantic categories: Holy Spirit, evil spirits, human spirit, life-force, disembodied spirits, wind/breath, figurative power

Key verses: Matt 27:50, John 3:8, Acts 2:4, 1 Thess 5:23, Jas 2:26, 1 Cor 15:45

Relevance: NT equivalent of ruach. The dominant NT usage is for the Holy Spirit. In anthropological contexts, pneuma is the animating breath/spirit — when it departs, the body is dead (Jas 2:26).

docs.title: G4157 — pnoe
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4157-pnoe.md

Occurrences: 2

Feminine noun, cognate of pneuma. Only 2 NT occurrences: Acts 2:2 (rushing mighty wind at Pentecost) and Acts 17:25 (God gives to all life, breath, and all things). LXX uses pnoe for neshamah 14 times — preserving the physical breath nuance of neshamah. Key relevance: Acts 17:25 affirms God as the sustainer of all breath/life.

Semantic categories: physical breath, wind

Key verses: Acts 2:2, Acts 17:25

Relevance: NT equivalent of neshamah via LXX bridge. Acts 17:25 parallels the OT theme of God sustaining all life through breath.

docs.title: H4194 — maveth
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H4194-maveth.md

Occurrences: 170

Masculine noun from muwth H4191 (to die). 153 unique verses, 170 tokens across 27 books. Translated 'death' (~92%), 'died/dead' (~8%). Seven semantic categories: biographical marker ('after the death of X'), legal penalty, death personified, life-death moral contrast (Deu 30:15), deliverance from death, realm/destination, death defeated (Isa 25:8). LXX maps to thanatos G2288 97 times (PMI 5.98). Paired with sheol H7585 in 15 verses in synonymous parallelism.

Semantic categories: biographical marker, legal penalty, personified power, moral contrast with life, deliverance from, realm/destination, defeated/swallowed up

Key verses: Deu 30:15, Isa 25:8, Hos 13:14, Psa 49:14, Job 38:17

Relevance: The primary Hebrew noun for death. The same word is used for all types of death — physical, judicial, and eschatological. No separate vocabulary exists for different 'kinds' of death.

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

Masculine noun from thnesko (to die). 106 unique verses, 119 tokens across 15 NT books. Translated 'death' (100% effectively). Primary LXX bridge from maveth H4194 (97 co-occurrences, PMI 5.98). Highest density in Romans (4.6/100v) and Philippians (4.8/100v). Used for physical death, spiritual death, and the second death — same vocabulary for all.

Semantic categories: physical death, spiritual death, second death, death personified, death defeated

Key verses: Rom 5:12, Rom 6:23, 1 Cor 15:54-55, Rev 20:14, Rev 21:8

Relevance: NT equivalent of maveth. The same word covers all kinds of death. 'Death is swallowed up in victory' (1 Cor 15:54 quoting Isa 25:8).

docs.title: G110 — athanasia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G110-athanasia.md

Occurrences: 3

Feminine noun. Alpha-privative (a-) + thanatos (death) = deathlessness. Only 3 NT occurrences: 1 Tim 6:16 (God ALONE has it), 1 Cor 15:53 and 15:54 (mortals PUT ON immortality at resurrection). All three in accusative singular feminine — functioning as direct object of 'having' or 'putting on.' Exclusively Pauline. No Hebrew source via LXX. Concept of deathlessness present in OT imagery (tree of life, Isa 25:8) but the word is uniquely Greek/NT.

Semantic categories: exclusive divine attribute, eschatological transformation

Key verses: 1 Tim 6:16, 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54

Relevance: The most critical word for the immortality question. Only 3 occurrences — God alone HAS it; humans must PUT IT ON at the resurrection. The word's extreme rarity and exclusive assignment to God (as present possession) or believers (as future acquisition) directly addresses whether humans have inherently immortal souls.

docs.title: G861 — aphtharsia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G861-aphtharsia.md

Occurrences: 8

Feminine noun. Alpha-privative (a-) + phtheiro (to corrupt/decay) = incorruptibility. 8 unique verses across 5 books. Translated 'incorruption' (50%), 'immortality' (25%), 'sincerity' (25%). Three semantic categories: resurrection transformation (1 Cor 15:42, 50, 53, 54), object of aspiration (Rom 2:7, 2 Tim 1:10), ethical purity (Eph 6:24, Tit 2:7). Exclusively Pauline. Paired with athanasia in 1 Cor 15:53-54: corruptible/incorruption and mortal/immortality.

Semantic categories: resurrection transformation, object of aspiration, ethical purity

Key verses: Rom 2:7, 1 Cor 15:42, 1 Cor 15:53-54, 2 Tim 1:10

Relevance: Something humans SEEK (Rom 2:7) and PUT ON at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54). Christ 'brought life and immortality to light through the gospel' (2 Tim 1:10). Not a present human possession.

docs.title: G862 — aphthartos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G862-aphthartos.md

Occurrences: 7

Adjective. Alpha-privative + phtheiro = incorruptible/undecaying. 7 verses across 4 books. Applied to God (Rom 1:23, 1 Tim 1:17), the resurrection body (1 Cor 15:52), the Christian's reward (1 Cor 9:25), and the believer's inheritance and new birth (1 Pet 1:4, 23; 3:4). Contrasted with phthartos (corruptible) applied to man (Rom 1:23).

Semantic categories: divine attribute, resurrection body, imperishable reward, incorruptible character

Key verses: Rom 1:23, 1 Tim 1:17, 1 Cor 15:52, 1 Pet 1:4

Relevance: Applied to God as an inherent attribute; applied to humans only in the future tense or through divine gift. The Rom 1:23 contrast (incorruptible God vs. corruptible man) is direct evidence against inherent human immortality.

docs.title: G2349 — thnetos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2349-thnetos.md

Occurrences: 6

Adjective from thnesko (to die) = mortal, liable to die. 6 verses across 3 books (exclusively Pauline). Applied to human body/flesh: the mortal body under sin (Rom 6:12), mortal bodies awaiting resurrection quickening (Rom 8:11), mortal putting on immortality (1 Cor 15:53-54), life manifested in mortal flesh (2 Cor 4:11), mortality swallowed up by life (2 Cor 5:4). Paired directly with athanasia (G110) in 1 Cor 15:53: 'this mortal must put on immortality.'

Semantic categories: mortal body under sin, mortal body awaiting resurrection, mortal-to-immortal transformation, life in mortal flesh

Key verses: Rom 6:12, Rom 8:11, 1 Cor 15:53-54, 2 Cor 4:11, 2 Cor 5:4

Relevance: Applied to human bodies 6 times. Confirms mortality as the present human condition. Paired with athanasia as its antonym — mortality must be REPLACED by immortality at the resurrection.

docs.title: H6754 — tselem
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H6754-tselem.md

Occurrences: 18

Masculine noun from unused root 'to shade.' 15 unique verses (18 tokens) across 8 books. Translated 'image/images' (87%), 'pictures' (7%), 'vain shew' (7%). Four semantic categories: humanity in God's image (Gen 1:26-27, 9:6), cult-images to destroy (Num 33:52), crafted figures (1 Sam 6:5), fleeting appearance (Psa 39:6). Paired with demuth (H1823, likeness) in Gen 1:26 and 5:3. LXX maps to eikon G1504 (10x, PMI 8.98). The image of God distinguishes humans from animals and is the basis for human dignity (Gen 9:6).

Semantic categories: image of God in humanity, cult-images, crafted figures, fleeting appearance

Key verses: Gen 1:26-27, Gen 5:3, Gen 9:6, Psa 39:6

Relevance: What makes humans unique is the image of God (tselem + demuth), not the possession of nephesh or ruach (which animals also have). The image persists after the Fall (Gen 9:6) and in the NT (1 Cor 11:7, Jas 3:9).

docs.title: H3820 — leb
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H3820-leb.md

Occurrences: 654

Masculine noun. 550 unique verses (654 tokens) across 33 books. Translated 'heart' (~85%), 'understanding' (2%), 'mind' (1%). Six semantic categories: emotion (Gen 6:6), will/intention (Gen 8:21), intellect/wisdom (1 Kgs 3:9), moral condition (Gen 6:5), devotion/religious orientation (Jer 3:10), center/midst (spatial). The most frequent anthropological term in Hebrew. What modern Western anthropology assigns to 'soul' or 'mind,' Hebrew assigns to 'heart.' LXX maps to kardia G2588 436 times (PMI 4.8) — one of the strongest cross-testament bridges.

Semantic categories: emotion, will/intention, intellect/wisdom, moral condition, devotion, spatial center

Key verses: Gen 6:5, 1 Kgs 3:9, Pro 4:23, Jer 17:9-10, Deu 6:5

Relevance: The most frequent OT anthropological term after nephesh. The heart is the executive center of the whole person — encompassing thought, will, and emotion. What Greek philosophy separates into 'mind,' 'soul,' and 'will,' Hebrew locates in the single concept of leb.

docs.title: G2588 — kardia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2588-kardia.md

Occurrences: 160

Feminine noun. 160 tokens in 152 unique verses across 22 NT books. Translated 'heart/hearts' (100%). Seven semantic categories: thought/reasoning, belief/faith, emotion/affection, moral character/will, surface for God's law, object of divine knowledge, hardened/opened. LXX bridge from leb H3820 (436 co-occurrences, PMI 4.8). Pervasive: 22 of 27 NT books. The NT center of the entire inner life — intellect, will, and emotion.

Semantic categories: thought/reasoning, belief/faith, emotion/affection, moral character, divine law surface, divine knowledge object, hardened/opened

Key verses: Rom 10:9-10, Mat 5:8, Mat 15:18-19, Heb 8:10, Heb 4:12

Relevance: NT continuation of the OT heart concept. The heart is where faith dwells (Rom 10:10), where God writes His law (Heb 8:10), and what God searches (Heb 4:12). The 'inner man' language (Rom 7:22, Eph 3:16) corresponds to the OT 'heart' rather than to a separable soul.

docs.title: H2416 — chay
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H2416-chay.md

Occurrences: 531

Adjective/noun. 449 unique verses (531 tokens) across 29 books. Translated variously: 'liveth' (12%), 'living' (8.5%), 'life' (7.3%), 'alive' (6.5%), 'beast' (5.1%). Six semantic categories: living creatures (Gen 1:20), life as vitality (Lev 17:11), being alive (Deu 4:4), oath formula ('as the LORD lives'), living water (Jer 2:13), beast/animal. Part of the nephesh chayyah compound in Gen 2:7. LXX maps to zoe G2222 (136x) and zao G2198 (195x).

Semantic categories: living creature, vitality, being alive, oath formula, living water, beast/animal

Key verses: Gen 1:20, Gen 2:7, Lev 17:11, Deu 30:19

Relevance: Part of the foundational creation compound nephesh chayyah (living soul/creature). Applied to both animals and humans.

docs.title: H7585 — sheol
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7585-showl.md

Occurrences: 68

Feminine noun. 64 unique verses (68 tokens) across 17 books. Translated 'hell' (48%), 'grave' (41%), 'pit' (5%). Six semantic categories: realm of the dead (Gen 37:35), descent (Num 16:33), paired with death (2 Sam 22:6), fate of the wicked (Psa 9:17), rescue from sheol (Psa 16:10), insatiable (Pro 27:20). Characterized by unconsciousness (Ecc 9:10 — no work, knowledge, wisdom in sheol), silence (Psa 115:17), and darkness. LXX maps to hades G86 (58x, PMI 8.31).

Semantic categories: realm of dead, descent, paired with death, fate of wicked, rescue from, insatiable

Key verses: Gen 37:35, Psa 16:10, Psa 9:17, Ecc 9:10, Isa 14:15

Relevance: The OT destination of the dead. Characterized by unconsciousness, silence, and inactivity. The righteous and wicked both go there. Rescue from sheol is associated with resurrection.

docs.title: G86 — hades
docs.text:
Occurrences: 11

Proper locative noun. Alpha-privative (a-) + idein (to see) = 'unseen.' 11 NT occurrences. Translated 'hell' (64%), 'grave' (9%). LXX equivalent of sheol H7585 (58 co-occurrences, PMI 8.31). Key verses: Mat 11:23, Mat 16:18 ('gates of hades'), Luk 10:15, Luk 16:23 (rich man in hades — parable), Acts 2:27 and 2:31 (quoting Psa 16:10), 1 Cor 15:55 ('O grave, where is thy victory?'), Rev 1:18 (Christ has the keys), Rev 6:8 (Death and Hades), Rev 20:13-14 (hades gives up its dead, then cast into lake of fire). Destroyed at the end — Rev 20:14.

Semantic categories: realm of dead, destination of dead, personified with death, destroyed at end

Key verses: Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, 1 Cor 15:55, Rev 20:13-14, Mat 16:18

Relevance: NT equivalent of sheol. Continues the OT concept of the realm of the dead. Notably destroyed in Rev 20:14 — hades is temporary, not eternal. Christ holds the keys (Rev 1:18).

docs.title: H1320 — basar
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1320-basar.md

Occurrences: 277

Masculine noun. 241 unique verses (277 tokens) across 27 books. Translated 'flesh' (~86%), 'body' (1%), 'kin' (1%). Used for physical flesh/body, kinship, all humanity ('all flesh'), and as contrast term to ruach/spirit. Key: Isa 31:3 — 'the Egyptians are men, not God; their horses flesh, not spirit' — the foundational OT flesh-spirit contrast is moral/qualitative, not ontological.

Semantic categories: physical flesh/body, kinship, all humanity, moral weakness vs divine power

Key verses: Gen 2:21, Gen 6:3, Isa 31:3, Lev 17:11

Relevance: The flesh-spirit contrast in the OT is about human weakness vs. divine power, not two ontological parts of man.

docs.title: G4561 — sarx
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4561-sarx.md

Occurrences: 151

Feminine noun. 130 unique verses (151 tokens) across 22 NT books. Translated 'flesh' (60%), 'the flesh' (26%). Multiple semantic domains: body, human beings, kinship, sinful nature, desire. In Paul, sarx becomes the sinful principle opposing the Spirit — but Gal 5:19-21 lists 'works of the flesh' that include hatred, envy, strife — clearly not bodily sins. This confirms the moral/volitional meaning of sarx in Paul.

Semantic categories: physical body, humanity, kinship, sinful nature, desire

Key verses: Rom 8:5-8, Gal 5:19-21, John 1:14, John 3:6, John 6:63

Relevance: The NT flesh-spirit contrast continues the OT pattern. Sarx in Paul means the sinful orientation of the whole person, not the physical body. Works of the flesh include jealousy, envy, strife — obviously not bodily sins.

docs.title: H4191 — muwth
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H4191-muwth.md

Occurrences: 1028

Primitive root verb. 694 unique verses (1,028 tokens) across 28 books. Primary Hebrew death verb. Four stems: Qal (74% — to die), Hiphil (16% — to cause to die), Hophal (8% — to be put to death), Piel (1% — to kill intensively). The mot tamut (infinitive absolute) construction in Gen 2:17 is the same form used for judicial death penalties throughout the Pentateuch. First occurrence: Gen 2:17.

Semantic categories: natural death, judicial death, state of being dead, killing

Key verses: Gen 2:17, Ezek 18:4, Exo 21:12

Relevance: The mot tamut construction (Gen 2:17) is the same used for capital punishment — it invariably means actual death, not metaphorical separation.

docs.title: G2222 — zoe
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2222-zoe.md

Occurrences: 134

Feminine noun from zao (to live). 126 unique verses (134 tokens) across 22 NT books. Translated 'life' (73%), 'of life' (25%). Highest density in 1 John (9.5/100v) and John (3.6/100v). Used for both physical life and eternal/spiritual life. Distinguished from psyche (soul/self who lives) and bios (livelihood). LXX bridge from chay H2416 (136 co-occurrences). Eternal life consistently presented as gift (Rom 6:23), promise (Tit 1:2), and something to seek (Rom 2:7) — conditional on Christ (1 John 5:11-12).

Semantic categories: physical life, eternal life, life as divine gift

Key verses: John 3:16, Rom 6:23, 1 John 5:11-12, John 14:6

Relevance: Eternal life is a gift, a promise, something conditional on Christ — not an inherent human possession. This supports the conditionalist anthropology.

docs.title: H1961 — hayah
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1961-hayah.md

Occurrences: 4280

Primitive root verb. 3,122 unique verses (4,280 tokens) across 39 books. The fundamental verb of existence and becoming. Two stems: Qal (3,540 — be, become, happen), Niphal (21 — emphatic). Seven semantic categories: simple existence (Gen 1:2), coming into being/becoming (Gen 2:7), creative command (Gen 1:3), narrative marker, divine self-identification (Exo 3:14), covenant formula, prophetic future. Critical for Gen 2:7: wayehi (Qal.Wayq.3ms) = 'became' — man BECAME a living soul, not received one. LXX splits between ginomai (1,236x — dynamic/becoming) and eimi (1,820x — stative/being).

Semantic categories: existence, becoming, creative command, narrative marker, divine name, covenant, prophetic future

Key verses: Gen 1:3, Gen 2:7, Exo 3:14, Gen 3:22

Relevance: The wayehi (became) in Gen 2:7 is critical — it is a transformation verb. Man did not receive a soul; the combined dust + breath entity BECAME a living soul.

docs.title: G1504 — eikon
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1504-eikon.md

Occurrences: 23

Feminine noun. NT equivalent of tselem H6754 via LXX bridge (10 co-occurrences, PMI 8.98). Used for image of God in man (1 Cor 11:7), image of the earthly/heavenly (1 Cor 15:49), image of the invisible God applied to Christ (Col 1:15), and literal images/coins (Mat 22:20). Man IS the image of God (1 Cor 11:7, present tense).

Semantic categories: image of God, image of Christ, earthly/heavenly image, literal image

Key verses: 1 Cor 11:7, 1 Cor 15:49, Col 1:15, Col 3:10

Relevance: NT continuation of the image of God concept. Man IS the image of God (present). Believers are being renewed after the image of the creator (Col 3:10).

docs.title: H3824 — lebab
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H3824-lebab.md

Occurrences: 267

Masculine noun. Fuller/emphatic form of leb H3820. 230 unique verses. Same meaning as leb — the inner directing center. Tends to appear in emphatic or covenantal contexts; Deuteronomy and Chronicles favor lebab for 'with all your heart.' LXX maps to kardia G2588 187 times (PMI 4.83).

Semantic categories: emotion, will/intention, intellect, moral condition, devotion

Key verses: Deu 6:5, Deu 30:6, 1 Chr 28:9

Relevance: Emphatic form of leb. Used in covenantal heart-language, especially Deuteronomy.

docs.title: G3667 — homoioma
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3667-homoioma.md

Occurrences: 6

Neuter noun meaning likeness, similitude, resemblance. Used in Rom 1:23 (image made like to corruptible man), Rom 5:14 (similitude of Adam's transgression), Rom 6:5 (likeness of his death), Rom 8:3 (likeness of sinful flesh), Phil 2:7 (likeness of men), Rev 9:7 (shapes like horses). Related to homoiosis (Jas 3:9 — similitude of God).

Semantic categories: likeness/resemblance, representation, form/shape

Key verses: Rom 8:3, Phil 2:7, Rom 1:23

Relevance: Part of the image/likeness vocabulary. Rom 1:23 contrasts the incorruptible God with images made like corruptible man.

docs.title: H2421 — chayah
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H2421-chayah.md

Occurrences: 361

Verb (primitive root). To live, to revive, to preserve alive. Cognate of chay H2416. Used for living, being restored to life, keeping alive. The verbal form underlying the life vocabulary.

Semantic categories: to live, to revive, to preserve alive

Key verses: Gen 3:22, Ezek 37:5-6

Relevance: In Gen 3:22 — wachai le'olam ('and live forever') — the verb form in the tree of life passage. Living forever was conditional on access to the tree.

docs.title: Evidence Classifications: What Is Man?
docs.text: Tool-verified classification audit trail for etc7-01-what-is-man. Each positional evidence item is presented with its claim, supporting evidence, and the full Decision Tree walkthrough. Hebrew/Greek parsing verified by running hebrew_parser.py and greek_parser.py against the actual text.

docs.title: E12 — Thoughts perish at death
docs.text:
Claim: "When breath (ruach) departs, in that very day his thoughts perish" Reference: Psalm 146:4 Evidence: The psalmist teaches: do not trust in princes or the son of man, for when his breath departs and he returns to the earth, "in that very day his thoughts perish."

Classification Walkthrough:

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — אָבְדוּ (אבד, "perish") applied to human thoughts at death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Subject is עֶשְׁתֹּנֹתָיו ("his thoughts") belonging to a literal human whose רוח departs — antecedent (v.3) is בן־אדם ("son of man"). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): אָבְדוּ — lemma אבד, Qal Perfect 3cp. Intransitive: "to perish, cease to exist." Subject עֶשְׁתֹּנֹתָיו (fp noun + 3ms suffix). No ambiguity. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm 146 is wisdom/hymnic psalm with direct didactic instruction (vv.3-4 teach not to trust in mortal princes). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E13 (no remembrance), E14 (silence), E15 (dead know nothing), E16 (no knowledge in sheol), E70 (land of forgetfulness). PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond.

docs.title: E13 — No remembrance in death
docs.text:
Claim: "In death there is no remembrance of God; in the grave none gives thanks" Reference: Psalm 6:5 Evidence: David appeals to God for deliverance on the basis that the dead cannot remember or praise him.

Classification Walkthrough:

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "death" (מות) and "no remembrance" describe cessation of conscious activity. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): David speaking of human beings in death generally; implicit subject of "gives thanks" is any person in Sheol. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): אֵין (negative particle of non-existence) + בַּמָּוֶת (prep ב + noun מות, "in death") + זִכְרֶךָ (noun זכר + 2ms suffix). יוֹדֶה — ידה Hiphil.Impf.3ms ("gives thanks") negated by rhetorical מִי ("who?"). PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm — individual lament, direct first-person speech stating theological premise. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E12, E14-E16, E70. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond.

docs.title: E14 — The dead go to silence
docs.text:
Claim: "The dead praise not the LORD; they go down into silence" Reference: Psalm 115:17 Evidence: A declarative statement contrasting the living (who praise the LORD) with the dead (who go to silence).

Classification Walkthrough:

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "dead" (מות, Qal participle) and "silence" (דומה) — cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): הַמֵּתִים (Qal.Ptcp.mp of מות) — literal dead humans as a class. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): מֵּתִים (מות, Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs) substantive = "the dead." יְהַלְלוּ (הלל, Piel.Impf.3mp) negated by לֹא = "they do not praise." יֹרְדֵי (ירד, Qal.Ptcp.mp.Cst) = "ones going down to." דוּמָה (Noun.fs.Abs) = "silence." PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Hymnic psalm with declarative theological statement. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E12, E13, E15, E16, E70. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond.

docs.title: E15 — The dead know nothing
docs.text:
Claim: "The dead know not any thing; their love, hatred, and envy have perished" Reference: Ecclesiastes 9:5-6 Evidence: Qoheleth states that the dead have no knowledge, no share in anything under the sun, and their emotions have perished.

Classification Walkthrough:

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "perished" (אָבְדָה from אבד, Qal Perf.) applied to the dead's faculties. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): הַמֵּתִים (מות, Qal.Ptcp.mp) — literal dead humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): אֵינָם יֹודְעִים (אין + ידע Qal.Ptcp.mp) = "they do not know"; מְאוּמָה = "anything" — total negation. אָבְדָה (אבד, Qal.Perf.3fs) = "has perished" applied to love/hatred/jealousy. חֵלֶק אֵין לָהֶם עוֹד לְעוֹלָם = "no share for them again forever." PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, direct didactic assertion. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E12, E13, E14, E16, E70. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond.

docs.title: E16 — No knowledge in sheol
docs.text:
Claim: "In sheol there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom" Reference: Ecclesiastes 9:10 Evidence: Qoheleth commands diligent work because there is absolutely no activity or cognition in sheol.

Classification Walkthrough:

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — אֵין ("there is not") + four nouns of activity/cognition applied to all in sheol. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Implied "you" (אַתָּה, 2ms) — generic literal human. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): אֵין (negation particle) governs מַעֲשֶׂה (deed), חֶשְׁבֹּון (account), דַעַת (knowledge), חָכְמָה (wisdom). Locative בְּשְׁאֹול = "in sheol." Total absence stated. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, direct didactic exhortation. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E12-E15, E70. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond.

docs.title: E20 — The soul that sins shall die
docs.text:
