Notes: Zoopoiesei (future active indicative of zoopoieo G2227 — 'will make alive') + ta thneta somata (the mortal bodies, accusative plural). The vivification is future — the mortal bodies are not yet made alive. The indwelling Spirit is the guarantee, not the present fulfillment. Thneta (G2349, accusative plural neuter) modifies somata (bodies).

docs.title: Life of Jesus manifested in mortal flesh
docs.text:
For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh.

Context: Paul's treasure-in-earthen-vessels argument (2 Cor 4:7-12). The apostolic paradox: continual dying so that divine life may be displayed.

Notes: Thnete (G2349, dative singular feminine) modifies sarki (flesh). Here thnetos agrees with sarx (flesh, feminine), hence the feminine form. The present condition is mortal; divine life is manifested through the mortal vessel.

docs.title: Mortal swallowed up by life — clothing metaphor for resurrection
docs.text:
For we know that if our earthly house of [this] tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked. For we that are in [this] tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing [is] God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit.

Context: Paul's extended clothing metaphor. The earthly tent (mortal body) vs. the heavenly building (resurrection body). Paul does NOT want to be unclothed (die/disembodied) but clothed upon (transformed).

Notes: V.4: to thneton (the mortal thing, neuter singular substantival — 'mortality') + katapino (swallowed up) + hypo zoes (by life). The ependyomai (G1902, clothed upon) in vv.2,4 describes super-addition — putting on the resurrection body OVER the mortal body, i.e., transformation without death. Paul explicitly rejects the intermediate disembodied state as desirable — he does NOT want to be unclothed (ekdysasthai, G1562) but clothed upon.

docs.title: Grace with those who love the Lord in sincerity/incorruption
docs.text:
Grace [be] with all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity. Amen.

Context: Closing benediction of Ephesians. Aphtharsia used in its ethical sense — love that is undecayed, genuine.

Notes: En aphtharsia (in incorruption/sincerity, dative) — the ethical/metaphorical use of aphtharsia. Not about physical immortality but about genuineness of love. One of 2 ethical uses (with Tit 2:7) out of 8 total occurrences.

docs.title: Doctrine showing uncorruptness — ethical use of aphtharsia
docs.text:
In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine [shewing] uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity,

Context: Paul's instructions to Titus about sound doctrine. Aphtharsia describes the quality of teaching — un-corrupted, pure.

Notes: Aphtharsian (uncorruptness) in the ethical sense — doctrine that is not decayed or corrupted. Second ethical use of aphtharsia (with Eph 6:24). These two ethical uses demonstrate that aphtharsia's core meaning is 'un-decay' — applied physically to the resurrection body and metaphorically to moral character.

docs.title: Changed the glory of the INCORRUPTIBLE God into corruptible images
docs.text:
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.

Context: Paul's indictment of pagan idolatry. God is aphthartos (incorruptible) by nature; idolaters exchanged this for images of corruptible (phthartos) creatures.

Notes: Aphthartos (G862, genitive singular masculine) modifies theou (God) — God is inherently incorruptible. Phthartos (G5349) describes man, birds, beasts — all creatures are corruptible. The contrast is between Creator (aphthartos) and creature (phthartos). God's incorruptibility is intrinsic; creature-corruptibility is intrinsic.

docs.title: The King eternal, immortal, invisible — divine doxology
docs.text:
Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, [be] honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Pauline doxology interrupting the charge to Timothy. Three divine attributes: eternal (aionon), immortal (aphthartos), invisible (aoratos).

Notes: Aphtharto (G862, dative singular masculine) — God described as aphthartos (incorruptible/immortal). Used alongside monos (only) — the only wise God. This parallels 1 Tim 6:16 where God alone (monos) has athanasia. Two Pauline doxologies, both attributing immortality exclusively to God.

docs.title: Dead raised incorruptible — transformation at the last trumpet
docs.text:
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

Context: The mystery revealed (v.51): not all will sleep, but all will be changed. The resurrection occurs instantaneously at the last trumpet.

Notes: Aphthartoi (G862, nominative plural masculine) — the dead are raised incorruptible. This is a predicate adjective describing what the dead BECOME at resurrection, not what they currently are. The verb egerthesontai (future passive of egeiro) + aphthartoi = 'shall be raised incorruptible.' Change is instantaneous: en atomo (in an atom/indivisible moment).

docs.title: Corruptible crown vs. incorruptible crown — athlete metaphor
docs.text:
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they [do it] to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.

Context: Paul's athlete analogy. Athletic victors receive perishable laurel wreaths; believers pursue an imperishable reward.

Notes: Phtharton (G5349, corruptible) vs. aphtharton (G862, incorruptible). The believer's reward is a future possession — something obtained through striving, not presently worn.

docs.title: Inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, unfading — reserved in heaven
docs.text:
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,

Context: Peter's opening praise. The inheritance is described with triple negation: aphtharton (incorruptible), amiantos (undefiled), amarantos (unfading). It is reserved — not yet possessed.

Notes: Aphtharton (G862, accusative singular feminine) modifies kleronomian (inheritance). The inheritance is reserved (tetērēmenēn, perfect passive participle) in heaven — a future possession, not a present attribute of the soul.

docs.title: Born again of incorruptible seed — the word of God
docs.text:
Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.

Context: Peter contrasts corruptible and incorruptible seed. The word of God is the incorruptible seed of regeneration.

Notes: Phthartēs (G5349, genitive singular feminine, corruptible) vs. aphthartou (G862, genitive singular feminine, incorruptible) — modifying sporas (seed). Applied to the word of God, not to the human soul.

docs.title: The hidden person of the heart, in that which is not corruptible
docs.text:
But [let it be] the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, [even the ornament] of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.

Context: Peter's instruction on inner vs. outer adornment. The 'incorruptible' ornament is a meek and quiet spirit — a moral quality, not a statement about the soul's inherent immortality.

Notes: Aphtharto (G862, dative singular neuter) — applied to the spiritual quality of meekness, not to the soul as an entity. This is a character description, not an ontological statement.

docs.title: The soul that sinneth, it shall die — soul mortality stated
docs.text:
Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

Context: God's declaration of individual responsibility. All souls belong to God; the sinning soul will die. Repeated in v.20.

The nephesh is the subject of dying — not the body only, but the nephesh itself. The verb muth is the standard Hebrew verb for dying.

docs.title: The soul that sinneth, it shall die — restatement
docs.text:
The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

Context: Repetition of v.4's principle. The soul dies — individual responsibility.

Notes: Same construction as v.4. God reiterates: the soul that sins SHALL DIE. If the soul were inherently immortal, this statement would be misleading at best.

docs.title: God is able to DESTROY both soul and body in gehenna
docs.text:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: Jesus' instruction to the twelve. Human enemies can kill the body but not the soul; God can destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna.

The distinction is between human limitation (can kill body only) and divine power (can destroy the whole person).

docs.title: Man BECAME a living soul — the creation formula
docs.text:
And the LORD God formed man [of] the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

Context: The creation of man. Three elements: dust (material), breath of life (divine animation), living soul (the result). Man did not receive a soul; man BECAME a soul.

Neshamath chayyim (breath of life, H5397 + H2416) is the divine animating force breathed into the dust.

docs.title: Man barred from tree of life — immortality was not inherent
docs.text:
And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever: Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken. So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

Context: After the fall, God bars access to the tree of life. The purpose clause 'lest he live forever' (pen...wachay leolam) implies that without the tree of life, man will NOT live forever — immortality was not inherent.

The purpose clause reveals that God deliberately prevented Adam from accessing immortality after sin. If man already had an immortal soul, barring access to the tree of life would be pointless — he would live forever regardless.

docs.title: To him that overcometh — access to the tree of life as conditional reward
docs.text:
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.

Context: Promise to the Ephesian church. The tree of life reappears — access is conditional on overcoming. Echoes Gen 3:22-24.

Notes: The tree of life (to xylon tes zoes) — same concept as Genesis. Access is conditional: 'to him that overcometh.' Life remains a gift/reward, not an inherent possession.

docs.title: Wages of sin is death; gift of God is eternal life — the binary
docs.text:
For the wages of sin [is] death; but the gift of God [is] eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Context: Paul's climactic statement on sin and salvation. Two outcomes: death (opsonia = wages, military pay) vs. eternal life (charisma = free gift). No third option.

Notes: Opsonia (wages/payment) + hamartias (of sin) = thanatos (death). Charisma (free gift) + theou (of God) = zoe aionios (eternal life). The binary is exhaustive: wages of sin is death (not eternal conscious torment), and eternal life is a gift (not an inherent possession). Life comes through (en) Christ Jesus.

docs.title: Perish vs. have everlasting life — exhaustive alternatives
docs.text:
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

Context: Jesus' explanation of salvation to Nicodemus. The two alternatives: perish (apollymi, middle voice) or have (echo) everlasting life (zoen aionion).

Notes: Me apoletai (should not perish, aorist middle subjunctive of apollymi G622) vs. eche zoen aionion (have everlasting life). The alternatives are exhaustive — perishing or everlasting life. If all humans had immortal souls, 'perish' could not mean actual cessation; it would have to mean something else entirely.

docs.title: I GIVE them eternal life — life as Christ's gift
docs.text:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any [man] pluck them out of my hand.

Context: Jesus as the Good Shepherd. He gives (didomi, present active) eternal life to his sheep.

Notes: Didomi (I give, present active) + zoen aionion (eternal life). Life is given by Christ — not inherent. The sheep 'shall never perish' (ou me apolontai eis ton aiona) — double negative for emphasis.

docs.title: Power to give eternal life — divine authority over life
docs.text:
As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him. And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.

Context: Jesus' high priestly prayer. The Father gave the Son authority (exousia) to give eternal life. Life is defined as knowing God and Christ.

Notes: Exousia (authority/power) + didomi (give) + zoen aionion (eternal life). Life is under divine authority — given by the Father to the Son, then by the Son to believers. The definition of eternal life is relational: knowing (ginosko) the only true God and Jesus Christ.

docs.title: Life is in the Son — absolute negation of life apart from Christ
docs.text:
And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; [and] he that hath not the Son of God hath not life.

Context: John's summation. God gave (edoken, aorist active) eternal life. This life is located in (en) the Son. Having the Son = having life; not having the Son = not having life.

Notes: The absolute negation: 'he that hath not the Son of God hath not life' (ouk echei ten zoen). If all humans possessed inherent immortal souls, they would already have life apart from Christ — contradicting John's explicit statement.

docs.title: Eternal life as a promise — future expectation
docs.text:
And this is the promise that he hath promised us, [even] eternal life.

Context: John's exhortation to abide. Eternal life is a promise (epangelia) — something promised, not already possessed inherently.

Notes: Epangelia (promise) + zoe aionios (eternal life). A promise implies future fulfillment, not present inherent possession.

docs.title: In hope of eternal life, promised before the world began
docs.text:
In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began;

Context: Opening of Titus. Eternal life is the object of hope (elpis) and a divine promise (epaggello) from before time.

Notes: Ep' elpidi (upon/in hope) + zoes aioniou (of eternal life). Hope implies not-yet-realized possession. God promised eternal life before the ages — it is his to give, not inherent in human nature.

docs.title: The Father has life in himself — self-existent life as divine attribute
docs.text:
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life. Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live. For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself;

Context: Jesus' discourse on the Son's authority. The Father has life (zoe) 'in himself' (en heauto) — self-existent, underived life. This is then given (edoken) to the Son.

Notes: Hosper (just as) + ho pater echei zoen en heauto (the Father has life in himself) — the Father's life is self-existent. Edoken (aorist, gave) — the Son's self-existent life was given by the Father. Self-existent life is a divine attribute. Humans do not have life 'in themselves' — they receive it.

docs.title: Sow to Spirit, reap everlasting life — life as future harvest
docs.text:
For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.

Context: Paul's sowing/reaping metaphor. Two harvests: corruption (phthora, G5356) or everlasting life (zoe aionios).

Notes: Phthoran (corruption, G5356, accusative) vs. zoen aionion (life everlasting). Corruption is the natural outcome of the flesh; eternal life is the harvest of the Spirit. Life is a future reaping, not a present inherent possession.

docs.title: If God gathers spirit and breath, all flesh perishes — life depends on God
docs.text:
If he set his heart upon man, [if] he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath; All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust.

Context: Elihu's speech. If God withdrew his sustaining spirit and breath, all life would cease immediately.

  • יָשִׂ֣ים () — Verb.Qal.Impf.3ms — put
  • אֵלָ֣יו () — Prep.+3ms — to
  • לִבֹּ֑ו () — Noun.ms.Abs.+3ms — heart
  • רוּחֹ֥ו () — Noun.s.Abs.+3ms — wind
  • וְ֝ () — Conj.+NAN — and
  • נִשְׁמָתֹ֗ו () — Noun.fs.Abs.+3ms — breath
  • אֵלָ֥יו () — Prep.+3ms — to
  • יֶאֱסֹֽף () — Verb.Qal.Impf.3ms — gather

Notes: Rucho (his spirit, H7307 + 3ms suffix) + wenshmato (and his breath, H5397 + 3ms suffix) + elayv ye'esoph (unto himself he gathers, Qal imperfect of asaph H622). Yigwa' (expire, Qal imperfect of gawa H1478) + kol-basar (all flesh) + yachad (together). Adam (man) + al-aphar (unto dust) + yashub (shall return, Qal imperfect of shub H7725). Life is entirely dependent on God's sustaining breath — withdrawal means immediate death and return to dust. There is no surviving immortal component.

docs.title: Take away breath = death; send forth spirit = creation
docs.text:
Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust. Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth.

Context: Creation psalm. The cycle of life and death depends entirely on God's spirit/breath.

Notes: Toseph rucham (you take away their spirit/breath) = yigva'un (they expire) + we'el-apharam yeshubun (and to their dust they return). Teshalach ruchakha (you send forth your spirit) = yibbare'un (they are created). Life begins when God sends forth spirit; life ends when God withdraws spirit. No autonomous immortal soul persists.

docs.title: God gives to all life and breath — in him we live and move and have our being
docs.text:
Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things; And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

Context: Paul's Areopagus sermon. God is the source and sustainer of all life. Humans exist 'in him' — dependent, not autonomous.

Notes: Didous (giving, present active participle of didomi) + pasin zoen kai pnoen (to all life and breath). En auto zomen kai kinoumetha kai esmen (in him we live and move and have our being/exist). All human existence depends on God's ongoing sustaining. This is incompatible with inherent immortality — if humans had immortal souls, they would exist independently of God's sustaining power.

docs.title: Many that sleep in the dust shall awake — resurrection from death-sleep
docs.text:
And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame [and] everlasting contempt.

Context: Daniel's eschatological vision. The dead 'sleep' in the dust — resurrection is the awakening. Two outcomes: everlasting life or everlasting contempt.

Notes: Yeshene (sleeping, Qal participle of yashen H3463) + admath-aphar (dust of the ground) — the dead are sleeping in the dust. Yaqitsu (shall awake, Hiphil imperfect of quts H6974) — resurrection as awakening. If the dead had immortal conscious souls, calling their state 'sleep in the dust' would be misleading.

docs.title: The dead know not anything — unconsciousness in death
docs.text:
For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any [thing] that is done under the sun.

Context: Qoheleth's observation on death. The dead have no knowledge, no reward, no emotions, no participation in anything under the sun.

Notes: Hammetim enam yod'im me'umah (the dead know not anything). If the dead possessed conscious immortal souls, this statement would be false. Qoheleth describes total cessation of consciousness, activity, and emotion in death.

docs.title: No work, device, knowledge, wisdom in sheol — death as cessation
docs.text:
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do [it] with thy might; for [there is] no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.

Context: Qoheleth's exhortation to industry. Death is the end of all activity — sheol is a place of total inactivity.

Notes: 'Ein ma'aseh wecheshbon weda'ath wechokmah bishe'ol (no work, device, knowledge, wisdom in sheol). Comprehensive negation of any activity or consciousness in death. Consistent with soul mortality.

docs.title: His breath goeth forth, his thoughts perish — cessation of consciousness
docs.text:
His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

Context: Warning against trusting in human rulers. When a person dies (breath departs), their thoughts perish — that very day.

Notes: Tetse rucho (his spirit/breath goes out) + yashub le'admato (he returns to his earth/ground) + bayyom hahu (in that very day) + abdu eshtonotayv (his thoughts perish, Qal perfect of abad H6). The verb abad (perish/be lost) applied to thoughts at the moment of death — consciousness ceases when the breath departs.

docs.title: By man came death; by man came resurrection — Adam/Christ typology
docs.text:
For since by man [came] death, by man [came] also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.

Context: Paul's Adam/Christ parallel. Death entered through Adam; resurrection comes through Christ. The remedy for death is resurrection, not an already-immortal soul.

Notes: Di' anthropou thanatos (through man, death) vs. di' anthropou anastasis nekron (through man, resurrection of dead). The parallel is exact: the problem is death, the solution is resurrection. If humans already had immortal souls, resurrection would be unnecessary — the soul would survive death regardless.

docs.title: The last enemy destroyed is death — death as enemy, not gateway
docs.text:
The last enemy [that] shall be destroyed [is] death.

Context: Christ's eschatological victory. Death is the final enemy to be abolished (katargeo).

Notes: Eschatos echthros katargeitai ho thanatos (last enemy abolished [is] death). Death is called an 'enemy' — not a friend, not a gateway to immortal bliss. It is 'destroyed/abolished' (katargeo G2673, present passive — being rendered inoperative). If death were merely the liberation of an immortal soul from the body, calling it the last 'enemy' would be strange.

docs.title: We shall all be changed — transformation at the last trumpet
docs.text:
Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

Context: The mystery revealed: some believers will be alive at Christ's return and transformed without dying. The dead are raised incorruptible.

Notes: Allagesometha (we shall be changed, future passive of allasso G236). The transformation is a discrete event at the last trumpet — not a gradual process or an already-existing state.

docs.title: He will swallow up death in victory — OT promise of death's abolition
docs.text:
He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken [it].

Context: Isaiah's eschatological banquet vision. God will swallow up (bala') death (maveth) for victory (lanetsach). Quoted in 1 Cor 15:54.

Notes: Billa' hamaveth lanetsach (he has swallowed death forever/to victory). This is the OT background for Paul's 'death swallowed up in victory' (1 Cor 15:54). Death is to be destroyed, not perpetuated.

docs.title: Upholding all things by the word of his power — divine sustaining
docs.text:
Who being the brightness of [his] glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;

Context: The prologue to Hebrews. Christ upholds (phero, present active participle) all things (ta panta) by his powerful word.

Notes: Pheron (bearing/upholding, present active participle of phero G5342) + ta panta (all things) + to rhemati tes dynameos autou (by the word of his power). All things — including human life — are sustained by Christ's active power. If human souls were inherently immortal, they would not need sustaining.

docs.title: By him all things consist — Christ holds all together
docs.text:
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.

Context: Paul's Christological hymn. Christ is both temporally prior to and sustainer of all created reality.

Notes: Ta panta en auto synesteken (all things in him hold together, perfect active of synistemi G4921). Without Christ's sustaining power, all things — including human existence — would not hold together.

docs.title: Every living soul died in the sea — psyche dies
docs.text:
And the second angel poured out his vial upon the sea; and it became as the blood of a dead [man]: and every living soul died in the sea.

Context: Second bowl judgment. Every living soul (pasa psyche zosa) in the sea died.

Notes: Pasa psyche zosa apethanen (every living soul died). Psyche (G5590) is the subject of apethanen (died, aorist active of apothnesko G599). Souls die. This is a direct statement that psyche is mortal.

docs.title: Dead body (nephesh met) — nephesh used for corpses
docs.text:
Neither shall he go in to any dead body, nor defile himself for his father, or for his mother;

Context: Priestly holiness code. The high priest may not approach a dead body — literally 'dead souls' (nephesh met).

Notes: Nephesh met (H5315 + dead) — literally 'dead soul.' The word nephesh is used for corpses, proving that nephesh is not inherently immortal. A nephesh can be dead.

docs.title: Dead body (nephesh met) — Nazirite separation
docs.text:
All the days that he separateth [himself] unto the LORD he shall come at no dead body.

Context: Nazirite vow regulations. The Nazirite must not approach a dead body (nephesh met).

Notes: Al-nephesh met (unto/near a dead soul) — same construction as Lev 21:11. Nephesh used for a dead person/corpse. The 'soul' is the dead person, not a surviving conscious entity.

docs.title: Animals as nephesh chayyah — same term as for man in Gen 2:7
docs.text:
And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl [that] may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven. And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that [it was] good.

Context: Day 5 of creation. Sea creatures and birds called nephesh chayyah — the same term applied to man in Gen 2:7.

Notes: Nephesh chayyah (living soul/creature) — used for sea animals and birds. The same phrase describes man in Gen 2:7. Man does not receive a qualitatively different type of nephesh from animals in the creation account.

docs.title: If no resurrection, the dead in Christ are PERISHED — no hope without resurrection
docs.text:
Now if Christ be preached that he rose from the dead, how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: And if Christ be not risen, then [is] our preaching vain, and your faith [is] also vain. Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God; because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ: whom he raised not up, if so be that the dead rise not. For if the dead rise not, then is not Christ raised: And if Christ be not raised, your faith [is] vain; ye are yet in your sins. Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished. If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.

Context: Paul's reductio ad absurdum argument against denying the resurrection. Without resurrection: faith is vain, sins unforgiven, the dead in Christ have PERISHED.

Notes: V.18: apollonto (perished, aorist middle indicative of apollymi G622) — those fallen asleep in Christ have perished if there is no resurrection. If they had immortal souls already in God's presence, Paul could not say they have 'perished' — they would be alive in heaven regardless of resurrection. V.19: 'If in this life only we have hope' — the hope is resurrection, not disembodied survival.

docs.title: The endyo (put on) metaphor — acquisition across Paul
docs.text:
Rom 13:14: But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to [fulfil] the lusts [thereof]. Gal 3:27: For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. Eph 4:24: And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness. Eph 6:11: Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. Col 3:10: And have put on the new [man], which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him. Col 3:12: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering.

Context: Every Pauline use of endyo (G1746) describes acquiring/receiving something not previously possessed — clothing oneself with Christ, the new man, armor, virtues.

  • δεῖ (G1163) — V-PAI-3S — Pres Act Ind Sg thirdPers
  • γὰρ (G1063) — CONJ — τὸ ὁ G3588 [T-NSN] Nom Sg N
  • φθαρτὸν (G5349) — A-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • τοῦτο (G3778) — D-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • ἐνδύσασθαι (G1746) — V-AMN — Aor Mid Inf
  • ἀφθαρσίαν (G861) — N-ASF — Acc Sg F
  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — τὸ ὁ G3588 [T-NSN] Nom Sg N
  • θνητὸν (G2349) — A-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • ἀθανασίαν. (G110) — N-ASF — Acc Sg F

Notes: Endyo in Paul always means acquisition: put on Christ (Rom 13:14, Gal 3:27), put on the new man (Eph 4:24, Col 3:10), put on armor (Eph 6:11), put on virtues (Col 3:12). Never does endyo describe unveiling or revealing something already present. In 1 Cor 15:53-54, when the mortal must 'put on' (endyo) immortality, the consistent Pauline usage demands the acquisition reading — immortality is received, not revealed.

docs.title: Equal unto the angels; neither can they die any more — immortality as resurrection quality
docs.text:
But they which shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry, nor are given in marriage: Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection.

Context: Jesus' response to the Sadducees about resurrection. Those who attain the resurrection can no longer die — immortality is a quality of the resurrected state.

Notes: Oute apothanein eti dynantai (neither can they die any more). The inability to die (immortality) is a quality of the resurrection state — not of the present human condition. They become 'equal to angels' and 'children of God' through being 'children of the resurrection.' Without resurrection, they CAN die.

docs.title: Creation delivered from bondage of corruption — phthora as bondage
docs.text:
Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.

Context: Paul's cosmic eschatology. All creation groans under the bondage of corruption (phthora) and will be delivered at the revelation of God's children.

Notes: Douleias tes phthoras (bondage of corruption, G5356). Phthora here describes the universal condition of decay and mortality afflicting all creation since the fall. Deliverance from corruption parallels the resurrection transformation from mortal to immortal.

docs.title: Christ's body did not see corruption — diaphthora in messianic resurrection proof
docs.text:
Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.

Context: Peter's Pentecost sermon. David prophesied (Ps 16:10) that the Messiah's body would not undergo decay (diaphthora). Applied to Christ's resurrection.

Notes: Diaphthoran (G1312, corruption/decay) — Christ's body was preserved from decomposition because he was raised. David's body DID see corruption (Acts 13:36). The resurrection prevented physical decay. Diaphthora is used 6 times, all in Acts 2 and 13, all in the context of messianic resurrection proof.

docs.title: David saw corruption; Christ did not — diaphthora continued
docs.text:
And as concerning that he raised him up from the dead, [now] no more to return to corruption, he said on this wise, I will give you the sure mercies of David. Wherefore he saith also in another [psalm], Thou shalt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. For David, after he had served his own generation by the will of God, fell on sleep, and was laid unto his fathers, and saw corruption: But he, whom God raised again, saw no corruption.

Context: Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch. Same argument as Peter's in Acts 2. David fell asleep (ekoimēthē) and saw corruption; Christ was raised and did not see corruption.

Notes: Diaphthoran (G1312) used 4 times in vv.34-37. David ekoimēthē (fell asleep, aorist passive of koimao G2837) — death described as sleep. David's body decayed; Christ's was raised before decay. The contrast proves resurrection is bodily, not merely spiritual. Note the death-as-sleep vocabulary.

docs.title: Christ destroyed him who had the power of death — death as enemy defeated
docs.text:
Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.

Context: Christ's incarnation purpose. He shared human nature (flesh and blood) to destroy the devil's power of death and deliver those enslaved by death-fear.

Notes: Katargesei (render inoperative, aorist active subjunctive of katargeo G2673) + ton to kratos echonta tou thanatou (him having the power of death). Death is a power to be destroyed, not a friend. Christ took on flesh and blood (mortal nature) to defeat death through death. If humans had immortal souls, death-fear bondage would be irrational — they would know they could not truly die.

docs.title: The dead in Christ shall rise first — resurrection sequence
docs.text:
But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him. For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive [and] remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep. For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:

Context: Paul comforts the Thessalonians about dead believers. They are 'asleep' — the resurrection at Christ's coming is the hope, not present conscious existence in heaven.

Notes: Koimomenon (those sleeping, present passive participle of koimao G2837) — the dead are sleeping. If they were conscious in heaven, Paul's comfort would be 'they are alive with the Lord' — but his comfort is the coming resurrection. The dead in Christ 'shall rise first' (anastesontai proton) — they are currently dead, not alive in heaven.

docs.title: Dust returns to earth, spirit returns to God — dissolution, not immortal soul departing
docs.text:
Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

Context: Qoheleth's description of death. The body (dust) returns to earth; the spirit (ruach) returns to God who gave it.

Notes: Weharuach tashuv el-ha'elohim asher netanah (and the spirit returns to God who gave it). The ruach (spirit/breath) returns to God — this is the life-force, not a conscious immortal soul. God gave the ruach (Gen 2:7); at death it returns. This reverses the creation process: dust + breath = living soul; death reverses it.

docs.title: Death and hell cast into the lake of fire — the second death
docs.text:
And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Context: After the final judgment. Death and hades are destroyed — cast into the lake of fire, which IS the second death.

Notes: Ho thanatos kai ho hades (death and hades) are personified and destroyed. 'This is the second death' (houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin) — the lake of fire is identified as a second death, not as eternal living in torment.

docs.title: No more death — death abolished in the new creation
docs.text:
And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

Context: The new heaven and new earth. Death is abolished — it will no longer exist. This is the fulfillment of Isa 25:8 and 1 Cor 15:26.

Notes: Ho thanatos ouk estai eti (death shall not be any more). Death is abolished only in the new creation — not in the present age. Immortality is a future state, not a present possession.

docs.title: Right to the tree of life — conditional access
docs.text:
Blessed [are] they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.

Context: Epilogue of Revelation. Access to the tree of life is conditional on obedience — echoing Gen 3:22-24.

Notes: Hina estai he exousia auton epi to xylon tes zoes (that their authority/right may be upon the tree of life). Conditional access: those who do his commandments. The tree of life represents ongoing immortality from an external source, not inherent in human nature.

docs.title: I am alive for evermore — Christ holds the keys of death and hades
docs.text:
[I am] he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.

Context: Christ's self-identification in the opening vision. He died and is now alive forever, holding authority (keys) over death and hades.

Notes: Zon (living, present active participle of zao G2198) — Christ possesses life. Egenomen nekros (I became dead) — Christ truly died. Zon eimi eis tous aionas ton aionon (alive I am unto the ages of the ages) — Christ now possesses everlasting life. Christ holds the keys (authority) of death and hades — death is under his dominion.

docs.title: Athenian philosophers mocked resurrection — Greek immortal-soul believers rejected apostolic message
docs.text:
Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection. And they took him, and brought him unto Areopagus, saying, May we know what this new doctrine, whereof thou speakest, [is]? For thou bringest certain strange things to our ears: we would know therefore what these things mean. (For all the Athenians and strangers which were there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell, or to hear some new thing.) Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, [Ye] men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things; And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device. And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent: Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by [that] man whom he hath ordained; [whereof] he hath given assurance unto all [men], in that he hath raised him from the dead. And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this [matter].

Context: Paul's sermon at the Areopagus. Greek philosophers (Epicurean and Stoic) — who already accepted some form of soul immortality — mocked the resurrection. The apostolic message was resurrection-centered, not inherent-immortality-centered.

Notes: The Athenians mocked specifically when they heard of 'the resurrection of the dead' (v.32). Philosophers who already believed in soul immortality found bodily resurrection absurd — confirming that the Christian message was NOT soul immortality but resurrection of the whole person.

docs.title: The dead praise not the LORD — dead are silent
docs.text:
The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence.

Context: Psalm contrasting the living who bless God with the silent dead. The dead are in silence — no conscious activity.

Notes: Lo' hammetim yehallu-Yah — the dead do not praise Yah. If the dead had conscious immortal souls in God's presence, they would certainly praise him. Their silence indicates unconsciousness.

docs.title: Thou shalt surely die — death as penalty for sin
docs.text:
But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.

Context: God's command and warning to Adam. The penalty for eating the forbidden fruit is death — moth tamuth (dying you shall die), emphatic construction.

Notes: Moth tamuth (dying you shall die) — infinitive absolute + imperfect of muth (H4191), the strongest possible expression of certainty. Death was introduced as the consequence of sin, not as the natural state. If Adam had an immortal soul, the threat of death would be empty.

docs.title: No remembrance of God in death — cessation of relationship
docs.text:
For in death [there is] no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?

Context: David's plea for deliverance from death. Death is characterized by absence of memory and thanksgiving — no conscious activity.

Notes: Ki ein bammaveth zikhrekha (for there is no remembrance of thee in death). If the dead had conscious immortal souls, they would remember and thank God. David's argument for deliverance depends on death being a state of unconsciousness.

docs.title: Not leave my soul in sheol — messianic resurrection hope
docs.text:
For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence [is] fulness of joy; at thy right hand [there are] pleasures for evermore.

Context: Messianic psalm quoted by Peter in Acts 2:27,31. The psalmist's hope is not disembodied survival but resurrection — not being left in sheol, not seeing corruption.

Notes: Lo'-ta'azob napshi lish'ol (you will not abandon my soul to sheol). The hope is resurrection from sheol, not escape of an immortal soul FROM sheol. Quoted in Acts 2:27,31 as proof of Christ's bodily resurrection — his flesh did not see corruption (diaphthora).

docs.title: Man lieth down and riseth not till heavens be no more — resurrection hope
docs.text:
So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens [be] no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep. O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me! If a man die, shall he live [again]? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands.

Context: Job's meditation on death and the hope of future restoration. Death is sleep from which there is no waking until the appointed time. Job asks the fundamental question: 'If a man die, shall he live again?'

Notes: V.12: lo'-yaqitsu welo'-ye'oru mishenatam (they shall not awake nor be raised from their sleep) — death is sleep, unconsciousness. V.14: im-yamuth geber hayichyeh (if a man die, shall he live?) — the question presupposes that death is real, not just bodily while the soul lives on. V.15: tiqra' wa'anokhi e'enekka (you shall call and I will answer) — the hope is future resurrection at God's call, not present disembodied consciousness.

docs.title: In my flesh shall I see God — bodily resurrection hope
docs.text:
For I know [that] my redeemer liveth, and [that] he shall stand at the latter [day] upon the earth: And [though] after my skin [worms] destroy this [body], yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; [though] my reins be consumed within me.

Context: Job's declaration of faith in a future redeemer. His hope is to see God 'in my flesh' — bodily resurrection, not disembodied immortality.

Notes: Umibbesari echezeh Eloah (and from my flesh I shall behold God). Job's hope is explicitly embodied — he expects to see God in/from his flesh, with his own eyes. This is resurrection hope, not the hope of a disembodied immortal soul.

docs.title: Ransom from the power of the grave — redemption from death
docs.text:
I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction: repentance shall be hid from mine eyes.

Context: God's promise of redemption from death and sheol. Quoted/alluded to in 1 Cor 15:55. Death and the grave are enemies to be overcome.

Notes: Miyad she'ol epha'dem mimaveth eg'alem (from the hand of sheol I will ransom them, from death I will redeem them). Ehi devareyikha maveth ehi qatabkha she'ol (where are your plagues, O death? where is your destruction, O sheol?). Death is personified as an enemy from which God will redeem. Paul adapts this in 1 Cor 15:55.

docs.title: If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection — resurrection as goal
docs.text:
That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death; If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead.

Context: Paul's personal aspiration. The resurrection of the dead is the goal — not presupposed as automatic but something to be attained.

Notes: Ei pos katanteso eis ten exanastasin ten ek nekron (if somehow I may attain to the out-resurrection from the dead). Paul uses exanastasis (G1815) — only here in the NT — a strengthened form of anastasis. If Paul already had an immortal soul guaranteed to survive death, 'attaining' the resurrection would be unnecessary.

docs.title: Change our vile body — body transformation at Christ's coming
docs.text:
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.

Context: Paul's expectation of bodily transformation at Christ's return. The body of humiliation (to soma tes tapeinoseos) is changed to conform to Christ's glorious body.

Notes: Metaschematizei (will transform) + to soma tes tapeinoseos hemon (the body of our humiliation). The transformation is future, at Christ's coming. The hope is bodily transformation, not soul release from the body.

docs.title: Made to be taken and destroyed — destruction language for the wicked
docs.text:
But these, as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed, speak evil of the things that they understand not; and shall utterly perish in their own corruption;

Context: Peter's condemnation of false teachers. They shall perish (phtheiro) in their own corruption (phthora) — language of destruction, not eternal conscious torment.

Notes: En te phthora auton kai phtharesontai (in their corruption they also shall be corrupted/destroyed). Phthora (G5356, corruption) and phtheiro (G5351, to corrupt/destroy) from the same root. The wicked perish in their own corruption — the same corruption/decay vocabulary that is contrasted with aphtharsia (incorruption) in the immortality passages.

docs.title: Raise him up at the last day — resurrection as the mechanism of eternal life
docs.text:
And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day. And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.

Context: Jesus' bread of life discourse. Eternal life is connected to being raised 'at the last day' — four times in this discourse (vv.39,40,44,54).

Notes: Anasteso auto en te eschate hemera (I will raise it/him up at the last day). The mechanism for receiving eternal life is resurrection at the last day — not immediate possession of an immortal soul. Jesus repeats this phrase four times for emphasis.

docs.title: I am the resurrection and the life — life inseparable from Christ and resurrection
docs.text:
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?

Context: Jesus' declaration to Martha before raising Lazarus. Life is identified with Christ himself AND with resurrection — not as an inherent human quality.

Notes: Ego eimi he anastasis kai he zoe (I am the resurrection and the life). Jesus does not say 'I am the immortality of the soul' but 'I am the resurrection and the life.' Life and resurrection are inseparable — life comes through resurrection, not through an inherent immortal soul. The believer who dies 'shall live' (zesetai, future) — through resurrection.

docs.title: David's flesh rested in hope — messianic resurrection, not disembodied soul survival
docs.text:
Therefore did my heart rejoice, and my tongue was glad; moreover also my flesh shall rest in hope: Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. Thou hast made known to me the ways of life; thou shalt make me full of joy with thy countenance. Men [and] brethren, let me freely speak unto you of the patriarch David, that he is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day. Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne; He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.

Context: Peter's Pentecost sermon quoting Psalm 16. David is 'both dead and buried' (v.29) — not alive in heaven. The prophecy is about Christ's resurrection, not David's present conscious survival.

Notes: Peter explicitly states David is 'dead and buried' and his tomb is with them (v.29). David prophesied about Christ's resurrection, not about his own immortal soul. The soul (psyche) was not left in hades, and the flesh did not see corruption (diaphthora) — both soul and body language refers to resurrection, not to disembodied survival.

docs.title: O death where is thy sting — victory over death through Christ
docs.text:
O death, where [is] thy sting? O grave, where [is] thy victory? The sting of death [is] sin; and the strength of sin [is] the law. But thanks [be] to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Context: Triumphant conclusion of Paul's resurrection argument. Quoting/adapting Hos 13:14. Victory over death comes through Christ, not through inherent immortality.

Notes: Pou sou, thanate, to kentron? pou sou, hade, to nikos? (where, O death, is your sting? where, O hades, is your victory?). The victory is God's gift through Christ (v.57). Death is mocked ONLY because of the resurrection — without resurrection, death would have the final word (cf. vv.12-19).

docs.title: Promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come
docs.text:
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.

Context: Paul's instruction to Timothy on the value of godliness. Life — both present and future — is a promise (epangelia), not an inherent possession.

Notes: Epangelian echousa zoes tes nyn kai tes mellouses (having promise of life, the present and the coming). Life is described as a promise — both present and future. The 'life to come' is not presupposed as already possessed through an immortal soul.

docs.title: God will redeem my soul from the power of sheol
docs.text:
None [of them] can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him: (For the redemption of their soul [is] precious, and it ceaseth for ever:) That he should still live for ever, [and] not see corruption. Like sheep they are laid in the grave; death shall feed on them; and the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning; and their beauty shall consume in the grave from their dwelling. But God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me. Selah.

Context: Psalm contrasting human inability to redeem from death with God's power. No human can pay a ransom to avoid death (vv.7-9), but God will redeem the psalmist's soul from sheol's power (v.15).

Notes: V.7-9: No human can ransom another or pay God enough to live forever. V.14: Death feeds on the wicked — they are consumed. V.15: Ak-Elohim yiph'deh napshi miyad-she'ol (but God will redeem my soul from the hand/power of sheol). The hope is divine redemption from death, not inherent survival of death.

docs.title: Thy dead men shall live — OT resurrection promise
docs.text:
Thy dead [men] shall live, [together with] my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew [is as] the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead.

Context: Isaiah's eschatological vision. The dead will live, arise, awake from the dust — resurrection language, not disembodied survival.

Notes: Yichyu metheyikha (your dead shall live) + nevelati yequmun (my dead body shall arise) + haqitsu weranenu shokhenei aphar (awake and sing, dwellers in dust). The dead are in the dust (like Gen 3:19) and will arise from it. This is bodily resurrection, not the continuation of immortal souls.

docs.title: The wicked shall be cut off; the wicked shall not be — cessation of existence
docs.text:
For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the LORD, they shall inherit the earth. For yet a little while, and the wicked [shall] not [be]: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it [shall] not [be].

Context: David's contrast between the righteous and the wicked. The wicked will cease to exist — they 'shall not be' and their place will be empty.

Notes: We'od me'at we'ein rasha' (yet a little while and there is no wicked one). Wehithbonanta al-meqomo we'einennu (and you consider his place and he is not). The wicked cease to exist — they are 'not.' Their very place is empty. This is cessation, not eternal conscious torment.

docs.title: Wicked as stubble, ashes under feet — destruction imagery
docs.text:
For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do [this], saith the LORD of hosts.

Context: Malachi's eschatological prophecy. The wicked are burned up completely — stubble consumed, leaving neither root nor branch. They become ashes underfoot.

Notes: V.1: wehayah lahem qash (they shall be stubble) + welibat otam (and it shall burn them up) + lo'-ya'azob lahem shoresh we'anaph (it shall leave them neither root nor branch). V.3: ki-yihyu epher tachath kappoth ragleykhem (for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet). The imagery is total consumption — the wicked are reduced to ashes. This is incompatible with eternal conscious torment but consistent with conditional immortality.

docs.title: Eat and not die — life through Christ's provision, not inherent
docs.text:
This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.

Context: Jesus' bread of life discourse continued. Life depends on eating the bread from heaven — an external provision, not an inherent quality.

Notes: Hina tis ex autou phage kai me apothane (that a man may eat of it and not die). Ean tis phage ek toutou tou artou zesei eis ton aiona (if anyone eat of this bread he shall live forever). Life forever depends on partaking of Christ — it is conditional and externally provided, not inherent in human nature.

docs.title: Clothing metaphor — clothed upon, not unclothed
docs.text:
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked. For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit.

Context: Paul discusses the resurrection body. He does not want disembodiment (unclothed) but transformation (clothed upon). V.5 identifies God as the one who has prepared this transformation and given the Spirit as guarantee.

Notes: Supporting verse added for compliance. Full range includes v.5 which adds the divine initiative and Spirit-guarantee elements.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Who possesses immortality? Is the soul inherently immortal or is immortality a divine gift? Examine athanasia (G110), aphtharsia (G861), thnetos (G2349).

docs.title: 1 Timothy 6:15-16
docs.text:
Context: Paul's doxological climax in his charge to Timothy. This is a formal declaration of God's attributes — part of a creedal formula listing exclusive divine characteristics.

Direct statement: God alone (monos) has immortality (athanasia). He dwells in unapproachable light. No man has seen him or can see him.

Original language: The Greek parsing shows monos (G3441, Nom Sg M) + echon (G2192, Present Active Participle, Nom Sg M) + athanasiān (G110, Acc Sg F). The present active participle echon describes ongoing, continuous possession. Monos functions as an attributive adjective — "the only one having." Athanasia is the direct object of echon — immortality is what God possesses. The construction is an exclusive attribution: monos + participle = "the one who alone does X."

Cross-references: 1 Tim 1:17 parallels this doxology — the King eternal, immortal (aphthartos, G862), invisible, the only (monos) wise God. Two independent doxologies from the same author attribute immortality/incorruptibility exclusively to God using monos. John 17:3 uses monos for "the only true God." Jude 25 uses mono for "the only wise God." In every doxological use of monos with a divine attribute, the exclusivity is unqualified.

Relationship to other evidence: This is the crux text for the entire study. If God alone has immortality, then no creature — including the human soul — possesses it inherently. Every other passage about immortality must be read in light of this exclusive attribution. The question is whether monos admits the qualification "self-existent vs. derived." The text contains no such qualifier; adding it requires importing a concept not present in the verse.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:42-44
docs.text:
Context: Paul's resurrection argument, answering "with what body do they come?" (v.35). He uses seed/harvest and celestial/terrestrial analogies before stating four paired contrasts between the present and resurrection bodies.

Direct statement: The present body is sown in corruption, dishonor, weakness, as a natural body. It is raised in incorruption, glory, power, as a spiritual body.

Original language: Phthora (G5356) is paired with aphtharsia (G861) as antonyms. The body is characterized by corruption (decay, mortality) in its present state and by incorruption (un-decay) in its resurrection state.

Cross-references: The corruption/incorruption pairing in v.42 is expanded in vv.53-54 where phthartos/aphtharsia and thnetos/athanasia run in parallel. The four contrasts build toward the climax: the mortal must put on immortality.

Relationship to other evidence: Establishes that the present human condition is one of corruption — decay, mortality, weakness. Transformation is required. The body is not currently incorruptible; it must become so.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:50
docs.text:
Context: Transitional verse between Paul's resurrection body argument (vv.35-49) and the mystery of transformation (vv.51-54).

Direct statement: Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God. Corruption cannot inherit incorruption.

Original language: Phthora (G5356, corruption) and aphtharsia (G861, incorruption) stand in absolute opposition. The present corruptible state is incompatible with the kingdom.

Cross-references: This reinforces vv.42-44 and sets up vv.53-54. The logic is: (1) the present body is corrupt, (2) corruption cannot enter the kingdom, therefore (3) transformation is necessary — immortality must be acquired.

Relationship to other evidence: Directly opposes any claim that immortality is presently possessed. If it were, the incompatibility problem would not exist.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:53-54
docs.text:
Context: The climax of Paul's resurrection chapter. The "mystery" (v.51) is now stated: not all will die, but all will be changed.

Direct statement: This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. When this happens, the prophecy of Isaiah 25:8 is fulfilled: "Death is swallowed up in victory."

Original language: The parsing confirms two parallel pairs: phtharton (G5349, Nom Sg N, corruptible) + aphtharsian (G861, Acc Sg F, incorruption) and thneton (G2349, Nom Sg N, mortal) + athanasiān (G110, Acc Sg F, immortality). The verb endysasthai (G1746, Aorist Middle Infinitive) in v.53 means "to clothe oneself with." In v.54, endysetai shifts to Aorist Middle Subjunctive. Thneton is used substantivally — "this mortal" (touto to thneton), not restricted to "this mortal body."

The verb endyo across Paul's letters always means acquisition of something not previously worn: put on Christ (Rom 13:14, Gal 3:27), put on the new man (Eph 4:24, Col 3:10), put on armor (Eph 6:11), put on virtues (Col 3:12). It never means unveiling or revealing something already present.

Cross-references: Death is "swallowed up" (katepothe, G2666, Aorist Passive) quoting Isaiah 25:8. The OT promise and the NT fulfillment agree: death will be destroyed, not perpetuated.

Relationship to other evidence: This passage makes the case for acquisition most directly. The mortal does not already have immortality; it must put it on. The verb of acquisition and the future tense both point to something not yet possessed.

docs.title: Romans 2:7
docs.text:
Context: Paul describing God's impartial judgment. Those who by patient well-doing seek glory, honor, and immortality receive eternal life.

Direct statement: Immortality (aphtharsia) is something humans seek. Eternal life is the reward for seeking it.

Original language: Zetousin (G2212, Present Active Participle, Dat Pl M) — "seeking." The present tense indicates ongoing seeking. Aphtharsian (G861, Acc Sg F) is the object of seeking, listed alongside doxan (glory) and timen (honor) as future rewards. Zoen aionion (eternal life, Acc Sg F) is the result.

Cross-references: The seeking implies present non-possession. You do not seek what you already have. This parallels 1 Cor 15:53-54 where immortality is acquired, not revealed.

Relationship to other evidence: Consistent with 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has it) and 1 Cor 15:53-54 (mortals must put it on). If immortality were inherent, seeking it would be nonsensical.

docs.title: 2 Timothy 1:10
docs.text:
Context: Paul describes Christ's appearing and its twofold effect.

Direct statement: Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality (aphtharsia) to light through the gospel.

Original language: Katargesantos (G2673, Aorist Active Participle, Gen Sg M — "having abolished/rendered inoperative") + thanaton (death). Photisantos (G5461, Aorist Active Participle, Gen Sg M — "having brought to light") + zoen (life) + aphtharsian (incorruption). Christ's double action: death abolished, life and immortality illuminated.

Cross-references: The verb photizo means to illuminate, reveal, make visible. Christ did not create immortality ex nihilo; he revealed what was previously hidden and made it available through the gospel.

Relationship to other evidence: Christ's gospel reveals immortality — it is available through him. This aligns with the gift/promise pattern (Rom 6:23, 1 John 2:25, Tit 1:2).

docs.title: Romans 6:12
docs.text:
Context: Paul's ethical exhortation following the death-to-sin argument (Rom 6:1-11).

Direct statement: Do not let sin reign in your mortal (thnetos) body.

Original language: Thneto (G2349, Dat Sg N) modifies somati (body). Paul describes the present human body as mortal — subject to death.

Cross-references: Paul does not mention an immortal soul alongside the mortal body. The mortal body is the arena of sin because mortality and sin are linked (Rom 5:12).

Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the present human condition as mortal. Paul has no concept of a mortal body housing an immortal soul.

docs.title: Romans 8:11
docs.text:
Context: Paul's Spirit-life argument. The indwelling Spirit guarantees future vivification.

Direct statement: The Spirit that raised Jesus will also "make alive" (zoopoieo) the believers' mortal bodies.

Original language: Zoopoiesei (G2227, Future Active Indicative, Sg 3rd — "will make alive") + ta thneta somata (the mortal bodies, G2349 Acc Pl N + G4983 Acc Pl N). The vivification is future tense — not yet accomplished. The mortal bodies await transformation.

Cross-references: The Spirit's indwelling is the guarantee (cf. 2 Cor 5:5, Eph 1:14), not the fulfillment. Present: mortal bodies. Future: made alive.

Relationship to other evidence: Consistent with 1 Cor 15:53-54. The mortal body must be made alive — transformation is future.

docs.title: 2 Corinthians 4:11
docs.text:
Context: Paul's treasure-in-earthen-vessels argument. The apostolic paradox: continual dying so that divine life is displayed.

Direct statement: The life of Jesus is made manifest in "our mortal flesh" (thnete sarki).

Original language: Thnete (G2349, Dat Sg F) modifies sarki (flesh, feminine). Present condition: mortal flesh. Divine life is manifested through the mortal vessel, not because the vessel is immortal.

Cross-references: Parallels Rom 6:12 (mortal body) and Rom 8:11 (mortal bodies). All three use thnetos to describe the present human condition.

Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces the pattern: humans are mortal now; immortality is future.

docs.title: 2 Corinthians 5:1-5
docs.text:
Context: Paul's extended clothing metaphor. The earthly tent (mortal body) vs. the heavenly building (resurrection body).

Direct statement: Paul does not want to be unclothed (die, become disembodied) but clothed upon (transformed). Mortality is swallowed up by life. God has prepared this and given the Spirit as the guarantee.

Original language: Ependyomai (G1902, "clothed upon") in vv.2,4 describes super-addition — putting on the resurrection body over the mortal body, i.e., transformation without death. Ekdysasthai (G1562, "to unclothe") = death/disembodiment. To thneton (the mortal, G2349, Nom Sg N, substantival) + katapothe (swallowed up) + hypo zoes (by life).

Cross-references: The clothing metaphor connects to 1 Cor 15:53-54 (endyo = put on). Paul rejects the intermediate disembodied state as desirable — he wants transformation, not escape from the body.

Relationship to other evidence: Paul's anthropology is holistic. He does not want soul-release from the body; he wants the mortal to be swallowed up by life. This is resurrection theology, not immortal-soul theology.

docs.title: Ephesians 6:24
docs.text:
Context: Closing benediction of Ephesians.

Direct statement: Grace with all who love the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity (aphtharsia).

Original language: En aphtharsia (in incorruption/sincerity, Dative) — ethical/metaphorical use. Not about physical immortality but about genuineness of love.

Cross-references: One of two ethical uses of aphtharsia (with Tit 2:7). Demonstrates that aphtharsia's core meaning is "un-decay" — applied physically to the resurrection body and metaphorically to moral character.

Relationship to other evidence: Shows aphtharsia has a range of meaning, but its physical usage (resurrection, immortality) is the dominant one (6 of 8 occurrences). Ethical uses do not affect the immortality argument.

docs.title: Titus 2:7
docs.text:
Context: Paul's instructions to Titus about sound doctrine.

Direct statement: In doctrine showing uncorruptness (aphtharsia).

Original language: Aphtharsian — ethical sense. Doctrine that is not decayed or corrupted.

Cross-references: Second ethical use of aphtharsia (with Eph 6:24).

Relationship to other evidence: Same as Eph 6:24 — ethical metaphor, not relevant to the physical immortality question.

docs.title: Romans 1:23
docs.text:
Context: Paul's indictment of pagan idolatry.

Direct statement: Humans exchanged the glory of the incorruptible (aphthartos) God for images of corruptible (phthartos) man and animals.

Original language: Aphthartos (G862, Gen Sg M) modifies theou (God). Phthartos (G5349) describes man, birds, beasts — all creatures are corruptible. The contrast is Creator (aphthartos) vs. creature (phthartos).

Cross-references: God's incorruptibility is intrinsic; creature-corruptibility is intrinsic. This parallels 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has immortality) and 1 Tim 1:17 (God as aphthartos).

Relationship to other evidence: Establishes a binary: God is incorruptible; created things (including humans) are corruptible. Humans are classified on the creature side.

docs.title: 1 Timothy 1:17
docs.text:
Context: Pauline doxology.

Direct statement: The King eternal, immortal (aphthartos), invisible, the only wise God.

Original language: Aphtharto (G862, Dat Sg M) — God described as aphthartos. Used alongside monos (only).

Cross-references: Parallels 1 Tim 6:16. Two Pauline doxologies, both attributing immortality/incorruptibility exclusively to God with the qualifier "only."

Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces that immortality is a divine attribute. Paul consistently links immortality/incorruptibility to God, not to humans.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:52
docs.text:
Context: The mystery revealed — transformation at the last trumpet.

Direct statement: The dead shall be raised incorruptible (aphthartoi), and we shall be changed.

Original language: Aphthartoi (G862, Nom Pl M) — predicate adjective describing what the dead become at resurrection. Egerthesontai (Future Passive) = "shall be raised." The dead become incorruptible; they are not incorruptible already.

Cross-references: Links directly to vv.53-54. Incorruptibility is a quality of the resurrection state, acquired at the transformation.

Relationship to other evidence: The dead must be raised incorruptible — this is a change in their state, not a continuation of it.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 9:25
docs.text:
Context: Paul's athlete analogy.

Direct statement: Athletes compete for a corruptible (phthartos) crown; believers pursue an incorruptible (aphthartos) one.

Original language: Phtharton (G5349, corruptible) vs. aphtharton (G862, incorruptible). The believer's crown is future — obtained through striving, not presently worn.

Cross-references: The corruptible/incorruptible contrast mirrors the mortal/immortal contrast in 1 Cor 15:53-54.

Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces the acquisition pattern — the incorruptible crown is future, not present.

docs.title: 1 Peter 1:4
docs.text:
Context: Peter's opening praise.

Direct statement: An inheritance incorruptible (aphthartos), undefiled, unfading — reserved in heaven.

Original language: Aphtharton (G862, Acc Sg F) modifies kleronomian (inheritance). The inheritance is reserved (teteremenēn, Perfect Passive Participle) — not yet possessed but kept in heaven.

Cross-references: The "reserved in heaven" language shows this is a future possession, not a present attribute of the soul.

Relationship to other evidence: Consistent with the acquisition/future pattern: immortality and incorruptibility belong to the resurrection and the inheritance, not to the present human condition.

docs.title: 1 Peter 1:23
docs.text:
Context: Peter contrasts corruptible and incorruptible seed.

Direct statement: Born again of incorruptible (aphthartos) seed — the word of God.

Original language: Phthartēs (G5349, Gen Sg F, corruptible) vs. aphthartou (G862, Gen Sg F, incorruptible) — modifying sporas (seed). Applied to the word of God, not to the human soul.

Cross-references: The word of God is the incorruptible source of regeneration.

Relationship to other evidence: Aphthartos is applied to God's word, not to the human soul. The soul is not called incorruptible.

docs.title: 1 Peter 3:4
docs.text:
Context: Peter's instruction on inner vs. outer adornment.

Direct statement: Let the hidden person of the heart be adorned with the incorruptible (aphthartos) ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.

Original language: Aphtharto (G862, Dat Sg N) — applied to a spiritual quality (meekness), not to the soul as an entity. This is a character description, not an ontological statement about the soul's nature.

Cross-references: This is the closest any passage comes to applying aphthartos to something internal in a human being, but the referent is a moral quality (meekness), not the soul itself.

Relationship to other evidence: Does not support inherent soul immortality. The "incorruptible" quality described is a character trait, not the soul's substance.

docs.title: Ezekiel 18:4
docs.text:
Context: God's declaration of individual responsibility. All souls belong to God.

Direct statement: The soul (nephesh) that sins shall die (tamut).

Original language: The parsing confirms: hannephesh (the soul, H5315 with article) + hachote't (the sinning one, Qal Participle of chata H2398, fs) + hi' (she/it, 3fs pronoun) + tamut (shall die, Qal Imperfect 3fs of muth H4191). The nephesh is the grammatical subject of dying. Muth is the standard Hebrew verb for dying — the same verb used for physical death throughout the OT.

Cross-references: Repeated in v.20. Directly contradicts the claim that the soul is inherently immortal. If the soul cannot die, this statement is false.

Relationship to other evidence: This is one of the most direct statements in Scripture against soul immortality. The soul dies. Combined with Matt 10:28 (God can destroy soul and body), the biblical picture is that the soul is mortal.

docs.title: Ezekiel 18:20
docs.text:
Context: Restatement of v.4's principle.

Direct statement: The soul that sins shall die.

Original language: Same construction as v.4. God reiterates the principle.

Cross-references: The repetition underscores the point. This is not a passing comment but a deliberate theological assertion made twice in the same chapter.

Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces v.4.

docs.title: Matthew 10:28
docs.text:
Context: Jesus instructing the twelve disciples before sending them out.

Direct statement: Fear not those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear God, who is able to destroy (apollymi) both soul (psyche) and body in gehenna.

Original language: Apolesai (G622, Aorist Active Infinitive — "to destroy") + kai psychen kai soma (both soul and body) + en geenne (in gehenna). The verb apollymi with God as agent and in active voice means destruction. God's ability to destroy the psyche is stated explicitly.

Cross-references: The distinction is between human limitation (can kill body only) and divine power (can destroy the whole person). If the soul were inherently immortal, God's ability to "destroy" it would need redefining to mean something other than destruction.
