  • Μή (G3361) — PRT-N — μου ἐγώ G1473 [P-1GS] Gen Sg
  • ἅπτου, (G680) — V-PMM-2S — Pres Mid Impv Sg secondPers
  • οὔπω (G3768) — ADV-N — γὰρ γάρ G1063 [CONJ]
  • ἀναβέβηκα (G305) — V-RAI-1S — Perf Act Ind Sg firstPers
  • πρὸς (G4314) — PREP — τὸν ὁ G3588 [T-ASM] Acc Sg M
  • Πατέρα· (G3962) — N-ASM — Acc Sg M
  • πορεύου (G4198) — V-PNM-2S — Pres M/P Impv Sg secondPers
  • δὲ (G1161) — CONJ — πρὸς πρός G4314 [PREP]
  • τοὺς (G3588) — T-APM — Acc Pl M
  • ἀδελφούς (G80) — N-APM — Acc Pl M
  • μου (G1473) — P-1GS — Gen Sg
  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — εἰπὲ λέγω G3004 [V-2AAM-2S] Aor Act Impv Sg secondPers
  • ὑμῶν (G4771) — P-2GP — Gen Pl

Notes: Greek: oupo (G3768, not yet, ADV-N) gar (for) anababeka (G305, Perf Act Ind 1s of anabaino = I have ascended) pros ton Patera (to the Father). The perfect tense anababeka indicates a state resulting from a completed action — and Jesus says this state has NOT YET occurred. If paradise = the Father's presence (2 Cor 12:2-4, Rev 2:7), Jesus was not there on Friday. This makes the traditional reading of Luke 23:43 impossible — Jesus could not have been 'in paradise' on the day of crucifixion.

docs.title: Crown of righteousness given 'at that day' — not at death
docs.text:
For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished [my] course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.

Context: Paul's final letter, written facing imminent death. Despite anticipating death, Paul places his reward 'at that day' — the day of Christ's appearing (epiphaneia G2015), not the day of his death.

Notes: Greek: apodosei (G591, Fut Act Ind 3s of apodidomi = will give) moi (to me) ho kurios (the Lord) en ekeine te hemera (on that day). The crown is given 'at that day' — and the qualifying phrase is 'but unto all them also that love his appearing (epiphaneian, G2015 Acc Sg F).' The reward comes at the appearing/coming of Christ, not at individual death. If Paul expected immediate heavenly bliss at death, why specify 'that day' as the future moment of reward?

docs.title: Paul seeks resurrection — same letter as Phil 1:23
docs.text:
That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death; If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead.

Context: Paul's aspiration in the SAME LETTER as Phil 1:23 ('to depart and be with Christ'). He strives to 'attain unto the resurrection' — why seek resurrection if he would already be with Christ at death?

Notes: Greek: ten exanastasin (G1815, Acc Sg F = the out-resurrection) ten ek nekron (the one from among dead ones). Paul uses the rare compound exanastasis (only here in NT) to emphasize bodily resurrection from among the dead. This is in the same letter where he speaks of 'departing to be with Christ' — demonstrating that being 'with Christ' and 'resurrection' are the same event from Paul's perspective.

docs.title: Saviour from heaven shall change our body — future transformation
docs.text:
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.

Context: Still in the same letter as Phil 1:23. Paul looks for (apekdechometha = eagerly await) the Saviour FROM heaven, who SHALL CHANGE (metaschematizo, Fut Act Ind 3s) our body. Transformation is future, at the coming of Christ.

Notes: This is the same Paul, in the same letter, who said 'to depart and be with Christ.' Here he clarifies: being with Christ involves the future transformation of the body at Christ's coming from heaven. The hope is resurrection and transformation, not disembodied intermediate existence.

docs.title: Tree of life barred — immortality is not inherent; man must eat
docs.text:
And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever: Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken. So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

Context: After the fall, God bars access to the tree of life to prevent man from living forever in a sinful state. The cherubim and flaming sword guard the way. This implies immortality was conditional on eating from the tree, not inherent in human nature.

Notes: The phrase 'lest he...take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever' (pen-yishlach yado velaqach gam meetz hachayyim veakhal vachai leolam) proves immortality was not inherent. Man needed the tree of life to live forever. Being barred from it meant death was certain. This is foundational to conditional immortality.

docs.title: Death as rest — kings, princes, servants all quiet and still in death
docs.text:
For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest, With kings and counsellers of the earth, which built desolate places for themselves; Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver: Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants [which] never saw light. There the wicked cease [from] troubling; and there the weary be at rest. [There] the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor. The small and great are there; and the servant [is] free from his master.

Context: Job, lamenting his birth, describes what death would have been like. Death is portrayed as rest, quiet, sleep — a state where all distinctions (king/servant, wicked/weary, prisoner/free) cease. The dead 'hear not the voice of the oppressor' — absence of perception.

Notes: Key vocabulary: shakabti (I would have lain down, from shakab H7901), shenah (sleep), nuwach (rest H5117). V.17: 'the wicked cease (chadal) from troubling (rogez)' — cessation of activity. V.18: 'they hear not (lo shamu) the voice of the oppressor' — explicit absence of hearing/perception. V.19: 'the servant is free (chophshi) from his master' — liberation through cessation, not through conscious reward.

docs.title: He that goes down to sheol shall come up no more; shall not return to his house
docs.text:
[As] the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away: so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no [more]. He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more.

Context: Job compares human death to a cloud that vanishes. The one who descends to sheol does not return to earthly life. His place no longer knows him — complete severance from the living world.

Notes: Hebrew: yored sheol (he who goes down to sheol) lo yaaleh (shall not come up). Lo-yashuv od lebeito (shall not return again to his house). Velo-yakkirennu od meqomo (and his place shall not recognize him any more). Three negations emphasizing the finality of death from the perspective of earthly existence. The dead do not return, do not resume life, are not recognized.

docs.title: Land of darkness and shadow of death; no order, light as darkness
docs.text:
Before I go [whence] I shall not return, [even] to the land of darkness and the shadow of death; A land of darkness, as darkness [itself; and] of the shadow of death, without any order, and [where] the light [is] as darkness.

Context: Job describes death as a journey to a land of darkness from which there is no return. The accumulation of darkness vocabulary (choshek, tsalmaveth, ophel, lo sedarim) paints sheol as the utter absence of light, order, and life.

Notes: Hebrew: eretz choshek vetsalmaveth (land of darkness and shadow-of-death). Lo sedarim (without any order). Vattopha kemo-ophel (and it shines as deep darkness). Fourfold repetition of darkness language makes this the most intensive death-as-darkness passage in the OT. No light = no awareness, no perception.

docs.title: Sheol is my house; bed in darkness; corruption is my father, the worm my mother
docs.text:
If I wait, the grave [is] mine house: I have made my bed in the darkness. I have said to corruption, Thou [art] my father: to the worm, [Thou art] my mother, and my sister. And where [is] now my hope? as for my hope, who shall see it? They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when [our] rest together [is] in the dust.

Context: Job describes sheol as his dwelling place. He has made his bed in darkness and calls corruption (shachath) his father and the worm his mother and sister — complete identification with decay and decomposition.

Notes: Hebrew: sheol beiti (sheol is my house). Bachoshek riddadti yetsuai (in the darkness I have spread my bed). Lashachath qarati abi (to corruption I have called 'my father'). Larimmah immi vaachoti (to the worm 'my mother and my sister'). Rest (nuchah from nuwach H5117) together is in the dust. The imagery is decomposition and unconsciousness, not conscious existence.

docs.title: Shall the dust praise thee? Shall it declare thy truth?
docs.text:
What profit [is there] in my blood, when I go down to the pit? Shall the dust praise thee? shall it declare thy truth?

Context: David appeals to God for healing by arguing that the dead cannot praise God or declare His truth. If the dead were conscious in God's presence, this argument would be pointless.

Notes: Hebrew: hayodekha aphar (shall dust praise you)? hayaggid amittekha (shall it declare your truth)? Rhetorical questions expecting 'no.' Parallels Psa 6:5, 88:10-12, 115:17, Isa 38:18-19 — the dead cannot praise, thank, declare, hope, or remember God. If the righteous dead were consciously praising God in heaven, David's argument to God would be invalid.

docs.title: Made to dwell in darkness, as those that have been long dead
docs.text:
For the enemy hath persecuted my soul; he hath smitten my life down to the ground; he hath made me to dwell in darkness, as those that have been long dead.

Context: David compares his suffering to the state of the dead — dwelling in darkness. The dead are characterized by darkness, a consistent OT theme (Job 10:21-22, Psa 88:6,12).

Notes: Hebrew: hoshivani bemachashakim kemethey olam (he made me dwell in dark places like the dead of old/eternity). The phrase methey olam (dead of eternity/long-dead) describes those who have been dead for a long time — they dwell in darkness. Darkness is the defining characteristic of the death state.

docs.title: They are dead, they shall not live; deceased, they shall not rise
docs.text:
[They are] dead, they shall not live; [they are] deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them, and made all their memory to perish.

Context: Isaiah describes the fate of oppressive rulers. The dead are dead — they shall not live or rise. Their memory perishes. This describes the finality of death for the wicked apart from God's resurrection power.

Notes: Hebrew: methim bal-yichyu (dead ones, they shall not live). Refaim bal-yaqumu (shades/deceased, they shall not rise). Vateabbed kol-zeker lamo (and you destroyed all memory of them). The term refaim (shades) describes the dead as powerless, and the explicit statement 'they shall not rise' reinforces their unconscious state. Their memory (zeker) perishes — even the record of their existence is erased.

docs.title: The righteous perisheth; he shall enter into peace; they shall rest in their beds
docs.text:
The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth [it] to heart: and merciful men [are] taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil [to come]. He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds, [each one] walking [in] his uprightness.

Context: Isaiah describes the death of the righteous as entering peace and resting in their beds. Death is rest (nuwach) — a positive description but still describing unconscious repose, not conscious heavenly activity.

Notes: Hebrew: yavo shalom (he shall enter peace). Yanuchuu al-mishkevotam (they shall rest upon their beds). Holek nekocho (walking in his uprightness — describing their character in life). The verb nuwach (H5117, rest) is the same used in Dan 12:13 for Daniel's death-rest. 'Beds' (mishkab, from shakab H7901) connects to the death-as-sleep vocabulary. Peace and rest characterize righteous death — but rest is cessation, not activity.

docs.title: Sheol personification — the dead stirred up to meet the king of Babylon
docs.text:
Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet [thee] at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, [even] all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us? Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, [and] the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee.

Context: Isaiah's taunt-song (mashal) against the king of Babylon. Sheol is personified as stirring up the dead (refaim) to meet him. This is widely recognized as poetic personification — the same literary device used when trees clap hands (Isa 55:12) and mountains sing (Isa 44:23).

Notes: Hebrew: sheol mittachat ragezah lekha (sheol beneath is stirred for you). The refaim (shades/dead) are 'stirred up' — but the genre is mashal (v.4, taunt/proverb). V.11: tola (worm) spread under, rimmah (maggots) cover — the reality behind the personification is decomposition. The dead 'speak' in the same way Abel's blood 'cries' (Gen 4:10) — forensic/poetic personification, not literal consciousness.

docs.title: They shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake
docs.text:
In their heat I will make their feasts, and I will make them drunken, that they may rejoice, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the LORD.

Context: God's judgment on Babylon. The Babylonians will sleep a perpetual sleep (shenath olam) and not awake. Death is described as sleep from which there is no awakening — apart from divine intervention.

Notes: Hebrew: veyashnu shenat-olam (and they shall sleep a sleep of eternity) velo yaqitsu (and not awake). Uses yashen (H3462, to sleep) — the death-sleep word also used in Dan 12:2. The perpetual sleep (shenath olam) describes death as unbroken unconsciousness. The negation 'not awake' reinforces the point — without divine resurrection, the dead remain in this sleep state.

docs.title: Thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days
docs.text:
But go thou thy way till the end [be]: for thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.

Context: The angel's final words to Daniel. Two phases: (1) rest (nuwach) — death as rest/cessation, and (2) stand in thy lot — resurrection at the end of days. Death is rest; resurrection is standing.

Notes: Hebrew: tanuwach (you shall rest, from nuwach H5117) vetaamod legoralekha leqets hayyamim (and you shall stand in your lot at the end of the days). The sequence is explicit: death = rest, resurrection = standing at the end. Daniel will not be conscious between death and resurrection — he rests. The reward comes 'at the end of the days,' not at death.

docs.title: Thou shalt sleep with thy fathers — OT sleep-death formula (shakab)
docs.text:
And the LORD said unto Moses, Behold, thou shalt sleep with thy fathers; and this people will rise up, and go a whoring after the gods of the strangers of the land, whither they go [to be] among them, and will forsake me, and break my covenant which I have made with them.

Context: God tells Moses he will die. The death formula 'sleep with thy fathers' (shakab im-abotekha) is used — the standard OT euphemism for death. God himself uses this language, calling death 'sleep.'

Notes: Hebrew: shokeb im-abotekha (lying down with your fathers, from shakab H7901). This is God himself speaking, using the sleep metaphor for death. The same formula appears for David (1 Ki 2:10), Solomon (1 Ki 11:43), and dozens of other kings. If God calls death 'sleep,' the metaphor carries divine authority.

docs.title: David slept with his fathers — standard OT death formula
docs.text:
So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David.

Context: The record of David's death using the standard regnal death formula. David 'slept' (shakab) with his fathers and was buried. This is the same David whom Peter declares has NOT ascended into the heavens (Acts 2:34).

Notes: Hebrew: vayyishkab david im-abotav (and David lay down with his fathers). The Qal consecutive imperfect of shakab (H7901). The LXX translates with ekoimathe (from koimao G2837) — the same word used for death-sleep in the NT. Acts 2:29,34 explicitly states David is 'both dead and buried' and has 'NOT ascended into the heavens' — directly contradicting any idea that David is consciously in heaven.

docs.title: The soul that sinneth, it shall die — nephesh can die
docs.text:
Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

Context: God declares ownership of all souls (nephesh) and states the principle: the sinning soul dies. If the soul were inherently immortal, it could not die. This directly contradicts the concept of an immortal soul.

Notes: Hebrew: hannephesh hachote't hi tamut (the soul that sins, it shall die). The pronoun hi (it/she) is emphatic — the soul ITSELF dies. Nephesh (H5315) here means the person/being, not an immaterial component. If the soul is immortal, God's statement is false. Combined with Gen 2:7 (man became a nephesh chayyah), the whole person dies at death.

docs.title: Jesus: the maid is not dead but sleepeth — Jesus calls death sleep (katheudo)
docs.text:
He said unto them, Give place: for the maid is not dead, but sleepeth. And they laughed him to scorn.

Context: Jesus arrives at Jairus's house where the daughter has died. He declares she is 'not dead but sleepeth' (katheudei, from katheudo G2518). The crowd laughs because they know she is dead. Jesus uses the sleep metaphor with full knowledge of her death.

Notes: Greek: ou gar apethanen (for she did not die) to korasion (the girl) alla katheudei (but sleeps, G2518 Pres Act Ind 3s). Jesus redefines death as sleep. This is the same vocabulary pattern as John 11:11-14 (Lazarus sleepeth/is dead). Katheudo (G2518) is used here as a death euphemism by Jesus himself, making it authoritative. The crowd's laughter confirms she was genuinely dead — Jesus is reframing death, not denying it.

docs.title: Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in gehenna
docs.text:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: Jesus teaches about whom to fear. Humans can kill the body but not the soul (psyche); God can destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna. The soul CAN be destroyed — it is not inherently indestructible.

Notes: Greek: apollesai (G622, Aor Act Inf of apollymi = to destroy utterly) kai psychen kai soma (both soul and body) en geenne (in gehenna, G1067). The verb apollymi means to destroy, ruin, put to death — not to torment forever. If the soul were inherently immortal and indestructible, Jesus's statement that God is 'able to destroy' it would be meaningless. This is Jesus teaching conditional immortality — the soul can perish.

docs.title: All in the graves shall hear his voice and come forth — resurrection
docs.text:
Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.

Context: Jesus describes the future resurrection. ALL who are in the graves shall hear his voice and come forth — some to life, some to judgment. The dead are IN THE GRAVES, not in heaven or hell, until the hour of resurrection.

Notes: Greek: pantes hoi en tois mnemeois (all those in the tombs) akousousin (shall hear, Fut Act Ind 3P of akouo G191) tes phones autou (his voice). The dead are located 'in the tombs' — not in heaven, purgatory, or conscious intermediate state. They come forth (ekporeusontai) at the resurrection. Two outcomes: anastasis zoes (resurrection of life) and anastasis kriseos (resurrection of judgment). Both groups are in the graves until they hear Christ's voice.

docs.title: Martha: I know he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day
docs.text:
Jesus saith unto her, Thy brother shall rise again. Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:

Context: Jesus and Martha's exchange about Lazarus. Martha's theology is clear: resurrection happens 'at the last day' — not at the moment of death. Jesus does not correct her timing; he affirms he IS the resurrection and the life.

Notes: Greek: anastesetai (G450, Fut Mid Ind 3s of anistemi = he will rise) en te anastasei (in the resurrection) en te eschate hemera (on the last day). Martha's understanding of resurrection timing — at the last day — is identical to Jesus's four-fold statement in John 6:39,40,44,54. Jesus does not correct her eschatology; he personalizes it: 'I AM the resurrection.' The hope is still future resurrection, embodied in the person of Christ.

docs.title: David fell on sleep (koimao) and was laid unto his fathers and saw corruption
docs.text:
For David, after he had served his own generation by the will of God, fell on sleep, and was laid unto his fathers, and saw corruption:

Context: Paul's sermon at Antioch. He distinguishes David from Christ: David fell asleep (ekoimathe, from koimao G2837), was buried, and saw corruption. Christ was raised and did NOT see corruption (v.37).

Notes: Greek: ekoimathe (G2837, Aor Pass Ind 3s of koimaomai = fell asleep). Paul uses the standard NT death-sleep word for David. Combined with Acts 2:29,34 (David is dead, buried, and has NOT ascended), this establishes David's current state: asleep in death, awaiting resurrection. David's body 'saw corruption' (eiden diaphthoran) — he decomposed. He is not in conscious heavenly bliss.

docs.title: Some are fallen asleep (koimao) — Paul uses sleep for dead believers
docs.text:
After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep.

Context: Paul lists witnesses to the resurrection of Christ. Of the 500+ who saw the risen Christ, some have since died — Paul says they 'are fallen asleep' (ekoimathasan, from koimao G2837).

Notes: Greek: ekoimathasan (G2837, Aor Pass Ind 3P of koimaomai = fell asleep). Paul naturally uses sleep language for dead believers. This is not a euphemism for polite conversation — it reflects Paul's theology of death as unconscious sleep until resurrection, as the rest of 1 Cor 15 makes clear (vv.18,20,51).

docs.title: Christ the firstfruits of them that slept (koimao)
docs.text:
But now is Christ risen from the dead, [and] become the firstfruits of them that slept.

Context: The turning point of Paul's argument. Christ IS risen — and is the firstfruits (aparche) of those who have died ('slept,' kekoimamenon). The firstfruits metaphor implies a harvest to follow — the general resurrection.

Notes: Greek: aparche ton kekoimamenon (G2837, Perf Pass Ptcp Gen Pl M of koimaomai = of those having fallen asleep). The perfect participle indicates an ongoing state — those who have fallen asleep and remain asleep. Christ is the FIRST to rise permanently; the sleepers will follow at the harvest (resurrection). The firstfruits/harvest metaphor demands that the dead are currently sleeping (not yet harvested/resurrected).

docs.title: Whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him
docs.text:
Who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him.

Context: Paul's conclusion to the resurrection passage (4:13-5:11). Whether alive ('wake,' gregoromen from gregoreo G1127) or dead ('sleep,' katheudomen from katheudo G2518), believers will live together with Christ — at his coming.

Notes: Greek: eite gregoromen eite katheudomen (whether we wake or sleep) hama syn auto zesomen (together with him we should live). Katheudo (G2518) is used here for death — the same word Jesus used in Matt 9:24. The living together (zesomen, Aor Act Subj 1P of zao) is FUTURE — connected to the resurrection event of 4:16-17. The assurance is that both living and dead believers share the same resurrection hope.

docs.title: Christ brought life and immortality to light through the gospel
docs.text:
But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel:

Context: Paul describes the effect of Christ's appearing. Christ ABOLISHED death (katargeo) and brought life (zoe) and immortality (aphtharsia G861) to light. Immortality had to be brought to light — it was not already possessed.

Notes: Greek: katargesantos (G2673, Aor Act Ptcp Gen Sg M of katargeo = having abolished/rendered inoperative) men ton thanaton (death). Photisantos (G5461, Aor Act Ptcp Gen Sg M of photizo = having brought to light) de zoen kai aphtharsian (life and incorruption/immortality G861). If humans already possessed immortal souls, immortality would not need to be 'brought to light' — it would already be evident. Christ's work is precisely to bring immortality as a gift (Rom 2:7, 1 Cor 15:53-54).

docs.title: Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord; they REST from their labours
docs.text:
And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed [are] the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.

Context: A beatitude for the dead in the Lord. The Spirit declares they REST (anapauomai G373) from their labours. Rest = cessation of activity, consistent with death-as-rest/sleep throughout Scripture.

Notes: Greek: anapausontai (G373, Fut Mid Ind 3P of anapauomai = they shall rest) ek ton kopon auton (from their labours). Same word used in Rev 6:11 where the souls under the altar are told to 'rest' (anapausontai). The Spirit's characterization of the dead is REST — cessation from labour. Their works 'follow' (akolouthei) them, implying future reward at resurrection, not immediate recompense at death.

docs.title: Death and hades delivered up the dead — hades is temporary storage
docs.text:
And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works. And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Context: The final judgment. Death and hades DELIVER UP the dead — they held the dead until this point. Then death and hades are themselves cast into the lake of fire and destroyed. Hades is temporary, not eternal.

Notes: Greek: ho thanatos kai ho hades edokan (G1325, Aor Act Ind 3P of didomi = gave up/delivered) tous nekrous tous en autois (the dead who were in them). The dead were IN death and hades — held there, not conscious elsewhere. After giving up the dead, thanatos (death) and hades (G86) are cast into the lake of fire (limnen tou pyros). This is the second death (ho thanatos ho deuteros). Death itself is destroyed — consistent with 1 Cor 15:26 ('the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death').

docs.title: Spirits of just men made perfect — alleged conscious state
docs.text:
To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,

Context: The author of Hebrews lists what believers have come to in the new covenant. 'Spirits of just men made perfect' is often cited as evidence of conscious disembodied existence. However, 'made perfect' (teteleiosmenon, from teleioo G5048) is the same word used in Heb 11:40 — where these same people 'received NOT the promise.'

Notes: Greek: pneumasi dikaion teteleiosmenon (G5048, Perf Pass Ptcp Gen Pl M of teleioo = having been made perfect/complete). The key is Heb 11:39-40: the OT faithful 'received NOT the promise' and are 'not made perfect' apart from us. The perfection here is covenantal/legal — achieved through Christ's sacrifice (Heb 10:14), not through conscious existence in heaven. 'Spirits' (pneumasi) may refer to the spiritual legacy/record of the just, not disembodied consciousness. The passage lists realities of the heavenly Jerusalem, not a description of an intermediate state.

docs.title: In the resurrection they neither marry; God is not God of the dead but of the living
docs.text:
And Jesus answering said unto them, The children of this world marry, and are given in marriage: But they which shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry, nor are given in marriage: Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection. Now that the dead are raised, even Moses shewed at the bush, when he calleth the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him.

Context: Jesus answers the Sadducees about the resurrection. His argument is about RESURRECTION (v.35-36), not about a conscious intermediate state. 'All live unto him' (v.38) is proleptic — God counts the dead patriarchs as living because their resurrection is certain (cf. Rom 4:17).

Notes: Greek v.38: pantes gar auto zosin (for all live unto/for him). The dative auto (unto him) is key — they live 'unto him' (from God's perspective), not 'unto themselves' (in present conscious experience). Cf. Rom 4:17: God 'calleth those things which be not as though they were.' Jesus introduces this as proof 'that the dead ARE RAISED' (v.37, hoti egeirontai hoi nekroi) — resurrection language, not intermediate state language. The Sadducees denied resurrection (not intermediate state), and Jesus's answer addresses resurrection.

docs.title: Paradise vision — living person's experience, not about death-state
docs.text:
I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven. And I knew such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.

Context: Paul describes a visionary experience — being caught up to the third heaven/paradise while ALIVE. This is a living person's vision, not a death experience. It tells us about paradise's existence but nothing about the death-state.

Notes: Greek: harpagenta (G726, Aor Pass Ptcp Acc Sg M of harpazo = caught up/snatched away) eis ton paradeison (into paradise, G3857 Acc Sg M). Paul equates the third heaven (v.2) with paradise (v.4). This was a LIVING person's experience — Paul was alive, not dead. It proves paradise exists but says nothing about dead people being conscious there. The phrase 'whether in the body or out of the body' describes the visionary mode, not a death-state.

docs.title: Michael contended about the body of Moses — Moses was resurrected
docs.text:
Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.

Context: Jude references a tradition about Michael's dispute with the devil over Moses' body. The dispute is about the BODY — why contend for a body unless resurrection was at stake? Moses appeared at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3), but as a resurrected being, not a disembodied spirit.

Notes: Greek: peri tou Mouseos somatos (G4983, Gen Sg N = about the body of Moses). The dispute was specifically about Moses' body (soma) — physical remains. The devil contested the body's disposition. This implies resurrection: Michael claimed the body for resurrection, the devil disputed it. Moses' appearance at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3) is thus explained as a RESURRECTED Moses, not a disembodied spirit — eliminating the transfiguration as evidence for conscious intermediate state.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Condition of the dead -- conscious or unconscious? What happens between death and resurrection?

docs.title: OT Death-State Passages: Unconsciousness, Silence, and Cessation
Psalm 146:4
docs.text: Context: A psalm of praise warning against trusting in mortal leaders (v.3). When a human dies, three things happen in sequence: breath departs, body returns to earth, thoughts perish. Direct statement: "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish." Original language: Ruach (H7307, breath/spirit) goes out (yatsa, Qal Impf 3fs). The subject returns (yashuv, Qal Impf 3ms) to his earth (adamah). On that very day (bayyom hahu), his thoughts (eshtonoth, from eshtonah -- a rare word for plans/thoughts) PERISH (avdu, Qal Perf 3cp of abad). The perfect tense of abad indicates completed, definitive action. The word abad means to perish, be destroyed, be lost -- the same word used for destruction throughout the OT. Cross-references: Direct reversal of Gen 2:7 (dust + breath = living being). Parallels Ecc 12:7 (dust returns, spirit returns to God). Combined with Ecc 9:5 (the dead know nothing), establishes that consciousness ceases at death. Relationship to other evidence: Foundational text -- links creation anthropology (Gen 2:7) to the death-state. The cessation of eshtonoth (thoughts/plans) directly contradicts any notion of conscious activity after death.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 9:5-6
docs.text: Context: Qoheleth's reflection on the common fate of all. The living know they will die; the dead know nothing at all. Comprehensive negation of every cognitive and emotional capacity. Direct statement: "The dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished." Original language: Hammetim (the dead, Qal ptcp of muwth H4191) einam yodim (are-not knowing) meumah (anything/something). Double negation: ein + meumah = absolute nothing. Their love (ahavah), hatred (sinah), and envy/jealousy (qinah) have PERISHED (avdah, Qal Perf 3fs of abad H6). Nishkach (Niphal Perf 3ms of shakach) = their memory IS forgotten. Every volitional, cognitive, and emotional capacity is negated. Cross-references: Parallels Psa 146:4 (thoughts perish), Psa 6:5 (no remembrance), Psa 115:17 (dead praise not), Job 14:21 (dead know nothing of sons). Relationship to other evidence: This is the single most comprehensive negation of consciousness in death. It covers knowledge, reward, memory, love, hatred, and envy. Any theory of conscious intermediate state must account for this text.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 9:10
docs.text: Context: Qoheleth's imperative to act now, grounded in the total cessation of all activity in sheol. Four categories of human capacity are negated. Direct statement: "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave [sheol], whither thou goest." Original language: Ein (there is not) + four nouns: maaseh (deed/work), cheshbon (account/planning), daath (knowledge), chokmah (wisdom). Bisheol (in sheol, H7585) asher attah holek shammah (where you are going). The existential negation "ein X in sheol" is a categorical statement: these things do not exist there. Sheol is named explicitly. Cross-references: Sheol as the destination described in Psa 6:5, Psa 115:17, Job 10:21-22. Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces the characterization of sheol as a place of total inactivity. The negation of knowledge and wisdom directly parallels the negation of knowing in v.5.

docs.title: Psalm 6:5
docs.text: Context: David pleads for healing from God. His argument: the dead cannot remember or praise God, so God should preserve his life. Direct statement: "In death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave [sheol] who shall give thee thanks?" Original language: Bammavet (in death) ein (there is not) zikrekha (remembrance of you). Bisheol (in sheol) mi (who?) yodeh (will praise, Hiphil Impf 3ms of yadah) lakh (you?). Rhetorical question expecting "no one." Cross-references: Parallels Psa 115:17, Psa 88:10-12, Psa 30:9, Isa 38:18-19. Relationship to other evidence: David's argument assumes that the dead cannot praise God. If the righteous dead were conscious in God's presence, praising Him, David's appeal would be nonsensical.

docs.title: Psalm 115:17
docs.text: Context: A psalm contrasting the living God with lifeless idols. The dead do not praise God; those who die descend into silence. Direct statement: "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence." Original language: Lo (not) hammetim (the dead) yehallu-yah (will praise the LORD). Velo (and not) kol-yordey (all who descend into) dumah (silence, H1745). Death is equated with descent into dumah -- the cessation of sound and speech. Cross-references: Parallels Psa 6:5, 30:9, 88:10-12, Isa 38:18-19. Relationship to other evidence: The word dumah (silence) is the defining characteristic of the death-state from this psalmist's perspective. Silence is incompatible with conscious praise, prayer, or communication.

docs.title: Psalm 88:10-12
docs.text: Context: The darkest psalm in the Psalter. Six rhetorical questions expecting "no" as the answer. The dead cannot experience wonders, praise, lovingkindness, faithfulness, or righteousness. Direct statement: "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction? Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?" Original language: Four locations named: qeber (grave), abaddon (destruction/perdition), choshek (darkness), eretz neshiyah (land of forgetfulness). Refaim (shades/dead) are used to describe the dead as powerless beings. Interrogative he + lamedh construction expects negative answer. Cross-references: Psa 6:5, 115:17, Isa 38:18-19. Relationship to other evidence: The phrase "land of forgetfulness" (eretz neshiyah) adds forgetfulness to the profile of the death-state. The dead not only cannot praise but cannot even remember.

docs.title: Job 14:10-14
docs.text: Context: Job reflects on human mortality. Man dies and "where is he?" -- a rhetorical question. Job uses the sleep metaphor and expresses hope in a future change. Direct statement: "Man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he? ... So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep." Original language: Yishkab (lies down, from shakab H7901) velo-yaqum (and does not arise). "Till the heavens be no more" = until the end of the present age. Job's question "if a man die, shall he live again?" and his answer "I will wait till my change come" (v.14) express resurrection hope alongside unconscious sleep. Cross-references: Dan 12:2 (sleep in dust, awake), 1 Thess 4:16-17 (dead in Christ shall rise). Relationship to other evidence: Combines death-as-sleep with resurrection hope. The dead lie down and do not rise until the eschatological event.

docs.title: Job 14:21
docs.text: Context: Continuing Job's meditation on death. After describing death as sleep, Job states that the dead have no awareness of what happens to their children. Direct statement: "His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them." Original language: Two parallel clauses: yikbedu (come to honour) velo-yeda (and he knows not); yitsaru (are brought low) velo-yabin (and he perceives not). Double negation of perception. Cross-references: Ecc 9:5-6 (the dead know nothing). Relationship to other evidence: Directly contradicts any notion of the dead observing or being aware of earthly events.

docs.title: Isaiah 38:18-19
docs.text: Context: Hezekiah's testimony after recovering from a fatal illness. He contrasts the dead (no praise, no celebration, no hope) with the living. Direct statement: "The grave cannot praise thee, death cannot celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. The living, the living, he shall praise thee." Original language: Sheol (H7585) cannot todekha (praise you). Mavet (death, H4194) cannot yehalelekha (celebrate you). Yordey-bor (those descending to the pit) cannot yesabberu (hope for) thy truth. Triple negation followed by emphatic contrast: chai chai (the living, the living -- emphatic repetition). Cross-references: Psa 6:5, 115:17, 88:10-12, 30:9. Relationship to other evidence: Adds the category of "hope" to the list of things the dead cannot do. The dead have no hope -- hope belongs to the living.

docs.title: Psalm 30:9
docs.text: Context: David appeals to God for healing, arguing that the dead cannot praise or declare God's truth. Direct statement: "Shall the dust praise thee? shall it declare thy truth?" Original language: Hayodekha aphar (shall dust praise you)? Hayaggid amittekha (shall it declare your truth)? Rhetorical questions expecting "no." Cross-references: Psa 6:5, 88:10-12, 115:17. Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces the consistent OT pattern: the dead cannot praise, declare, remember, or hope.

docs.title: Psalm 143:3
docs.text: Context: David compares his suffering to the state of the dead -- dwelling in darkness. Direct statement: "He hath made me to dwell in darkness, as those that have been long dead." Original language: Hoshivani bemachashakim kemethey olam (he made me dwell in dark places like the dead of old/eternity). Darkness is the defining characteristic of the death state. Cross-references: Job 10:21-22, Psa 88:6,12. Relationship to other evidence: Darkness as the defining condition of the dead, consistent with Job 10:21-22 (land of darkness, shadow of death).

docs.title: Isaiah 26:14
docs.text: Context: Isaiah describes the fate of oppressive rulers. Their death is final apart from God's intervention. Direct statement: "They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them, and made all their memory to perish." Original language: Methim bal-yichyu (dead ones, they shall not live). Refaim bal-yaqumu (shades/deceased, they shall not rise). Vateabbed kol-zeker lamo (and you destroyed all memory of them). The refaim (shades) are powerless dead. Cross-references: Psa 88:10-12 (refaim shall not arise and praise). Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces the finality of death apart from divine resurrection.

docs.title: Deuteronomy 31:16
docs.text: Context: God tells Moses he will die, using the sleep formula. Direct statement: "Behold, thou shalt sleep with thy fathers." Original language: Shokeb (lying down, from shakab H7901) im-abotekha (with your fathers). God himself uses this language, calling death "sleep." The same formula appears for David (1 Ki 2:10), Solomon (1 Ki 11:43), and approximately 36 other kings. Cross-references: 1 Ki 2:10 (David slept with his fathers), Dan 12:2 (sleep in dust). Relationship to other evidence: God uses the death-as-sleep metaphor, giving it divine authority.

docs.title: 1 Kings 2:10
docs.text: Context: The record of David's death using the standard regnal death formula. Direct statement: "So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David." Original language: Vayyishkab david im-abotav (and David lay down with his fathers). Qal consecutive imperfect of shakab (H7901). The LXX translates with ekoimathe (from koimao G2837) -- the same word used for death-sleep in the NT. Cross-references: Acts 2:29,34 (David is dead and buried, has NOT ascended into the heavens). Acts 13:36 (David fell on sleep, was laid unto his fathers, saw corruption). Relationship to other evidence: Establishes the LXX semantic chain: shakab (H7901) -> koimao (G2837). David's current state: asleep in death, not ascended to heaven.

docs.title: Daniel 12:2
docs.text: Context: Daniel's final vision, after the time of trouble. The dead described as sleeping in the dust, who shall awake at resurrection. Direct statement: "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." Original language: Yesheney (sleepers of, from yashen H3462, Adj.mp.Cst) admat-aphar (soil of dust). Yaqitsu (shall awake, Hiphil Impf 3mp of quts). Both righteous and wicked sleep until awakening. The word olam (eternity) modifies both outcomes. Cross-references: Dan 12:13 (thou shalt rest and stand at the end of days), 1 Thess 4:16-17 (dead in Christ shall rise), John 5:28-29 (all in graves shall come forth). Relationship to other evidence: The resurrection model: death = sleep, resurrection = awakening. Both righteous and wicked are in the same sleep state until the eschatological event.

docs.title: Jeremiah 51:39
docs.text: Context: God's judgment on Babylon. Death described as perpetual sleep. Direct statement: "They shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the LORD." Original language: Veyashnu shenat-olam (and they shall sleep a sleep of eternity, from yashen H3462) velo yaqitsu (and not awake). Death as unbroken unconsciousness. Cross-references: Dan 12:2 (sleep in dust, awake), Job 14:12 (lies down, rises not). Relationship to other evidence: Reinforces the sleep metaphor. Without divine intervention (resurrection), the dead remain in unconscious sleep.

docs.title: John 11:11-14
docs.text: Context: Jesus deliberately uses the sleep metaphor for Lazarus's death, then explicitly clarifies. Direct statement: "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep. ... Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead." Original language: Kekoimetai (G2837, Perf Pass Ind 3s of koimaomai) = "has fallen asleep." Perfect tense indicates a completed state. Jesus uses exypniso (G1852, Aor Act Subj 1s) = "that I may awaken him." John's editorial note confirms: Jesus spoke of his death (thanatos). Cross-references: Matt 9:24 (the maid sleepeth), Dan 12:2 (sleep, awake). Relationship to other evidence: Jesus's own interpretive framework for death: it is sleep. Resurrection is awakening. The narrator explicitly confirms the equation: sleep = death.

docs.title: Matthew 9:24
docs.text: Context: Jesus at Jairus's house declares the dead girl is "not dead but sleepeth." Direct statement: "The maid is not dead, but sleepeth." Original language: Ou gar apethanen (for she did not die) to korasion (the girl) alla katheudei (but sleeps, G2518, Pres Act Ind 3s). Jesus redefines death as sleep. The crowd's laughter confirms she was genuinely dead. Cross-references: John 11:11-14, Luke 8:52, Mark 5:39. Relationship to other evidence: Jesus uses katheudo (G2518) for death, just as He uses koimao in John 11. Both are authoritative sleep-death designations.

docs.title: Acts 7:59-60
docs.text: Context: Stephen's martyrdom. He commends his spirit to Jesus, then "falls asleep." Direct statement: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. ... And when he had said this, he fell asleep." Original language: Dexai (G1209, Aor Mid Impv 2s, receive) to pneuma mou (my spirit). Ekoimathe (G2837, Aor Pass Ind 3s of koimaomai) = "he fell asleep." Stephen commends his pneuma to Christ (paralleling Jesus's own words in Luke 23:46 and fulfilling Ecc 12:7), yet Luke immediately uses sleep language for his death. Cross-references: Luke 23:46 (Jesus commends spirit to Father), Ecc 12:7 (spirit returns to God). Relationship to other evidence: The combination is significant: spirit commended = trust in God's keeping; sleep = unconscious death until resurrection. If commending the spirit meant immediate conscious presence with Christ, the sleep language would be contradictory.

docs.title: Acts 13:36
docs.text: Context: Paul's sermon distinguishing David from Christ. David died and decomposed. Direct statement: "David, after he had served his own generation by the will of God, fell on sleep, and was laid unto his fathers, and saw corruption." Original language: Ekoimathe (G2837, Aor Pass Ind 3s). Paul uses the standard NT death-sleep word for David. David's body "saw corruption" (eiden diaphthoran) -- he decomposed. Cross-references: Acts 2:29,34 (David dead, buried, NOT ascended). Relationship to other evidence: David -- "a man after God's own heart" -- is asleep in death, not in conscious heavenly existence.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:6,18,20,51
docs.text: Context: Paul's resurrection argument throughout 1 Cor 15. Direct statement (v.18): "Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished." (v.20): "Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept." (v.51): "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed." Original language: V.18: koimethentes (G2837, Aor Pass Ptcp Nom Pl M) = "those having fallen asleep." Apolonto (G622, Aor Mid Ind 3P) = "perished/are destroyed." V.20: kekoimamenon (G2837, Perf Pass Ptcp Gen Pl M) = "of those having fallen asleep" -- perfect tense indicates ongoing state. V.51: koimethesometha (G2837, Fut Pass Ind 1P) = "we shall sleep." Cross-references: 1 Thess 4:13-17, Dan 12:2. Relationship to other evidence: 1 Cor 15:18 is the decisive logical test for every alleged conscious intermediate state passage. If believers were already in conscious bliss with Christ at death, Paul's reductio ad absurdum -- "they have perished" without resurrection -- makes no sense. Paul's entire argument assumes that without resurrection, the dead have no conscious existence at all.

docs.title: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-17
docs.text: Context: Paul addresses the Thessalonians' concern about dead believers. Three times he uses koimao for death. Direct statement: "Them which are asleep ... the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them ... and so shall we ever be with the Lord." Original language: V.14: koimethentas (G2837, Aor Pass Ptcp Acc Pl M). V.16: nekroi en Christo anastesontai (dead in Christ will rise, Fut Mid Ind 3P of anistemi G450) proton (first). The chronology: (1) Lord descends, (2) dead rise, (3) living caught up, (4) THEN "so shall we ever be with the Lord." Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:51-54, John 6:39-40. Relationship to other evidence: Being "ever with the Lord" is the RESULT of resurrection, not something that happens at death. If the dead were already with the Lord, Paul's comfort -- that they will be raised -- is unnecessary.

docs.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:10
docs.text: Context: Paul's conclusion to the resurrection passage. Direct statement: "Whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him." Original language: Eite gregoromen eite katheudomen (whether we wake or sleep) hama syn auto zesomen (together with him we should live). Katheudo (G2518) used for death. Cross-references: Matt 9:24 (katheudo for death). Relationship to other evidence: The future living together is connected to the resurrection event of 4:16-17.

docs.title: Sheol/Hades Characterization
docs.text: The OT death-state passages above (Ecc 9:10, Psa 6:5, Psa 115:17, Psa 88:10-12, Job 10:21-22) all characterize sheol. Summary: sheol is characterized by no work, no knowledge, no wisdom (Ecc 9:10); no remembrance of God (Psa 6:5); silence (Psa 115:17); darkness and no order (Job 10:21-22); forgetfulness (Psa 88:12). The LXX translates sheol as hades 58 times. Acts 2:27,31 confirm the equivalence by quoting Psa 16:10. Hades (G86, 11 NT occurrences) is TEMPORARY -- Rev 20:13-14 describes death and hades delivering up their dead and then being cast into the lake of fire.

docs.title: Job 3:13-19
docs.text: Context: Job laments his birth and describes what death would have been. Direct statement: "For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest. ... There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest." Original language: Shakabti (from shakab H7901), shenah (sleep), nuwach (rest H5117). V.17: the wicked cease (chadal) from troubling. V.18: "they hear not (lo shamu) the voice of the oppressor." Explicit absence of hearing/perception. Cross-references: Isa 57:1-2 (righteous enter peace, rest in beds), Dan 12:13 (rest, then stand). Relationship to other evidence: Death is rest -- cessation for both wicked and righteous. The dead "hear not" -- perception ceases.

docs.title: Job 7:9-10
docs.text: Context: Job on the finality of death. Direct statement: "He that goeth down to the grave [sheol] shall come up no more. He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more." Original language: Yored sheol lo yaaleh (he who goes down to sheol shall not come up). Three negations emphasizing severance from the living world. Relationship to other evidence: The dead do not return to earthly life -- they are severed from the living.

docs.title: Job 10:21-22
docs.text: Context: Job describes death as a journey to darkness from which there is no return. Direct statement: "The land of darkness and the shadow of death; A land of darkness, as darkness itself; and of the shadow of death, without any order, and where the light is as darkness." Original language: Eretz choshek vetsalmaveth (land of darkness and shadow-of-death). Lo sedarim (without any order). Fourfold repetition of darkness language. Cross-references: Psa 143:3, Psa 88:6,12. Relationship to other evidence: Sheol is defined by darkness -- the utter absence of light, order, and awareness.

docs.title: Job 17:13-16
docs.text: Context: Job describes sheol as his dwelling place. Direct statement: "If I wait, the grave is mine house: I have made my bed in the darkness. I have said to corruption, Thou art my father: to the worm, Thou art my mother." Original language: Sheol beiti (sheol is my house). Bachoshek riddadti yetsuai (in the darkness I have spread my bed). Nuchah (rest, from nuwach H5117) together in the dust. Relationship to other evidence: Sheol characterized by decomposition and unconsciousness, not conscious existence.

docs.title: Isaiah 14:9-11
docs.text: Context: Isaiah's taunt-song (mashal, v.4) against the king of Babylon. Direct statement: "Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee." Original language: Sheol mittachat ragezah lekha. The refaim (shades/dead) are "stirred up." But the genre is mashal (taunt/proverb). V.11: tola (worm) spread under, rimmah (maggots) cover. Reality behind the personification is decomposition. Cross-references: Gen 4:10 (Abel's blood "cries"), Isa 55:12 (trees clap hands). Relationship to other evidence: Poetic personification. The dead "speak" in the same way Abel's blood "cries" -- forensic/literary device, not literal consciousness.

docs.title: Isaiah 57:1-2
docs.text: Context: Isaiah describes the death of the righteous. Direct statement: "The righteous perisheth... He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness." Original language: Yavo shalom (he shall enter peace). Yanuchuu al-mishkevotam (they shall rest upon their beds). Nuwach (H5117, rest) + mishkab (from shakab H7901, beds) -- death-as-sleep vocabulary. Cross-references: Dan 12:13 (thou shalt rest and stand). Relationship to other evidence: Righteous death is rest and peace -- positive but still describing cessation, not conscious activity.

docs.title: Daniel 12:13
docs.text: Context: The angel's final words to Daniel. Direct statement: "Thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days." Original language: Tanuwach (you shall rest, from nuwach H5117) vetaamod legoralekha (and you shall stand in your lot) leqets hayyamim (at the end of the days). Two phases: death = rest, resurrection = standing. Cross-references: Dan 12:2 (sleep, awake), Rev 14:13 (rest from labours). Relationship to other evidence: The reward comes "at the end of the days," not at death. Daniel rests until resurrection.

docs.title: Revelation 20:13-14
docs.text: Context: The final judgment. Death and hades deliver up their dead and are then cast into the lake of fire. Direct statement: "Death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them ... And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire." Original language: Ho thanatos kai ho hades edokan (G1325, Aor Act Ind 3P, gave up) tous nekrous tous en autois (the dead who were in them). Hades is temporary storage for the dead -- not a place of conscious experience. After giving up the dead, death and hades are destroyed. Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:26 (last enemy destroyed is death). Relationship to other evidence: Hades is temporary. The dead were IN death and hades -- held there until judgment. Death itself is destroyed at the end.

docs.title: Genesis 2:7
docs.text: Context: The creation of the first human. Direct statement: "The LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Original language: Creation formula: dust (aphar H6083) + breath (neshamah H5397) = living being (nephesh chayyah). Man BECOMES a soul -- he does not receive one. The same term (nephesh chayyah) is used for animals (Gen 1:24). Cross-references: Gen 3:19 (dust to dust), Ecc 12:7 (reversal), Psa 146:4 (thoughts perish). Relationship to other evidence: The foundational text for holistic anthropology. Death reverses this formula: when breath departs, the living being ceases to exist as a conscious entity.

docs.title: Genesis 3:19
docs.text: Context: God's pronouncement after the fall. Direct statement: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Original language: Aphar attah veel-aphar tashuv (dust you are and to dust you shall return). Death defined as reversal of creation -- no mention of a conscious soul surviving. Cross-references: Gen 2:7, Ecc 12:7, Ecc 3:19-20. Relationship to other evidence: The first biblical definition of death: return to dust. Not separation of soul from body.

docs.title: Genesis 3:22-24
docs.text: Context: God bars access to the tree of life after the fall. Direct statement: "Lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever." Original language: Pen-yishlach yado velaqach gam meetz hachayyim veakhal vachai leolam. Man needed the tree of life to live forever. Being barred from it means death is certain. Cross-references: Rev 2:7 (tree of life in paradise), Rev 22:2 (tree of life in new Jerusalem). Relationship to other evidence: Immortality was not inherent -- it was conditional on access to the tree of life.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 12:7
docs.text: Context: Qoheleth's death allegory. The two components of the creation formula are separated at death. Direct statement: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." Original language: Veyashov heaphar al-haaretz keshehayah (the dust shall return to the earth as it was). Veharuach tashuv el-haelohim asher netanah (and the spirit/breath shall return to God who gave it). Ruach (H7307) returns to God who GAVE it -- it was God's to begin with. Cross-references: Gen 2:7, Gen 3:19, Psa 146:4, Ecc 3:19-21. Relationship to other evidence: Not the departure of a conscious soul but the return of the animating principle. Animals have the same ruach (Ecc 3:19). Combined with Psa 146:4 (thoughts perish when ruach departs), the result: when ruach departs, consciousness ceases.

docs.title: Ecclesiastes 3:19-21
docs.text: Context: Qoheleth's observation about the commonality between human and animal death. Direct statement: "As the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast." Original language: Ruach echad lakkol (one breath/spirit for all). If ruach were the conscious, immortal soul, then animals would also have immortal souls. V.21 asks rhetorically who knows whether human ruach goes upward and animal downward. Cross-references: Gen 2:7, Ecc 12:7. Relationship to other evidence: The shared ruach proves it is the animating principle, not a conscious immaterial entity unique to humans.

docs.title: Ezekiel 18:4
docs.text: Context: God declares the principle of individual accountability. Direct statement: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die." Original language: Hannephesh hachote't hi tamut (the soul that sins, it shall die). Emphatic: the soul ITSELF dies. Nephesh (H5315) here means the person/being. Cross-references: Gen 2:7 (man became a nephesh), Matt 10:28 (God can destroy soul and body). Relationship to other evidence: If the soul were inherently immortal, God's statement is false. The soul can die.

docs.title: Matthew 10:28
docs.text: Context: Jesus teaches about whom to fear. Direct statement: "Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." Original language: Apollesai (G622, Aor Act Inf of apollymi = to destroy) kai psychen kai soma (both soul and body) en geenne (in gehenna, G1067). The verb apollymi means to destroy, not to torment forever. Cross-references: Ezek 18:4 (the soul that sins shall die). Relationship to other evidence: Jesus teaches that the soul (psyche) CAN be destroyed. This contradicts the concept of an inherently indestructible, immortal soul.

docs.title: 1 Timothy 6:15-16
docs.text: Context: Paul's doxology to God. Direct statement: "Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto." Original language: Monos echon (alone having) athanasin (immortality, G110). Monos (G3440) = alone/only -- the exclusivity is absolute. Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:53-54 (mortals must put on immortality), Rom 2:7 (seek for immortality). Relationship to other evidence: If God alone possesses immortality, no human soul inherently possesses it. Immortality is a divine gift acquired at resurrection.

docs.title: 1 Corinthians 15:51-54
docs.text: Context: Climax of Paul's resurrection argument. Direct statement: "This mortal must put on immortality. ... then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory." Original language: Endysasthai (aorist middle infinitive of endyo G1746) -- "putting on" immortality implies it is not currently possessed. The timing: "at the last trump." Cross-references: 1 Tim 6:16, 2 Cor 5:4 ("mortality swallowed up of life"). Relationship to other evidence: Immortality acquired at resurrection, not possessed at creation or maintained through death.

docs.title: 2 Timothy 1:10
docs.text: Context: Paul describes the effect of Christ's appearing. Direct statement: "Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel." Original language: Katargesantos (G2673, having abolished) men ton thanaton (death). Photisantos (G5461, having brought to light) de zoen kai aphtharsian (life and incorruption, G861). Cross-references: 1 Tim 6:16, Rom 2:7. Relationship to other evidence: If humans already possessed immortal souls, immortality would not need to be "brought to light."

docs.title: John 6:39-40
docs.text: Context: Jesus's bread of life discourse. The phrase "I will raise him up at the last day" is repeated four times (vv.39,40,44,54). Direct statement: "I will raise him up at the last day." Original language: Anasteso (G450, Fut Act Ind 1s of anistemi) auto (him) en te eschate hemera (on the last day). Four-fold repetition for emphasis. Cross-references: John 11:24 (Martha: "I know he shall rise again at the last day"), 1 Thess 4:16-17. Relationship to other evidence: Resurrection at the last day, not at the moment of death, is the consistent biblical hope. If believers immediately go to heaven at death, resurrection becomes superfluous.

docs.title: John 5:28-29
docs.text: Context: Jesus describes future resurrection. Direct statement: "All that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth." Original language: Pantes hoi en tois mnemeois (all those in the tombs) akousousin (shall hear) tes phones autou (his voice). The dead are located "in the tombs" -- not in heaven or hell. Cross-references: Dan 12:2, John 6:39-40, 1 Thess 4:16. Relationship to other evidence: The dead are in the graves until resurrection. Two outcomes: resurrection of life and resurrection of judgment.

docs.title: Acts 2:29-34
docs.text: Context: Peter's Pentecost sermon. Explicit denial that David is in heaven. Direct statement: "David is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day. ... For David is not ascended into the heavens." Original language: V.34: ou gar Daueid anebe (G305, Aor Act Ind 3s of anabaino = ascended) eis tous ouranous (into the heavens). Peter, under the Holy Spirit's inspiration at Pentecost, explicitly denies David's conscious heavenly existence. Cross-references: 1 Ki 2:10 (David slept with his fathers), Acts 13:36 (David fell on sleep, saw corruption). Relationship to other evidence: If David -- "a man after God's own heart" -- has not ascended to heaven, the doctrine of immediate conscious heavenly existence after death lacks biblical warrant.

docs.title: Hebrews 11:39-40
docs.text: Context: The conclusion of the faith hall of fame. Direct statement: "These all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect." Original language: Ouk ekomisanto (G2865, Aor Mid Ind 3P, received not) ten epaggelian (the promise). Teleiothosin (G5048, Aor Pass Subj 3P of teleioo = be perfected). If these OT heroes were already in conscious bliss, the author's statement would be false. Cross-references: Heb 12:23 (spirits of just men made perfect -- same word teleioo). Relationship to other evidence: The OT faithful await corporate completion "with us" at the resurrection.

docs.title: Revelation 20:4-6
docs.text: Context: The first resurrection. Direct statement: "They lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years. But the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished." Original language: Ezasan (Aor Act Ind 3P of zao G2198) = "they lived" -- ingressive aorist: they came to life. If they were already consciously alive, this statement is meaningless. Cross-references: Rev 6:9-11 (souls under altar told to rest). Relationship to other evidence: The same "souls" from Rev 6:9 are described as having "lived" at the first resurrection. They were not alive before. The rest of the dead "lived not again" until later.

docs.title: Matthew 22:31-32
docs.text: Context: Jesus answers the Sadducees about resurrection. Direct statement: "God is not the God of the dead, but of the living." Original language: Ouk estin ho theos nekron alla zonton (Pres Act Ptcp Gen Pl M of zao). Jesus explicitly introduces this as "touching the resurrection of the dead" (v.31) -- not about the current state of the dead. Cross-references: Luke 20:37-38 ("all live unto him"), Rom 4:17 (God "calleth those things which be not as though they were"). Relationship to other evidence: Jesus's argument is proleptic: God counts the patriarchs as living because their resurrection is certain. The Sadducees denied resurrection (Acts 23:8), and Jesus's answer addresses resurrection, not intermediate state.

docs.title: Luke 20:34-38
docs.text: Context: Luke's version of the Sadducees' challenge. Direct statement: "For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him." Original language: Pantes gar auto zosin (for all live unto him). The dative auto (unto him) is key -- they live "unto him" (from God's perspective), not "unto themselves" (in present conscious experience). Cf. Rom 4:17. Cross-references: Matt 22:31-32, Mark 12:26-27. Relationship to other evidence: The Sadducees challenged RESURRECTION, not intermediate state. Jesus's answer proves resurrection, not present consciousness.

docs.title: John 11:23-25
docs.text: Context: Jesus and Martha's exchange about Lazarus. Direct statement: "Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Original language: Anastesetai (G450, Fut Mid Ind 3s, he will rise) en te anastasei en te eschate hemera (in the resurrection at the last day). Martha's understanding matches Jesus's four-fold statement in John 6. Jesus does not correct her timing. Cross-references: John 6:39-40,44,54. Relationship to other evidence: Martha's theology: resurrection at the last day. Jesus affirms he IS the resurrection, personalizing the hope without changing the timing.

docs.title: 2 Timothy 4:6-8
docs.text: Context: Paul's final letter, facing imminent death. Direct statement: "There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing." Original language: Apodosei (G591, Fut Act Ind 3s, will give) moi (to me) en ekeine te hemera (on that day). The crown is given "at that day" -- the day of Christ's appearing (epiphaneian G2015), not the day of death. Cross-references: Phil 1:23 (same author anticipates being with Christ), 1 Thess 4:16-17. Relationship to other evidence: Even facing death, Paul places his reward at the future appearing of Christ, not at the moment of death.

docs.title: Difficult or Complicating Passages: Alleged Conscious Intermediate State
2 Corinthians 5:1-9
docs.text:
Context: Paul's discussion of the believer's hope. Often cited as proof of conscious intermediate state. Direct statement: "We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord." Original language: V.8: ekdemesai (G1553, Aor Act Inf, to be absent from) ek tou somatos (the body) kai (and) endemesai (G1736, Aor Act Inf, to be at home with) pros ton Kurion (the Lord). Two aorist infinitives connected by kai. The aorist does NOT specify temporal relationship or duration between the two events.

V.4 is key: Paul explicitly does NOT want to be ekdysasthai (unclothed/stripped) but ependysasthai (clothed upon). His stated purpose: "that mortality might be swallowed up of life" (hina katapoth to thneton hypo tes zoes) -- direct language from 1 Cor 15:54.

From the perspective of an unconscious dead person, the next conscious moment after death IS being with the Lord at resurrection. The passage does not require a conscious intermediate state; it requires that death leads to being with Christ, which resurrection accomplishes. Cross-reference: 1 Cor 15:18 -- if no resurrection, the dead have "perished." This is the same Paul, in the same letter corpus, making an argument that only works if the dead are NOT already in conscious bliss. Relationship to other evidence: Paul's clothing metaphor aligns with resurrection, not disembodied intermediate existence. He wants to be clothed upon, not unclothed.

docs.title: Philippians 1:21-24
docs.text:
Context: Paul writing from prison considers two options: remaining alive or departing to be with Christ. Direct statement: "Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better." Original language: Analysai (G360, Aor Act Inf of analyo, to depart) kai (and) syn Christo einai (to be with Christ, Pres Act Inf of eimi). The articular infinitive to analysai is paired with syn Christo einai without specifying temporal relationship.

The SAME LETTER contains Phil 3:10-11: "if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead" -- why seek resurrection if already with Christ at death? And Phil 3:20-21: "we look for the Saviour...who shall change our vile body" -- future transformation, not present bliss. Also 2 Tim 4:8: crown given "at that day" (the appearing), not at death.

From the dead person's subjective perspective (no conscious interval), departure = next conscious moment with Christ at resurrection. Relationship to other evidence: The same-letter context (Phil 3:11, 3:20-21) shows Paul's hope is resurrection, not disembodied intermediate existence.

docs.title: Philippians 3:10-11,20-21
docs.text: Context: Same letter as Phil 1:23. Direct statement: "If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead. ... We look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: Who shall change our vile body." Original language: Ten exanastasin (G1815, the out-resurrection) ten ek nekron. Paul uses the rare compound exanastasis (only here in NT). Metaschematizo (Fut Act Ind 3s, shall change) -- transformation is future, at Christ's coming. Relationship to other evidence: Demonstrates that being "with Christ" and "resurrection" are the same event from Paul's perspective.

docs.title: Luke 23:43
docs.text:
Context: Jesus's response to the repentant thief on the cross. Direct statement: "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." Original language: Amen soi lego (truly to you I say) semeron (G4594, today, ADV) met emou (with me) ese (Fut Mid Ind 2s of eimi, you will be) en to Paradeiso (in paradise, G3857).

Three issues: (1) Greek manuscripts have NO punctuation. The comma placement -- "I say unto thee, Today..." vs. "I say unto thee today, Thou shalt..." -- is entirely editorial. Semeron can modify either lego or ese. The Syriac Peshitta and Curetonian manuscripts place "today" with "I say."

(2) Jesus was NOT in paradise on that day. John 20:17, three days later: "I am not yet ascended (oupo anababeka, Perf Act Ind 1s of anabaino G305) to my Father." If paradise = God's presence (2 Cor 12:4, Rev 2:7), Jesus was not there on Friday.

(3) Paradeisos (G3857) occurs only 3 times in the NT. Rev 2:7 links it to the tree of life -- eschatological paradise. LXX uses it for Eden (Gen 2:8).

The thief's request was "when thou comest into thy kingdom" -- a future reference. Relationship to other evidence: John 20:17 is the decisive cross-reference. Jesus was not in paradise on crucifixion day, making the traditional comma placement untenable.

docs.title: Luke 16:19-31
docs.text:
Context: The rich man and Lazarus, situated in Luke 15-16, a continuous parabolic discourse. Direct statement: The rich man in hades, in torments; Lazarus in Abraham's bosom. Original language: V.23: en to Hade (in hades, G86). Basanois (G931, torments) -- this is basanos (touchstone/torment), NOT basanizo/basanismos used in eschatological judgment. "Abraham's bosom" (kolpos G2859) appears ONLY in this passage in all of Scripture.

Genre: Luke 15:3 provides a single parabole label for three stories. The opening formula "a certain rich man" (anthropos tis plousios) matches Luke 12:16 (labeled parabole) and 16:1 (universally accepted as parabolic).

Stated teaching point: "They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them" (vv.29,31) -- the lesson is about listening to Scripture, not afterlife geography.

Same author Luke records "David is not ascended" (Acts 2:34) and Stephen "fell asleep" (Acts 7:60).

Prior study (etc6-09): Tree 3 Gates 1 and 3 FAIL (parabolic character, parabolic genre). Classification: Neutral. Relationship to other evidence: A parable cannot override 9+ OT death-state passages and Jesus's own teachings about death as sleep and resurrection as the hope. The genre determines the hermeneutical weight.

docs.title: Revelation 6:9-11
docs.text:
Context: Fifth seal of Revelation's vision sequence. All surrounding elements are symbolic. Direct statement: "I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God ... they cried with a loud voice." Original language: Psychas (G5590, Acc Pl F) = souls/lives. Esphagmenon (G4969, Perf Pass Ptcp, slain) -- same word used for the Lamb (Rev 5:6). Ekraxan (G2896, Aor Act Ind 3P of krazo, cried out).

Abel parallel: Gen 4:10 -- Abel's blood "cries" from the ground. This is forensic personification, not literal voice. Rev 16:7: the altar itself speaks. If souls speaking proves consciousness, the altar is also conscious.

Rev 6:11: anapausontai (G373, rest) -- same word as Rev 14:13 ("rest from labours"). Rev 20:4-5: these same souls "LIVED" (ezasan) at the first resurrection -- they were not alive before.

Prior study (etc6-10): Tree 3 Gate 1 FAIL (symbolic vision-figure), Gate 3 FAIL (apocalyptic genre). Classification: Neutral. Relationship to other evidence: Apocalyptic imagery with clear OT precedent (Abel's blood crying). The same souls "lived" at resurrection -- meaning they were not alive before.

docs.title: 1 Samuel 28:3-20
docs.text:
Context: Saul, abandoned by God, consults a medium to reach the dead Samuel. Direct statement: The woman sees "gods ascending." Saul asks Samuel questions.

Key observations: (1) Only the woman saw the apparition -- Saul saw nothing (vv.12-14). (2) No new information was given beyond what Samuel had prophesied while alive (cf. 1 Sam 15:28). (3) God explicitly condemned Saul for this act (1 Chr 10:13). (4) Comprehensive OT prohibition against necromancy (Exo 22:18, Lev 19:31, 20:6,27, Deu 18:9-14). (5) If the dead are unconscious (as Ecc 9:5 and Psa 146:4 state), this was demonic impersonation. (6) The passage uses the woman's perspective to narrate what she claimed to see. Relationship to other evidence: The passage does not require that Samuel actually appeared. It is narrated from the woman's perspective, and God condemned the entire act.

docs.title: Matthew 17:1-9
docs.text:
Context: Three disciples witness Jesus transfigured with Moses and Elijah. Direct statement: "There appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him." Original language: V.9: to horama (G3705, Acc Sg N) = "the vision." Jesus himself calls the transfiguration "the vision" (horama). This word is used for supernatural visual experiences (Acts 7:31, 9:10, 10:3, etc.), not ordinary reality.

Neither figure requires a conscious intermediate state: Moses was resurrected (Jude 1:9 -- Michael's dispute about the BODY of Moses), Elijah was translated without dying (2 Ki 2:11). Relationship to other evidence: Jesus classifies this as a "vision." Moses's appearance is explained by resurrection (Jude 1:9), Elijah's by translation (2 Ki 2:11). No conscious intermediate state is required.

docs.title: 1 Peter 3:18-20
docs.text:
Context: Peter discusses Christ's suffering and triumph. Direct statement: "By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison; Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah." Original language: En ho (in which, Dat Sg N of hos G3739) connects to pneumati (Spirit) in v.18. Poreutheis (G4198, having gone) ekeruxen (G2784, Aor Act Ind 3s, proclaimed). The spirits (pneumasin G4151) are "in prison" (en phylake G5438).

The preaching occurred "in the days of Noah" (v.20), not between Christ's death and resurrection. 1 Pet 1:10-11 establishes that "the Spirit of Christ was in" OT prophets. 2 Pet 2:5: Noah was "a preacher of righteousness." The preaching was by the Spirit of Christ through Noah.

Alternative reading: spirits = fallen angels (Gen 6:1-4, 2 Pet 2:4, Jude 1:6), prison = tartaroo.
