1 Pet 4:6: eueggelisthe (G2097, Aor Pass Ind 3s) = "was preached." Aorist passive = completed past action. The gospel WAS preached (past) to those who ARE dead (present state) -- preached while alive. Relationship to other evidence: The passage does not teach post-mortem preaching. The spirits were preached to during Noah's time through the Spirit of Christ in Noah.

docs.title: 1 Peter 4:6
docs.text: Context: Peter explains why the gospel was preached to those who are now dead. Direct statement: "For this cause was the gospel preached also to them that are dead." Original language: Nekrois (G3498, Dat Pl M, dead ones) eueggelisthe (G2097, Aor Pass Ind 3s, was preached). Aorist passive indicates completed past action to present dead -- the gospel was preached to these people while they were alive. Relationship to other evidence: Does not teach post-mortem preaching. Past action to present dead.

docs.title: Hebrews 12:23
docs.text: Context: The author lists realities of the new covenant. Direct statement: "The spirits of just men made perfect." Original language: Pneumasi dikaion teteleiosmenon (G5048, Perf Pass Ptcp Gen Pl M of teleioo, having been made perfect). The key is Heb 11:39-40: the OT faithful "received NOT the promise" and are "not made perfect" apart from us. The perfection is covenantal/legal -- achieved through Christ's sacrifice (Heb 10:14), not through conscious existence in heaven. Relationship to other evidence: If literal, contradicts Heb 11:39-40 (same author: they received not the promise). The perfection described is covenantal, not locational.

docs.title: 2 Corinthians 12:2-4
docs.text: Context: Paul describes being caught up to the third heaven / paradise. Direct statement: "Caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words." Original language: Harpagenta (G726, caught up) eis ton paradeison (into paradise G3857). This was a LIVING person's experience, not a death experience. It tells us paradise exists but nothing about the death-state. Relationship to other evidence: Proves paradise exists but says nothing about dead people being conscious there. Paul was alive during this vision.

docs.title: Genesis 4:10
docs.text: Context: Abel's blood cries from the ground. Direct statement: "Thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground." Original language: Forensic personification -- blood does not literally have a voice. This is the OT precedent for the "crying" of the souls under the altar in Rev 6:9-11. Relationship to other evidence: If Rev 6:9-11 proves consciousness because the souls cry out, then Gen 4:10 proves Abel's blood is conscious. Both are personification.

docs.title: Jude 1:9
docs.text: Context: Michael's dispute with the devil over Moses's body. Direct statement: "Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses." Original language: Peri tou Mouseos somatos (about the body of Moses, G4983). The dispute was about the physical body. Why contend for a body unless resurrection was at stake? Relationship to other evidence: Explains Moses's appearance at the transfiguration: he was resurrected, not a disembodied spirit. Eliminates the transfiguration as evidence for conscious intermediate state.

docs.title: Revelation 14:13
docs.text: Context: A beatitude for the dead in the Lord. Direct statement: "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours." Original language: Anapausontai (G373, Fut Mid Ind 3P, they shall rest) ek ton kopon auton (from their labours). Same word used in Rev 6:11 for the souls told to "rest." Cross-references: Rev 6:11, Dan 12:13. Relationship to other evidence: The Spirit's characterization of the dead is REST -- cessation from labor. Their works "follow" them, implying future reward at resurrection.

docs.title: Pattern 1: OT Unanimity on Death as Unconsciousness
docs.text: At least 8 OT authors across 6+ books describe the dead as unconscious. The psalms (David, Heman, anonymous), the wisdom literature (Qoheleth), the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel), and the patriarchs (Job) all consistently characterize death as silence, darkness, forgetfulness, cessation of thought, cessation of praise, and ignorance. There is no OT passage that describes the dead as conscious in an intermediate state.

docs.title: Pattern 2: Death as Sleep Across Both Testaments
docs.text: The sleep metaphor spans from Moses (Deu 31:16) through the kings (1 Ki 2:10), wisdom literature (Dan 12:2, Jer 51:39), Jesus himself (John 11:11, Matt 9:24), and the apostles (Acts 7:60, 13:36, 1 Cor 15:6,18,20,51, 1 Thess 4:13-15, 5:10). At least 7 biblical authors use this language. God himself uses it (Deu 31:16). The LXX's translation of shakab (H7901) as koimao (G2837) creates a unifying semantic chain across testaments.

docs.title: Pattern 3: Resurrection as the Moment of Being with the Lord
docs.text: Every passage that specifies WHEN believers receive their reward, are transformed, or are "with the Lord" places this at the resurrection, not at death: John 6:39,40,44,54 (at the last day), 1 Thess 4:16-17 (dead rise first, THEN we are with the Lord), Dan 12:2,13 (awake/stand at the end of days), 2 Tim 4:8 (at that day), Rev 20:4-6 (lived at the first resurrection).

docs.title: Pattern 4: The 1 Corinthians 15:18 Test
docs.text: Paul's own logic: if there is no resurrection, those who have died in Christ have PERISHED (apollymi G622). This argument only works if the dead are NOT already in conscious bliss. Every alleged conscious intermediate state passage must be tested against this: if believers were already with Christ at death, Paul's reductio fails.

docs.title: Pattern 5: All Alleged Conscious State Passages Involve Genre, Grammar, or Context Issues
docs.text: Every passage cited for conscious intermediate state involves at least one of: (a) parabolic genre (Luke 16:19-31), (b) apocalyptic genre (Rev 6:9-11), (c) editorial punctuation absent from the Greek (Luke 23:43), (d) aorist infinitives that do not specify temporal relationships (2 Cor 5:8, Phil 1:23), (e) condemned necromancy (1 Sam 28), (f) a "vision" (Matt 17:1-9), (g) preaching in Noah's time, not post-mortem (1 Pet 3:18-20), or (h) covenantal rather than locational language (Heb 12:23). None of them is a didactic, unambiguous statement that the dead are conscious.

docs.title: Pattern 6: Anthropological Foundation -- Man IS a Soul
docs.text: Gen 2:7 establishes that man BECAME a living soul (nephesh chayyah) -- the same term used for animals (Gen 1:24). Nephesh can die (Ezek 18:4), be destroyed (Matt 10:28), and refer to corpses (Lev 21:11, Num 6:6). Ruach (spirit/breath) is the animating principle shared with animals (Ecc 3:19), not a conscious immaterial entity. When ruach departs, thoughts perish (Psa 146:4).

docs.title: Word Study Integration
docs.text: The word studies confirm the following: - Sheol (H7585, 68 occ.) and hades (G86, 11 occ.) are semantically equivalent (LXX: 58x). Both describe the holding place of all dead, characterized by unconsciousness, silence, and darkness. Hades is temporary (Rev 20:13-14). - Shakab (H7901, 262 occ.) maps to koimao (G2837, 19 occ.) in the LXX, creating the OT-NT sleep-death chain. Approximately 36 kings use the shakab death formula. - Yashen (H3462, 21 occ.) and katheudo (G2518, 23 occ.) provide additional sleep-death vocabulary. - Nephesh (H5315, 788 occ.) and psyche (G5590, 105 occ.) mean "life/being/self" rather than "immortal soul." Both can die/be destroyed. - Ruach (H7307, 434 occ.) and pneuma (G4151, 385 occ.) mean "breath/spirit/wind" -- the animating principle, not the conscious self. Animals share the same ruach (Ecc 3:19). - Athanasia (G110, 3 occ.) and aphtharsia (G861, 8 occ.) establish immortality as a divine gift acquired at resurrection, not a human possession. - Paradeisos (G3857, 3 occ.) does not establish a conscious intermediate state. One use is a living person's vision (2 Cor 12:4), one is eschatological (Rev 2:7), and one involves editorial punctuation issues (Luke 23:43). - Horama (G3705, 12 occ.) is Jesus's own classification of the transfiguration as a "vision."

docs.title: Cross-Testament Connections
docs.text:
1. Gen 2:7 -> Ecc 12:7 -> Psa 146:4: Creation formula and its reversal at death. Dust + breath = living being. At death: dust returns, spirit returns, thoughts perish.
  2. Psa 16:10 -> Acts 2:27,31: Sheol/hades chain. David's psalm about not being left in sheol applied to Christ's resurrection. Peter explicitly states David himself HAS NOT ascended (Acts 2:34).
  3. Shakab (H7901) -> koimao (G2837): The LXX translates the OT death-sleep word with the NT death-sleep word, creating a unified cross-testament vocabulary.
  4. Dan 12:2 -> 1 Thess 4:16-17: OT sleep-awakening language fulfilled in NT resurrection chronology. Both describe the dead as sleeping until the eschatological event.
  5. Gen 4:10 -> Rev 6:9-11: Abel's blood crying from the ground -> souls under the altar crying. Same literary device (forensic personification) across testaments.
  6. Lev 4:7,18,25,30 -> Rev 6:9: OT sacrificial blood poured at the altar base -> souls under the altar. The OT sacrificial system provides the imagery.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The evidence divides into two categories: (1) direct, didactic statements about the state of the dead, and (2) passages that allegedly describe conscious intermediate state.

Category 1 is overwhelmingly consistent. At least 8 OT authors across 6+ books describe the dead as unconscious (no thoughts, no knowledge, no praise, no remembrance, silence, darkness, forgetfulness). The NT continues this pattern with death-as-sleep vocabulary used by Jesus and the apostles. Resurrection, not death, is presented as the moment of receiving eternal life and being with the Lord. Paul's own argument in 1 Cor 15:18 confirms: without resurrection, the dead have perished.

Category 2 involves passages that, upon examination, each involve genre complications (parabolic, apocalyptic), grammatical ambiguity (aorist infinitives, editorial punctuation), contextual qualifications (same-letter resurrection hope, condemned necromancy, "the vision"), or covenantal rather than locational language. None is a direct didactic statement that the dead are conscious.

The weight of evidence points in a single direction: the dead are unconscious between death and resurrection. Resurrection is the biblical hope.

Analysis completed: 2026-06-03

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Condition of the dead -- conscious or unconscious? What happens between death and resurrection? Examine ALL Old Testament death-state passages (the dead know nothing, thoughts perish, no praise, silence, forgetfulness, sleep), ALL New Testament death-as-sleep passages, and ALL alleged conscious intermediate state passages (2 Cor 5:1-9, Phil 1:23, Luke 23:43, Luke 16:19-31, Rev 6:9-11, 1 Sam 28:3-20, Matt 17:1-9, 1 Pet 3:18-20). Examine the Hebrew and Greek 'sleep' vocabulary (shakab H7901, yashen H3462, koimao G2837, katheudo G2518) and 'rest/waiting' vocabulary. Investigate sheol (H7585) and hades (G86) as the abode of the dead.

docs.title: H7585 — sheol
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7585-showl.md

Occurrences: 68

Sheol (shᵉʼôwl) — feminine noun from uncertain root. The abode/world of the dead (subterranean retreat). 68 tokens across 64 unique verses in 17 books. KJV translates as 'hell' (48.4%), 'grave' (40.6%), 'pit' (4.7%). Receives both righteous (Jacob Gen 37:35, David Psa 16:10, Hezekiah Isa 38:10) and wicked (Korah Num 16:30-33). Characterized by silence (Psa 115:17), no work/knowledge/wisdom (Ecc 9:10), darkness (Job 10:21-22), no praise (Psa 6:5, Isa 38:18-19), forgetfulness (Psa 88:12).

Semantic categories: the grave/abode of all dead, unconsciousness and silence, temporary holding until resurrection

Key verses: Gen 37:35, Psa 16:10, Ecc 9:10, Psa 6:5, Psa 115:17, Isa 38:18-19

Relevance: Central term for where the dead go. Every sheol characterization describes unconsciousness, silence, and cessation — not conscious existence. This is the E-item foundation for the conditionalist position.

docs.title: G86 — hades
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G86-háidēs.md

Occurrences: 11

Hades (háidēs) — from alpha-privative + eido = 'unseen.' NT equivalent of sheol. 11 occurrences across 5 books. LXX translates sheol as hades 58 times. Acts 2:27,31 confirm equivalence by quoting Psa 16:10. Three semantic categories: (1) general realm of the dead (Acts 2:27,31; 1 Cor 15:55), (2) judgment context (Matt 11:23, Luke 10:15, Luke 16:23), (3) defeated power (Rev 1:18, 6:8, 20:13-14). Hades is TEMPORARY — cast into lake of fire (Rev 20:14).

Semantic categories: realm of the dead (= sheol), defeated power, temporary holding

Key verses: Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, Matt 16:18, Rev 1:18, Rev 20:13-14, Luke 16:23

Relevance: NT equivalent of sheol. The sheol→hades equivalence (confirmed by Acts 2:27,31 quoting Psa 16:10) means all OT sheol characterizations (unconsciousness, silence) apply to hades. Hades is temporary — not the final state.

docs.title: H3462 — yashen
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H3462-yâshên.md

Occurrences: 21

Yashen (yâshên) — primitive root verb meaning to be slack/languid, to sleep; figuratively to die; also to grow old. 21 occurrences across 12+ books. Used for death-sleep in Dan 12:2 ('many of them that sleep in the dust'), Jer 51:39 ('sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake'), Psa 13:3 ('lest I sleep the sleep of death'). The death-sleep metaphor implies unconsciousness — sleep is a state without awareness.

Semantic categories: literal sleep, death as sleep, perpetual sleep

Key verses: Dan 12:2, Jer 51:39, Psa 13:3

Relevance: One of four key sleep-death vocabulary words. Dan 12:2 uses yashen for the dead who await resurrection ('awake'). The metaphor of sleep for death is foundational — it implies unconsciousness between death and resurrection.

docs.title: G2837 — koimao
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2837-koimao.md

Occurrences: 19

Koimao (κοιμάω) — verb meaning to put to sleep, to fall asleep, to die. 19 occurrences across 7 books. The standard NT term for death as sleep. Used by Jesus (John 11:11), Luke (Acts 7:60, 13:36), Paul (1 Cor 15:6,18,20,51; 1 Thess 4:13-15), and Peter (2 Pet 3:4). 1 Cor 15:18: if no resurrection, those 'fallen asleep' (koimethentes) have PERISHED — proving sleep = unconscious state, not conscious heavenly existence.

Semantic categories: literal sleep, death as sleep (euphemism), resurrection awaited

Key verses: John 11:11, Acts 7:60, 1 Cor 15:6, 1 Cor 15:18, 1 Cor 15:51, 1 Thess 4:14

Relevance: The NT standard death-sleep word. Used by 4+ authors including Jesus. 1 Cor 15:18 is the decisive test: if koimao meant conscious existence with Christ, Paul could not say the dead have 'perished' without resurrection.

docs.title: H5315 — nephesh
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5315-nephesh.md

Occurrences: 788

Nephesh — feminine noun from naphash (to breathe). 788 tokens across 682 verses in 31 books. Extraordinary breadth: 214 unique KJV translations. Primary meanings: soul (64%), life (14%), person (4%), reflexive self (2%), desire/appetite (3%), creature (1%), dead body (1%). Man BECAME a nephesh chayyah (Gen 2:7) — did not receive one. Animals are also nephesh chayyah (Gen 1:24). Nephesh can DIE (Ezek 18:4, Num 31:19), be DESTROYED (Matt 10:28 psyche), and refer to CORPSES (Lev 21:11, Num 6:6).

Semantic categories: living being/creature, life/vitality, person/self, desire/appetite, corpse/dead body

Key verses: Gen 2:7, Gen 1:24, Ezek 18:4, Lev 21:11, Num 6:6

Relevance: Foundational for understanding what 'dies' at death. Man IS a soul (holistic), not HAS a soul (dualistic). Nephesh can die (Ezek 18:4) and refers to corpses — it is not an inherently immortal entity.

docs.title: G5590 — psyche
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5590-psyche.md

Occurrences: 105

Psyche (ψυχή) — feminine noun from psycho (to breathe/blow cool). 105 NT occurrences. NT equivalent of nephesh. Semantic domains: psychological faculties, life/death, person, creature, attitudes. Can be destroyed (Matt 10:28). Rev 6:9 'souls' (psychas) under the altar = lives/selves of martyrs, not disembodied spirits. The lexicon note on 'immortal soul' is a Greek-philosophical import, not a biblical doctrine.

Semantic categories: life/vitality, person/self, psychological faculty, creature

Key verses: Matt 2:20, Matt 10:28, Rev 6:9, Acts 2:41

Relevance: NT equivalent of nephesh. Rev 6:9 uses psychas for the martyrs under the altar — understanding psyche as 'life/self' rather than 'immaterial soul' changes the interpretation of this passage entirely.

docs.title: H7307 — ruach
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7307-ruach.md

Occurrences: 434

Ruach (rûwach) — feminine noun. 434 occurrences. Translated as spirit (53.7%), wind (21.4%), breath (7.6%), and other. The animating principle shared by humans and animals (Ecc 3:19). Returns to God at death (Ecc 12:7). Never used for corpses. When ruach departs, thoughts PERISH (Psa 146:4) — ruach is the life-force, not the conscious self.

Semantic categories: wind/breath, divine Spirit, human spirit/disposition, life-force/animating principle

Key verses: Gen 1:2, Ecc 12:7, Ecc 3:19, Psa 146:4, Psa 104:29-30

Relevance: What returns to God at death. Shared with animals (Ecc 3:19), proving ruach is the animating principle, not a conscious immaterial soul. Combined with Psa 146:4 (thoughts perish when ruach departs), ruach's departure = cessation of consciousness.

docs.title: G4151 — pneuma
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4151-pneuma.md

Occurrences: 385

Pneuma (πνεῦμα) — neuter noun from pneo (to blow/breathe). 385 occurrences. Extremely wide semantic range: Holy Spirit, demonic spirits, angels, wind, breath, life-force, inner disposition. Stephen commits his pneuma to Jesus (Acts 7:59) — paralleling Jesus (Luke 23:46) and fulfilling Ecc 12:7. The next verse says Stephen 'fell asleep' — pneuma commitment is not immediate conscious presence but trust in God's keeping.

Semantic categories: Holy Spirit, human spirit/disposition, breath/wind, demonic spirits, life-force

Key verses: Acts 7:59, Luke 23:46, 1 Pet 3:19, James 2:26

Relevance: NT equivalent of ruach. Stephen's pneuma-commitment + sleep language (Acts 7:59-60) demonstrates that commending one's spirit to God is an act of trust, not immediate conscious transfer.

docs.title: H5397 — neshamah
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5397-nshamah.md

Occurrences: 25

Neshamah (nᵉshâmâh) — feminine noun from nasham (to blow away). 25 tokens across 24 verses in 10 books. Translated as breath (42%), breathe (21%), blast (12.5%), spirit (8.3%), inspiration (4.2%). The breath God breathed into man at creation (Gen 2:7). Appears in destruction contexts (breath of God's nostrils = divine judgment). Psa 150:6: 'let everything that hath breath praise the LORD' — this ceases at death (Psa 115:17).

Semantic categories: breath of life (creation), divine breath (judgment), all breathing things

Key verses: Gen 2:7, Job 33:4, Isa 2:22, Psa 150:6

Relevance: The specific term in Gen 2:7 — what God breathed into man. When neshamah ceases (Psa 146:4 uses ruach, the parallel term), the living being ceases. Not a conscious soul but the breath of life.

docs.title: H4194 — maveth
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H4194-maveth.md

Occurrences: 170

Maveth — masculine noun, primary Hebrew word for death. From muwth (H4191, to die). Paired frequently with sheol. Used for the death sentence (Gen 2:17), the state of death, and personified death. Isa 38:18: 'death (maveth) cannot celebrate thee.'

Semantic categories: physical death, death personified, death as a state

Key verses: Gen 2:17, Psa 6:5, Isa 38:18, Hos 13:14

Relevance: Primary Hebrew death term. Every maveth context describes cessation, not conscious survival. Paired with sheol to describe the state of the dead.

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

Thanatos — masculine noun, primary Greek word for death. 119 occurrences. Includes 'second death' (Rev 20:14, 21:8). Defeated enemy that shall be destroyed (1 Cor 15:26). Death and hades cast into lake of fire (Rev 20:14) — death itself is abolished.

Semantic categories: physical death, second death, death as enemy, spiritual death (metaphorical)

Key verses: Rom 6:23, 1 Cor 15:26, Rev 20:14, Heb 2:14

Relevance: NT death vocabulary. The 'second death' uses the same word, showing death means death, not eternal conscious existence.

docs.title: G110 — athanasia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G110-athanasia.md

Occurrences: 3

Athanasia — feminine noun from alpha-privative + thanatos = 'deathlessness/immortality.' Only 3 occurrences: 1 Cor 15:53 (mortals must PUT ON immortality), 1 Cor 15:54 (mortal puts on immortality → death swallowed), 1 Tim 6:16 (God ALONE has immortality). The rarity and exclusivity are significant — immortality is not a human possession but a divine gift acquired at resurrection.

Semantic categories: divine attribute, resurrection gift, deathlessness

Key verses: 1 Tim 6:16, 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54

Relevance: Only 3 occurrences, all establishing that immortality belongs to God alone and is acquired by believers at resurrection. The phrase 'immortal soul' never appears in Scripture.

docs.title: G861 — aphtharsia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G861-aphtharsia.md

Occurrences: 8

Aphtharsia — incorruption/immortality. 8 occurrences. Something to SEEK (Rom 2:7), brought to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10), PUT ON at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54). Every usage presents incorruption as a future acquisition, not a present possession.

Semantic categories: incorruption, immortality as gift, resurrection quality

Key verses: Rom 2:7, 1 Cor 15:53-54, 2 Tim 1:10

Relevance: Paired with athanasia. Both terms describe what mortals ACQUIRE at resurrection. If humans already had an incorruptible/immortal component, these passages would be meaningless.

docs.title: G386 — anastasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G386-anastasis.md

Occurrences: 42

Anastasis — feminine noun from anistemi (to stand up again). 42 occurrences. The consistent biblical hope for the dead: bodily resurrection. Used by Jesus (Matt 22:23-32, John 5:29, 6:39-40,44,54, 11:25), Paul (1 Cor 15, Phil 3:11, 1 Thess 4:16), Peter (Acts 2:31, 4:2), and Hebrews author (6:2, 11:35). Acts 4:2: the Sadducees were grieved that the apostles 'preached through Jesus the resurrection from the dead.'

Semantic categories: bodily resurrection, the biblical hope, eschatological event

Key verses: John 11:25, 1 Cor 15:42, Phil 3:11, Acts 2:31, Rev 20:5-6

Relevance: The consistent biblical alternative to 'going to heaven at death.' Resurrection — not death — is when believers receive their reward, are transformed, and are 'with the Lord.'

docs.title: G373 — anapauo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G373-anapauo.md

Occurrences: 13

Anapauo — verb from ana + pauo (to cease). 13 tokens across 12 verses in 8 books. Means to cause to rest, to give rest, to take rest. Rev 6:11: souls told to 'rest' (anapausontai). Rev 14:13: dead in the Lord 'rest from their labours.' The death-rest vocabulary treats death as cessation of activity.

Semantic categories: physical rest, spiritual rest, death as rest/cessation

Key verses: Matt 11:28, Rev 6:11, Rev 14:13

Relevance: Links Rev 6:11 (souls told to rest) with Rev 14:13 (dead rest from labours). Death is described as rest/cessation — not conscious activity.

docs.title: H5117 — nuwach
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5117-nuwach.md

Occurrences: 108

Nuwach — verb meaning to rest, settle, be quiet. Dan 12:13: 'thou shalt rest (tanuwach), and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.' Death = rest, resurrection = standing in one's lot. The OT rest-death vocabulary.

Semantic categories: physical rest, cessation from activity, death as rest

Key verses: Dan 12:13, Isa 57:2, Job 3:13

Relevance: Dan 12:13 explicitly connects rest (nuwach) with death and standing in one's lot (resurrection) 'at the end of the days.' Death is rest until the eschatological awakening.

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

Apollymi — to destroy utterly, to perish, to lose. Used in 1 Cor 15:18: if no resurrection, believers have 'perished' (apolonto, Aor Mid Ind 3P). This is the decisive cross-reference for conscious intermediate state claims — if the dead were already in conscious bliss, they could not 'perish' without resurrection.

Semantic categories: destruction, perishing, loss

Key verses: 1 Cor 15:18, Matt 10:28, John 3:16

Relevance: 1 Cor 15:18 is the logical test for every conscious intermediate state claim. Paul's own argument proves that without resurrection, dead believers are destroyed — impossible if they are already consciously with Christ.

docs.title: G4983 — soma
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4983-soma.md

Occurrences: 146

Soma — body. Used in 2 Cor 5:8 (absent from the body), Phil 1:20 (Christ magnified in my body), Phil 3:21 (shall change our vile body). The soma is what is transformed at resurrection, not discarded for disembodied existence.

Semantic categories: physical body, resurrection body, embodied existence

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:8, Phil 3:21, 1 Cor 15:44

Relevance: Key to the 2 Cor 5 and Phil 1-3 passages. Paul's hope is a resurrection BODY, not disembodied existence. He explicitly does not want to be 'unclothed' (2 Cor 5:4).

docs.title: G3705 — horama
docs.text:
Occurrences: 12

Horama — vision, that which is seen. Jesus uses this word to describe the transfiguration in Matt 17:9: 'Tell the vision (horama) to no man.' Used elsewhere for supernatural visions (Acts 7:31, 9:10, 10:3, 10:17, 10:19, 11:5, 12:9, 16:9-10, 18:9). The transfiguration was a visionary experience, not proof of conscious intermediate state.

Semantic categories: supernatural vision, that which is seen

Key verses: Matt 17:9, Acts 10:3, Acts 16:9

Relevance: Jesus himself classifies the transfiguration as a 'vision' (horama), not as evidence that Moses was consciously alive in an intermediate state. Moses was resurrected (Jude 1:9), Elijah was translated (2 Ki 2:11).

docs.title: H7901 — shakab
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7901-shâkab.md

Occurrences: 262

Shakab (shâkab) — primitive root verb meaning to lie down for rest, sexual connection, decease, or any other purpose. 262 occurrences. The most theologically significant usage is the death formula 'slept with his fathers' (wayyishkab 'im-'abotayw) used for ~36 kings in 1-2 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Also used in Job 14:12 ('man lieth down and riseth not'), Isa 14:18, Ezek 32 (slain warriors in sheol). LXX maps primarily to koimaomai (G2837, 141x, PMI 6.6) and katheudo (G2518, 19x, PMI 6.61). Death formula presents death as lying down to sleep among ancestors — unconscious repose.

Semantic categories: death formula: slept with his fathers, death and the grave (non-formulaic), physical rest and sleep, sexual relations (euphemistic)

Key verses: 1 Ki 2:10, 1 Ki 11:43, Deu 31:16, Job 14:12, Job 3:13, Isa 14:18

Relevance: OT 'lie down/sleep' used for death; 'sleep with thy fathers' formula appears ~36 times for kings. LXX translates with koimaomai (G2837), which becomes the NT death-as-sleep word. The semantic chain shakab → koimao establishes death-as-sleep as a unified biblical concept across Testaments.

docs.title: G2518 — katheudo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2518-katheudo.md

Occurrences: 23

Katheudo (καθεύδω) — verb from kata (G2596) + heudo (to sleep); to lie down to rest, fall asleep. 23 occurrences across 5 books (Matt 8, Mark 8, Luke 2, Eph 1, 1 Thess 4). Three semantic categories: (1) literal physical sleep, (2) sleep of death/euphemism — Jesus uses this for death in Matt 9:24, Mark 5:39, Luke 8:52, and Paul in 1 Thess 5:10, (3) spiritual lethargy/moral unconsciousness. Antonym: gregoreo (G1127, to watch/be vigilant).

Semantic categories: literal physical sleep, sleep of death (euphemism), spiritual lethargy or moral unconsciousness

Key verses: Matt 9:24, Mark 5:39, Luke 8:52, 1 Thess 5:10, 1 Thess 5:6

Relevance: NT 'sleep' used for death by Jesus himself (Matt 9:24). Distinguished from koimao (G2837): katheudo is the common word for literal sleep occasionally extended to death, while koimao is the standard NT death-euphemism. Both words used by Jesus for death establish the sleep metaphor as authoritative.

docs.title: G3857 — paradeisos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3857-paradeisos.md

Occurrences: 3

Paradeisos (παράδεισος) — masculine noun of Oriental origin (cf. H6508 pardes); a park, Eden, place of future happiness. Only 3 NT occurrences: Luke 23:43 (Jesus to the thief), 2 Cor 12:4 (Paul caught up to paradise = third heaven), Rev 2:7 (tree of life in the paradise of God). LXX uses paradeisos to translate Hebrew gan (garden, H1588) especially for the Garden of Eden. The eschatological paradise (Rev 2:7) connects to the restored Eden with the tree of life (Rev 22:2), identifying paradise as the future new creation rather than a present intermediate state.

Semantic categories: present abode of the righteous dead (alleged), heavenly/third heaven realm, eschatological restored Eden

Key verses: Luke 23:43, 2 Cor 12:4, Rev 2:7

Relevance: Only 3 NT uses. Luke 23:43 is the key death-state passage — but Jesus was NOT in paradise on that day (John 20:17). 2 Cor 12:4 describes a living person's vision. Rev 2:7 is eschatological (tree of life in paradise of God). The word itself does not establish a conscious intermediate state.

docs.title: Classification Audit Trail — etc7-04 State of the Dead
docs.text: This document contains the full Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for every E-item classified Cond. or ECT, and every N-item. Each walkthrough uses actual parser output for Gate 2 verification.

docs.title: E-Items Classified Cond.
docs.text:
E1 (Psa 146:4) -- "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "perish" (abad) applied to thoughts of the dying person. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject is a generic human being (context: "princes," v.3, i.e. mortal men). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: abad (Verb.Qal.Perf.3p = "perish," completed action); eshtonoth (Noun.fp.Abs.+3ms = "his thoughts"). Grammar unambiguously states thoughts perish when breath departs. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm -- direct didactic statement within a hymn of praise. Not parabolic or apocalyptic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E2 (Ecc 9:5, dead know nothing), E3 (Ecc 9:6, love/hatred/envy perished), E4 (Ecc 9:10, no knowledge in sheol), E5 (Psa 6:5, no remembrance), E9 (Job 14:21, dead know not). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E2 (Ecc 9:5) -- "The dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- negation of knowledge/awareness applied to the dead. Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The dead" (hammetim, Qal ptcp of muwth) -- literal dead human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: hammetim (Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs) einam (Noun.ms.Abs.+3mp = NEG) yodim (Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs = knowing) meumah (Noun.fs.Abs = something/anything). Double negation: ein + meumah = absolute nothing. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, direct didactic observation. Not parabolic or apocalyptic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1, E3-E12, E14. No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E3 (Ecc 9:6) -- "Their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "perished" (abad) applied to emotional/volitional capacities of the dead. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead (continuing from v.5). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: ahavah (love), sinah (hatred), qinah (jealousy) -- avdah (Verb.Qal.Perf.3fs = perished, completed action). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1, E2, E4-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E4 (Ecc 9:10) -- "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave [sheol]" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- negation of all activity and cognition in sheol. Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Generic human going to sheol ("whither thou goest"). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: ein (Noun.ms.Cst = NEG) + maaseh (deed) + cheshbon (account) + daath (knowledge) + chokmah (wisdom) + bisheol (in sheol). Four-fold existential negation. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, didactic imperative. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E3, E5-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E5 (Psa 6:5) -- "In death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave [sheol] who shall give thee thanks?" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- negation of remembrance and thanksgiving in death/sheol. Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): David speaking about the dead generically. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: bammavet ein zikrekha (in death there is not remembrance of you). Bisheol mi yodeh lakh (in sheol who will praise you -- rhetorical question expecting "no one"). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of lament, direct didactic statement about death. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E4, E6-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E6 (Psa 115:17) -- "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- negation of praise; descent into "silence" (dumah). Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The dead" (hammetim) -- literal dead humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: lo (Neg) hammetim (Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs = the dead) yehallu (Verb.Piel.Impf.3mp = will praise) Yah (the LORD). Kol-yordey (Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Cst = all descending into) dumah (Noun.fs.Abs = silence). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of praise, didactic statement. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E5, E7-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E7 (Psa 88:10-12) -- "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee?" etc. -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- series of rhetorical negations about the dead: no wonders, no praise, no lovingkindness, no faithfulness, no righteousness, "land of forgetfulness." Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The dead" (hammetim), refaim (shades). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: ha-lammetim (interrogative + to-the-dead) taaseh-pele (will you do wonder)? im-refaim (if-shades) yaqumu (will arise) yodukha (praise you)? Interrogative construction expecting "no." Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of lament, didactic questions. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E6, E8-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E8 (Job 14:12) -- "Man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "riseth not," "shall not awake," "sleep" -- cessation/death-sleep vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "Man" (generic human being). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Yishkab (from shakab H7901) velo-yaqum (and does not arise). Grammar unambiguous: death is lying down without rising. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, direct speech in didactic poetry. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E7, E9-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E9 (Job 14:21) -- "His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- double negation of perception: "knoweth it not," "perceiveth it not." Cessation of awareness. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): A dead man (continuing from the death described in vv.10-14). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Velo-yeda (and he knows not) ... velo-yabin (and he perceives not). Two distinct verbs (yada, bin) both negated. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, direct speech. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E8, E10-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E10 (Isa 38:18-19) -- "The grave cannot praise thee, death cannot celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- triple negation: cannot praise, cannot celebrate, cannot hope. Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead generically (sheol, mavet, yordey-bor). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Sheol cannot todekha (praise you), mavet cannot yehalelekha (celebrate you), yordey-bor cannot yesabberu (hope for). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Hezekiah's prayer -- direct speech, didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E9, E11-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E11 (Psa 30:9) -- "Shall the dust praise thee? shall it declare thy truth?" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- rhetorical questions expecting "no." The dead (dust) cannot praise or declare. Cessation. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "Dust" = the dead (metonymy for dead person). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hayodekha aphar (will dust praise you)? Hayaggid amittekha (will it declare your truth)? Interrogative expecting "no." Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of thanksgiving, didactic rhetorical question. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E10, E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E12 (Isa 26:14) -- "They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou ... made all their memory to perish" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "dead," "shall not live," "shall not rise," "memory to perish." Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Oppressive rulers -- literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Methim bal-yichyu (dead, shall not live). Refaim bal-yaqumu (deceased, shall not rise). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Prophetic song, direct statement. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E11. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E13 (Job 3:17-18) -- "There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest. There the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "cease," "rest," "hear not." Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): All dead humans (wicked, weary, prisoners). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Chadal (cease) from rogez (troubling). Lo shamu (hear not) the voice. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature, direct speech. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E12. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E14 (Acts 2:34) -- "David is not ascended into the heavens" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- explicit denial of heavenly ascent for a dead righteous person. Cessation/unconsciousness direction. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): David -- literal, historical human being. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: ou (PRT-N) gar (CONJ) Daueid (N-PRI, Nom Sg M) anebe (V-2AAI-3S, Aor Act Ind 3s of anabaino G305 = ascended) eis tous ouranous (into the heavens). Negation particle ou + aorist verb = "David did not ascend." Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Apostolic sermon -- direct didactic teaching under Holy Spirit inspiration (Acts 2:4). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E13. If the righteous dead ascend to heaven, Peter's statement is false. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E15 (Heb 11:39-40) -- "These all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- OT saints "received NOT the promise." They are not yet in their reward. Death did not bring them fulfillment. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): OT heroes of faith (Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, etc.) -- literal humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: ouk (PRT-N) ekomisanto (V-AMI-3P, Aor Mid Ind Pl 3rd of komizo = received/carried off) ten epaggelian (the promise). Grammar unambiguous: they did not receive the promise. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Epistle -- direct didactic teaching. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E14 (David not ascended). If OT saints are already in heaven, the author's statement is false. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E16 (1 Cor 15:18) -- "Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "perished" (apollymi) applied to dead believers if there is no resurrection. Destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Dead believers ("fallen asleep in Christ") -- literal humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: koimethentes (V-APP-NPM, Aor Pass Ptcp of koimaomai G2837 = those having fallen asleep) en Christo (in Christ) apolonto (V-2AMI-3P, Aor Mid Ind 3P of apollymi G622 = perished). Grammar unambiguous: Paul states that without resurrection, the dead in Christ have perished. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Epistle -- direct didactic argument (reductio ad absurdum). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1-E15. If dead believers were already in conscious bliss, they could not "perish" without resurrection. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E17 (Ezek 18:4) -- "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "die" (muwth) applied to the soul (nephesh). Death vocabulary applied to the soul itself. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The soul" (nephesh) = the person. Literal human. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hannephesh hachote't hi tamut (the soul sinning, it shall die). Emphatic pronoun hi (it). Grammar unambiguous: the soul itself dies. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Prophetic oracle -- direct speech of God ("Thus says the Lord GOD"). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E18 (Matt 10:28, soul can be destroyed). PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E18 (Matt 10:28) -- "Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destroy" (apollymi G622) applied to soul and body. Destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Soul and body of a human being. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Apollesai (Aor Act Inf of apollymi G622 = to destroy) kai psychen kai soma (both soul and body) en geenne (in gehenna). Grammar unambiguous: God is able to destroy (not merely torment) both soul and body. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Jesus's direct teaching -- didactic instruction. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E17 (soul that sins shall die). PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E19 (1 Tim 6:16) -- "Who only hath immortality" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- God ALONE has immortality; implies no human possesses it inherently. Supports conditional immortality. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): God. Statement is about divine exclusivity. Implication falls on humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Monos (G3440, alone/only) echon (having) athanasin (immortality G110). Grammar unambiguous: "alone having" admits no exceptions. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Epistle -- doxology within didactic letter. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E16 (dead perish without resurrection), E17-E18 (soul can die/be destroyed). PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E20 (Gen 3:19) -- "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- death defined as return to dust. No surviving consciousness mentioned. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Adam / generic humanity. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Aphar attah veel-aphar tashuv (dust you are and to dust you shall return). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Narrative -- direct speech of God. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1 (thoughts perish), E21 (Gen 2:7, creation formula). PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E-Items with Candidate ECT (Tree 3 Walkthrough)
docs.text:
E41 (Luke 16:23) -- "In hell [hades] he lift up his eyes, being in torments" -- Candidate: ECT

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "torments" (basanois G931), conscious experience in hades. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "A certain rich man" (anthropos tis plousios) -- a character in a parabolic narrative. The opening formula matches Luke 12:16 (labeled parabole) and 16:1 (universally parabolic). Luke 15:3 provides a single parabole label for the discourse. FAIL. Subject is a parabolic character, not a literal human.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Parabolic discourse (Luke 15:3-16:31). FAIL. Genre is parabolic.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Gate 1 fails (parabolic character). Gate 3 fails (parabolic genre).
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "A parabolic character is depicted in torments in hades within a parable whose stated point is 'they have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them' (vv.29,31)."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1/V2: Parabolic depiction does not constitute didactic teaching about the literal state of the dead. Neither V1 nor V2 applies to a parabolic character as evidence about human fate.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Classification revised to: Neutral.

E42 (Rev 6:9-11) -- "I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain ... they cried with a loud voice" -- Candidate: ECT

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "cried out" could suggest conscious activity. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "Souls" (psychas G5590) under the altar in an apocalyptic vision. Every surrounding element is symbolic (seals, horsemen, stars falling, sky rolling up). Parallel: Abel's blood "cries" from the ground (Gen 4:10) -- forensic personification. Rev 16:7: the altar itself speaks. FAIL. Subjects are symbolic vision-figures, not literal humans.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Apocalyptic vision (Revelation's seal sequence). FAIL. Genre is apocalyptic.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Gate 1 fails (symbolic vision-figures). Gate 3 fails (apocalyptic genre).
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, symbolic figures under a symbolic altar cry out in the manner of Abel's blood crying from the ground."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1/V2: Apocalyptic personification does not constitute didactic teaching about human consciousness in death. Rev 20:4-5 states these same souls "LIVED" at the first resurrection -- they were not alive before.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Classification revised to: Neutral.

E43 (2 Cor 5:8) -- "Absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord" -- Candidate: ECT

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "present with the Lord" could suggest conscious existence after death. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Paul speaking about believers generally. Literal humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: ekdemesai (V-AAN, Aor Act Inf of ekdemeo G1553 = to be absent from) ek tou somatos (from the body) kai (CONJ) endemesai (V-AAN, Aor Act Inf of endemeo G1736 = to be at home with) pros ton Kurion (with the Lord). Two aorist infinitives connected by kai. The aorist DOES NOT specify temporal relationship or duration between the two events. The reading "absent from body THEREFORE IMMEDIATELY present with Lord" requires importing temporal simultaneity that the grammar does not contain. FAIL. Grammar allows alternative: death (absent from body) leads to resurrection (present with Lord) without specifying intervening duration.
  • Gate 2 additional: V.4 (same passage): Paul explicitly does NOT want to be ekdysasthai (unclothed/disembodied) but ependysasthai (clothed upon). Purpose: "that mortality (to thneton G2349) might be swallowed up by life (tes zoes G2222)" -- resurrection language from 1 Cor 15:54.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Gate 2 fails -- aorist infinitives do not specify temporal relationship; "immediately" is imported.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "Paul expresses willingness to depart from the body and be at home with the Lord, using two aorist infinitives that state both events without specifying the temporal relationship between them."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1/V2: The corrected observation contains neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary. It is a statement of Paul's preference and confidence.
  • Result: Gate 2 fails. Classification revised to: Neutral.

E44 (Phil 1:23) -- "Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" -- Candidate: ECT

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "to be with Christ" could suggest conscious intermediate state. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Paul. Literal human. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: analysai (V-AAN, Aor Act Inf of analyo G360 = to depart) kai (CONJ) syn Christo (with Christ) einai (V-PAN, Pres Act Inf of eimi = to be). The articular infinitive to analysai is paired with syn Christo einai via kai without specifying temporal duration between them. Same grammatical pattern as 2 Cor 5:8. FAIL. Grammar does not specify temporal immediacy between departing and being with Christ.
  • Gate 2 additional: Same letter -- Phil 3:11: "if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead" (ten exanastasin ten ek nekron). Phil 3:20-21: "we look for the Saviour...who shall change our vile body." Paul's hope is resurrection, not disembodied intermediate existence.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Gate 2 fails -- kai connecting two infinitives does not establish temporal immediacy.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "Paul expresses desire to depart and be with Christ, using two infinitives connected by kai that state both events without specifying temporal relationship."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1/V2: Corrected observation contains neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary.
  • Result: Gate 2 fails. Classification revised to: Neutral.

E45 (Luke 23:43) -- "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" -- Candidate: ECT

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "paradise" with "today" could suggest immediate conscious presence. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Jesus and the thief. Literal humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser: semeron (G4594, ADV = today). The adverb semeron can grammatically modify either lego (V-PAI-1S = I say) or ese (V-FDI-2S = you will be). Greek manuscripts contain NO punctuation. The comma placement is entirely editorial (inserted by translators). FAIL. Reading depends on editorial punctuation absent from the original Greek.
  • Gate 2 additional: John 20:17 -- three days later, Jesus told Mary: oupo (G3768, ADV-N = not yet) anababeka (V-RAI-1S, Perf Act Ind 1s of anabaino G305 = I have ascended) pros ton Patera (to the Father). If paradise = God's presence, Jesus was not there on Friday. The proposed ECT reading creates a direct contradiction with John 20:17.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Gate 2 fails -- reading depends on editorial comma placement absent from original Greek. John 20:17 contradicts the proposed reading.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "Jesus uses the formula 'Truly I say unto thee today' (semeron modifying lego, as in the Syriac Peshitta reading) followed by a promise of future paradise."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1/V2: Corrected observation contains neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary. It is a promise with unspecified timing.
  • Result: Gate 2 fails. Classification revised to: Neutral.

docs.title: N-Items (Tree 4 Walkthrough)
docs.text:
N1 -- "When ruach/breath departs, the entire person ceases conscious existence" -- Based on: E1, E2, E20, E21 -- Candidate: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): E1 says thoughts perish when breath departs. E2 says the dead know nothing. E20 says man returns to dust. E21 says man became a living being via dust + breath. If breath departs and dust returns, the living being ceases. Would an ECT scholar agree? An ECT scholar would argue that the "soul" continues. But that requires ADDING a concept (immortal soul) that E1-E2 explicitly negate (thoughts perish, know nothing). PASS -- the disagreement requires adding a concept the texts do not contain.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion from "thoughts perish" + "dead know nothing" + "dust returns"? Yes -- these statements together leave no room for continuing consciousness. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the E-items? No -- it merely states their combined entailment. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates:
  • V1: Cessation of consciousness. Candidate: COND.
  • Gate 1: Subject is humanity generically. PASS.
  • Gate 2: Grammar verified in E1, E2, E20, E21 parsers. PASS.
  • Gate 3: Source passages are didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4: Consistent with all Cond. E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

N2 -- "Resurrection, not death, is the moment when believers are 'with the Lord'" -- Based on: E16, E26, E27, E28 -- Candidate: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1: E16 says without resurrection the dead have perished. E27 says dead rise THEN "ever with the Lord." E28 says "raise him up at the last day" (4x). Would an ECT scholar agree that these texts place being-with-the-Lord at resurrection? An ECT scholar must acknowledge the texts say this -- they would add that other texts (2 Cor 5:8, Phil 1:23) indicate intermediate fellowship, but those texts were classified Neutral at E-tier. The N-item follows from the cited E-items without addition. PASS.
  • N-Test 2: Is this the only possible conclusion from "perished without resurrection" + "dead rise first, THEN ever with the Lord" + "raise him up at the last day"? Yes. PASS.
  • N-Test 3: Zero added concepts. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates: V1: Cessation direction. Gates 1-4 PASS (literal subjects, unambiguous grammar, didactic genre, no E-item conflict).
  • Result: Classification: Cond. stands.

N3 -- "The death-as-sleep metaphor, used by God, Jesus, and multiple biblical authors, describes death as unconscious repose" -- Based on: E24-E25, E30, E34-E35 -- Candidate: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1: Both sides acknowledge the sleep metaphor exists. An ECT scholar would say "sleep" is merely a euphemism, not a statement about consciousness. But the metaphor is used by God himself (E34, Deu 31:16), Jesus (E25, John 11:11), and multiple authors -- at minimum 7. The observation that these authors use this metaphor is factual. PASS.
  • N-Test 2: The observation itself (the metaphor exists and is widely used) is not disputed. PASS.
  • N-Test 3: No added concepts. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates: V1/V2: Neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary. The observation is about a shared literary pattern. Neutral.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

N4 -- "Sheol/hades is characterized by unconsciousness, silence, darkness, and cessation, not by conscious activity" -- Based on: E4, E5, E6, E7 -- Candidate: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1: E4 says no work, knowledge, wisdom in sheol. E5 says no remembrance in sheol. E6 says dead go into silence. E7 says no wonders, praise, faithfulness in the grave. Would an ECT scholar agree? An ECT scholar typically distinguishes sheol (OT) from the post-Christ situation, but they must acknowledge what THESE TEXTS say about sheol. The implication follows from the cited E-items. PASS.
  • N-Test 2: Only possible conclusion from these texts. PASS.
  • N-Test 3: No added concepts. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates: V1: Cessation vocabulary. Gates 1-4 PASS.
  • Result: Classification: Cond. stands.

N5 -- "Since God alone has immortality (E19) and the soul can die (E17, E18), human consciousness does not survive death by its own nature" -- Based on: E17, E18, E19 -- Candidate: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1: E19 says God alone has immortality. E17 says the soul that sins shall die. E18 says God can destroy soul and body. Would an ECT scholar agree that these texts, taken together, mean human consciousness does not survive death by its own nature? An ECT scholar would typically argue for immortality as a gift already given. But "God alone has immortality" (monos) and "the soul shall die" leave no room for inherent human immortality. PASS.
  • N-Test 2: Only possible conclusion from "God alone has immortality" + "souls can die." PASS.
  • N-Test 3: No concepts added beyond the E-items. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates: V1: Cessation/death vocabulary. Gates 1-4 PASS.
  • Result: Classification: Cond. stands.

N6 -- "The creation formula (Gen 2:7) and its reversal at death (Gen 3:19, Ecc 12:7, Psa 146:4) define death as the dissolution of the whole living being, not the liberation of a conscious soul" -- Based on: E1, E20, E21, E22 -- Candidate: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1: E21 says dust + breath = living being. E20 says dust returns to dust. E22 says dust returns, spirit returns to God. E1 says thoughts perish. Would an ECT scholar agree that these texts describe death as the reversal of creation? Yes -- the description is textually clear. The disagreement is about whether something else (an immortal soul) also exists alongside this formula, but that requires adding a concept not in these texts. PASS.
  • N-Test 2: Only possible conclusion from creation + reversal + thoughts perish. PASS.
  • N-Test 3: No added concepts. PASS.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Condition of the dead -- conscious or unconscious? What happens between death and resurrection?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The Old Testament consistently describes the dead as unconscious across at least 8 authors and 6+ books: thoughts perish, knowledge ceases, no praise, no remembrance, silence, darkness, forgetfulness. The New Testament continues this pattern with death-as-sleep vocabulary used by Jesus and the apostles. Resurrection, not death, is the biblical moment when believers receive their reward and are "with the Lord." All 10 alleged conscious intermediate state passages (2 Cor 5:1-9, Phil 1:21-24, Luke 23:43, Luke 16:19-31, Rev 6:9-11, 1 Sam 28, Matt 17:1-9, 1 Pet 3:18-20, 1 Pet 4:6, Heb 12:23) involve genre, grammar, or context qualifications that prevent them from producing E-tier ECT evidence.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Thoughts Perish at Death (Psalm 146:4) His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

The Dead Know Nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:5-6) For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun.

No Knowledge in Sheol (Ecclesiastes 9:10) There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.

David Not Ascended (Acts 2:34) For David is not ascended into the heavens.

Without Resurrection, the Dead Have Perished (1 Corinthians 15:18) Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished.

God Alone Has Immortality (1 Timothy 6:16) Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto.

Resurrection at the Last Day (John 6:40) And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.

Being with the Lord Follows Resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17) The dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.

docs.title: The OT Foundation: Eight Authors, One Testimony
docs.text:
The Old Testament presents a unified picture of the death-state across multiple authors, genres, and centuries. The psalmists declare that thoughts perish at death (Psa 146:4), the dead cannot praise God (Psa 6:5, 115:17, 30:9), death is silence (Psa 115:17), darkness (Psa 88:6, 143:3), and the land of forgetfulness (Psa 88:12). Qoheleth states that the dead know nothing at all (Ecc 9:5), that their love, hatred, and envy have perished (Ecc 9:6), and that there is no work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom in sheol (Ecc 9:10). Job affirms that the dead lie down and do not rise (Job 14:12), that they know nothing of their children's fortunes (Job 14:21), that the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at rest (Job 3:17), and that the dead "hear not the voice of the oppressor" (Job 3:18). Isaiah records Hezekiah's testimony that sheol cannot praise God, death cannot celebrate Him, and those in the pit cannot hope for His truth (Isa 38:18-19). Isaiah also states that the dead "shall not live" and "shall not rise" and their memory perishes (Isa 26:14). Jeremiah describes death as a "perpetual sleep" from which there is no awakening apart from divine intervention (Jer 51:39). Daniel describes the dead as "sleeping in the dust of the earth" until they awake at the eschatological event (Dan 12:2) and tells Daniel he shall "rest" and "stand in thy lot at the end of the days" (Dan 12:13).

The Hebrew vocabulary reinforces this picture. The word abad (perish, H6) is applied to thoughts (Psa 146:4), emotional capacities (Ecc 9:6), and memory (Isa 26:14). The negation particles ein and lo are combined with cognitive verbs (yada, bin, zakar) to produce absolute negation of awareness. Sheol (H7585, 68 occurrences) is characterized by silence (dumah), darkness (choshek, tsalmaveth), no work (maaseh), no knowledge (daath), and no wisdom (chokmah). There is no OT passage that describes the dead as conscious in a sheol-based intermediate state. Isaiah 14:9-11 uses personification (mashal genre, v.4) -- the same literary device used when trees clap hands (Isa 55:12) and Abel's blood cries from the ground (Gen 4:10).

docs.title: The Sleep Vocabulary Chain: OT to NT
docs.text:
The Bible uses four primary words for death as sleep: shakab (H7901, 262 occurrences -- the "sleep with thy fathers" formula used for approximately 36 kings), yashen (H3462, 21 occurrences -- Dan 12:2, Jer 51:39, Psa 13:3), koimao (G2837, 19 occurrences -- John 11:11, Acts 7:60, 13:36, 1 Cor 15:6,18,20,51, 1 Thess 4:13-15), and katheudo (G2518, 23 occurrences -- Matt 9:24, Mark 5:39, 1 Thess 5:10). The LXX translates shakab as koimao 141 times, creating a unified semantic chain across testaments.

The sleep metaphor is used by God himself (Deu 31:16), Jesus (John 11:11, Matt 9:24), Luke (Acts 7:60), Paul (1 Cor 15:6,18,20,51, 1 Thess 4:13-15, 5:10), and Peter (2 Pet 3:4). At least 7 biblical authors employ this language. Sleep is a state without awareness. When Jesus uses koimao for Lazarus's death and then explicitly clarifies "Lazarus is dead" (John 11:14), He establishes the interpretive equivalence: death IS sleep.

docs.title: The Anthropological Foundation
docs.text:
Genesis 2:7 establishes the creation formula: dust (aphar H6083) + breath of life (neshamah H5397) = living being (nephesh chayyah). Man BECAME a living being -- he did not receive a separate soul. The same term nephesh chayyah is applied to animals (Gen 1:24). Death reverses this formula: dust returns to earth (Gen 3:19, Ecc 12:7), spirit/breath returns to God who gave it (Ecc 12:7), and thoughts perish (Psa 146:4).

The spirit (ruach H7307) that returns to God is the animating principle, not a conscious entity. Animals possess the same ruach (Ecc 3:19). If ruach were the conscious immortal soul, animals would also have immortal souls. When ruach departs, consciousness ceases (Psa 146:4). The nephesh (soul) can die (Ezek 18:4), be destroyed (Matt 10:28 -- psyche G5590, the Greek equivalent), and even refers to corpses (Lev 21:11, Num 6:6). The phrase "immortal soul" does not appear in Scripture.

God alone possesses immortality (athanasia G110 -- 1 Tim 6:16, with the exclusive monos). Immortality is something mortals must "put on" at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54), something to "seek" (Rom 2:7), and something Christ "brought to light through the gospel" (2 Tim 1:10). If humans already had immortal souls, these statements would be meaningless.

docs.title: Resurrection as the Biblical Hope
docs.text:
Every passage that specifies WHEN believers receive their reward and are "with the Lord" places this at the resurrection, not at the moment of death:

  • Jesus: "I will raise him up at the last day" -- repeated four times (John 6:39,40,44,54)
  • Paul: "The dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them ... and so shall we ever be with the Lord" (1 Thess 4:16-17)
  • Daniel: "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake" (Dan 12:2)
  • Daniel: "Thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days" (Dan 12:13)
  • Paul: "There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord shall give me at that day" (2 Tim 4:8)
  • John: "They lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years. ... This is the first resurrection" (Rev 20:4-5)
  • Jesus: "All that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth" (John 5:28-29)

The dead are described as IN the graves (John 5:28-29), sleeping in the dust (Dan 12:2), and resting (Dan 12:13, Rev 14:13) until the resurrection event. Peter, under the Holy Spirit's inspiration at Pentecost, explicitly states that David -- "a man after God's own heart" -- "is not ascended into the heavens" (Acts 2:34). The author of Hebrews confirms that the OT heroes of faith "received not the promise" and await perfection "with us" (Heb 11:39-40).

docs.title: The 1 Corinthians 15:18 Test
docs.text:
Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 15:12-19 provides the decisive logical test. His reductio ad absurdum: "If there is no resurrection... then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished" (v.18). The Greek is unambiguous: koimethentes (Aor Pass Ptcp of koimao -- those having fallen asleep) en Christo (in Christ) apolonto (Aor Mid Ind 3P of apollymi G622 -- perished/are destroyed).

Paul's argument works only if the dead are NOT already in conscious bliss with Christ. If dead believers were already in heaven, they could not "perish" simply because there is no resurrection -- they would still be consciously alive. The fact that Paul considers "no resurrection" equivalent to "perished" proves that for Paul, resurrection is not optional consolation for those already in heaven; it is the sole mechanism by which the dead receive life.

docs.title: The Ten Alleged Conscious Intermediate State Passages
docs.text:
Each of the 10 passages alleged to teach conscious intermediate state was examined. Every one involves genre, grammar, or context qualifications:

2 Corinthians 5:1-9: Paul's clothing metaphor expresses a desire to be "clothed upon" (ependysasthai) -- NOT unclothed/disembodied. His stated purpose: "that mortality might be swallowed up of life" -- resurrection language from 1 Cor 15:54. The phrase "absent from the body, present with the Lord" (v.8) uses two aorist infinitives connected by kai, which does not specify temporal relationship or duration between the two events. From the dead person's subjective perspective (no conscious interval), death leads directly to being with Christ at resurrection. (Prior study: 2-corinthians-5-unclothed-intermediate-state)

Philippians 1:21-24: "To depart and be with Christ" (analysai kai syn Christo einai) uses the same grammatical pattern -- two infinitives connected by kai without specifying temporal duration. The same letter contains Phil 3:11 ("if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead") and Phil 3:20-21 ("we look for the Saviour...who shall change our vile body"). Paul's hope in his own letter is resurrection and bodily transformation, not disembodied intermediate existence.

Luke 23:43: Greek manuscripts contain no punctuation. The comma placement ("I say unto thee, Today..." vs. "I say unto thee today, Thou shalt...") is editorial. Jesus was NOT in paradise on that day -- John 20:17, three days later: "I am not yet ascended to my Father" (oupo anababeka, Perf Act Ind 1s). If paradise = God's presence (2 Cor 12:4, Rev 2:7), Jesus was not there on Friday. The Syriac Peshitta and Curetonian manuscripts place "today" with "I say."

Luke 16:19-31: A parable within a continuous parabolic discourse (Luke 15:3 provides the genre label). The opening formula "a certain rich man" (anthropos tis plousios) matches Luke 12:16 (labeled parabole) and 16:1 (universally accepted as parabolic). "Abraham's bosom" appears only in this passage. The stated teaching point is "they have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them" (vv.29,31). The same author records David "is not ascended" (Acts 2:34) and Stephen "fell asleep" (Acts 7:60). Tree 3: Gates 1 and 3 fail. (Prior study: etc6-09-rich-man-lazarus)

Revelation 6:9-11: Apocalyptic vision with symbolic elements throughout. "Souls under the altar" = OT sacrificial imagery (blood poured at altar base, Lev 4:7,18,25,30). Abel's blood "cries" from the ground (Gen 4:10) -- forensic personification. The altar itself speaks (Rev 16:7). The same souls "LIVED" at the first resurrection (Rev 20:4-5) -- they were not alive before. Tree 3: Gates 1 and 3 fail. (Prior study: etc6-10-souls-under-altar)

1 Samuel 28:3-20: Necromancy comprehensively prohibited by God (Exo 22:18, Lev 19:31, 20:6,27, Deu 18:9-14). Saul saw nothing -- only the woman saw (vv.12-14). No new information was given beyond Samuel's prior prophecy (1 Sam 15:28). God condemned Saul for this act (1 Chr 10:13). The passage uses the woman's perspective. (Prior study: saul-witch-endor-necromancy)

Matthew 17:1-9: Jesus calls the transfiguration "the vision" (horama G3705, v.9). Moses was resurrected (Jude 1:9 -- Michael's dispute about the BODY of Moses). Elijah was translated without dying (2 Ki 2:11). Neither requires a conscious intermediate state.

1 Peter 3:18-20: "By which" (en ho) connects to "the Spirit" (v.18). The preaching occurred "in the days of Noah" (v.20) through Noah, "a preacher of righteousness" (2 Pet 2:5). The Spirit of Christ was in OT prophets (1 Pet 1:10-11). Alternative: spirits = fallen angels (2 Pet 2:4, Jude 1:6). (Prior study: 1-peter-3-spirits-in-prison)

1 Peter 4:6: "Was the gospel preached" (eueggelisthe, Aor Pass Ind 3s) to those who ARE dead -- aorist passive = past action to present dead. They were preached to while alive, not after death.

Hebrews 12:23: "Spirits of just men made perfect" -- the word "made perfect" (teleioo G5048) is the same as Heb 11:40, where the OT faithful were NOT YET perfected apart from us. The perfection is covenantal (through Christ's sacrifice, Heb 10:14), not locational. (Prior study: spirits-of-just-men-made-perfect)

docs.title: Stephen's Prayer: Spirit Commended, Body Sleeps
docs.text: Acts 7:59-60 combines both elements in a single narrative: Stephen says "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (pneuma), and the very next clause says "he fell asleep" (ekoimathe, from koimao G2837). The spirit-commitment parallels Jesus's own words (Luke 23:46) and fulfills Ecc 12:7 (spirit returns to God). But Luke immediately uses sleep language. Spirit-commitment is an act of trust in God's keeping; sleep describes the unconscious death-state until resurrection.
