docs.title: Pattern 1: Sheol/Hades = Unconscious, Temporary Realm of All Dead
docs.text: Eight or more OT authors across multiple genres describe sheol as characterized by unconsciousness, silence, darkness, no work, no knowledge, no wisdom, no praise, and forgetfulness. Both righteous and wicked go there. The LXX translates sheol as hades 58 times. Acts 2:27,31 and 1 Corinthians 15:55 confirm this equivalence in the NT. Hades is temporary — cast into the lake of fire (Rev 20:14).

docs.title: Pattern 2: Gehenna = Final Destruction (Not Torment)
docs.text: In all 12 gehenna occurrences, the vocabulary is destruction (apollymi), not torment (basanizo). The contrast is "enter life" vs. gehenna. The OT background (Isaiah 66:24) describes corpses (peger), not living beings. The prophetic name for the Valley of Hinnom is "Valley of Slaughter," not "Valley of Torment."

docs.title: Pattern 3: Four Distinct Concepts, Not One
docs.text: Sheol/hades = general realm of the dead (temporary). Gehenna = eschatological destruction (final). Tartaroo = angelic imprisonment (temporary). Lake of fire = second death (final, for all enemies of God). These cannot be substituted for one another without producing absurdity.

docs.title: Pattern 4: Torment Vocabulary Restricted to Non-Human Subjects
docs.text: Basanizo appears in Revelation 20:10 — subjects are devil, beast, false prophet. When humans encounter the lake of fire (Rev 20:15; 21:8), the text uses "second death." Basanizo never co-occurs with gehenna in any passage.

docs.title: Pattern 5: "Eternal Fire/Smoke" = OT Destruction Formula
docs.text: Isaiah 34:9-10 (Edom's "smoke ascending forever") is the OT source for Revelation 14:11 and 19:3. Edom is not still burning. Sodom "suffered the vengeance of eternal fire" (Jude 1:7) but is not still burning. The formula describes the finality and completeness of destruction.

docs.title: Pattern 6: The Perish/Life Contrast
docs.text: John 3:16: perish vs. everlasting life. Romans 6:23: death vs. eternal life. Matthew 7:13-14: destruction vs. life. Gehenna passages: gehenna vs. "enter into life." The contrast is consistently cessation/destruction vs. life, not torment vs. bliss.

docs.title: Pattern 7: KJV Translation Obscures Distinctions
docs.text: The KJV translates four distinct Hebrew/Greek words as "hell," creating a unified concept that does not exist in the original languages. It further translates sheol as "grave" for righteous subjects and "hell" for wicked subjects — a theological, not linguistic, decision.

docs.title: Sheol (H7585) — 68 occurrences
docs.text: The word study confirms: realm of the dead, paired with death (maveth), Abaddon, pit. LXX: hades 58 times. Receives both righteous and wicked. No lexicon defines sheol as "a place of eternal conscious torment."

docs.title: Hades (G86) — 11 occurrences
docs.text: Semantic equivalent of sheol. Temporary (cast into lake of fire). Only passage associating it with consciousness is Luke 16:23 (parable genre). KJV: "hell" 10 times, "grave" once.

docs.title: Gehenna (G1067) — 12 occurrences
docs.text: From ge-Hinnom. Jesus uses it 11 times; James once. Collocates: fire 6 times, apollymi 3 times. Never collocates with basanizo. The verb in gehenna passages is "destroy," not "torment."

docs.title: Tartaroo (G5020) — 1 occurrence
docs.text: Hapax legomenon verb. Angels only. Temporary ("reserved unto judgment"). No bearing on human fate.

docs.title: Apollymi (G622) — 102 occurrences
docs.text: The verb Jesus uses in gehenna contexts. Active: destroy. Middle/passive: perish. The LXX maps the Hebrew abad (H6) to apollymi 141 times. This is the dominant verb for the fate of the wicked.

docs.title: Basanizo (G928) — 12 occurrences
docs.text: Wide semantic range: sickness, waves, moral distress, childbirth, punishment. NEVER co-occurs with gehenna. In eschatological contexts, applied to devil, beast, false prophet (Rev 20:10), not to human beings in gehenna.

docs.title: Kolasis (G2851) — 2 occurrences
docs.text: Punishment, curtailment. Only in Matt 25:46 (eschatological) and 1 John 4:18 (fear). Etymology: curtail/prune, not torture. The passage does not use gehenna, sheol, hades, or tartaroo.

docs.title: Aionios (G166) — 69 occurrences
docs.text: Adjective from aion. Modifies both positive (life) and negative (punishment, destruction, fire) outcomes. Hebrew source: olam (H5769), which is applied to things that ended (Aaron's priesthood, hills).

docs.title: Peger (H6297) — 24 occurrences
docs.text: Carcass, corpse, dead body. NEVER used for a living person. This is the word in Isaiah 66:24 that Jesus quotes in Mark 9:48. The subjects of worm and fire in Isaiah 66:24 are dead bodies.

docs.title: Skolex (G4663) / Tolaath (H8438) — Worm
docs.text: Decomposition agent. Acts on corpses, not living beings.

docs.title: Asbestos (G762) — 4 occurrences
docs.text: Unquenchable fire = fire completing its work, not fire burning forever. Chaff is totally consumed (Matt 3:12).

docs.title: Luke 16:23 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
docs.text: This is the only passage associating hades with consciousness and torment. It uses hades (G86) + basanos (G931, torment). The passage is a parable — part of a series in Luke 15-16. It fails Tree 3 Gate 1 (subject is a parabolic character) and Gate 3 (genre is parabolic). One parable cannot override 65+ consistent didactic passages characterizing sheol/hades as unconscious. The word used is basanos (touchstone), not basanismos (ongoing torment). If taken as literal teaching about the intermediate state, it contradicts every didactic passage about sheol's nature.

docs.title: Revelation 14:10-11 — Smoke of Torment Ascending Forever
docs.text: This is the strongest ECT proof text after Revelation 20:10. It uses basanizo (torment) vocabulary. Two qualifications: (1) the genre is apocalyptic vision, and (2) the "smoke ascending forever" language is drawn from Isaiah 34:9-10, where it describes the completed destruction of Edom. The OT source establishes the convention: this language describes the permanence of destruction, not the duration of a process.

docs.title: Revelation 20:10 — Tormented Day and Night Forever
docs.text: This applies basanizo to three subjects: devil, beast, false prophet. The complication: humans are later cast into the same lake of fire (Rev 20:15). Does what applies to the three also apply to humans? The text itself makes a vocabulary distinction: when the three supernatural/symbolic entities enter the lake of fire, the word is basanizo (torment); when humans enter it, the word is thanatos (second death). The text draws the distinction; the question is whether to honor or override it.

docs.title: Matthew 25:46 — Everlasting Punishment
docs.text: The same adjective (aionios) modifies both outcomes (punishment and life). Does "everlasting" mean the same thing for both? Grammatically, the same adjective in the same construction likely carries the same force. The question is what aionios modifies: the process (eternal punishing) or the result (permanent punishment). Kolasis means punishment/curtailment, not torment. The passage does not specify what the punishment consists of.

docs.title: Daniel 12:2 — Everlasting Contempt
docs.text: The wicked awake to "shame and everlasting contempt" (deraon). This word appears only here and in Isaiah 66:24, where the context is corpses viewed with abhorrence. Contempt/abhorrence can be the reaction of the living to the aftermath of destruction, not a description of ongoing conscious experience.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The evidence across all 93 verse entries points consistently in one direction at the explicit and necessary implication tiers:

  1. Sheol and hades designate the same concept — the temporary realm of all the dead, characterized by unconsciousness in every didactic passage. Neither word means eternal torment.

  2. Gehenna designates final destruction, not ongoing torment. Jesus' vocabulary is "destroy" (apollymi), not "torment" (basanizo). The OT background describes corpse disposal, not torture of the living. The prophetic name is "Valley of Slaughter."

  3. Tartaroo applies to angels, not humans. It describes temporary imprisonment, not final punishment.

  4. The four words are not interchangeable. They designate distinct concepts: general realm of the dead (sheol/hades), final destruction (gehenna), angelic imprisonment (tartaroo), and final death (lake of fire).

  5. No word inherently means eternal conscious torment. The semantic ranges established by lexicons, usage patterns, and LXX translations do not include "eternal conscious torment" for any of these four words.

  6. Torment vocabulary in eschatological contexts applies to supernatural/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet in Rev 20:10). When humans encounter the same lake of fire, the text switches to death vocabulary ("second death").

  7. The KJV's translation of all four words as "hell" creates a unified concept that obscures the original distinctions and introduces a theological framework not present in the Hebrew and Greek texts.

The passages that complicate this picture (Luke 16:23; Rev 14:10-11; Rev 20:10; Matt 25:46) involve genre qualifications (parable, apocalyptic), subject qualifications (symbolic entities, not literal humans), or vocabulary questions (what does aionios modify?). At the E-tier, no passage applies eternal conscious torment vocabulary to human beings in a didactic context.

Analysis completed: 2026-06-03

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Semantic range of Sheol (H7585), Hades (G86), Gehenna (G1067), Tartaroo (G5020). Interchangeability? Does any inherently mean eternal torment? LXX translation patterns.

docs.title: H7585 — sheol
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7585-showl.md

Occurrences: 68

The realm of the dead. 64 verses, 68 tokens. KJV: 'hell' 31x, 'grave' 26x, 'pit' 3x. LXX: hades 58x (PMI 8.31). Receives both righteous and wicked. Characterized by unconsciousness in didactic passages. Paired with death (maveth), Abaddon, pit.

Semantic categories: realm of the dead, descent/below, death parallelism, wicked fate, rescue from sheol, insatiability

Key verses: Gen 37:35, Ps 6:5, Ps 16:10, Ecc 9:10, Hos 13:14

Relevance: Primary study word — Hebrew term behind the 'hell' question.

docs.title: G86 — hades
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G86-háidēs.md

Occurrences: 11

NT equivalent of sheol. 11 occurrences. LXX: sheol to hades 58x. Categories: realm of the dead (Acts 2:27,31), judgment (Matt 11:23), defeated power (Rev 1:18; 20:13-14). Temporary — cast into lake of fire. KJV: 'hell' 10x, 'grave' 1x.

Semantic categories: realm of the dead, judgment/humiliation, defeated power

Key verses: Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, Rev 20:13-14, 1 Cor 15:55, Luke 16:23

Relevance: Second study word — Greek equivalent of sheol confirmed by Acts 2:27,31.

docs.title: G1067 — gehenna
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1067-geenna.md

Occurrences: 12

Transliteration of ge-Hinnom. 12 NT occurrences. Jesus 11x, James 1x. Collocates: fire 6x, apollymi 3x. Contrast: 'enter life' vs. gehenna. Matt 10:28 uses apollymi (destroy), NOT basanizo (torment). No gehenna passage applies torment vocabulary to humans.

Semantic categories: fiery destruction, self-denial imperative, soul/body destruction, divine judgment

Key verses: Matt 5:22, Matt 10:28, Mark 9:43-48, Luke 12:5, James 3:6

Relevance: Third study word — NT term most associated with 'hell' in popular understanding.

docs.title: G5020 — tartaroo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5020-tartaroo.md

Occurrences: 1

Hapax legomenon — verb, not noun. 2 Pet 2:4 only. Applied exclusively to fallen angels. 'Reserved unto judgment' = temporary imprisonment, not final punishment.

Semantic categories: divine incarceration of angels

Key verses: 2 Pet 2:4

Relevance: Fourth study word — single occurrence, angel-only application.

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

To destroy fully, perish, lose. 86 verses, 102 tokens. Active: destroy/kill. Middle/passive: perish. Hebrew source: abad (H6), LXX 141x. Used in gehenna (Matt 10:28: 'destroy both soul and body').

Semantic categories: physical destruction, divine judgment, eschatological perishing, losing life/soul, losing possession

Key verses: Matt 10:28, John 3:16, Luke 17:27,29, 2 Pet 3:9

Relevance: The verb Jesus uses in gehenna passages — 'destroy,' not 'torment.'

docs.title: G684 — apoleia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G684-apoleia.md

Occurrences: 20

Destruction, perdition, waste. 20 tokens. KJV: 'destruction' 5x, 'perdition' 5x. Noun form of apollymi (G622). Broad way leading to destruction (Matt 7:13), son of perdition.

Semantic categories: eschatological ruin, son of perdition, waste

Key verses: Matt 7:13, John 17:12, Rev 17:8, Phil 3:19

Relevance: Noun form of destroy/perish vocabulary.

docs.title: G929 — basanismos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G929-basanismos.md

Occurrences: 6

Torment. 6 occurrences, all Revelation. Demonic torment (Rev 9:5), smoke of torment (Rev 14:11), Babylon's torment (Rev 18:7,10,15). Alludes to Isa 34:9-10.

Semantic categories: demonic torment, eschatological judgment, commercial/imperial torment

Key verses: Rev 14:11, Rev 9:5, Rev 18:7,10,15

Relevance: Torment noun — Revelation-specific contexts. Smoke imagery = OT destruction-completion formula.

docs.title: G2851 — kolasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2851-kolasis.md

Occurrences: 2

Punishment, penal infliction. Only 2 NT occurrences: Matt 25:46, 1 John 4:18. Root kolazo = curtail/prune — corrective punishment.

Semantic categories: eschatological punishment, fear/anguish

Key verses: Matt 25:46, 1 John 4:18

Relevance: Key word in Matt 25:46. Etymology: curtailment, not torture.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 69

Adjective from aion (G165). 71 tokens. KJV: 'eternal' 32x, 'everlasting' 21x. Dominant: 'eternal life' (~43 of 69). Also modifies fire, punishment, destruction, chains. Hebrew source: olam (H5769), 100x.

Semantic categories: eternal life, eternal judgment, divine attributes, eternal realities

Key verses: John 3:16, Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, Jude 1:7, Rom 6:23

Relevance: Modifies both positive (life) and negative (punishment, destruction, fire) outcomes.

docs.title: G126 — aidios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G126-aidios.md

Occurrences: 2

Everduring, eternal. 2 NT occurrences: Rom 1:20 (God's eternal power), Jude 1:6 (everlasting chains). From aei (always). Absolute eternality.

Semantic categories: divine attributes, eschatological judgment

Key verses: Rom 1:20, Jude 1:6

Relevance: Used for chains binding fallen angels — absolute permanence, but 'unto judgment' (temporary holding).

docs.title: G762 — asbestos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G762-ásbestos.md

Occurrences: 4

Unquenchable. 4 NT occurrences: Matt 3:12, Mark 9:43, Mark 9:45, Luke 3:17. All modify fire. 'Unquenchable' = cannot be extinguished before completing its work.

Semantic categories: eschatological judgment fire

Key verses: Mark 9:43, Mark 9:45, Matt 3:12, Luke 3:17

Relevance: 'Unquenchable' = fire completing its work. Chaff is totally consumed (Matt 3:12).

docs.title: G4663 — skolex
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4663-skṓlēx.md

Occurrences: 3

Worm, maggot. 3 NT occurrences (Mark 9:44,46,48), quoting Isa 66:24. Decomposition agent feeding on corpses. Hebrew source: tolaath (H8438).

Semantic categories: decay of unburied dead

Key verses: Mark 9:44, Mark 9:46, Mark 9:48

Relevance: Worm = decomposition agent on CORPSES (peger), not living souls.

docs.title: H8438 — tolaath
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H8438-tôwlâʻ.md

Occurrences: 44

Maggot; also crimson-grub dye. 44 occurrences. Dominant: scarlet dye (70%+). Literal worm: Isa 14:11, 66:24. LXX: skolex (G4663) 7x.

Semantic categories: scarlet dye, purification rituals, literal worm/decay, metaphor for lowliness, eschatological judgment

Key verses: Isa 66:24, Isa 14:11, Psa 22:6

Relevance: Hebrew behind Isa 66:24's worm (Mark 9:48). Decomposition agent.

docs.title: H11 — abaddon
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H11-ʼabaddown.md

Occurrences: 5

Destruction — place/realm. 5 OT occurrences. Intensive of abad (H6). Always paired with sheol/death. LXX: apoleia (G684) 4x. NT Rev 9:11: Abaddon = Apollyon (Destroyer).

Semantic categories: place of destruction, personified destruction, consuming ruin

Key verses: Job 26:6, Psa 88:11, Pro 15:11, Rev 9:11

Relevance: Sheol's constant companion — associates sheol with DESTRUCTION, not torment.

docs.title: H6297 — peger
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H6297-peger.md

Occurrences: 24

Carcass, corpse, dead body. 24 occurrences. NEVER used for a living person. In Isa 66:24: subjects of worm and fire are dead bodies.

Semantic categories: battlefield dead, divine judgment, prophetic imagery

Key verses: Isa 66:24, Num 14:29, Isa 34:3

Relevance: The word in Isa 66:24 Jesus quotes. Worm and fire consume CORPSES, not living souls.

docs.title: H1516 — gay/ge
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1516-gayʼ.md

Occurrences: 67

Valley, gorge. 67 occurrences. The ge- in ge-Hinnom (gehenna). Geographic feature with steep sides. H2011 Hinnom collocates 13x.

Semantic categories: geographic feature, named valleys, battlefield geography

Key verses: Jos 15:8, Jer 7:31, 2Ki 23:10

Relevance: Hebrew noun behind gehenna's first element. Establishes gehenna as a physical place name.

docs.title: H2011 — Hinnom
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H2011-hinnom.md

Occurrences: 13

Proper name (Jebusite). 13 occurrences. Trajectory: boundary (Joshua) → sacrifice site (Kings) → prophetic curse (Jeremiah) → settlement (Nehemiah).

Semantic categories: geographic boundary, child sacrifice site, prophetic judgment, post-exilic settlement

Key verses: Jos 15:8, 2Ki 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, Neh 11:30

Relevance: Proper noun behind gehenna. OT trajectory: geography → abomination → slaughter → geographic ref.

docs.title: H8612 — Topheth
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H8612-tôpheth.md

Occurrences: 10

Burning site in Valley of Hinnom. 10 occurrences. Where children sacrificed to Molech. Possibly from taphaph (to drum). Jeremiah: renamed 'Valley of Slaughter.'

Semantic categories: child sacrifice site, divine judgment, cultic reform

Key verses: Jer 7:31, 2Ki 23:10, Jer 19:6, Isa 30:33

Relevance: Specific location of burning in ge-Hinnom. Establishes fire-association.

docs.title: H7496 — rapha/rephaim
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7496-râphâʼ.md

Occurrences: 8

Shades/dead ones in sheol. 8 occurrences. Weak, powerless shadows. From raphah (H7503, to be feeble). LXX: nekros 3x, hades 3x.

Semantic categories: the dead in sheol, death as destination, resurrection/non-resurrection

Key verses: Job 26:5, Isa 14:9, Isa 26:14, Psa 88:10

Relevance: Inhabitants of sheol — characterized by WEAKNESS, not consciousness.

docs.title: H7845 — shachath (pit)
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7845-shachath.md

Occurrences: 23

Pit, corruption, destruction. 23 occurrences. From H7843 (destroy/corrupt). Sheol parallel. LXX: diaphthora (G1312) 8x. Ps 16:10 'corruption' quoted in Acts 2:27.

Semantic categories: literal pit/trap, death/grave parallel, corruption/decay, deliverance from pit

Key verses: Psa 16:10, Job 33:18,24, Isa 38:17

Relevance: Sheol parallel — associates realm of dead with corruption/decay.

docs.title: G930 — basanistes
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G930-basanistēs.md

Occurrences: 1

Tormentor. Hapax: Matt 18:34 (parable). Agent noun from basanizo. Originally touchstone tester; then torturer/jailer.

Semantic categories: punitive authority

Key verses: Matt 18:34

Relevance: Part of basanizo family. Only in a parable about earthly debt, not eschatology.

docs.title: G931 — basanos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G931-basanos.md

Occurrences: 3

Touchstone; then torment. 3 occurrences: Matt 4:24 (disease), Luke 16:23,28 (hades parable). Original: testing stone for gold purity.

Semantic categories: physical suffering, afterlife torment, testing

Key verses: Luke 16:23, Luke 16:28, Matt 4:24

Relevance: Torment noun in Luke 16:23 (parable). Original meaning: testing, not eternal punishment.

docs.title: G3041 — limne
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3041-limne.md

Occurrences: 10

Lake. 10 occurrences: 5 Luke (Gennesaret), 5 Revelation (lake of fire). 'Lake of fire' = 'second death' (Rev 20:14; 21:8). Collocates: pyr 5x, ballo 4x, thanatos 2x.

Semantic categories: natural body of water, eschatological place of punishment

Key verses: Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14-15, Rev 21:8

Relevance: Lake of fire DISTINCT from hades (hades cast INTO it). Identified as second DEATH.

docs.title: G165 — aion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G165-aion.md

Occurrences: 120

Age, era, perpetuity. 95 verses, 120 tokens. From aei (always). Root of aionios. KJV: 'ever' 50x, 'world' 29x. Hebrew source: olam (H5769) 287x.

Semantic categories: duration, age/era, universe/world

Key verses: Rev 20:10, Heb 1:2, Matt 12:32

Relevance: Root word of aionios. 'Eis tous aionas ton aionon' = emphatic duration formula.

docs.title: G3639 — olethros
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3639-olethros.md

Occurrences: 4

Destruction, ruin. 4 Pauline occurrences. From ollymi (destroy). 2 Thess 1:9: 'everlasting destruction.' KJV consistently: 'destruction.' No lexicon defines as torment.

Semantic categories: disciplinary destruction, sudden destruction, everlasting destruction

Key verses: 2 Thess 1:9, 1 Thess 5:3, 1 Tim 6:9

Relevance: Paul's word for wicked's fate. Destruction, not torment.

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

Death. 106 verses. Hebrew source: maveth (H4194) 97x LXX. 'Second death' in Rev 20:14; 21:8. Death = enemy to be destroyed (1 Cor 15:26).

Semantic categories: physical death, second death, death as enemy, death personified

Key verses: Rev 20:14, Rev 21:8, 1 Cor 15:26, Rom 6:23

Relevance: Lake of fire = second DEATH. Human fate: thanatos (death), not basanizo (torment).

docs.title: G4442 — pyr
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4442-pyr.md

Occurrences: 73

Fire. 73 verses. Hebrew source: esh (H784) 316x LXX. Concentrated in Revelation (25x). Collocates: gehenna 6x, limne 5x, aionios 3x.

Semantic categories: literal fire, divine judgment fire, purification fire, theophany fire

Key verses: Matt 5:22, Mark 9:43, Rev 20:14-15, Matt 25:41

Relevance: Fire is dominant image in gehenna and lake of fire. Fire CONSUMES.

docs.title: H5769 — owlam
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5769-owlam.md

Occurrences: 432

Time out of mind, eternity. 406 verses. Core: horizon beyond sight. KJV: 'for ever' 49%, 'everlasting' 13%. LXX: aion 287x, aionios 100x. Applied to things that ended (Aaron's priesthood, hills).

Semantic categories: indefinite duration, divine attributes, covenant permanence

Key verses: Dan 12:2, Gen 3:22, Ps 90:2, Isa 34:10

Relevance: Hebrew behind 'everlasting.' Core = 'beyond the horizon' — indefinite, not necessarily infinite.

docs.title: H784 — esh
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H784-esh.md

Occurrences: 400

Fire. 348 verses. LXX: pyr 316x. In judgment contexts: fire consumes/destroys, does not preserve.

Semantic categories: literal fire, sacrificial fire, divine theophany, judgment fire

Key verses: Deu 32:22, Isa 66:24, Mal 4:1

Relevance: OT fire in judgment = consumption/destruction.

docs.title: G5590 — psyche
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5590-psyche.md

Occurrences: 105

Soul, life, self. ~105 occurrences. LXX: nephesh to psyche ~599x. Can be DESTROYED in gehenna (Matt 10:28).

Semantic categories: inner self, life/living being, person, object lost/saved/destroyed

Key verses: Matt 10:28, Matt 16:25, John 3:16

Relevance: Matt 10:28: God destroys psyche in gehenna. Soul is not indestructible.

docs.title: H5315 — nephesh
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5315-nephesh.md

Occurrences: 788

Breathing creature, soul, life. 682 verses. Applied to animals. Can die (Ezek 18:4). Used for corpses. Never modified by 'immortal.'

Semantic categories: living being, life force, person/self, corpse

Key verses: Gen 2:7, Ezek 18:4, Lev 21:11

Relevance: Soul (nephesh) is mortal and destructible. Prerequisite for Matt 10:28.

docs.title: G3709 — orge
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3709-orge.md

Occurrences: 36

Wrath, anger. 36 occurrences. Hebrew source: aph (H639) 135x LXX. Dual domain: anger (emotion) and punishment (judicial). God's wrath results in destruction.

Semantic categories: divine wrath, human anger, eschatological punishment

Key verses: Rom 2:5, Rev 14:10, Matt 3:7

Relevance: Wrath vocabulary. God's wrath → destruction (olethros, apollymi), not eternal torment.

docs.title: G12 — abyssos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G12-abyssos.md

Occurrences: 9

Bottomless pit, abyss. 9 occurrences (7 Revelation). Confinement for demonic beings. Hebrew: tehom (H8415) 30x LXX.

Semantic categories: demonic realm, primordial deep

Key verses: Rev 9:1-2,11, Rev 20:1,3, Luke 8:31

Relevance: Related underworld term. Distinct from hades, gehenna, and lake of fire.

docs.title: H7843 — shachath (verb)
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7843-shachath.md

Occurrences: 164

To destroy, corrupt, ruin. 136 occurrences. KJV: 'destroy' ~48%, 'corrupt' ~16%. LXX: diaphtheiro 48x. Root of H7845 (pit/corruption).

Semantic categories: moral corruption, physical destruction, divine judgment

Key verses: Gen 6:11-12, Psa 78:38, Deu 4:16

Relevance: Root verb of shachath (pit/corruption) in Ps 16:10, quoted Acts 2:27.

docs.title: H639 — aph
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H639-aph.md

Occurrences: 305

Nose, nostril; anger, wrath. 269 verses. Anger/wrath 67%. LXX: orge 135x. Idiom erek appayim = longsuffering.

Semantic categories: anatomy, divine anger, human anger, patience idiom

Key verses: Exo 34:6, Num 25:3-4, Deu 32:22

Relevance: Hebrew anger/wrath. God's wrath (aph) in judgment uses destruction vocabulary.

docs.title: H6 — abad
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H6-abad.md

Occurrences: 219

To wander away, perish, be destroyed. 174 verses, 219 tokens. Qal: perish. Piel/Hiphil: destroy. LXX: apollymi 141x (PMI 6.14).

Semantic categories: perishing, being lost, destruction, covenant curse

Key verses: Psa 1:6, Deu 4:26, Jer 50:6

Relevance: Hebrew parent of apollymi-apoleia chain. OT destruction vocabulary → NT perish/destroy.

docs.title: H4194 — maveth
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H4194-maveth.md

Occurrences: 170

Death. 153 verses. Sheol's most frequent parallel partner (15 pairings). LXX: thanatos 97x.

Semantic categories: physical death, metaphorical death, death personified

Key verses: Hos 13:14, Isa 25:8, Psa 23:4

Relevance: Sheol's partner term. Sheol-maveth pairing = sheol IS the realm of death.

docs.title: H2416 — chay
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H2416-chay.md

Occurrences: 531

Alive, living, life. 449 verses. Antonym of maveth/sheol. Greek: zoe (G2222).

Semantic categories: alive, living creature, life

Key verses: Gen 2:7, Deu 30:19

Relevance: Alternative to sheol/gehenna: LIFE. Contrast = life vs. death/destruction.

docs.title: H2822 — choshek
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H2822-choshek.md

Occurrences: 83

Darkness. 77 verses. LXX: skotos 67x. Sheol characterized by darkness (Job 10:21-22, Ps 88:12).

Semantic categories: primordial chaos, judgment darkness, death/sheol darkness

Key verses: Job 10:21-22, Ps 88:12, Isa 9:2

Relevance: Sheol's darkness supports unconsciousness characterization.

docs.title: H8415 — tehom
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H8415-thowm.md

Occurrences: 42

Deep, abyss, primordial waters. 35 verses. LXX: abyssos 30x (PMI 9.16).

Semantic categories: primordial deep, cosmic waters

Key verses: Gen 1:2, Exo 15:5

Relevance: Hebrew source of abyssos. Related depth vocabulary.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Occurrences: 12

Basanizo (G928) -- to test by touchstone, to torture, to torment. 12 total occurrences in the NT. Wide semantic range: Matt 8:6 (servant 'grievously tormented' = sick/paralyzed), Matt 8:29 (demons: 'art thou come to torment us?'), Matt 14:24 (ship 'tossed' by waves), Mark 5:7/Luke 8:28 (demons: 'torment me not'), Mark 6:48 (disciples 'toiling' in rowing), 2 Pet 2:8 (Lot 'vexed' his righteous soul), Rev 9:5 (scorpion torment), Rev 11:10 (two prophets 'tormented' the earth-dwellers), Rev 12:2 (woman 'pained' in childbirth), Rev 14:10 (tormented with fire and brimstone), Rev 20:10 (devil/beast/false prophet tormented day and night). CRITICAL: basanizo NEVER co-occurs with gehenna in any NT passage. Jesus uses apollymi (destroy) in gehenna contexts but never basanizo.

Semantic categories: physical suffering/illness, demonic distress, natural forces (waves), moral anguish, divine judgment, torment/punishment

Key verses: Matt 8:6, Matt 8:29, Matt 14:24, Rev 14:10, Rev 20:10

Relevance: Central to the eternal torment question. If eternal conscious torment is the biblical teaching about the fate of the wicked, basanizo should appear in gehenna passages. It does not. The torment vocabulary in Revelation is applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet (symbolic/supernatural entities), not to ordinary human beings entering gehenna.

docs.title: Classification Audit Trail — etc7-05-four-hell-words
docs.text: This document contains the full Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for every E-item classified Cond. or ECT and every N-item. Each walkthrough was performed using actual parser tool output for Gate 2.

docs.title: E1 (Ps 6:5) -- "In death there is no remembrance of thee; in sheol who shall give thee thanks?" -- Classified: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "no remembrance," inability to praise; cessation of consciousness applied to the dead. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead (hammethim) -- literal humans who have died. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: lo (Neg) + zakar (remembrance) + sheol (nether world) + yadah (Hiphil.Impf.3fs = praise). Negation particle lo directly governs both clauses. No ambiguous parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of lament -- didactic direct address to God. Not parable, not apocalyptic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E2 (Ps 88:10-12), E3 (Ps 115:17), E4 (Ecc 9:10), E5 (Isa 38:18). No conflicting E-item. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E2 (Ps 88:10-12) -- "Shall the dead praise thee? Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction?" -- Classified: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- Comprehensive negation of consciousness in sheol: no wonders, no praise, no lovingkindness, no faithfulness, darkness, forgetfulness. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead (methim), rephaim (H7496, shades/dead). Literal dead humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: ha-interrogative + methim (Qal.Ptcp = the dead) + asah (make/do) + pele (miracle). Rhetorical questions with ha-interrogative expecting "no." Rephaim (Noun.mp.Abs = ghosts/shades) + qum (Qal.Impf.3mp = arise). Sheol paralleled with Abaddon, dark, land of forgetfulness. No ambiguous parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of lament -- didactic. Not parable, not apocalyptic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1 (Ps 6:5), E3 (Ps 115:17), E4 (Ecc 9:10). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E3 (Ps 115:17) -- "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence." -- Classified: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- Dead cannot praise; sheol characterized as "silence" (dumah). Cessation of activity. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead (hammethim) -- literal dead humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: lo (Neg) + hammethim (Art + muth Qal.Ptcp.mp = the dead) + halal (Piel.Impf.3mp = praise). Yoredey dumah (Qal.Ptcp.mp.Cst + Noun.fs = those descending to silence). Clear negation; no alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm -- didactic contrast between living and dead. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1, E2, E4, E5. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: Conclusion — Semantic Range of Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, Tartaroo
Question
docs.text: Semantic range of Sheol (H7585), Hades (G86), Gehenna (G1067), Tartaroo (G5020). Interchangeability? Does any inherently mean eternal torment? LXX translation patterns.

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The four words translated "hell" in the KJV designate four distinct concepts: sheol/hades is the temporary, unconscious realm of all the dead; gehenna is the place of final destruction; tartaroo is angelic imprisonment awaiting judgment; and the lake of fire is identified as "the second death." None of the four words inherently means eternal conscious torment. The LXX translates sheol as hades 58 times, confirming their semantic equivalence, and the secondary translations (death, descent, destruction) contain no torment vocabulary. Jesus' vocabulary in gehenna passages is apollymi (G622, destroy), not basanizo (G928, torment), and the OT background of gehenna describes corpse disposal in the Valley of Slaughter, not ongoing conscious suffering.

docs.text: # Claim Type Position What the Bible actually says Why this is an inference Criteria I1 Sheol/hades is a state of conscious existence for the dead I-B ECT-direction E1-E5 (Ps 6:5; 88:10-12; 115:17; Ecc 9:10; Isa 38:18): didactic passages describe sheol as unconscious. E14 (Luke 16:23): a parable depicts a character conscious in hades. E45 (Isa 14:9-10): a mashal depicts rephaim speaking. Choosing between didactic descriptions of unconsciousness and parabolic/poetic depictions of consciousness requires interpretation. The parable and mashal are genre-qualified; the didactic passages are not. I026 I2 Gehenna is a place of eternal conscious torment for human beings I-B ECT-direction E6 (Matt 10:28): God "destroys" soul and body in gehenna. E7 (Matt 5:29-30): apollymi vocabulary. E8 (Luke 12:5): kill-then-cast sequence. E22 (Isa 66:24): corpses consumed. E57 (Mark 9:48 quotes Isa 66:24 corpse text). AGAINST: No gehenna passage uses torment vocabulary for humans (N7). Asserting eternal conscious torment in gehenna requires overriding the apollymi (destroy) vocabulary Jesus uses and the peger (corpse) context of the OT source. E51 (Rev 20:15): humans cast into same lake of fire. E52: text uses "second death" for humans, not "tormented." Extending the torment of three non-human/symbolic entities to all human beings requires adding the premise that same destination = same experience. The text itself makes a vocabulary distinction. All four words have different semantic ranges, different subjects, and different temporal scopes. This claim requires overriding the textual distinctions established at E and N tier. E46 (sheol-Abaddon pairing in 5+ passages), E47 (Abaddon = Apollyon = Destroyer). Systematizes the pairing pattern. All components observable in E-items. docs.title: The Four Words Are Not One Concept
docs.text:
The English word "hell" in the KJV translates four distinct Hebrew and Greek terms. This study examines all occurrences of each word to establish what the biblical text actually says about each one.

Sheol (H7585) appears 68 times in the OT. The KJV translates it as "grave" 26 times, "hell" 31 times, and "pit" 3 times. The distribution is not random: when righteous individuals go to sheol (Jacob in Genesis 37:35, Job in Job 14:13, David in Psalm 86:13), the KJV tends toward "grave." When the wicked go to sheol (Psalm 9:17, Proverbs 15:24, Isaiah 5:14), the KJV uses "hell." The underlying Hebrew makes no such distinction. The same word, sheol, designates the same destination for both.

Hades (G86) appears 11 times in the NT. The LXX translates sheol as hades in 58 of approximately 65 instances. Acts 2:27 and 2:31 provide definitive evidence: Peter quotes Psalm 16:10, which uses sheol, and the NT text uses hades. Paul does the same in 1 Corinthians 15:55, quoting Hosea 13:14 with hades for sheol. These inspired quotations establish that the NT authors understood hades as the Greek equivalent of sheol.

Gehenna (G1067) appears 12 times in the NT — 11 from Jesus, 1 from James. It derives from ge-Hinnom, the Valley of the son of Hinnom, a physical location south of Jerusalem. The OT traces this valley from a boundary marker (Joshua 15:8) to a site of child sacrifice (2 Chronicles 28:3; 33:6) to a prophetically cursed location Jeremiah renamed the "Valley of Slaughter" (Jeremiah 7:31-32; 19:6). The trajectory moves from geography to abomination to prophetic curse to eschatological metaphor.

Tartaroo (G5020) appears once in all of Scripture — 2 Peter 2:4. It is a verb (not a noun), applied exclusively to fallen angels, describing their temporary imprisonment "reserved unto judgment." It has no bearing on human eschatology.

These four words cannot substitute for one another. Jacob expects to go to sheol (Genesis 37:35) — substituting "gehenna" produces absurdity (a righteous patriarch expects fiery destruction). Christ went to hades (Acts 2:27) — substituting "gehenna" makes Christ go to the place of final judgment. Angels are cast to tartaroo (2 Peter 2:4) — substituting "sheol" puts them in the general human abode. The substitution test confirms four distinct concepts, not one.

docs.title: Sheol: The Unconscious Realm of All the Dead
docs.text:
The OT characterization of sheol is remarkably consistent across multiple authors and centuries. David writes that there is "no remembrance" and "no praise" in sheol (Psalm 6:5). The sons of Korah describe sheol as a place of "no wonders," "no lovingkindness," "darkness," and "forgetfulness" (Psalm 88:10-12). The psalmist of Psalm 115 says the dead go to "silence" (Psalm 115:17). Solomon teaches that in sheol there is "no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom" (Ecclesiastes 9:10) and that "the dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5). Hezekiah states that "sheol cannot praise" and "death cannot celebrate" (Isaiah 38:18).

These are not isolated proof texts. They represent a consistent pattern across psalms, wisdom literature, and prophetic thanksgiving. Every didactic passage that characterizes sheol's nature describes it as unconscious, silent, dark, and devoid of activity.

The sheol-Abaddon pairing reinforces this. In Job 26:6, Psalm 88:11, Proverbs 15:11, and Proverbs 27:20, sheol is paired with Abaddon (H11). Abaddon is an intensive form of abad (H6, to perish/destroy). In Revelation 9:11, Abaddon is explicitly equated with Apollyon (Destroyer, from apollymi G622). The Hebrew authors consistently paired the realm of the dead with destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

The rephaim (H7496, shades/dead ones) who inhabit sheol are characterized by weakness. Isaiah 14:10 says to the fallen king: "Art thou also become weak as we?" These are not conscious beings suffering; they are feeble shades in death.

Both righteous and wicked go to sheol. Jacob expects it (Genesis 37:35). David needs deliverance from it (Psalm 86:13). Job requests it as a hiding place (Job 14:13). Christ goes there (Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27,31). And the wicked go there too (Psalm 9:17; Numbers 16:33). This dual occupancy conclusively demonstrates that sheol is not a place of punishment. It is the common destination of all the dead.

docs.title: Hades: Sheol's Greek Equivalent
docs.text:
All 11 hades occurrences align with sheol's semantic range. Hades is paired with death (Revelation 1:18; 6:8; 20:13-14) just as sheol is paired with maveth in the OT. Hades is used in the heaven-hades merism (Matthew 11:23; Luke 10:15) just as sheol is used in the heaven-sheol merism (Psalm 139:8; Amos 9:2). Hades is a domain Christ has conquered (Revelation 1:18) just as sheol is a domain God destroys (Hosea 13:14).

Hades is temporary. Revelation 20:13-14 states this explicitly: "death and hades delivered up the dead which were in them... and death and hades were cast into the lake of fire." Hades empties itself, then ceases to exist. It cannot be the final state of the wicked because it is itself destroyed.

Luke 16:23 — the rich man conscious in hades — is the only passage associating hades with consciousness. It is a parable, part of a series in Luke 15-16 (lost sheep, lost coin, prodigal son, unjust steward, rich man and Lazarus). Parabolic genre fails Gate 1 (allegorical character) and Gate 3 (parabolic, not didactic). A single parable cannot override the consistent testimony of 65+ passages that characterize sheol/hades by unconsciousness.

docs.title: Gehenna: Final Destruction, Not Eternal Torment
docs.text:
The vocabulary Jesus uses in gehenna passages is the decisive evidence. In Matthew 10:28, Jesus says God can "destroy" (apollymi G622, aorist active infinitive) both soul (psyche) and body (soma) in gehenna. The Greek parser confirms: apolesai = to destroy. The verb is apollymi, not basanizo. If Jesus intended to teach eternal conscious torment in gehenna, "destroy" is the wrong word.

In Matthew 5:29-30, the member "perishes" (apollymi) and the body is "cast" into gehenna — disposal language. In Luke 12:5, God kills first, THEN casts into gehenna — a temporal sequence (meta + articular infinitive) that places death before gehenna. In Mark 9:43-48, Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24. In Isaiah, the subjects of the worm and fire are peger (H6297, carcasses/corpses) — a word never used for a living person. The worm (tolaath/skolex) is a decomposition agent feeding on dead bodies. The fire is "unquenchable" — in OT usage, this means fire that cannot be extinguished before completing its work (cf. Jeremiah 17:27, where Jerusalem's gates burned with unquenchable fire but are not still burning).

The contrast pattern reinforces this: "enter into life" vs. gehenna (Matthew 18:9; Mark 9:43,45,47). If gehenna were eternal conscious torment, the opposite would not be "life" but something like "bliss." The contrast is life vs. destruction, not happiness vs. suffering.

Basanizo (G928, torment) never co-occurs with gehenna in any NT passage. This is a verifiable textual fact. The torment vocabulary in eschatological contexts (Revelation 14:10-11; 20:10) applies to the devil, beast, and false prophet in the lake of fire — not to human beings in gehenna.

docs.title: The OT Background of Gehenna
docs.text:
The Valley of Hinnom's trajectory through the OT establishes gehenna's semantic foundation. It begins as a boundary marker (Joshua 15:8; 18:16). It becomes the site of child sacrifice to Molech and Baal (2 Chronicles 28:3; 33:6; Jeremiah 32:35). God condemns this practice emphatically: "which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart" (Jeremiah 7:31). Josiah defiles Topheth to end the sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10).

Jeremiah then pronounces judgment: the valley will be renamed the "Valley of Slaughter" (Jeremiah 7:32; 19:6). The prophetic name is haregah (slaughter), not any word for torment. The valley becomes a place of burial — "they shall bury in Topheth, till there be no place" (Jeremiah 7:32). The imagery throughout is slaughter, death, and corpse disposal.

Isaiah 66:24 completes the picture: the righteous "look upon the carcasses (peger) of the men that have transgressed." The subjects are dead bodies. The worm and fire consume corpses. Daniel 12:2 shares the rare word deraon (contempt/abhorrence) with Isaiah 66:24, connecting the resurrection judgment to the corpse imagery.

docs.title: Tartaroo: Angelic Imprisonment
docs.text: Tartaroo (G5020) is the simplest of the four to analyze. It occurs once (2 Peter 2:4), as a verb ("having cast down to tartaroo"), applied exclusively to fallen angels. They are delivered into "chains of darkness" and "reserved unto judgment." Jude 1:6 provides the parallel: "everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day." The chains are permanent (aidios G126), but the purpose is temporal ("unto judgment"). Tartaroo describes a temporary holding facility for angels, not a final destination and not a human one.

docs.title: LXX Translation Patterns
docs.text: The LXX translates sheol as hades in approximately 58 of 65 instances. The secondary translations are significant: thanatos (death), katabaino (to descend), katago (to lead down), and apoleia (destruction). Every secondary translation uses death, descent, or destruction vocabulary. None uses torment vocabulary. The translators — working centuries before the NT — understood sheol as the realm of the dead characterized by death and descent, not by torment.

docs.title: The Lake of Fire and the Second Death
docs.text:
The lake of fire must be distinguished from both hades and gehenna. Hades is cast INTO the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14) — they are not the same. The lake of fire is identified twice as "the second death" (Revelation 20:14; 21:8). When the devil, beast, and false prophet are cast into it, the text uses basanizo (torment, Revelation 20:10). When humans are cast into it, the text uses thanatos (death, Revelation 20:14-15; 21:8). This vocabulary distinction is consistent and appears to be intentional.

The three subjects of torment in Revelation 20:10 are the devil (a non-human spirit being), the beast (a symbolic entity in apocalyptic vision), and the false prophet (another symbolic entity). Extending the torment vocabulary from these three to all human beings requires adding a premise the text does not state: that same destination means same experience. The text draws a vocabulary distinction; whether to honor or override that distinction is an interpretive choice.

docs.title: Does Any Word Inherently Mean Eternal Conscious Torment?
docs.text:
The lexical evidence is clear for each word:

Sheol: No lexicon defines it as "a place of eternal conscious torment." Standard definition: "the realm of the dead, the underworld." Every didactic passage characterizes it by unconsciousness.

Hades: No lexicon defines it as "a place of eternal conscious torment." Standard definition: "the realm of the dead, the underworld" (Greek equivalent of sheol). Temporary — destroyed in Revelation 20:14.

Gehenna: No lexicon defines it as "a place of eternal conscious torment." Standard definition: "Valley of Hinnom; place of final punishment/destruction." The vocabulary Jesus uses in gehenna is destruction (apollymi), not torment (basanizo).

Tartaroo: No lexicon defines it as "a place of eternal conscious torment." Standard definition: "to cast into Tartarus" (a verb of imprisonment). Applied to angels, temporary.

The concept of "eternal conscious torment" as a single unified doctrine requires combining elements from different words, different passages, different genres, and different subjects. No single word carries that meaning, and no single passage states it for human beings in a didactic context.

docs.title: Word Studies
docs.text:
Apollymi (G622): The verb Jesus uses in gehenna passages. Active = destroy; middle/passive = perish. Hebrew source: abad (H6), with 141 LXX mappings. This is the dominant vocabulary for the fate of the wicked.

Basanizo (G928): Wide semantic range including sickness, waves, moral distress, and punishment. In eschatological contexts, applied to devil, beast, and false prophet (Revelation 20:10) — never to humans in gehenna.

Kolasis (G2851): Only 2 NT occurrences. Etymologically from kolazo = curtail/prune. Punishment, not specifically torment.

Aionios (G166): Adjective meaning pertaining to the age. Modifies both positive (life) and negative (punishment, destruction, fire) outcomes. Hebrew source: olam (H5769), applied to things that ended.

Peger (H6297): Carcass, corpse. Never used for a living person. The subjects in Isaiah 66:24 (quoted in Mark 9:48) are dead bodies.

docs.title: Luke 16:23 — Rich Man and Lazarus
docs.text: The only passage associating hades with consciousness. Genre: parable. Fails Gate 1 (parabolic character) and Gate 3 (parabolic genre). If read as literal teaching about the intermediate state, it contradicts every didactic passage about sheol/hades. The I-B resolution (I1) found 6 Plain didactic items against 2 Ambiguous genre-qualified items. Resolution: Strong toward conditionalist.

docs.title: Revelation 14:10-11 — Smoke of Torment
docs.text: Uses basanizo and basanismos. Apocalyptic genre. Alludes to Isaiah 34:9-10, where "smoke ascending forever" describes the completed destruction of Edom (which is not still burning). The OT source establishes the convention: this language describes finality, not duration.

docs.title: Revelation 20:10 — Tormented Day and Night
docs.text: Applies basanizo to devil, beast, false prophet — non-human and symbolic entities. Gate 1 fails (non-human subjects). The extension to humans requires adding a premise the text does not contain. When humans enter the same lake of fire, the text switches to "second death" vocabulary.

docs.title: Matthew 25:46 — Everlasting Punishment
docs.text: The parallel structure (aionios modifying both kolasis and zoe) is genuine. The question is process vs. result: eternal punishing or permanent punishment. The I-B resolution (I8) found the defining passages (Matt 10:28, John 3:16, Rom 6:23, 2 Thess 1:9) use destruction/death vocabulary for the penalty. Resolution: Moderate toward conditionalist.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies)
docs.text:
• Sheol and hades are semantically equivalent (LXX data, Acts 2:27,31, 1 Cor 15:55)
  • Sheol/hades is characterized by unconsciousness in every didactic passage (Ps 6:5; 88:10-12; 115:17; Ecc 9:5,10; Isa 38:18)
  • Both righteous and wicked go to sheol (Gen 37:35; Ps 9:17; Ps 16:10; Acts 2:27)
  • Hades is temporary — delivers up the dead, then is cast into the lake of fire (Rev 20:13-14)
  • Gehenna and sheol/hades are distinct concepts with distinct semantic ranges
  • Hades and the lake of fire are distinct — one is cast into the other
  • Tartaroo applies only to angels, not humans (2 Pet 2:4)
  • Jesus uses apollymi (destroy) in gehenna passages, never basanizo (torment)
  • The OT background of gehenna is the Valley of Slaughter with corpse disposal imagery
  • Isaiah 66:24's subjects (quoted in Mark 9:48) are peger (corpses/dead bodies)
  • The lake of fire is identified as "the second death" (Rev 20:14; 21:8)
  • When humans encounter the lake of fire, the text uses death vocabulary; when the devil/beast/false prophet encounter it, the text uses torment vocabulary
  • The KJV translation of four distinct words as "hell" obscures distinct semantic ranges
  • No lexicon defines any of the four words as "a place of eternal conscious torment"

docs.title: What CANNOT Be Said (not explicitly stated or necessarily implied by Scripture)
docs.text:
• That sheol/hades is a place of conscious torment (only one parable depicts this; all didactic passages contradict it)
  • That gehenna involves eternal conscious torment (no gehenna passage uses torment vocabulary for humans)
  • That the four "hell" words designate a single unified concept (they have different semantic ranges, subjects, and temporal scopes)
  • That Revelation 20:10's torment of the devil/beast/false prophet applies to all human beings (the text uses different vocabulary for humans)
  • That "everlasting punishment" (Matt 25:46) specifies the nature of the punishment as ongoing torment (the text says "punishment," not "torment," and does not specify process vs. result)
  • That "unquenchable fire" means fire that burns forever (OT precedent shows it means fire that completes its work)
  • That tartaroo has any bearing on human eschatology (single occurrence, angel-only)
  • That the soul survives death in a conscious state to experience eternal torment (no "four hell words" passage teaches this)
  • That any specific verse in a didactic genre states "the wicked will be consciously tormented forever" (no such verse exists in any genre for human subjects)

docs.title: Tally Summary
docs.text:
Explicit statements: 58 - Cond.: 18 (E1-E11, E15-E22) - ECT: 0 - Neutral: 40 (E12-E14, E23-E58)

Necessary implications: 9 - Cond.: 0 - ECT: 0 - Neutral: 9 (N1-N9)

Inferences: 8 - I-A (Evidence-Extending): 3 (I5, I6, I7 — all Cond.) - I-B (Competing-Evidence): 3 (I1, I2, I8 — all resolved: I1 Strong Cond., I2 Strong Cond., I8 Moderate Cond.) - I-C (Compatible External): 1 (I3 — ECT-direction) - I-D (Counter-Evidence External): 1 (I4 — ECT)

Totals: E: 18 Cond. / 0 ECT / 40 Neutral; N: 0 Cond. / 0 ECT / 9 Neutral; I-A: 3 Cond.; I-B: 3 (all resolved toward Cond.); I-C: 1 ECT-direction; I-D: 1 ECT.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The four words translated "hell" in the KJV designate four distinct concepts with non-overlapping semantic ranges. Sheol (H7585) and hades (G86) are the temporary, unconscious realm of all the dead — both righteous and wicked — confirmed as semantically equivalent by the LXX (58 mappings) and by inspired NT quotations (Acts 2:27,31; 1 Corinthians 15:55). Gehenna (G1067) is the place of final destruction, rooted in the Valley of Hinnom's OT trajectory from child sacrifice to prophetic curse ("Valley of Slaughter") to eschatological metaphor. Tartaroo (G5020) is a single-occurrence verb describing temporary angelic imprisonment with no application to humans.

At the E-tier, 18 explicit statements use destruction, death, cessation, or unconsciousness vocabulary for the fate of the wicked and the nature of the afterlife realm. Zero explicit statements use eternal conscious torment vocabulary for human beings in a didactic context. The three passages most cited for eternal conscious torment (Luke 16:23; Revelation 14:10-11; Revelation 20:10) are reclassified to Neutral after Gate failures: Luke 16:23 is a parable; Revelation 14:10-11 is apocalyptic genre alluding to an OT destruction formula; Revelation 20:10 applies torment to non-human and symbolic entities.

At the N-tier, all 9 necessary implications are Neutral — factual observations both sides accept: the words are distinct, hades is temporary, sheol receives both righteous and wicked, the KJV obscures distinctions.

At the I-tier, all three I-B items (sheol-as-conscious, gehenna-as-torment, everlasting-punishment-as-process) resolve toward conditionalist — the first two with Strong resolution, the third with Moderate resolution. The ECT position at the inference tier rests on one I-C item (extending Rev 20:10 torment to humans) and one I-D item (treating the four words as a unified concept). The I-D item requires overriding multiple E/N-tier distinctions between the words.

The evidence tiers contain what they contain. At the highest tier (Explicit), the vocabulary is destruction, death, and unconsciousness. The concept of eternal conscious torment for human beings does not appear in any passage using sheol, hades, gehenna, or tartaroo in a didactic context.

  • Ezekiel 32:27 — Gone down to sheol with weapons — sheol receives warriors
  • Amos 9:2 — Though they dig into sheol, thence shall mine hand take them — God's inescapable reach
  • Habakkuk 2:5 — Enlarges his desire as sheol — sheol used as simile for insatiability
  • Matthew 25:41 — Everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels — fire language in judgment context
  • Matthew 25:46 — Everlasting punishment (kolasis G2851) — key disputed passage
  • Jude 1:6 — Angels kept in everlasting chains under darkness unto judgment — parallel to 2 Pet 2:4
  • Revelation 6:8 — Death and hades followed — hades personified with death
  • Revelation 20:10 — Devil tormented day and night for ever — torment language applied to devil/beast/false prophet
  • Revelation 20:15 — Whosoever not found in book of life cast into lake of fire — human fate: death vocabulary
  • Revelation 21:8 — Lake of fire = second death — lake of fire identified as second death
  • 1 Corinthians 15:55 — O death, where is thy sting? O grave (hades), where is thy victory? — quotes Hosea 13:14
  • Jude 1:7 — Sodom suffering vengeance of eternal fire — but Sodom is not still burning
  • Isaiah 34:9-10 — Edom's land: smoke ascending for ever — OT 'eternal fire' language for temporal destruction
  • Malachi 4:1-3 — Day that burns as oven; wicked become ashes under feet — destruction imagery
  • Obadiah 1:16 — They shall be as though they had not been — cessation language
  • Revelation 14:10-11 — Smoke of their torment ascendeth — alludes to Isa 34; key ECT proof text
  • Revelation 19:20 — Beast and false prophet cast into lake of fire — symbolic entities
  • Daniel 12:2 — Everlasting life vs. shame and everlasting contempt — key judgment text
  • Isaiah 26:14 — They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased (rephaim), they shall not rise
  • Nehemiah 11:30 — Valley of Hinnom as geographic reference — post-exilic mention
  • John 3:16 — Perish (apollymi) vs. everlasting life — the contrast pattern
  • Romans 6:23 — Wages of sin is death vs. gift of God eternal life — death/life contrast
  • 2 Thessalonians 1:9 — Everlasting destruction (olethros G3639) from the presence of the Lord — destruction vocabulary

docs.title: Focus Areas
docs.text:
FA1. Semantic Range of Sheol (H7585): This area must establish what sheol actually means in its OT contexts before comparing it to Greek NT terms. The KJV's inconsistent translation of the same word as both 'grave' and 'hell' raises immediate questions about whether theological assumptions drove translation choices. Verses: Genesis 37:35, Numbers 16:30, Deuteronomy 32:22, 1 Samuel 2:6, Job 7:9, Job 14:13, Job 26:5-6, Psalm 6:5, Psalm 9:17, Psalm 16:10, Psalm 49:14-15, Psalm 86:13, Psalm 88:10-12, Psalm 115:17, Psalm 139:8, Proverbs 5:5, Proverbs 15:24, Proverbs 27:20, Ecclesiastes 9:5-6, Ecclesiastes 9:10, Song of Solomon 8:6, Isaiah 5:14, Isaiah 14:9-11, Isaiah 14:15, Isaiah 28:15, Isaiah 38:18, Ezekiel 32:21, Ezekiel 32:27, Hosea 13:14, Amos 9:2, Jonah 2:2, Habakkuk 2:5 Strong's: H7585, H7496, H11, H7845, H4194

FA2. Semantic Range of Hades (G86): If hades is semantically equivalent to sheol (as Acts 2:27,31 confirms), then the NT concept of hades should carry the same characteristics: temporary, receives both righteous and wicked, characterized by unconsciousness in didactic passages. Luke 16:23 is the key test case. Verses: Matthew 11:23, Matthew 16:18, Luke 10:15, Luke 16:23, Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, 1 Corinthians 15:55, Revelation 1:18, Revelation 6:8, Revelation 20:13-14 Strong's: G86, H7585, G2288

FA3. Semantic Range of Gehenna (G1067): This area must carefully distinguish between what the text actually says about gehenna and what theological tradition has read into it. The vocabulary Jesus chooses (destroy vs. torment) and the OT background (valley of slaughter, corpse disposal) are the primary evidence. Verses: Matthew 5:22, Matthew 5:29-30, Matthew 10:28, Matthew 18:9, Matthew 23:15, Matthew 23:33, Mark 9:43-48, Luke 12:5, James 3:6, Joshua 15:8, 2 Kings 23:10, 2 Chronicles 28:3, 2 Chronicles 33:6, Jeremiah 7:31-32, Jeremiah 19:2-6, Jeremiah 32:35, Isaiah 30:33, Isaiah 66:24 Strong's: G1067, G622, H1516, H2011, H8612, H6297, G4663, H8438

FA4. Tartaroo (G5020) — Single Occurrence Analysis: Tartaroo is the most specialized of the four words. Its restriction to a single verse about angelic imprisonment makes it the easiest to analyze but also the most important to correctly delimit — it should not be conflated with human eschatology. Verses: 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 1:6, Jude 1:7 Strong's: G5020, G126

FA5. LXX Translation Patterns — Sheol to Greek: The LXX data is critical evidence. The overwhelming sheol→hades mapping (58 times) establishes the semantic equivalence. But the secondary mappings (thanatos 14x, katabaino 17x, katago 10x, apoleia 3x) show that translators sometimes chose context-sensitive renderings — all of which point to death/descent/destruction, never to torment. Verses: Psalm 16:10, Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, Hosea 13:14, 1 Corinthians 15:55, Isaiah 38:18, Psalm 6:5 Strong's: H7585, G86, G2288, G2609, G2597, G684, G5590

FA6. Interchangeability — Can These Words Substitute for Each Other?: If these four words designated a single concept, they should be interchangeable in context. The test is whether you can substitute 'gehenna' for 'sheol' in passages like Psalm 6:5 or Genesis 37:35 without absurdity. If Jacob expected to go to a place of fiery punishment to be with his dead son, the text becomes incoherent. Verses: Genesis 37:35, Psalm 6:5, Psalm 16:10, Acts 2:27, Matthew 10:28, Mark 9:43-48, 2 Peter 2:4, Revelation 20:13-14, Luke 16:23, Matthew 25:41 Strong's: H7585, G86, G1067, G5020

FA7. Does Any Word Inherently Mean Eternal Conscious Torment?: The lexical evidence must be presented word by word. Each word's actual semantic range — as defined by lexicons and demonstrated by usage — is the primary evidence. If no lexicon defines any of these four words as 'a place of eternal conscious torment,' that is a significant finding. Verses: Matthew 10:28, Mark 9:43-48, Isaiah 66:24, Matthew 25:41, Matthew 25:46, Revelation 20:10, Revelation 14:10-11, Jude 1:7, Isaiah 34:9-10, 2 Thessalonians 1:9, Psalm 6:5, Ecclesiastes 9:10 Strong's: H7585, G86, G1067, G5020, G622, G928, G929, G2851, G166, G762, H784, G4442

FA8. The 'Grave' vs. 'Hell' Translation Controversy: If the KJV translates sheol as 'grave' when Jacob, David, or Job go there but as 'hell' when the wicked go there, this reveals a theological interpretive layer imposed on the translation. The underlying Hebrew makes no such distinction. Verses: Genesis 37:35, Genesis 42:38, 1 Samuel 2:6, Job 14:13, Psalm 9:17, Psalm 16:10, Psalm 31:17, Psalm 49:14-15, Psalm 55:15, Proverbs 7:27, Proverbs 23:14, Isaiah 14:9, Isaiah 14:15, Deuteronomy 32:22, Hosea 13:14 Strong's: H7585

FA9. Who Goes to Sheol/Hades? Righteous and Wicked?: The data should show conclusively whether sheol is a general abode of all the dead or a punishment for the wicked. If righteous individuals (Jacob, David, Job, Christ) go to sheol, this establishes that sheol is not a punitive destination. Verses: Genesis 37:35, Genesis 44:29, 1 Kings 2:6, Job 17:13, Psalm 9:17, Psalm 16:10, Psalm 49:14-15, Psalm 88:3, Isaiah 38:10, Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, Hosea 13:14 Strong's: H7585, G86

FA10. Gehenna's OT Background — Valley of Hinnom and Child Sacrifice: The Valley of Hinnom trajectory moves from geography to abomination to prophetic curse to eschatological metaphor. At every stage, the imagery is slaughter, death, and corpse disposal — never ongoing conscious existence in torment. Verses: Joshua 15:8, Joshua 18:16, 2 Kings 23:10, 2 Chronicles 28:3, 2 Chronicles 33:6, Jeremiah 7:31-32, Jeremiah 19:2-6, Jeremiah 32:35, Isaiah 30:33, Isaiah 66:24, Nehemiah 11:30 Strong's: G1067, H1516, H2011, H8612, H6297

FA11. Sheol-Abaddon Pairing Pattern: The sheol-abaddon pairing associates sheol with destruction, not torment. This word association is evidence about how the Hebrew authors conceptualized the realm of the dead. Verses: Job 26:6, Job 28:22, Job 31:12, Psalm 88:11, Proverbs 15:11, Proverbs 27:20, Revelation 9:11 Strong's: H7585, H11, H6

FA12. Hades vs. Lake of Fire — The Distinction: This focus area establishes the biblical framework: temporary holding (sheol/hades) → judgment → final outcome (lake of fire = second death). The two destinations are sequential, not identical. Verses: Revelation 20:10, Revelation 20:13-14, Revelation 20:15, Revelation 21:8, Revelation 19:20, Revelation 6:8, Revelation 1:18 Strong's: G86, G3041, G4442, G2288, G928, G929

docs.title: The Four "Hell" Words of the Bible
docs.text: The King James Version translates four different Hebrew and Greek words as "hell." But these four words mean very different things. Understanding the distinctions changes how we read the Bible's teaching on the fate of the wicked.

docs.title: Sheol and Hades — The Grave
docs.text:
Sheol (Hebrew) and Hades (Greek) are the same concept in two languages. We know this because the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) translates sheol as hades 58 times, and the New Testament confirms it — Peter quotes Psalm 16:10 using hades where the Hebrew has sheol (Acts 2:27).

Sheol/hades is simply the realm of the dead. Everyone goes there — righteous and wicked alike. Jacob expected to go there (Genesis 37:35). Christ went there (Acts 2:27). The wicked go there too (Psalm 9:17).

What is sheol like? Every teaching passage that describes it says the same thing: unconsciousness.

  • "The dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
  • "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom" in sheol (Ecclesiastes 9:10)
  • "In death there is no remembrance of thee" (Psalm 6:5)
  • "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)

Sheol/hades is also temporary. Revelation 20:13-14 says death and hades deliver up their dead and are then cast into the lake of fire. Hades itself is destroyed.

docs.title: Gehenna — Final Destruction
docs.text:
Gehenna comes from the Valley of Hinnom, a real place south of Jerusalem. In the Old Testament, it was the site of child sacrifice to Molech. The prophet Jeremiah cursed it and renamed it the "Valley of Slaughter" — a place of death and burial (Jeremiah 7:31-32).

Jesus uses gehenna 11 of the 12 times it appears in the New Testament. The critical detail is the vocabulary he chooses. In Matthew 10:28, Jesus says God can "destroy" (Greek: apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna. In Luke 12:5, God kills first, then casts into gehenna. When Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24 about the "worm" and "fire" in Mark 9:48, the original passage describes corpses — dead bodies, not living, suffering people.

The word for "torment" (Greek: basanizo) never appears in a single gehenna passage. Jesus consistently uses destruction language, not torment language.

docs.title: Tartaroo — Angels Only
docs.text: Tartaroo appears exactly once in the entire Bible (2 Peter 2:4). It describes fallen angels cast into a prison of darkness, "reserved unto judgment." It is a temporary holding place for angels. It says nothing about the fate of human beings.

docs.title: The Lake of Fire — The Second Death
docs.text:
The lake of fire is distinct from all four words above. Hades is cast into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14), so they cannot be the same thing. The Bible identifies the lake of fire as "the second death" (Revelation 20:14; 21:8).

When the devil, the beast, and the false prophet are cast into the lake of fire, the text uses the word "torment" (Revelation 20:10). But when human beings are cast in, the text switches to "death" (Revelation 20:14-15; 21:8). This vocabulary shift appears deliberate.

docs.title: The Bottom Line
docs.text:
No single passage, in any of these four words, states in plain teaching language that human beings will be consciously tormented forever. The Bible's own vocabulary for the fate of the wicked is consistent: destroy, perish, death (Matthew 10:28; John 3:16; Romans 6:23). The concept of eternal conscious torment requires combining elements from different words, different genres, and different subjects — and overriding the destruction vocabulary that the biblical authors actually used.

"For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." — Romans 6:23

docs.title: 2 Peter 2:4
docs.text: ====================================================================== 2 Peter 2:4 - GRAMMATICAL ANALYSIS ====================================================================== Greek Text: εἰ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς ἀγγέλων ἁμαρτησάντων οὐκ ἐφείσατο, ἀλλὰ σειροῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας παρέδωκεν εἰς κρίσιν τηρουμένους, Key words: tartarosas (G5020, Aor Act Ptcp Nom Sg M = having cast down to tartarus), seirois zophou (chains of darkness), krisin (G2920, Acc Sg F = judgment), teroumenous (G5083, Pres Pass Ptcp Acc Pl M = being reserved).

docs.title: 2 Thessalonians 1:9
docs.text: ====================================================================== 2 Thessalonians 1:9 - GRAMMATICAL ANALYSIS ====================================================================== Greek Text: οἵτινες δίκην τίσουσιν ὄλεθρον αἰώνιον ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, Key words: olethron (G3639, Acc Sg M = destruction), aionion (G166, Acc Sg M = everlasting), apo prosopou (from the face/presence of). Paul's word is OLETHROS (destruction), not basanismos (torment).

Key words: psychen (G5590, Acc Sg F = soul), Haiden (G86, Acc Sg M = Hades), diaphthoran (G1312, Acc Sg F = corruption). Direct quotation of Psalm 16:10 with hades for sheol.

docs.text: ====================================================================== Matthew 25:46 - GRAMMATICAL ANALYSIS ====================================================================== Greek Text: καὶ ἀπελεύσονται οὗτοι εἰς κόλασιν αἰώνιον, οἱ δὲ δίκαιοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον. docs.text: ====================================================================== Revelation 20:10 - GRAMMATICAL ANALYSIS ====================================================================== Greek Text: καὶ ὁ διάβολος ὁ πλανῶν αὐτοὺς ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρὸς καὶ θείου, ὅπου καὶ τὸ θηρίον καὶ ὁ ψευδοπροφήτης, καὶ βασανισθήσονται ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Key words: diabolos (G1228 = devil), therion (G2342 = beast), pseudoprophetes (G5578 = false prophet), basanisthesontai (G928, Fut Pass Ind 3P = shall be tormented), limnen (G3041 = lake), pyros (G4442 = fire), aionas ton aionon (G165 = for the ages of the ages). Subjects of torment: devil, beast, false prophet — all supernatural/symbolic.

docs.title: Revelation 20:14
docs.text: ====================================================================== Revelation 20:14 - GRAMMATICAL ANALYSIS ====================================================================== Greek Text: καὶ ὁ θάνατος καὶ ὁ Ἅιδης ἐβλήθησαν εἰς τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός. οὗτος ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερός ἐστιν, ἡ λίμνη τοῦ πυρός. Key words: thanatos (G2288, Nom Sg M = death), Hades (G86, Nom Sg M), eblethesan (G906 ballo, Aor Pass Ind 3P = were cast), limnen (G3041, Acc Sg F = lake), pyros (G4442, Gen Sg N = fire), deuteros (G1208, Nom Sg M = second). 'This is the second death, the lake of fire.'

docs.title: Isaiah 66:24
docs.text: ====================================================================== Isaiah 66:24 ====================================================================== Key words: pigre (peger H6297, mp.Cst = corpses/carcasses), tolaatam (tolaath H8438, fs.Abs+3mp = their worm), lo tamuth (not die, Qal Impf 3fs of muth H4191), ishsam (esh H784, s.Abs+3mp = their fire), lo tikhbeh (not go out/quench, Qal Impf 3fs of kabah H3518), deraon (H1860, ms.Abs = abhorrence). Subjects = CORPSES (peger = dead bodies). Worm = decomposition agent. Fire = consuming agent on dead bodies.

docs.title: Cross-Testament Parallels
docs.text:
• Psalm 16:10 → Acts 2:27 (nt, direct quotation — sheol (H7585) rendered as hades (G86) confirming semantic equivalence)
  • Hosea 13:14 → 1 Corinthians 15:55 (nt, direct quotation — sheol rendered as hades; death-sheol triumph)
  • Isaiah 66:24 → Mark 9:48 (nt, direct quotation — worm/fire imagery; peger (corpses) behind skolex/pyr)
  • Isaiah 34:9-10 → Revelation 14:11 (nt, vocabulary + structural allusion — 'smoke ascending forever' formula; Edom completed destruction)
  • Isaiah 34:9-10 → Revelation 19:3 (nt, vocabulary allusion — smoke ascending forever for Babylon's destruction)
