docs.title: Question
docs.text: Hebrew/Greek destruction vocabulary: abad/apollumi (H6/G622), shamad (H8045), kalah (H3615), shachath (H7843), apoleia (G684), olethros (G3639). Lexical definitions, eschatological usage.

docs.title: First Death Threat in Scripture
docs.text:
But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.

Context: The foundational mot tamut construction establishing death as the penalty for sin. All destruction vocabulary builds on this original sentence.

Notes: mot tamut = infinitive absolute + imperfect = emphatic 'you shall certainly die.' Foundation for all destruction vocabulary.

docs.title: First Divine Destruction Declaration
docs.text:
And the LORD said, I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth; both man, and beast, and the creeping thing, and the fowls of the air; for it repenteth me that I have made them.

Context: God's first declaration of intent to destroy humanity. Uses machah (H4229, 'blot out') rather than shachath. The Flood is the paradigm case for divine destruction of the wicked.

Notes: Uses machah (blot out) — the destruction language escalates to shachath in vv. 11-13.

docs.title: Threefold Shachath — Corruption-to-Destruction Pattern
docs.text:
The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth. And God said unto Noah, The end of all flesh is come before me; for the earth is filled with violence through them; and, behold, I will destroy them with the earth.

Context: The same root shachath (H7843) describes both the sin (corruption, vv.11-12) and the judgment (destruction, v.13). Three forms: Niphal wayyiqtol (v.11, 'was corrupt'), Niphal perfect (v.12, 'it was corrupt'), Hiphil perfect (v.12, 'had corrupted'), Hiphil participle (v.13, 'I will destroy them'). This creates a principle: corruption leads to destruction, and destruction is the natural end of corruption.

Notes: Three forms of shachath: v.11 Niphal wayq 3fs (earth was corrupt), v.12 Niphal perf 3fs (was corrupt) + Hiphil perf 3ms (had corrupted), v.13 Hiphil ptcp ms+3mp (I will destroy them).

docs.title: Destruction of Sodom — Paradigm Case
docs.text:
Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven; And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.

Context: Sodom's destruction is the paradigm case for eschatological judgment (cf. Jude 1:7, 2 Pet 2:6). Fire and brimstone produced ashes, not ongoing torment. The verb 'overthrew' (haphak) emphasizes complete reversal/annihilation.

Notes: Key paradigm: Sodom reduced to ashes (2 Pet 2:6), proving 'eternal fire' (Jude 1:7) produces permanent destruction, not endless burning.

docs.title: Divine Destruction of the Wicked — abad H6
docs.text:
And repayeth them that hate him to their face, to destroy them: he will not be slack to him that hateth him, he will repay him to his face.

Context: Direct divine destruction language. Uses abad (H6) in Hiphil — causative 'to destroy.' God directly and deliberately destroys those who hate him.

Notes: abad H6 Hiphil — causative active: God actively destroys the wicked.

docs.title: Covenant Curse — abad H6
docs.text:
And it shall be, if thou do at all forget the LORD thy God, and walk after other gods, and serve them, and worship them, I testify against you this day that ye shall surely perish. As the nations which the LORD destroyeth before your face, so shall ye perish; because ye would not be obedient unto the voice of the LORD your God.

Context: Covenant-curse language using abad. The infinitive absolute intensification (abad + tabad = 'surely perish') emphasizes certainty. V.20 draws explicit parallel: as the destroyed nations perished, so will apostate Israel.

Notes: Infinitive absolute construction: abad toadedun = 'you shall surely perish.' Same fate as destroyed nations.

docs.title: Covenant Curse Cluster — abad/shamad H6/H8045
docs.text:
The LORD shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke, in all that thou settest thine hand unto for to do, until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly; because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me. The LORD shall make the pestilence cleave unto thee, until he have consumed thee from off the land, whither thou goest to possess it. The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish.

Context: Dense covenant-curse passage using shamad ('until thou be destroyed') and abad ('until thou perish'). Both destruction words operate in the same judgment context, showing they share the same semantic domain of total destruction.

Notes: V.20 uses both shamad (Niphal, 'be destroyed') and abad (Qal, 'perish') together. V.22 adds abad again.

docs.title: Righteous/Wicked Contrast — Chaff Simile + abad H6
docs.text:
The ungodly [are] not so: but [are] like the chaff which the wind driveth away. Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.

Context: First psalm establishes the binary: righteous flourish like a tree (v.3), wicked are chaff that blows away (v.4). The way of the ungodly 'shall perish' (abad, Qal imperfect) — the way itself ceases to exist. Chaff is a cessation simile: it does not continue to exist in a ruined state.

Notes: abad Qal impf 3fs — intransitive: the way itself perishes. LXX: apollymi.

docs.title: Non-Existence Declaration — ayin
docs.text:
For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the LORD, they shall inherit the earth. For yet a little while, and the wicked [shall] not [be]: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it [shall] not [be].

Context: Explicit non-existence statement. Hebrew ayin (H369) = 'not be, non-existent.' The wicked 'shall not be' — not 'shall be in torment' or 'shall be ruined.' The place of the wicked is also non-existent. Combined with Jesus' quotation of v.11 (Matt 5:5, 'the meek shall inherit the earth').

Notes: v.10 parsed: ayin rasha ('not-be wicked') = the wicked SHALL NOT BE. ayin = noun of non-existence. hitbonanta al-meqomo we-einennu = 'you look at his place and it is not (there).'

docs.title: Triple Destruction — abad + kalah — Smoke Simile
docs.text:
But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD [shall be] as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away.

Context: Two destruction words in one verse: abad (Qal impf 3mp, 'shall perish') and kalah (Qal perf 3p, 'shall consume,' twice). The 'fat of lambs' simile is cessation imagery: fat on the altar is completely consumed, nothing remains. 'Into smoke shall they consume away' — smoke dissipates into nothing.

Notes: Parsed: yobedu (abad Qal impf 3mp, 'shall perish') + kalu (kalah Qal perf 3p, 'consumed') + be'ashan kalu (kalah Qal perf 3p, 'in smoke consumed'). Double kalah intensifies the cessation.

docs.title: Non-Existence Statement — 'he was not'
docs.text:
Yet he passed away, and, lo, he [was] not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found.

Context: Third non-existence statement in Psalm 37 (with v.10 and v.20). The wicked 'passed away and was not' — emphatic cessation. 'I sought him, but he could not be found' — the wicked person has ceased to exist.

Notes: Hebrew: einennu = 'he is not.' Same ayin construction as v.10.

docs.title: shamad H8045 — Transgressors Destroyed Together
docs.text:
But the transgressors shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off.

Context: Third destruction word in Psalm 37: shamad (Niphal perf 3p, 'shall be destroyed'). Combined with karath (Niphal perf 3fs, 'shall be cut off'). The 'end' (acharith) of the wicked is cutting off — termination, not continuation in torment.

Notes: Parsed: nishmedu (shamad Niphal perf 3p, 'were destroyed') + nichratah (karath Niphal perf 3fs, 'was cut off'). Prophetic perfect = future certainty.

docs.title: Kalah + Non-Existence — 'that they may not be'
docs.text:
Consume [them] in wrath, consume [them], that they [may] not [be]: and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah.

Context: Prayer using kalah (H3615) with explicit non-existence result clause: 'that they may not be' (ayin). The purpose of the consumption (kalah) is non-existence (ayin). This verse directly connects destruction vocabulary to cessation of existence.

Notes: kalah Piel imperative + we-einemo ('and they are not') = consume them so that they do not exist.

docs.title: Wax/Fire Simile — abad H6
docs.text:
As smoke is driven away, [so] drive [them] away: as wax melteth before the fire, [so] let the wicked perish at the presence of God.

Context: Double cessation simile: smoke driven away + wax melting before fire. Both describe substances that cease to exist. The wicked 'perish' (abad, Qal impf) at the presence of God — God's presence causes destruction, not preservation in torment.

Notes: v.2 parsed: yaqum elohim (Qal impf 3ms, God arises) + yobedu (abad Qal impf 3mp, perish). The KJV v.2 is the wax/fire verse; v.1 in Hebrew numbering.

docs.title: shamad H8045 — 'Destroyed Forever'
docs.text:
When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; [it is] that they shall be destroyed for ever:

Context: shamad with adey-ad duration modifier. 'Destroyed for ever' — the 'for ever' modifies the permanence of the RESULT (destroyed state), not the duration of a process. The wicked flourish temporarily but are destroyed permanently.

Notes: Hebrew: lehishamdam adey-ad = 'to be destroyed to perpetuity.' shamad Niphal infinitive + adey-ad. The grass simile (spring, flourish) emphasizes temporary existence followed by permanent destruction.

docs.title: abad H6 — Enemies Perish
docs.text:
For, lo, thine enemies, O LORD, for, lo, thine enemies shall perish; all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered.

Context: abad (Qal impf 3mp) in parallel with 'scattered.' Two destruction words in Psalm 92 (shamad v.7, abad v.9). The enemies of the LORD perish — the same verb used of substances that cease to exist.

Notes: abad Qal impf 3mp = intransitive 'shall perish.' Parallel: enemies perish AND workers of iniquity are scattered = total dissolution.

docs.title: Non-Existence — 'Let the wicked be no more'
docs.text:
Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless thou the LORD, O my soul. Praise ye the LORD.

Context: Uses tamam (H8552, 'be consumed/completed') with explicit non-existence result: 'let the wicked be no more' (ayin). Third passage pairing destruction vocabulary with explicit non-existence language (with Psa 37:10, 59:13).

Notes: tamam (consumed/completed) + ayin (be no more). The prayer is for the wicked to cease existing, not to be tormented.

docs.title: Preserve/Destroy Contrast — shamar vs. shamad
docs.text:
The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy.

Context: Binary contrast using antonyms: shamar (Qal ptcp, 'preserves/guards') vs. shamad (Hiphil impf 3ms, 'will destroy'). The same God who preserves the righteous utterly annihilates the wicked. The contrast is preservation vs. destruction, not preservation-in-blessing vs. preservation-in-torment.

Notes: Parsed: shomer (shamar Qal ptcp ms, 'preserves') vs. yashmid (shamad Hiphil impf 3ms, 'will destroy'). Hiphil = causative active: God actively destroys.

docs.title: abad H6 — 'Perish forever like his own dung'
docs.text:
[Yet] he shall perish for ever like his own dung: they which have seen him shall say, Where [is] he?

Context: abad with permanence indicator ('for ever') and cessation simile (dung — decomposing substance). The rhetorical question 'Where is he?' emphasizes absence/non-existence, not continued suffering.

Notes: abad Qal impf 3ms + lanetsach ('forever'). The dung simile = decomposition to nothing.

docs.title: Wicked Cut Off from the Earth
docs.text:
But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it.

Context: karath (cut off) + nacah (rooted out). Both verbs describe removal from existence, not preservation in suffering. Rooting out a plant = it ceases to exist in that location.

Notes: karath Niphal impf + nacah Qal impf = double removal/cessation.

docs.title: kalah + Fire Destruction
docs.text:
And the destruction of the transgressors and of the sinners [shall be] together, and they that forsake the LORD shall be consumed. And the strong shall be as tow, and the maker of it as a spark, and they shall both burn together, and none shall quench [them].

Context: v.28 uses kalah (consumed). v.31 provides the fire simile: the strong become tow (flax fiber), the maker becomes a spark — both burn together. 'None shall quench' does not mean endless burning but that nothing stops the consumption until it is complete.

Notes: kalah = consumed. 'Unquenchable' fire = fire that cannot be stopped until it has consumed its fuel, not fire that burns forever.

docs.title: shamad H8045 — Day of the LORD Passage
docs.text:
Behold, the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it.

Context: Eschatological Day-of-the-LORD passage using shamad (Hiphil impf 3ms). God destroys the sinners OUT OF the land — removal/elimination, not preservation. The Day of the LORD consistently uses destruction vocabulary.

Notes: shamad Hiphil impf 3ms = 'he shall destroy' — causative active. Day of the LORD = eschatological judgment context.

docs.title: Dead Shall Not Rise — Destruction Language
docs.text:
[They are] dead, they shall not live; [they are] deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them, and made all their memory to perish.

Context: Triple negation: dead + shall not live + shall not rise. Their very memory perishes (abad). God has 'visited and destroyed them' — shamad used for the destruction. This is permanent non-existence: no resurrection, no memory.

Notes: Uses shamad ('destroyed them') + abad ('memory perish'). Both destruction words for permanent cessation.

docs.title: Duration Language — Edom's 'Forever' Smoke
docs.text:
It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever.

Context: Key duration-language text. Edom's 'smoke shall go up for ever' — but Edom is now habitable territory. This proves prophetic 'for ever' (olam) language describes the permanence of the judgment result, not literal endlessness of the burning process. Critical parallel to Rev 14:11.

Notes: olam (H5769) = 'for ever' — context-dependent. Edom's fire has long been out, proving 'forever' describes permanence of result.

docs.title: Source Text for Mark 9:43-48 — Corpses
docs.text:
And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

Context: Mark 9:43-48 quotes this verse. Critical: the Hebrew word is peger (H6297) = CORPSES, dead bodies. The worm feeds on dead bodies, not living beings. 'Their fire shall not be quenched' parallels Isa 34:10 (Edom) — unquenchable fire that produces complete consumption, not endless burning.

Notes: Parsed: pigrey (peger H6297 mp cst, 'corpses of'). The entire scene describes dead bodies being decomposed by worms and consumed by fire — not living beings in torment.

docs.title: Four Dissipation Similes
docs.text:
Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff [that] is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.

Context: Four cessation similes in one verse: morning cloud (dissipates), early dew (evaporates), chaff (blown away), smoke (disperses). Every simile depicts a substance that CEASES TO EXIST. No simile depicts ongoing existence in a ruined state.

Notes: Four similes, all depicting cessation: cloud, dew, chaff, smoke. This is the densest collection of cessation similes in one verse.

docs.title: Strongest Non-Existence Language — 'as though they had not been'
docs.text:
For as ye have drunk upon my holy mountain, [so] shall all the heathen drink continually, yea, they shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been.

Context: The strongest possible non-existence language in the OT: kelo hayu = 'as though they had not been.' This goes beyond 'not existing anymore' to 'as if they never existed.' This is the ultimate cessation formula.

Notes: kelo hayu = 'as if they had not been.' Strongest OT cessation formula — not merely death but retroactive non-existence.

docs.title: Comprehensive Destruction Passage — Stubble, Ashes, Root/Branch
docs.text:
For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do [this], saith the LORD of hosts.

Context: The most comprehensive OT destruction passage. Five elements: (1) burn as an oven, (2) wicked are stubble, (3) burned up completely, (4) neither root nor branch remaining, (5) become ashes under feet. The righteous tread on ASHES — not living beings. Ashes are the end product of complete combustion.

docs.title: kalah — 'Utter End' + Stubble Simile
docs.text:
But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies. What do ye imagine against the LORD? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time. For while [they be] folden together [as] thorns, and while they are drunken [as] drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry.

Context: kalah (H3615) used twice: 'utter end' (kalah construct). 'Affliction shall not rise up the second time' — the destruction is so complete there is nothing left to afflict again. The stubble simile (v.10) depicts complete consumption.

Notes: kalah = 'complete end/consumption.' Double use emphasizes finality. 'Not rise up the second time' = nothing left to cause further trouble.

docs.title: Even Powers Behind Tyre — Ashes, 'Never Any More'
docs.text:
Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee. All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never [shalt] thou [be] any more.

Context: Directed at the power behind the king of Tyre (often interpreted as Satan/the cherub figure). Fire from WITHIN devours. Result: brought to ashes + 'never shalt thou be any more' (ayin). Even the most exalted evil power is reduced to ashes and non-existence.

Notes: Fire devours from within → ashes → 'never any more' (we-eyneka ad-olam, 'and you are not, to eternity'). Same ayin + olam construction.

docs.title: Apoleia G684 — Broad Way to Destruction vs. Narrow Way to Life
docs.text:
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide [is] the gate, and broad [is] the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait [is] the gate, and narrow [is] the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

Context: Binary contrast: two ways, two gates, two destinations — destruction (apoleia) vs. life (zoe). If life means continued conscious existence with God, then destruction means the opposite: cessation of existence. Jesus frames the choice as existence vs. non-existence, not two forms of eternal existence.

Notes: apoleia (G684) as destination. Structural binary: destruction ≠ life. If life = conscious existence, destruction = non-existence.

docs.title: Apollymi G622 — God Destroys Soul and Body in Gehenna
docs.text:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: Jesus' most explicit destruction statement. Two key observations: (1) Jesus uses apollymi (G622, 'destroy') for what God does, not apokteinō (G615, 'kill') — apollymi is STRONGER than mere killing. (2) God destroys BOTH soul AND body in gehenna — the entire person is destroyed, not just the body while the soul survives in torment.

Notes: Parsed: apokteinontwn (apokteinō G615, Pres Act Ptcp, 'those killing') vs. apolesai (apollymi G622, Aor Act Inf, 'to destroy'). Deliberate word change: humans KILL the body; God DESTROYS soul and body. apollymi is lexically stronger than apokteinō.

docs.title: Apollymi G622 — Central Perish-vs-Life Contrast
docs.text:
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

Context: The central NT soteriology verse. apollymi (Aor Mid Subj 3s, 'should not perish') contrasted with echō zōēn aiōnion ('have everlasting life'). The subjunctive mood (me apolelatai) in a purpose clause: the PURPOSE of God's gift is that believers NOT perish. Perishing is the default; eternal life is the alternative.

Notes: Parsed: apoletai (apollymi G622, Aor Mid Subj 3s, 'should perish') + eche zoen aionion (echō G2192 Pres Act Subj 3s + zōē G2222 + aiōnios G166). Structural binary: perish ≠ eternal life.

docs.title: Apollymi G622 — Universal Perishing Without Repentance
docs.text:
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.

Context: Jesus uses apollymi twice (vv. 3 and 5, identical wording). Destruction is the DEFAULT fate of ALL — not a special punishment for the especially wicked. Repentance is the only escape from perishing.

Notes: apollymi Fut Mid Ind 2p = 'you shall perish.' Said twice for emphasis. Universal scope: ALL perish without repentance.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence — apollymi as 'Lost' (Recoverable)
docs.text:
What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it? And when he hath found [it], he layeth [it] on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he cometh home, he calleth together [his] friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.

Context: apollymi in its 'lost/straying' semantic category (recoverable). The sheep is apollymi (lost) but still alive and recoverable. ECT proponents argue this shows apollymi's core meaning is 'lost/ruined' rather than 'destroyed.' Counter-argument: illegitimate totality transfer — a word used in four semantic categories does not carry all four in every context. Luke 15 uses 'recoverable loss'; Matt 10:28 uses 'destroy utterly.'

Notes: apollymi here = 'lost' (recoverable). Context: parable of seeking the lost. In judgment contexts (Matt 10:28, John 3:16), no recovery is possible.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence — Prodigal Son 'Lost and Found'
docs.text:
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry. ... It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.

Context: apollymi for the prodigal son — 'lost' but recoverable. The father describes him as 'dead and alive again, lost and found.' This is the 'recoverable loss' sense of apollymi, not the 'destroy utterly' sense. The parable context (seeking sinners) determines the meaning.

Notes: apollymi = 'lost' (recoverable). Dead/alive language is metaphorical (spiritual death). Not applicable to eschatological judgment passages.

docs.title: Apollymi G622 — Historical Destructions as Paradigms
docs.text:
They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all. ... But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed [them] all.

Context: Jesus uses apollymi for two historical destructions: the Flood and Sodom. Both describe people who CEASED TO EXIST — the flood victims drowned and died; the Sodomites were incinerated. apollymi in these contexts unambiguously means 'killed/destroyed,' not 'lost but still existing.'

Notes: apollymi Aor Act Ind 3s = 'destroyed them all.' Historical referent: people who ceased to exist. This fixes the eschatological meaning of apollymi.

docs.title: Death vs. Eternal Life — The Wages Statement
docs.text:
For the wages of sin [is] death; but the gift of God [is] eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Context: Paul's definitive contrast: death (thanatos) vs. eternal life (zōē aiōnios). The 'wages of sin' is DEATH — not torment, not suffering, not separation, but death. The contrast is existence (eternal life) vs. non-existence (death). Death is the natural result of sin; eternal life is a gift.

Notes: thanatos (death) vs. zoe aionios (eternal life). Binary: death ≠ life. If eternal life = conscious existence, death = non-existence.

docs.title: Apoleia G684 — 'Whose End Is Destruction'
docs.text:
Whose end [is] destruction, whose God [is their] belly, and [whose] glory [is] in their shame, who mind earthly things.)

Context: apoleia as the TELOS (end/outcome) for enemies of the cross. The end is destruction — not ongoing existence in a ruined state. Paul uses telos (end) + apoleia (destruction) to describe the final outcome.

Notes: hon to telos apoleia = 'whose end [is] destruction.' telos = final outcome/termination. apoleia as the end state.

docs.title: Olethros G3639 — Sudden Eschatological Destruction
docs.text:
For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape.

Context: olethros (G3639) with aiphnidios ('sudden'). The destruction is sudden and inescapable — not gradual or ongoing. The labor-pains simile emphasizes surprise and inescapability, not duration.

Notes: aiphnidios olethros = 'sudden destruction.' olethros here is a single catastrophic event, not an ongoing process.

docs.title: Olethros Aionios — Everlasting Destruction
docs.text:
[Which is] a manifest token of the righteous judgment of God, that ye may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which ye also suffer: Seeing [it is] a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you; And to you who are troubled rest with us, when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, In flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ: Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power; When he shall come to be glorified in his saints, and to be admired in all them that believe (because our testimony among you was believed) in that day.

Context: The key olethros eschatological passage. v.9: olethros aionios = 'everlasting destruction.' Two exegetical questions: (1) 'everlasting destruction' = permanent result or ongoing process? The Hebrews pattern (eternal redemption, judgment, salvation — all permanent results) favors permanent result. (2) 'from the presence of the Lord' (apo prosopou) = 'away from' (separation) or 'proceeding from' (source)? Greek apo can mean either; if source, the Lord's presence CAUSES the destruction.

Notes: Parsed: olethron (olethros G3639, Acc Sg M) aionion (aionios G166, Acc Sg M) apo prosopou (from face/presence). olethros in accusative = penalty suffered. aionios modifies the destruction noun.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence — Olethros as Remedial Discipline
docs.text:
To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

Context: olethros used for DISCIPLINARY purpose ('that the spirit may be saved'). ECT counter-argument: if olethros can be remedial here, it might be remedial eschatologically. Evaluation: this is a living church member under discipline, not an impenitent person at final judgment. The 'that the spirit may be saved' clause explicitly shows this is NOT final destruction — it is categorically different from 2 Thess 1:9.

Notes: olethros here = disciplinary, not eschatological. The salvation-purpose clause ('that the spirit may be saved') distinguishes this from final judgment.

docs.title: Olethros + Apoleia Together — Double Destruction
docs.text:
But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and [into] many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.

Context: Both olethros (G3639) and apoleia (G684) together in one verse — double destruction vocabulary. The verb 'drown' (bythizo) adds a cessation image: drowning = death by submersion. The doubling of destruction words intensifies the sense of total ruin.

Notes: olethron kai apoleian = 'destruction and perdition.' Both destruction nouns together. bythizo = 'drown/plunge' — vivid cessation imagery.

docs.title: Apoleia Concentration — False Teachers
docs.text:
But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction. And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of. And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.

Context: Three uses of apoleia in three verses — the densest NT concentration. v.1: 'swift destruction' (tachinēn apoleian), v.2: 'pernicious ways' (tais apoleiais), v.3: 'their damnation' (hē apoleia). Peter's polemic against false teachers is saturated with destruction vocabulary.

Notes: apoleia 3x in 3 verses. 2 Peter has 5x apoleia in 61 verses — the epicenter of NT destruction vocabulary.

docs.title: Sodom → Ashes — Destruction Paradigm
docs.text:
And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned [them] with an overthrow, making [them] an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

Context: Peter explicitly states Sodom was turned to ASHES (tephrōsas) and made an EXAMPLE (hupodeigma) of eschatological judgment. If Sodom is the paradigm ('ensample'), and Sodom was reduced to ashes, then the eschatological fate of the ungodly is also reduction to ashes — not eternal conscious torment.

Notes: tephrōsas (tephroō, 'to reduce to ashes'). hupodeigma = 'example/pattern.' The paradigm case for eschatological judgment is reduction to ashes.

docs.title: Apoleia/Apollymi — Perdition of Ungodly / Not Willing Any Perish
docs.text:
But the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men. ... The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

Context: v.7: apoleia — the heavens and earth are reserved for fire 'against the day of judgment and perdition (apoleia) of ungodly men.' v.9: apollymi — God is 'not willing that any should perish (apollymi).' The verb and noun of the same root appear in the same context: perishing IS the perdition/destruction that awaits the ungodly at judgment.

Notes: v.7 apoleia (noun), v.9 apollymi (verb). Same root, same context. God's delay in judgment is motivated by desire that none perish.

docs.title: Fire Devours — Drawing Back to Perdition
docs.text:
But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries. ... But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.

Context: v.27: Fire 'devours' (esthiō) the adversaries — fire consumes, it does not preserve. v.39: apoleia vs. peripoiēsis ('saving/preserving') of the soul. Binary: drawing back to destruction OR believing to salvation. The soul is either saved or destroyed — not preserved in torment.

Notes: v.27 esthiō = 'to eat/devour.' Fire eats/consumes its fuel. v.39 apoleia vs. peripoiēsis psychēs = destruction vs. preservation of soul.

docs.title: ECT Proof-Text — Torment with Fire and Brimstone
docs.text:
The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

Context: Strongest ECT proof-text. Key observations: (1) Genre = apocalyptic symbolism (Revelation). (2) OT source = Isa 34:10 (Edom's 'smoke forever' — fire now out). (3) basanisthēsetai (basanizō G928, Fut Pass Ind 3s, 'shall be tormented') — TORMENT vocabulary, not destruction vocabulary. Different word family. (4) 'No rest day nor night' — applied to beast-worshipers during the judgment period. (5) 'Smoke ascends' echoes Gen 19:28 (Sodom) — smoke rises from completed destruction, not from ongoing burning.

Notes: Parsed: basanisthēsetai (basanizō G928, Fut Pass Ind 3s, 'shall be tormented') + kapnos (G2586, 'smoke') + basanismou (basanismos G929, 'torment'). Note: basanizō/basanismos are TORMENT words, not destruction words. Different semantic domain from apollymi/apoleia/olethros.

docs.title: ECT Proof-Text — Everlasting Fire/Punishment
docs.text:
Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels: ... And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

Context: Key ECT proof-text. 'Everlasting fire' (pur aionion) and 'everlasting punishment' (kolasin aiōnion). The aionios pattern from Hebrews applies: eternal redemption (Heb 9:12), eternal judgment (Heb 6:2), eternal salvation (Heb 5:9) — all permanent results, not ongoing processes. 'Everlasting punishment' = punishment whose result (death/destruction) is permanent. Note: 'fire prepared for the devil and his angels' — the fire was prepared for supernatural beings, not originally for humans.

Notes: aionion modifies kolasin (punishment), not a process verb. Hebrews pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result. kolasin = punishment (corrective, from kolazō), not basanismos (torment).

docs.title: ECT Proof-Text — Gehenna, Unquenchable Fire, Worm
docs.text:
And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. And if thy foot offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter halt into life, than having two feet to be cast into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out: it is better for thee to enter into the kingdom of God with one eye, than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.

Context: Jesus quotes Isa 66:24 three times. Critical: the source text (Isa 66:24) describes CORPSES (peger), not living beings. The worm feeds on dead bodies. 'Unquenchable fire' means fire that CANNOT BE STOPPED until it has consumed its fuel (cf. Jer 17:27, where 'unquenchable' fire burned Jerusalem — now long extinguished). The binary is 'life' vs. 'gehenna' = existence vs. destruction, not two forms of eternal existence.

Notes: Quotes Isa 66:24 (peger = corpses). 'Unquenchable' (asbestos G762) = fire that cannot be put out, not fire that burns forever. Jer 17:27 proves this: Jerusalem's 'unquenchable' fire has been out for millennia.

docs.title: Sodom — 'Eternal Fire' Produces Ashes
docs.text:
Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

Context: Sodom suffers 'the vengeance of eternal fire' (puros aiōniou). But Sodom is now ASHES (2 Pet 2:6). The 'eternal fire' produced permanent DESTRUCTION, not endless burning. This definitively proves that 'eternal fire' describes fire whose RESULTS are eternal, not fire that burns endlessly. Key interpretive text for Matt 25:41 and Rev 14:10-11.

Notes: puros aioniou = 'of eternal fire.' But Sodom's fire is long out. 'Eternal' modifies the RESULT (permanent destruction), not the DURATION (endless burning). This governs interpretation of 'everlasting fire' in Matt 25:41.

docs.title: Final Destruction — Fire Devours
docs.text:
And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them.

Context: The final destruction scene. Fire from God 'devoured' (katesthiō, G2719) them — the fire EATS/CONSUMES. katesthiō is an intensified form of esthiō ('to eat'). Fire that devours its fuel produces ashes, not ongoing existence. This is the last mention of the wicked before the lake of fire (v.14-15).

Notes: katephagen (katesthiō G2719, Aor Act Ind 3s, 'devoured'). kata- intensifier + esthiō ('to eat') = 'to eat up completely, devour.' Fire consumes; it does not preserve.

docs.title: Apoleia — Beast 'Goes Into Perdition'
docs.text:
The beast that thou sawest was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition: and they that dwell on the earth shall wonder... And the beast that was, and is not, even he is the eighth, and is of the seven, and goeth into perdition.

Context: apoleia as a DESTINATION for the beast. The beast 'goes into' (hupagei eis) perdition — apoleia functions as a terminus/end-state. Combined with 'was, and is not' language (echoing non-existence formulas), the beast's end is cessation.

Notes: hupagei eis apoleian = 'goes into perdition.' apoleia as destination/terminus. 'Was, and is not' = non-existence language.

docs.title: Second Death — Lake of Fire
docs.text:
And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Context: The lake of fire IS the second death. Not 'the second torment' or 'the second separation' but 'the second DEATH.' Death is the end of life, not the continuation of life in suffering. Even death and hades are destroyed — the instruments of death are themselves consumed.

Notes: houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin = 'this is the second death.' The lake of fire = death, not torment.

docs.title: Duration Pattern — 'Eternal Redemption'
docs.text:
Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption [for us].

Context: aionios + result-noun pattern. 'Eternal redemption' (aiōnian lytrōsin) = a once-for-all act of redemption whose RESULT endures forever, not an ongoing process of redeeming. This pattern governs 2 Thess 1:9 ('everlasting destruction').

Notes: aiōnian lytrōsin = 'eternal redemption.' One-time act, permanent result. Pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result.

docs.title: Duration Pattern — 'Eternal Judgment'
docs.text:
Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.

Context: aionios + result-noun pattern. 'Eternal judgment' (aiōniou krimatos) = a judgment whose RESULT is permanent, not an ongoing process of judging. The judgment happens once; the verdict endures forever.

Notes: aiōniou krimatos = 'eternal judgment.' Judgment is an event; 'eternal' modifies the permanence of the result.

docs.title: Duration Pattern — 'Eternal Salvation'
docs.text:
And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him;

Context: aionios + result-noun pattern. 'Eternal salvation' (sōtērias aiōniou) = salvation whose RESULT endures forever, not an ongoing process of saving. Three Hebrews passages establish the pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result.

Notes: sōtērias aiōniou = 'eternal salvation.' The third instance of the pattern. Applied to 2 Thess 1:9: 'everlasting destruction' = destruction whose result is permanent.

docs.title: Duration Word Test — olam = 3 Days
docs.text:
I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars [was] about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God.

Context: olam (H5769) = 'for ever' — but Jonah was in the fish for 3 DAYS. This proves olam is context-dependent, not always 'endless.' When applied to things that end (Jonah's confinement, Edom's smoke, a slave's service), olam means 'for the duration of' or 'permanently within the relevant timeframe.'

Notes: olam = '3 days' in context. Proof that olam/aionios duration words are context-dependent.

docs.title: Duration Word Test — olam = Until Death
docs.text:
Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever.

Context: olam = 'for ever' in the context of a slave serving his master — obviously meaning 'for the rest of his life,' not 'endlessly.' Another proof that olam is not inherently 'eternal' but context-dependent.

Notes: olam = 'for the rest of his life.' Context determines duration, not the word itself.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence — Apoleia as 'Waste'
docs.text:
But when his disciples saw [it], they had indignation, saying, To what purpose [is] this waste?

Context: apoleia used for 'waste' of ointment. ECT proponents argue the ointment still exists in a 'wasted' state. Counter-evaluation: the ointment was USED UP, GONE, CONSUMED — it ceased to exist as a useful substance. This actually SUPPORTS cessation: apoleia = the state of being used up/gone.

Notes: apoleia = 'waste.' The ointment was consumed/used up — it ceased to exist as ointment. Supports cessation rather than 'ruined but still existing.'

docs.title: God Able to Save AND Destroy
docs.text:
There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?

Context: James pairs sōzō (save) and apollymi (destroy) as the two things God is able to do. Binary: save OR destroy. Not save-to-blessing OR save-to-torment. God's power extends to both preservation and annihilation.

Notes: sōsai kai apolesai = 'to save and to destroy.' The apollymi-sōzō antonym pair: God's two options are preservation and destruction.

docs.title: The Soul That Sins Shall Die
docs.text:
Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

Context: Foundation text from etc7-01: the nephesh (soul) CAN DIE. If the soul is destructible, then apollymi (destroy both soul and body in gehenna, Matt 10:28) is literal, not metaphorical. The soul is not inherently immortal.

Notes: hannephesh hachote't hi' tamut = 'the soul that sins, it shall die.' nephesh = soul. The soul is mortal and destructible.

docs.title: God Alone Has Immortality
docs.text:
Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom [be] honour and power everlasting. Amen.

Context: Foundation text from etc7-02: God ALONE has athanasia (immortality). If only God possesses immortality, the wicked do not have it — they cannot live forever in torment. This removes the theological prerequisite for ECT (inherent soul immortality).

Notes: monos echōn athanasian = 'alone having immortality.' If only God has immortality, the wicked cannot have eternal conscious existence in torment.

docs.title: Two Groups — Perishing vs. Saved
docs.text:
For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.

Context: Paul's binary: tois apollymenois ('those perishing') vs. tois sōzomenois ('those being saved'). Present participles indicate ongoing states leading to final outcomes. The two destinies are perishing and salvation — not two forms of eternal existence.

Notes: apollymenois (Pres Mid/Pass Ptcp) vs. sōzomenois (Pres Pass Ptcp). Present participles = ongoing process toward final destiny.

docs.title: Two Groups — Saved and Perishing
docs.text:
For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish:

Context: Same binary as 1 Cor 1:18: sōzomenois ('being saved') vs. apollymenois ('perishing'). Paul consistently uses the apollymi/sōzō antonym pair to describe the two destinies.

Notes: Same apollymenois/sōzomenois binary. Paul's consistent framework: perishing vs. salvation.

docs.title: Never Perish — Negated apollymi
docs.text:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any [man] pluck them out of my hand.

Context: Jesus gives eternal life and promises believers 'shall never perish' (ou me apolōntai, emphatic double negative). The assurance is that believers will NOT perish — implying that perishing is the fate of those who do not receive eternal life.

Notes: ou me apolōntai = 'they shall by no means perish.' Emphatic double negative. The promise of not-perishing presupposes that perishing is the default fate.

docs.title: God's Will — None of These Little Ones Perish
docs.text:
Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.

Context: God's will is that none perish (apollymi). Parallel to 2 Pet 3:9 ('not willing that any should perish'). The Father's desire is that people NOT be destroyed — implying destruction is the alternative to salvation.

Notes: apoletai (apollymi Aor Mid Subj 3s, 'should perish'). The Father's will = preservation, not destruction.

docs.title: Son of Perdition — Judas
docs.text:
While I was with them in the world, I kept them in thy name: those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition; that the scripture might be fulfilled.

Context: ho huios tēs apōleias = 'the son of perdition/destruction.' Semitic destiny-genitive: the one whose destiny IS apoleia. Judas is characterized by and destined for destruction. Same title applied to the Antichrist in 2 Thess 2:3.

Notes: ho huios tēs apōleias = 'the son of destruction.' Destiny-genitive = the person whose end is destruction.

docs.title: Apoleia — Peter's Curse on Simon
docs.text:
But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.

Context: eis apōleian = 'unto destruction.' Peter wishes destruction on Simon Magus's money and potentially on Simon himself. The curse invokes destruction, not preservation in suffering.

Notes: eis apōleian = directional: heading toward destruction.

docs.title: Vessels of Wrath Fitted for Destruction
docs.text:
[What] if God, willing to shew [his] wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:

Context: skeuē orgēs katērtismena eis apōleian = 'vessels of wrath fitted/prepared for destruction.' The vessels are FITTED FOR destruction — apoleia is their purpose/destination. Paul uses apoleia as the final end of vessels of wrath.

Notes: katērtismena eis apōleian = 'having been prepared for destruction.' Perfect passive participle = already fitted for their end.

docs.title: Non-Existence Declaration — Wicked Shall Not Be
docs.text:
For yet a little while, and the wicked [shall] not [be]: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it [shall] not [be].

Context: Psalm 37 is a wisdom psalm contrasting the fate of the righteous and wicked. Verse 10 uses explicit non-existence language (ayin) to describe the future state of the wicked.

Notes: Uses ayin (non-existence particle) twice — the wicked shall not be, his place shall not be. This is cessation language, not ruin-while-continuing. Part of Psalm 37 triple destruction vocabulary cluster (abad v.20, kalah v.20, shamad v.38).

docs.title: Olethros Aionios — Everlasting Destruction from the Presence of the Lord
docs.text:
Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

Context: Paul describes the punishment awaiting those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel. This is the key eschatological olethros passage.

Notes: Key passage combining olethros (G3639) with aionios (G166). The construction 'olethros aionios' could mean destruction that is everlasting in its result (conditionalist) or destruction that is everlasting in its process (ECT). The phrase 'from the presence of the Lord' (apo prosopou) is debated.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence: Apollymi as 'Lost' (Recoverable) — Lost Sheep, Coin, Son
docs.text:
What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it? And when he hath found [it], he layeth [it] on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he cometh home, he calleth together [his] friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost. I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance. Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find [it]? And when she hath found [it], she calleth [her] friends and [her] neighbours together, saying, Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost. Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth. And he said, A certain man had two sons: And the younger of them said to [his] father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth [to me]. And he divided unto them [his] living. And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living. And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want. And he went and joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine. And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him. And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants. And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son. But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put [it] on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on [his] feet: And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill [it]; and let us eat, and be merry: For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry. Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing. And he called one of the servants, and asked what these things meant. And he said unto him, Thy brother is come; and thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound. And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came his father out, and intreated him. And he answering said to [his] father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends: But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf. And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.

Context: Jesus tells three parables about lost things in response to Pharisees criticizing him for receiving sinners. All three use apollymi (G622) in the sense of 'lost' — something that can be recovered.

Notes: Critical counter-evidence for conditionalist reading of apollymi. In these parables, apollymi means 'lost' not 'destroyed' — the sheep, coin, and son are all recovered. ECT proponents argue this shows apollymi does not necessarily mean annihilation. However, the recoverable sense of apollymi in parables about seeking the lost does not govern eschatological judgment passages where destruction is explicitly irreversible (Matt 10:28, John 3:16). The context of each usage determines meaning.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Hebrew/Greek destruction vocabulary: abad/apollumi (H6/G622), shamad (H8045), kalah (H3615), shachath (H7843), apoleia (G684), olethros (G3639). Lexical definitions, eschatological usage.

docs.title: 1. Genesis 2:17 — First Death Threat
docs.text:
Text: "But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die."

Context: The mot tamut construction (infinitive absolute + imperfect) establishes the emphatic certainty of death as penalty for sin. This is the foundation on which all destruction vocabulary builds. The punishment for sin is death, not torment.

Original language: mot tamut — the same emphatic form used for judicial death penalties throughout Torah (Exo 21:12ff), where it invariably means actual death.

Cross-references: Rom 6:23 (wages of sin is death); Gen 3:19 (dust returns to dust); 1 Cor 15:21-22 (by man came death).

Relevance: Establishes that the original divine penalty for sin is death. All subsequent destruction vocabulary describes the execution of this sentence.

docs.title: 2. Genesis 6:7 — First Divine Destruction Declaration
docs.text:
Text: "And the LORD said, I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth..."

Context: Uses machah (H4229, "blot out"). God's first declaration of intent to destroy humanity. The Flood is the paradigm case for divine destruction.

Original language: machah = "to blot out, wipe away." The destruction language escalates to shachath in vv. 11-13.

Cross-references: 2 Pet 2:5 (God spared not the old world); Luke 17:27 (the flood destroyed them all).

Relevance: Establishes the pattern of divine destruction: God announces judgment, executes it, and the result is death of the wicked.

docs.title: 3. Genesis 6:11-13 — Threefold Shachath (H7843)
docs.text:
Text: "The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth. And God said unto Noah... I will destroy them with the earth."

Context: Three forms of shachath in three verses. The same root describes the sin (corruption) and the judgment (destruction).

Original language: v.11 Niphal wayyiqtol 3fs (earth was corrupt — reflexive/passive), v.12 Niphal perfect 3fs (was corrupt — stative) + Hiphil perfect 3ms (had corrupted — causative, flesh as agent), v.13 Hiphil participle ms + 3mp (I will destroy them — causative, God as agent).

Cross-references: 2 Pet 2:5-6 (flood and Sodom as paradigms); Rev 11:18 (destroy them which destroy the earth — same diaphtheiro root in LXX).

Relevance: Establishes the corruption-to-destruction principle. The same root describes both the disease (corruption) and the cure (destruction). Corruption naturally terminates in destruction.

docs.title: 4. Genesis 19:24-25 — Destruction of Sodom
docs.text:
Text: "Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven; And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities..."

Context: Sodom's destruction is the paradigm case for eschatological judgment. The verb haphak ("overthrew") emphasizes complete reversal/annihilation.

Cross-references: Jude 1:7 (suffering vengeance of eternal fire); 2 Pet 2:6 (turned to ashes as example); Luke 17:29 (fire destroyed them all).

Relevance: The fire-and-brimstone judgment produced ashes (2 Pet 2:6), not ongoing torment. This is the biblical paradigm for "eternal fire."

docs.title: 5. Deuteronomy 7:10 — abad H6 in Hiphil
docs.text:
Text: "And repayeth them that hate him to their face, to destroy them: he will not be slack to him that hateth him, he will repay him to his face."

Context: Direct divine destruction language. God actively and personally destroys those who hate him.

Original language: abad H6 Hiphil — causative active. God is the agent; destruction is the action.

Cross-references: Psa 145:20 (the LORD preserveth... but all the wicked will he destroy); 2 Thess 1:8-9 (taking vengeance... punished with everlasting destruction).

Relevance: God's response to those who hate him is destruction, not preservation in torment.

docs.title: 6. Deuteronomy 8:19-20 — Covenant Curse with abad
docs.text:
Text: "...I testify against you this day that ye shall surely perish. As the nations which the LORD destroyeth before your face, so shall ye perish..."

Context: Covenant-curse language using the infinitive absolute intensification (abad toadedun = "surely perish").

Original language: Infinitive absolute + finite verb = emphatic certainty. The fate is explicitly parallel to destroyed nations who ceased to exist.

Cross-references: Deut 28:20-22 (same curse cluster with shamad and abad together).

Relevance: Covenant disobedience results in perishing — the same perishing that befell destroyed nations.

docs.title: 7. Deuteronomy 28:20-22 — Covenant Curse Cluster (abad + shamad)
docs.text:
Text: "The LORD shall send upon thee cursing... until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly... The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption... until thou perish."

Context: Dense covenant-curse passage using both shamad ("be destroyed") and abad ("perish") in the same judgment context.

Original language: v.20 shamad Niphal ("be destroyed") + abad Qal ("perish") together. v.22 abad again.

Cross-references: Deut 7:10 (God destroys those who hate him); Deut 8:19-20 (surely perish).

Relevance: Both destruction words operate in the same context, showing shared semantic domain of total destruction.

docs.title: 8. Psalm 1:4-6 — Chaff Simile + abad
docs.text:
Text: "The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away... the way of the ungodly shall perish."

Context: The first psalm establishes the binary: righteous flourish like a tree (v.3), wicked are chaff (v.4). The way of the ungodly "shall perish" (abad Qal imperfect 3fs).

Original language: abad Qal impf 3fs — intransitive: the way itself perishes. LXX translates with apollymi.

Cross-references: Matt 3:12 (burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire); Hos 13:3 (chaff driven with the whirlwind); Mal 4:1 (stubble).

Relevance: Chaff is a cessation simile — it does not continue to exist in a ruined state but ceases to exist. This is the first of many cessation similes applied to the wicked.

docs.title: 9. Psalm 37:10 — Non-Existence Declaration (ayin)
docs.text:
Text: "For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be."

Context: Explicit non-existence language. Hebrew ayin (H369) is a noun of non-existence.

Original language: ayin rasha = "the wicked is not" (non-existence). einennu = "he is not" (emphatic non-existence with 3ms suffix). Two ayin statements in one verse.

Cross-references: Psa 37:20 (consume into smoke); Psa 37:36 (he was not); Psa 37:38 (destroyed together); Psa 59:13 (that they may not be); Psa 104:35 (be no more).

Relevance: The explicit result of destruction is non-existence — not torment, not ruin, but the absence of the wicked entirely.

docs.title: 10. Psalm 37:20 — Triple Destruction (abad + kalah + Smoke Simile)
docs.text:
Text: "But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD shall be as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away."

Context: Two destruction words in one verse: abad (perish) and kalah (consume, twice). The "fat of lambs" simile: fat on the altar is completely consumed. "Into smoke shall they consume away" — smoke dissipates into nothing.

Original language: yobedu (abad Qal impf 3mp, "shall perish") + kalu (kalah Qal perf 3p, "consumed") + be'ashan kalu ("in smoke consumed"). Double kalah intensifies the cessation.

Cross-references: Psa 68:2 (wax melting); Hos 13:3 (four dissipation similes); Mal 4:1-3 (ashes).

Relevance: Two destruction words plus cessation imagery. The smoke simile describes complete dissipation — the wicked cease to exist.

docs.title: 11. Psalm 37:36 — Non-Existence: "He Was Not"
docs.text:
Text: "Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found."

Context: Third non-existence statement in Psalm 37 (with v.10 and v.20).

Original language: einennu = "he is not." Same ayin construction as v.10.

Cross-references: Psa 37:10 (wicked shall not be); Oba 1:16 (as though they had not been).

Relevance: The wicked person ceases to exist entirely — sought but not found. Emphatic cessation.

docs.title: 12. Psalm 37:38 — shamad H8045 (Transgressors Destroyed Together)
docs.text:
Text: "But the transgressors shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off."

Context: Third destruction word in Psalm 37: shamad. Combined with karath ("cut off"). The "end" (acharith) of the wicked is cutting off.

Original language: nishmedu (shamad Niphal perf 3p, "were destroyed") + nichratah (karath Niphal perf 3fs, "was cut off"). Prophetic perfects = future certainty.

Cross-references: Psa 92:7 (destroyed for ever); Psa 145:20 (all the wicked will he destroy).

Relevance: Psalm 37 uses three destruction words (abad v.20, kalah v.20, shamad v.38), three non-existence statements (v.10, v.20, v.36), and karath (v.38) — the densest single-chapter destruction vocabulary cluster in the OT.

docs.title: 13. Psalm 59:13 — kalah + Non-Existence
docs.text:
Text: "Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be..."

Context: kalah (Piel imperative) used twice with explicit non-existence result clause.

Original language: kalah Piel imperative + we'einemo ("and they are not") = consume them so that they do not exist.

Cross-references: Psa 37:10 (shall not be); Psa 104:35 (be no more).

Relevance: The PURPOSE of consumption (kalah) is non-existence (ayin). Destruction vocabulary produces cessation of existence.

docs.title: 14. Psalm 68:2 — Wax/Fire Simile with abad
docs.text:
Text: "As smoke is driven away, so drive them away: as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God."

Context: Double cessation simile: smoke driven away + wax melting before fire. Both substances cease to exist.

Original language: yobedu (abad Qal impf 3mp, "let the wicked perish"). The wicked perish "at the presence of God" — God's presence causes destruction.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:9 (destruction from the presence of the Lord); Psa 37:20 (consume into smoke).

Relevance: Wax and smoke are cessation images. Neither continues to exist in a ruined state. The wicked perish at God's presence, not survive in torment.

docs.title: 15. Psalm 92:7 — shamad with adey-ad ("Destroyed Forever")
docs.text:
Text: "When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; it is that they shall be destroyed for ever."

Context: shamad with adey-ad duration modifier. Temporary flourishing followed by permanent destruction.

Original language: lehishamdam adey-ad = "to be destroyed to perpetuity." shamad Niphal infinitive + adey-ad. The grass simile emphasizes temporary existence.

Cross-references: Psa 37:38 (destroyed together); Job 20:7 (perish forever like dung).

Relevance: "For ever" modifies the permanence of the RESULT (destruction), not the duration of a process. The wicked are permanently destroyed.

docs.title: 16. Psalm 92:9 — abad (Enemies Perish)
docs.text:
Text: "For, lo, thine enemies, O LORD, for, lo, thine enemies shall perish; all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered."

Context: abad (Qal impf 3mp) paralleled with "scattered." Two destruction words in Psalm 92 (shamad v.7, abad v.9).

Original language: abad Qal impf 3mp = intransitive "shall perish."

Cross-references: Psa 37:20 (wicked shall perish); Psa 68:2 (wicked perish at presence of God).

Relevance: The enemies of the LORD perish — the same verb used of substances that cease to exist.

docs.title: 17. Psalm 104:35 — Consumed Out of the Earth, Be No More
docs.text:
Text: "Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more."

Context: tamam ("be consumed/completed") with explicit non-existence: "let the wicked be no more" (ayin).

Original language: tamam + ayin = consumed to non-existence.

Cross-references: Psa 37:10 (shall not be); Psa 59:13 (that they may not be).

Relevance: Third passage pairing destruction with explicit non-existence language.

docs.title: 18. Psalm 145:20 — Preserve/Destroy Contrast (shamar vs. shamad)
docs.text:
Text: "The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy."

Context: Binary antonym contrast: shamar (preserve) vs. shamad (destroy). The same God who preserves the righteous destroys the wicked.

Original language: shomer (shamar Qal ptcp ms, "preserves") vs. yashmid (shamad Hiphil impf 3ms, "will destroy"). Hiphil = causative active.

Cross-references: John 3:16 (not perish but have everlasting life); Jam 4:12 (able to save and to destroy).

Relevance: The contrast is preservation vs. destruction — not preservation-in-blessing vs. preservation-in-torment.

docs.title: 19. Job 20:7 — abad with Permanence Indicator
docs.text:
Text: "Yet he shall perish for ever like his own dung: they which have seen him shall say, Where is he?"

Context: abad with "for ever" (lanetsach) and cessation simile (dung). The rhetorical question "Where is he?" emphasizes absence.

Original language: abad Qal impf 3ms + lanetsach. Dung = decomposing substance that ceases to exist.

Cross-references: Psa 92:7 (destroyed for ever); Psa 37:36 (he was not).

Relevance: Permanent perishing with cessation imagery. The wicked are sought but not found.

docs.title: 20. Proverbs 2:22 — Cut Off from the Earth
docs.text:
Text: "But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it."

Context: karath (cut off) + nacah (rooted out). Both verbs describe removal from existence.

Original language: karath Niphal impf + nacah Qal impf = double removal/cessation.

Cross-references: Psa 37:9,34 (evildoers cut off); Psa 37:38 (end of wicked cut off).

Relevance: Cutting off and rooting out describe termination — the wicked cease to be part of the earth.

docs.title: 21. Isaiah 1:28,31 — kalah + Fire
docs.text:
Text: "...they that forsake the LORD shall be consumed. And the strong shall be as tow, and the maker of it as a spark, and they shall both burn together, and none shall quench them."

Context: v.28 uses kalah (consumed). v.31 provides the fire simile: tow (flax fiber) + spark = both burn together.

Original language: kalah = consumed. "None shall quench" = the fire cannot be stopped until consumption is complete, not that it burns endlessly.

Cross-references: Mark 9:43-48 (unquenchable fire); Jer 17:27 (unquenchable fire burned Jerusalem — now long extinguished).

Relevance: "Unquenchable" fire means fire that cannot be resisted or put out, not fire that burns forever. The result is complete consumption.

docs.title: 22. Isaiah 13:9 — shamad H8045 (Day of the LORD)
docs.text:
Text: "Behold, the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it."

Context: Eschatological Day-of-the-LORD passage using shamad.

Original language: shamad Hiphil impf 3ms = "he shall destroy" — causative active. God destroys sinners OUT OF the land.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:7-9 (Lord Jesus revealed from heaven in flaming fire... everlasting destruction); Mal 4:1 (the day cometh that shall burn).

Relevance: Day-of-the-LORD language consistently uses destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

docs.title: 23. Isaiah 26:14 — Dead Shall Not Rise
docs.text:
Text: "They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them, and made all their memory to perish."

Context: Triple negation: dead + shall not live + shall not rise. Uses both shamad ("destroyed them") and abad ("memory perish").

Original language: shamad + abad for permanent cessation. No resurrection, no memory.

Cross-references: Ecc 9:5 (their memory is forgotten); Psa 37:10 (shall not be).

Relevance: The destroyed are permanently dead — no life, no rising, no memory. Two destruction words reinforce permanence.

docs.title: 24. Isaiah 34:10 — Edom's "Forever" Smoke
docs.text:
Text: "It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever."

Context: Edom's smoke "goes up for ever" (olam) — but Edom is now habitable territory (animals dwell there, Isa 34:11-17).

Original language: olam = context-dependent duration word. Edom's fire has long been out.

Cross-references: Rev 14:11 (smoke of their torment ascendeth for ever and ever); Gen 19:28 (smoke of Sodom). Both passages echo this language.

Relevance: Proves that prophetic "for ever" smoke language describes the permanence of the judgment result, not literal endless burning. This governs interpretation of Rev 14:11.

docs.title: 25. Isaiah 66:24 — Corpses (peger)
docs.text:
Text: "And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh."

Context: Source text for Mark 9:43-48. The Hebrew word is peger (H6297) = corpses, dead bodies.

Original language: pigrey (peger mp cst, "corpses of"). The worm feeds on dead bodies (decomposition); the fire consumes dead bodies (cremation). The scene describes aftermath of destruction.

Cross-references: Mark 9:43-48 (Jesus quotes this three times); Isa 66:16-17 (slain and consumed before v.24).

Relevance: The source text for the "unquenchable fire" and "worm dieth not" phrases describes corpses, not living beings in torment.

docs.title: 26. Hosea 13:3 — Four Dissipation Similes
docs.text:
Text: "Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney."

Context: Four cessation similes in one verse: morning cloud (dissipates), early dew (evaporates), chaff (blown away), smoke (disperses).

Cross-references: Psa 1:4 (chaff); Psa 37:20 (smoke); Psa 68:2 (smoke and wax).

Relevance: Every simile depicts a substance that ceases to exist. No simile depicts ongoing existence in a ruined state. The densest collection of cessation similes in one verse.

docs.title: 27. Obadiah 1:16 — Strongest Non-Existence Language
docs.text:
Text: "...they shall be as though they had not been."

Context: kelo hayu — the strongest possible non-existence language in the OT.

Original language: kelo hayu = "as if they had not been." Goes beyond "not existing anymore" to "as if they never existed."

Cross-references: Psa 37:10 (shall not be); Psa 59:13 (may not be); Psa 104:35 (be no more).

Relevance: The ultimate cessation formula. Not merely death but retroactive non-existence. Destruction produces this result.

docs.title: 28. Nahum 1:8-10 — kalah: "Utter End" + Stubble
docs.text:
Text: "But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof... he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time. For while they be folden together as thorns... they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry."

Context: kalah used twice for "utter end." "Affliction shall not rise up the second time" = nothing left to cause further trouble.

Original language: kalah = complete end/consumption. Double use emphasizes finality.

Cross-references: Mal 4:1 (stubble burned up); Isa 1:31 (tow and spark burn together).

Relevance: The destruction is so complete that nothing remains to cause further affliction. Utter finality.

docs.title: 29. Malachi 4:1-3 — Comprehensive Destruction Passage
docs.text:
Text: "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch... And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet..."

Context: The most comprehensive OT destruction passage. Five elements: (1) burn as an oven, (2) wicked are stubble, (3) burned up completely, (4) neither root nor branch, (5) become ashes under feet.

Original language: qash (stubble) + lahat Piel perf 3ms ("devour/burn up") + lo ya'azov shoresh we'anaph ("shall not leave root or branch") + epher ("ashes").

Cross-references: Psa 37:20 (consume into smoke); Nah 1:10 (stubble fully dry); 2 Pet 2:6 (Sodom turned to ashes).

Relevance: Every image is of complete destruction producing ashes. The righteous tread on ASHES — not living beings. Ashes are the end product of complete combustion.

docs.title: 30. Ezekiel 28:18-19 — Ashes and Never Any More
docs.text:
Text: "...therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth... thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more."

Context: Directed at the power behind the king of Tyre. Fire devours from within; result = ashes + "never any more."

Original language: we-eyneka ad-olam = "and you are not, to eternity." ayin + olam = permanent non-existence.

Cross-references: Isa 14:12-15 (fall of Lucifer); Psa 37:10 (shall not be).

Relevance: Even the most exalted evil power is reduced to ashes and permanent non-existence. If this applies to the power behind Tyre, it applies to all the wicked.

docs.title: 31. Matthew 7:13-14 — apoleia: Destruction vs. Life
docs.text:
Text: "...wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life..."

Context: Binary contrast: two ways, two gates, two destinations — destruction (apoleia) vs. life (zoe).

Original language: apoleia (G684) as destination.

Cross-references: John 3:16 (perish vs. life); Rom 6:23 (death vs. life); Phil 3:19 (whose end is destruction).

Relevance: Structurally decisive. If life means continued conscious existence, destruction means the opposite.

docs.title: 32. Matthew 10:28 — apollymi: God Destroys Soul and Body in Gehenna
docs.text:
Text: "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."

Context: Jesus' most explicit destruction statement. Two key observations: (1) apollymi ("destroy"), not apokteino ("kill") — a stronger word. (2) God destroys BOTH soul AND body.

Original language: apokteinonton (apokteino G615, Pres Act Ptcp, "those killing") vs. apolesai (apollymi G622, Aor Act Inf, "to destroy"). Deliberate word change: humans kill the body; God destroys soul and body.

Cross-references: Ezek 18:4 (the soul that sins shall die); Luke 12:4-5 (fear him who can destroy); Matt 7:13 (destruction vs. life).

Relevance: The combined apollymi + soul + body + gehenna is the most explicit NT statement that the whole person is destroyed in final judgment. apollymi is lexically stronger than apokteino.

docs.title: 33. John 3:16 — apollymi: Central Perish-vs-Life Contrast
docs.text:
Text: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

Context: The central NT soteriology verse. apollymi contrasted with eternal life.

Original language: apoletai (apollymi G622, Aor Mid Subj 3s, "should perish") in purpose clause (hina me). Structural binary: me apoletai vs. eche zoen aionion.

Cross-references: Rom 6:23 (death vs. eternal life); Matt 7:13 (destruction vs. life); 2 Pet 3:9 (not willing any should perish).

Relevance: The binary is perishing vs. eternal life. Perishing is the default fate; eternal life is the alternative. These are antithetical outcomes.

docs.title: 34. Luke 13:3,5 — apollymi: Universal Perishing Without Repentance
docs.text:
Text: "I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."

Context: Jesus uses apollymi twice (vv. 3 and 5, identical wording). Destruction is the DEFAULT fate of ALL.

Original language: apollymi Fut Mid Ind 2p = "you shall perish."

Cross-references: John 3:16 (should not perish); 2 Pet 3:9 (not willing any should perish).

Relevance: Universal scope: ALL perish without repentance. Perishing is not a special punishment but the natural end of all sinners.

docs.title: 35. Luke 15:4-32 — Counter-Evidence: apollymi as "Lost" (Recoverable)
docs.text:
Text: Lost sheep (vv.4-7), lost coin (vv.8-10), lost son (vv.11-32). All use apollymi for "lost."

Context: Three parables about lost things. apollymi in its "lost/straying" semantic category (recoverable).

Original language: apollymi = "lost" (recoverable). The sheep is alive; the coin exists; the son returns.

Cross-references: Matt 10:28 (destroy in gehenna — not recoverable); John 3:16 (should not perish — permanent).

Relevance: This is the strongest counter-evidence that apollymi does not always mean cessation. However, the "recoverable loss" sense operates in a different semantic category from the "destroy utterly" sense used in judgment contexts. Context determines meaning — the illegitimate totality transfer fallacy applies to importing the "lost" meaning into "destroy" contexts.

docs.title: 36. Luke 17:27,29 — apollymi for Historical Destructions
docs.text:
Text: "...the flood came, and destroyed them all... it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all."
