Context: Jesus uses apollymi for two historical destructions: the Flood and Sodom. Both describe people who ceased to exist.

Original language: apollymi Aor Act Ind 3s = "destroyed them all."

Cross-references: Gen 6:7 (I will destroy man); Gen 19:24-25 (overthrew those cities); 2 Pet 2:5-6 (examples).

Relevance: Historical referents fix the eschatological meaning. apollymi in these contexts means people who died and ceased to exist — not people preserved in a ruined state.

docs.title: 37. Romans 6:23 — Death vs. Eternal Life
docs.text:
Text: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Context: Paul's definitive contrast: thanatos (death) vs. zoe aionios (eternal life).

Original language: thanatos vs. zoe aionios. Death is the natural result of sin; eternal life is a gift.

Cross-references: John 3:16 (perish vs. life); Matt 7:13 (destruction vs. life); Gen 2:17 (thou shalt surely die).

Relevance: The "wages of sin" is death — not torment, not suffering, not separation. The binary is existence (eternal life) vs. non-existence (death).

docs.title: 38. Philippians 3:19 — apoleia: "Whose End Is Destruction"
docs.text:
Text: "Whose end is destruction..."

Context: apoleia as the telos (end/outcome) for enemies of the cross.

Original language: hon to telos apoleia = "whose end is destruction." telos = final outcome.

Cross-references: Matt 7:13 (broad way to destruction); 2 Pet 2:1 (swift destruction).

Relevance: The end of enemies of the cross is destruction — not ongoing existence.

docs.title: 39. 1 Thessalonians 5:3 — olethros: Sudden Destruction
docs.text:
Text: "For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape."

Context: olethros with aiphnidios ("sudden"). The destruction is sudden and inescapable.

Original language: aiphnidios olethros = "sudden destruction." Not gradual or ongoing.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:9 (everlasting destruction); Luke 17:27,29 (flood and Sodom — sudden).

Relevance: Eschatological destruction is described as sudden, not as an ongoing process.

docs.title: 40. 2 Thessalonians 1:5-10 — olethros aionios: Everlasting Destruction
docs.text:
Text: "...punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power."

Context: The key olethros eschatological passage. Full context: v.7 rest for believers; v.8 flaming fire; v.9 everlasting destruction; v.10 glorified in saints.

Original language: olethron aionion (olethros G3639 Acc Sg M + aionios G166 Acc Sg M) = "everlasting destruction." apo prosopou = "from the presence/face." Both in accusative = penalty they will pay.

Cross-references: Heb 9:12 (eternal redemption — permanent result); Heb 6:2 (eternal judgment — permanent result); Heb 5:9 (eternal salvation — permanent result).

Relevance: Two exegetical questions: (1) "everlasting destruction" = permanent result or ongoing process? The Hebrews pattern strongly favors permanent result. (2) "from the presence of the Lord" = "away from" (separation) or "proceeding from" (source/cause)? If source, the Lord's presence causes the destruction.

docs.title: 41. 1 Corinthians 5:5 — Counter-Evidence: olethros as Remedial
docs.text:
Text: "To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus."

Context: olethros used for disciplinary purpose — the salvation clause ("that the spirit may be saved") shows this is not final destruction.

Original language: olethros = destruction of flesh (disciplinary). The purpose clause is salvific.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:9 (eschatological olethros — no salvation clause); 1 Tim 6:9 (olethros + apoleia).

Relevance: This is counter-evidence: olethros CAN be remedial in a disciplinary context. However, context determines application — discipline of a church member is categorically different from eschatological judgment of the impenitent. The salvation-purpose clause is absent from all eschatological uses.

docs.title: 42. 1 Timothy 6:9 — olethros + apoleia Together
docs.text:
Text: "But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition."

Context: Both olethros and apoleia in one verse — double destruction vocabulary.

Original language: olethron kai apoleian = "destruction and perdition." bythizo = "drown/plunge."

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:9 (olethros alone); Phil 3:19 (apoleia alone); Matt 7:13 (apoleia alone).

Relevance: The doubling of destruction words creates rhetorical intensification. The drowning verb adds vivid cessation imagery.

docs.title: 43. 2 Peter 2:1-3 — apoleia Concentration (3x in 3 Verses)
docs.text:
Text: "...bring upon themselves swift destruction... their pernicious ways... whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not."

Context: Three uses of apoleia in three verses — densest NT concentration.

Original language: v.1 tachinēn apoleian ("swift destruction"), v.2 tais apoleiais, v.3 hē apoleia.

Cross-references: 2 Pet 2:6 (Sodom → ashes); 2 Pet 3:7 (perdition of ungodly men); 2 Pet 3:9 (not willing any should perish).

Relevance: 2 Peter has 5x apoleia in 61 verses — the epicenter of NT destruction vocabulary. Peter's consistent framework for the wicked is destruction.

docs.title: 44. 2 Peter 2:6 — Sodom → Ashes as Paradigm
docs.text:
Text: "And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly."

Context: Peter explicitly states Sodom was turned to ashes (tephrosas) and made an example (hupodeigma).

Original language: tephrosas (tephroo, "to reduce to ashes"). hupodeigma = "example/pattern."

Cross-references: Jude 1:7 (suffering eternal fire); Gen 19:24-25 (original destruction); Luke 17:29 (destroyed them all).

Relevance: If Sodom is the paradigm ("ensample"), and Sodom was reduced to ashes, then the eschatological fate of the ungodly is reduction to ashes.

docs.title: 45. 2 Peter 3:7,9 — apoleia/apollymi
docs.text:
Text: v.7: "...reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men." v.9: "...not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

Context: The verb (apollymi) and noun (apoleia) of the same root in the same context.

Original language: v.7 apoleia (noun); v.9 apollymi (verb). Same root, same eschatological context.

Cross-references: John 3:16 (should not perish); 2 Thess 1:9 (everlasting destruction); 2 Pet 2:6 (ashes as example).

Relevance: God's delay in judgment is motivated by desire that none perish (v.9). Perishing IS the perdition that awaits the ungodly (v.7).

docs.title: 46. Hebrews 10:27,39 — Fire Devours; Drawing Back to Perdition
docs.text:
Text: v.27: "But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries." v.39: "But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul."

Context: v.27 fire "devours" (esthio) adversaries — fire consumes. v.39 apoleia vs. peripoiesis ("saving/preserving").

Original language: esthio = "to eat/devour." apoleia vs. peripoiesis psyches = destruction vs. preservation of soul.

Cross-references: Rev 20:9 (fire devoured them); Matt 10:28 (destroy soul and body); Mal 4:1 (burn them up).

Relevance: Fire devours (consumes) rather than preserves. The binary is destruction vs. preservation — the soul is either saved or destroyed.

docs.title: 47. Revelation 14:10-11 — ECT Proof-Text: Torment Language
docs.text:
Text: "...he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image..."

Context: Strongest ECT proof-text. Several factors: (1) Genre = apocalyptic symbolism. (2) OT source = Isa 34:10 (Edom — fire now out). (3) basanizo (torment) is a different word family from apollymi/apoleia/olethros. (4) "Smoke ascends" echoes Gen 19:28 (Sodom — smoke from completed destruction).

Original language: basanisthesetai (basanizo G928, Fut Pass Ind 3s, "shall be tormented"). kapnos basanismou = "smoke of torment." basanizo/basanismos are TORMENT words, not destruction words.

Cross-references: Isa 34:10 (Edom's smoke for ever — ended); Gen 19:28 (smoke of Sodom ascending); Rev 20:9 (fire devoured them).

Relevance: This passage uses torment vocabulary (basanizo), not destruction vocabulary. It is apocalyptic in genre. The OT source text (Isa 34:10) describes a judgment whose fire has long been extinguished. (Examined in depth in etc7-11 and etc7-15.)

docs.title: 48. Matthew 25:41,46 — ECT Proof-Text: Everlasting Fire/Punishment
docs.text:
Text: v.41: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels." v.46: "And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal."

Context: aionios modifies both "fire" (v.41) and "punishment" (v.46). The fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels," not originally for humans.

Original language: aionion modifies kolasin (punishment), not a process verb. kolasin = punishment (from kolazo), not basanismos (torment).

Cross-references: Heb 9:12 (eternal redemption — permanent result); Jude 1:7 (eternal fire → ashes); 2 Thess 1:9 (everlasting destruction).

Relevance: The Hebrews pattern (aionios + result-noun = permanent result) governs: "everlasting punishment" = punishment whose result is permanent, not punishment that continues as an ongoing process. (Examined in depth in etc7-08 and etc7-14.)

docs.title: 49. Mark 9:43-48 — ECT Proof-Text: Gehenna, Unquenchable Fire, Worm
docs.text:
Text: "...go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched."

Context: Jesus quotes Isa 66:24 three times. The source text describes corpses (peger), not living beings. "Unquenchable fire" = fire that cannot be stopped until consumption is complete.

Original language: asbestos (G762) = "unquenchable" — fire that cannot be put out, not fire that burns forever.

Cross-references: Isa 66:24 (corpses); Jer 17:27 (unquenchable fire burned Jerusalem — now extinguished); Isa 1:31 (none shall quench).

Relevance: The source text (Isa 66:24) controls the interpretation. The worm and fire act on dead bodies, not living beings. (Examined in depth in etc7-05, etc7-14, and etc7-15.)

docs.title: 50. Jude 1:7 — "Eternal Fire" Produces Ashes
docs.text:
Text: "Even as Sodom and Gomorrha... are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire."

Context: Sodom suffers "the vengeance of eternal fire" (puros aioniou). But Sodom is now ashes (2 Pet 2:6).

Original language: puros aioniou = "of eternal fire." But Sodom's fire is long out.

Cross-references: 2 Pet 2:6 (turned to ashes); Gen 19:24-25 (original destruction); Matt 25:41 (everlasting fire).

Relevance: "Eternal fire" produced permanent destruction, not endless burning. This governs interpretation of "everlasting fire" in Matt 25:41.

docs.title: 51. Revelation 20:9 — Final Destruction: Fire Devours
docs.text:
Text: "...and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them."

Context: The final destruction scene. Fire "devoured" (katesthio G2719) them — intensified form of esthio ("to eat").

Original language: katephagen (katesthio G2719, Aor Act Ind 3s, "devoured"). kata- intensifier + esthio = "to eat up completely."

Cross-references: Heb 10:27 (fiery indignation devours); Mal 4:1-3 (burn up, ashes); Rev 20:14 (second death).

Relevance: The last mention of the wicked before the lake of fire describes fire that devours/consumes. Fire that devours produces ashes, not ongoing existence.

docs.title: 52. Revelation 20:14 — Second Death
docs.text:
Text: "And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death."

Context: The lake of fire IS the second death. Not "the second torment" but "the second death."

Original language: houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin = "this is the second death."

Cross-references: Rev 21:8 (second death); Rev 2:11 (not hurt of the second death); Rom 6:23 (wages of sin is death).

Relevance: The defining term for the lake of fire is "death" — the end of life, not the continuation of life in suffering.

docs.title: 53. Revelation 17:8,11 — apoleia: Beast Goes into Perdition
docs.text:
Text: "The beast... shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition... goeth into perdition."

Context: apoleia as destination for the beast. Combined with "was, and is not" non-existence language.

Original language: hupagei eis apoleian = "goes into perdition." apoleia as terminus.

Cross-references: Phil 3:19 (whose end is destruction); 2 Thess 2:3 (son of perdition).

Relevance: The beast's end is apoleia (perdition/destruction). The "was, and is not" echoes non-existence formulas.

docs.title: 54. John 17:12 — Son of Perdition (Judas)
docs.text:
Text: "...none of them is lost, but the son of perdition..."

Context: ho huios tes apoleias = "the son of perdition/destruction." Semitic destiny-genitive.

Original language: Destiny-genitive: the one whose destiny IS apoleia.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 2:3 (son of perdition — Antichrist); Phil 3:19 (whose end is destruction).

Relevance: The "son of perdition" title designates someone whose destiny is destruction.

docs.title: 55. Acts 8:20 — Peter's Curse
docs.text:
Text: "But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee..."

Context: eis apoleian = "unto destruction." Peter wishes destruction on Simon Magus's money.

Cross-references: Phil 3:19 (end is destruction); Rom 9:22 (fitted for destruction).

Relevance: apoleia as directional curse — heading toward destruction.

docs.title: 56. Romans 9:22 — Vessels Fitted for Destruction
docs.text:
Text: "...the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction."

Context: katartismena eis apoleian = "having been prepared/fitted for destruction."

Original language: Perfect passive participle = already fitted for their end.

Cross-references: Phil 3:19 (whose end is destruction); 2 Pet 3:7 (perdition of ungodly men).

Relevance: The vessels of wrath are fitted FOR destruction — apoleia is their purpose/destination.

docs.title: 57. 1 Corinthians 1:18 — Perishing vs. Saved
docs.text:
Text: "For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God."

Context: tois apollymenois ("those perishing") vs. tois sozomenois ("those being saved"). Present participles.

Original language: apollymenois (Pres Mid/Pass Ptcp) vs. sozomenois (Pres Pass Ptcp).

Cross-references: 2 Cor 2:15 (saved and perishing); John 3:16 (perish vs. life).

Relevance: Paul's binary: two groups heading toward two outcomes — perishing vs. salvation.

docs.title: 58. 2 Corinthians 2:15 — Saved and Perishing
docs.text:
Text: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish."

Context: Same apollymi/sozo binary as 1 Cor 1:18.

Cross-references: 1 Cor 1:18; John 3:16.

Relevance: Paul's consistent framework: perishing vs. salvation.

docs.title: 59. John 10:28 — Never Perish
docs.text:
Text: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish..."

Context: Emphatic double negative: ou me apolontai = "they shall by no means perish."

Original language: Emphatic double negative with apollymi.

Cross-references: John 3:16 (should not perish); 2 Pet 3:9 (not willing any should perish).

Relevance: The promise of not-perishing presupposes that perishing is the default fate. Eternal life prevents perishing.

docs.title: 60. Matthew 18:14 — God's Will: None Perish
docs.text:
Text: "Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish."

Context: God's will is that none perish (apollymi).

Cross-references: 2 Pet 3:9 (not willing any should perish); John 3:16 (should not perish).

Relevance: The Father's desire is preservation, not destruction — implying destruction is the alternative.

docs.title: 61. James 4:12 — God Able to Save and Destroy
docs.text:
Text: "There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy..."

Context: sozo (save) and apollymi (destroy) as God's two powers. Binary: save OR destroy.

Original language: sosai kai apolesai = "to save and to destroy."

Cross-references: Psa 145:20 (preserves... destroys); Matt 10:28 (destroy soul and body).

Relevance: God's two options are preservation and destruction — not two forms of preservation.

docs.title: 62. Ezekiel 18:4 — The Soul That Sins Shall Die
docs.text:
Text: "Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die."

Context: Foundation text: the nephesh can die. If the soul is destructible, then apollymi in Matt 10:28 is literal.

Cross-references: Matt 10:28 (destroy both soul and body); 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has immortality).

Relevance: The soul is not inherently immortal — it can and does die. This means destruction vocabulary applies to the whole person.

docs.title: 63. 1 Timothy 6:16 — God Alone Has Immortality
docs.text:
Text: "Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto..."

Context: monos echon athanasian = "alone having immortality." If only God possesses immortality, the wicked do not have it.

Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:53-54 (mortal puts on immortality at resurrection); Rom 2:7 (seek for immortality).

Relevance: Removes the theological prerequisite for ECT. If the wicked do not have immortality, they cannot live forever in torment.

docs.title: 64. Matthew 26:8 / Mark 14:4 — Counter-Evidence: apoleia as "Waste"
docs.text:
Text: "To what purpose is this waste?"

Context: apoleia for "waste" of ointment. ECT proponents argue the ointment still exists in a "wasted" state.

Cross-references: Phil 3:19 (whose end is destruction); Matt 7:13 (broad way to destruction).

Relevance: Counter-evaluation: the ointment was used up, gone, consumed — it ceased to exist as usable ointment. This actually supports cessation rather than "ruined but still existing."

docs.title: 65. Hebrews 9:12 — Duration Pattern: Eternal Redemption
docs.text:
Text: "...having obtained eternal redemption for us."

Context: aionios + result-noun. "Eternal redemption" = a once-for-all act whose result endures forever, not an ongoing process.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:9 (everlasting destruction); Heb 6:2 (eternal judgment); Heb 5:9 (eternal salvation).

Relevance: Establishes the aionios + result-noun pattern: permanent result, not ongoing process.

docs.title: 66. Hebrews 6:2 — Duration Pattern: Eternal Judgment
docs.text:
Text: "...of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment."

Context: aionios + result-noun. "Eternal judgment" = judgment whose result is permanent, not ongoing judging.

Cross-references: Heb 9:12 (eternal redemption); Heb 5:9 (eternal salvation); 2 Thess 1:9 (everlasting destruction).

Relevance: Second instance of the pattern. Judgment is an event; "eternal" modifies the permanence of the result.

docs.title: 67. Hebrews 5:9 — Duration Pattern: Eternal Salvation
docs.text:
Text: "...he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him."

Context: aionios + result-noun. Third instance of the pattern.

Cross-references: Heb 9:12; Heb 6:2; 2 Thess 1:9.

Relevance: Three Hebrews passages establish the pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result. Applied to 2 Thess 1:9: "everlasting destruction" = destruction whose result is permanent.

docs.title: 68. Jonah 2:6 — Duration Word Test: olam = 3 Days
docs.text:
Text: "...the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God."

Context: olam = "for ever" — but Jonah was in the fish 3 days.

Cross-references: Exo 21:6 (olam = until death); Isa 34:10 (olam = Edom's smoke — ended).

Relevance: Proves olam is context-dependent, not always "endless."

docs.title: 69. Exodus 21:6 — Duration Word Test: olam = Until Death
docs.text:
Text: "...and he shall serve him for ever."

Context: olam for a slave serving his master — "for the rest of his life."

Cross-references: Jon 2:6 (olam = 3 days); 1 Sam 1:22 (olam = Samuel's lifetime).

Relevance: Another proof that olam is context-dependent.

docs.title: 70. Genesis 6:11-13 — LXX Verification: shachath → diaphtheiro
docs.text:
Text: (See #3 above)

Context: LXX translates shachath as diaphtheiro — preserving the corruption-destruction semantic bridge.

Cross-references: Rev 11:18 (destroy them which destroy the earth — same diaphtheiro); 2 Pet 2:12 (utterly perish in their own corruption — phthora).

Relevance: The LXX translators chose a Greek word that carries both corruption and destruction meanings, confirming they understood shachath as a word of actual destruction.

docs.title: 71. Psalm 37:20 (LXX) — kalah → synteleo
docs.text:
Text: (See #10 above)

Context: LXX translates kalah with synteleo (85x mapping). synteleo = "to complete entirely/consume."

Cross-references: Matt 13:39 (synteleia tou aionos, "end of the age").

Relevance: The LXX translators chose a Greek word emphasizing completeness of consumption.

docs.title: 72. Psalm 145:20 (LXX) — shamad → apollymi
docs.text:
Text: (See #18 above)

Context: LXX translates shamad with apollymi (23x mapping). shamad → apollymi confirms cross-testament vocabulary continuity.

Cross-references: Matt 10:28 (apollymi for eschatological destruction); John 3:16 (apollymi for perishing).

Relevance: When Paul and Jesus use apollymi for the fate of the wicked, they use the LXX's chosen translation for the OT's most extreme destruction word (shamad).

docs.title: 73. Isaiah 13:9 (LXX) — shamad → apollymi
docs.text:
Text: (See #22 above)

Context: Same shamad → apollymi mapping in an eschatological Day-of-the-LORD passage.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:7-9 (Day-of-the-LORD language + olethros).

Relevance: Confirms the cross-testament vocabulary chain in eschatological contexts.

docs.title: Pattern 1: The abad-apollymi Lexical Chain
docs.text: The LXX translates abad as apollymi 141 times (PMI 6.14, score 30.45). This is the dominant Hebrew-to-Greek destruction mapping. When the NT uses apollymi for the fate of the wicked, it carries the full semantic weight of the OT's primary destruction verb. Both abad and apollymi are classified in the Non-Exist semantic domain by standard lexicographic authorities (UBS and Louw-Nida).

docs.title: Pattern 2: The Perish-vs-Life Binary
docs.text: Five passages from four authors present destruction and life as antithetical outcomes: John 3:16 (perish vs. eternal life), Matt 7:13-14 (destruction vs. life), Rom 6:23 (death vs. eternal life), Phil 3:19 (end is destruction), Psa 145:20 (preserve vs. destroy). The consistent structure across multiple authors, both testaments, and multiple genres is: life = continued existence; destruction/death/perishing = cessation of existence.

docs.title: Pattern 3: Cessation Similes
docs.text: Every biblical simile for the fate of the wicked depicts a substance that ceases to exist: chaff burned (Psa 1:4; Matt 3:12), wax melting (Psa 68:2), smoke dissipating (Psa 37:20; Hos 13:3), fat consumed (Psa 37:20), stubble burned (Mal 4:1; Nah 1:10), ashes remaining (Mal 4:3; 2 Pet 2:6), morning clouds and dew passing (Hos 13:3), dung decomposing (Job 20:7). No biblical simile for the wicked depicts something that continues to exist in a ruined state.

docs.title: Pattern 4: Non-Existence Language
docs.text: Four passages explicitly describe the result of destruction as non-existence using the Hebrew noun ayin (H369): "shall not be" (Psa 37:10), "that they may not be" (Psa 59:13), "be no more" (Psa 104:35), "as though they had not been" (Oba 1:16). These are not poetic hyperbole — they describe the stated result of the destruction vocabulary used in context.

docs.title: Pattern 5: Destruction vs. Torment as Distinct Word Families
docs.text: Destruction vocabulary (apollymi G622, apoleia G684, olethros G3639, abad H6, shamad H8045, kalah H3615, shachath H7843) and torment vocabulary (basanizo G928, basanismos G929, kolasis G2851) are different word families with non-overlapping semantic ranges. No lexicon defines any of the seven destruction words as "torment" or "ongoing conscious suffering." The destruction family outnumbers the torment family by approximately 30:1 when applied to the fate of the wicked.

docs.title: Pattern 6: The aionios + Result-Noun Pattern
docs.text: Three Hebrews passages (eternal redemption 9:12, eternal judgment 6:2, eternal salvation 5:9) establish that when aionios modifies a result-noun, it describes the permanence of the result, not the duration of an ongoing process. Applied to 2 Thess 1:9: "everlasting destruction" = destruction whose result (cessation of existence) is permanent.

docs.title: Pattern 7: LXX Translation Consistency
docs.text: The LXX translators consistently chose Greek destruction words with cessation semantics: abad → apollymi (141x), shamad → apollymi (23x), kalah → synteleo (85x), shachath → diaphtheiro (48x). They did not choose torment words or "ongoing suffering" words. This is a translator's semantic judgment: the LXX translators understood Hebrew destruction vocabulary as words of actual destruction.

docs.title: Pattern 8: Historical Destruction Paradigms
docs.text: The Flood and Sodom are used as paradigms for eschatological judgment by Jesus (Luke 17:27,29), Peter (2 Pet 2:5-6), and Jude (1:7). In both cases, apollymi describes people who ceased to exist. Sodom is explicitly said to be "ashes" (2 Pet 2:6) and an "example" (hupodeigma) of eschatological judgment.

docs.title: H6 abad — 219 occurrences
docs.text: The broadest Hebrew destruction verb. Qal (intransitive, "perish") dominates at ~61% (119x). UBS semantic domain: Non-Exist. The Qal describes the subject ceasing to exist; the Piel and Hiphil describe active destruction by an agent. Key eschatological uses: Psa 1:6, 37:20, 68:2, 92:9, Deut 7:10, 8:19-20, Job 20:7.

docs.title: G622 apollymi — 102 occurrences
docs.text: Primary Greek destruction verb and canonical NT heir to abad (LXX mapping 141x, PMI 6.14). Louw-Nida dual classification: Violence/Destroy (20.003) AND Exist/Non-exist (13.003). No lexicon places apollymi in a "torment" domain. The sozo antonym relationship (14 verses in direct opposition) defines the two destinies.

docs.title: H8045 shamad — 101 occurrences
docs.text: The most absolute Hebrew destruction word. Total extermination with no remnant. Almost exclusively Hiphil (69x, causative) or Niphal (21x, passive). KJV renders as "destroy/destroyed" ~94%. No milder meanings. LXX maps to apollymi 23x.

docs.title: H3615 kalah — 258 occurrences
docs.text: Bridges completion and destruction. In judgment contexts, consistently means "consume to nothing." Three key non-existence passages pair kalah with ayin: Psa 37:20, 59:13, 104:35. LXX maps to synteleo 85x.

docs.title: H7843 shachath — 164 occurrences
docs.text: Bridges corruption and destruction. Gen 6:11-13 establishes the principle: the same root describes the sin (corruption) and the judgment (destruction). Hiphil dominates (98x). LXX maps to diaphtheiro 48x.

docs.title: G684 apoleia — 20 occurrences
docs.text: Noun form of apollymi's action. Matt 7:13 structurally decisive: two ways → destruction vs. life. 2 Peter has 5x in 61 verses — the NT epicenter of destruction vocabulary. Every eschatological use describes a terminal state.

docs.title: G3639 olethros — 4 occurrences
docs.text: All Pauline. 2 Thess 1:9 is the key passage: olethros aionios = "everlasting destruction." 1 Cor 5:5 is the only remedial use, with an explicit salvation-purpose clause absent from eschatological uses.

docs.title: Cross-Testament Connections
docs.text:
1. abad (Psa 37:20) → apollymi (John 3:16): Same verb through LXX, same perish-vs-life contrast across testaments.

  2. shamad (Psa 145:20) → apollymi (Matt 10:28): Preserve/destroy contrast (OT) maps to kill/destroy contrast (NT). Both use the most extreme vocabulary available.

  3. shachath (Gen 6:11-13) → diaphtheiro (Rev 11:18): The corruption-destruction principle established in the Flood narrative echoes in Revelation's judgment.

  4. kalah (Psa 37:20, 59:13) → synteleo (Matt 13:39): The "consumption to nothing" concept carries into the NT "end of the age" language.

  5. Sodom paradigm: Gen 19:24-25 → Luke 17:29 (apollymi) → 2 Pet 2:6 (ashes) → Jude 1:7 (eternal fire). The paradigm case runs from original event through Jesus' teaching through apostolic interpretation.

  6. Isa 66:24 → Mark 9:43-48: Jesus quotes the OT source text about corpses (peger), connecting OT destruction imagery to NT gehenna teaching.

  7. Isa 34:10 → Rev 14:11: "Smoke ascending forever" language originates in the judgment of Edom (whose fire is out), establishing the meaning for the same formula in Revelation.

docs.title: Rev 14:10-11 — Torment Vocabulary in Apocalyptic Context
docs.text: This passage uses basanizo (torment), not destruction vocabulary. It is the strongest ECT proof-text. Key factors: (1) genre is apocalyptic symbolism, (2) OT source text (Isa 34:10) describes a completed judgment, (3) "smoke ascending" is shared imagery with Gen 19:28 (smoke from completed destruction), (4) "no rest day nor night" applies to beast-worshipers during the judgment period. The passage requires analysis within its genre and OT source context. (Full analysis in etc7-11 and etc7-15.)

docs.title: Matt 25:41,46 — Everlasting Fire/Punishment
docs.text: "Everlasting fire" and "everlasting punishment" use aionios. The Hebrews pattern (aionios + result-noun = permanent result) and the Jude 1:7 + 2 Pet 2:6 paradigm (eternal fire → ashes) favor interpreting "everlasting punishment" as punishment whose result is permanent. However, the passage also says "prepared for the devil and his angels," raising questions about human participation in a judgment originally designed for supernatural beings. (Full analysis in etc7-08 and etc7-14.)

docs.title: Mark 9:43-48 — Unquenchable Fire and Worm
docs.text: Jesus quotes Isa 66:24. The source text describes corpses (peger), not living beings. "Unquenchable fire" (asbestos) means fire that cannot be put out (cf. Jer 17:27 — Jerusalem's "unquenchable" fire, now extinguished for millennia). The binary is "life" vs. "gehenna" = existence vs. destruction. (Full analysis in etc7-05 and etc7-15.)

docs.title: Luke 15:4-32 — apollymi as "Lost"
docs.text: apollymi in its "recoverable loss" sense. The three parables use apollymi for things that are lost but recoverable. However, the recoverable-loss semantic category is distinct from the "destroy utterly" category used in judgment contexts (Matt 10:28, John 3:16). Context determines meaning. Importing the "lost" meaning into every apollymi occurrence is the illegitimate totality transfer fallacy.

docs.title: 1 Cor 5:5 — Remedial olethros
docs.text: The only remedial use of olethros. The salvation-purpose clause ("that the spirit may be saved") distinguishes this from eschatological uses where no such clause appears. Disciplinary destruction of a church member is categorically different from final judgment of the impenitent.

docs.title: 2 Thess 1:9 — "From the Presence of the Lord"
docs.text: The phrase apo prosopou can mean "away from" (separation — ECT reading) or "proceeding from" (source — the Lord's presence causes destruction). Greek apo allows both meanings. The OT parallel (Psa 68:2, "wicked perish at the presence of God") and the context (v.8, "in flaming fire taking vengeance") favor "proceeding from" — the Lord's presence is the source of the destruction.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The research data shows the following:

Lexical evidence: All seven destruction words (abad, shamad, kalah, shachath, apollymi, apoleia, olethros) share a common semantic core: the ending or cessation of the object. None has "ongoing conscious suffering" as even a secondary meaning in any standard lexicon. abad and apollymi are classified in the Non-Exist semantic domain. shamad means total extermination with no remnant. kalah paired with ayin produces explicit non-existence statements. shachath bridges corruption and destruction.

Cross-testament continuity: The LXX translations (abad→apollymi 141x, shamad→apollymi 23x, kalah→synteleo 85x, shachath→diaphtheiro 48x) chose Greek destruction words, not torment words. The LXX translators understood Hebrew destruction vocabulary as words of actual destruction.

Eschatological usage: When destruction vocabulary is used in eschatological contexts, it is accompanied by cessation similes (chaff, wax, smoke, ashes, stubble, dung), non-existence language (ayin), and perish-vs-life contrasts. The consistent picture is cessation of existence.

Counter-evidence: The Luke 15 "lost" sense of apollymi, the 1 Cor 5:5 remedial sense of olethros, and the Matt 26:8 "waste" sense of apoleia operate in different semantic categories from eschatological judgment uses. Rev 14:10-11 uses torment vocabulary (basanizo), not destruction vocabulary, and is apocalyptic in genre with OT source texts describing completed judgments.

The distinction between destruction and torment vocabulary: These are different word families with non-overlapping semantic ranges. The Bible uses destruction words for the fate of the wicked approximately 30 times more frequently than torment words. The few torment references occur in apocalyptic contexts (Revelation) or parabolic contexts (Luke 16), while destruction vocabulary appears across all genres and all biblical authors.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Hebrew/Greek destruction vocabulary: abad/apollumi (H6/G622), shamad (H8045), kalah (H3615), shachath (H7843), apoleia (G684), olethros (G3639). Lexical definitions, eschatological usage.

docs.title: H6 — abad
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H6-abad.md

Occurrences: 219

Primitive root verb: 'to wander away, lose oneself; by implication to perish (causative, destroy).' Qal (intransitive, 'perish') dominates at ~61% (119x). Piel 41x and Hiphil 26x provide causative 'destroy.' KJV: 'perish' ~55%, 'destroy' ~32%, 'lost' ~6%. UBS semantic domain: Non-Exist (002002002006). The broadest Hebrew destruction verb, covering simple straying through to total annihilation.

Semantic categories: Physical loss of objects/animals, Individual death/personal destruction, Covenant-curse/divine judgment, Divine active destruction of enemies/nations, Fate of the wicked (wisdom literature), Loss of abstract qualities, Idiom: ready to perish

Key verses: Psa 1:6, Psa 37:20, Psa 68:2, Psa 92:9, Deu 7:10, Deu 8:19-20, Deu 28:20, Job 20:7, Pro 2:22

Relevance: Primary Hebrew destruction verb. Core study word. LXX maps to apollymi 141 times (PMI 6.14, score 30.45) — the strongest Hebrew-Greek verb pairing in the OT-NT destruction chain.

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

From apo (G575) + ollymi ('to destroy'): 'to destroy fully.' Active = destroy, ruin; Middle/Passive = perish, be lost. Louw-Nida: Violence/Destroy (20.003) AND Exist/Non-exist (13.003). KJV: 'perish' 36%, 'destroy' 30%, 'lose/lost' 27%. Critical antonym: sozo (G4982, 'to save') — 14 verses in direct opposition. The primary Greek destruction/perishing verb and canonical NT heir to Hebrew abad.

Semantic categories: Physical destruction/killing (active), Divine judgment/eschatological ruin, Perishing in eternal judgment (middle/passive), Losing one's life/soul, Losing/finding a possession, Decay/perishability, Safety/preservation (negated)

Key verses: Mat 10:28, Joh 3:16, Luk 13:3, Luk 13:5, Luk 17:27, Luk 17:29, 2 Pet 3:9, 1 Cor 1:18, Jam 4:12

Relevance: Primary Greek destruction verb. Core study word. LXX heir to abad (141x co-occurrence). No lexicon places apollymi in a 'torment' or 'ongoing suffering' domain.

docs.title: H8045 — shamad
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H8045-shamad.md

Occurrences: 101

Primitive root verb: 'to desolate — destroy, destruction, bring to nought, overthrow.' The most absolute Hebrew destruction word — total extermination with no remnant. Almost exclusively Hiphil (69x, causative) or Niphal (21x, passive). No Qal form = always carries intensive/causative force. KJV: 'destroy/destroyed' ~94%. Never means anything less than total destruction.

Semantic categories: YHWH exterminating Canaanite nations, Covenant curse against apostate Israel, Destruction of dynasties/royal houses, Destruction of idolatry/false worship, Extermination plots against God's people, Eschatological/prophetic final destruction, Divine restraint/non-destruction (negated)

Key verses: Psa 37:38, Psa 92:7, Psa 145:20, Isa 13:9, Deu 28:20, Deu 28:45, Deu 28:48, Deu 28:51, Deu 28:61

Relevance: Most extreme Hebrew destruction word. Core study word. LXX maps to apollymi 23 times. UBS domain: Non-Exist. No remnant language — total annihilation.

docs.title: H3615 — kalah
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H3615-kalah.md

Occurrences: 258

Primitive root verb: 'to end, whether intransitive (cease, be finished, perish) or transitive (complete, prepare, consume).' Broadest usage range of the four Hebrew destruction words. Piel dominates (141x = intensive/factitive). KJV: 'consume/consumed' ~18%, 'made an end' ~20%, 'finished' ~13%. In judgment contexts, consistently means 'consume to nothing.' Three key non-existence passages pair kalah with ayin: Psa 37:20, 59:13, 104:35.

Semantic categories: Completion of task/work, Finishing speaking, Divine judgment/consumption, Wrath/fury accomplished, Eyes failing/longing, Time/resources spent, Determination/decided evil

Key verses: Psa 37:20, Psa 59:13, Psa 104:35, Isa 1:28, Nah 1:8-9, Eze 22:31, Jer 14:12, Deu 28:21, Deu 32:23

Relevance: Core study word. Bridges completion and destruction semantics. LXX maps to synteleo 85 times. In judgment/eschatological contexts, kalah consistently means 'consume to nothing,' paired with explicit non-existence (ayin) language.

docs.title: H7843 — shachath
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7843-shachath.md

Occurrences: 164

Primitive root verb: 'to decay, ruin (causatively) — batter, corrupt, destroy, lose, mar, perish, spoil, waste.' Bridges corruption and destruction semantics. Hiphil dominates (98x = deliberate destruction by external agent). Piel (39x = intensive corruption/ruin). KJV: 'destroy/destroyed' ~48%, 'corrupt' ~16%. Gen 6:11-13 threefold use establishes the hermeneutical principle: corruption leads to destruction.

Semantic categories: Moral/spiritual corruption, Physical destruction of cities/nations/armies, Ruining/marring objects, Divine restraint from destruction (negated), The Destroyer as active agent, Self-destruction/reflexive ruin

Key verses: Gen 6:11-13, Gen 19:13-14, Psa 14:1, Psa 53:1, Eze 28:17, Deu 31:29, Deu 32:5, Exo 32:7

Relevance: Core study word. Bridges corruption and destruction. LXX maps to diaphtheiro 48 times. Gen 6:11-13 principle: the same root describes sin (corruption) and judgment (destruction) — corruption naturally results in destruction.

docs.title: G684 — apoleia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G684-apoleia.md

Occurrences: 20

Feminine noun from G622 apollymi: 'ruin or loss (physical, spiritual, or eternal).' Louw-Nida: 20.031 (Violence/Destroy). KJV: 'destruction' 25%, 'perdition' 25%. Concentrated in 2 Peter (5x in 61 verses) and eschatological contexts. All 20 occurrences classified: eschatological destruction, 'son of perdition' (destiny-genitive), beast's end, waste/squandering, false teachers' ruin.

Semantic categories: Final/eschatological ruin, Son of perdition (destiny-genitive), Beast goes into perdition, Waste/squandering, Perishing/immediate ruin, False teachers and their followers, Apostasy (drawing back)

Key verses: Mat 7:13, Phi 3:19, 2 Th 2:3, 2 Pet 2:1, 2 Pet 2:3, 2 Pet 3:7, Rev 17:8, Rev 17:11, 1 Tim 6:9, Joh 17:12

Relevance: Core study word. NT noun form of apollymi's action. Matt 7:13 structurally decisive: two ways → destruction vs. life. 2 Peter epicenter (5x in 61 verses).

docs.title: G3639 — olethros
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3639-olethros.md

Occurrences: 4

Masculine noun from ollymi (to destroy): 'ruin, death, punishment.' Only 4 NT occurrences, all Pauline. KJV: uniformly 'destruction.' Four semantic categories: (1) disciplinary destruction of flesh (1 Cor 5:5), (2) sudden eschatological destruction (1 Thess 5:3), (3) everlasting destruction from God's presence (2 Thess 1:9), (4) destruction paired with perdition (1 Tim 6:9). Hebrew source (LXX): eid (H343, calamity), shod (H7701, violence/devastation).

Semantic categories: Disciplinary destruction, Sudden eschatological destruction, Everlasting destruction from God's presence, Destruction paired with perdition

Key verses: 2 Th 1:9, 1 Th 5:3, 1 Cor 5:5, 1 Tim 6:9

Relevance: Core study word. Specifically Pauline destruction vocabulary. 2 Thess 1:9 is the most important single verse for this focus area: olethros aionios = 'everlasting destruction.'

docs.title: G4982 — sozo
docs.text:
Occurrences: 120

Verb: 'to save, deliver, heal, make whole.' The primary NT salvation verb and critical antonym of apollymi. 14 verses set apollymi and sozo in direct opposition (Mat 16:25; Luk 9:24; 19:10; Jas 4:12; 2 Cor 2:15 etc.). What sozo rescues from is what apollymi inflicts. KJV: 'save' ~52%, 'be saved' ~17%, 'whole/healed' ~8%.

Semantic categories: Spiritual salvation from sin/judgment, Physical healing, Deliverance from danger, Preservation of life

Key verses: Mat 16:25, Luk 9:24, Luk 19:10, Jam 4:12, 1 Cor 1:18, 2 Cor 2:15

Relevance: Critical antonym of apollymi. The apollymi-sozo pair defines the two destinies: perishing vs. being saved. If sozo = preservation of life/existence, then apollymi = loss of life/existence.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Occurrences: 71

Adjective: 'eternal, everlasting.' From aion (G165, 'age'). KJV: 'eternal' 45%, 'everlasting' 30%. Applied to both life (zoe aionios, ~40x) and judgment/destruction contexts (olethros aionios 2 Thess 1:9, pur aionion Matt 25:41, kolasis aionios Matt 25:46). The Hebrews pattern (eternal redemption, judgment, salvation — all permanent results) is decisive for interpretation.

Semantic categories: Eternal life, Everlasting punishment/fire, Everlasting destruction, Age-lasting duration

Key verses: 2 Th 1:9, Mat 25:41, Mat 25:46, Joh 3:16, Heb 9:12, Heb 6:2, Heb 5:9, Jud 1:7

Relevance: Duration modifier applied to destruction vocabulary. Key for temporal vs. permanent analysis. Hebrews pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result, not ongoing process.

docs.title: H5769 — olam
docs.text:
Occurrences: 432

Noun/adjective: 'concealed, eternity, long duration, perpetual, everlasting, for ever.' Context-dependent duration word. Can mean '3 days' (Jon 2:6), 'until death' (Exo 21:6), 'for a generation' (Isa 34:10 — Edom), or 'truly endless' (of God's nature). In eschatological destruction contexts, olam describes the permanence of the RESULT, not the duration of the process.

Semantic categories: Truly eternal (of God), Age-lasting/generational, Life-long, Permanent result

Key verses: Jon 2:6, Exo 21:6, Isa 34:10, Psa 92:7

Relevance: Hebrew duration word. Context-dependent — not always 'endless.' Proves that 'forever' language in destruction contexts can describe permanent result rather than endless process.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Occurrences: 12

Verb: 'to test by rubbing on a touchstone; to torture, torment, vex.' From basanos (G931, 'touchstone'). KJV: 'torment/tormented' ~75%, 'tossed/vexed/pained' ~25%. Used in Rev 14:10 for torment of beast-worshipers. DIFFERENT word family from apollymi/apoleia/olethros. Torment vocabulary ≠ destruction vocabulary.

Semantic categories: Physical torment, Testing/examination, Distress/vexation

Key verses: Rev 14:10, Rev 20:10, Mat 8:29, Luk 8:28

Relevance: Must be distinguished from destruction vocabulary as a DIFFERENT word family. basanizo/basanismos = torment; apollymi/apoleia/olethros = destruction. The Bible uses destruction words ~30x more frequently than torment words for the fate of the wicked.

docs.title: G4931 — synteleo
docs.text:
Occurrences: 7

Verb: 'to complete entirely, consummate, execute.' From syn (G4862, 'together/completely') + teleo (G5055, 'to end'). Primary LXX translation of kalah (H3615) at 85 co-occurrences (PMI 27.17). The syn- prefix doubles the completeness emphasis. Cognate noun synteleia (G4930) = 'consummation' (Matt 13:39, 'end of the age').

Semantic categories: Completing/finishing discourse, Fulfilling prophecy, Consummating/making covenant

Key verses: Mat 7:28, Rom 9:28, Heb 8:8, Mar 13:4

Relevance: LXX bridge word for kalah. Preserves kalah's dual semantic of completion and consumption. synteleo = 'to complete entirely' — when applied to judgment, means complete consumption/finishing.

docs.title: G1311 — diaphtheiro
docs.text:
Occurrences: 6

Verb: 'to rot thoroughly, corrupt utterly, destroy.' From dia (G1223, 'through/thoroughly') + phtheiro (G5351, 'to corrupt/decay'). Primary LXX translation of shachath (H7843) at 48 co-occurrences (PMI 7.00, score 27.24). Rev 11:18 creates a Flood echo: 'destroy them which destroy (diaphtheiro) the earth' — same word as Gen 6:11 LXX 'the earth was corrupt (diaphtheiro).'

Semantic categories: Physical corruption/decay, Moral corruption, Eschatological destruction, Moths corrupting

Key verses: Rev 11:18, 2 Cor 4:16, 1 Tim 6:5, Luk 12:33

Relevance: LXX bridge word for shachath. Preserves shachath's corruption-destruction semantic bridge. Rev 11:18 = the corrupt are destroyed by the same word that describes their corruption.

docs.title: G5356 — phthora
docs.text:
Occurrences: 9

Noun: 'corruption, decay, destruction, perishing.' From phtheiro (G5351, 'to corrupt'). Connected to shachath (H7843) through the LXX diaphtheiro chain. Used in 2 Pet 2:12 ('shall utterly perish in their own corruption'), Gal 6:8 ('of the flesh reap corruption'), 1 Cor 15:42,50 (resurrection body contrasted with corruption).

Semantic categories: Physical corruption/decay, Moral corruption leading to destruction, Perishability of the body

Key verses: 2 Pet 2:12, Gal 6:8, 1 Cor 15:42, 1 Cor 15:50, 2 Pet 1:4

Relevance: NT corruption/destruction noun connected to shachath through LXX. 2 Pet 2:12: wicked 'perish in their own corruption' — the corruption-destruction principle from Gen 6:11-13 extends into the NT.

docs.title: H3772 — karath
docs.text:
Occurrences: 360

Verb: 'to cut off, cut down.' Frequently used for covenant-curse destruction: being 'cut off' from the people, from the land, from existence. Shares 'extinction' sense with abad in Psa 37:9,34 ('evildoers shall be cut off'). LXX maps to apollymi 21x, showing overlap with the destruction vocabulary chain.

Semantic categories: Covenant-curse cutting off, Judicial excision from community, Physical cutting down, Making/cutting covenant

Key verses: Psa 37:9, Psa 37:22, Psa 37:28, Psa 37:34, Psa 37:38, Pro 2:22

Relevance: Related Hebrew destruction term. 'Cut off' = removal from existence. Appears 5x in Psalm 37 alongside abad, kalah, and shamad. LXX maps to apollymi 21x.

docs.title: H1820 — damah
docs.text:
Occurrences: 18

Verb: 'to cease, be silent, be destroyed, be brought to silence.' Emphasizes ceasing to speak/exist — the silence of death and non-existence. Used in judgment contexts for complete cessation. Related to domiyyah ('silence').

Semantic categories: Ceasing to exist, Being silenced, Being destroyed/cut off

Key verses: Hos 4:6, Oba 1:5, Jer 47:5

Relevance: Related Hebrew destruction term. Emphasizes the silence and cessation aspect of destruction — the destroyed cease to speak, act, or exist.

docs.title: Classification Audit Trail
docs.text: This file contains the full Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for every E-item classified as Cond. or ECT and every N-item in this study.

docs.title: E1 — "The way of the ungodly shall perish (abad)" (Psa 1:6)
docs.text:
Candidate: Cond.

Step 1 — Vocabulary Scan: V1: "perish" (abad) = destruction/cessation vocabulary applied to the wicked. YES → Candidate: Cond.

Step 2 — Four Validation Gates:

Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject is "the way of the ungodly" — this is an abstract concept (a way/path), not a literal human. However, the "way" metonymically represents the people who walk it. The verse contrasts "the righteous" (literal humans, v.6a) with "the ungodly" (literal humans, v.6b). PASS — the subject through metonymy is the ungodly (literal humans).

Gate 2 (Grammar): abad Qal impf 3fs — intransitive "shall perish." No alternative parsing. The Qal of abad means "to perish" without ambiguity. PASS.

Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom poetry (Psalm 1). Didactic in function — direct teaching about the two paths. PASS.

Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E2 (Psa 37:20), E3 (Psa 37:10), E7 (Psa 92:9), E9 (Psa 145:20), and all other destruction vocabulary E-items. No conflict. PASS.

Classification: Cond. — CONFIRMED.

docs.title: E2 — "The wicked shall perish (abad)... consume (kalah); into smoke shall they consume away" (Psa 37:20)
docs.text:
Candidate: Cond.

Step 1 — Vocabulary Scan: V1: "perish" (abad) + "consume" (kalah) + "into smoke" = destruction/cessation vocabulary. YES → Candidate: Cond.

Step 2 — Four Validation Gates:

Gate 1 (Subject): "The wicked" and "the enemies of the LORD" — literal humans. PASS.

Gate 2 (Grammar): abad Qal impf 3mp ("shall perish") + kalah Qal perf 3p ("consumed") x2. Standard forms, no alternative parsing. PASS.

Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom psalm. Didactic function — direct teaching on the fate of the wicked. PASS.

Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with all other destruction vocabulary E-items. The smoke simile reinforces cessation. No conflict. PASS.

Classification: Cond. — CONFIRMED.

docs.title: E3 — "Yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be (ayin)" (Psa 37:10)
docs.text:
Candidate: Cond.

Step 1 — Vocabulary Scan: V1: "shall not be" (ayin) = non-existence/cessation language. YES → Candidate: Cond.

Step 2 — Four Validation Gates:

Gate 1 (Subject): "The wicked" — literal humans. PASS.

Gate 2 (Grammar): ayin rasha = "the wicked is not." ayin = noun of non-existence (H369). einennu = "he is not" with 3ms suffix. No alternative parsing for ayin. PASS.

Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom psalm. Didactic. PASS.

Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E4 (Psa 59:13), E5 (Psa 104:35), E6 (Oba 1:16), and all non-existence statements. No conflict. PASS.

Classification: Cond. — CONFIRMED.

docs.title: E4 — "Consume (kalah) them in wrath, that they may not be (ayin)" (Psa 59:13)
docs.text:
Candidate: Cond.

Step 1 — Vocabulary Scan: V1: "consume" (kalah) + "may not be" (ayin) = destruction + non-existence. YES → Candidate: Cond.

Step 2 — Four Validation Gates:

Gate 1 (Subject): "Them" — refers to enemies/wicked in context. Literal humans. PASS.

Gate 2 (Grammar): kalah Piel imperative + we'einemo ("and they are not"). Standard forms. PASS.

Gate 3 (Genre): Imprecatory psalm (prayer). Didactic in its theological content — expresses belief about what consumption produces. PASS.

Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E3 (Psa 37:10), E5 (Psa 104:35). No conflict. PASS.

Classification: Cond. — CONFIRMED.

docs.title: E5 — "Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more (ayin)" (Psa 104:35)
docs.text:
Candidate: Cond.

Step 1 — Vocabulary Scan: V1: "consumed" (tamam) + "be no more" (ayin) = destruction + non-existence. YES → Candidate: Cond.

Step 2 — Four Validation Gates:

Gate 1 (Subject): "Sinners" and "the wicked" — literal humans. PASS.

Gate 2 (Grammar): tamam + ayin. Standard forms. PASS.

Gate 3 (Genre): Praise psalm with wisdom element. Didactic. PASS.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Hebrew/Greek destruction vocabulary: abad/apollumi (H6/G622), shamad (H8045), kalah (H3615), shachath (H7843), apoleia (G684), olethros (G3639). Lexical definitions, eschatological usage.

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The seven destruction words studied (abad, shamad, kalah, shachath, apollymi, apoleia, olethros) share a common semantic core: the ending or cessation of the object. No standard lexicon defines any of these words as "torment" or "ongoing conscious suffering." When used in eschatological contexts, these words are accompanied by cessation similes (chaff, wax, smoke, ashes, stubble, dung), explicit non-existence language (ayin), and perish-vs-life contrasts across four authors and both testaments. The LXX translators chose Greek destruction words for Hebrew destruction terms, not torment words, confirming that ancient translators understood these as words of actual destruction.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Psalm 37:10 — "For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be." (Explicit non-existence: Hebrew ayin = "not be." The wicked person and his place cease to exist.)

Psalm 37:20 — "But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD shall be as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away." (Two destruction words: abad + kalah. The smoke simile depicts complete dissipation into nothing.)

Psalm 145:20 — "The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy." (Binary antonym contrast: shamar/shamad. The same God who preserves the righteous utterly destroys the wicked.)

Matthew 10:28 — "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." (Jesus uses apollymi — lexically stronger than apokteino ["kill"] — for what God does to the whole person in gehenna.)

John 3:16 — "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." (The central perish-vs-life contrast: apollymi as the opposite of eternal life.)

Romans 6:23 — "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." (Paul's definitive statement: the penalty for sin is death, not torment. Death contrasted with eternal life.)

2 Thessalonians 1:9 — "Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power." (olethros aionios: the key Pauline eschatological passage. "Everlasting destruction" — the destruction noun modified by the permanence adjective.)

Malachi 4:1,3 — "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch... And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet." (The most comprehensive OT destruction passage: burn up, stubble, neither root nor branch, ashes under feet.)

Obadiah 1:16 — "...and they shall be as though they had not been." (The strongest OT non-existence formula: kelo hayu. Not merely death but the retroactive language of never having existed.)

Jude 1:7 — "Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire." (Sodom suffered "eternal fire" — but Sodom is now ashes [2 Pet 2:6]. "Eternal fire" produces permanent destruction, not endless burning.)

docs.title: The Lexical Evidence
docs.text:
The four Hebrew destruction words and three Greek destruction words form a coherent semantic domain with destruction/cessation as the common core.

abad (H6) has 219 occurrences across 25 books. The primitive root means "to wander away, lose oneself; by implication to perish (causative, destroy)." The Qal stem dominates at approximately 61% (119 occurrences), and in the Qal the word is intransitive: the subject perishes — ceases to exist. The Piel (41 occurrences) and Hiphil (26 occurrences) provide the causative "destroy." The KJV translates abad as "perish" approximately 55% of the time and "destroy" approximately 32%. The UBS semantic domain classification places abad in the Non-Exist domain (002002002006). This is not an interpretive judgment but a standard lexicographic classification: the word belongs to the domain of non-existence.

shamad (H8045) has 101 occurrences and represents the most absolute end of the destruction spectrum. While abad can mean "lose" or "wander," shamad never means anything less than total destruction. The KJV renders shamad as "destroy/destroyed" approximately 94% of the time. The word appears almost exclusively in the Hiphil (69 occurrences, causative — someone deliberately exterminates) or Niphal (21 occurrences, passive — the subject is exterminated). There is no Qal form, which means shamad always carries intensive or causative force. When Psalm 145:20 pairs shamar ("preserve") with shamad ("destroy"), the contrast is between preservation and total annihilation.

kalah (H3615) has 258 occurrences and the broadest usage range of the four Hebrew words. It can mean "to finish" (Gen 2:1, completing creation) or "to consume" (Psa 37:20, wicked consumed into smoke). In judgment contexts, kalah consistently means "consume to nothing." Three key passages pair kalah with the Hebrew noun of non-existence (ayin): Psalm 37:20 ("consume into smoke"), Psalm 59:13 ("consume them, that they may not be"), and Psalm 104:35 ("let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more"). Each of these states the result of kalah as non-existence.

shachath (H7843) has 164 occurrences and bridges corruption and destruction. Genesis 6:11-13 uses shachath three times: the earth "was corrupt" (Niphal), flesh "had corrupted" its way (Hiphil), and God declares "I will destroy them" (Hiphil participle). The same root describes the sin and the judgment, establishing a principle: corruption leads to destruction, and destruction is the natural end of corruption. The Hiphil dominates (98 occurrences), showing that most uses describe deliberate destruction by an external agent.

apollymi (G622) has 102 occurrences and is the primary Greek destruction verb. The LXX maps the Hebrew abad to this Greek verb 141 times (PMI 6.14, score 30.45) — one of the strongest Hebrew-Greek verb pairings in the LXX, making apollymi the canonical NT heir to abad. Louw-Nida classifies apollymi in two semantic domains: Violence/Destroy (20.003) and Exist/Non-exist (13.003). No lexicon places apollymi in a "torment" or "ongoing suffering" domain. The critical antonym relationship is apollymi-sozo: 14 verses set "destroy/perish" and "save" in direct opposition (Matt 16:25; Luke 9:24; 19:10; Jam 4:12; 1 Cor 1:18; 2 Cor 2:15, among others). What sozo rescues from is what apollymi inflicts. If sozo means "to preserve life/existence," then apollymi means "to end life/existence."

apoleia (G684) has 20 occurrences and is the noun form of apollymi's action. The Louw-Nida classification is 20.031 (Violence/Destroy). The word is concentrated in 2 Peter (5 occurrences in 61 verses), making that book the epicenter of NT destruction vocabulary. Matthew 7:13 is structurally decisive: two ways, two gates, two destinations — apoleia (destruction) and zoe (life). The binary structure means the two outcomes are antithetical.

olethros (G3639) has only 4 occurrences, all Pauline. It is a masculine noun from ollymi ("to destroy"), the same root behind apollymi. The KJV renders olethros uniformly as "destruction." The key passage is 2 Thessalonians 1:9: olethros aionios ("everlasting destruction"). The other occurrences are 1 Thessalonians 5:3 (sudden eschatological destruction), 1 Corinthians 5:5 (disciplinary destruction of flesh), and 1 Timothy 6:9 (destruction paired with apoleia).

docs.title: The Cross-Testament Vocabulary Chain
docs.text:
The LXX translation patterns establish direct cross-testament vocabulary continuity. The LXX translates abad as apollymi 141 times, shamad as apollymi 23 times, kalah as synteleo ("to complete entirely/consume") 85 times, and shachath as diaphtheiro ("to rot thoroughly/destroy") 48 times.

The translators consistently chose Greek words with cessation semantics. They did not choose basanizo ("torment"), odunao ("grieve/suffer"), or any word carrying "ongoing conscious suffering" as its meaning. This is a translator's semantic judgment made by scholars who read both languages natively: they understood Hebrew abad, shamad, kalah, and shachath as words of actual destruction and chose Greek equivalents that carry the same meaning.

The synteleo mapping for kalah is significant because synteleo itself combines syn ("together/completely") + teleo ("to bring to an end"), doubling the completeness emphasis. The diaphtheiro mapping for shachath preserves the corruption-destruction bridge: diaphtheiro means "to rot thoroughly/destroy," maintaining shachath's dual semantic of corruption and destruction. This chain extends into the NT: 2 Peter 2:12 says the wicked "shall utterly perish in their own corruption (phthora)" — phthora is from the same root as diaphtheiro.

docs.title: The Perish-vs-Life Binary
docs.text:
Five passages from four authors across both testaments present destruction/death and life as antithetical binary outcomes:

  1. John 3:16 — "should not perish (apollymi) but have everlasting life (zoe aionios)"
  2. Matthew 7:13-14 — "broad way to destruction (apoleia)" vs. "narrow way to life (zoe)"
  3. Romans 6:23 — "wages of sin is death (thanatos)" vs. "gift of God is eternal life (zoe aionios)"
  4. Philippians 3:19 — "whose end is destruction (apoleia)"
  5. Psalm 145:20 — "the LORD preserveth (shamar) all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy (shamad)"

The consistency of this pattern across David, Jesus, Paul, and the author of Hebrews, in both poetry and prose, in both testaments, in both direct teaching and epistolary argument, establishes a multi-author, cross-genre, cross-testament framework: life is one outcome, destruction/death/perishing is the other. They are not two forms of eternal existence but two opposite endpoints.

docs.title: Cessation Similes
docs.text:
Every biblical simile comparing the fate of the wicked to a physical substance depicts a substance that ceases to exist:

  • Chaff burned in fire (Psa 1:4; Matt 3:12; Hos 13:3) — chaff burns completely and ceases to exist
  • Wax melting before fire (Psa 68:2) — wax melts away to nothing
  • Smoke dissipating (Psa 37:20; Psa 68:2; Hos 13:3) — smoke disperses and vanishes
  • Fat of lambs consumed on the altar (Psa 37:20) — fat is entirely consumed
  • Stubble burned (Mal 4:1; Nah 1:10; Isa 1:31) — stubble is completely consumed by fire
  • Ashes remaining after combustion (Mal 4:3; 2 Pet 2:6) — ashes are the end product of total destruction
  • Morning cloud and early dew passing away (Hos 13:3) — both dissipate completely
  • Dung decomposing (Job 20:7) — dung decomposes and disappears
  • Tow/flax burning (Isa 1:31) — tow catches fire and is consumed instantly

No biblical simile depicts something that continues to exist in a ruined state. No simile depicts ongoing conscious suffering. The consistent imagery across multiple authors is cessation: the object is consumed, dissipated, dissolved, or decomposed until nothing remains.

docs.title: Non-Existence Language
docs.text:
Four passages use explicit non-existence language (the Hebrew noun ayin, H369, "not-be/non-existence") to describe the result of destruction:

  1. Psalm 37:10 — "the wicked shall not be (ayin)" and "his place shall not be (ayin)"
  2. Psalm 59:13 — "consume them, that they may not be (ayin)"
  3. Psalm 104:35 — "let the wicked be no more (ayin)"
  4. Obadiah 1:16 — "they shall be as though they had not been (kelo hayu)"

These are not poetic hyperbole. They are the stated result of the destruction vocabulary used in context. When the psalmist says "consume them, that they may not be," the PURPOSE of the consumption is explicitly non-existence. When Obadiah says "as though they had not been," the result goes beyond mere death to the language of retroactive non-existence.

docs.title: Destruction vs. Torment: Distinct Word Families
docs.text:
The destruction words studied here (apollymi, apoleia, olethros, and their Hebrew antecedents) and the torment words used in ECT proof-texts (basanizo G928, basanismos G929, kolasis G2851) are different Greek word families with different roots, different semantic ranges, and non-overlapping definitions.

apollymi is from apo + ollymi ("to destroy"); basanizo is from basanos ("touchstone/testing stone"). apoleia is the noun state of destruction; basanismos is the noun state of torment/testing. These are not synonyms. They do not share a root. They do not appear in the same semantic domains in any standard lexicon.

The quantitative disparity is significant. When applied to the fate of the wicked: - Destruction vocabulary (apollymi, apoleia, olethros, and related words) appears in approximately 75-80 verses across the full range of biblical genres (law, wisdom, prophecy, gospel, epistle, apocalyptic) - Torment vocabulary (basanizo, basanismos) applied to eschatological judgment of humans appears in 2-3 verses, all in the apocalyptic genre (Revelation)

The Bible describes the fate of the wicked with destruction words approximately 30 times more frequently than with torment words. The torment passages are limited to a single genre (apocalyptic symbolism), while destruction passages appear across all genres.

docs.title: The Historical Destruction Paradigms
docs.text:
The Flood and Sodom function as paradigms for eschatological judgment. Jesus uses apollymi for both: "the flood came, and destroyed (apollymi) them all... fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed (apollymi) them all" (Luke 17:27,29). Peter uses Sodom as an explicit "ensample" (hupodeigma) of what will happen to the ungodly: "turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly" (2 Pet 2:6). Jude says Sodom suffered "the vengeance of eternal fire" (Jude 1:7).

The paradigm is decisive. Sodom suffered "eternal fire" (Jude 1:7). Sodom was turned to "ashes" (2 Pet 2:6). Sodom is set forth as an "example" of eschatological judgment (2 Pet 2:6). If the paradigm case of "eternal fire" produced ashes rather than endless burning, then "eternal fire" describes fire whose results are permanent, not fire that burns endlessly. This governs interpretation of "everlasting fire" (Matt 25:41) and "tormented with fire and brimstone" (Rev 14:10).

docs.title: Counter-Evidence Evaluated
docs.text:
apollymi as "lost" (Luke 15:4-32): Three parables use apollymi in its "lost/straying" sense — the sheep, coin, and son are all recoverable. ECT proponents argue this shows apollymi does not mean annihilation. The counter-argument is the illegitimate totality transfer fallacy: apollymi has four semantic categories (destroy utterly, perish/die, be lost/straying, lose/waste), and a word used in four categories does not carry all four meanings in every occurrence. In Luke 15, the context is parables about seeking the lost — recoverable loss. In Matt 10:28, the context is God destroying soul and body in gehenna — irreversible destruction. Context, not etymology, determines which meaning applies.

olethros as remedial (1 Cor 5:5): olethros is used for the "destruction of the flesh" of a living church member, with the explicit purpose "that the spirit may be saved." ECT proponents argue this shows olethros can be something less than final annihilation. The response: disciplinary action against a living church member under discipline is categorically different from eschatological judgment of the impenitent. The salvation-purpose clause ("that the spirit may be saved") is present in 1 Cor 5:5 and absent from every eschatological use of olethros (2 Thess 1:9; 1 Thess 5:3). The disciplinary context determines the meaning; the eschatological context determines a different meaning.

apoleia as "waste" (Matt 26:8): apoleia is used for the "waste" of expensive ointment. ECT proponents argue the ointment still exists in a "wasted" state. Counter-evaluation: the ointment was poured out — used up, gone, consumed. It ceased to exist as usable ointment. The "waste" meaning actually supports cessation rather than "ruined but still existing."

Rev 14:10-11: This passage uses basanizo (torment), not destruction vocabulary. It is the strongest passage supporting ECT. It must be evaluated on its own terms: (1) The genre is apocalyptic symbolism (Revelation). (2) The OT source text for "smoke ascending for ever" is Isaiah 34:10 (Edom's judgment — fire long extinguished). (3) "Smoke ascending" also echoes Genesis 19:28 (Abraham watching smoke rise from Sodom's completed destruction). (4) basanizo is a different word family from apollymi/apoleia/olethros. This passage uses torment vocabulary, and it warrants full treatment in its own study. (Examined in depth in etc7-11 and etc7-15.)

Matt 25:41,46: "Everlasting fire" and "everlasting punishment" use aionios. The word kolasin (punishment, from kolazo) is distinct from basanismos (torment). The Hebrews pattern (eternal redemption Heb 9:12, eternal judgment Heb 6:2, eternal salvation Heb 5:9 — all permanent results of completed actions) and the Sodom paradigm (Jude 1:7 + 2 Pet 2:6: "eternal fire" → ashes) bear on how aionios functions when modifying a result-noun. (Examined in depth in etc7-08 and etc7-14.)

Mark 9:43-48: Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24 three times. The source text describes peger (H6297) — corpses, dead bodies. The worm feeds on dead bodies (decomposition); the fire consumes dead bodies (cremation). "Unquenchable" (asbestos G762) means fire that cannot be put out (cf. Jer 17:27 — Jerusalem's "unquenchable" fire, extinguished for millennia), not fire that burns forever. (Examined in depth in etc7-05 and etc7-15.)

docs.title: H6 abad — 219 occurrences
docs.text: Primitive root: "to wander away, lose oneself; by implication to perish (causative, destroy)." Qal dominates (~61%, 119 occurrences) — intransitive "perish." Piel 41 occurrences, Hiphil 26 occurrences — causative "destroy." UBS semantic domain: Non-Exist. KJV: "perish" ~55%, "destroy" ~32%, "lost" ~6%. LXX maps to apollymi 141 times (PMI 6.14). The broadest Hebrew destruction verb. Key eschatological uses: Psa 1:6 (way of ungodly perishes), Psa 37:20 (wicked perish), Psa 68:2 (wicked perish at God's presence), Psa 92:9 (enemies perish), Deut 7:10 (God destroys those who hate him), Job 20:7 (perish forever like dung).

docs.title: G622 apollymi — 102 occurrences
docs.text: From apo + ollymi: "to destroy fully." Active = destroy; Middle/Passive = perish, be lost. Louw-Nida: Violence/Destroy (20.003) AND Exist/Non-exist (13.003). KJV: "perish" 36%, "destroy" 30%, "lose/lost" 27%. Critical antonym: sozo (G4982, 14 verses in direct opposition). No lexicon places apollymi in a "torment" domain. LXX heir to abad (141 co-occurrences). Key eschatological uses: Matt 10:28 (destroy soul and body), John 3:16 (should not perish), Luke 13:3,5 (all likewise perish), Luke 17:27,29 (flood and Sodom destroyed them all), 2 Pet 3:9 (not willing any should perish).

docs.title: H8045 shamad — 101 occurrences
docs.text: Primitive root: "to desolate — destroy, destruction, bring to nought, overthrow." Most absolute Hebrew destruction word. Almost exclusively Hiphil (69 occurrences) or Niphal (21 occurrences). No Qal form = always intensive/causative force. KJV: "destroy/destroyed" ~94%. LXX maps to apollymi 23 times. Key eschatological uses: Psa 37:38 (transgressors destroyed together), Psa 92:7 (destroyed for ever), Psa 145:20 (all the wicked will he destroy), Isa 13:9 (destroy sinners out of the land).

docs.title: H3615 kalah — 258 occurrences
docs.text: Primitive root: "to end, cease, be finished, perish; to complete, consume." Piel dominates (141 occurrences = intensive). In judgment contexts, consistently means "consume to nothing." Three passages pair kalah with ayin (non-existence): Psa 37:20, 59:13, 104:35. LXX maps to synteleo 85 times. Key eschatological uses: Psa 37:20 (consume into smoke), Psa 59:13 (consume that they may not be), Nah 1:8-10 (utter end), Isa 1:28 (consumed).

docs.title: H7843 shachath — 164 occurrences
docs.text: Primitive root: "to decay, ruin (causatively) — batter, corrupt, destroy." Hiphil dominates (98 occurrences). Bridges corruption and destruction. Gen 6:11-13 principle: the same root describes sin (corruption) and judgment (destruction). LXX maps to diaphtheiro 48 times. The corruption-destruction chain extends into NT through phthora (2 Pet 2:12; Gal 6:8; 1 Cor 15:42,50).

docs.title: G684 apoleia — 20 occurrences
docs.text: Feminine noun from G622 apollymi: "ruin or loss." Louw-Nida: 20.031 (Violence/Destroy). Concentrated in 2 Peter (5 occurrences in 61 verses). Matt 7:13: structurally decisive binary — destruction vs. life. Phil 3:19: "whose end is destruction" — telos + apoleia = final outcome is destruction. 2 Pet 3:7: "perdition of ungodly men" — reserved for judgment day. Rev 17:8,11: beast "goeth into perdition" — apoleia as terminus.

docs.title: G3639 olethros — 4 occurrences
docs.text: Masculine noun from ollymi: "ruin, death, punishment." All Pauline. KJV: uniformly "destruction." 2 Thess 1:9: olethros aionios = "everlasting destruction" — the key eschatological passage. 1 Thess 5:3: "sudden destruction" — eschatological. 1 Cor 5:5: "destruction of the flesh" — disciplinary (the only remedial use, with salvation-purpose clause). 1 Tim 6:9: olethros + apoleia together — double destruction.
