Notes: Focus Area 1. Aion as created order -- the ages are things God made, not self-existent infinity.

docs.title: Aionios covenant -- 'the blood of the everlasting covenant'
docs.text:
Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,

Context: Aionios covenant -- the new covenant established through Christ's blood. It does not expire. Hebrews pattern.

Notes: Focus Area 6. The covenant is established (completed act); its validity is aionios.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological -- 'glory for ever and ever'
docs.text:
Make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ; to whom [be] glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Doxological formula: eis tous aionas ton aionon.

Notes: Focus Area 7. Doxological use applied to God/Christ.

docs.title: Aionios glory -- 'called us unto his eternal glory'
docs.text:
But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle [you].

Context: Aionios modifying God's glory -- heavenly reality.

Notes: Focus Area 12.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological -- 'praise and dominion for ever and ever'
docs.text:
If any man speak, [let him speak] as the oracles of God; if any man minister, [let him do it] as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Doxological formula.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological -- 'glory and dominion for ever and ever'
docs.text:
To him [be] glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Doxological formula.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: Aionios kingdom -- 'the everlasting kingdom of our Lord'
docs.text:
For so an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

Context: Aionios modifying Christ's kingdom. The kingdom has no end (Luk 1:33).

Notes: Focus Area 12.

docs.title: Context: Sodom became ASHES -- example of judgment
docs.text:
And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned [them] with an overthrow, making [them] an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

Context: Sodom reduced to ASHES (tephrosas). Made an ENSAMPLE (deigma) -- an example of what happens to the ungodly. Jude 1:7 calls this same fire 'eternal fire.'

Notes: Focus Areas 2, 5, 15. The 'eternal fire' of Jude 1:7 produced ashes. Sodom is not still burning. The fire's eternality is in its divine source and irreversible effect.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'that eternal life, which was with the Father'
docs.text:
(For the life was manifested, and we have seen [it], and bear witness, and shew unto you that eternal life, which was with the Father, and was manifested unto us;)

Context: Eternal life was WITH the Father before being manifested. Life as pre-existent divine attribute.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'the promise... even eternal life'
docs.text:
And this is the promise that he hath promised us, [even] eternal life.

Context: Eternal life is a PROMISE -- something given, not inherent.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him'
docs.text:
Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.

Context: Murderers do NOT HAVE eternal life. If all humans had inherent eternal existence, this statement would be meaningless.

Notes: Focus Areas 4, 14. Critical for the immortality question: eternal life is something that 'abides in' believers but is ABSENT from murderers.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son'
docs.text:
And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.

Context: Eternal life is GIVEN by God and is IN HIS SON -- not inherent in all humans.

Notes: Focus Area 4. Life is in the Son; without the Son, no eternal life (cf. 1 John 5:12).

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'that ye may know that ye have eternal life'
docs.text:
These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God.

Context: Written to believers so they may KNOW they have eternal life. Believers possess it; unbelievers do not.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'This is the true God, and eternal life'
docs.text:
And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, [even] in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.

Context: Christ IS the true God AND eternal life. Life is identified with Christ himself.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: CRITICAL: Aidios (G126) -- 'everlasting chains [desmois aidiois]'
docs.text:
And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

Context: One of only 2 NT uses of aidios. Jude uses aidios for the chains binding fallen angels -- absolute, unbreakable permanence. In the NEXT verse (v.7) he switches to aionios for Sodom's fire.

Notes: Focus Area 2. Parsing: desmois (G1199, Dat Pl M) aidiois (G126, Dat Pl M). Jude chose aidios (from aei, 'always') for genuinely unbreakable chains, then aionios (from aion, 'age') for fire that historically reduced cities to ashes. Same author, adjacent verses, different words.

docs.title: CRITICAL: Aionios fire -- 'the vengeance of eternal fire [pyros aioniou]'
docs.text:
Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

Context: Sodom's fire is called 'eternal' (aioniou), yet Sodom became ashes (2Pe 2:6). Adjacent to v.6 where aidios is used for angelic chains.

Notes: Focus Area 2, 5, 8. Parsing: pyros (G4442, Gen Sg N) aioniou (G166, Gen Sg N). Jude calls Sodom's fire 'eternal fire' and says it is 'set forth for an example' (deigma). The example is of cities destroyed, not cities eternally burning. 2Pe 2:6 confirms: Sodom became ASHES.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'looking for... eternal life'
docs.text:
Keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.

Context: Believers LOOK FOR eternal life -- a future hope to be received.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios gospel -- 'having the everlasting gospel'
docs.text:
And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

Context: Aionios modifying the gospel -- God's message that spans all ages.

Notes: Focus Area 12.

docs.title: CRITICAL: 'Ages of ages' in judgment -- smoke of torment ascends
docs.text:
The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

Context: The smoke (kapnos) of their torment (basanismos) ascends eis aionas aionon. Echoes Isa 34:10 (Edom's smoke 'shall go up for ever'). Subjects: those who worship the beast.

Notes: Focus Area 7, 11. Parsing: kapnos (G2586, Nom Sg M) tou basanismou (G929, Gen Sg M) auton -- 'the smoke of the torment of them.' eis aionas (G165, Acc Pl M) aionon (G165, Gen Pl M) -- 'into ages of ages.' Note: the SMOKE ascends -- evidence of completed destruction (cf. Gen 19:28). Basanismos (G929) appears only 6x in NT, ALL in Revelation. 'No rest day and night' (anapausis G372) -- same word used in Rev 4:8 of living creatures who 'rest not day and night' in praise.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' in judgment -- Babylon's smoke
docs.text:
And again they said, Alleluia. And her smoke rose up for ever and ever.

Context: Symbolic Babylon's smoke rises eis tous aionas ton aionon. Rev 17:5 identifies her as 'MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT' -- symbolic, not literal.

Notes: Focus Area 7, 11. Babylon is explicitly symbolic (Rev 17:5). Her smoke's 'forever' rising is evidence of completed destruction, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Context: Beast/false prophet cast alive vs. humans slain
docs.text:
And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet that wrought miracles before him, with which he deceived them that had received the mark of the beast, and them that worshipped his image. These both were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone. And the remnant were slain with the sword of him that sat upon the horse, which [sword] proceeded out of his mouth: and all the fowls were filled with their flesh.

Context: Sharp distinction: beast and false prophet cast 'alive' (zontes) into the lake. The human 'remnant were SLAIN' (apektanthesan) -- different verbs for symbolic entities vs. humans.

Notes: Focus Area 11. Symbolic entities go alive into the lake; humans are killed/slain. Different vocabulary = different fates.

docs.title: CRITICAL: Humans 'devoured' vs. devil/beast/false prophet 'tormented'
docs.text:
And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them. And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet [are], and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Context: V.9: Human enemies are DEVOURED (katephagen) by fire from God. V.10: The devil, beast, false prophet are tormented eis tous aionas ton aionon. NOT ONE of the three is a literal human being.

Notes: Focus Area 7, 11. Parsing (v.10): diabolos (G1228) = devil; therion (G2342) = beast; pseudoprophetes (G5578) = false prophet. basanisthesontai (G928, Fut Pass Ind 3P) = 'shall be tormented.' eis tous aionas (G165, Acc Pl M) ton aionon (G165, Gen Pl M) = 'into the ages of the ages.' Katephagen (v.9, G2719) = devoured/consumed -- destruction vocabulary for humans.

docs.title: Context: Second death -- lake of fire = 'second death'
docs.text:
And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Context: When humans enter the lake of fire (Rev 20:15; 21:8), the text's term is 'the SECOND DEATH' -- not 'torment.'

Notes: Focus Area 11. The lake of fire IS the second death. Death, not torment.

docs.title: Context: Lake of fire = 'the second death' for humans
docs.text:
But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

Context: Lists human categories (fearful, unbelieving, murderers, etc.) whose fate is the lake of fire = 'the second death.'

Notes: Focus Area 11. Human fate in the lake = second DEATH, not second life of torment.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological -- 'glory and dominion for ever and ever'
docs.text:
And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him [be] glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Doxological formula applied to God.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' applied to Christ -- 'I am alive for evermore'
docs.text:
[I am] he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.

Context: Christ alive eis tous aionas ton aionon -- His post-resurrection immortality. Nature-of-subject: Christ IS now immortal.

Notes: Focus Area 7. Applied to Christ who received immortality through resurrection.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' applied to God -- 'him that liveth for ever and ever'
docs.text:
And when those beasts give glory and honour and thanks to him that sat on the throne, who liveth for ever and ever, The four and twenty elders fall down before him that sat on the throne, and worship him that liveth for ever and ever, and cast their crowns before the throne, saying,

Context: God 'liveth for ever and ever' -- the formula reflects God's genuinely endless nature.

Notes: Focus Area 7. Nature-of-subject: God IS genuinely eternal; the formula reflects His nature.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological
docs.text:
And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, [be] unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever.

Context: Universal doxology: every creature ascribing blessing to God and the Lamb eis tous aionas ton aionon.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological
docs.text:
Saying, Amen: Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honour, and power, and might, [be] unto our God for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Doxological formula.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' applied to God -- 'who liveth for ever and ever'
docs.text:
And sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth, and the things that therein are, and the sea, and the things which are therein, that there should be time no longer:

Context: Angel swears by God who lives eis tous aionas ton aionon.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' for divine reign -- 'he shall reign for ever and ever'
docs.text:
And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become [the kingdoms] of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.

Context: Christ's reign eis tous aionas ton aionon. Nature-of-subject: Christ's kingdom genuinely has no end.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' applied to God -- 'God, who liveth for ever and ever'
docs.text:
And one of the four beasts gave unto the seven angels seven golden vials full of the wrath of God, who liveth for ever and ever.

Context: God who lives eis tous aionas ton aionon.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' for saints' reign -- 'they shall reign for ever and ever'
docs.text:
And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever.

Context: Saints reign eis tous aionas ton aionon. Nature-of-subject: saints receive immortality (1Co 15:53), hence genuinely endless reign.

Notes: Focus Area 7. The only 'ages of ages' passage applied to human saints -- they receive immortality at resurrection.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological -- 'glory for ever and ever'
docs.text:
To whom [be] glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Doxological formula.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: Aionios life vs corruption -- 'reap life everlasting'
docs.text:
For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.

Context: Sowing to flesh = reap CORRUPTION (phthora G5356). Sowing to Spirit = reap LIFE EVERLASTING. Corruption (decay/dissolution) vs. life.

Notes: Focus Area 14. Corruption (phthora) = decay/dissolution -- the opposite of life. Not torment.

docs.title: Context: 'whose end is destruction [apoleia]'
docs.text:
Whose end [is] destruction, whose God [is their] belly, and [whose] glory [is] in their shame, who mind earthly things.)

Context: The 'end' (telos) of the wicked is destruction (apoleia G684) -- not eternal torment.

Notes: Focus Area 14. Apoleia = destruction/perdition -- destruction vocabulary, not torment.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' doxological -- 'glory for ever and ever'
docs.text:
Now unto God and our Father [be] glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Doxological formula.

Notes: Focus Area 7.

docs.title: Context: God can 'destroy both soul and body in hell'
docs.text:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: God can DESTROY (apollymi) both soul (psyche) and body (soma) in gehenna. Destruction vocabulary, not preservation for torment.

Notes: Focus Area 14. God destroys soul AND body -- total destruction, not preservation in torment.

docs.title: Context: 'the way that leadeth to destruction [apoleia]'
docs.text:
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide [is] the gate, and broad [is] the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:

Context: Two ways: one leads to life (v.14), one leads to DESTRUCTION (apoleia). Not two forms of eternal existence.

Notes: Focus Area 14.

docs.title: Context: 'this world [aion]... the world [aion] to come' -- aion as distinct eras
docs.text:
And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the [world] to come.

Context: Aion used for 'this world/age' and 'the world/age to come' -- two distinct eras.

Notes: Focus Area 1. Aion clearly means 'age/era' -- two ages, not two eternities.

docs.title: Context: 'end of the world [aion]' -- synteleia tou aionos = end of the AGE
docs.text:
And as he sat upon the mount of Olives, the disciples came unto him privately, saying, Tell us, when shall these things be? and what [shall be] the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world?

Context: Synteleia tou aionos = 'consummation/end of the age.' The age has an END.

Notes: Focus Area 1.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?'
docs.text:
And, behold, one came and said unto him, Good Master, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?

Context: Supporting: aionios life as sought blessing.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'shall inherit everlasting life'
docs.text:
And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.

Context: Everlasting life as inheritance.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Context: 'hell fire' [gehenna] -- parallel with 18:8 'everlasting fire'
docs.text:
And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast [it] from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire.

Context: Gehenna fire in v.9 = everlasting fire in v.8. Same fire, two descriptions.

Notes: Focus Area 5.

docs.title: Context: 'outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth'
docs.text:
And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Judgment imagery from the parable of the talents.

Notes: Supporting context for Mat 25:41-46.

docs.title: Aionios life -- synoptic parallel
docs.text:
And when he was gone forth into the way, there came one running, and kneeled to him, and asked him, Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?

Context: Synoptic parallel to Mat 19:16.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'what shall I do to inherit eternal life?'
docs.text:
And, behold, a certain lawyer stood up, and tempted him, saying, Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?

Context: Synoptic parallel.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios habitations -- 'everlasting habitations'
docs.text:
And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations.

Context: Aionios modifying skenas (habitations/tents). Heavenly dwelling places.

Notes: Focus Area 12.

docs.title: Aionios life -- synoptic parallel
docs.text:
And a certain ruler asked him, saying, Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?

Context: Synoptic parallel.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'in the world to come life everlasting'
docs.text:
Who shall not receive manifold more in this present time, and in the world to come life everlasting.

Context: Synoptic parallel to Mar 10:30.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'water springing up into everlasting life'
docs.text:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.

Context: Living water imagery for eternal life.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'gathereth fruit unto life eternal'
docs.text:
And he that reapeth receiveth wages, and gathereth fruit unto life eternal: that both he that soweth and he that reapeth may rejoice together.

Context: Harvest imagery.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'in them ye think ye have eternal life'
docs.text:
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

Context: Scriptures testify of Christ who gives eternal life.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'meat which endureth unto everlasting life'
docs.text:
Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you: for him hath God the Father sealed.

Context: Perishable food vs. food enduring to eternal life.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'may have everlasting life... raise him up at the last day'
docs.text:
And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.

Context: Everlasting life connected to RESURRECTION -- future bodily raising.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'He that believeth on me hath everlasting life'
docs.text:
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life.

Context: Present possession of everlasting life through faith.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'eateth my flesh... hath eternal life'
docs.text:
Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.

Context: Eucharistic imagery connected to eternal life and resurrection.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'thou hast the words of eternal life'
docs.text:
Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.

Context: Peter's confession: Christ has the words of eternal life.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'shall keep it unto life eternal'
docs.text:
He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal.

Context: The paradox: lose life (psyche) to keep it unto life eternal (zoen aionion).

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'his commandment is life everlasting'
docs.text:
And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak.

Context: God's commandment = life everlasting.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him'
docs.text:
As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him.

Context: Eternal life is GIVEN by Christ to those given to him by the Father.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life'
docs.text:
Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.

Context: Jews who rejected the gospel judged themselves unworthy of eternal life.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Aionios life -- 'as many as were ordained to eternal life believed'
docs.text:
And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.

Context: Those ordained to eternal life believed.

Notes: Focus Area 4.

docs.title: Context: olethros -- 'destruction of the flesh'
docs.text:
To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

Context: Olethros (G3639) used for disciplinary destruction -- not torment but ruin of the flesh.

Notes: Focus Area 10. Olethros = destruction in all 4 NT occurrences.

docs.title: Context: 'sudden destruction [olethros]'
docs.text:
For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape.

Context: Olethros as sudden, inescapable destruction.

Notes: Focus Area 10.

docs.title: Context: 'destruction [olethros] and perdition [apoleia]'
docs.text:
But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and [into] many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.

Context: Olethros paired with apoleia -- both are destruction/ruin vocabulary, not torment.

Notes: Focus Area 10.

docs.title: Context: Mortal must PUT ON immortality
docs.text:
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal [must] put on immortality. So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

Context: Immortality is PUT ON (endyo) at resurrection -- it is not inherent. Mortal beings do not currently possess it.

Notes: Focus Area 14. Immortality (athanasia G110) and incorruption (aphtharsia G861) must be RECEIVED. They are not inherent human attributes.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Olam smoke judgment (Edom) echoed by Rev 14:11
docs.text:
It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever.

Context: Edom's judgment: smoke goes up le-olam ('for ever'), lies waste le-netsach netsachim ('for ever and ever' -- the strongest Hebrew 'forever' form). Yet Isa 34:11-17 describes animals inhabiting the territory -- the judgment ENDED.

Notes: Focus Areas 7, 8, 11, 15. Hebrew parsing: le-olam (H5769) = 'for eternity'; le-netsach (H5331) netsachim = 'to perpetuity of perpetuities.' The STRONGEST Hebrew 'forever' form -- and it describes a judgment that historically ended. This is the direct OT source for Rev 14:11.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Sodom fire-brimstone paradigm
docs.text:
Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven;

Context: The first occurrence of fire-and-brimstone judgment. Sodom was destroyed -- became ashes (2Pe 2:6). Jude 1:7 calls this 'eternal fire.'

Notes: Focus Area 15. The fire-brimstone paradigm: divine judgment that produces permanent destruction, not ongoing burning. Hebrew: gophryith (sulphur/brimstone) va-esh (and fire) from YHWH.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Abraham sees smoke of Sodom's completed destruction
docs.text:
And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace.

Context: Abraham sees ascending smoke from Sodom -- evidence of COMPLETED destruction. Same imagery as Rev 14:11 and Rev 19:3.

Notes: Focus Area 11. Ascending smoke as evidence of completed destruction.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: 'everlasting life... everlasting contempt' -- olam modifying both
docs.text:
And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame [and] everlasting contempt.

Context: Identical grammar: chayyei olam ('everlasting life') and dir'on olam ('everlasting contempt'). Same word olam modifying both outcomes. Nature-of-subject principle applies.

Notes: Focus Areas 8, 9. Hebrew parsing: chayyei (H2416, 'life' mp Cst) olam (H5769, 'eternity' ms Abs); dir'on (H1860, 'abhorrence' ms Cst) olam (H5769, 'eternity' ms Abs). Deraon occurs only twice: here and Isa 66:24 where it describes reaction to CORPSES (peger). The 'everlasting contempt' is the everlasting abhorrence evoked by the memory of the wicked's fate -- not everlasting conscious experience of shame.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Deraon context -- onlookers view CORPSES (peger), not living beings
docs.text:
And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

Context: The redeemed VIEW CORPSES (peger = dead bodies, not living sufferers). The worm and fire consume the corpses. Deraon = the visceral revulsion of onlookers at the sight.

Notes: Focus Area 15. Hebrew parsing confirms: pigerey (corpses, H6297 mp Cst) -- the objects viewed are dead bodies. The worm 'shall not die' and fire 'shall not be quenched' = agents of consumption are not interrupted until the task is complete. Deraon (H1860) = abhorrence of the onlookers, not suffering of the dead.

docs.title: Context: Satan becomes ASHES and exists NO MORE
docs.text:
Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee. All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never [shalt] thou [be] any more.

Context: The being behind the king of Tyre (Satan) becomes ASHES and exists 'NO MORE.' Same being tormented 'for ever and ever' in Rev 20:10.

Notes: Focus Area 11. The same fire produces ashes and cessation ('never shalt thou be any more'). Either Eze 28 or Rev 20:10 must be interpreted non-literally; both cannot be literal simultaneously.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Jerusalem's olam fire ended
docs.text:
But if ye will not hearken unto me to hallow the sabbath day, and not to bear a burden, even entering in at the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath day; then will I kindle a fire in the gates thereof, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem, and it shall not be quenched.

Context: Jerusalem's fire 'shall not be quenched' -- same formula as Isa 34:10 and Isa 66:24. Yet this fire ended with the Babylonian destruction in 586 BC.

Notes: Focus Area 15. 'Not quenched' means the fire cannot be extinguished by human effort -- it burns until it has consumed its fuel. It does not mean it burns forever.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Wicked become STUBBLE -- burned up
docs.text:
For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

Context: Wicked = STUBBLE burned up. Leaves NEITHER ROOT NOR BRANCH -- total consumption.

Notes: Focus Area 15. Destruction vocabulary: 'burn them up' and 'leave them neither root nor branch.'

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Wicked become ASHES
docs.text:
And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do [this], saith the LORD of hosts.

Context: The wicked become ASHES underfoot. Cessation/consumption, not preservation.

Notes: Focus Area 15.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: 'the wicked shall not be' -- cessation
docs.text:
For yet a little while, and the wicked [shall] not [be]: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it [shall] not [be].

Context: The wicked SHALL NOT BE -- cessation of existence. Their place is gone.

Notes: Focus Area 15.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: 'they shall be as though they had not been'
docs.text:
For as ye have drunk upon my holy mountain, [so] shall all the heathen drink continually, yea, they shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been.

Context: The wicked 'shall be as though they had not been' -- as if they never existed.

Notes: Focus Area 15. Incompatible with eternal conscious existence.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Olam slave -- 'he shall serve him for ever [le-olam]'
docs.text:
Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever.

Context: Le-olam = 'for ever' meaning 'for the rest of his life.' Same word (olam) used for both slave service and God's eternity.

Notes: Focus Area 13, 15. Nature-of-subject: olam applied to a mortal slave = 'for life.' The Phm 1:15 (aionion) usage is the NT parallel.

docs.title: OT SOURCE: Olam slave -- 'he shall be thy servant for ever [le-olam]'
docs.text:
Then thou shalt take an aul, and thrust [it] through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise.

Context: Parallel to Exo 21:6. Le-olam = 'for life' in the context of human service.

Notes: Focus Area 13, 15.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' in judgment -- smoke of torment ascending forever
docs.text:
And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

Context: Third angel's message in Revelation 14. Warning about those who worship the beast and receive his mark. Uses the eis aionas aionon formula in a judgment context.

Notes: One of only 3 uses of the ages-of-ages formula in a judgment context (with Rev 19:3 and 20:10). Echoes Isa 34:10 (Edom's smoke). Subject is beast-worshipers. The smoke ascends, not the people -- smoke is evidence of completed burning.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' in judgment -- devil, beast, false prophet tormented
docs.text:
And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet [are], and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Context: After the millennium. The devil is cast into the lake of fire where the beast and false prophet already are. Uses eis tous aionas ton aionon.

Notes: Subjects are specifically the devil, beast, and false prophet -- non-human/symbolic entities. Humans enter the lake of fire in v.14-15 but the term used for them is the second death, not torment. Rev 20:9 uses devoured (katephagen) for human enemies.

docs.title: Satan's fate: "never shalt thou be any more"
docs.text:
All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never [shalt] thou [be] any more.

Context: Lamentation over the king of Tyre, widely understood as extending to the spiritual being behind the earthly king (Satan). Follows v.18 where this being becomes ashes upon the earth.

Notes: The phrase eynekha ad-owlam (you are no more to perpetuity) uses owlam to describe permanent cessation. The same being described with covering cherub imagery (v.14,16) will become ashes (v.18) and cease to exist (v.19). Relevant to Rev 20:10 -- same being, different vocabulary for outcome.

docs.title: Immortality put on at resurrection -- death swallowed in victory
docs.text:
So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

Context: Paul's resurrection chapter. Describes the transformation at the last trumpet (v.52). Mortals PUT ON immortality -- it is not inherent.

Notes: Immortality (athanasia G110) is PUT ON (enduo G1746) at a future point. Combined with 1Ti 6:16 (God alone has immortality), establishes that eternal existence is a gift given to the redeemed, not an inherent property of all humans. If the wicked also have eternal conscious existence, they too must receive immortality -- but Scripture never says this.

docs.title: Human remnant SLAIN -- destruction vocabulary for humans vs. symbolic entities
docs.text:
And the remnant were slain with the sword of him that sat upon the horse, which [sword] proceeded out of his mouth: and all the fowls were filled with their flesh.

Context: Battle of Armageddon. The beast and false prophet are cast alive into the lake of fire (v.20), but the human remnant are SLAIN (apektanthesan from apokteino).

Notes: Sharp distinction: symbolic entities (beast, false prophet) are cast alive into the lake; humans are slain/killed. Different verbs for different subjects. Confirms that the ages-of-ages torment applies to the symbolic entities, while humans experience death/destruction.

docs.title: Analysis: Aionios (G166) in the New Testament
Study Question
docs.text: Greek aionios (G166) -- all 71 NT occurrences. Compare aidios (G126). "Eis tous aionas ton aionon" in ~20 passages. LXX usage. Does aionios inherently mean "eternal/endless" or does it mean "pertaining to the age" with duration determined by the nature of the subject?

docs.title: Aionios (G166) from Aion (G165)
docs.text:
Strong's defines aionios as "from G165; perpetual (also used of past time, or past and future as well)." The root noun aion (G165) is defined as "properly, an age; by extension, perpetuity." Aion appears 120 times in the NT. The KJV translates it as "ever" (52.6%), "world" (30.5%), and "and ever" (22.1%).

The KJV translates aion as "world" 30 times. These are not arbitrary translation choices. They reflect the word's core meaning as "age" or "era":

  • Matt 24:3: "the end of the world" = synteleia tou aionos = "the consummation of the age." An age that has an END is not infinity.
  • Matt 12:32: "neither in this world, neither in the world to come" = two distinct aions (ages/eras), not two eternities.
  • 2 Cor 4:4: "the god of this world" = the god of this present age.
  • Heb 1:2: "by whom also he made the worlds" = the ages (aionas, plural) as created order.
  • Heb 9:26: "the end of the world" = synteleia tou aionos = end of the age.
  • Heb 11:3: "the worlds were framed by the word of God" = the ages are created things.

Mark 10:30 puts both words in the same sentence: "in the world [aion] to come eternal [aionios] life." The root noun and its adjective side by side. Eternal life belongs to the age to come. The adjective derives from the noun.

docs.title: Aidios (G126) from Aei (G104)
docs.text:
Aidios derives from aei (G104, "always"). Aei appears 8 times in the NT, always denoting habitual, continual patterns: "ye do always [aei] resist the Holy Ghost" (Acts 7:51); "the Cretians are alway [aei] liars" (Tit 1:12). The etymology chain: aei ("always") produces aidios ("everduring") -- inherent, absolute eternality.

The Greek language had two distinct words available for "eternal": aionios (from aion, "an age") and aidios (from aei, "always"). The existence of both as separate lexical items is itself a datum. If they were synonymous, one would be redundant.

docs.title: Romans 1:20
docs.text:
"For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal [aidios] power and Godhead."

Greek parsing: aidios (G126, Nom Sg F) modifying dynamis (G1411, Nom Sg F). Paul chooses aidios for God's "eternal power" -- attributes intrinsic to God's nature that have always existed and always will. The word theiotes (G2305, "divinity") appears alongside, reinforcing that aidios here describes what is inherently and absolutely divine.

Paul uses aionios dozens of times throughout his epistles. Here, describing God's own eternal power, he switches to aidios. The word choice is deliberate.

docs.title: Jude 1:6
docs.text:
"And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting [aidios] chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day."

Greek parsing: desmois (G1199, Dat Pl M) aidiois (G126, Dat Pl M). Jude uses aidios for chains binding fallen angels -- absolute, unbreakable permanence. These chains genuinely never fail until the appointed judgment.

docs.title: Jude's Word Switch (v.6 vs. v.7)
docs.text:
In verse 6, Jude uses aidios for the angelic chains. In the immediately next verse (v.7), he switches to aionios:

"Even as Sodom and Gomorrha... are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal [aionios] fire."

Greek parsing: pyros (G4442, Gen Sg N) aioniou (G166, Gen Sg N). The same author, in consecutive sentences, chooses different words. Aidios for chains that genuinely never break. Aionios for fire that historically reduced cities to ashes (2 Pet 2:6 confirms: "turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes"). Sodom is not still burning. The fire accomplished its purpose and ceased.

If aidios and aionios were synonymous, Jude would not alternate between them in adjacent verses when writing about related subjects (judgment of angels; judgment of Sodom). The distinction is functional: aidios = inherent, absolute permanence; aionios = age-pertaining, with actual duration determined by the subject.

docs.title: Part 3: Aionios for Past Time -- The Decisive Counter-Evidence
docs.text: Three passages use aionios to refer to past ages that have ended:

docs.title: Romans 16:25
docs.text:
"Now to him that is of power to stablish you... according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began [chronois aioniois]."

Greek parsing: chronois (G5550, Dat Pl M) aioniois (G166, Dat Pl M) = "in age-long/eternal times." The mystery WAS kept secret during these aionios times. It is NOW revealed. The aionios period has ended. If aionios inherently means "endless," the mystery could never have been revealed, because the period of secrecy would never conclude.

docs.title: 2 Timothy 1:9
docs.text:
"Who hath saved us... according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began [pro chronon aionion]."

Greek parsing: pro (G4253, "before") chronon (G5550, Gen Pl M) aionion (G166, Gen Pl M) = "before age-long/eternal times." God's grace was given BEFORE aionios times. If aionios means "endless," the phrase requires a starting point before endlessness -- a logical impossibility.

docs.title: Titus 1:2
docs.text:
"In hope of eternal life [zoes aioniou], which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began [pro chronon aionion]."

This verse is decisive. Aionios appears TWICE in a single verse: - First: zoes aioniou (Gen Sg F + Gen Sg F) = "eternal life" -- future hope. - Second: pro chronon aionion (Gen Pl M + Gen Pl M) = "before age-long times" -- past reference.

Same adjective. Same verse. Different temporal directions. One points forward (eternal life to be received). The other points backward (before the ages began). This verse alone falsifies the claim that aionios must carry identical duration every time it appears. If the Matt 25:46 symmetry argument requires identical duration for two uses of aionios, then Tit 1:2 is self-contradictory -- but no one reads it that way.

docs.title: Part 4: Aionios Modifying "Life" (~43 of 71 Occurrences)
docs.text:
Approximately 43 of the 71 NT uses of aionios modify zoe ("life"), making "eternal life" the dominant collocation at ~60% of all occurrences. The distribution across books:

  • John's Gospel: ~17 occurrences (John 3:15, 3:16, 3:36, 4:14, 4:36, 5:24, 5:39, 6:27, 6:40, 6:47, 6:54, 6:68, 10:28, 12:25, 12:50, 17:2, 17:3)
  • Pauline epistles: ~12 (Rom 2:7, 5:21, 6:22, 6:23; Gal 6:8; 1 Tim 1:16, 6:12, 6:19; 2 Tim 2:10; Tit 1:2, 3:7)
  • 1 John: ~6 (1:2, 2:25, 3:15, 5:11, 5:13, 5:20)
  • Synoptics/Acts: ~7 (Matt 19:16, 19:29, 25:46; Mark 10:17, 10:30; Luke 10:25, 18:18, 18:30; Acts 13:46, 13:48)
  • Jude: 1 (Jude 1:21)

The NT teaching on eternal life can be stated from the texts themselves:

It is a gift, not inherent. "The gift of God is eternal life" (Rom 6:23). "God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son" (1 John 5:11). Life is GIVEN, not possessed by nature.

It is received through faith. "Whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life" (John 3:15-16). "He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life" (John 3:36).

It is defined as knowing God. "This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God" (John 17:3). Eternal life is relational and qualitative, not merely quantitative.

Those without Christ do NOT have it. "No murderer hath eternal life abiding in him" (1 John 3:15). "He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life" (1 John 5:12). If all humans inherently have eternal existence, this statement is meaningless.

It is contrasted with perishing and death. "Should not perish, but have everlasting life" (John 3:16). "I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish" (John 10:28). "The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life" (Rom 6:23). "Soweth to the flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but... reap life everlasting" (Gal 6:8).

The contrasts are consistent: perish vs. eternal life (John 3:16). Death vs. eternal life (Rom 6:23). Corruption vs. eternal life (Gal 6:8). Destruction vs. life (Matt 7:13-14). In every case, the alternative to eternal life is cessation, not alternative eternal existence.

docs.title: Part 5: Aionios Modifying Judgment Subjects
docs.text: Only about 7 of 71 occurrences (~10%) apply aionios to judgment:

docs.title: Matthew 25:46 -- "Everlasting Punishment"
docs.text:
"And these shall go away into everlasting punishment [kolasin aionion]: but the righteous into life eternal [zoen aionion]."

Greek parsing: kolasin (G2851, Acc Sg F) aionion (G166, Acc Sg F) // zoen (G2222, Acc Sg F) aionion (G166, Acc Sg F). Identical grammatical construction.

The symmetry is real: same adjective, same case and gender agreement, parallel destinations. But the symmetry argument ("same adjective = same duration") must account for the following:

  1. Titus 1:2 precedent: Same adjective, same verse, different temporal scopes.
  2. The noun matters. Aionios modifies different nouns. Kolasis (punishment) and zoe (life) are different things. The Hebrews pattern (see Part 6) shows that aionios + a result-noun = permanent result of a completed act. "Eternal punishment" follows the same pattern as "eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12) -- the act happens once; the result stands permanently.
  3. Kolasis, not basanizo. The word is kolasis (G2851), not basanizo (G928). Kolasis occurs only twice in the NT (here and 1 John 4:18). Its root kolazo (G2849) means "to curtail, prune, correct." Jesus chose a word meaning punishment/correction, not a word meaning torment.
  4. Dan 12:2 parallel. The OT uses identical grammar: chayyei olam ("everlasting life") and dir'on olam ("everlasting contempt"). Olam modifies both. But the nature-of-subject principle (demonstrated across 50+ OT cases) shows olam's actual duration depends on the subject it modifies. The "everlasting contempt" (deraon) describes the permanent revulsion of onlookers at the sight of corpses (Isa 66:24), not the conscious experience of the dead.

docs.title: Matthew 25:41 -- "Everlasting Fire"
docs.text:
"Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

Greek parsing: to pyr (G4442, Acc Sg N) to aionion (G166, Acc Sg N) to hetoimasmenon (G2090, Perf Pass Ptcp Acc Sg N) to diabolo (G1228, Dat Sg M) kai tois angelois (G32, Dat Pl M) autou. Double article construction: "the fire, the eternal one." The fire was "prepared" (perfect passive -- a completed preparation) for the devil and his angels, not originally for humans.

docs.title: Matthew 18:8 -- "Everlasting Fire"
docs.text:
"It is better for thee to enter into life halt or maimed, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into everlasting fire."

The parallel in Matt 18:9 calls this same fire "hell fire" (gehenna). "Everlasting fire" = "gehenna fire." The two are synonymous descriptions of the same destination.

docs.title: 2 Thessalonians 1:9 -- "Everlasting Destruction"
docs.text:
"Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction [olethron aionion] from the presence of the Lord."

Greek parsing: olethron (G3639, Acc Sg M) aionion (G166, Acc Sg M). Paul wrote "everlasting DESTRUCTION." Olethros (G3639) occurs 4 times in the NT: 1 Cor 5:5 (destruction of the flesh), 1 Thess 5:3 (sudden destruction), 2 Thess 1:9 (everlasting destruction), 1 Tim 6:9 (destruction and perdition). In every occurrence, olethros means ruin, destruction, or death. No lexicon defines it as "torment" or "ongoing conscious suffering."

Paul had vocabulary for torment (basanizo/basanismos) and did not use it. He wrote "destruction" and meant destruction. "Everlasting destruction" = destruction that is permanent and irreversible. "From the presence of the Lord" = separation from the source of life, producing death.

docs.title: Mark 3:29 -- "Eternal Sin"
docs.text:
"He that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation [aioniou hamartematos]."

Greek parsing: aioniou (G166, Gen Sg F) hamartematos (G265, Gen Sg N) = "eternal sin." The critical text reads "eternal sin," not "eternal damnation" (KJV). The adjective modifies the SIN itself, not a process of punishment. The sin is irrevocable -- its guilt stands permanently. This matches the Hebrews "permanent result" pattern: an act committed once with permanent standing.

docs.title: Jude 1:7 -- "Eternal Fire"
docs.text:
"Even as Sodom and Gomorrha... are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire."

Greek parsing: pyros (G4442, Gen Sg N) aioniou (G166, Gen Sg N). Sodom's fire is called "eternal." But 2 Pet 2:6 says God turned Sodom into ASHES. Sodom is not still burning. The fire's "eternality" is in its divine source and irreversible effect, not in endless duration. The cities are "set forth for an example" -- an example of what? Ashes. Permanent destruction.

docs.title: Hebrews 6:2 -- "Eternal Judgment"
docs.text:
"Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment."

Greek parsing: krimatos (G2917, Gen Sg N) aioniou (G166, Gen Sg N). "Eternal judgment" is listed among foundational doctrines. The judgment is rendered once; its verdict stands permanently. Not "eternal judging" (ongoing process) but "eternal judgment" (permanent verdict).

docs.title: Part 6: The Hebrews Pattern -- Permanent Results of Completed Acts
docs.text: Hebrews uses aionios in a distinct pattern: the adjective modifies a noun describing a completed act, and the combination means the act's result is permanent.

docs.title: Hebrews 9:12 -- "Eternal Redemption"
docs.text:
"Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once [ephapax] into the holy place, having obtained [heuramenos] eternal redemption."

Greek parsing: aionian (G166, Acc Sg F) lytrosin (G3085, Acc Sg F). Heuramenos = aorist middle participle, "having obtained" (completed action). Ephapax = "once for all." Christ entered once. He obtained redemption once. The act of redemption is not ongoing. The result is aionios -- it stands permanently. Not "eternal redeeming" (process) but "eternal redemption" (result).

docs.title: Hebrews 5:9 -- "Eternal Salvation"
docs.text:
"And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation."

Greek parsing: soterias (G4991, Gen Sg F) aioniou (G166, Gen Sg F). Teleiotheis = "having been made perfect" (completed). Christ became (egeneto, aorist) the author (aitios) of salvation. The salvation was accomplished; its effect is permanent.

docs.title: Hebrews 9:15 -- "Eternal Inheritance"
docs.text:
"They which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance."

An inheritance received. Not an endless process of inheriting. The inheritance does not expire.

docs.title: Hebrews 13:20 -- "Everlasting Covenant"
docs.text:
"Through the blood of the everlasting covenant."

The covenant is established through Christ's blood. It does not need to be re-established. Its validity is permanent.

docs.title: The Pattern Applied to Judgment
docs.text: This pattern directly informs how to read "eternal punishment" (Matt 25:46), "eternal judgment" (Heb 6:2), and "eternal destruction" (2 Thess 1:9). In each case: - The noun describes an act or its result (punishment, judgment, destruction) - The adjective describes the permanence of that result - The act happens once; its result stands permanently - Not "eternal punishing/judging/destroying" (ongoing process) but "eternal punishment/judgment/destruction" (permanent result)

docs.title: Part 7: The "Eis Tous Aionas Ton Aionon" Formula
docs.text: The "ages of ages" formula appears approximately 22 times in the NT. The distribution is categorically lopsided:

docs.title: Doxological Uses (~19 passages)
docs.text:
Applied to God, Christ, or divine realities: - God's existence: Rev 4:9, 4:10, 10:6, 15:7 ("him that liveth for ever and ever") - God's reign: Rev 11:15 ("he shall reign for ever and ever") - Christ's life: Rev 1:18 ("I am alive for evermore") - God's throne: Heb 1:8 ("Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever") - Saints' reign: Rev 22:5 ("they shall reign for ever and ever") - Doxologies: Gal 1:5; Phil 4:20; 1 Tim 1:17; 2 Tim 4:18; Heb 13:21; 1 Pet 4:11; 5:11; Rev 1:6; 5:13; 7:12

In every doxological use, the formula reflects the genuinely endless nature of its subject. God IS genuinely eternal (Rev 4:9-10). Christ IS now immortal (Rev 1:18). Saints RECEIVE immortality at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53), hence their reign is genuinely endless (Rev 22:5).

docs.title: Judgment Uses (3 passages)
docs.text:
Only three uses of the formula appear in judgment contexts, all in Revelation's apocalyptic framework:

Rev 14:11: "The smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever [eis aionas aionon]."

The SMOKE ascends -- the evidence of burning, not the persons. The passage echoes Isa 34:10: "the smoke thereof shall go up for ever [le-olam]" -- Edom's judgment that historically ended (Isa 34:11-17 describes animals inhabiting the territory). The subjects are "those who worship the beast and his image" -- within the Revelation's symbolic framework. Basanismos (G929, "torment") appears only 6 times in the NT, ALL in Revelation. Three of six describe Babylon's completed destruction (Rev 18:7, 10, 15).

"No rest day and night" uses anapausis (G372) -- the same word used in Rev 4:8 of the living creatures who "rest not day and night" in praise. The phrase characterizes uninterrupted activity, not necessarily eternal duration.

Rev 19:3: "And her smoke rose up for ever and ever [eis tous aionas ton aionon]."

The subject is symbolic Babylon. Rev 17:5 explicitly labels her: "MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT." This is a symbolic entity, not a literal city eternally burning. Rev 18:8 says she is "utterly burned with fire"; Rev 18:21 says she "shall be found no more at all." The smoke's "forever" rising indicates the permanence of her destruction, not ongoing burning.

Rev 20:10: "The devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented [basanisthesontai] day and night for ever and ever [eis tous aionas ton aionon]."

Greek parsing: diabolos (G1228, Nom Sg M), therion (G2342, Nom Sg N), pseudoprophetes (G5578, Nom Sg M). Basanisthesontai (G928, Fut Pass Ind 3P). Three subjects: the devil (non-human supernatural being), the beast (symbolic political entity -- Rev 17:8 says it "was, and is not, and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit"), the false prophet (symbolic religious entity = the second beast of Rev 13:11-17). Not one of the three is a literal, generic human being.

When HUMANS enter the lake of fire, the vocabulary changes: - Rev 20:9: Fire from God "devoured" (katephagen, G2719) them -- destruction vocabulary - Rev 19:20-21: Beast and false prophet cast "alive" (zontes) into the lake; but the human "remnant were slain" (apektanthesan) -- different verbs - Rev 20:14-15: Humans in the lake of fire = "the second death" -- death vocabulary, not torment - Rev 21:8: Human categories (fearful, unbelieving, murderers, etc.) = "the second death"

Not a single "ages of ages" passage in the NT applies the torment formula to literal, generic human wicked.

docs.title: Part 8: LXX Usage -- Aionios Translating Olam
docs.text:
The LXX translates olam (H5769) as aionios 100 times (PMI 26.16, the strongest association). Aionios also translates: dor ("generation," 23x), chuqqah ("statute," 20x), berith ("covenant," 20x), choq ("enactment," 14x).

These translation patterns reveal how the LXX translators understood aionios: - "Everlasting statutes" (olam -> aionios): Mosaic ceremonies that have ceased with the temple's destruction - "Everlasting covenants" (olam -> aionios): Covenants that were superseded (circumcision, per Gal 5:2-6) - "Generational" contexts (dor -> aionios): Duration spanning generations, not infinity

Aidios (G126) has NO Hebrew source in the LXX. It is a distinctly Greek word with no equivalent in the Hebrew OT. The LXX translators, when rendering olam, consistently chose aion/aionios -- the age-related word -- rather than aidios -- the strictly-everduring word. If olam inherently meant "eternal" in the absolute sense, aidios would have been the natural translation choice. The consistent choice of aionios over aidios confirms that the translators understood olam (and therefore aionios) as "age-pertaining."

The nature-of-subject principle established in the olam studies (etc7-07, etc6-07) carries directly into the NT via this vocabulary bridge. Olam applied to God = genuinely eternal. Olam applied to slave service = lifetime. Olam applied to Jonah's confinement = 3 days. Olam applied to fire/smoke judgments = until completed. Aionios inherits this entire semantic range.

docs.title: Part 9: Aionios for Divine Attributes and Heavenly Realities
docs.text:
When aionios modifies something genuinely eternal, it carries its maximal force:

  • Rom 16:26: "the everlasting God" -- God IS eternal; aionios reflects that nature
  • Heb 9:14: "the eternal Spirit" -- the Holy Spirit is divine; genuinely eternal
  • Heb 13:20: "the everlasting covenant" -- supersedes the old; does not expire
  • 2 Pet 1:11: "the everlasting kingdom" -- Christ's kingdom has no end (Luke 1:33)
  • 2 Cor 4:17-18: "eternal weight of glory" / "things which are not seen are eternal" -- the contrast is proskaira (temporary) vs. aionios (eternal)
  • 2 Cor 5:1: "eternal in the heavens" -- the heavenly dwelling
  • Rev 14:6: "the everlasting gospel" -- God's message spanning all ages
  • 1 Tim 1:17: "the King eternal" -- God as sovereign over the ages
  • 2 Thess 2:16: "everlasting consolation" -- permanent comfort
  • 1 Pet 5:10: "his eternal glory" -- God's own glory
  • 2 Tim 2:10: "eternal glory" -- the glory believers receive

These uses establish the maximal range of aionios. But they simultaneously confirm the nature-of-subject principle: aionios carries full eternal force here because the subjects ARE genuinely eternal. God is eternal by nature. The Spirit is divine. The heavenly realities are imperishable. The word reflects the subject's nature; it does not impose a fixed duration regardless of context.

docs.title: Philemon 1:15 -- "For Ever" in a Human Context
docs.text:
"For perhaps he therefore departed for a season [pros horan], that thou shouldest receive him for ever [aionion]."

Greek parsing: aionion (G166, Acc Sg M) modifying auton ("him"). Paul contrasts pros horan ("for an hour/season") with aionion ("permanently"). This clearly means "for the rest of your life" or "permanently" -- not "for literal infinity." This is the NT parallel to the Hebrew olam slave (Exo 21:6; Deut 15:17), where le-olam means "for life."

This usage demonstrates that aionios can mean "permanent within the scope of the subject's existence" without implying absolute infinity. The same semantic range attested for olam in the OT appears in the NT with aionios.

docs.title: Luke 16:9 -- "Everlasting Habitations"
docs.text:
"Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations."

Aionios modifying skenas ("habitations/tents") -- heavenly dwelling places that last because the age they belong to does not end.

docs.title: Part 11: The Perish-vs-Life Contrast and the Immortality Question
docs.text:
The NT consistently presents two outcomes:

  • John 3:16: "should not PERISH [apollytai, G622], but have everlasting life" -- perish vs. life
  • Rom 6:23: "the wages of sin is DEATH [thanatos, G2288]; but the gift of God is eternal life" -- death vs. life
  • Gal 6:8: "shall of the flesh reap CORRUPTION [phthora, G5356]; but... reap life everlasting" -- corruption vs. life
  • Matt 7:13-14: "broad is the way, that leadeth to DESTRUCTION [apoleia, G684]; narrow is the way, which leadeth unto LIFE" -- destruction vs. life
  • Phil 3:19: "whose end is DESTRUCTION [apoleia]" -- destruction as the telos

The contrasting terms are: perish, death, corruption, destruction. Not "torment," not "alternative eternal existence." The binary is existence vs. non-existence, not bliss vs. suffering.

The immortality data reinforces this: - 1 Tim 6:16: God ALONE (monos) has athanasia (immortality) - 1 Cor 15:53: Mortal must PUT ON (endyo) immortality at resurrection - Rom 2:7: Believers SEEK immortality -- seeking what they do not yet possess - 1 John 3:15: "No murderer hath eternal life abiding in him"

If the wicked are tormented eternally, they must have eternal existence. But Scripture says God alone has immortality, believers must receive it as a gift, and murderers do not have eternal life. The wicked are never said to receive immortality, incorruptibility, or eternal existence.

docs.title: Isaiah 34:10 -- The Source of Rev 14:11
docs.text:
"It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever [le-olam]."

Hebrew parsing: le-olam (H5769) ya'aleh (H5927, "shall ascend") ashana-h (H6227, "its smoke"). Then: le-netsach (H5331) netsachim (H5331) = "to perpetuity of perpetuities" -- the STRONGEST Hebrew "forever" form. Yet Isa 34:11-17 describes animals inhabiting the territory. The judgment ended. The strongest possible "forever" language describes a completed judgment.

Rev 14:11 uses this same imagery: smoke ascending eis aionas aionon. The OT source demonstrates that ascending smoke is evidence of COMPLETED destruction, not ongoing burning. Gen 19:28 confirms: Abraham sees Sodom's smoke after the cities have been consumed.

docs.title: Daniel 12:2 -- The OT Parallel to Matt 25:46
docs.text:
"Some to everlasting life [chayyei olam], and some to shame and everlasting contempt [dir'on olam]."

Identical grammatical structure: Noun.Cst + olam.Abs for both outcomes. But deraon (H1860, "contempt/abhorrence") occurs only twice: here and Isa 66:24. In Isa 66:24, the objects viewed are pigerey (H6297, "corpses") -- dead bodies, not living sufferers. The "everlasting contempt" is the permanent abhorrence evoked by the memory of the wicked's fate, not everlasting conscious experience of shame.

docs.title: Genesis 19:24 / 2 Peter 2:6 -- The Fire-Brimstone Paradigm
docs.text: God rained fire and brimstone on Sodom (Gen 19:24). Jude 1:7 calls this "eternal fire." Peter says it produced ASHES and was made an "ensample" to the ungodly (2 Pet 2:6). The paradigmatic "eternal fire" burned completely, consumed its target, and ceased. The "eternity" is in the divine source and the irreversibility of the destruction, not in endless duration of the burning itself.

docs.title: Isaiah 66:24 -- Corpses, Not Living Beings
docs.text:
"They shall go forth, and look upon the carcases [pigerey] of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched."

Hebrew parsing: pigerey (H6297, "corpses" mp Cst). The objects viewed are dead bodies. The worm and fire consume the corpses -- they are agents of decomposition whose work is not interrupted ("shall not die," "shall not be quenched") until the task is complete. Deraon (H1860) = the visceral revulsion of onlookers at the sight. The onlookers are alive and conscious; the transgressing men are corpses.

docs.title: Ezekiel 28:18-19 -- Satan's Fate
docs.text:
"I will bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth... thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more."

The being behind the king of Tyre becomes ASHES and exists "NO MORE." This is the same being described in Rev 20:10 as "tormented for ever and ever." Both statements cannot be literal simultaneously. Either the ashes/cessation language of Ezekiel or the torment-forever language of Revelation's apocalyptic vision requires non-literal reading. Since Ezekiel 28 is prophetic direct speech and Revelation is acknowledged apocalyptic symbolism (Rev 1:1: "signified" = communicated through signs), the apocalyptic passage yields to the more didactic one.

docs.title: Part 13: The Complete Distribution of Aionios
docs.text:
Categorizing all 71 NT occurrences by subject modified:

Eternal life (~43 occurrences, ~60%): Matt 19:16, 19:29, 25:46b; Mark 10:17, 10:30; Luke 10:25, 18:18, 18:30; John 3:15, 3:16, 3:36, 4:14, 4:36, 5:24, 5:39, 6:27, 6:40, 6:47, 6:54, 6:68, 10:28, 12:25, 12:50, 17:2, 17:3; Acts 13:46, 13:48; Rom 2:7, 5:21, 6:22, 6:23; Gal 6:8; 1 Tim 1:16, 6:12, 6:19; 2 Tim 2:10; Tit 1:2a, 3:7; 1 John 1:2, 2:25, 3:15, 5:11, 5:13, 5:20; Jude 1:21

Divine attributes and heavenly realities (~12 occurrences, ~17%): Rom 16:26 (God); 2 Cor 4:17 (glory), 4:18 (unseen things), 5:1 (heavenly house); 2 Thess 2:16 (consolation); 1 Tim 1:17 (King); Heb 9:14 (Spirit), 13:20 (covenant); 1 Pet 5:10 (glory); 2 Pet 1:11 (kingdom); Rev 14:6 (gospel); Luke 16:9 (habitations)

Judgment/punishment (~7 occurrences, ~10%): Matt 18:8 (fire), 25:41 (fire), 25:46a (punishment); Mark 3:29 (sin); 2 Thess 1:9 (destruction); Jude 1:7 (fire); Heb 6:2 (judgment)

Completed-act results in Hebrews (~4 occurrences, ~6%): Heb 5:9 (salvation), 9:12 (redemption), 9:15 (inheritance) [Note: Heb 6:2 and 13:20 overlap with other categories]

Past time (~3 occurrences, ~4%): Rom 16:25 (times past); 2 Tim 1:9 (before times); Tit 1:2b (before times)

Human/relational (~1 occurrence, ~1%): Philemon 1:15 (permanently)

The distribution speaks for itself. The primary use of aionios is for the life God gives to believers through Christ. The judgment uses are a small minority, and within that minority, destruction vocabulary dominates (olethros in 2 Thess 1:9; kolasis in Matt 25:46). Torment vocabulary (basanizo/basanismos) is conspicuously absent from aionios-modified judgment. The only torment-forever language in the NT appears in the "ages of ages" formula, not with aionios as an adjective, and only in Revelation's apocalyptic framework applied to non-human/symbolic entities.

docs.title: Pattern 1: The Nature-of-Subject Principle
docs.text: Across all categories, aionios takes its actual duration from the nature of the subject: - Applied to God (Rom 16:26): genuinely eternal, because God is eternal - Applied to the Spirit (Heb 9:14): genuinely eternal, because the Spirit is divine - Applied to believers' life (John 3:16): genuinely endless, because believers receive immortality (1 Cor 15:53) - Applied to past times (Rom 16:25; 2 Tim 1:9; Tit 1:2): age-spanning but ended - Applied to human relationship (Phm 1:15): permanent within the scope of the relationship - Applied to Sodom's fire (Jude 1:7): permanent in effect, but the burning ceased (2 Pet 2:6) - Applied to completed acts (Heb 9:12): the result is permanent; the act is not ongoing

docs.title: Pattern 2: The LXX Vocabulary Bridge
docs.text: Aionios inherits olam's full semantic range through the LXX translation tradition (100x co-occurrence). Every pattern attested for olam in the OT has a corresponding aionios pattern in the NT: - Olam for God = aionios for God (genuinely eternal) - Olam for past time = aionios for past time - Olam for human service = aionios in human context (Philemon) - Olam for fire judgments that ended = aionios for fire judgments of Sodom (Jude 1:7 / 2 Pet 2:6)

docs.title: Pattern 3: The Two-Word System (Aionios vs. Aidios)
docs.text: Greek has two words. Aidios (from aei, "always") = inherent, absolute eternality. Aionios (from aion, "an age") = age-pertaining. Paul uses aidios for God's inherent eternal power (Rom 1:20). Jude uses aidios for genuinely unbreakable chains (Jude 1:6), then switches to aionios for fire that produced ashes (Jude 1:7). The word system itself testifies: when Greek speakers meant "strictly, absolutely eternal," they had a word for it -- and it was not aionios.

docs.title: Pattern 4: Destruction Not Torment
docs.text:
When aionios modifies judgment nouns: - "Eternal punishment" (Matt 25:46): kolasis, not basanizo - "Eternal destruction" (2 Thess 1:9): olethros, a destruction word - "Eternal sin" (Mark 3:29): the sin is permanent, not a process - "Eternal fire" (Matt 25:41; Jude 1:7): fire that produces ashes (2 Pet 2:6) - "Eternal judgment" (Heb 6:2): permanent verdict

In every case, the noun points to a result or act, not an ongoing process of conscious suffering. Basanizo/basanismos (the torment word family) never appears with aionios as a modifier.

docs.title: Pattern 5: The "Ages of Ages" Distribution
docs.text: ~19 of ~22 uses are doxological (God/Christ). Only 3 are in judgment contexts (Rev 14:11; 19:3; 20:10), all in Revelation, all with non-human or symbolic subjects, all echoing OT "forever" language for completed judgments. The formula is not a general statement about the wicked's fate. It is a Revelation-specific expression applied to symbolic entities within an apocalyptic vision.

docs.title: Part 15: Verses Addressed Individually (Supporting Verses)
docs.text:
The supporting verses (73 in the scope) largely repeat the patterns already established. For completeness:

"Eternal life" supporting passages (Matt 19:16, 19:29; Mark 10:17; Luke 10:25, 18:18, 18:30; John 3:15, 3:36, 4:14, 4:36, 5:39, 6:27, 6:40, 6:47, 6:54, 6:68, 12:25, 12:50, 17:2; Acts 13:46, 13:48; Rom 5:21, 6:22; 2 Cor 4:17, 5:1; Gal 6:8; 2 Thess 2:16; 1 Tim 1:16, 6:12, 6:19; 2 Tim 2:10; Tit 3:7; 1 Pet 5:10; 1 John 1:2, 2:25, 5:13, 5:20; Jude 1:21): All use aionios to describe the life God gives believers. Each confirms: life is a gift, received through faith, absent from those who reject Christ. None introduces a concept that modifies the core pattern.

"Ages of ages" doxological passages (Gal 1:5; Phil 4:20; 2 Tim 4:18; Heb 13:21; 1 Pet 4:11; 5:11; Rev 1:6; 4:9, 4:10; 5:13; 7:12; 10:6; 15:7): All apply the formula to God, Christ, or divine attributes. The formula reflects the genuinely endless nature of the divine subject.

Destruction/context passages (Matt 10:28; 2 Pet 2:6; Rev 20:14; 21:8; 20:9; 19:20-21; Matt 25:30; 1 Cor 5:5; 1 Thess 5:3; 1 Tim 6:9; 1 Cor 15:53-54; 1 Tim 6:16; Matt 7:13; Phil 3:19; Mal 4:1, 4:3; Psa 37:10; Oba 1:16): These provide the broader context of destruction vocabulary for the wicked's fate, immortality as a gift not inherent, and cessation language incompatible with eternal conscious existence.

OT background passages (Isa 34:10; Gen 19:24, 19:28; Dan 12:2; Isa 66:24; Jer 17:27; Ezek 28:18-19; Exo 21:6; Deut 15:17): These demonstrate the olam semantic range that aionios inherits, including fire/smoke judgments that ended, human "forever" = "lifetime," and the nature-of-subject principle.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The evidence converges on a clear answer to the study question. Aionios does not inherently mean "eternal/endless." It means "pertaining to the age(s)," with actual duration determined by the nature of the subject it modifies.

The evidence for this conclusion comes from multiple independent lines:

  1. Etymology: Aionios derives from aion ("an age"), not from aei ("always"). The strictly-eternal word is aidios.
  2. Past-time uses: Three passages use aionios for past ages that have ended (Rom 16:25; 2 Tim 1:9; Tit 1:2). If aionios inherently means "endless," these passages are incoherent.
  3. Tit 1:2: Same adjective, same verse, two different temporal directions. Falsifies "same adjective = same duration."
  4. The aidios/aionios distinction: Jude uses aidios for genuinely unbreakable chains, then aionios for fire that produced ashes, in adjacent verses.
  5. The LXX bridge: Aionios translates olam, which demonstrably means different durations for different subjects across 432 OT occurrences.
  6. Philemon 1:15: Aionios in a human context means "permanently" -- not "for literal infinity."
  7. The Hebrews pattern: Aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act, not ongoing process.
  8. Distribution: ~60% of aionios occurrences modify "life." Only ~10% modify judgment subjects. The judgment uses consistently employ destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.
  9. The "ages of ages" distribution: ~19 doxological vs. 3 judgment, with the judgment uses applying only to non-human/symbolic entities in Revelation's apocalyptic framework.

When aionios modifies God, the Spirit, or the believer's life (subjects that are genuinely eternal or receive eternality), the word carries full eternal force. When aionios modifies fire, punishment, destruction, or human relationships (subjects with inherent limits), the word means "permanent within the scope of the subject's existence." The adjective describes permanence. The noun determines what kind of permanence.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Greek aionios (G166) -- all 71 NT occurrences. Compare aidios (G126). 'Eis tous aionas ton aionon' in ~20 passages. LXX usage. Does aionios inherently mean 'eternal/endless' or does it mean 'pertaining to the age' with duration determined by the nature of the subject?

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Adjective from G165 aion ('an age'). 71 tokens in 69 unique verses across 19 books. Strong's: 'from G165; perpetual (also used of past time, or past and future as well).' KJV: 'eternal' (46.4%), 'everlasting' (30.4%). Dominant collocation: zoe (life) ~43x. Semantic categories: (1) Eternal life as gift, (2) Judgment/punishment, (3) Divine attributes, (4) Heavenly realities, (5) Pre-temporal reference, (6) Eschatological kingdom. Hebrew source: H5769 olam (100 co-occurrences, PMI 26.16), dor (23x), chuqqah (20x), beriyth (20x).

Semantic categories: Eternal life as gift, Judgment/punishment, Divine attributes, Heavenly realities, Pre-temporal reference, Eschatological kingdom

Key verses: Jhn 3:16, Mat 25:46, Rom 6:23, 2Th 1:9, Tit 1:2, Rom 16:25, Heb 9:12, Jud 1:7

Relevance: PRIMARY TARGET. The central word of the study. All 71 occurrences must be categorized. Etymology from aion ('age') vs. aidios from aei ('always'). Past-time uses (Rom 16:25, 2Ti 1:9, Tit 1:2) disprove inherent 'endless' meaning. LXX translation of olam carries context-dependent semantics into the NT.

docs.title: G165 — aion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G165-aion.md

Occurrences: 120

Masculine noun. 95 unique verses (120 tokens) across 22 books. Root noun of aionios. Strong's: 'properly, an age; by extension, perpetuity.' KJV: 'ever' (52.6%), 'world' (30.5%), 'and ever' (22.1%). 7 semantic categories: duration, intensified perpetuity ('ages of ages'), present age, age to come, time-span/epochs, created order, end of the age. Hebrew source: H5769 owlam (287x, PMI 31.41).

Semantic categories: Duration/perpetuity, Ages of ages formula, This present age, Age to come, Time-span/epochs, Created order/universe, End of the age

Key verses: Mat 24:3, Mat 12:32, 2Co 4:4, Heb 1:2, Rev 14:11, Rev 20:10

Relevance: Root noun of aionios. The KJV translation 'world' 30x (meaning 'age/era') confirms the basic meaning as an age, not infinity. The 'eis tous aionas ton aionon' formula (~22 NT passages) derives from this word.

docs.title: G126 — aidios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G126-aidios.md

Occurrences: 2

Adjective from G104 aei ('always'). Only 2 NT occurrences: Rom 1:20 (God's eternal power) and Jude 1:6 (everlasting chains). Strong's: 'everduring -- eternal, everlasting.' Denotes inherent, absolute eternality without reference to ages. Distinct from aionios which derives from aion ('age').

Semantic categories: Divine attributes, Eschatological judgment

Key verses: Rom 1:20, Jud 1:6

Relevance: The comparison word. Greek has TWO words for eternity: aidios (from aei, 'always' -- inherent, absolute) and aionios (from aion, 'age' -- age-pertaining). Their coexistence as distinct words is significant. Jude uses BOTH in adjacent verses (aidios v.6, aionios v.7), choosing different words for different subjects.

docs.title: G104 — aei
docs.text:
Occurrences: 8

Adverb meaning 'always, ever, continually.' 8 NT occurrences. Root of aidios (G126). KJV: 'alway' (50%), 'always' (37.5%). Used for habitual/continual patterns: 'ye do always resist the Holy Ghost' (Act 7:51), 'alway delivered unto death' (2Co 4:11), 'the Cretians are alway liars' (Tit 1:12). Denotes habitual pattern rather than infinite duration. Establishes aidios's etymology as 'from always' -- inherent, absolute eternality.

Semantic categories: Habitual/continual pattern, Persistent spiritual reality

Key verses: Act 7:51, 2Co 4:11, Tit 1:12, Heb 3:10, 1Pe 3:15

Relevance: Root adverb of aidios (G126). The etymology chain: aei ('always') -> aidios ('everduring') contrasts with aion ('age') -> aionios ('age-pertaining'). Different roots yield different semantic ranges.

docs.title: H5769 — owlam
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5769-owlam.md

Occurrences: 432

Masculine noun. 406 unique verses in OT (432 tokens). From unused root related to H5956 alam (concealment). Core image: 'the vanishing point' -- time receding beyond sight. KJV: 'for ever' (48.8%), 'everlasting' (13.3%), 'perpetual' (5.4%), 'of old' (3.2%). 6 semantic categories: divine attributes, covenants, cultic ordinances, immemorial past, eschatological, permanent judgment. LXX: aion (287x, PMI 5.55), aionios (100x, PMI 5.67).

Semantic categories: Divine eternity, Covenants, Cultic ordinances, Immemorial past, Eschatological, Permanent judgment

Key verses: Psa 90:2, Gen 17:7, Dan 12:2, Isa 34:10, Exo 21:6

Relevance: Hebrew source of aionios in LXX (100x). The nature-of-subject principle: olam applied to God = genuinely eternal; olam applied to slave service = lifetime; olam applied to Jonah = 3 days; olam applied to fire/smoke judgments = until completed. Aionios inherits this same context-dependent semantics.

docs.title: G2851 — kolasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2851-kolasis.md

Occurrences: 2

Feminine noun. Only 2 NT occurrences: Mat 25:46 ('everlasting punishment') and 1Jn 4:18 ('fear hath torment'). Root kolazo (G2849) from kolos ('dwarf, cut short') -- corrective pruning/curtailing.
