Parables regularly use cultural settings without endorsing them (the unjust judge in Luke 18, the unjust steward in Luke 16:1-12).

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The evidence converges from multiple independent lines on the parabolic classification of Luke 16:19-31:

  1. Literary-structural evidence: Identical formula (anthropos tis plousios) at 12:16 with explicit parabole label, at 16:1 universally accepted as parabolic, and at 16:19. Five-narrative discourse structure with single parabole label at 15:3 and no discourse break. Mid-discourse Pharisee reaction connecting the stories.

  2. Vocabulary evidence: Luke 16 uses basanos/odunao (grief/sorrow vocabulary), not basanizo/basanismos (standard eschatological torment vocabulary). Multiple standard judgment vocabulary terms are absent (apollymi, apoleia, geenna, orge, aionios).

  3. Unique imagery evidence: "Abraham's bosom" as afterlife destination appears only here. Chasma is a hapax legomenon. These concepts are not corroborated elsewhere in Scripture.

  4. Same-author evidence: Luke records both Luke 16 and Acts 2:29,34 (David dead, not ascended). Coherence requires Luke 16 = parabolic, Acts 2 = didactic.

  5. Didactic death-state evidence: Nine+ didactic passages from 6+ authors describe the dead as unconscious. The clarity hierarchy (didactic > parabolic) means these govern the reading of parabolic imagery.

  6. OT mashal precedent: Isaiah 14 (explicitly labeled mashal) uses the identical motif — dead speaking in sheol — without teaching literal afterlife consciousness.

  7. Logical evidence: Paul's argument in 1 Cor 15:18 collapses if the righteous dead are conscious in Abraham's bosom. The resurrection as the Christian hope (1 Thess 4:16) is incompatible with immediate conscious afterlife.

  8. The passage's self-identified teaching point: Luke 16:29,31 — the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets. The afterlife setting is the narrative framework, not the lesson.

The single indicator for the literal reading — the naming of Lazarus — is addressed by the thematic nature of the name, the unnamed rich man, OT precedent for named allegorical characters, and Nave's silence on this Lazarus as a historical person. One indicator does not override the cumulative weight of eight converging lines of evidence.

Tree 3 (Genre Gate) application: Gate 1 FAILS (subject is a parabolic character, not a verified historical human). Gate 3 FAILS (genre is parabolic, not didactic). Classification: E-items from this passage are Neutral — they describe what a parable depicts, not what didactic teaching establishes.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Luke 16:19-31 -- parable or literal? Genre, first-century Jewish context. Apply Tree 3 genre gate. Literary structure (five parables in Luke 15-16).

docs.title: G86 — hades
docs.text:
Source: G86-háidēs.md

Occurrences: 11

Realm of the dead, unseen world. LXX equivalent of sheol (H7585, 58 co-occurrences, PMI 8.31). Temporary — delivered up and cast into lake of fire (Rev 20:13-14). The one depiction of consciousness in hades (Luke 16:23) is in a parable.

Semantic categories: grave/realm of dead, judgment association, defeated power

Key verses: Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, Luke 16:23, Revelation 20:13-14, Matthew 16:18, 1 Corinthians 15:55

Relevance: Central location term in Luke 16:23. LXX equivalence with sheol means didactic characterizations of sheol as unconscious (Ecc 9:5,10; Ps 6:5; 115:17) directly inform the meaning of hades.

docs.title: G931 — basanos
docs.text:
Source: G931-basanos.md

Occurrences: 3

Originally a touchstone for testing metals, then torture/torment. Only 3 NT occurrences: Matt 4:24 (physical disease), Luke 16:23 (parabolic torment), Luke 16:28 (place of torment). 2 of 3 occurrences are in Luke 16.

Semantic categories: physical suffering/disease, afterlife torment (parabolic), testing/examination (etymological)

Key verses: Matthew 4:24, Luke 16:23, Luke 16:28

Relevance: Key vocabulary in Luke 16:23,28. Luke uses basanos (3 total NT occurrences) rather than basanizo (12 occ., the standard eschatological torment verb used in Rev 14:10; 20:10). This vocabulary divergence is a genre indicator.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Source: G928-basanizo.md

Occurrences: 12

Standard NT verb for torment. 5 of 12 occurrences in Revelation (eschatological). ABSENT from Luke 16. Used in Matt 8:6,29; Mark 5:7; Luke 8:28; 2 Pet 2:8; Rev 9:5; 11:10; 12:2; 14:10; 20:10.

Semantic categories: physical suffering, demonic encounters, moral distress, eschatological torment

Key verses: Revelation 14:10, Revelation 20:10, Matthew 8:29, 2 Peter 2:8

Relevance: The standard eschatological torment verb is ABSENT from Luke 16. This absence is significant: if Luke 16 were didactic eschatological teaching, we would expect basanizo, not basanos.

docs.title: G929 — basanismos
docs.text:
Source: G929-basanismos.md

Occurrences: 6

Torment (noun). All 6 occurrences exclusively in Revelation (9:5; 14:11; 18:7,10,15). ABSENT from Luke 16.

Semantic categories: demonic torment, eschatological judgment, imperial judgment

Key verses: Revelation 14:11, Revelation 9:5, Revelation 18:7

Relevance: The standard eschatological torment noun is ABSENT from Luke 16. Combined with the absence of basanizo, this confirms Luke 16 uses a different vocabulary register from standard eschatological judgment passages.

docs.title: G930 — basanistes
docs.text:
Source: G930-basanistēs.md

Occurrences: 1

Torturer/tormentor. Single occurrence in Matt 18:34 (parable of unforgiving servant). Agent noun from basanizo.

Semantic categories: punitive authority

Key verses: Matthew 18:34

Relevance: Background: the basanos word family includes this agent noun used in another parable (Matt 18:34).

docs.title: G3600 — odunao
docs.text:
Source: G3600-odynao.md

Occurrences: 4

To grieve, be in anguish. Used exclusively by Luke (3x Luke, 1x Acts). Luke 16:24,25 ('I am tormented/you are tormented'); Luke 2:48 (Mary's parental anxiety); Acts 20:38 (Ephesian elders' grief at Paul's departure). Grief/sorrow vocabulary, NOT punishment vocabulary.

Semantic categories: judgment anguish (parabolic), parental grief, separation grief

Key verses: Luke 16:24, Luke 16:25, Luke 2:48, Acts 20:38

Relevance: Critical vocabulary evidence. Luke uses odunao for the rich man's experience — the same word he uses for Mary's parental worry and the Ephesian elders' grief. This is grief/sorrow vocabulary, not eschatological punishment vocabulary.

docs.title: G3601 — odune
docs.text:
Source: G3601-odyne.md

Occurrences: 2

Grief, sorrow (noun form of odunao G3600). Used in Rom 9:2 and 1 Tim 6:10 for grief/sorrow contexts.

Semantic categories: grief, sorrow

Key verses: Romans 9:2, 1 Timothy 6:10

Relevance: Noun form of the verb Luke uses in Luke 16:24,25. The word family is consistently grief/sorrow, not judicial punishment.

docs.title: G2859 — kolpos
docs.text:
Source: G2859-kólpos.md

Occurrences: 6

Bosom, bay. 6 occurrences: Luke 6:38 (bosom/lap), Luke 16:22 (Abraham's bosom), Luke 16:23 (his bosom), John 1:18 (bosom of the Father), John 13:23 (leaning on Jesus' bosom), Acts 27:39 (bay/inlet). 'Abraham's bosom' as a destination for the righteous dead appears ONLY in Luke 16.

Semantic categories: intimate relational closeness, Abraham's bosom (unique), physical receptacle, geographical feature

Key verses: Luke 16:22, Luke 16:23, John 1:18, John 13:23

Relevance: The uniqueness of 'Abraham's bosom' as a scriptural concept is a significant genre indicator. If this were literal doctrine about where the righteous dead go, we would expect it to appear in other afterlife teaching passages. Its singular occurrence in a passage with multiple parabolic indicators suggests culturally familiar imagery.

docs.title: G5490 — chasma
docs.text:
Source: G5490-chásma.md

Occurrences: 1

Chasm, gulf, vacancy. Hapax legomenon — appears only once in the entire NT (Luke 16:26). From obsolete chaō (to gape/yawn).

Semantic categories: impassable spatial separation, geographical void

Key verses: Luke 16:26

Relevance: A hapax legomenon in the NT. The word appears nowhere else in Scripture. This unique vocabulary further marks Luke 16 as containing imagery found nowhere else in biblical afterlife teaching.

docs.title: G5395 — phlox
docs.text:
Source: G5395-phlóx.md

Occurrences: 7

Flame, blaze. 7 occurrences. Used primarily for divine theophany: Christ's eyes (Rev 1:14; 2:18; 19:12), burning bush (Acts 7:30), angels (Heb 1:7). Luke 16:24 ('this flame') and 2 Thess 1:8 ('flaming fire') are the non-theophanic uses.

Semantic categories: divine theophany, parabolic detail, eschatological judgment (2 Thess)

Key verses: Revelation 1:14, Acts 7:30, Luke 16:24, 2 Thessalonians 1:8

Relevance: In Luke 16:24, the 'flame' (phlox) is singular and specific to the parabolic narrative. The majority of phlox uses are theophanic, not eschatological judgment.

docs.title: G4145 — plousios
docs.text:
Source: G4145-ploúsios.md

Occurrences: 28

Rich, wealthy. 28 occurrences. Luke uses it 11 times (39% of all NT uses) — highest concentration of any book. Key to the 'certain rich man' formula (anthropos tis plousios) at Luke 12:16, 16:1, 16:19.

Semantic categories: material wealth (literal), spiritual wealth (figurative), Lukan wealth-reversal theme

Key verses: Luke 12:16, Luke 16:1, Luke 16:19, Luke 6:24, Luke 18:23

Relevance: The adjective that completes the parabolic formula. Luke's distinctive emphasis on wealth-reversal theology makes plousios a Lukan signature term.

docs.title: G4434 — ptochos
docs.text:
Source: G4434-ptōchós.md

Occurrences: 34

Poor, destitute, begging. Used in Luke 6:20 (Blessed are ye poor), Luke 16:20,22 (Lazarus the beggar).

Semantic categories: material poverty, spiritual receptivity

Key verses: Luke 6:20, Luke 16:20, Luke 16:22

Relevance: Lazarus's condition connects to Luke's Beatitude ('Blessed are ye poor,' 6:20) — the same wealth-reversal theology.

docs.title: G3870 — parakaleo
docs.text:
Source: G3870-parakaleo.md

Occurrences: 113

To comfort, encourage, exhort. In Luke 16:25, 'parakaleitai' (V-PPI-3S, 'he is comforted') describes Lazarus's state — contrasted with the rich man's odunao (grief).

Semantic categories: comfort, encouragement, exhortation

Key verses: Luke 16:25, 2 Corinthians 1:4, Matthew 5:4

Relevance: The comfort/grief contrast (parakaleo vs. odunao) in Luke 16:25 echoes the Beatitude reversal: 'Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted' (Matt 5:4, parakaleo).

docs.title: G2976 — Lazaros
docs.text:
Source: G2976-lazaros.md

Occurrences: 15

Lazarus (from Hebrew Eleazar, 'God helps'). 15 occurrences: 4 in Luke (all in 16:19-31 parable), 11 in John (brother of Mary and Martha). Nave's lists ONLY the John 11 Lazarus as historical — no separate entry for a historical beggar named Lazarus.

Semantic categories: named character in parable (Luke 16), historical person raised from dead (John 11-12)

Key verses: Luke 16:20, Luke 16:23-25, John 11:1, John 11:43, John 12:10

Relevance: The naming of Lazarus is the steelman argument for the literal reading. However: the name is thematic ('God helps'), the rich man is NOT named, Nave's does not list this Lazarus as historical, and OT parables also name characters symbolically (Ezek 23:4).

docs.title: G450 — anistemi
docs.text:
Source: G450-anistemi.md

Occurrences: 123

To rise, raise up. In Luke 16:31, anaste (V-2AAS-3S Aorist Active Subjunctive) — 'should rise from the dead.' Standard resurrection vocabulary.

Semantic categories: physical rising, resurrection, establishment

Key verses: Luke 16:31, Acts 2:24, 1 Thessalonians 4:16

Relevance: The climactic verse (16:31) uses resurrection vocabulary (anistemi), not intermediate-state vocabulary. The passage points toward resurrection, not Abraham's bosom, as the eschatological hope.

docs.title: G3850 — parabole
docs.text:
Source: G3850-parabole.md

Occurrences: 50

Parable, similitude, comparison. 50 tokens across 48 verses. Confined to Synoptic Gospels (46) and Hebrews (2). Luke uses it 18 times. LXX regularly translates mashal (H4912) as parabole.

Semantic categories: narrative comparison, short saying, object lesson, veiled speech, typological figure

Key verses: Luke 15:3, Matthew 13:3, Mark 4:2, Hebrews 9:9

Relevance: Luke 15:3 uses this word (singular, with demonstrative 'this') to introduce the discourse unit containing the Rich Man and Lazarus. The LXX bridge to mashal (H4912) connects the NT concept directly to the OT mashal genre exemplified in Isaiah 14:4.

docs.title: G1147 — daktylos
docs.text:
Source: G1147-daktylos.md

Occurrences: 8

Finger. 8 NT occurrences. In Luke 16:24, the rich man asks that Lazarus dip 'the tip of his finger' in water — a physical body part attributed to a supposedly disembodied soul.

Semantic categories: divine action, physical touch, proof by contact, burden-bearing

Key verses: Luke 16:24, Luke 11:20, John 20:25-27

Relevance: A physical body part in a scene depicting disembodied post-mortem existence. This is a physical impossibility in the literal reading — a genre indicator.

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

To destroy fully, to perish. 102 tokens. The standard NT destruction verb for divine judgment (Matt 10:28). ABSENT from Luke 16.

Semantic categories: physical destruction, divine judgment, perishing, losing life, lost possession, decay

Key verses: Matthew 10:28, John 3:16, Luke 13:3, 2 Peter 3:9

Relevance: The standard destruction vocabulary (apollymi/apoleia) is ABSENT from Luke 16. If Luke 16 were a didactic judgment passage, we would expect this vocabulary.

docs.title: G5590 — psyche
docs.text:
Source: G5590-psyche.md

Occurrences: 105

Soul, life, self. 105 occurrences. LXX equivalent of nephesh (H5315). Can die (Matt 10:28), be destroyed — not inherently immortal.

Semantic categories: inner self, physical life, person/individual, living creature, mind/will

Key verses: Matthew 10:28, Matthew 22:37, Luke 1:46, Revelation 16:3

Relevance: Background for the anthropological question: if psyche/nephesh can die and be destroyed, there is no inherent immortal component to sustain conscious existence between death and resurrection.

docs.title: G4151 — pneuma
docs.text:
Source: G4151-pneuma.md

Occurrences: 385

Spirit, breath, wind. 385 occurrences. In death contexts, pneuma is the life-force that departs (Matt 27:50; Luke 23:46; James 2:26).

Semantic categories: Holy Spirit, evil spirits, human spirit, life-force, disembodied spirits, wind

Key verses: Luke 23:46, James 2:26, John 3:8, Revelation 11:11

Relevance: Background for the spirit-at-death question. The life-force (pneuma) returns to God at death (Ecc 12:7/Luke 23:46) but is not depicted as a conscious entity that carries on activity.

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

Death. 119 tokens. Encompasses physical death, death as sin's consequence, death as cosmic power, Christ's atoning death, spiritual death, and the second death (Rev 20:14).

Semantic categories: physical death, sin consequence, cosmic power, atoning event, spiritual death, second death

Key verses: Romans 5:12, Romans 6:23, 1 Corinthians 15:26, Revelation 20:14

Relevance: The definition of death as cessation/reversal of creation is the foundation. If death = cessation, Luke 16's conscious post-mortem activity is parabolic imagery, not didactic teaching.

docs.title: G110 — athanasia
docs.text:
Source: G110-athanasia.md

Occurrences: 3

Immortality, deathlessness. Only 3 NT occurrences: 1 Cor 15:53, 15:54 (put on at resurrection), 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has it). Something received at resurrection, not possessed inherently.

Semantic categories: resurrection transformation, exclusive divine attribute

Key verses: 1 Corinthians 15:53-54, 1 Timothy 6:16

Relevance: If immortality is received at resurrection (not possessed at death), there is no mechanism for conscious intermediate existence. This undermines the literal reading of Luke 16.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Eternal, age-pertaining. 71 tokens. Duration determined by subject context. Three passages use aionios for past time that has ended (Rom 16:25; 2 Tim 1:9; Tit 1:2). ABSENT from Luke 16.

Semantic categories: eternal life, eternal judgment, divine attributes, heavenly realities, pre-temporal reference

Key verses: John 3:16, Matthew 25:46, Romans 6:23, 2 Thessalonians 1:9

Relevance: Luke 16 does NOT use aionios. The passage makes no claim about the eternal duration of the rich man's experience. This is another vocabulary absence distinguishing Luke 16 from didactic eschatological passages.

docs.title: G684 — apoleia
docs.text:
Source: G684-apoleia.md

Occurrences: 20

Destruction, perdition. 20 tokens. Used for final eschatological ruin, son of perdition, and waste. ABSENT from Luke 16.

Semantic categories: eschatological ruin, son of perdition, beast's end, waste, perishing

Key verses: Matthew 7:13, John 17:12, 2 Thessalonians 2:3, Revelation 17:8

Relevance: Standard eschatological destruction vocabulary is ABSENT from Luke 16. Another vocabulary absence distinguishing the passage from didactic judgment teaching.

docs.title: G1067 — geenna
docs.text:
Source: G1067-geenna.md

Occurrences: 12

Gehenna, Valley of Hinnom. 12 occurrences. 11 are Jesus' direct speech. Consistently associated with fire and destruction (apollymi). ABSENT from Luke 16.

Semantic categories: fiery destruction, self-denial warnings, destruction of soul and body, judicial judgment, moral corruption

Key verses: Matthew 10:28, Matthew 5:22, Mark 9:43, Luke 12:5

Relevance: Jesus' standard judgment-place term is geenna, NOT hades. Luke 16 uses hades, which Revelation shows is temporary and emptied at the final judgment.

docs.title: G3709 — orge
docs.text:
Source: G3709-orge.md

Occurrences: 36

Wrath, anger. 36 occurrences. Divine judicial wrath and eschatological wrath. ABSENT from Luke 16.

Semantic categories: eschatological wrath, judicial wrath, wrath and law, deliverance from wrath, human anger

Key verses: Romans 1:18, Revelation 6:16-17, 1 Thessalonians 1:10, Romans 5:9

Relevance: Standard judgment vocabulary (orge) is ABSENT from Luke 16. The passage does not use wrath terminology.

docs.title: G3992 — pempo
docs.text:
Source: G3992-pémpō.md

Occurrences: 82

To send, dispatch. 82 occurrences. Used in Luke 16:24,27 for the rich man's requests to 'send' Lazarus.

Semantic categories: authorized dispatch, divine mission, representative agency, urgent deployment

Key verses: Luke 16:24, Luke 16:27, John 4:34, John 20:21

Relevance: The rich man's requests to 'send' Lazarus serve the narrative's teaching point — building toward the climactic statement about the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets.

docs.title: G2198 — zao
docs.text:
Source: G2198-záō.md

Occurrences: 147

To live. 147 occurrences. Physical, spiritual, resurrection, and divine life.

Semantic categories: physical life, spiritual life, resurrection life, the living God, ethical conduct, judgment formula

Key verses: John 11:25, Romans 1:17, Revelation 1:18, Luke 20:38

Relevance: Background for understanding 'all live unto him' (Luke 20:38) as eschatological/resurrection life, not intermediate-state consciousness.

docs.title: G2222 — zoe
docs.text:
Source: G2222-zoe.md

Occurrences: 134

Life. 134 tokens. Dominant usage: eternal/eschatological life as God's gift through Christ. In Luke 16:25, 'en te zoe sou' = 'in thy lifetime' (earthly biographical life).

Semantic categories: eternal life, present possession in Christ, life vs. death, symbolic objects of life, earthly life, divine attribute

Key verses: John 3:16, John 5:24, Luke 16:25, Romans 6:23

Relevance: In Luke 16:25, zoe refers to earthly lifetime, not eternal life — consistent with the passage's reversal motif about earthly wealth and poverty.

docs.title: G599 — apothnesko
docs.text:
Source: G599-apothnēskō.md

Occurrences: 122

To die. 122 occurrences. Used in Luke 16:22 ('the beggar died... the rich man also died').

Semantic categories: physical death, Christ's death, dying to sin, death as sin's consequence, death overcome

Key verses: Luke 16:22, Romans 5:6, 1 Corinthians 15:3, John 11:25

Relevance: Both the beggar and the rich man 'died' (apethanen) in Luke 16:22 — standard death vocabulary, not specialized eschatological language.

docs.title: G861 — aphtharsia
docs.text:
Source: G861-aphtharsia.md

Occurrences: 8

Incorruptibility, immortality. 8 occurrences, exclusively Pauline. 4 in 1 Cor 15 (resurrection chapter). Something 'put on' at resurrection, not possessed before.

Semantic categories: resurrection transformation, aspiration/revealed hope, ethical purity

Key verses: 1 Corinthians 15:42, 1 Corinthians 15:53-54, Romans 2:7, 2 Timothy 1:10

Relevance: Paired with athanasia in 1 Cor 15:53-54: incorruption and immortality are both received at resurrection. Reinforces conditional immortality.

docs.title: G3306 — meno
docs.text:
Source: G3306-meno.md

Occurrences: 128

To remain, abide, stay. 128 tokens. Johannine signature term (54 of 105 verses).

Semantic categories: physical staying, mutual indwelling, remaining in teaching, enduring permanently, vine/branch metaphor, abiding of abstract realities

Key verses: John 15:4, 1 John 2:27, 1 Corinthians 13:13

Relevance: Background vocabulary. Not directly used in Luke 16 but relevant to the permanence concepts in the passage.

docs.title: G3551 — nomos
docs.text:
Source: G3551-nomos.md

Occurrences: 197

Law. 197 occurrences. Primary: Mosaic Law/Torah. Luke 16:29 refers to 'Moses and the prophets' — the authoritative Scripture the rich man's brothers should heed.

Semantic categories: Mosaic Law, OT Scriptures broadly, principle/rule, law of Christ, natural law, ceremonial law

Key verses: Matthew 5:17, Luke 16:29, Galatians 3:24, Romans 7:12

Relevance: The climactic teaching point of Luke 16 is the sufficiency of 'Moses and the prophets' — Scripture is authoritative for faith and practice.

docs.title: H3045 — yada
docs.text:
Source: H3045-yada.md

Occurrences: 1099

To know. 1099 tokens, 873 verses. Broadest OT knowledge verb. Ecclesiastes 9:5 uses yada in the didactic death-state statement: 'the dead know (yada) not anything.'

Semantic categories: cognitive knowing, experiential/relational knowing, covenantal recognition, sexual knowing, causative revelation, skill/expertise, perception/discernment

Key verses: Ecclesiastes 9:5, Genesis 3:5, Job 19:25, Amos 3:2

Relevance: The verb in Ecc 9:5's 'the dead know not anything.' Qal participle yod'im = 'knowing ones' — the dead are NOT knowing ones. Didactic genre, direct statement.

docs.title: H4191 — muwth
docs.text:
Source: H4191-muwth.md

Occurrences: 1028

To die. 1028 occurrences. The most common death verb in the OT. Covers natural death, capital punishment, divine decree, violent death, spiritual death, and ritual impurity from contact with the dead.

Semantic categories: natural death, judicial death penalty, divine death decree, violent killing, spiritual death, ritual impurity

Key verses: Genesis 2:17, Ezekiel 18:4, Ecclesiastes 9:5

Relevance: Background death vocabulary. Ecc 9:5 uses the Qal participle of muwth ('the dying ones' / 'the dead') as those who 'know not anything.'

docs.title: H5315 — nephesh
docs.text:
Source: H5315-nephesh.md

Occurrences: 788

Soul, living being, person, life. 788 tokens. Applied to animals and humans alike (Gen 1:20,24; 2:7 — same phrase 'nephesh chayyah'). Can die (Ezek 18:4; Num 6:6 'dead soul'). Not inherently immortal.

Semantic categories: breathing creature, whole person, life at risk, inner self/desire, wholehearted devotion, reflexive pronoun, corpse

Key verses: Genesis 2:7, Ezekiel 18:4, Numbers 6:6, Psalm 146:4

Relevance: Biblical anthropology: man BECAME a nephesh chayyah (Gen 2:7), he did not RECEIVE a separate nephesh. Nephesh can die. This undermines the prerequisite for conscious intermediate existence.

docs.title: H7585 — sheol
docs.text:
Source: H7585-showl.md

Occurrences: 68

Underworld, grave, realm of the dead. 68 tokens. LXX translates sheol as hades 58 times (PMI 8.31). Characterized by unconsciousness in didactic passages (Ecc 9:10; Ps 6:5; 115:17). Receives all dead, righteous and wicked.

Semantic categories: universal destination, descent language, death paired term, fate of wicked, rescue from sheol, insatiable

Key verses: Ecclesiastes 9:10, Psalm 6:5, Psalm 115:17, Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 14:9-15, Hosea 13:14

Relevance: The OT counterpart of hades (G86). Didactic passages characterize sheol as unconscious (Ecc 9:10; Ps 6:5; 115:17). The one parabolic depiction of consciousness in hades/sheol (Luke 16:23 / Isa 14:9-10) occurs in mashal/parabolic genre.

docs.title: H7496 — rapha
docs.text:
Source: H7496-râphâʼ.md

Occurrences: 8

Shades, dead ones in sheol. 8 occurrences. The rephaim are consistently portrayed as weak, powerless shadows — not active, conscious beings. Isaiah 14:9 'stirs up' the rephaim figuratively; Isaiah 26:14,19 discusses their non-rising/rising.

Semantic categories: dead in sheol, death as destination, resurrection contrast

Key verses: Isaiah 14:9, Job 26:5, Psalm 88:10, Proverbs 9:18, Isaiah 26:14, Isaiah 26:19

Relevance: The rephaim of Isaiah 14:9 — 'stirred up' to greet the king of Babylon in the mashal — are the same type of figurative dead-speaking that appears in Luke 16. Both are in mashal/parabolic genre.

docs.title: Classification Audit Trail — etc7-09-rich-man-lazarus
docs.text: This document contains the per-item Tree 3/4/5 walkthroughs for every E-item classified Cond. or ECT and every N-item. Each walkthrough uses tool-verified parsing for Gate 2.

docs.title: E-Item Classifications (Cond. or ECT)
docs.text:
E16 (Acts 2:34) — "David is not ascended into the heavens" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "not ascended into the heavens" applied to David. The righteous dead have not gone to heaven. This denies post-mortem conscious heavenly existence for the righteous dead. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): David — a literal historical human being, named individual. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: ou G3756 [PRT-N] + gar G1063 [CONJ] + Daueid G1138 [N-PRI] Nom Sg M + anebe G305 [V-2AAI-3S] Aor Act Ind ("ascended") + eis tous ouranous G3772 [N-APM] Acc Pl M ("the heavens"). Emphatic negative particle ou + gar. Grammar is unambiguous: David [subject] + has not ascended [verb] + into the heavens [destination]. No alternative parsing available. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Peter's Pentecost sermon, recorded as didactic prose/direct speech in Acts. Narrative report of apostolic teaching. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E15 (David is dead and buried, Acts 2:29), E19 (dead know not anything, Ecc 9:5), E21 (thoughts perish, Ps 146:4), and the full didactic death-state corpus. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. David, a righteous man, is dead and has not ascended to heaven. This denies conscious heavenly intermediate existence for the righteous dead.

E19 (Ecc 9:5) — "The dead know not any thing" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "know not any thing" applied to the dead. Cessation of consciousness/knowledge at death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The dead" (hammetim, Qal participle of muth H4191 with article) — literal dead humans, universal category. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: vehammetim = muth Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs with Art ("the dead") + einam = ain Noun.ms.Abs+3mp ("are not") + yod'im = yada H3045 Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs ("knowing") + meumah = Noun.fs.Abs ("anything"). Grammar is unambiguous: the dead [subject] + are not knowing [negated participle] + anything [universal object]. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Ecclesiastes 9 — wisdom literature, didactic teaching about the human condition. Direct statement about the nature of death. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E20 (no knowledge in sheol, Ecc 9:10), E21 (thoughts perish, Ps 146:4), E22 (no remembrance in death, Ps 6:5), E23 (dead go into silence, Ps 115:17), E24 (dead know not about children, Job 14:21), E25 (grave cannot praise, Isa 38:18-19). Multi-author consensus. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. The dead lack consciousness and knowledge.

E20 (Ecc 9:10) — "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "no knowledge, nor wisdom in sheol" — cessation of cognitive function at death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The person addressed ("thou") going to sheol — universal human experience. Literal humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: ein = ain Noun.ms.Cst ("there is not") + ma'aseh = Noun.ms.Abs ("deed") + cheshbon = Noun.ms.Abs ("account/device") + da'ath = Noun.fs.Abs ("knowledge") + chokmah = Noun.fs.Abs ("wisdom") + bishe'ol = Prep + sheol Noun.s.Abs ("in sheol"). Four nouns negated by one ain — no work, no device, no knowledge, no wisdom. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Ecclesiastes 9 — didactic wisdom literature. Direct teaching. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E19, E21-E25 and the full death-state corpus. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E21 (Ps 146:4) — "In that very day his thoughts perish" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "thoughts perish" (abad H6 = "perish") — cessation vocabulary applied to cognitive function at death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): A human being ("his" = the person whose breath departs). Literal human. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: bayom = Prep + Art + yom Noun.ms.Abs ("in the day") + hahu = Art + hu' PersPron.3ms ("that very") + abdu = abad Verb.Qal.Perf.3p ("they perish") + eshtonotav = eshtonot Noun.fp.Abs+3ms ("his thoughts"). Qal perfect 3rd plural of abad ("perish") with eshtonotav ("his thoughts") as subject. Grammar unambiguous: on the day of death, the person's thoughts perish. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm 146 — hymnic/didactic poetry. Direct statement about human mortality in the context of trusting God rather than princes. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E19 (dead know nothing), E20 (no knowledge in sheol), E22-E25. Multi-author consensus. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E22 (Ps 6:5) — "In death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "no remembrance" in death — cessation of cognitive function/awareness of God at death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead — those "in death" and "in the grave." Universal human category. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms negation of remembrance and thanksgiving in death/sheol. Grammar unambiguous: in death [location] + there is no remembrance [negated noun] + of thee [object]; in sheol [location] + who gives thee thanks? [rhetorical question expecting "no one"]. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm 6 — a petition psalm. David's direct statement about death as a state where God is not remembered. Didactic content within poetic genre. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E19-E21, E23-E25. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E23 (Ps 115:17) — "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "dead praise not" + "go down into silence (dumah)" — cessation of activity at death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The dead" (hammetim, Qal participle of muth with article) — universal human category. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: lo = Neg ("not") + hammetim = muth Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs with Art ("the dead") + yehalelu = halal Verb.Piel.Impf.3mp ("praise") + Yah = PropN ("the LORD"). Grammar unambiguous: the dead [subject] + do not praise [negated verb] + the LORD [object]. Second clause: yoredei dumah = "those descending into silence." PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm 115 — hymnic/didactic poetry. Direct statement about the dead's inability to praise God. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E19-E22, E24-E25. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E24 (Job 14:21) — "His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — the dead person "knoweth it not" and "perceiveth it not" — cessation of awareness at death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead man — a literal human being who has died (context: Job 14:10-12 describes man dying). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: yikbedu = kabad Verb.Qal.Impf.3mp ("they are honored") + banav = ben Noun.mp.Abs+3ms ("his sons") + velo = Conj + Neg ("and not") + yeda = yada Verb.Qal.Impf.3ms ("he knows") + veyits'aru = tsa'ar Verb.Qal.Impf.3mp ("they are brought low") + velo yavin = Neg + bin Verb.Qal.Impf.3ms ("he does not perceive") + lamo = Prep+3mp ("of them"). Grammar unambiguous: his sons [subject] + are honored/brought low [verb], but he [the dead man] + does not know/perceive [negated verbs]. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Job 14 — wisdom literature, didactic teaching about human mortality. Direct statement. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E19-E23, E25. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E25 (Isa 38:18-19) — "The grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee... The living, the living, he shall praise thee" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — the grave/death "cannot praise" — cessation of capacity at death, contrasted with the living. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The grave" (sheol) and "death" (maveth) as personified states, but the implicit subjects are the humans in those states. The living/dead contrast makes clear the teaching is about dead humans vs. living humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: lo = Neg ("not") + she'ol = Noun.s.Abs ("nether world/sheol") + todeka = yadah Verb.Hiphil.Impf.3fs+2ms ("praises you") + maveth = muth Noun.ms.Abs ("death") + yehallelka = halal Verb.Piel.Impf.3ms+2ms ("celebrates you"). Grammar unambiguous: sheol [subject] + does not praise you [negated verb]; death [subject] + does not celebrate you [negated verb]. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Hezekiah's prayer, recorded in Isaiah 38. Personal testimony within prophetic narrative. Didactic content — direct speech about the nature of death. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E19-E24. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E33 (Matt 10:28) — "Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "destroy" (apolesai, apollymi G622) applied to "soul and body" — destruction vocabulary applied to the whole person. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "Soul and body" (psychen kai soma) — literal human components. Direct reference to human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: ton dunamenon = dynamai G1410 [V-PNP-ASM] Pres M/P Ptcp Acc Sg M ("the one being able") + kai psychen kai soma = G5590 [N-ASF] + G4983 [N-ASN] ("both soul and body") + apolesai = apollymi G622 [V-AAN] Aor Act Inf ("to destroy"). Apollymi in aorist active infinitive — "to destroy." Subject and object are clear: God [the one being able] + to destroy [verb] + both soul and body [objects] + in Gehenna [location]. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Jesus' direct teaching to his disciples in the Matthean mission discourse. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E19-E25 (death-state unconsciousness) and the destruction vocabulary pattern (apollymi). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. God is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna — destruction, not preservation in torment.

docs.title: N-Item Classifications
docs.text:
N1 — "The absence of a parabole label at Luke 16:19 is uninformative about genre, given Luke's labeling pattern" — Based on: E1, E2, E3, E4 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that the absence of the parabole label at 16:19 is uninformative about genre, given that Luke 16:1 also lacks the label and is universally accepted as parabolic? Yes — both sides acknowledge Luke does not label every parable. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? Yes — the data shows Luke labels some parables but not others (12:16 has label, 16:1 does not, 16:19 does not). The absence of a label cannot establish either reading. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the cited E-items? No — it is the logical entailment of the observed pattern. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates:
  • V1/V2: Neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary. Neither applies.
  • Result: Neutral stands. This is an observation about Luke's labeling convention.

N2 — "The passage's self-identified teaching point is about hearing Moses and the prophets, not afterlife geography" — Based on: E12, E13 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that vv.29,31 are the passage's climactic teaching point? Yes — the narrative builds to this exchange. Both sides can identify vv.29,31 as the climactic statements. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? Some might argue the afterlife setting is also a teaching point. However, the text itself identifies "Moses and the prophets; let them hear them" as the directive. The climactic position (final statement in the narrative) is not disputed. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the cited E-items? No — it restates what E12 and E13 contain: the passage's final statements are about Scripture's sufficiency. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates:
  • V1/V2: Neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary in the teaching point itself. Neither applies.
  • Result: Neutral stands. The teaching point is about the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets.

N3 — "'Abraham's bosom' as a post-mortem location is unique to Luke 16:22-23 and lacks corroboration elsewhere in Scripture" — Based on: E7 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that "Abraham's bosom" as a post-mortem destination appears only in Luke 16:22-23? Yes — this is a verifiable distributional fact. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? Yes — kolpos Abraam as an afterlife location appears nowhere else in the NT or OT. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the cited E-item? No — it restates the distributional data. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates:
  • V1/V2: Neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary. Neither applies.
  • Result: Neutral stands. This is a distributional observation.

N4 — "Luke 16 uses different torment vocabulary (basanos/odunao) from the eschatological torment passages (basanizo/basanismos)" — Based on: E8, E9, E34 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that Luke 16 uses basanos G931 and odunao G3600 rather than basanizo G928 and basanismos G929? Yes — this is verifiable from the Greek text. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? Yes — the lexemes are different. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the cited E-items? No — it combines the distributional data from E8, E9, and E34. PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates:
  • V1/V2: Neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary in the observation itself. This is a vocabulary comparison. Neither applies.
  • Result: Neutral stands. This is a lexical observation that both sides can verify.

N5 — "Since David is dead and NOT ascended (Acts 2:29,34), Luke 16's depiction of the righteous dead in Abraham's bosom cannot be Luke's didactic teaching about the death-state" — Based on: E15, E16 — Classified: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar necessarily agree that David is dead and not ascended, and that therefore Luke 16 cannot be Luke's didactic teaching? An ECT scholar would agree David has not ascended into the heavens (the text says so). However, some ECT scholars would argue that Abraham's bosom is not "the heavens" — it is a different compartment. They would deny the implication that this proves Luke 16 is non-didactic. The implication adds a step beyond the E-items: equating "not ascended to heavens" with "not in Abraham's bosom." FAIL.
  • N-Test 2: Not reached (Test 1 failed).
  • N-Test 3: Not reached (Test 1 failed).
  • Gate 0 FAILS. Reclassify to I-tier.
  • Reclassification: N5 fails Gate 0. The implication adds an interpretive step (equating "not ascended to heavens" with "not in Abraham's bosom"). Reclassified as I-A (text-derived, aligns with E/N). Source test: all components from E-items (Acts 2:29,34). Direction test: aligns with death-state E-items. Requires criterion #5 (systematizing). Position: Cond.

N6 — "Since hades is temporary and emptied at the final judgment (Rev 20:13-14), Luke 16's setting in hades is not the final eschatological state" — Based on: E10, E26 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that hades is temporary and emptied? Yes — ECT scholars acknowledge that Luke 16:19-31 describes hades (intermediate state), not the final hell/lake of fire (see E422 in master evidence). Both sides agree hades is temporary. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? Yes — Revelation 20:13-14 states that death and hades deliver up their dead, then are cast into the lake of fire. The text itself establishes hades as temporary. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the cited E-items? No — it combines E10 (rich man is in hades) with E26 (hades is emptied and destroyed). PASS.
  • Tree 3 Gates:
  • V1/V2: Neither destruction nor conscious-torment vocabulary in the observation itself. It is a statement about the temporal nature of hades. Neither applies.
  • Result: Neutral stands. Both sides agree hades is temporary and is not the final eschatological state.

docs.title: I-Item Classifications
docs.text:
I1 — "Luke 16:19-31 is a parable, not a literal account" — Type: I-B — Classified: Neutral

  • Source test: All components from E/N tables — E1-E14, E17-E18, E30-E32, N1-N4, N6. Text-derived.
  • Direction test: Some E/N items support (E1-E4 formula, E7 unique imagery, E8-E9 vocabulary, E17-E18 mashal precedent, N1-N4); the naming of Lazarus (E6) is neutral but is cited by the opposing reading. Both sides have textual observations. Conflicts: I-B.
  • FOR (parabolic): E1 (parabole label at 15:3), E2-E4 (identical formula), E5 (rich man unnamed), E7 (Abraham's bosom unique), E8-E9 (vocabulary divergence), E11 (chasma hapax), E12-E13 (teaching point is Scripture sufficiency), E14 (Pharisees as money-lovers), E17-E18 (mashal precedent), E30 (physical impossibilities), E31-E32 (figurative precedents), N1-N4, N6.
  • AGAINST (literal): E6 (Lazarus named — unique among parables).
  • Result: Type I-B confirmed. Position: Neutral (genre determination, not inherently favoring either eschatological position). [SIS resolution in CONCLUSION.md]

I2 — "The naming of Lazarus proves the passage is a literal historical account" — Type: I-C — Classified: ECT-direction

  • Source test: The claim that naming = historicity requires an external principle (the assumption that named characters in Jesus' teaching must be historical). This principle is not stated in Scripture. External.
  • Direction test: Compatible with E/N items (E6 confirms the naming) but does not override any E/N item. I-C.
  • Result: Type I-C confirmed. Position: ECT-direction (supports the literal reading, which is the prerequisite for extracting afterlife doctrine from the passage).

I3 — "The physical details (tongue, water, flame, gulf) describe literal post-mortem conditions" — Type: I-C — Classified: ECT-direction

  • Source test: The claim that parabolic details are literal requires an external framework (literal reading of figurative genre). External.
  • Direction test: Does not override any E/N item directly — E30 observes the physical details but does not classify them as literal. I-C.
  • Result: Type I-C confirmed. Position: ECT-direction.

I4 — "Luke 16:19-31 teaches the literal geography of the afterlife" — Type: I-C — Classified: ECT-direction

  • Source test: Requires adding the concept "parabolic settings teach doctrine" — not found in any E/N item. External.
  • Direction test: Compatible with some E items (E7, E10, E11 describe the setting) but does not override them. However, it conflicts with N2 (teaching point is Scripture sufficiency, not afterlife geography). Borderline I-C/I-D.
  • Assessment: N2 states the passage's self-identified teaching point. I4 claims the setting is also doctrinal teaching. Since the passage itself identifies its teaching point and I4 must add a concept the text does not state ("parabolic settings are doctrinal"), this remains I-C: compatible external that supplements but does not directly override N2 (N2 does not say the setting teaches nothing; it says the climactic teaching point is Scripture sufficiency).
  • Result: Type I-C confirmed. Position: ECT-direction.

I5 — "Luke 16:19-31 proves conscious post-mortem suffering consistent with ECT" — Type: I-D — Classified: ECT-direction

  • Source test: Requires (a) taking the parable as literal, (b) extracting doctrinal content from the narrative setting rather than the teaching point, (c) overriding the didactic death-state passages (E19-E25) that characterize death as unconsciousness. External.
  • Direction test: Conflicts with E19 (dead know nothing), E21 (thoughts perish), E22 (no remembrance in death), E23 (dead go into silence), E24 (dead perceive nothing about their children), E25 (grave cannot praise). To maintain this claim, these E-items must be qualified, limited, or overridden. I-D.
  • Result: Type I-D confirmed. Position: ECT-direction. This is the weakest inference type — it requires the didactic death-state passages to mean something other than what they say.

I6 — "The didactic death-state passages establish that the dead are unconscious, making Luke 16's conscious afterlife imagery parabolic" — Type: I-A — Classified: Cond.

  • Source test: All components from E/N tables: E19-E25 (didactic death-state), E8-E9 (vocabulary divergence), N4 (vocabulary difference). Text-derived.
  • Direction test: Aligns with E/N items. Does not require any E/N item to mean something other than its lexical value. I-A.
  • Consistency check: Requires only criterion #5 (systematizing multiple E/N items into a broader pattern). Does not require #1, #2, or #3.
  • Result: Type I-A confirmed. Position: Cond.

I7 — "Paul's logic in 1 Cor 15:18 requires the dead NOT to be in conscious bliss; this rules out a literal reading of Luke 16's afterlife imagery" — Type: I-A — Classified: Cond.

  • Source test: All components from E/N tables: E27 (1 Cor 15:18 — dead have perished without resurrection). Text-derived.
  • Direction test: Aligns with E/N items. Paul's argument requires that without resurrection, the dead are simply gone — not in Abraham's bosom. Does not require any E/N item to mean something other than its lexical value. I-A.
  • Consistency check: Requires criterion #5 (systematizing — combining Paul's logic with Luke 16's imagery) and #4a (SIS connection — same vocabulary field, same author corpus). Does not require #1, #2, or #3.
  • Result: Type I-A confirmed. Position: Cond.

Reclassified Item: N5 → I-A8

I-A8 — "Since David is dead and NOT ascended (Acts 2:29,34), and Abraham's bosom is a post-mortem heavenly destination, Luke 16's depiction is inconsistent with Luke's own didactic teaching" — Type: I-A — Classified: Cond.

  • Source test: Components from E-items: E15 (David dead and buried), E16 (David not ascended), E7 (Abraham's bosom unique to Luke 16). Text-derived.
  • Direction test: Aligns with E/N items. The step from "not ascended to heavens" to "not in Abraham's bosom" requires systematizing but uses only text-internal vocabulary. I-A.
  • Consistency check: Requires criterion #5 (systematizing) and arguably #4b (bridging Luke 16 to Acts 2 — though same-author connection is strong). The connection is same-author, so #4a applies.
  • Result: Type I-A confirmed. Position: Cond.

docs.title: Conclusion — etc7-09: Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31)
Question
docs.text: Luke 16:19-31 -- parable or literal? Genre, first-century Jewish context. Apply Tree 3 genre gate. Literary structure (five parables in Luke 15-16).

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: Luke 16:19-31 is a parable, as established by multiple converging lines of textual evidence: the identical Lukan "certain rich man" formula (anthropos tis plousios) used in two other passages both recognized as parables; the five-narrative discourse structure of Luke 15-16 governed by a single parabole label at 15:3; the vocabulary divergence from standard eschatological judgment passages; the uniqueness of "Abraham's bosom" and "great chasm" (hapax legomenon) as concepts found nowhere else in Scripture; the OT mashal precedent for figurative speech from the dead; and the same-author evidence from Acts 2:29,34 where Luke records that David is dead, buried, and NOT ascended to heaven. The passage's self-identified teaching point is the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets (vv.29,31), not afterlife geography.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Luke 16:19 — "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day." (Opening formula "anthropos tis plousios" — identical to Luke 12:16 with explicit parabole label and Luke 16:1, universally recognized as parabolic.)

Luke 16:23 — "And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom." (The torment word is basanos, Strong's G931, appearing only 3 times in the NT — not basanizo G928, the standard eschatological torment verb.)

Luke 16:29 — "Abraham saith unto him, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them." (The passage's climactic teaching point — sufficiency of Scripture.)

Luke 16:31 — "And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead." (Ironic foreshadowing: a Lazarus DID rise from the dead, John 11:43-44; leaders plotted murder, John 12:10-11.)

Luke 15:3 — "And he spake this parable unto them, saying," (Singular parabole with demonstrative tauten introduces the discourse unit. Three stories follow under this label in ch.15; two more in ch.16 with no discourse-closing formula.)

Acts 2:34 — "For David is not ascended into the heavens." (Same author as Luke. Didactic prose. If the righteous dead were in Abraham's bosom, David should be there — but Peter says David has not ascended.)

Ecclesiastes 9:5 — "For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing." (Didactic death-state. Multi-author consensus: the dead lack consciousness.)

Isaiah 14:4,9 — "Thou shalt take up this proverb [mashal] against the king of Babylon... Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee." (Explicitly labeled mashal. Dead kings depicted as conscious and speaking in sheol — identical motif to Luke 16, universally recognized as figurative.)

1 Corinthians 15:18 — "Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished." (Paul's argument works only if the dead are NOT already in conscious bliss. If believers were in Abraham's bosom, they would not have "perished" even without resurrection.)

docs.title: The Lukan "Certain Rich Man" Formula
docs.text:
The Greek construction "anthropos tis plousios" (a certain rich man) appears three times in Luke's Gospel. At Luke 12:16, it is explicitly labeled parabole: "And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully." At Luke 16:1, the identical formula introduces the unjust steward, universally recognized as a parable. At Luke 16:19, the formula appears a third time. Parser verification confirms identical morphology at all three sites: anthropos G444 [N-NSM] + tis G5100 [X-NSM] + plousios G4145 [A-NSM].

The pattern establishes a Lukan convention: "anthropos tis plousios" is a parabolic opening formula. The absence of the parabole label at 16:19 is uninformative — Luke 16:1 also lacks the label and is universally accepted as parabolic.

docs.title: The Five-Narrative Discourse Structure of Luke 15-16
docs.text:
Luke 15:1-2 establishes the audience: publicans and sinners drawing near, Pharisees and scribes murmuring. Luke 15:3 introduces the discourse with a singular parabole label covering what follows. Three stories follow in chapter 15: lost sheep (15:4-7), lost coin (15:8-10), prodigal son (15:11-32). Chapter 16 opens with Jesus speaking (16:1), using the "anthropos tis plousios" formula for the unjust steward — the fourth narrative. No discourse-closing formula appears.

At 16:14-15, the Pharisees react mid-discourse: they are identified as philargyroi (lovers of money) and they deride Jesus. This mid-discourse reaction proves the audience is continuous from 15:1-2 and provides the thematic bridge to the fifth narrative — the rich man and Lazarus (16:19-31), directed at the money-loving Pharisees.

The wealth theme runs through the entire unit: mammon (16:13), Pharisees as money-lovers (16:14), the rich man's daily feasting (16:19), the reversal of rich and poor (16:25). This thematic continuity, combined with the unbroken discourse structure, places the Rich Man and Lazarus within the parabolic sequence introduced at 15:3.

docs.title: Vocabulary Divergence: Luke 16 vs. Standard Eschatological Passages
docs.text:
The parable uses basanos G931 (appearing 3 times in the NT: Matt 4:24 for physical diseases, and twice in this parable at vv.23,28) and odunao G3600 (appearing 4 times in the NT, all Lukan: Luke 2:48 for Mary's parental anxiety, vv.24-25 for the rich man's grief, Acts 20:38 for the Ephesian elders' grief at Paul's departure).

The standard eschatological torment passages (Rev 14:10-11; 20:10) consistently use basanizo (G928, 12 NT occurrences, 5 in Revelation) and basanismos (G929, 6 NT occurrences, exclusively Revelation). Neither basanizo nor basanismos appears in Luke 16.

Additionally absent from Luke 16: apollymi (G622, the standard destruction verb, 102 occ.); apoleia (G684, destruction noun, 20 occ.); geenna (G1067, Jesus' standard judgment location, 12 occ.); orge (G3709, wrath, 36 occ.); aionios (G166, eternal/age-pertaining, 71 occ.). Luke 16 uses a fundamentally different vocabulary register from both the eschatological torment passages and the destruction-judgment passages. The rich man's experience is described with grief/sorrow vocabulary, not judicial punishment vocabulary.

docs.title: Abraham's Bosom and the Hapax Legomenon
docs.text:
"Abraham's bosom" (kolpos Abraam) as a post-mortem destination appears exclusively in Luke 16:22-23. Kolpos (G2859, 6 NT occurrences) elsewhere means intimate relational closeness (John 1:18 — bosom of the Father; John 13:23 — disciple leaning on Jesus), garment fold (Luke 6:38), or geographic bay (Acts 27:39). No other biblical author — not Paul, not John, not Peter, not the OT — describes the righteous dead as going to "Abraham's bosom."

Chasma (G5490, "great gulf/chasm") is a hapax legomenon — it appears only in Luke 16:26 in the entire NT. The perfect passive of sterizo (G4741, esteriktai — "has been permanently established") describes a barrier found nowhere else in biblical afterlife teaching.

If Luke 16 were didactic teaching about afterlife geography, these unique concepts would require corroboration elsewhere in Scripture. Their singular occurrence within a passage that has multiple parabolic indicators marks them as narrative elements specific to this story.

docs.title: Same-Author Evidence: Luke vs. Acts
docs.text:
The same author who narrates Luke 16:19-31 also records, in didactic prose, Peter's Pentecost sermon. Acts 2:29 states that David "is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day." Acts 2:34 states emphatically: "David is not ascended into the heavens" (ou gar Daueid anebe eis tous ouranous — emphatic negative confirmed by parser: ou G3756 [PRT-N] + anebe G305 [V-2AAI-3S] Aor Act Ind). Acts 13:36 records Paul confirming that David "fell on sleep, and was laid unto his fathers, and saw corruption."

If Luke understood Luke 16 as teaching that the righteous dead are conscious in Abraham's bosom, he would be directly contradicting what he records Peter saying about David. David, a man after God's own heart, is dead, buried, and has NOT ascended to heaven. The only way both Luke 16:22 and Acts 2:34 can coexist from the same author is if Luke 16 uses parabolic imagery and Acts 2 presents the didactic teaching.

docs.title: The OT Mashal Precedent
docs.text:
Isaiah 14:4 explicitly labels what follows as a mashal (H4912): "thou shalt take up this proverb [mashal] against the king of Babylon." Hebrew parser confirms: hammashal H4912, Noun.ms.Abs with article — "the mashal." Verses 9-10 then depict dead kings rising from thrones in sheol, speaking, greeting the king of Babylon. No interpreter claims Isaiah 14:9-10 teaches literal afterlife consciousness — it is universally recognized as a figurative taunt-song.

The motif is identical to Luke 16: dead persons depicted as conscious, speaking, aware of new arrivals, engaging in dialogue. Ezekiel 32:21 presents the same pattern: "The strong among the mighty shall speak to him out of the midst of hell." Genesis 4:10 presents Abel's blood "crying" from the ground — figurative speech from the dead. The OT has an established convention of figurative/personified speech attributed to the dead in sheol, operating under the mashal genre. Luke 16 follows the same convention.

docs.title: The Didactic Death-State Consensus and Clarity Hierarchy
docs.text:
The didactic passages that describe the state of the dead are multi-author, cross-testament, and in the highest-clarity genre (didactic):

  • Ecclesiastes 9:5 — "the dead know not any thing" (Solomon, didactic wisdom)
  • Ecclesiastes 9:10 — "no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in sheol" (Solomon, didactic wisdom)
  • Psalm 146:4 — "in that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalmist, didactic hymn)
  • Psalm 6:5 — "in death there is no remembrance of thee" (David, petition psalm)
  • Psalm 115:17 — "the dead praise not the LORD; they go down into silence" (Psalmist, didactic hymn)
  • Job 14:21 — "His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not" (Job, didactic wisdom)
  • Isaiah 38:18-19 — "the grave cannot praise thee... the living, the living, he shall praise thee" (Hezekiah, personal testimony)
  • Psalm 30:9 — "Shall the dust praise thee?" (David, petition psalm)
  • Psalm 88:10-12 — "Shall the dead arise and praise thee?" (Sons of Korah, lamentation)

These nine passages from six authors across multiple genres consistently describe the dead as unconscious, unknowing, silent, and unable to praise or perceive. This is didactic teaching in the highest-clarity genre.

Against this consensus, the literal reading of Luke 16 would introduce conscious post-mortem existence based on a single passage in parabolic genre. The clarity hierarchy — didactic > parabolic — means the didactic passages govern the reading of the parabolic imagery. Clear passages interpret unclear passages (SIS principle).

docs.title: Paul's Logic in 1 Corinthians 15:18
docs.text:
Paul argues: "If Christ be not raised... then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished" (1 Cor 15:18). The verb is apolonto (apollymi G622 — "they have perished"). Paul's argument works logically ONLY if the dead are NOT already in conscious bliss. If believers who had died were already in Abraham's bosom enjoying conscious fellowship with the patriarchs, they would not have "perished" even if Christ had not been raised. The word "perished" would be nonsensical if the dead were conscious and blessed.

Paul's argument requires that without resurrection, death is the end — the dead have perished, they are gone. Resurrection is the sole mechanism by which they are recovered. This is consistent with the didactic death-state passages and inconsistent with a literal reading of Luke 16 where the righteous dead are conscious and comforted before resurrection.

docs.title: The Passage's Self-Identified Teaching Point
docs.text:
The Rich Man and Lazarus builds to a climactic exchange in vv.27-31. The rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers. Abraham replies: "They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them" (v.29). The rich man objects: "If one went unto them from the dead, they will repent" (v.30). Abraham concludes: "If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead" (v.31).

Every parable has a teaching point, and the teaching point is not the setting but the climax. The Prodigal Son's teaching point is about the Father's welcome, not pig-farming economics. The Good Samaritan's point is about loving one's neighbor, not travel routes from Jerusalem to Jericho. The Rich Man and Lazarus's teaching point is about the sufficiency of Scripture and the hardness of unbelief — not about afterlife geography.

The ironic foreshadowing in v.31 confirms this: "neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead." A Lazarus DID rise from the dead (John 11:43-44). The response of the leaders was not repentance but a plot to kill both Jesus and Lazarus (John 12:10-11). Jesus himself would rise from the dead, and many would still not believe. The parable's teaching point was vindicated by history.

docs.title: The Steelman: Naming of Lazarus
docs.text:
The naming of Lazarus is the single strongest indicator for the literal reading. No other parable of Jesus names a human character. This must be taken seriously.

The response involves five observations: (1) The name Lazaros (from Hebrew Eleazar = "God helps") is thematic — it describes the character's role. The poor man whom no human helped is the one God helped. (2) The rich man is NOT named — unprecedented for a real historical person described in such vivid detail (purple, fine linen, daily feasting). (3) Ezekiel 23:4 provides OT precedent for named characters in figurative literature: Aholah ("her own tent") and Aholibah ("my tent is in her") in an explicitly allegorical passage. (4) Nave's Topical Bible lists only the Lazarus of John 11 (brother of Mary and Martha) as a historical person — no separate entry for a historical beggar named Lazarus. (5) The naming must be weighed against the cumulative weight of multiple converging indicators for the parabolic reading. One indicator does not override eight converging lines of evidence.

docs.title: Physical Impossibilities in the Literal Reading
docs.text:
The rich man asks for Lazarus to "dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue" (16:24). These are physical body parts — finger (daktylos G1147), tongue (glossa G1100) — attributed to supposedly disembodied souls between death and resurrection. If the dead are disembodied spirits awaiting resurrection (as the literal reading requires), they do not have tongues, fingers, or physical needs for water.

Prior studies in this series established that biblical anthropology is holistic: man BECAME a living soul (Gen 2:7), not received a separate soul component (etc7-01). Death reverses the creation formula: body to dust, spirit to God, living soul ceases (etc7-03). Immortality is conditional and received at resurrection (etc7-02). Under this anthropology, the dead do not have conscious, embodied existence between death and resurrection. The physical details in Luke 16 make perfect sense as parabolic specificity (expressing desperation through vivid imagery) but create logical problems as literal description.

docs.title: Tree 3 Genre Gate Application
docs.text:
Gate 1 (Subject Gate): The rich man is unnamed, has no genealogy, no historical markers, and no cross-reference anywhere in Scripture. Lazarus, if taken as historical, would need to be a different person from the Lazarus of John 11, since the parable's Lazarus dies in destitution with no one to help while the historical Lazarus of Bethany has sisters wealthy enough to host dinners (John 12). The characters function as parabolic figures representing types (the rich who ignore the poor, the poor whom God helps). Gate 1: FAIL — subjects are parabolic characters, not verified historical individuals.

Gate 3 (Genre Gate): The passage is situated within the Luke 15-16 parabolic discourse introduced by the parabole label at 15:3. It uses the Lukan "anthropos tis plousios" parabolic formula. It contains unique narrative elements (Abraham's bosom, great chasm) found nowhere else in Scripture. Its vocabulary diverges from standard eschatological passages. The OT mashal tradition provides the literary precedent. Gate 3: FAIL — genre is parabolic, not didactic.

Classification result: E-items derived from Luke 16:19-31 are classified Neutral per the reclassification check. The text says what it says — a parable depicts a rich man in torment and a poor man in comfort. But a parabolic depiction does not constitute didactic teaching about human fate. The positional significance of the passage's details is determined by genre: parabolic imagery does not override didactic teaching.

Step 1 — Tension: - FOR (parabolic reading): E1 (parabole label at 15:3), E2 (identical formula at 12:16 with label), E3 (identical formula at 16:1 — universally parabolic), E4 (identical formula at 16:19), E5 (rich man unnamed), E7 (Abraham's bosom unique), E8 (basanos not basanizo), E9 (odunao = grief vocabulary), E11 (chasma hapax), E12-E13 (teaching point is Scripture sufficiency), E14 (Pharisees as money-lovers — audience context), E17 (mashal label in Isa 14:4), E18 (dead speaking in mashal), E30 (physical impossibilities), E31 (Abel's blood "crying"), E32 (named characters in Ezek 23 allegory), N1-N4, N6. - AGAINST (literal reading): E6 (Lazarus is the only named human character in Jesus' parables).

Step 2 — Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E1 Plain Greek text directly states "this parable" (singular) — observable grammatical fact E2 Plain Greek text at 12:16 uses identical formula with explicit parabole label — observable fact E3 Plain 16:1 uses identical formula — universally accepted as parabolic E4 Plain 16:19 uses identical formula — observable grammatical fact E5 Plain The rich man has no name in the Greek text — observable fact E6 Contextually Clear Lazarus is named — observable fact. But the significance (historical vs. thematic) requires contextual assessment. The name means "God helps." OT precedent exists for named allegory characters (E32). E7 Plain Kolpos Abraam as afterlife destination: distributional fact, verifiable E8 Plain Basanos G931 vs. basanizo G928: lexical fact, verifiable E9 Plain Odunao G3600 used for Mary's grief and Ephesian elders' grief: distributional fact E11 Plain Chasma G5490 is a hapax: distributional fact E12-E13 Plain The text's climactic statements are about Moses and the prophets: observable structural fact E17-E18 Plain Mashal label in Isa 14:4 and dead speaking in sheol: observable fact E30 Contextually Clear Physical body parts for disembodied souls: requires understanding that the literal reading implies disembodiment E31-E32 Plain Abel's blood "crying" and named allegory characters: observable facts N1-N4, N6 Plain Distributional and lexical observations: all verifiable

Step 3 — Weight: FOR the parabolic reading: 15+ Plain items, 1 Contextually Clear item. The evidence is converging from multiple independent lines — literary structure, vocabulary, unique imagery, OT precedent, same-author evidence. AGAINST the literal reading: 1 Contextually Clear item (E6 — naming of Lazarus). The naming is a genuine observation, but its interpretive weight (historical vs. thematic) requires choosing between readings.

Step 4 — SIS Application: The Plain statements on the parabolic side determine the reading of the Contextually Clear item on the literal side. The naming of Lazarus, when read in light of the converging Plain-level evidence (identical formula, discourse structure, vocabulary divergence, unique imagery, mashal precedent, same-author didactic contradiction), is best understood as thematic naming (Eleazar = "God helps") — consistent with the OT precedent in Ezekiel 23:4. The naming does not override the cumulative weight of the parabolic indicators.

Step 5 — Resolution: Strong The parabolic reading is supported by 15+ Plain-level items from multiple independent lines of evidence. The literal reading is supported by 1 Contextually Clear item (the naming of Lazarus) whose significance is ambiguous (historical vs. thematic). The resolution is Strong toward the parabolic reading.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said
docs.text:
Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies:

  • The "certain rich man" formula (anthropos tis plousios) is used by Luke at 12:16 with an explicit parabole label and at 16:1 for a universally recognized parable (E2, E3, E4)
  • "Abraham's bosom" as a post-mortem destination appears only in Luke 16:22-23 (E7, N3)
  • Luke 16 uses basanos/odunao (grief vocabulary), not basanizo/basanismos (standard eschatological torment vocabulary) (E8, E9, N4)
  • The passage's climactic teaching point is the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets (E12, E13, N2)
  • David is dead, buried, and has NOT ascended to heaven — recorded by the same author as Luke 16 (E15, E16)
  • The dead know not anything, their thoughts perish, they go down into silence, the grave cannot praise God — from nine didactic passages across six authors (E19-E25)
  • God alone has immortality; humans receive it at resurrection, not at death (E28, E29)
  • Paul's logic in 1 Cor 15:18 requires that without resurrection, the dead have perished (E27)
  • Hades is temporary — it delivers up its dead and is itself destroyed at the final judgment (E26, N6)
  • Isaiah 14:4 explicitly labels what follows as a mashal, and vv.9-10 depict dead kings speaking in sheol — universally recognized as figurative (E17, E18)

docs.title: What CANNOT Be Said
docs.text:
The following claims are not explicitly stated or necessarily implied by Scripture:

  • "Luke 16:19-31 teaches the literal geography of the afterlife" — no verse says this; the passage identifies its teaching point as Scripture sufficiency (I4: I-C)
  • "The naming of Lazarus proves the passage is a historical account" — requires adding a principle not stated in Scripture; contradicted by OT precedent for named allegory characters (I2: I-C)
  • "The physical details (tongue, water, flame) describe literal post-mortem conditions" — requires reading parabolic narrative details as literal and requires an anthropology (separable conscious soul) not established by didactic passages (I3: I-C)
  • "Luke 16:19-31 proves conscious post-mortem suffering" — requires overriding seven didactic death-state passages from six authors with one parabolic passage (I5: I-D)
  • "Abraham's bosom is a real place where the righteous dead go" — found only in Luke 16; no corroboration elsewhere in Scripture; absent from Paul, John, Peter, and the OT (N3)
  • "The parable endorses the first-century Jewish imagery of compartmentalized afterlife" — parables use culturally familiar settings without endorsing them as doctrine

docs.title: Word Studies
docs.text:
Basanos (G931): 3 NT occurrences — Matt 4:24 (physical diseases) and twice in this parable (vv.23,28). Originally a touchstone for testing metals. Not the standard eschatological torment word. Two of its three occurrences are in the Rich Man and Lazarus passage.

Odunao (G3600): 4 NT occurrences, all Lukan — Luke 2:48 (Mary's parental anxiety), Luke 16:24,25 (rich man's grief), Acts 20:38 (Ephesian elders' grief). Grief/sorrow vocabulary. Luke uses the same word for Mary worrying about the boy Jesus that he uses for the rich man's parabolic experience.

Basanizo (G928): 12 NT occurrences, 5 in Revelation. The standard NT verb for eschatological torment (Rev 14:10; 20:10). ABSENT from Luke 16.

Basanismos (G929): 6 NT occurrences, all in Revelation. The standard eschatological torment noun (Rev 14:11). ABSENT from Luke 16.

Hades (G86): 11 NT occurrences. LXX equivalent of sheol (H7585, 68 co-occurrences). Temporary — delivered up and destroyed at the final judgment (Rev 20:13-14). Characterized by unconsciousness in didactic passages via the sheol equivalence (Ecc 9:5,10; Ps 6:5; 115:17). Luke 16:23 is the sole NT depiction of consciousness in hades, and it occurs in a parable.

Kolpos (G2859): 6 NT occurrences. "Abraham's bosom" as afterlife destination unique to Luke 16:22-23. Other uses: intimate relational closeness (John 1:18; 13:23), garment fold (Luke 6:38), geographic bay (Acts 27:39).

Chasma (G5490): 1 NT occurrence (Luke 16:26). Hapax legomenon. Found nowhere else in biblical afterlife teaching.

Parabole (G3850): 50 NT occurrences. Luke 15:3 uses the singular with demonstrative to introduce the discourse unit. LXX translates mashal (H4912) as parabole, connecting the NT parable concept to the OT mashal genre.

Apollymi (G622): 102 NT occurrences. Standard destruction verb for divine judgment (Matt 10:28: "destroy both soul and body in Gehenna"). ABSENT from Luke 16. Also ABSENT: apoleia (G684), geenna (G1067), orge (G3709), aionios (G166).

docs.title: The Naming of Lazarus
docs.text: The naming of Lazarus is the single strongest indicator for the literal reading. This study addresses it through five observations: the name is thematic (Eleazar = "God helps"), the rich man is unnamed, OT precedent exists for named characters in allegory (Ezek 23:4), Nave's does not list this Lazarus as historical, and one indicator does not override eight converging lines of evidence. The I-B resolution evaluates this as 1 Contextually Clear item against 15+ Plain items and resolves Strong toward the parabolic reading.

docs.title: The Vivid Afterlife Setting
docs.text: The specificity of the afterlife imagery (Abraham's bosom, torment, flame, chasm, dialogue) can create the impression of literal reporting. Parabolic specificity is a consistent feature of Jesus' teaching (the prodigal son's pig-farming, the unjust steward's financial dealings, the good Samaritan's travel details). The parable's setting draws on culturally familiar imagery (parallels in Second Temple Jewish literature, particularly 1 Enoch 22's compartmentalized afterlife). Parables use cultural settings without endorsing them as doctrine — the unjust judge (Luke 18) does not endorse corrupt judges, the unjust steward (Luke 16:1-12) does not endorse embezzlement.

docs.title: Cultural Familiarity of the Imagery
docs.text: The compartmentalized afterlife imagery has parallels in intertestamental literature (1 Enoch 22 describes four compartments for the conscious dead; Josephus reports Pharisaic beliefs about intermediate conscious existence). Jesus uses this culturally familiar imagery as a narrative setting. He does not correct or endorse the setting — his teaching point bypasses the setting entirely. The climactic statements (vv.29,31) address the sufficiency of Scripture and the hardness of unbelief. The afterlife imagery serves as the framework for this teaching, not as its content.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
This study examines Luke 16:19-31 through the Tree 3 Genre Gate and finds the parabolic classification supported by converging evidence from multiple independent lines.

At E-tier, 9 items point in the Conditionalist direction (the didactic death-state passages and Acts 2:34) and 0 items point in the ECT direction. The 28 Neutral E-items are predominantly literary-structural and vocabulary observations that both sides can verify from the text. All ECT-direction claims are at inference tier: 3 at I-C (compatible external — requiring added concepts) and 1 at I-D (counter-evidence external — requiring the didactic death-state passages to be overridden).

The I-B resolution of the genre question resolves Strong toward the parabolic reading: 15+ Plain-level items from eight independent evidentiary lines against 1 Contextually Clear item (the naming of Lazarus). The naming is addressed by the thematic nature of the name, the unnamed rich man, OT precedent for named allegory characters, Nave's silence, and the cumulative weight of the parabolic indicators.

The passage's contribution to the eschatological debate is determined by its genre. As a parable, its afterlife imagery does not constitute didactic teaching about the death-state or the fate of the wicked. Its teaching point — the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets — is not about afterlife geography. The didactic death-state passages (E19-E25, from nine passages across six authors) remain uncontradicted at E-tier, and per the clarity hierarchy (didactic > parabolic), they govern the reading of parabolic imagery.
