docs.title: Focus Areas
docs.text:
1. The Genre of Revelation as Apocalyptic Literature: Revelation opens by declaring its mode of communication: God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ, who 'signified' (esēmanen) it through his angel to John. The verb sēmainō means to communicate through signs or symbols, not through direct literal description. Every other NT use of this verb confirms the symbolic-communication sense. Nave's Topical Bible classifies the entire content of Revelation under the heading VISION. This is not a neutral observation -- it means the standard biblical reference work treats everything from Rev 1:10 onward as vision-content. When a book self-identifies as sign-communicated prophecy, its imagery requires interpretation through the symbolic code the book itself establishes, not as literal reportage of heavenly geography. The contrast with didactic passages like Ecclesiastes 9:5 ('the dead know not any thing') or Psalm 146:4 ('his thoughts perish') is stark: those are propositional truth-claims made in non-visionary genres. Verses: Rev 1:1, Rev 1:3, Rev 1:10, Rev 4:1, John 12:33, John 18:32, John 21:19, Acts 11:28 Strong's: G4591, G4394

  2. The Altar Imagery and OT Sacrificial System Background: Revelation uses the word thysiastērion (altar) eight times, spanning all three judgment sequences. A critical grammatical observation governs the identification: when Revelation refers to the golden altar of incense, it explicitly qualifies with chrysoun ('golden') at Rev 8:3 and Rev 9:13. Rev 6:9 uses the unqualified form, pointing to the burnt offering altar -- the altar of sacrifice, not the altar of prayer. In the OT sacrificial system, the blood of the sin offering was poured 'at the bottom of the altar of burnt offering' (Lev 4:7,18,25,30,34). The nephesh/psyche = blood = life equation (Lev 17:11,14; Gen 9:4; Deut 12:23) means that 'souls under the altar' corresponds typologically to 'blood-life at the base of the sacrifice altar.' This is a sanctuary-liturgical image, not a location report. The altar that receives the martyrs' blood in Rev 6:9 is the same altar that speaks to confirm God's justice in Rev 16:7. Verses: Rev 6:9, Rev 8:3, Rev 9:13, Rev 16:7, Lev 4:7, Lev 4:18, Lev 4:25, Lev 4:30, Lev 4:34, Exo 29:12, Exo 27:1-8, Lev 17:11 Strong's: G2379, H4196, G5259

  3. Abel's Blood Parallel (Gen 4:10) -- Forensic Personification: God says to Cain: 'The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.' No reader takes this to mean that Abel was literally conscious inside the earth, speaking audible words through the soil. Abel's blood 'cries' as a forensic metaphor -- shed blood demands justice from the righteous Judge. Hebrews 11:4 reinforces this: Abel 'being dead yet speaketh' (lalei, present tense) -- but the speaking is 'through his sacrifice' (di autēs), not through conscious existence in an afterlife. Hebrews 12:24 extends the metaphor: Christ's blood 'speaketh better things than that of Abel.' Blood speaks. Wages cry (Jas 5:4). Stones would cry out (Luke 19:40). The beam answers the stone (Hab 2:11). The altar itself speaks (Rev 16:7). This is an established biblical pattern where non-personal entities are given voice to express a theological truth -- in this case, that the blood of martyrs demands divine vindication. The sphazō vocabulary chain (1 John 3:12 -> Rev 5:6 -> Rev 6:9) explicitly links Abel's slaughter with the Lamb's slaughter and the martyrs' slaughter, all in the same sacrificial framework. Verses: Gen 4:10, Heb 11:4, Heb 12:24, Matt 23:35, Luke 11:50-51, 1 John 3:12, Jas 5:4, Luke 19:40, Hab 2:11, Rev 16:7, Rev 5:6 Strong's: H6963, G2896, G4969

  4. The Meaning of Psyche (G5590) in Rev 6:9: The word psyche (G5590) in Rev 6:9 is the Greek equivalent of Hebrew nephesh (H5315). When Leviticus 17:11 says 'the life [nephesh] of the flesh is in the blood,' it establishes a direct equation: nephesh = blood-life. When sacrificial blood was poured at the base of the altar, it was the nephesh/psyche of the animal that was symbolically placed there. In Rev 6:9, the psychas ('lives/souls') under the altar are positioned exactly where sacrificial blood collects in the OT system. Revelation itself uses psyche for marine animal life that dies during the trumpet and bowl judgments (Rev 8:9; 16:3) -- demonstrating that the word does not inherently mean 'immortal soul.' In Rev 12:11, the same martyrs 'loved not their lives [psychas] unto the death' -- here psyche means mortal life that can be lost. The same word appears in Rev 20:4 where the same group identified by matching vocabulary (psychas + martyria + logos tou Theou) 'lived and reigned' only at the first resurrection. Verses: Rev 6:9, Rev 8:9, Rev 12:11, Rev 16:3, Rev 18:13, Rev 20:4, Lev 17:11, Lev 17:14, Gen 9:4, Deut 12:23, Gen 2:7, Ezek 18:4, Matt 10:28 Strong's: G5590, H5315

  5. The Identity of the 'Souls' -- Who or What Are They?: In the same sequence of visions, the Lamb appears as a slain animal with seven horns and seven eyes (Rev 5:6) -- no one concludes that Christ literally has seven horns. Death rides a pale horse with Hades following behind (Rev 6:8) -- no one concludes that abstract concepts literally ride horses. A woman appears clothed with the sun, standing on the moon (Rev 12:1) -- no one concludes this is a literal human being. Within this consistently symbolic visionary context, the 'souls under the altar' appear as one element in an apocalyptic tableau. They are given white robes (garments for bodiless souls?) and told to rest for a little season. The verbal parallel between Rev 6:9 and Rev 20:4 (sharing psychas, martyria, logos tou Theou, and a killed-verb) identifies the same group -- and Rev 20:4-5 explicitly says they 'lived and reigned with Christ' only at 'the first resurrection.' If they were already consciously alive in heaven, the statement 'they lived' at the first resurrection would be meaningless. Verses: Rev 6:9-11, Rev 5:6, Rev 6:8, Rev 12:1, Rev 16:7, Rev 20:4-5 Strong's: G5590, G4969

  6. 'Under the Altar' -- Significance of Position: The preposition hypokatō ('under, beneath') places the psychas at the base of the altar. In the OT sacrificial system, the priest poured the remaining blood of the sin offering at the base of the altar of burnt offering (Lev 4:7,18,25,30,34; Exo 29:12; Lev 8:15). This was where the blood-life (nephesh) of the sacrificial animal ended up after the sacrifice was completed. The bronze altar was five cubits square and three cubits high (Exo 27:1), overlaid with bronze -- the metal of judgment. It was 'the place of slaughter' (mizbeach, from zabach, H2076, 'to slaughter in sacrifice'). The spatial correspondence is exact: souls/lives under the altar = blood-life at the altar base. This is not a description of a dwelling place for conscious spirits but a typological identification of the martyrs as sacrificial victims whose shed blood cries for vindication, just as Abel's blood cried from the ground (Gen 4:10). Verses: Rev 6:9, Lev 4:7, Lev 4:18, Lev 4:25, Lev 4:30, Exo 29:12, Lev 8:15, Exo 27:1-8, Gen 4:10 Strong's: G5270, G2379, H4196, H2076

  7. White Robes and 'Rest' (Anapauō, G373): The martyrs are told to 'rest' (anapausōntai, G373) for a little season. This is the same Greek word used in Rev 14:13 for the blessed dead who 'rest from their labours.' Daniel receives the same instruction: 'thou shalt rest [nuach], and stand in thy lot at the end of the days' (Dan 12:13). The pattern is consistent: rest = death-state cessation of activity, followed by resurrection ('stand in thy lot'). If the martyrs were already consciously active in heaven -- crying out, receiving robes, engaging in dialogue -- telling them to 'rest' would be peculiar. The white robes (stolai leukai) are the same garments worn by the great multitude who 'came out of great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb' (Rev 7:9,14). They represent vindication and righteousness, not literal clothing for disembodied souls. Notably, if these are disembodied spirits without bodies, the giving of physical garments would be an incongruous detail -- unless the entire scene is symbolic. Verses: Rev 6:11, Rev 14:13, Dan 12:13, Dan 12:2, Rev 7:9, Rev 7:13-14, Rev 3:4-5 Strong's: G373, G4749

  8. The Cry for Vindication/Judgment (Ekdikeō, G1556): The cry 'How long, O Lord (despota), holy and true?' echoes the ancient Israelite lament formula found across the OT. Psalm 79:5,10 combines the exact elements: 'How long, LORD?' with 'let him be known among the heathen... by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed.' Zechariah 1:12 places the formula in an angelic speaker's mouth: 'O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy?' Daniel 8:13 and 12:6 use it in apocalyptic vision contexts. Habakkuk 1:2 cries 'How long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!' The formula is a theological convention expressing the problem of theodicy, not a transcript of literal speech by conscious dead people. The vindication vocabulary arc runs from ekdikeis (present active, Rev 6:10, ongoing/unresolved) through the progressive judgment sequences to exedikēsen (aorist active, Rev 19:2, completed). The tense shift from present to aorist marks the narrative resolution. Deut 32:43 promises that God 'will avenge the blood of his servants' -- the martyrs' cry invokes this covenantal promise. Verses: Rev 6:10, Rev 19:2, Ps 79:5, Ps 79:10, Zech 1:12, Dan 8:13, Hab 1:2, Deut 32:43, 2 Thess 1:6-8, Ps 6:3, Ps 13:1, Ps 94:3 Strong's: G1556, G1203, G2193

  9. Tree 3 Gate 1 (Subject Gate) -- Literal Humans or Symbolic Vision-Figures?: Tree 3 Gate 1 asks whether the subject is a literal human person making a propositional claim. The 'souls under the altar' exist within John's apocalyptic vision, introduced by the standard vision-frame formula 'I saw' (eidon). They are not persons encountered in ordinary space and time. They are positioned in a symbolically loaded location (under a heavenly altar that corresponds to no physical structure). They perform actions that parallel what non-personal entities do elsewhere in Scripture -- crying out (as Abel's blood cries, as wages cry, as stones would cry). They receive physical objects (white robes) while apparently lacking physical bodies. The prior study (etc6-10) concluded Gate 1 FAILS: these are symbolic vision-figures, not literal human subjects. They function within the apocalyptic tableau like the four horsemen, the woman clothed with the sun, or the beast rising from the sea -- as symbolic carriers of theological meaning rather than as literal beings making propositional truth-claims about the nature of post-mortem existence. Verses: Rev 6:9-11, Rev 5:6, Rev 6:8, Rev 12:1, Rev 16:7, Gen 4:10, Jas 5:4 Strong's: G5590, G1492

  10. Tree 3 Gate 3 (Genre Gate) -- Apocalyptic Vision vs. Didactic Prose: Revelation is apocalyptic literature. This is not a debatable classification -- the book opens by declaring its mode as sēmainō (sign-communication), identifies itself repeatedly as propheteia, and employs the standard apocalyptic apparatus: vision-frames (eidon), symbolic decoding keys (Rev 1:20; 17:15), cosmic imagery, angelic mediators, and numerological patterns. The genre classification has direct hermeneutical consequences. When Ecclesiastes 9:5 says 'the dead know not any thing,' it is a propositional truth-claim made by a wisdom teacher in a didactic genre. When Paul writes 'if the dead rise not, then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished' (1 Cor 15:18), it is a logical argument in an epistle. When Peter declares 'David is not ascended into the heavens' (Acts 2:34), it is a factual assertion in a kerygmatic speech. These are all didactic-genre passages making direct claims. Rev 6:9-11 is none of these things. It is a vision-scene within a sign-communicated apocalyptic prophecy, and Gate 3 filters it accordingly. The passage cannot serve as E-tier evidence for conscious intermediate state because its genre does not permit direct doctrinal extraction without interpretive mediation. Verses: Rev 1:1, Rev 1:3, Rev 1:20, Rev 17:15, Ecc 9:5, Ps 146:4, 1 Cor 15:18, Acts 2:34 Strong's: G4591, G4394

docs.title: The "Souls Under the Altar" — What Does Revelation 6:9-11 Actually Teach?
The Passage
docs.text:
When the fifth seal is opened, John sees "under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God" (Rev 6:9). They cry out asking God how long until He avenges their blood. They receive white robes and are told to rest a little longer (Rev 6:10-11).

At first glance this looks like dead martyrs consciously talking in heaven. But several features of the passage point in a different direction.

docs.title: Revelation Communicates Through Signs
docs.text: The very first verse of Revelation tells us how to read the book. God "signified" its message to John (Rev 1:1) — the Greek word is semainō, meaning to communicate through signs and symbols. Throughout Revelation, stars represent angels, candlesticks represent churches, and waters represent nations. A slain Lamb has seven horns and seven eyes (Rev 5:6). Death rides a horse (Rev 6:8). A woman stands on the moon (Rev 12:1). No one takes these literally. The souls under the altar appear in the same symbolic framework.

docs.title: Blood at the Base of the Altar
docs.text: In the Old Testament sacrificial system, the blood of the offering was poured out at the base of the altar (Lev 4:7, 18, 25, 30, 34). Scripture teaches that "the life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) — where "life" is the Hebrew word nephesh, the same word translated "soul." So "souls under the altar" corresponds exactly to blood-life poured at the altar's base. This is sacrificial imagery, not a location report for conscious spirits.

docs.title: Abel's Blood Already Set the Pattern
docs.text:
Genesis 4:10 says Abel's blood "crieth unto me from the ground." No one believes Abel was literally conscious inside the earth, speaking through the soil. Hebrews 11:4 clarifies: Abel "being dead yet speaketh" — through his sacrifice, not through conscious existence. This is forensic personification: shed blood demands justice from God.

The Bible uses this pattern repeatedly. Unpaid wages "cry out" (Jas 5:4). Stones would "cry out" (Luke 19:40). Even the altar itself speaks in Rev 16:7. If the altar can talk, the blood-souls crying beneath it need not imply literal consciousness.

docs.title: "Rest" Points to Resurrection, Not Heavenly Activity
docs.text:
The martyrs are told to "rest" (anapauō) for a little season (Rev 6:11). The same Greek word describes the blessed dead who "rest from their labours" in Rev 14:13. Daniel receives the same instruction: rest, then "stand in thy lot at the end of the days" (Dan 12:13). The pattern is consistent — rest in death, then resurrection.

Revelation 20:4-5 identifies the same group of martyrs and says "they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years. This is the first resurrection." If they were already consciously alive in heaven, saying they "lived" at the resurrection would be meaningless.

docs.title: What the Passage Can and Cannot Prove
docs.text:
Rev 6:9-11 is a powerful scene of martyrs awaiting vindication. But it appears within an apocalyptic vision full of symbolic imagery, not within a teaching passage that makes direct doctrinal claims about what happens after death.

The Bible's direct teaching passages on this topic are clear: "The dead know not any thing" (Ecc 9:5). "In that very day his thoughts perish" (Ps 146:4). "David is not ascended into the heavens" (Acts 2:34). Without the resurrection, those who have died in Christ "are perished" (1 Cor 15:18).

These straightforward statements in teaching genres carry more interpretive weight than symbolic imagery in an apocalyptic vision. The souls under the altar cry out for justice the way Abel's blood cried out — not because they are conscious, but because their sacrifice demands a divine response.

docs.title: Cross-Testament Parallels
docs.text:
• Rev 6:9 → Lev 4:7 (ot, Blood poured at the bottom/base (yesod) of the burnt offering altar -- spatial correspondence with 'under the altar' (hypokatō tou thysiastēriou))
  • Rev 6:9 → Lev 17:11 (ot, Nephesh/psyche = blood = life equation. Blood on the altar is the nephesh. Souls 'under' the altar = blood-life at the altar base)
  • Rev 6:9 → Gen 4:10 (ot, Abel's blood 'cries' (qol demey tsoaqim) from the ground -- forensic personification origin. Blood cries for justice without the dead being conscious)
  • Rev 6:9 → 1 John 3:12 (nt, sphazō vocabulary chain origin: Cain 'slew' (esphaxen) Abel. Same verb links Abel to the Lamb (Rev 5:6) and martyrs (Rev 6:9))
  • Rev 6:9 → Rev 5:6 (nt, Identical perfect passive participle esphagmenon. Lamb and martyrs share the same sacrificial framework)
  • Rev 6:9 → Rev 20:4 (nt, Verbal Parallel VP075 (Strong, 5 links): psychas, martyria, logos tou Theou, killed-verb, eidon. Same group -- 'they lived' at the first resurrection)
  • Rev 6:10 → Ps 79:5 (ot, 'How long, LORD?' (ad-mah YHWH) + blood vindication (v.10). OT formula paralleling heōs pote in Rev 6:10)
  • Rev 6:10 → Ps 79:10 (ot, 'Revenging of the blood of thy servants' -- combines 'how long' with blood vindication, exact elements of Rev 6:10)
  • Rev 6:10 → Deut 32:43 (ot, 'He will avenge the blood of his servants' -- covenantal promise invoked by the martyrs' cry)
  • Rev 6:10 → Zech 1:12 (ot, Angel uses 'how long' formula. Non-dead entity (angel) employs the same lament convention)
  • Rev 6:10 → Rev 19:2 (nt, Vindication arc resolution VP076: ekdikeis (present, 6:10) → exedikēsen (aorist, 19:2). Tense shift marks completed vindication)
  • Rev 6:11 → Dan 12:13 (ot, 'Thou shalt rest (nuach), and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.' Same pattern: rest = death-state, then resurrection)
  • Rev 6:11 → Rev 14:13 (nt, Same verb anapauō -- blessed dead 'rest from their labours')
  • Rev 6:11 → Rev 20:4-5 (nt, Same group 'lived and reigned with Christ' at 'the first resurrection.' The transition from resting (6:11) to living (20:4) occurs at the resurrection)
  • Gen 4:10 → Heb 11:4 (nt, Abel 'being dead yet speaketh' (lalei) -- through his sacrifice (di autēs), not through conscious existence)
  • Gen 4:10 → Heb 12:24 (nt, Blood of Christ 'speaketh better things than Abel.' Blood speaks metaphorically -- forensic personification extended)
  • Gen 4:10 → Matt 23:35 (nt, 'All the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel.' Jesus connects Abel to the whole martyrdom tradition)
  • Gen 4:10 → Luke 11:50-51 (nt, 'The blood of all the prophets... from the blood of Abel.' Blood 'required' -- forensic language)
  • Rev 6:9 → Jas 5:4 (nt, Non-personal entity (wages) 'crieth' (krazō) -- same personification pattern as blood/souls crying)
  • Rev 6:9 → Hab 2:11 (ot, Stone 'cries out' of the wall, beam 'answers' -- OT personification of inanimate objects)
  • Rev 6:9 → Rev 16:7 (nt, The altar itself speaks -- personification. If the altar can speak, blood/souls 'crying' under it need not imply literal consciousness)

docs.text: Rev 14:9-11, 19:3 -- OT source imagery (Isa 34:9-10, Gen 19:28, Mal 4:1-3). Ongoing torment vs. permanent destruction? Apply Tree 3 genre gate.

docs.title: Primary crux text: the third angel's warning — smoke of torment ascending forever
docs.text:
And the third angel followed them, saying with a loud voice, If any man worship the beast and his image, and receive [his] mark in his forehead, or in his hand, The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

Context: Part of the three angels' messages in Revelation 14. The first angel proclaims the everlasting gospel (v.6-7), the second announces Babylon's fall (v.8), and the third warns against worshipping the beast. This is within an apocalyptic vision sequence — the Lamb on Mount Zion with 144,000 (vv.1-5), the three angels (vv.6-12), the harvest of the earth (vv.14-20). Every element is symbolic: Lamb, Mount Zion, harps, angels, sickle, winepress.

Notes: Rev 14:10 — basanisthesetai (G928) is future passive indicative 3S, matching the conditional 'if any man' in v.9. The torment occurs enopion (G1799) the holy angels and the Lamb — throne-room/judgment language. Rev 14:11 — kapnos (G2586) is nominative singular, anabainei (G305) is present active indicative — the smoke 'ascends' using the same present tense as the living creatures' ceaseless praise in 4:8. The 'ages of ages' formula (eis aionas aionon) uses accusative plural + genitive plural of aion (G165). The anapausis (G372) construction 'ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos' exactly parallels Rev 4:8.

docs.title: Second crux text: Babylon's smoke rises forever — identical formula applied to completed destruction
docs.text:
And again they said, Alleluia. And her smoke rose up for ever and ever.

Context: Follows the exhaustive destruction of Babylon in Rev 18. After 'utterly burned with fire' (18:8), 'in one hour' (18:10,17,19), and fivefold 'found no more at all' (18:21-23), heaven celebrates Babylon's destruction. The identical 'smoke ascending for ever and ever' (eis tous aionas ton aionon) formula is applied to an entity whose destruction is explicitly complete and total.

Notes: The Greek construction is nearly identical to Rev 14:11: kapnos (G2586) nominative + anabainei (G305) present active + eis tous aionas ton aionon. Key difference: Rev 19:3 has the full article (tous) before aionas. Both use the same 'ages of ages' formula. Applied to Babylon — a symbolic entity 'found no more at all' — this formula cannot mean ongoing burning, since the thing is gone. It means permanent memorial/evidence of completed destruction.

docs.title: Primary OT source: Edom's smoke ascending forever — the formula Rev 14:11 draws upon
docs.text:
And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever.

Context: Isaiah 34 is a judgment oracle against Edom (Idumea). The chapter opens with universal judgment language (vv.1-4), then focuses on Edom (vv.5-17). The fire-and-brimstone imagery (v.9) and the smoke-ascending-forever formula (v.10) are the primary OT source for Rev 14:11's language. Critically, vv.11-17 describe animals DWELLING in the territory — pelicans, hedgehogs, owls, ravens, wild goats. The 'forever' fire has ended.

Notes: Hebrew parsing of v.10: le-olam (H5769, 'to eternity') governs ya'aleh (Qal imperfect 3ms of alah H5927, 'ascend') ashanah (H6227+3fs, 'its smoke'). The le-netsach netsachim (H5331, 'to perpetuity of perpetuities') is the STRONGEST Hebrew 'forever' form — construct + plural, intensifying. Yet animals dwell there in vv.11-17. The olam fire terminated. This is THE interpretive key for Rev 14:11.

docs.title: The continuation: animals dwelling in Edom's ruins — the 'forever' fire has ended
docs.text:
But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness. They shall call the nobles thereof to the kingdom, but none [shall be] there, and all her princes shall be nothing. And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of dragons, [and] a court for owls. The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest. There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow: there shall the vultures also be gathered, every one with her mate. Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read: no one of these shall fail, none shall want her mate: for my mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them. And he hath cast the lot for them, and his hand hath divided it unto them by line: they shall possess it for ever, from generation to generation shall they dwell therein.

Context: Immediately following the 'smoke ascending forever' declaration in v.10. The same prophet, in the same oracle, describes the RESULT of the judgment: not ongoing fire but permanent desolation inhabited by wild animals. The animals 'rest' (v.14) and 'dwell' (v.17) — activities impossible if the fire were still burning. The 'for ever' in v.17 (le-olam) describes the animals' permanent habitation of the ruins.

Notes: V.14 uses 'rest' (manoach H4494) for the screech owl — the same concept (cessation, settling) that anapausis expresses in Greek. The territory has become habitable. V.17 says 'they shall possess it for ever (le-olam), from generation to generation shall they dwell therein.' The same olam applied to the animals' habitation as was applied to the smoke's ascent in v.10. This proves olam-fire = permanent result, not endless process.

docs.title: Foundational fire-and-brimstone paradigm: Sodom destroyed, Abraham sees smoke aftermath
docs.text:
Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven; And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground. But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt. And Abraham gat up early in the morning to the place where he stood before the LORD: And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace.

Context: The foundational narrative establishing the fire-and-brimstone judgment paradigm. Every subsequent fire-and-brimstone passage references this event. Key: the fire 'destroyed' (overthrew), and Abraham sees smoke as AFTERMATH — visible evidence of completed destruction. The smoke is not evidence of ongoing torment but of the destruction that already happened.

Notes: Hebrew parsing: v.28 uses qitor (H7008, 'dense smoke/vapor') not ashan (H6227). Qitor emphasizes thick, furnace-like quality. The smoke 'went up' (alah H5927, Qal perfect 3ms) — completed action. Abraham sees the aftermath the morning AFTER the destruction. NT interpretation: Luke 17:29 says fire 'destroyed them all' (apollymi G622); 2 Pet 2:6 says Sodom became 'ashes' (tephroo); Jude 1:7 calls it 'eternal fire' yet the result is ashes.

docs.title: Eschatological fire producing ashes: the wicked become stubble, burned up, leaving ashes
docs.text:
For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do [this], saith the LORD of hosts.

Context: The OT's most explicit eschatological fire passage. Malachi uses total consumption language: wicked = stubble (qash H7179), burned up (lahat H3857 Piel), leaving neither root nor branch. The RESULT is ashes (epher H665) under the soles of the righteous' feet. No torment vocabulary — only destruction and cessation vocabulary.

Notes: Hebrew parsing (Mal 3:19 in Hebrew = 4:1 in English): bo'er (H1197 Qal participle) 'burning'; qash (H7179) 'stubble'; lihat (H3857 Piel perfect 3ms) 'devour'. V.3 (Heb 3:21): epher (H665) 'ashes/dust' — the stated RESULT. The wicked are ashes, not tormented beings. The stubble simile is decisive: stubble ceases to exist when burned. Corroborated by 2 Pet 2:6 where Sodom's fire-and-brimstone result is also 'ashes'.

docs.title: Babylon's destruction: torment and utter burning with fire — time-limited basanismos
docs.text:
How much she hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously, so much torment and sorrow give her: for she saith in her heart, I sit a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no sorrow. Therefore shall her plagues come in one day, death, and mourning, and famine; and she shall be utterly burned with fire: for strong [is] the Lord God who judgeth her.

Context: Babylon's judgment described as basanismos (G929) — the same word used in Rev 14:11 for the beast-worshippers' torment. Yet the result is 'utterly burned with fire' and plagues come 'in one day.' Three of six basanismos occurrences describe Babylon's judgment (18:7,10,15).

Notes: Basanismos (G929) occurrence 4 of 6. The basanismos of Babylon is time-limited ('one day,' 'one hour'), followed by complete destruction ('utterly burned'). This same basanismos whose smoke rises 'for ever and ever' in 19:3 is explicitly finite in duration and total in result.

docs.title: Basanismos occurrence: Babylon's torment comes 'in one hour'
docs.text:
Standing afar off for the fear of her torment, saying, Alas, alas, that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come.

Context: Kings of the earth witness Babylon's basanismos and note it comes 'in one hour' — explicitly time-bounded torment.

Notes: Basanismos (G929) occurrence 5 of 6. Time-limited: 'in one hour.' The merchants (v.15) also stand afar off 'for the fear of her basanismos' — occurrence 6 of 6.

docs.title: Basanismos occurrence: merchants fear Babylon's completed torment
docs.text:
The merchants of these things, which were made rich by her, shall stand afar off for the fear of her torment, weeping and wailing,

Context: The third Babylon-basanismos occurrence. Merchants weep at the completed destruction of their source of wealth.

Notes: Basanismos (G929) occurrence 6 of 6. Total distribution: Rev 9:5 (twice, five-month limit), Rev 14:11 (crux text), Rev 18:7, 18:10, 18:15 (all Babylon's completed destruction). 3 of 6 = Babylon's time-limited, completed destruction. 1 of 6 = five-month limit. Only 1 (14:11) is the crux text.

docs.title: Fivefold 'found no more at all': the most total destruction language in Scripture
docs.text:
And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast [it] into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all. And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft [he be], shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee; And the light of a candle shall shine no more at all in thee; and the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride shall be heard no more at all in thee: for thy merchants were the great men of the earth; for by thy sorceries were all nations deceived.

Context: Five 'no more at all' declarations for Babylon: (1) city found no more, (2) music heard no more, (3) craftsmen found no more, (4) light shines no more, (5) wedding voices heard no more. Total, exhaustive cessation language. Yet the smoke of this same Babylon 'rises for ever and ever' in 19:3.

Notes: The entity whose smoke rises 'for ever and ever' in 19:3 is described here with the most comprehensive cessation language in Scripture. Every aspect of life — music, industry, light, marriage — ceases completely. The smoke formula therefore CANNOT mean the entity is still burning; it means permanent memorial of completed destruction.

docs.title: Same-book same-author anapausis parallel: living creatures 'rest not day and night'
docs.text:
And the four beasts had each of them six wings about [him]; and [they were] full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come.

Context: The four living creatures before God's throne. Same author (John), same book (Revelation), same word (anapausis G372), same grammatical construction (ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos). In 4:8, 'rest not day and night' characterizes uninterrupted activity during its occurrence — not eternal duration. No one interprets this as the creatures being eternally conscious without rest in a torment-like sense.

Notes: Greek parsing confirms identical construction to Rev 14:11: anapausin (G372, accusative singular feminine) + ouk echousin (G2192, present active indicative 3P) + hemeras kai nuktos (genitive of time). The only difference: in 4:8, the activity is praise (positive); in 14:11, the activity is torment (negative). The phrase characterizes the NATURE of the activity (uninterrupted, without respite), not its eternal duration.

docs.title: Genre marker: Revelation communicated through 'signs' (semaino G4591)
docs.text:
The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified [it] by his angel unto his servant John:

Context: The programmatic opening verse of Revelation. The verb esemainen (G4591, aorist active indicative 3S) — 'signified' — establishes that the entire book communicates through signs and symbols. This is the foundation for the Tree 3 genre gate: Revelation is apocalyptic/symbolic, not didactic/plain.

Notes: Semaino (G4591) means to communicate through signs rather than direct statement. All 4 Johannine uses (John 12:33; 18:32; 21:19; Rev 1:1) involve indirect, symbolic communication of future events. The word establishes the book's hermeneutical framework: its imagery is sign-language, not literal description.

docs.title: Basanismos with five-month time limit: torment can be temporally bounded
docs.text:
And to them it was given that they should not kill them, but that they should be tormented five months: and their torment [was] as the torment of a scorpion, when he striketh a man.

Context: The fifth trumpet judgment. Basanismos (G929) occurs twice in this verse — both with an explicit five-month time limit. This demonstrates that basanismos is not inherently eternal; it can be time-bounded.

Notes: Basanismos (G929) occurrences 1-2 of 6. Both are explicitly time-limited (five months). This falsifies any claim that basanismos inherently implies eternal duration.

docs.title: Fire 'devoured' human enemies: destruction vocabulary for humans at the lake of fire
docs.text:
And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them.

Context: After the millennium, human enemies surround the beloved city. Fire from God devours (katephagen, G2719, aorist active indicative 3S) them. The NEXT verse (20:10) uses 'tormented' (basanisthesonai) for the devil, beast, and false prophet — different vocabulary for different subjects.

Notes: Katephagen (G2719) = 'devoured/consumed.' Aorist active — completed, decisive action. This is destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary. The human enemies are devoured; only the non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet) in v.10 are 'tormented.' When humans enter the lake of fire in vv.14-15, the term is 'second death' — death vocabulary.

docs.title: Tormented for ever and ever: applied to devil, beast, and false prophet — non-human subjects
docs.text:
And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet [are], and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Context: Three named subjects: the devil (non-human spirit being), the beast (symbolic: 7 heads, 10 horns, 'was and is not'), and the false prophet (symbolic: second beast of Rev 13:11-17). None is a literal human. The 'tormented for ever and ever' formula is NEVER applied to generic human wicked anywhere in Scripture.

Notes: Basanisthesontai (G928, future passive indicative 3P) — plural, matching the three subjects. This is the ONLY verse applying 'tormented for ever and ever' to any entity. Subject differentiation: v.9 humans = devoured; v.10 devil/beast/false prophet = tormented; vv.14-15 humans = second death. Different vocabulary for different subjects.

docs.title: Second death: when humans enter the lake of fire, the term is death, not torment
docs.text:
And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.

Context: The conclusion of the judgment scene. When the human wicked ('whosoever was not found written in the book of life') enter the lake of fire, the operative term is 'second death' — death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

Notes: Thanatos (G2288) — 'death.' The lake of fire IS the second death. For humans, the result is death. Death and Hades themselves are cast in — the destruction of death itself. Rev 21:4 confirms: 'there shall be no more death' — death is consumed/destroyed, not tormented.

docs.title: Lake of fire = second death for human wicked: death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary
docs.text:
But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

Context: The final statement on the fate of human wicked in Revelation. Their 'part' in the lake of fire is explicitly identified as 'the second death.' Not 'the second torment' or 'eternal conscious suffering' — death. Thanatos, the antonym of zoe (life).

Notes: This verse lists specific categories of humans (fearful, unbelieving, murderers, etc.) and says their fate in the lake of fire is 'the second death.' Combined with Rev 20:9 (humans devoured) and 20:14 (lake = second death), the consistent vocabulary for human fate is death/destruction, never torment.

docs.title: Beast and false prophet cast into lake of fire: non-human/symbolic entities
docs.text:
And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet that wrought miracles before him, with which he deceived them that had received the mark of the beast, and them that worshipped his image. These both were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone.

Context: The beast and false prophet are cast into the lake of fire BEFORE the millennium (Rev 19:20). The devil joins them AFTER the millennium (Rev 20:10). Both are symbolic entities — the beast has 7 heads and 10 horns (Rev 13:1), the false prophet is the second beast of Rev 13:11-17.

Notes: The entities in the lake of fire receiving 'torment' language are symbolic/non-human: beast (political power symbol), false prophet (religious deception symbol), devil (spirit being). None is a generic human.

docs.title: Fire-and-brimstone paradigm: permanent desolation, not ongoing process
docs.text:
[And that] the whole land thereof [is] brimstone, and salt, [and] burning, [that] it is not sown, nor beareth, nor any grass groweth therein, like the overthrow of Sodom, and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath:

Context: Moses describes the covenant-curse consequence using the Sodom paradigm. Brimstone + salt + burning = permanent desolation of the land. The result is barrenness and uninhabitability, not ongoing burning.

Notes: Gophrith (H1614) + melach (H4417) + seraphah (burning). The result vocabulary is desolation, not torment.

docs.title: Fire and brimstone rained on the wicked: OT judgment paradigm
docs.text:
Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and an horrible tempest: [this shall be] the portion of their cup.

Context: Psalm of trust. God's judgment on the wicked uses fire-and-brimstone language echoing Sodom.

Notes: Esh (H784) + gophrith (H1614). The Sodom paradigm applied to individual wicked. Result is their 'portion' — not ongoing torment but judgment outcome.

docs.title: Topheth prepared with fire and brimstone: divine preparation for judgment
docs.text:
For Tophet [is] ordained of old; yea, for the king it is prepared; he hath made [it] deep [and] large: the pile thereof [is] fire and much wood; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of brimstone, doth kindle it.

Context: Topheth — the burning place — prepared for judgment. Brimstone as kindling agent.

Notes: Gophrith (H1614) as kindling agent. The breath of the LORD kindles the judgment fire. Topheth is a place of burning (consumption), not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Fire and brimstone on Gog: OT brimstone judgment producing destruction
docs.text:
And I will plead against him with pestilence and with blood; and I will rain upon him, and upon his bands, and upon the many people that [are] with him, an overflowing rain, and great hailstones, fire, and brimstone.

Context: God's judgment against Gog. Fire and brimstone rain from heaven — Sodom paradigm applied to eschatological warfare. Rev 20:9 echoes this event.

Notes: Esh (H784) + gophrith (H1614). Result: destruction of Gog's armies, not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Jesus interprets the Sodom paradigm: fire 'destroyed them all'
docs.text:
But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed [them] all.

Context: Jesus recounting the Sodom event. His chosen verb for the result of fire-and-brimstone is apollymi (G622) — 'destroyed.' Not basanizo, not tormented — destroyed.

Notes: Apolesen (G622, aorist active indicative 3S) — 'destroyed them all.' Jesus himself interprets the fire-and-brimstone paradigm with destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

docs.title: Sodom turned to ashes as an example: permanent result language
docs.text:
And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned [them] with an overthrow, making [them] an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

Context: Peter's interpretation of the Sodom judgment. The fire-and-brimstone produced 'ashes' (tephroo G5077, only NT occurrence). Sodom is an 'ensample' (example) — the result of fire-and-brimstone judgment is ashes, not ongoing torment.

Notes: Tephrosas (G5077, aorist active participle) — 'having turned to ashes.' The only NT occurrence. Peter says the fire-and-brimstone paradigm produces ASHES. This is the NT interpretation of the same paradigm Rev 14:10 uses.

docs.title: Sodom suffered 'eternal fire' — yet the result is ashes
docs.text:
Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

Context: Jude describes Sodom as suffering the vengeance of 'eternal fire' (puros aioniou). Yet 2 Pet 2:6 says the result was ashes. The fire is 'eternal' in the permanence of its result, not in its endless burning. Sodom is not still burning.

Notes: Puros aioniou (G4442+G166) — 'eternal fire.' Yet Sodom is ashes. Aionios describes the permanence of the judgment's result, not the duration of the burning process.

docs.title: Abraham sees smoke as aftermath: smoke ascending = evidence of completed destruction
docs.text:
And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace.

Context: Abraham looks toward Sodom the morning AFTER the destruction. The smoke is not evidence of ongoing torment but visible aftermath of completed destruction.

Notes: Uses qitor (H7008, 'dense smoke/vapor') rather than ashan (H6227). Alah (H5927) Qal perfect 3ms — 'went up' (completed). The smoke is aftermath evidence. The furnace comparison (kibshan H3536) echoes Sinai (Exod 19:18) and connects to Rev 9:2.

docs.title: Ai's smoke ascending: smoke as evidence of completed conquest
docs.text:
And when the men of Ai looked behind them, they saw, and, behold, the smoke of the city ascended up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that way: and the people that fled to the wilderness turned back upon the pursuers. And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had taken the city, and that the smoke of the city ascended, then they turned again, and slew the men of Ai.

Context: The destruction of Ai. Smoke ascending is a military signal and evidence that the city has been taken. The smoke proves the destruction is DONE, not ongoing.

Notes: Ashan (H6227) + alah (H5927) — 'smoke ascended.' Same vocabulary as Isa 34:10. Smoke ascending = the destruction is complete. OT pattern: smoke is the visible evidence AFTER destruction, not during ongoing torment.

docs.title: Wicked consume into smoke: transience/vanishing simile
docs.text:
But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD [shall be] as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away.

Context: Wisdom psalm contrasting righteous and wicked. The wicked are compared to the fat of lambs — consumed in sacrifice, vanishing into smoke. The smoke is the EVIDENCE of consumption, not an ongoing state.

Notes: Kalah (H3615, 'consume/complete') + ba-ashan (H6227, 'into smoke'). The wicked consume AWAY into smoke. The smoke marks their vanishing, not their preservation. Same ashan vocabulary as Isa 34:10.

docs.title: Wicked perish as wax melts before fire: cessation at God's presence
docs.text:
As smoke is driven away, [so] drive [them] away: as wax melteth before the fire, [so] let the wicked perish at the presence of God.

Context: Psalm of triumph. Two cessation similes: (1) smoke driven away — dispersed, gone; (2) wax melting before fire — ceasing to exist in its current form. 'At the presence of God' (mipene Elohim) echoes Rev 14:10's enopion language.

Notes: Ashan (H6227) + abad (H6) — smoke driven away, wicked perish. Both similes describe CESSATION, not ongoing torment. The 'presence of God' language connects to Rev 14:10's enopion.

docs.title: Wicked compared to transient substances: all vanish
docs.text:
Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff [that] is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.

Context: Hosea compares the wicked to four transient substances: morning cloud, early dew, chaff, smoke from a chimney. All four vanish completely — none depicts ongoing conscious existence.

Notes: Ashan (H6227) out of arubbah (H699, 'chimney/window') — smoke that rises and dissipates. Every simile in this verse depicts something that ceases to exist: cloud dissipates, dew evaporates, chaff blows away, smoke vanishes.

docs.title: Enopion: torment 'in the presence of' the holy angels and the Lamb — judgment event
docs.text:
The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb:

Context: The torment occurs enopion (G1799) the holy angels and the Lamb. This is throne-room/judgment language. Enopion appears 36 times in Revelation, consistently marking public events before a throne or authority.

Notes: Enopion (G1799) appears twice in this verse. Throughout Revelation, enopion marks public events before the throne (4:5, 4:10, 7:9, 8:2, 20:12). The torment is a public judgment execution event, not an eternal condition. The redeemed do not watch torment forever — they witness judgment being executed.

docs.title: Destroy both soul and body in Gehenna: apollymi for human fate
docs.text:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: Jesus teaching about the fear of God. The verb for God's action on the human soul and body is apollymi (G622) — 'destroy,' not basanizo (torment).

Notes: Apolesai (G622, aorist active infinitive) — 'to destroy.' Jesus uses destruction vocabulary for human fate in Gehenna, not torment vocabulary. Soul AND body are destroyed.

docs.title: Perish vs. everlasting life: the fundamental binary
docs.text:
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

Context: The programmatic soteriological statement. The alternative to everlasting life is perishing (apollymi G622) — not everlasting torment.

Notes: Apoletai (G622, aorist middle subjunctive 3S) — 'should perish.' The binary is perish/life, not torment/life. Two outcomes: apollymi (destruction) or zoe aionios (eternal life). Not two forms of eternal existence.

docs.title: Wages of sin is death — not eternal torment
docs.text:
For the wages of sin [is] death; but the gift of God [is] eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Context: Paul's statement of the sin-consequence binary. Death (thanatos G2288) is the opposite of eternal life — not eternal torment.

Notes: Thanatos (G2288) — 'death.' Paul's binary: death/eternal life. Consistent with John 3:16's perish/life binary.

docs.title: Everlasting destruction — olethros aionios, not torment vocabulary
docs.text:
Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

Context: Paul describes the punishment of those who do not know God. The noun is olethros (G3639, 'destruction') modified by aionios (G166, 'everlasting'). Destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

Notes: Olethron aionion (G3639+G166) — 'everlasting destruction.' Paul uses destruction vocabulary for eschatological punishment. No NT author outside Revelation's apocalyptic framework uses basanizo/basanismos for human fate.

docs.title: Satan's fate: devoured, brought to ashes, never any more
docs.text:
Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee. All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never [shalt] thou [be] any more.

Context: Prophetic oracle against the king of Tyre, widely understood as describing Satan's ultimate fate. Uses total cessation vocabulary: 'devour,' 'ashes,' 'never any more' (ayin + olam).

Notes: Akal (H398) 'devour' + epher (H665) 'ashes' + ayin (H369) + olam (H5769) 'never any more.' The same being described in Rev 20:10 as 'tormented for ever and ever' is described in Ezekiel with total cessation language. The OT original uses destruction/cessation vocabulary for the same entity.

docs.title: As though they had not been: non-existence language for the wicked
docs.text:
For as ye have drunk upon my holy mountain, [so] shall all the heathen drink continually, yea, they shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been.

Context: Obadiah's judgment oracle. The fate of the wicked is expressed as non-existence: 'as though they had not been' (ke-lo hayu).

Notes: Ke-lo hayu — 'as though they had not been.' Uses Hebrew ayin/negation for non-existence. Compatible with destruction, incompatible with eternal conscious torment.

docs.title: God alone has immortality: wicked never said to receive it
docs.text:
Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom [be] honour and power everlasting. Amen.

Context: Paul states that God ALONE possesses immortality (athanasia G110). Humans must RECEIVE it (1 Cor 15:53). The wicked are never said to receive immortality — a prerequisite for eternal conscious torment.

Notes: Monos echon athanasian (G3441+G2192+G110) — 'alone having immortality.' ECT requires the wicked to possess indestructible souls — but Scripture says only God has inherent immortality.

docs.title: Genre context: apocalyptic vision sequence with symbolic elements
docs.text:
And I looked, and, lo, a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him an hundred forty [and] four thousand, having his Father's name written in their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps: And they sung as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four beasts, and the elders: and no man could learn that song but the hundred [and] forty [and] four thousand, which were redeemed from the earth. These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men, [being] the firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb. And in their mouth was found no guile: for they are without fault before the throne of God.

Context: The immediate context of the three angels' messages (Rev 14:6-12). Every element is symbolic: the Lamb (not a literal lamb), Mount Zion (heavenly, not earthly), 144,000 (symbolic number), Father's name in foreheads, harps, new song. Rev 14:9-11 is embedded in apocalyptic vision, not didactic teaching.

Notes: For Tree 3 genre gate: Rev 14:1-5 establishes the apocalyptic/symbolic context. The Lamb = Christ (symbolic). Mount Zion = heavenly (Heb 12:22). 144,000 = symbolic number. Harps = worship imagery. The 'third angel' speaks within this symbolic framework. Rev 14:14-20 continues with harvest imagery (sickle, winepress, grapes, blood to horse bridles = symbolic, not literal).

docs.title: Harvest of the earth: symbolic imagery following the third angel
docs.text:
And I looked, and behold a white cloud, and upon the cloud [one] sat like unto the Son of man, having on his head a golden crown, and in his hand a sharp sickle. And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat on the cloud, Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe. And he that sat on the cloud thrust in his sickle on the earth; and the earth was reaped. And another angel came out of the temple which is in heaven, he also having a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe. And the angel thrust in his sickle into the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast [it] into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden without the city, and blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles, by the space of a thousand [and] six hundred furlongs.

Context: The passage following the three angels' messages. Entirely symbolic: sickle, harvest, winepress, blood reaching horse bridles for 1,600 furlongs. No one reads this as literal blood. The smoke-ascending imagery of 14:11 is in the same symbolic register.

Notes: Blood reaching horse bridles for 200 miles = symbolic imagery. This is the same literary context as Rev 14:9-11. The entire chapter uses apocalyptic symbolism.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' formula: doxological use for God's eternal existence
docs.text:
And when those beasts give glory and honour and thanks to him that sat on the throne, who liveth for ever and ever, The four and twenty elders fall down before him that sat on the throne, and worship him that liveth for ever and ever, and cast their crowns before the throne, saying,

Context: The doxological use of 'for ever and ever' (eis tous aionas ton aionon). Applied to God who genuinely lives eternally. This is the formula's primary use (~18 of ~21 occurrences).

Notes: Eis tous aionas ton aionon — same formula as Rev 14:11 and 19:3. In doxological uses, the formula describes genuinely eternal realities (God lives forever). In the 3 judgment uses (14:11, 19:3, 20:10), it is applied within apocalyptic genre to entities whose destruction is described as complete elsewhere.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' formula: doxological — blessing to God and the Lamb forever
docs.text:
And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, [be] unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever.

Context: Universal doxology. Every creature ascribes glory 'for ever and ever' to God and the Lamb.

Notes: Doxological use: genuinely eternal — God's glory and honor.

docs.title: 'Ages of ages' formula: doxological — glory to God forever
docs.text:
To whom [be] glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Context: Pauline doxology using the identical formula.

Notes: Doxological use. Paul uses the same formula for God's eternal glory.

docs.title: Destruction as the end of the wicked: apoleia vocabulary
docs.text:
Whose end [is] destruction, whose God [is their] belly, and [whose] glory [is] in their shame, who mind earthly things.)

Context: Paul describes the enemies of the cross. Their 'end' (telos G5056) is 'destruction' (apoleia G684). Not torment — destruction.

Notes: Apoleia (G684) — 'destruction/perdition.' Paul uses destruction vocabulary for the fate of the wicked.

docs.title: Heavens vanishing like smoke: smoke as transience/cessation imagery
docs.text:
Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath: for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment, and they that dwell therein shall die in like manner: but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.

Context: Isaiah's contrast between transient creation and permanent salvation. The heavens 'vanish like smoke' — smoke as the epitome of vanishing.

Notes: Ashan (H6227) as vanishing simile. Smoke = that which disperses and ceases to exist. Consistent with all OT smoke-as-transience passages.

docs.title: Worm and unquenchable fire: applied to corpses, not living beings
docs.text:
And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

Context: The final verse of Isaiah. The righteous look upon 'carcases' (peger H6297) — dead bodies. The worm and fire consume dead bodies, not torment living beings.

Notes: Peger (H6297) = corpses, not living beings. The worm and fire act on dead bodies. 'Not quenched' means nothing can stop the fire until its work is complete, not that it burns eternally. Unquenchable fire = fire that cannot be extinguished (by human effort), not fire that never goes out.

docs.title: Everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels — not originally for humans
docs.text:
Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

Context: The sheep-and-goats judgment. The 'everlasting fire' was 'prepared for the devil and his angels' — non-human entities. Humans are sent into what was designed for non-human beings.

Notes: Pur aionion (G4442+G166) 'everlasting fire' + hetoimasmenon (G2090 perfect passive participle) 'prepared' + to diabolo kai tois aggelois autou 'for the devil and his angels.' The fire is designed for non-human entities.

docs.title: Everlasting punishment: kolasis aionios — nature of punishment debated
docs.text:
And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

Context: The conclusion of the sheep-and-goats judgment. Kolasis aionios ('everlasting punishment') parallels zoe aionios ('eternal life').

Notes: Kolasin aionion (G2851+G166) — 'everlasting punishment.' Kolasis = judicial penalty/punishment (not basanismos/torment). The Hebrews pattern (Heb 5:9 'eternal salvation' = permanently effective act; Heb 9:12 'eternal redemption' = obtained once) suggests aionios + result-noun = permanent result of a completed act. 'Everlasting punishment' = punishment whose result is permanent, not punishment that is endlessly inflicted.

docs.title: Basanizo for labor pains: demonstrating broader semantic range
docs.text:
And she being with child cried, travailing in birth, and pained to be delivered.

Context: Basanizo (G928) used for the pain of childbirth — not torment in the eschatological sense. Demonstrates the word's broader semantic range.

Notes: Basanizomene (G928, present passive participle) — 'being pained/tormented.' Used for labor pains. Shows basanizo does not inherently mean eternal torment.

docs.title: The wicked shall not be: explicit non-existence language
docs.text:
For yet a little while, and the wicked [shall] not [be]: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it [shall] not [be].

Context: Wisdom psalm. The wicked's future is non-existence — 'shall not be' (ayin).

Notes: Ayin (H369) = non-existence. The wicked will not exist. Compatible with annihilation, incompatible with eternal conscious torment.

docs.title: Babylon is fallen: contextual flow leading to the smoke imagery
docs.text:
And there followed another angel, saying, Babylon is fallen, is fallen, that great city, because she made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication.

Context: The second angel's message, immediately preceding the third angel (14:9-11). Babylon's fall is announced before the smoke imagery. The same Babylon whose smoke rises in 19:3.

Notes: Sets up the Babylon connection: the entity whose 'fall' is announced in 14:8 is the same entity whose smoke rises in 19:3 with the identical formula used in 14:11.

docs.title: Anapausis in Revelation: the souls rest (positive usage)
docs.text:
And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they [were], should be fulfilled.

Context: The souls under the altar told to 'rest' (anapausis-related vocabulary). Connects to the Rev 14:11 denial of rest.

Notes: Anapausontai (G373, future middle indicative 3P) — 'they should rest.' The verb form of the noun used in 14:11. Rest is given to the righteous; denied to beast-worshippers during judgment.

docs.title: Sinners consumed out of the earth, wicked be no more
docs.text:
Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless thou the LORD, O my soul. Praise ye the LORD.

Context: The psalmist's prayer for the wicked to be consumed and be no more. Cessation/non-existence language.

Notes: Tamam (H8552) 'consumed/completed' + ayin (H369) 'no more.' Both cessation words.

docs.title: Utter end and devoured as stubble: total destruction language
docs.text:
What do ye imagine against the LORD? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time. For while [they be] folden together [as] thorns, and while they are drunken [as] drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry.

Context: Nahum's oracle against Nineveh. 'Utter end' (kalah) + 'devoured as stubble fully dry' (akal + qash) — total consumption language.

Notes: Kalah (H3617) 'utter end/complete destruction' + akal (H398) 'devoured' + qash (H7179) 'stubble.' The same stubble vocabulary as Mal 4:1. Total consumption, not preservation in torment.

docs.title: Stubble consumed: not a coal to warm at, not fire to sit before
docs.text:
Behold, they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them; they shall not deliver themselves from the power of the flame: [there shall] not [be] a coal to warm at, [nor] fire to sit before it.

Context: Oracle against Babylon. The wicked are stubble consumed by fire. The result: 'not a coal to warm at' — the fire has completed its work. Nothing remains.

Notes: Qash (H7179) 'stubble' + saraph (H8313) 'burn.' Result: no coal, no fire — the burning ends because the fuel is consumed. This is cessation, not eternal burning.

docs.title: Basanizo for waves tossing a ship (non-torment usage)
docs.text:
But the ship was now in the midst of the sea, tossed with waves: for the wind was contrary.

Context: Disciples crossing the Sea of Galilee after the feeding of the 5000. Jesus has gone to a mountain to pray. The ship was basanizo (G928) — tossed/harassed by waves. This usage demonstrates that basanizo does not inherently mean conscious torment; here it describes physical stress on an inanimate object.

Notes: basanizo (G928) applied to a ship being tossed — clearly non-torment usage. Demonstrates the word can mean distress/harassment/testing without implying conscious suffering.

docs.title: People as fuel of the fire — cessation/consumption imagery
docs.text:
Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts is the land darkened, and the people shall be as the fuel of the fire: no man shall spare his brother.

Context: Isaiah describes divine judgment on Israel. The people become fuel (ma'akholeth, H3980) for fire — consumed by it, not perpetually burning in it. The fire consumes its fuel; the fuel does not endure forever.

Notes: People as fuel of fire — fuel is consumed by fire, not preserved in it. Cessation/consumption imagery for divine wrath.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Rev 14:9-11, 19:3 -- OT source imagery (Isa 34:9-10, Gen 19:28, Mal 4:1-3). Ongoing torment vs. permanent destruction? Apply Tree 3 genre gate.

docs.title: Rev 14:9-11
docs.text:
Context: The third angel's message, embedded in an apocalyptic vision sequence. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 (vv.1-5); three angels proclaim messages (vv.6-12); the harvest of the earth follows (vv.14-20). Every element in the chapter is symbolic: Lamb, Mount Zion, harps, 144,000, sickle, winepress, blood to horse bridles for 1,600 furlongs.

Direct statement: Anyone worshipping the beast and receiving its mark will drink unmixed wrath, be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels and the Lamb, and the smoke of their torment ascends for ever and ever; they have no rest day nor night.

Original language: Basanisthesetai (G928, future passive indicative 3S) — "shall be tormented." Kapnos (G2586, nominative singular) — "smoke." Basanismou (G929, genitive singular) — "of torment." Anabainei (G305, present active indicative 3S) — "ascends." Anapausin (G372, accusative singular feminine) — "rest." The phrase eis aionas aionon ("unto ages of ages") uses accusative plural + genitive plural of aion (G165). Enopion (G1799) appears twice — "in the presence of."

Cross-references: The smoke-ascending-forever formula draws directly from Isa 34:10 (parallel score 0.401 — highest OT match). The fire-and-brimstone language echoes Gen 19:24 (Sodom paradigm). The "no rest day nor night" phrase uses the identical construction as Rev 4:8 (living creatures "rest not day and night" in praise). Rev 19:3 applies the identical smoke formula to Babylon's completed destruction.

Relationship to other evidence: This is the primary crux text. The surface reading in English suggests ongoing conscious torment. The OT source (Isa 34:10) describes an ended fire — animals dwell in the ruins (34:11-17). The same smoke formula in Rev 19:3 applies to an entity "found no more at all" (18:21). The anapausis parallel in Rev 4:8 characterizes uninterrupted activity during occurrence, not eternal duration. The passage is apocalyptic genre (Rev 1:1 semaino; chapter context of symbolic imagery). Tree 3 Gate 3 applies: apocalyptic vision, not didactic teaching.

docs.title: Rev 19:3
docs.text:
Context: Heaven celebrates Babylon's destruction. Rev 18 exhaustively describes Babylon's judgment: "utterly burned with fire" (18:8), "in one hour" (18:10,17,19), fivefold "found no more at all" (18:21-23). After this total destruction, heaven says "Alleluia. And her smoke rose up for ever and ever."

Direct statement: The smoke of destroyed Babylon ascends for ever and ever (eis tous aionas ton aionon).

Original language: Kapnos (G2586, nominative singular) + anabainei (G305, present active indicative 3S) + eis tous aionas ton aionon. Nearly identical construction to Rev 14:11. Rev 19:3 includes the full article (tous) before aionas.

Cross-references: Uses the identical formula as Rev 14:11. Parallel to Isa 34:10 (score 0.330). Babylon's completed destruction (Rev 18:8-23) proves the formula describes permanent evidence of ended destruction, not ongoing burning.

Relationship to other evidence: This verse is decisive for interpreting the smoke formula. The entity whose smoke "rises for ever and ever" is described five verses earlier as "found no more at all." Every mark of life — music, industry, light, marriage — has ceased (18:21-23). The smoke formula therefore means permanent memorial of completed destruction. The same formula in Rev 14:11 must carry the same meaning.

docs.title: Isa 34:9-10
docs.text:
Context: A judgment oracle against Edom (Idumea). The chapter opens with universal judgment language (vv.1-4), narrows to Edom (vv.5-17). Brimstone and pitch imagery in v.9, smoke-ascending-forever in v.10.

Direct statement: The land becomes burning pitch, not quenched night nor day; its smoke goes up forever (le-olam); from generation to generation it lies waste; none passes through it for ever and ever (le-netsach netsachim).

Original language: Le-olam (H5769, "to eternity") governs ya'aleh (alah H5927, Qal imperfect 3ms) ashanah (ashan H6227 + 3fs suffix, "its smoke"). Le-netsach netsachim (H5331, construct + plural — "to perpetuity of perpetuities") is the strongest Hebrew "forever" expression, intensified by the construct-plural combination.

Cross-references: This is the primary OT source for Rev 14:11 (parallel score 0.401). The verbal parallels are unmistakable: smoke ascending, not quenched, forever. Yet the continuation in vv.11-17 describes animals inhabiting the territory.

Relationship to other evidence: This is THE interpretive key for Rev 14:11. The strongest Hebrew "forever" form (le-netsach netsachim) describes a fire that ended — animals live in the ruins. If the OT source describes completed destruction with permanent aftermath, the same formula in Revelation cannot introduce a meaning the original never carried. Olam (H5769) means "concealed time" with duration determined by subject (432 occurrences ranging from three days to genuinely eternal).

docs.title: Isa 34:11-17
docs.text:
Context: Immediately following the "smoke ascending forever" declaration. Same prophet, same oracle, same audience.

Direct statement: Animals possess the territory — cormorant, bittern, owl, raven, thorns, nettles, dragons, wild beasts, satyrs, screech owl, great owl, vultures. They "rest" there (v.14), "dwell" there (v.17), "possess it for ever" (v.17).

Original language: V.14 uses manoach (H4494) for "rest" — the Hebrew concept behind the Greek anapausis. V.17 uses le-olam ("for ever") for the animals' permanent habitation, the same word applied to the smoke's ascent in v.10.

Cross-references: The animals' habitation proves the "forever" fire is no longer burning. The same olam governs both the smoke (v.10) and the animals' dwelling (v.17). Activities like nesting, hatching, and gathering (v.15) require the fire to have ended.

Relationship to other evidence: Falsifies the reading that le-olam fire means endless burning. The same word describes both the fire/smoke and the animals' post-fire habitation. Olam fire = permanent result (desolation), not endless process (burning).

docs.title: Gen 19:24-28
docs.text:
Context: The foundational fire-and-brimstone narrative. God rains brimstone and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah. Abraham sees smoke the next morning.

Direct statement: The LORD rained brimstone and fire, overthrew the cities, the plain, the inhabitants, and the vegetation. Abraham saw the smoke of the country going up "as the smoke of a furnace."

Original language: V.28 uses qitor (H7008, "dense smoke/vapor") rather than ashan (H6227). Alah (H5927, Qal perfect 3ms) — "went up" (completed action). Abraham observes the aftermath the morning after the destruction.

Cross-references: Luke 17:29 — Jesus says fire "destroyed them all" (apollymi G622). 2 Pet 2:6 — Sodom turned to "ashes" (tephroo G5077). Jude 1:7 — Sodom suffered "eternal fire." The NT consistently interprets this event with destruction/cessation vocabulary.

Relationship to other evidence: Establishes the fire-and-brimstone paradigm: fire from God produces total destruction; smoke is aftermath evidence. Every subsequent fire-and-brimstone passage references this event. The smoke Abraham sees is evidence that the destruction is done, not that it is continuing.

docs.title: Mal 4:1-3
docs.text:
Context: The OT's most explicit eschatological fire passage. The day comes burning as an oven; the wicked become stubble; fire leaves them neither root nor branch. The wicked become ashes under the righteous' feet.

Direct statement: The coming day burns as an oven, the proud and wicked are stubble, the fire burns them up leaving neither root nor branch (v.1). The wicked are ashes under the soles of the righteous' feet (v.3).

Original language: Bo'er (H1197, Qal participle) — "burning." Qash (H7179) — "stubble." Lihat (H3857, Piel perfect 3ms) — "devour." Epher (H665) — "ashes." The ashes vocabulary names the stated RESULT of eschatological fire.

Cross-references: The stubble simile is decisive: stubble ceases to exist when burned. The "neither root nor branch" language describes total consumption. 2 Pet 2:6 uses the same ashes-as-result pattern for Sodom.

Relationship to other evidence: This passage names what eschatological fire produces: ashes. Not tormented beings, not conscious entities in ongoing suffering — ashes. The righteous tread on the ashes. This is didactic prophecy (direct speech of the LORD through the prophet), placing it at the highest genre clarity level.

docs.title: Rev 18:7-8
docs.text:
Context: Babylon's judgment described. Three of six basanismos occurrences describe Babylon.

Direct statement: Babylon receives torment (basanismos G929) and sorrow. Her plagues come "in one day" — death, mourning, famine. She is "utterly burned with fire."

Original language: Basanismon (G929, accusative singular). Katakauthesetai (G2618, future passive) — "shall be utterly burned." The basanismos is time-limited ("one day") and followed by complete destruction ("utterly burned").

Cross-references: The same basanismos word appears in Rev 14:11. If Babylon's basanismos produces utter burning, the word does not inherently require eternal conscious suffering.

Relationship to other evidence: Basanismos occurrence 4 of 6. Time-limited, followed by total destruction. The entity whose basanismos-smoke rises "for ever" in 19:3 is here described as "utterly burned."

docs.title: Rev 18:10
docs.text:
Context: Kings of the earth witnessing Babylon's fall.

Direct statement: The kings stand afar off "for the fear of her torment (basanismos)," noting that "in one hour" her judgment has come.

Original language: Basanismou (G929, genitive singular). "One hour" (mia hora) — explicit time boundary.

Cross-references: Basanismos occurrence 5 of 6. The torment is bounded: "in one hour."

Relationship to other evidence: Confirms basanismos can describe time-bounded events. The entity experiencing basanismos is destroyed within "one hour."

docs.title: Rev 18:15
docs.text:
Context: Merchants weep over Babylon's completed destruction.

Direct statement: Merchants stand afar off "for the fear of her torment (basanismos)."

Original language: Basanismou (G929, genitive singular). Occurrence 6 of 6.

Cross-references: Final basanismos occurrence. Summary: 6 total, all Revelation, 3/6 = Babylon's completed destruction, 1/6 = five-month time limit (Rev 9:5), 1 crux text (14:11), 1 secondary (14:11 implied through the torment context).

Relationship to other evidence: The word basanismos appears nowhere outside Revelation. Three of its six uses describe the destruction of an entity that is "found no more at all." One use has an explicit five-month limit.

docs.title: Rev 18:21-23
docs.text:
Context: The climax of Babylon's destruction sequence.

Direct statement: Babylon is thrown down "with violence" and "shall be found no more at all." Five aspects of life cease: music, craftsmanship, millstone, candlelight, wedding voices — each with "no more at all" (ou me ... eti).

Original language: Ou me heurethe eti — "shall by no means be found any longer." The double negative (ou me) with subjunctive is the strongest Greek negation.

Cross-references: The entity whose smoke "rises for ever and ever" in Rev 19:3 is described here as utterly gone in every dimension of existence.

Relationship to other evidence: This is the most comprehensive cessation language in Scripture. If this entity's smoke "rises forever," and this entity is simultaneously "found no more at all," then the smoke-formula means permanent memorial of completed destruction, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Rev 4:8
docs.text:
Context: The four living creatures before God's throne, worshipping ceaselessly.

Direct statement: The four living creatures "rest not day and night" (ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos), saying "Holy, holy, holy."

Original language: Anapausin (G372, accusative singular feminine) + ouk echousin (G2192, present active indicative 3P) + hemeras kai nuktos (genitive of time). Identical construction to Rev 14:11.

Cross-references: Same word (anapausis G372), same grammatical construction, same book, same author. In 4:8, "rest not day and night" characterizes the uninterrupted nature of praise during its occurrence. No one reads this as the creatures being tormented without rest.

Relationship to other evidence: The strongest same-book same-author parallel. The phrase "have no rest day and night" characterizes the quality of activity (uninterrupted, without pause), not its guaranteed eternal duration. Applied to Rev 14:11, the phrase describes the uninterrupted nature of the judgment during its execution, not necessarily its eternal continuation.

docs.title: Rev 1:1
docs.text:
Context: The programmatic opening verse of Revelation.

Direct statement: God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ to show His servants things to come, and "he sent and signified (esemainen) it by his angel."

Original language: Esemainen (G4591, aorist active indicative 3S) — "signified." The verb means to communicate through signs rather than direct statement. All 4 Johannine uses involve indirect, symbolic communication.

Cross-references: John 12:33, 18:32, 21:19 — signifying manner of death; Acts 11:28 — prophetic revelation; Acts 25:27 — formal communication. The Johannine pattern is symbolic, indirect communication.

Relationship to other evidence: This verse establishes the hermeneutical framework for the entire book of Revelation: sign-language, not literal description. It is the foundation for Tree 3 Gate 3 (genre gate). All Revelation imagery, including Rev 14:9-11, is communicated through signs.

docs.title: Rev 9:5
docs.text:
Context: The fifth trumpet judgment. Locusts from the abyss torment those without God's seal.

Direct statement: The locusts torment (basanismos G929) for "five months." The torment is compared to a scorpion's sting.

Original language: Basanismos (G929) occurs twice — both with an explicit five-month time limit.
