Composite body parts from four Daniel 7 beasts confirm symbolic entity. The therion word study documents 38 of 46 NT occurrences in Revelation — in Revelation, therion is ALWAYS the apocalyptic beast-entity.

docs.title: Earth beast (= false prophet): symbolic characteristics, identified in Rev 19:20
docs.text:
Rev 13:11 And I beheld another beast coming up out of the earth; and he had two horns like a lamb, and he spake as a dragon. Rev 13:12 And he exerciseth all the power of the first beast before him, and causeth the earth and them which dwell therein to worship the first beast, whose deadly wound was healed. Rev 13:13 And he doeth great wonders, so that he maketh fire come down from heaven on the earth in the sight of men, Rev 13:14 And deceiveth them that dwell on the earth by [the means of] those miracles which he had power to do in the sight of the beast; saying to them that dwell on the earth, that they should make an image to the beast, which had the wound by a sword, and did live.

Context: Second beast rises from the earth with entirely symbolic characteristics: two horns like a lamb (counterfeiting Christ), speaks as a dragon (channeling Satan's authority), exercises delegated authority from the first beast, performs signs (semeia), makes fire come down from heaven, deceives earth-dwellers. Rev 19:20 identifies this entity as 'the false prophet' by matching vocabulary: 'wrought miracles before him' = 'miracles which he had power to do in the sight of the beast.'

Notes: The identification link between the earth beast (Rev 13:11-17) and the false prophet (Rev 19:20) is established by matching vocabulary: poiesas ta semeia enopion autou (Rev 19:20) refers back to poiei semeia megala (Rev 13:13) and the deception 'in the sight of' (enopion) the beast. The earth beast's characteristics (two horns like a lamb, speaks as dragon, gives pneuma to an image) are entirely symbolic — no literal human has these features.

docs.title: Beast 'was, and is not, and shall ascend' — temporal description impossible for human
docs.text:
Rev 17:8 The beast that thou sawest was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition: and they that dwell on the earth shall wonder, whose names were not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, when they behold the beast that was, and is not, and yet is.

Context: Angel explains the mystery of the beast to John. The beast 'was, and is not, and shall ascend' describes a temporal existence pattern spanning centuries — impossible for a single human individual. The beast ascends from the bottomless pit (abyssos) and goes into perdition (apoleia). Rev 17:9-11 further decodes: seven heads = seven mountains = seven kings.

Notes: The triple temporal formula 'was, and is not, and shall ascend' (en kai ouk estin kai mellei anabainein) describes a political-religious system that exists, disappears, and re-emerges — a pattern that no individual human being can fulfill. This confirms the beast as a symbolic entity representing a multi-century system.

docs.title: Counterfeit trinity: dragon, beast, false prophet as unit
docs.text:
Rev 16:13 And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs [come] out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet.

Context: Sixth bowl plague. Three unclean spirits (pneumata tria akatharta) proceed from the mouths of the dragon, beast, and false prophet. This presents the three as a unified counterfeit trinity (mimicking Father, Son, Spirit). The unclean spirits 'like frogs' further emphasize the symbolic/visionary nature of the scene.

Notes: The counterfeit trinity unit: dragon (= devil/Satan per 12:9), beast (symbolic political-religious system per 13:1), false prophet (= earth beast per 19:20). All three members of this unholy trinity are non-human/symbolic entities. pseudoprophetes (G5578) appears here in the singular without article — one of only 3 singular Revelation occurrences (16:13, 19:20, 20:10), all referring to the same specific apocalyptic entity.

docs.title: Eight categories of human wicked: lake = second death, no torment formula
docs.text:
Rev 21:8 But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

Context: New heaven/new earth context (Rev 21:1-8). After describing the absence of death, sorrow, and pain (v.4), the text lists eight categories of human wicked and assigns them 'the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.' No torment formula is applied. The terminology is 'second death' — death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

Notes: This is the most comprehensive list of human categories at the lake of fire: fearful (deilois), unbelieving (apistois), abominable (ebdelygmenois), murderers (phoneusin), whoremongers (pornois), sorcerers (pharmakois), idolaters (eidololatrais), all liars (pasin tois pseudesin). For ALL these human categories, the outcome is 'the second death' — not torment. The basanizo/basanisthesontai formula is never applied to any human category.

docs.title: Revelation 'signified' — genre marker for symbolic communication
docs.text:
Rev 1:1 The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified [it] by his angel unto his servant John:

Context: Opening verse of Revelation establishes the genre. 'Signified' (esemanen, from semaino G4591) means 'communicated by signs/symbols.' This is the literary genre declaration for the entire book — apocalyptic vision communicated through symbolic imagery. This is relevant for Tree 3 Gate 3 (Genre Gate): Revelation is classified as apocalyptic vision per Nave's VISION topic and per its own opening declaration.

Notes: esemanen (V-AAI-3S from semaino G4591) — 'he signified' or 'communicated by signs.' The verb semaino means to give a sign, indicate by signs, signify symbolically. This genre marker affects every passage in Revelation for Tree 3 purposes: all Revelation-sourced positional candidates pass through the Genre Gate, which automatically classifies them as requiring interpretation through symbolic lens.

docs.title: Christ destroys (katargeo) the one having power of death — the devil
docs.text:
Hebrews 2:14 Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;

Context: Epistle to the Hebrews, discussing Christ's incarnation. Christ took on flesh and blood specifically so that 'through death he might destroy (katargese) him that had the power of death, that is, the devil.' The purpose clause (hina + subjunctive) states the goal of Christ's death: to destroy the devil. Even the supernatural entity receives destruction vocabulary.

  • ἐπεὶ (G1893) — CONJ — οὖν οὖν G3767 [CONJ]
  • τὰ (G3588) — T-NPN — Nom Pl N
  • παιδία (G3813) — N-NPN — Nom Pl N
  • κεκοινώνηκεν (G2841) — V-RAI-3S — Perf Act Ind Sg thirdPers
  • αἵματος (G129) — N-GSN — Gen Sg N
  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — σαρκός, σάρξ G4561 [N-GSF] Gen Sg F
  • παραπλησίως (G3898) — ADV — μετέσχεν μετέχω G3348 [V-2AAI-3S] Aor Act Ind Sg thirdPers
  • αὐτῶν, (G846) — P-GPN — Gen Pl N
  • ἵνα (G2443) — CONJ — διὰ διά G1223 [PREP]
  • θανάτου (G2288) — N-GSM — Gen Sg M
  • καταργήσῃ (G2673) — V-AAS-3S — Aor Act Subj Sg thirdPers
  • κράτος (G2904) — N-ASN — Acc Sg N
  • ἔχοντα (G2192) — V-PAP-ASM — Pres Act Ptcp Acc Sg M
  • τοῦτ’ (G3778) — D-NSN — Nom Sg N
  • ἔστιν (G1510) — V-PAI-3S — Pres Act Ind Sg thirdPers
  • διάβολον, (G1228) — A-ASM — Acc Sg M

Notes: katargese (V-AAS-3S from katargeo G2673) — aorist active subjunctive, 'might destroy/render powerless.' katargeo has 27 NT occurrences with semantic range including abolish, render powerless, nullify, destroy, do away with. The G2673-katargeo word study documents this range. The devil (ton diabolon, A-ASM) is explicitly identified as the one having the power (kratos) of death. Christ's purpose (hina clause): to destroy this non-human adversary. touto estin ton diabolon — 'that is, the devil' — explicit identification using touto estin formula.

docs.title: Eternal fire 'prepared for the devil and his angels' — primary non-human designation
docs.text:
Matthew 25:41 Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

Context: Sheep and goats judgment parable. Jesus addresses those on the left with a command to depart 'into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels.' The primary designation of the eternal fire is for non-human entities: the devil (to diabolo) and his angels (tois aggelois autou). Humans are sent there secondarily. The verb is kolasis in v.46, not basanizo.

Notes: The fire was 'prepared' (hetoimasmenon, V-RPP-ASN from hetoimazo) for the devil and his angels — the primary design is for non-human entities. The dative to diabolo kai tois aggelois autou indicates the intended recipients. Humans who reject Christ are sent to a place originally designated for supernatural beings. Note: v.46 uses kolasis (G2851, judicial punishment), NOT basanizo (G928, torment) — different vocabulary from Rev 20:10.

docs.title: Son of God manifested to destroy (luo) works of the devil
docs.text:
1 John 3:8 He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sinneth from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil.

Context: Johannine epistle, didactic genre. The devil 'sinneth from the beginning' — a being whose activity predates humanity. The purpose of Christ's manifestation: to 'destroy' (luse, from luo G3089) the works of the devil. Destruction vocabulary applied to the devil's works in a didactic epistle context.

Notes: luse (V-AAS-3S from luo G3089) — aorist active subjunctive, 'might destroy/dissolve/undo.' luo means to loose, untie, dissolve, destroy. 'From the beginning' (ap arches) indicates the devil's activity predates human history, consistent with non-human supernatural identity. The devil 'sinneth from the beginning' — a pre-human origin of sin.

docs.title: Demons anticipate basanizo: 'art thou come to torment us before the time?'
docs.text:
Matthew 8:29 And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?

Context: Gadarene demoniacs encounter Jesus. The demons (non-human spirit beings) cry out using basanizo (basanisai, aorist active infinitive). They recognize Jesus as 'Son of God' and acknowledge an appointed time (kairos) of judgment. The demons themselves associate basanizo with their own future fate — basanizo used by demonic beings speaking of their own expected punishment.

Notes: basanisai (V-AAN from basanizo G928) — aorist active infinitive, 'to torment.' The demons use basanizo to describe what they expect Jesus to do to them. 'Before the time' (pro kairou) indicates awareness of a future appointed judgment — a time-bounded expectation. This is the only place in the Gospels where basanizo appears in a judgment context, and the speakers are demons, not Jesus or a human teacher.

docs.title: Basanizo for ship 'tossed' by waves — word does not require consciousness
docs.text:
Matthew 14:24 But the ship was now in the midst of the sea, tossed with waves: for the wind was contrary.

Context: Jesus walks on water narrative. The ship (ploion, an inanimate object) is 'basanized' by waves. This demonstrates that basanizo does NOT inherently require a conscious subject experiencing punishment. KJV translates as 'tossed' — recognizing the non-punitive semantic range.

Notes: basanizomenon (V-PPP-NSN from basanizo G928) — present passive participle, neuter singular, 'being tossed/battered.' Applied to a ship (to ploion, neuter noun) — an inanimate object. This occurrence proves basanizo does not inherently mean 'conscious torment' but rather 'severe distress/battering.' One of the 7 non-judgment occurrences.

docs.title: Demon begs Jesus 'torment me not' — demonic speech, basanizo
docs.text:
Mark 5:7 And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, [thou] Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not.

Context: Gerasene demoniac encounter, Markan parallel to Matt 8:29. The demon (singular, 'Legion') adjures Jesus by God not to basanize him. Same pattern: demonic being anticipates basanizo at Jesus' hands.

Notes: basanises (V-AAS-2S from basanizo G928) — aorist active subjunctive 2nd singular, 'that thou torment.' The demon speaks in singular ('me'), addressed to Jesus ('thee'). Parallel to Matt 8:29 and Luke 8:28 — all three Synoptic accounts use basanizo for demonic speech about their anticipated fate.

docs.title: Lot 'vexed' (basanizo) his soul — moral distress, not punishment
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:8 (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed [his] righteous soul from day to day with [their] unlawful deeds;)

Context: Peter discussing Lot's experience in Sodom. Lot 'basanized' his righteous soul — the word describes moral distress at witnessing wickedness, not divine punishment. KJV translates as 'vexed.' This is the only epistle occurrence of basanizo, and it is non-judgment.

Notes: ebasanizen (V-IAI-3S from basanizo G928) — imperfect active indicative 3rd singular, 'was vexing/tormenting.' The subject is Lot (a righteous man), the object is his own soul, and the cause is witnessing unlawful deeds. No judgment or punishment context. The only basanizo occurrence in any epistle — and it means 'moral distress.' hemeras ex hemeras ('from day to day') parallels the 'day and night' formula in Rev 20:10.

docs.title: Basanizo with explicit five-month time limit
docs.text:
Rev 9:5 And to them it was given that they should not kill them, but that they should be tormented five months: and their torment [was] as the torment of a scorpion, when he striketh a man.

Context: Fifth trumpet judgment. Locust-like beings from the abyss are given permission (divine passive: edothe) to torment (basanizo) for five months (menas pente). The explicit time limit demonstrates that basanizo does NOT inherently mean 'eternal' — the word itself requires duration modifiers to specify length. 'They should not kill' (me apokteinosin) establishes torment as distinct from death in this context.

  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — ἐδόθη δίδωμι G1325 [V-API-3S] Aor Pass Ind Sg thirdPers
  • αὐτοῖς (G846) — P-DPM — Dat Pl M
  • ἵνα (G2443) — CONJ — μὴ μή G3361 [PRT-N]
  • ἀποκτείνωσιν (G615) — V-AAS-3P — Aor Act Subj Pl thirdPers
  • ἀλλ’ (G235) — CONJ — ἵνα ἵνα G2443 [CONJ]
  • βασανισθήσονται (G928) — V-FPI-3P — Fut Pass Ind Pl thirdPers
  • πέντε· (G4002) — A-NUI — καὶ καί G2532 [CONJ]
  • ὁ (G3588) — T-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • βασανισμὸς (G929) — N-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • ὡς (G5613) — ADV — βασανισμὸς βασανισμός G929 [N-NSM] Nom Sg M
  • σκορπίου, (G4651) — N-GSM — Gen Sg M
  • ὅταν (G3752) — CONJ — παίσῃ παίω G3817 [V-AAS-3S] Aor Act Subj Sg thirdPers

Notes: basanisthesontai (V-FPI-3P from basanizo G928) — same morphological form as in Rev 20:10 (future passive indicative 3rd plural). The five-month time limit (menas pente, accusative of duration) proves the word does not carry inherent duration — it requires modifiers. edothe (V-API-3S from didomi, divine passive) marks God's sovereign permission. basanismos (G929) appears twice in the same verse — 'their torment was as the torment of a scorpion.' The word family is explicitly time-bounded here.

docs.title: Basanizo for childbirth pain — non-judgment use in Revelation itself
docs.text:
Rev 12:2 And she being with child cried, travailing in birth, and pained to be delivered.

Context: Woman clothed with the sun in labor. Basanizo is used for the pain of childbirth — in Revelation itself, the word is used in a non-judgment context. KJV translates as 'pained.' This undermines any claim that basanizo in Revelation always means eschatological torment.

Notes: basanizomene (V-PPP-NSF from basanizo G928) — present passive participle, nominative singular feminine, 'being pained.' Applied to the woman (a positive symbolic figure representing God's people). This is a non-judgment use of basanizo WITHIN Revelation's apocalyptic framework, proving the word's semantic range extends beyond punishment even in this book.

docs.title: Beast-worshippers: basanizo with fire and brimstone, smoke ascending formula
docs.text:
Rev 14:10 The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: Rev 14:11 And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

Context: Third angel's message. Describes the fate of beast-worshippers. The smoke of their basanismos ascends eis tous aionas ton aionon. The etc7-11 study established that this formula draws on Isa 34:10 (ended fire with same language) and that basanismos is time-bounded in 4 of 6 occurrences. This passage concerns human beast-worshippers but uses the apocalyptic framework vocabulary — subject to Genre Gate classification.

Notes: basanisthesetai (V-FPI-3S from basanizo G928) — future passive indicative 3rd singular in v.10 (singular subject: 'he' = the beast-worshipper). basanismou (G929, genitive) in v.11. The 'for ever and ever' formula here parallels Rev 20:10 but is applied to the smoke (kapnos) of torment, not to the torment itself. Rev 19:3 uses the same formula for Babylon's smoke — an entity described as 'found no more at all' (Rev 18:21). Cross-reference with etc7-11-smoke-ascending-forever findings.

docs.title: Babylon's smoke rises 'for ever and ever' — same formula for an ended entity
docs.text:
Rev 19:3 And again they said, Alleluia. And her smoke rose up for ever and ever.

Context: Following the fall of Babylon (Rev 18). Babylon's smoke (kapnos) rises eis tous aionas ton aionon — the identical formula used in Rev 20:10 and 14:11. Yet Babylon is described in Rev 18:21-23 as 'found no more at all' with fivefold cessation. The smoke formula describes a completed, permanent destruction — the same formula can describe a permanent result rather than an ongoing process.

Notes: The 'for ever and ever' formula (eis tous aionas ton aionon) is applied here to the smoke of an entity (Babylon) that is explicitly and repeatedly described as having ceased to exist: 'shall be found no more at all' (Rev 18:21), 'shall be heard no more at all' (18:22 x3), 'shall shine no more at all' (18:23), 'shall be heard no more at all' (18:23). This demonstrates the formula can describe a permanent, irreversible result rather than an ongoing process.

docs.title: OT: Morning star/Lucifer brought down to sheol — OT background for Satan's fate
docs.text:
Isaiah 14:12 How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! [how] art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations! Isaiah 14:13 For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: Isaiah 14:14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High. Isaiah 14:15 Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.

Context: Isaiah's taunt (mashal) against the king of Babylon. While the primary referent is the king of Babylon, the language transcends any human king — five 'I will' statements of cosmic self-exaltation followed by descent to sheol/pit. The NT applies this pattern to Satan (Luke 10:18: 'I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven'). The fate described is descent and humiliation, not ongoing torment.

  • נָפַ֥לְתָּ () — Verb.Qal.Perf.2ms — fall
  • שָּׁמַזִים () — Noun.mp.Abs — heavens
  • הֵילֵ֣ל () — Noun.ms.Abs — morning-star
  • בֶּן () — Noun.ms.Cst — son
  • שָׁחְבחַר () — Noun.ms.Abs — dawn
  • נִגְדַּ֣עְתָּ () — Verb.Niphal.Perf.2ms — cut off
  • אָהָרֶץ () — Noun.s.Abs — earth
  • חוֹלֵזשׁ () — Verb.Qal.Ptcp.unknownms.Abs — defeat
  • גּוֹיִיםֽ () — Noun.mp.Abs — people

Notes: Hebrew heylel (H1966) — 'morning star/shining one,' hapax legomenon. napalta (Qal perf 2ms of naphal) — 'you have fallen.' nigdatta (Niphal perf 2ms of gada) — 'you are cut off.' The fate is descent to sheol (H7585) and to the sides of the pit (bor H953). Destruction/descent language, not ongoing torment. Luke 10:18 applies the 'fall from heaven' to Satan explicitly.

docs.title: OT: Anointed cherub becomes ashes, shall never be any more
docs.text:
Ezekiel 28:14 Thou [art] the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee [so]: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God; thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire. Ezekiel 28:15 Thou [wast] perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee. Ezekiel 28:16 By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned: therefore I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of God: and I will destroy thee, O covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire. Ezekiel 28:17 Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty, thou hast corrupted thy wisdom by reason of thy brightness: I will cast thee to the ground, I will lay thee before kings, that they may behold thee. Ezekiel 28:18 Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee. Ezekiel 28:19 All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never [shalt] thou [be] any more.

Context: Oracle against the king of Tyre, but with language transcending any human king — 'anointed cherub that covereth' (v.14), 'upon the holy mountain of God' (v.14), 'perfect from the day created till iniquity found' (v.15). The same entity referenced in Rev 20:10 as 'tormented forever' is described here as becoming ASHES (epher, v.18) and existing NO MORE (eneka od lo olam, v.19). This is the most striking OT parallel: absolute destruction language for the Satan-figure.

Notes: Key Hebrew terms: kerub (H3742, 'cherub') — identifies the figure as a non-human angelic being. epher (H665, 'ashes/dust') — v.18: 'I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth.' akal (Qal perf 3fs, 'devour/consume') — v.18: fire 'shall devour thee.' eneka (ain + 2ms suffix, 'you are not') plus ad olam (unto eternity) — v.19: 'and never shalt thou be any more.' This is absolute cessation language: the cherub becomes ashes and ceases to exist. The SAME entity that Rev 20:10 says is 'tormented for ever and ever' is described in Ezek 28 as becoming ashes and existing no more.

docs.title: OT: Edom's smoke 'shall go up for ever' — identical language for ended judgment
docs.text:
Isaiah 34:9 And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. Isaiah 34:10 It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever.

Context: Oracle against Edom. Uses identical 'for ever' language: smoke goes up 'for ever' (le-olam), 'not quenched night nor day,' 'for ever and ever' (le-olam wa-ed). Yet Isa 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the ruins — the land is inhabited, not still burning. This demonstrates that the 'for ever' smoke formula in the OT describes a permanent, completed destruction, not an ongoing fire. The identical language in Rev 20:10 draws on this OT paradigm.

Notes: Hebrew: le-olam (H5769, 'for ever') appears twice in v.10. 'Night nor day' (laylah va-yomam) parallels Rev 20:10's 'day and night' (hemeras kai nuktos). The smoke 'going up for ever' formula is used for Edom — a nation that demonstrably ceased to burn. Isa 34:11-17 describes birds and animals inhabiting the ruins, proving the 'for ever' language describes a permanent result (devastation), not an ongoing process (burning). This OT usage directly informs the meaning of the same formula in Rev 14:11, 19:3, and 20:10.

docs.title: OT: Fourth beast slain, body destroyed and given to burning flame
docs.text:
Daniel 7:11 I beheld then because of the voice of the great words which the horn spake: I beheld [even] till the beast was slain, and his body destroyed, and given to the burning flame.

Context: Daniel's vision of four beasts. The fourth beast (the conceptual predecessor of Revelation's beast) is 'slain' and its body 'destroyed and given to the burning flame.' Destruction vocabulary (qetilat, body destroyed) applied to a symbolic beast-entity. This is the OT paradigm for the fate of symbolic beast-powers: they are destroyed, not tormented forever.

Notes: Aramaic: qetilat (from qetal, 'to kill/slay') — the beast is slain. geshmah hoobad (body was destroyed). yehibat liqedat esha (given to the burning of fire). All three terms describe destruction/consumption — not ongoing torment. This is the OT source material for Revelation's beast imagery, and the OT consistently uses destruction, not torment, for these symbolic entities.

docs.title: Babylon 'found no more at all' — fivefold cessation of a symbolic entity
docs.text:
Rev 18:21 And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast [it] into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all. Rev 18:22 And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft [he be], shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee; Rev 18:23 And the light of a candle shall shine no more at all in thee; and the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride shall be heard no more at all in thee: for thy merchants were the great men of the earth; for by thy sorceries were all nations deceived.

Context: Fall of Babylon. The passage describes Babylon's total cessation with fivefold 'no more at all' (ou me ... eti): found no more, heard no more (music), found no more (craftsmen), heard no more (millstone), shine no more (light), heard no more (bridegroom/bride). Yet Rev 19:3 says Babylon's smoke rises 'for ever and ever.' The same entity that is completely ceased is described with the ages-of-ages smoke formula — proving the formula describes a permanent result of destruction, not an ongoing process.

Notes: ou me heurethē eti — 'shall be found no more at all.' The emphatic double negative (ou me) with eti (anymore) repeated five times establishes absolute cessation. This is the same entity whose smoke rises eis tous aionas ton aionon in Rev 19:3. The coexistence of total cessation language and 'forever' smoke language in the same literary context proves the 'forever' formula can describe a permanent destruction.

docs.title: The serpent — pre-human, more subtil than any beast
docs.text:
Genesis 3:1 Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?

Context: Garden of Eden narrative. The serpent exists before any human sin — a pre-human being. Rev 12:9 and 20:2 identify this serpent as the Devil and Satan. The serpent's pre-human existence confirms the devil is not and has never been a human being.

Notes: The serpent (nachash H5175) is identified as 'more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made' — a created being distinct from humanity. Rev 12:9 explicitly links 'that old serpent' (ho ophis ho archaios) back to this Genesis figure. The devil's activity predates all of human history.

docs.title: Sodom destroyed by fire and brimstone — OT paradigm for lake of fire imagery
docs.text:
Genesis 19:24 Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven;

Context: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. The fire-and-brimstone paradigm originates here: divine judgment from heaven producing total destruction. Jesus interprets Sodom as 'destroyed them all' (Luke 17:29). Peter: 'turned to ashes' (2 Pet 2:6). Jude: 'suffering the vengeance of eternal fire' — yet the fire produced ashes, not ongoing torment.

Notes: gaphrith (H1614, brimstone) and esh (H784, fire). This is the archetypal fire-and-brimstone judgment. Every subsequent use of the fire/brimstone imagery draws on this paradigm. The result is total destruction: cities turned to ashes (2 Pet 2:6), 'destroyed them all' (Luke 17:29). Jude 1:7 calls this 'eternal fire' — yet the fire is not still burning and the cities are ruins.

docs.title: Devil as 'prince of the power of the air' — spirit being, not human
docs.text:
Ephesians 2:2 Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:

Context: Pauline epistle, didactic genre. The devil is identified as 'the prince of the power of the air, the spirit (to pneuma) that now worketh in the children of disobedience.' The label 'the spirit' (to pneuma) explicitly identifies the devil as a spirit being — a non-human, non-material entity. This categorizes the devil as a supernatural spirit being for Tree 3 Gate 1 purposes.

Notes: to pneuma to nun energoun — 'the spirit that now worketh.' The devil is explicitly called 'the spirit' (pneuma) — a spirit being. This is the clearest NT identification of the devil's ontological nature: he is a spirit, not a human. Combined with Rev 12:9 (dragon/serpent), Gen 3:1 (pre-human serpent), Ezek 28:14 (cherub), this establishes the devil as a non-human supernatural spirit being.

docs.title: Last enemy destroyed is death — parallels death cast into lake in Rev 20:14
docs.text:
1 Corinthians 15:26 The last enemy [that] shall be destroyed [is] death.

Context: Paul's resurrection chapter. Death personified as 'the last enemy' that shall be 'destroyed' (katargeitai, from katargeo G2673). This parallels Rev 20:14 where death and hades are cast into the lake of fire. The result of casting death into the lake is its destruction — 'there shall be no more death' (Rev 21:4). The lake destroys death itself.

Notes: katargeitai (V-PPI-3S from katargeo G2673) — present passive indicative, 'is being destroyed/abolished.' The same verb (katargeo) used in Heb 2:14 for the destruction of the devil. Death is personified as an enemy to be destroyed — when cast into the lake of fire (Rev 20:14), the result is 'no more death' (Rev 21:4). The lake is an instrument of destruction, producing cessation.

docs.title: Wages of sin is death — same word as 'second death'
docs.text:
Romans 6:23 For the wages of sin [is] death; but the gift of God [is] eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Context: Pauline didactic epistle. The wages of sin is thanatos (death) — the same word used in 'second death' (ho thanatos ho deuteros) in Rev 20:14 and 21:8. The contrast is death vs. eternal life, not torment vs. eternal life.

Notes: thanatos (G2288) — the same noun used in Rev 20:14 'this is the second death' and 21:8 'which is the second death.' Paul contrasts death (thanatos) with eternal life (zoe aionios) — the antithesis is death vs. life, not torment vs. life. This didactic, cross-genre statement informs the meaning of 'second death' in Revelation.

docs.title: Jesus interprets Sodom fire: 'destroyed them all'
docs.text:
Luke 17:29 But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed [them] all.

Context: Jesus' eschatological discourse. He references the Sodom destruction as a paradigm for future judgment. Jesus' own interpretation of the fire-and-brimstone paradigm is 'destroyed them all' (apolesen hapantas) — destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary. Jesus uses apollymi (G622, destroy/perish), not basanizo.

Notes: apolesen (V-AAI-3S from apollymi G622) — aorist active indicative, 'destroyed.' Jesus himself interprets the fire-and-brimstone paradigm as producing destruction, not ongoing torment. This is a didactic saying of Jesus in the Gospels — higher genre weight than apocalyptic vision under SIS principles.

docs.title: Angels that sinned + Sodom turned to ashes — supernatural punishment + destruction paradigm
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:4 For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast [them] down to hell, and delivered [them] into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment; 2 Peter 2:6 And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned [them] with an overthrow, making [them] an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

Context: Peter's epistle uses three OT examples of divine judgment: fallen angels (v.4), the Flood (v.5), Sodom (v.6). The fallen angels are cast to Tartarus and reserved for judgment — supernatural beings receive imprisonment vocabulary. Sodom is turned to 'ashes' (tephrosas, from tephroo) — the fire-and-brimstone paradigm produces ashes, not ongoing torment. Peter calls this 'an ensample' (hupodeigma) for future judgment of the ungodly.

Notes: tephrosas (V-AAP-NSM from tephroo G5077) — aorist active participle, 'having turned to ashes.' This is Peter's inspired interpretation of Sodom's fire-and-brimstone judgment: the result is ASHES. katastrophe (G2692) — 'overthrow/destruction.' hupodeigma (G5262) — 'example/ensample' — Peter explicitly says this destruction paradigm is the example for future judgment of the ungodly. Jude 1:7 calls the same event 'eternal fire' — yet the result was ashes, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Angels in chains + Sodom's 'eternal fire' — yet reduced to ashes
docs.text:
Jude 1:6 And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day. Jude 1:7 Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

Context: Jude parallels 2 Peter 2. Angels who sinned are reserved in 'everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day' — supernatural beings receive supernatural imprisonment. Sodom suffers 'the vengeance of eternal fire' (puros aioniou) — yet is now ashes (per 2 Pet 2:6). The fire is 'eternal' in its result (permanent destruction), not in its duration (still burning).

Notes: puros aioniou (fire eternal) — genitive construction. aionios (G166) modifies the fire, yet the fire produced ashes (2 Pet 2:6). This is a key datum for understanding 'eternal' punishment language: aionios describes the permanence of the result (the cities are permanently destroyed), not the duration of the process (the fire is not still burning). deigma (G1164) — 'example' — Jude also calls this event an example, parallel to Peter's hupodeigma.

docs.title: Day shall burn as oven — wicked become stubble, burned up completely
docs.text:
Malachi 4:1 For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

Context: OT prophetic eschatology. The wicked become 'stubble' (qash) burned up completely — 'it shall leave them neither root nor branch.' Total consumption language for human wicked in an eschatological context. The vocabulary is destruction (burn up as stubble), not ongoing torment.

Notes: Hebrew: qash (H7179, stubble) — quickly consumed by fire. lihhat (Piel perf 3ms of lahat, 'burn up/set ablaze'). 'Neither root nor branch' — absolute destruction with nothing remaining. This is OT eschatological vocabulary for the fate of human wicked — total consumption, not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Wicked 'as though they had not been' — cessation language
docs.text:
Obadiah 1:16 For as ye have drunk upon my holy mountain, [so] shall all the heathen drink continually, yea, they shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been.

Context: Obadiah's prophecy against Edom and the nations. The wicked 'shall be as though they had not been' (vehayu kelo hayu). Absolute cessation language — not ongoing conscious existence in torment, but as if they never existed.

Notes: kelo hayu — 'as though they had not been.' This is cessation language incompatible with eternal conscious torment. The wicked do not continue to exist in any form — they are as if they never were. This OT eschatological language (from a non-apocalyptic prophet) describes the fate of human wicked.

docs.title: Wicked 'shall not be' — OT destruction language for human wicked
docs.text:
Psalm 37:10 For yet a little while, and the wicked [shall] not [be]: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it [shall] not [be].

Context: Wisdom psalm. The wicked 'shall not be' (enenu) — their very existence ceases. 'His place' (meqomo) shall not be. The psalmist describes cessation of existence, not ongoing torment in a different location.

Notes: enenu (ain + 3ms suffix) — 'he is not/shall not be.' The same negative existential construction used in Ezek 28:19 for the Satan-figure ('thou shalt never be any more'). Applied to human wicked in a wisdom psalm — cessation of existence.

docs.title: Generic false prophets (plural) — class of humans, distinct from Rev singular
docs.text:
Matthew 7:15 Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.

Context: Sermon on the Mount. Jesus warns of 'false prophets' (pseudoprophetai, PLURAL) — a class of human deceivers. This is distinct from the SINGULAR 'false prophet' (pseudoprophetes) in Revelation (16:13, 19:20, 20:10), which always refers to one specific apocalyptic entity. The plural/singular distinction is critical for identifying the subject of Rev 20:10.

Notes: pseudopropheton (G5578, genitive plural) — 'of false prophets.' The word study documents all 11 occurrences: 7x plural (class of human deceivers: Matt 7:15, 24:11, 24:24, Mark 13:22, Luke 6:26, 2 Pet 2:1, 1 John 4:1), 1x singular with name (Acts 13:6 Bar-Jesus), and 3x singular in Revelation (16:13, 19:20, 20:10 — all the same specific apocalyptic entity). The false prophet of Rev 20:10 is not a generic human false prophet.

docs.title: Demon begs Jesus 'torment me not' — Lukan parallel, basanizo in demonic speech
docs.text:
Luke 8:28 When he saw Jesus, he cried out, and fell down before him, and with a loud voice said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, [thou] Son of God most high? I beseech thee, torment me not.

Context: Lukan parallel to the Gerasene demoniac (cf. Matt 8:29, Mark 5:7). The demon uses basanizo to describe what it fears from Jesus. All three Synoptic accounts record demons using basanizo — the word appears in judgment contexts primarily through demonic speech about their own anticipated fate.

Notes: basanises (from basanizo G928) — the demon begs not to be basanized. This is the third Synoptic parallel using basanizo in demonic speech. The pattern: basanizo as a judgment term originates in demonic anticipation of their own fate, not in didactic teaching about human eschatological destiny.

docs.title: 'For ever and ever' formula applied to God — genuinely endless
docs.text:
Rev 4:9 And when those beasts give glory and honour and thanks to him that sat on the throne, who liveth for ever and ever, Rev 4:10 The four and twenty elders fall down before him that sat on the throne, and worship him that liveth for ever and ever, and cast their crowns before the throne, saying,

Context: Throne room vision. The formula 'eis tous aionas ton aionon' (for ever and ever) is applied to God's existence: 'who liveth for ever and ever.' Applied to the eternal God, the formula is genuinely endless. This is the baseline usage of the formula — its meaning appears subject-determined: applied to the eternal God = genuinely eternal; applied to judgment = requires contextual assessment.

Notes: eis tous aionas ton aionon — the same formula as Rev 20:10. In Rev 4:9-10, applied to God's life — unquestionably eternal. The formula appears ~13 times in Revelation: 9x for God's existence/reign, 1x for saints' reign, 3x for judgment contexts (14:11, 19:3, 20:10). The meaning is demonstrably subject-determined, as shown by the Isa 34:9-10 parallel where identical language describes an ended fire.

docs.title: Detailed Analysis — Rev 20:10 Named Subjects and Basanizo Usage
Question
docs.text: Rev 20:10 — named subjects (devil, beast, false prophet). Applied to humans or supernatural/symbolic entities? Basanizo (G928) usage. Apply Tree 3 subject gate.

docs.title: Rev 20:7-8 — Satan released, deceives nations
docs.text: Context: After the millennium, Satan is released from his prison and goes out to deceive the nations (Gog and Magog) for battle. The subject (Satanas) is the same entity identified in Rev 20:2 and 12:9 by the four-fold chain: dragon = old serpent = devil = Satan. Direct statement: Satan is loosed and deceives nations globally. Original language: Satanas (G4567) is a transliteration of Hebrew satan (H7854, "adversary"). The four-fold identification chain in Rev 20:2 confirms the subject is a non-human supernatural spirit being. Cross-references: Rev 12:9 provides the fullest identification: "the great dragon... that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world." The deception activity in 20:8 matches 12:9's "deceiveth the whole world." Gen 3:1 identifies the serpent as pre-human. Relationship to other evidence: Establishes the narrative context for Rev 20:10. The subject who is cast into the lake (v.10) is the same non-human entity released here.

docs.title: Rev 20:9 — Humans devoured by fire from heaven
docs.text: Context: The deceived nations surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Fire from God out of heaven devours them. Direct statement: Fire from God devours the human nations. Original language: katephagen (V-2AAI-3S from katesthio G2719) — aorist active indicative, "devoured." This is consumption/destruction vocabulary applied to human subjects. Cross-references: Ezek 38:22 describes fire and brimstone against Gog — the same Gog/Magog referenced here. The destruction vocabulary parallels the Sodom paradigm (Gen 19:24, Luke 17:29). Relationship to other evidence: The vocabulary distinction is critical. In v.9, human nations receive "devoured" (katephagen, destruction). In v.10, the non-human/symbolic trio receives "tormented" (basanisthesontai). Different vocabulary for different subjects in the same literary unit.

docs.title: Rev 20:10 — Devil, beast, false prophet tormented
docs.text: Context: The devil is cast into the lake of fire and brimstone where the beast and false prophet already are. All three are tormented day and night for ever and ever. Direct statement: The three named subjects — the devil, the beast, and the false prophet — are tormented (basanisthesontai) day and night unto the ages of the ages. Original language: basanisthesontai (V-FPI-3P from basanizo G928) — future passive indicative 3rd plural. The singular subject ho diabolos shifts to a plural verb to include the beast (to therion, G2342, neuter) and the false prophet (ho pseudoprophetes, G5578, masculine). hemeras kai nuktos (genitive of time) — "day and night." eis tous aionas ton aionon — "unto the ages of the ages." Cross-references: Rev 12:9 and 20:2 identify the devil as non-human. Rev 13:1-2 identifies the beast as a symbolic composite entity. Rev 19:20 identifies the false prophet as the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17. The torment formula (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) occurs only here in Scripture. Relationship to other evidence: This verse is the only place in the Bible that applies the "tormented for ever and ever" formula to any subject. All three subjects fail Tree 3 Gate 1 (Subject Gate): the devil is a non-human spirit being, the beast is a symbolic entity, and the false prophet is a symbolic entity.

docs.title: Rev 20:14 — Death and hades cast into lake; "this is the second death"
docs.text: Context: After the great white throne judgment (vv.11-13), death and hades are cast into the lake of fire. The text self-interprets: "This is the second death." Direct statement: Death and hades are cast into the lake of fire. The lake of fire is the second death. Original language: eblethēsan (V-API-3P from ballo G906) — aorist passive indicative 3rd plural. The predicate nominative: "houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin he limne tou pyros" — the X=Y symbol-decoding formula identifies the lake as "the second death." Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:26 — "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." Rev 21:4 — "there shall be no more death." Death personified as an enemy is destroyed when cast into the lake, resulting in the cessation of death itself. Relationship to other evidence: No torment vocabulary is applied to death, hades, or to humans in this verse. The self-interpreting formula defines the lake as a death concept, not a torment concept. The vocabulary distinction from v.10 (basanizo for non-human/symbolic entities) vs. v.14 (thanatos for the human outcome) is maintained.

docs.title: Rev 20:15 — Humans cast into the lake of fire
docs.text: Context: Those not found in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire. Direct statement: Humans not in the book of life are cast into the lake. Original language: eblethe (V-API-3S from ballo G906) — aorist passive indicative 3rd singular. Cross-references: Rev 21:8 lists eight categories of human wicked and assigns them "the second death." No torment formula is applied to any human category at the lake. Relationship to other evidence: When humans enter the lake, the text uses "cast into" and "second death" — not basanizo, not "day and night," not "for ever and ever." The vocabulary distinction between human and non-human/symbolic subjects is consistent throughout Rev 19-21.

docs.title: Rev 19:20 — Beast and false prophet cast alive into the lake
docs.text: Context: Battle of Armageddon conclusion. The beast is captured along with the false prophet (identified by matching vocabulary from Rev 13:13-14). Both are cast alive into the lake of fire. Direct statement: The beast and the false prophet are cast alive (zontes) into the lake of fire burning with brimstone. Original language: zontes (V-PAP-NPM from zao G2198) — present active participle, nominative plural masculine, "living/alive." eblethēsan (V-API-3P from ballo G906) — aorist passive indicative. The false prophet is identified by "ho poiesas ta semeia enopion autou" ("the one who wrought signs before him"), matching Rev 13:13-14. Cross-references: Rev 13:13-14 describes the earth beast performing signs (semeia) in the sight of the first beast. Rev 19:20 uses the same vocabulary to identify the false prophet as this entity. The beast and false prophet are cast "alive" — a different verb than what is applied to humans. Relationship to other evidence: In Rev 19:21, the human remnant is "slain" (apektanthesan, aorist passive from apokteino G615). The text uses different vocabulary for symbolic entities (cast alive) and humans (slain) in the same narrative.

docs.title: Rev 19:21 — Human remnant slain
docs.text: Context: Following the capture of beast and false prophet, the remaining human followers are slain by the sword proceeding from Christ's mouth. Direct statement: The remnant (hoi loipoi, the remaining humans) were slain (apektanthesan). Original language: apektanthesan (V-API-3P from apokteino G615) — aorist passive indicative 3rd plural, "were slain." Cross-references: This parallels Rev 20:9 where human followers of Satan are "devoured" (katephagen). In both cases, humans receive destruction vocabulary while the symbolic entities receive different treatment. Relationship to other evidence: The vocabulary differentiation within a single verse-pair (19:20 cast alive vs. 19:21 slain) is the clearest internal evidence that Revelation deliberately distinguishes what happens to symbolic entities from what happens to humans.

docs.title: Rev 12:9 — Four-fold identification: dragon = serpent = devil = Satan
docs.text: Context: War in heaven. Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, who is cast to earth. Direct statement: The great dragon is identified as "that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world." His angels are cast out with him. Original language: The four-fold articular apposition: ho drakon ho megas (the great dragon), ho ophis ho archaios (that old serpent), ho kaloumenos Diabolos kai ho Satanas (called the Devil and Satan). Each title carries non-human semantic content. "His angels" (hoi aggeloi autou) confirms command of angelic forces. Cross-references: Rev 20:2 restates this identification in the immediate context of Rev 20:10. Gen 3:1 identifies the serpent as pre-human. Eph 2:2 identifies the devil as "the spirit" (to pneuma) — a spirit being. Relationship to other evidence: This verse conclusively establishes that the devil of Rev 20:10 is not a human being but a supernatural spirit entity with angelic forces.

docs.title: Rev 20:2 — Restated identification in immediate context
docs.text: Context: Opening of the millennium. An angel binds the dragon for 1000 years. Direct statement: The angel lays hold on "the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan," and binds him for a thousand years. Original language: Same four-fold identification as 12:9, restated in the immediate chapter context of the crux verse. Cross-references: The binding of a supernatural being for 1000 years confirms non-human identity. Angel-on-spirit-being interaction is consistent throughout Scripture (cf. Jude 1:9, Michael and the devil). Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the subject of v.10 (ho diabolos) is the same non-human entity bound in v.2.

docs.title: Rev 13:1-2 — Sea beast: composite symbolic entity
docs.text: Context: John sees a beast rise from the sea with seven heads, ten horns, composite body parts from four Daniel 7 beasts (leopard, bear, lion in reverse order). The dragon gives the beast its authority. Direct statement: The beast has seven heads, ten horns, and body parts from multiple animals. The dragon gives it power, seat, and authority. Original language: therion (G2342, N-ASN) — neuter noun. The beast has kephalas hepta (seven heads) and kerata deka (ten horns). The composite body incorporates pardalis (leopard), arktos (bear), leon (lion) — Daniel 7's four beasts in reverse order. Cross-references: Dan 7:3-7 describes four separate beasts; Rev 13 combines all four into one. Rev 17:9-11 decodes the heads: seven heads = seven mountains = seven kings. Rev 17:8 describes the beast with a temporal existence pattern ("was, and is not, and shall ascend") that no single human can fulfill. Relationship to other evidence: The composite nature, multi-headed form, and centuries-spanning existence pattern make it impossible for the beast to be a literal human individual. This is the second subject of Rev 20:10.

docs.title: Rev 13:11-14 — Earth beast (= false prophet): symbolic characteristics
docs.text: Context: A second beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb and speech like a dragon. It exercises the first beast's authority, performs signs, deceives earth-dwellers, and commands image-worship. Direct statement: The earth beast has entirely symbolic characteristics: horns like a lamb, speaks as a dragon, exercises delegated authority, performs signs (semeia), makes fire come down from heaven. Original language: The vocabulary match with Rev 19:20 is exact: "poiei semeia megala" (13:13) corresponds to "poiesas ta semeia enopion autou" (19:20). Cross-references: Rev 19:20 explicitly identifies the false prophet by this matching vocabulary, confirming the earth beast IS the false prophet. Rev 16:13 places the false prophet in the counterfeit trinity alongside the dragon and beast. Relationship to other evidence: The false prophet of Rev 20:10 is this symbolic entity — not a generic human false prophet. No literal human has two horns like a lamb, speaks like a dragon, or gives breath to an image.

docs.title: Rev 17:8 — Beast "was, and is not, and shall ascend"
docs.text: Context: An angel explains the mystery of the beast to John. Direct statement: The beast "was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit, and go into perdition (apoleia)." Original language: en kai ouk estin kai mellei anabainein — a temporal existence pattern spanning multiple eras. Cross-references: Rev 17:9-11 further decodes: seven heads = seven mountains = seven kings, with the beast itself being "the eighth" and "of the seven." This multi-century, multi-kingdom existence is impossible for a single human individual. Relationship to other evidence: The beast goes into "perdition" (apoleia, G684) — destruction vocabulary. Even within Revelation's own description, the beast's destination is expressed with destruction terminology.

docs.title: Rev 16:13 — Counterfeit trinity as a unit
docs.text: Context: Sixth bowl plague. Three unclean spirits like frogs proceed from the dragon, beast, and false prophet. Direct statement: Three unclean spirits (pneumata tria akatharta) come from the mouths of the dragon, beast, and false prophet. Original language: pseudoprophetes (G5578) appears here as singular without the article — one of only three singular Revelation occurrences (16:13, 19:20, 20:10). Cross-references: The counterfeit trinity mirrors the divine Trinity: dragon (counterfeiting the Father), beast (counterfeiting the Son via the sphazo death-resurrection counterfeit), false prophet (counterfeiting the Spirit). Relationship to other evidence: All three members of the unholy trinity are non-human/symbolic entities. They function as a unit, and they receive the same fate as a unit in Rev 20:10.

docs.title: Rev 21:8 — Eight human categories: lake = second death
docs.text: Context: The new heaven and new earth. After describing the absence of death, sorrow, and pain (v.4), the text lists eight categories of wicked humans. Direct statement: The fearful, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, whoremongers, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars shall have their part in the lake burning with fire and brimstone, "which is the second death." Original language: Eight human categories, each a substantival adjective or noun describing human moral failures. The outcome: ho thanatos ho deuteros — "the second death." Cross-references: Rev 20:14-15 uses the same "second death" identification. Rom 6:23: "the wages of sin is death (thanatos)." The consistent term for human fate at the lake is death, not torment. Relationship to other evidence: This is the most comprehensive list of human categories at the lake of fire. For every human category, the outcome is "the second death." The basanizo/basanisthesontai formula is never applied to any human category.

docs.title: Rev 1:1 — Revelation "signified"
docs.text: Context: Opening verse of Revelation establishing the genre. Direct statement: God gave the revelation to Christ to show his servants things to come, and "he sent and signified it by his angel." Original language: esemanen (V-AAI-3S from semaino G4591) — "he communicated by signs/symbols." Cross-references: The verb semaino establishes the literary genre: apocalyptic vision communicated through symbolic imagery. This genre declaration applies to every passage in Revelation. Relationship to other evidence: For Tree 3 Gate 3 (Genre Gate), Revelation is classified as apocalyptic vision. Every positional candidate from Revelation passes through the Genre Gate, which requires symbolic/apocalyptic genre recognition.

docs.title: Heb 2:14 — Christ destroys the one having the power of death — the devil
docs.text: Context: Didactic epistle discussing Christ's incarnation. Christ took on flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy the devil. Direct statement: Christ became human "that through death he might destroy (katargese) him that had the power of death, that is, the devil." Original language: katargese (V-AAS-3S from katargeo G2673) — aorist active subjunctive, "might destroy/render powerless." The purpose clause (hina + subjunctive) states the goal of Christ's incarnation. ton diabolon (A-ASM from diabolos G1228) — the devil explicitly identified by the touto estin formula. Cross-references: 1 Cor 15:26 uses the same verb (katargeo) for the destruction of death. 1 John 3:8: "to destroy (luo) the works of the devil." Relationship to other evidence: Even the supernatural entity (the devil) receives destruction vocabulary in a didactic epistle — not torment vocabulary. The genre is didactic (higher weight under SIS than apocalyptic).

docs.title: Matt 25:41 — Eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels
docs.text: Context: Sheep and goats judgment. Jesus addresses those on the left. Direct statement: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels." Original language: to pur to aionion to hetoimasmenon to diabolo kai tois aggelois autou — the fire was "prepared" (hetoimasmenon, perfect passive participle from hetoimazo) for the devil and his angels. The primary designation is for non-human entities. Cross-references: Rev 20:10 describes the devil being cast into this same fire/lake. Matt 25:46 uses kolasis (G2851, judicial punishment), NOT basanizo (G928) — different vocabulary from Rev 20:10. Relationship to other evidence: The fire was originally designated for non-human entities (the devil and his angels). Humans are sent there secondarily. The vocabulary here is kolasis, not basanizo.

docs.title: 1 John 3:8 — Son of God manifested to destroy the devil's works
docs.text: Context: Johannine didactic epistle. Direct statement: The devil sinneth from the beginning. The Son of God was manifested "that he might destroy (luse) the works of the devil." Original language: luse (V-AAS-3S from luo G3089) — "might destroy/dissolve." ap arches ("from the beginning") — the devil's activity predates human history. Cross-references: Heb 2:14 uses katargeo; 1 John uses luo. Both are destruction verbs applied to the devil or his works. Gen 3:15 — the proto-evangelium promises the serpent's head will be crushed. Relationship to other evidence: Destruction vocabulary for the devil's works appears in multiple didactic contexts — a genre with higher interpretive weight than apocalyptic.

docs.title: Matt 8:29 — Demons anticipate basanizo
docs.text: Context: Gadarene demoniacs. The demons cry out to Jesus. Direct statement: "Art thou come hither to torment (basanisai) us before the time?" Original language: basanisai (V-AAN from basanizo G928) — aorist active infinitive. The demons use basanizo for what they expect from Jesus. "Before the time" (pro kairou) — a time-bounded expectation. Cross-references: Mark 5:7 and Luke 8:28 are Synoptic parallels. All three record demons using basanizo for their anticipated fate. Relationship to other evidence: This is the only Gospel occurrence of basanizo in a judgment context, and the speakers are demons — non-human spirit beings — describing their own expected fate. Basanizo in judgment contexts originates in demonic speech, not in didactic teaching about human destiny.

docs.title: Matt 14:24 — Ship "tossed" (basanizo) by waves
docs.text: Context: Jesus walks on water. The ship is battered by waves. Direct statement: The ship was "tossed" (basanizomenon) with waves. Original language: basanizomenon (V-PPP-NSN from basanizo G928) — present passive participle, neuter singular. Applied to a ship (ploion, neuter) — an inanimate object. Cross-references: Mark 6:48 uses basanizo for the disciples "toiling" in rowing. Relationship to other evidence: Basanizo applied to an inanimate object proves the word does not inherently require consciousness or punishment. The KJV translates it "tossed" — recognizing the broader semantic range.

docs.title: Mark 5:7 — Demon begs "torment me not"
docs.text: Context: Gerasene demoniac, Markan parallel. Direct statement: The demon adjures Jesus "by God, that thou torment me not." Original language: basanises (V-AAS-2S from basanizo G928) — aorist active subjunctive. Parallel to Matt 8:29 and Luke 8:28. Cross-references: All three Synoptics record this encounter with basanizo. The pattern is consistent: demons use basanizo for their anticipated judgment. Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the pattern that basanizo in judgment contexts appears in demonic speech about their own fate.

docs.title: Mark 6:48 — Disciples "toiling" (basanizo) in rowing
docs.text: Context: Disciples struggle against the wind on the sea. Direct statement: Jesus saw them "toiling" (basanizomenous) in rowing. Original language: basanizomenous (V-PPP-APM from basanizo G928) — present passive participle, accusative plural masculine. Applied to physical exertion. Cross-references: Parallel to Matt 14:24 (ship tossed). Both non-judgment uses of basanizo. Relationship to other evidence: Another non-judgment occurrence confirming basanizo's broad semantic range: physical strain, not punishment.

docs.title: Luke 8:28 — Demon begs "torment me not" (Lukan parallel)
docs.text: Context: Lukan parallel to the Gerasene demoniac. Direct statement: The demon cries out, "I beseech thee, torment me not." Original language: basanises (from basanizo G928). Third Synoptic parallel. Cross-references: Matt 8:29, Mark 5:7. Relationship to other evidence: Completes the Synoptic triad of demonic basanizo usage.

docs.title: 2 Pet 2:8 — Lot "vexed" (basanizo) his soul
docs.text: Context: Peter's epistle uses Lot as an example. Lot's righteous soul was vexed by Sodom's wickedness. Direct statement: The righteous man "vexed (ebasanizen) his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds." Original language: ebasanizen (V-IAI-3S from basanizo G928) — imperfect active indicative, "was vexing/tormenting." Applied to moral distress experienced by a righteous man. Cross-references: This is the only basanizo occurrence in any epistle. The context is moral distress, not divine punishment. "From day to day" (hemeras ex hemeras) uses a day-based temporal formula similar to Rev 20:10's "day and night." Relationship to other evidence: The sole epistle occurrence of basanizo describes moral distress, not eschatological torment. This confirms that basanizo's NT semantic range extends well beyond punishment.

docs.title: Rev 9:5 — Basanizo with explicit five-month time limit
docs.text: Context: Fifth trumpet. Locust-like beings from the abyss are given permission to torment for five months. Direct statement: "They should be tormented (basanisthesontai) five months." Original language: basanisthesontai (V-FPI-3P from basanizo G928) — same morphological form as Rev 20:10. menas pente (accusative of duration) — five months. edothe (divine passive from didomi) — God's sovereign permission. Cross-references: Rev 20:10 uses the same verb form but with "day and night for ever and ever" instead of "five months." The explicit time limit here demonstrates that basanizo does not carry inherent duration — it requires modifiers. Relationship to other evidence: The word itself is neutral on duration. In Rev 9:5 it is explicitly time-bounded; in Rev 20:10 it has the ages-of-ages formula. The duration depends on the modifier, not on the word.

docs.title: Rev 12:2 — Woman "pained" (basanizo) in childbirth
docs.text: Context: The woman clothed with the sun in labor. Direct statement: She was "pained (basanizomene) to be delivered." Original language: basanizomene (V-PPP-NSF from basanizo G928) — present passive participle, feminine singular. Applied to a positive symbolic figure (the woman representing God's people). Cross-references: Within Revelation itself, basanizo is used for childbirth pain — a non-judgment, non-punitive context. Relationship to other evidence: This occurrence proves that basanizo in Revelation does not always mean eschatological torment. The word appears in Revelation for childbirth pain, prophetic witness (11:10), time-limited scorpion torment (9:5), and eschatological judgment (14:10, 20:10).

docs.title: Rev 11:10 — Two prophets "tormented" earth-dwellers
docs.text: Context: The two witnesses' ministry distressed those dwelling on earth. Direct statement: "These two prophets tormented (ebasanisan) them that dwelt on the earth." Original language: ebasanisan (V-AAI-3P from basanizo G928) — aorist active indicative. The prophets' message caused distress to earth-dwellers — prophetic ministry, not eschatological punishment. Cross-references: This non-judgment Revelation use of basanizo further broadens the word's semantic range within the book. Relationship to other evidence: Another non-judgment use of basanizo within Revelation itself.

docs.title: Rev 14:10-11 — Beast-worshippers: torment with fire, smoke ascending
docs.text: Context: Third angel's message. The fate of those who worship the beast. Direct statement: The beast-worshipper "shall be tormented (basanisthesetai) with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb." The smoke of their basanismos "ascendeth up for ever and ever." Original language: basanisthesetai (V-FPI-3S from basanizo G928) — future passive indicative 3rd singular. kapnos tou basanismou auton (the smoke of their torment) — the "for ever" formula applies to the smoke, not directly to the torment. The etc7-11 study analyzed this passage in depth. Cross-references: Rev 19:3 uses the identical formula for Babylon's smoke, and Rev 18:21-23 describes Babylon as "found no more at all." Isa 34:9-10 uses identical language for Edom's ended fire. Relationship to other evidence: (Examined in depth in etc7-11-smoke-ascending-forever.) The smoke formula draws on Isa 34:10 and can describe a permanent result rather than an ongoing process.

docs.title: Rev 19:3 — Babylon's smoke rises "for ever and ever"
docs.text: Context: After Babylon's fall. Direct statement: "Her smoke rose up for ever and ever (eis tous aionas ton aionon)." Original language: Same formula as Rev 20:10 and 14:11. Cross-references: Rev 18:21-23 describes Babylon with fivefold "no more at all" cessation language. The entity whose smoke rises "for ever" is explicitly described as having ceased to exist. Relationship to other evidence: Demonstrates that the "for ever and ever" formula can describe a permanent, irreversible result of destruction, not an ongoing process. The formula's meaning is subject-determined.

docs.title: Isa 14:12-15 — Morning star brought down to sheol
docs.text: Context: Isaiah's taunt against the king of Babylon, with language transcending any human king. Direct statement: "How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer (heylel)... thou shalt be brought down to hell (sheol), to the sides of the pit." Original language: heylel (H1966) — hapax legomenon, "morning star/shining one." napalta (Qal perfect 2ms from naphal) — "you have fallen." nigdatta (Niphal perfect 2ms from gada) — "you are cut off." Cross-references: Luke 10:18 — Jesus: "I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven." The NT applies this pattern to Satan. Relationship to other evidence: The OT describes the Satan-figure's fate as descent and humiliation, not ongoing torment. The vocabulary is fall/cut off/descent to sheol and pit.

docs.title: Ezek 28:14-19 — Anointed cherub becomes ashes, "never any more"
docs.text: Context: Oracle against the king of Tyre, with language transcending any human king — "anointed cherub," "upon the holy mountain of God," "perfect from the day created." Direct statement: "I will bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth... thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more." Original language: kerub (H3742) — cherub, an angelic being. akal (Qal perfect 3fs from akal) — "devour/consume." epher (H665) — "ashes/dust." eneka (ain + 2ms, "you are not") plus ad olam (H5769, "unto eternity") — absolute cessation: "you are not unto eternity." Cross-references: This is the same entity described in Rev 20:10 as "tormented for ever and ever." In Ezek 28, that entity becomes ashes and exists no more — absolute destruction language. Relationship to other evidence: This is the most striking cross-testament parallel. The OT describes the Satan-figure with destruction/cessation vocabulary (ashes, devour, never any more), while Rev 20:10 uses torment vocabulary for the same being. Under SIS principles, the didactic/prophetic Ezekiel passage (direct divine speech: "I will bring forth fire") has higher genre weight than the apocalyptic vision of Revelation.

docs.title: Isa 34:9-10 — Edom's smoke "shall go up for ever"
docs.text: Context: Oracle against Edom. Direct statement: "It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever (le-olam)." Yet Isa 34:11-17 describes animals inhabiting the ruins. Original language: le-olam (H5769) — "for ever." laylah va-yomam — "night nor day," paralleling Rev 20:10's "day and night." Cross-references: The identical language ("for ever," "night nor day," "not quenched") appears in Rev 20:10. Edom is demonstrably not still burning — animals dwell in the ruins (Isa 34:11-17). Relationship to other evidence: Establishes the OT precedent: "for ever" smoke language describes a permanent result (total devastation), not an ongoing process (still burning). This directly informs the meaning of the same formula in Rev 20:10.

docs.title: Dan 7:11 — Fourth beast slain, body destroyed, given to burning flame
docs.text: Context: Daniel's vision of four beasts. The fourth beast receives judgment. Direct statement: "I beheld even till the beast was slain, and his body destroyed, and given to the burning flame." Original language: Aramaic: qetilat (from qetal, "to kill/slay"). geshmah hoobad (body was destroyed). yehibat liqedat esha (given to the burning of fire). Cross-references: Revelation's beast is the conceptual successor to Daniel 7's fourth beast. The OT uses destruction vocabulary (slain, body destroyed, given to burning) for symbolic beast-entities. Relationship to other evidence: The OT paradigm for symbolic beast-powers is destruction, not eternal torment. Daniel 7's beast is slain and destroyed; Revelation's beast is cast into the lake. The vocabulary shift from destruction to torment occurs only in Revelation's apocalyptic framework.

docs.title: Rev 18:21-23 — Babylon "found no more at all"
docs.text: Context: Fall of Babylon. Direct statement: Babylon shall be "found no more at all," with fivefold cessation (found, heard, found, shine, heard — each "no more at all"). Original language: ou me heurethe eti — emphatic double negative with eti (anymore). Repeated five times for absolute cessation. Cross-references: Rev 19:3 says Babylon's smoke rises "for ever and ever." The coexistence of total cessation language and "forever" smoke language proves the formula describes a permanent result of destruction. Relationship to other evidence: The same formula applied to Babylon (Rev 19:3) is applied to the devil/beast/false prophet (Rev 20:10). Babylon's case demonstrates the formula describes permanent destruction.

docs.title: Gen 3:1 — The serpent pre-human
docs.text: Context: Garden of Eden. The serpent exists before any human sin. Direct statement: "The serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made." Original language: nachash (H5175) — serpent. A created being distinct from humanity, existing before human sin. Cross-references: Rev 12:9 and 20:2 identify "that old serpent" as the Devil and Satan. The serpent's pre-human existence confirms the devil is not and never has been a human being. Relationship to other evidence: Establishes the pre-human origin of the entity named in Rev 20:10 as "the devil."

docs.title: Eph 2:2 — Devil as "the spirit" — spirit being
docs.text: Context: Paul describes the believer's former walk. Direct statement: They walked "according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit (to pneuma) that now worketh in the children of disobedience." Original language: to pneuma — "the spirit." The devil is explicitly called a spirit being. Cross-references: Combined with Rev 12:9 (dragon/serpent), Gen 3:1 (pre-human serpent), Ezek 28:14 (cherub), this establishes the devil's ontological category: non-human spirit being. Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the devil is not a human for Tree 3 Gate 1 purposes.

docs.title: 1 Cor 15:26 — Last enemy destroyed is death
docs.text: Context: Paul's resurrection chapter. Direct statement: "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." Original language: katargeitai (V-PPI-3S from katargeo G2673) — present passive indicative, "is being destroyed/abolished." Same verb as Heb 2:14. Cross-references: Rev 20:14 — death cast into lake of fire. Rev 21:4 — "no more death." The lake destroys death. Relationship to other evidence: The result of casting death into the lake is its destruction and cessation. The lake functions as an instrument of destruction.

docs.title: Rom 6:23 — Wages of sin is death
docs.text: Context: Pauline didactic epistle. Direct statement: "The wages of sin is death (thanatos); but the gift of God is eternal life." Original language: thanatos (G2288) — same noun as "second death" in Rev 20:14 and 21:8. The contrast is death vs. eternal life. Cross-references: Rev 20:14, 21:8. The didactic contrast is death vs. life, not torment vs. life. Relationship to other evidence: The cross-genre, didactic statement defines sin's consequence as death, using the same word that defines the human outcome at the lake.

docs.title: Luke 17:29 — Jesus interprets Sodom fire: "destroyed them all"
docs.text: Context: Jesus' eschatological discourse. Direct statement: "It rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed (apolesen) them all." Original language: apolesen (V-AAI-3S from apollymi G622) — "destroyed." Jesus uses destruction vocabulary for the fire-and-brimstone paradigm. Cross-references: Gen 19:24 — the original event. 2 Pet 2:6 — "turned to ashes." Jude 1:7 — "eternal fire." Relationship to other evidence: Jesus himself interprets fire and brimstone as destruction, not ongoing torment. This is a didactic saying with higher genre weight than apocalyptic vision.

docs.title: 2 Pet 2:4, 6 — Angels cast to Tartarus; Sodom turned to ashes
docs.text: Context: Peter's examples of divine judgment. Direct statement: Angels that sinned are cast to Tartarus, reserved for judgment. Sodom is turned to ashes, "an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly." Original language: tephrosas (V-AAP-NSM from tephroo G5077) — "having turned to ashes." hupodeigma (G5262) — "example." Cross-references: Peter explicitly calls Sodom's destruction by fire an example for future ungodly judgment. The result was ashes, not ongoing torment. Relationship to other evidence: The inspired interpretation of "eternal fire" (Jude 1:7) producing "ashes" (2 Pet 2:6) informs the meaning of fire-and-brimstone language throughout Scripture.

docs.title: Jude 1:6-7 — Angels in chains; Sodom's "eternal fire"
docs.text: Context: Jude parallels 2 Peter 2. Direct statement: Angels kept in "everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day." Sodom suffers "the vengeance of eternal fire (puros aioniou)." Original language: puros aioniou — "eternal fire." Yet the fire produced ashes (2 Pet 2:6), not ongoing burning. Cross-references: The "eternal" quality of the fire describes the permanence of its result, not the duration of the process. Relationship to other evidence: Demonstrates that "eternal fire" in biblical usage produces permanent destruction, not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Mal 4:1 — Wicked become stubble, burned up completely
docs.text: Context: OT prophetic eschatology. Direct statement: "All that do wickedly shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up... it shall leave them neither root nor branch." Original language: qash (H7179) — stubble (quickly consumed). "Neither root nor branch" — nothing remains. Cross-references: This OT eschatological language describes total consumption of human wicked — not ongoing torment. Relationship to other evidence: OT prophetic vocabulary for human eschatological fate is destruction/consumption, consistent across genres.

docs.title: Obad 1:16 — Wicked "as though they had not been"
docs.text: Context: Obadiah's prophecy against Edom and the nations. Direct statement: "They shall be as though they had not been." Original language: kelo hayu — "as though they had not been." Absolute cessation language. Cross-references: Psa 37:10 — "the wicked shall not be." Relationship to other evidence: Cessation language for human wicked in non-apocalyptic prophecy.

docs.title: Psa 37:10 — Wicked "shall not be"
docs.text: Context: Wisdom psalm. Direct statement: "Yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be." Original language: enenu (ain + 3ms suffix) — "he is not." Same negative existential construction as Ezek 28:19 for the Satan-figure. Cross-references: Obad 1:16. Relationship to other evidence: The same "not be" language is used for both human wicked (Psa 37:10) and the Satan-figure (Ezek 28:19).

docs.title: Matt 7:15 — Generic false prophets (plural)
docs.text: Context: Sermon on the Mount. Direct statement: "Beware of false prophets (pseudoprophetai), which come to you in sheep's clothing." Original language: pseudopropheton (G5578, genitive plural) — a class of human deceivers. Cross-references: Matt 24:11 — "many false prophets shall rise." The plural form refers to a generic class of humans, distinct from Revelation's singular apocalyptic entity. Relationship to other evidence: The plural/singular distinction confirms the false prophet of Rev 20:10 is not a member of the generic human class but a specific symbolic entity.

docs.title: Matt 24:11 — Many false prophets (plural)
docs.text: Context: Olivet discourse. Direct statement: "Many false prophets (pseudoprophetai, plural) shall rise." Cross-references: The plural form across the Gospels refers to a class of human individuals. Revelation's singular form refers to one specific entity. Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the plural/singular distinction.

docs.title: Acts 13:6 — Bar-Jesus, a human false prophet (singular)
docs.text: Context: Paul's first missionary journey. Direct statement: "They found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus." Original language: pseudopropheten (G5578, accusative singular) — with a definite article and personal name. A specific human individual.
