Cross-references: This is the one singular occurrence outside Revelation — but with a personal name (Bar-Jesus) and Jewish ethnicity, making it clearly a specific human individual, not an apocalyptic entity. Relationship to other evidence: Even the singular usage outside Revelation is identifiably human. Revelation's singular usage is identifiably symbolic (Rev 19:20 identification key).

docs.title: 1 John 4:1 — Many false prophets (plural)
docs.text: Context: Johannine epistle. Direct statement: "Many false prophets (pseudoprophetai, plural) are gone out into the world." Cross-references: Same plural pattern as Matt 7:15, 24:11. Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the consistent plural = class of humans pattern.

docs.title: Rev 4:9-10 — "For ever and ever" for God
docs.text: Context: Throne room vision. Direct statement: God "liveth for ever and ever (eis tous aionas ton aionon)." Original language: Same formula as Rev 20:10. Applied to God's existence — genuinely endless. Cross-references: The formula appears approximately 13 times in Revelation. Applied to God, it is genuinely eternal. Relationship to other evidence: Establishes the baseline: when applied to the eternal God, the formula means genuinely eternal. The formula's meaning is demonstrably subject-determined.

docs.title: Matt 18:34 — Basanistes (tormentors) in parable
docs.text: Context: Parable of the unforgiving servant. Direct statement: The lord "delivered him to the tormentors (basanistais)." Original language: basanistais (N-DPM from basanistes G930) — dative plural, "to the tormentors/jailers." Cross-references: The one occurrence of basanistes is in a parable — subject to Genre Gate (Tree 3 Gate 3: parabolic). Relationship to other evidence: Completes the basanizo word family. The agent noun appears only in a parable, not in didactic teaching about eschatological fate.

docs.title: Matt 8:6 — Servant "grievously tormented" (basanizo)
docs.text: Context: Centurion's servant ill with paralysis. Direct statement: "My servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented." Original language: basanizomenos (from basanizo G928) — physical illness, not punishment. Cross-references: Matt 4:24 uses basanizo similarly for physical diseases. Relationship to other evidence: Non-judgment use of basanizo for physical suffering.

docs.title: Rev 14:11 — Smoke ascending "for ever and ever"
docs.text: Context: Third angel's message (continued from 14:10). Direct statement: "The smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night." Original language: Same "ages of ages" formula. (Examined in depth in etc7-11-smoke-ascending-forever.) Cross-references: Isa 34:10 uses identical "for ever" smoke language for Edom (not still burning). Rev 19:3 uses it for Babylon (found no more). Relationship to other evidence: Cross-reference to etc7-11 findings: the formula draws on OT paradigm of permanent results from completed destruction.

docs.title: Gen 19:24 — Sodom destroyed by fire and brimstone
docs.text: Context: Original fire-and-brimstone judgment. Direct statement: "The LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven." Cross-references: Luke 17:29 — Jesus: "destroyed them all." 2 Pet 2:6 — "turned to ashes." Jude 1:7 — "eternal fire." Relationship to other evidence: The paradigmatic fire-and-brimstone event produces total destruction, ashes, and cessation — not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Rev 13:3 — Beast's deadly wound healed
docs.text: Context: One of the beast's heads receives a deadly wound that heals. Direct statement: "One of his heads as it were wounded to death; and his deadly wound was healed." Original language: esphagmenen (from sphazo G4969) — same verb as Rev 5:6 (Lamb slain). Counterfeit death-and-resurrection pattern. Cross-references: The beast counterfeits Christ through shared sphago vocabulary. A seven-headed entity with a healing mortal wound is symbolic, not literal. Relationship to other evidence: Further confirms the beast as a symbolic entity, not a literal human.

docs.title: Rev 17:9-11 — Seven heads decoded
docs.text: Context: Angel interprets beast symbolism. Direct statement: "The seven heads are seven mountains, on which the woman sitteth. And there are seven kings." Original language: Self-interpreting X=Y formula. heads = mountains = kings. Multi-layered symbolism spanning multiple kingdoms and eras. Cross-references: The beast spans multiple kingdoms. No single human fulfills this. Relationship to other evidence: The self-interpretation confirms the beast as a symbolic composite representing successive political-religious powers.

docs.title: 2 Pet 2:6 — Sodom turned to ashes
docs.text: Context: Peter's example of divine judgment. Direct statement: "Turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample." Cross-references: The inspired interpretation: fire and brimstone produces ashes. Relationship to other evidence: Peter calls ashes-producing destruction "an ensample" for future judgment.

docs.title: Jude 1:7 — Sodom's "eternal fire" — yet destroyed
docs.text: Context: Jude's example. Direct statement: Sodom suffers "the vengeance of eternal fire." Cross-references: 2 Pet 2:6 — ashes. Relationship to other evidence: "Eternal fire" produces ashes, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Rev 20:1-3 — Satan bound
docs.text: Context: Angel binds Satan for 1000 years. Direct statement: Four-fold identification: dragon, old serpent, Devil, Satan. Bound a thousand years, cast into the bottomless pit. Cross-references: Rev 12:9 provides the same identification. Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the supernatural, non-human identity of the entity named in v.10.

docs.title: Pattern 1: Consistent vocabulary differentiation between human and non-human/symbolic subjects
docs.text:
Throughout Rev 19-21, the text uses distinct vocabulary for distinct subjects: - Humans: devoured (katephagen, 20:9), slain (apektanthesan, 19:21), second death (20:14-15, 21:8) - Non-human/symbolic entities: cast alive (zontes, 19:20), tormented (basanisthesontai, 20:10) - Personified abstractions (death/hades): cast into (eblethēsan, 20:14)

This vocabulary differentiation is consistent across multiple passages and is a neutral observation both sides must acknowledge.

docs.title: Pattern 2: Basanizo judgment uses confined to apocalyptic framework and demonic speech
docs.text: Of the 12 NT occurrences of basanizo: 7 are non-judgment (illness, waves, rowing, moral distress, childbirth, prophetic witness). The 5 judgment uses are all either in Revelation's apocalyptic framework (Rev 9:5, 14:10, 20:10) or involve demons speaking of their own future (Matt 8:29, Mark 5:7, Luke 8:28). No epistle, Gospel didactic section, or OT passage uses basanizo for human eschatological fate.

docs.title: Pattern 3: OT destruction vocabulary for the same entities
docs.text: The OT describes the Satan-figure with destruction/cessation vocabulary: - Isa 14:12-15: fallen, cut off, brought down to sheol - Ezek 28:18-19: fire devours, becomes ashes, "never any more" - Dan 7:11: beast slain, body destroyed, given to burning flame

docs.title: Pattern 4: The "for ever" formula is subject-determined
docs.text: The eis tous aionas ton aionon formula in Revelation: - Applied to God: genuinely eternal (9x) - Applied to saints' reign: genuinely eternal (1x) - Applied to judgment: parallels OT usage where identical language describes ended events (Isa 34:9-10, Edom; Rev 19:3, Babylon "found no more")

docs.title: Pattern 5: Destruction vocabulary spans all genres; torment vocabulary is genre-specific
docs.text: Destruction/death vocabulary for the fate of the wicked appears in OT prophets (Mal 4:1, Obad 1:16), wisdom literature (Psa 37:10), Pauline epistles (Rom 6:23, 1 Cor 15:26), Johannine epistles (1 John 3:8), Petrine epistles (2 Pet 2:6), and Jesus' own words (Luke 17:29). Torment vocabulary for judgment appears only in Revelation's apocalyptic framework and in demonic speech.

docs.title: Basanizo (G928) — 12 occurrences
docs.text:
The word derives from basanos (G931), a touchstone for testing the purity of metals. The metaphorical extension to "torment" is secondary. The KJV translators recognized the semantic breadth, using five different English words: tormented, tossed, toiling, vexed, pained.

The non-judgment uses (7 of 12) reveal the word's broader range: physical illness (Matt 4:24, 8:6), ship battered by waves (Matt 14:24), physical exertion in rowing (Mark 6:48), moral distress (2 Pet 2:8), childbirth pain (Rev 12:2), prophetic distress (Rev 11:10). The application to an inanimate ship (Matt 14:24) demonstrates the word does not inherently require conscious experience of punishment.

docs.title: Basanismos (G929) — 6 occurrences
docs.text: All 6 occurrences are in Revelation. Time-bounded in 4 of 6: five months (Rev 9:5) and one hour for Babylon (Rev 18:7, 10, 15). The word family is genre-specific.

docs.title: Basanos (G931) — 3 occurrences
docs.text: The root noun. Physical diseases (Matt 4:24) and parabolic context (Luke 16:23, 28). The etymological base confirms the testing/examination root meaning.

docs.title: Basanistes (G930) — 1 occurrence
docs.text: The agent noun. One occurrence in a parable (Matt 18:34). No occurrences in didactic teaching.

docs.title: Therion (G2342) — 46 occurrences
docs.text: 38 of 46 in Revelation. In Revelation, therion is always the apocalyptic beast-entity. The concentration confirms "the beast" is a technical term in Revelation for the symbolic political-religious power.

docs.title: Pseudoprophetes (G5578) — 11 occurrences
docs.text: Singular in Revelation (3x: 16:13, 19:20, 20:10) = one specific apocalyptic entity. Plural elsewhere (7x) = class of human deceivers. Acts 13:6 is singular outside Revelation but with a personal name (Bar-Jesus). The distinction is clear and consistent.

docs.title: Diabolos (G1228) — 38 occurrences
docs.text: The proper-name uses (always articular/singular) refer to the supernatural adversary. Identified as: dragon, old serpent, spirit being (Eph 2:2), pre-human (Gen 3:1), commander of angels (Matt 25:41), subject of destruction (Heb 2:14, katargeo; 1 John 3:8, luo).

docs.title: Katargeo (G2673) — 32 occurrences
docs.text: Applied to the devil (Heb 2:14) and to death (1 Cor 15:26). The semantic range includes abolish, render powerless, destroy. Regardless of the exact nuance, the verb is destruction-class vocabulary, not torment-class.

docs.title: OT → NT: Satan-figure's fate
docs.text: Ezek 28:18-19 (ashes, never any more) → Rev 20:10 (tormented for ever). The same entity receives destruction vocabulary in the OT prophetic oracle and torment vocabulary in the NT apocalyptic vision. Under SIS principles, the prophetic direct divine speech ("I will bring forth fire... I will bring thee to ashes") has higher genre weight than apocalyptic symbolism.

docs.title: OT → NT: "For ever" smoke formula
docs.text: Isa 34:9-10 (Edom, smoke ascending forever, not quenched day nor night) → Rev 14:11 (smoke ascending for ever), Rev 19:3 (Babylon's smoke for ever), Rev 20:10 (tormented for ever). The OT paradigm shows this formula describes permanent results of completed destruction.

docs.title: OT → NT: Fire-and-brimstone paradigm
docs.text: Gen 19:24 (Sodom destroyed) → Luke 17:29 (Jesus: "destroyed them all") → 2 Pet 2:6 (turned to ashes) → Jude 1:7 (eternal fire, yet ashes) → Rev 19:20, 20:10 (lake of fire and brimstone). The paradigm consistently produces destruction and ashes.

docs.title: OT → NT: Symbolic beast destruction
docs.text: Dan 7:11 (fourth beast slain, body destroyed, given to burning) → Rev 13:1-2 (composite beast from Daniel 7) → Rev 19:20 (beast cast into lake) → Rev 20:10 (beast "tormented"). The OT paradigm for symbolic beast-powers is destruction.

docs.title: Rev 14:10-11 — Beast-worshippers and the torment formula
docs.text: This is the closest the text comes to applying torment vocabulary to human subjects. The beast-worshippers are human individuals who "shall be tormented with fire and brimstone." Two points complicate a straightforward reading: (1) the passage is in Revelation's apocalyptic framework (Genre Gate), and (2) the "for ever and ever" formula applies to the smoke of their torment, not directly to the torment itself. The etc7-11 study analyzed this passage in depth and classified all Revelation-sourced positional candidates as Neutral via the Genre Gate. The passage remains a key I-B item requiring SIS resolution.

docs.title: The "same lake" argument
docs.text: All three non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet), the personified death/hades, and unsaved humans end up in the same lake of fire. The argument: if the lake is the same destination, the experience must be the same for all. Against this: the text itself differentiates vocabulary (devoured, slain, second death for humans vs. tormented for non-human/symbolic entities). Different subjects receive different descriptions at the same destination. The text's own vocabulary argues against automatic transfer.

docs.title: The "beast-as-representative" counter-argument
docs.text: The beast represents a system composed of human adherents. Does the torment of the beast-symbol transfer to the humans within that system? The text addresses this directly: Rev 19:20-21 has the beast and false prophet cast alive into the lake, while the human adherents are slain. Rev 20:9 has human followers of Satan devoured while Satan himself receives the torment formula. Rev 21:8 assigns the human wicked "the second death." The text consistently applies different vocabulary to the system and to the humans within it.

docs.title: Katargeo ambiguity (Heb 2:14)
docs.text: Katargeo has a broad semantic range (abolish, render powerless, destroy). Whether Christ "destroys" the devil or "renders him powerless" is a genuine lexical question. However, regardless of the exact nuance, the verb is in the destruction/cessation category, not the torment category. The didactic epistle describes the devil's fate with destruction-class vocabulary.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The evidence consistently distinguishes between the subjects of Rev 20:10 and human beings at three levels:

  1. Subject identification: All three subjects of the "tormented for ever and ever" formula are non-human or symbolic: the devil (supernatural spirit being), the beast (symbolic political-religious system), the false prophet (symbolic entity = earth beast of Rev 13:11-17). None is a literal human being.

  2. Vocabulary differentiation: The text uses distinct vocabulary for distinct subjects — humans receive destruction/death vocabulary (devoured, slain, second death); non-human/symbolic entities receive torment vocabulary. This distinction is maintained across Rev 19-21.

  3. Cross-genre distribution: Destruction/death vocabulary for the fate of the wicked spans all genres and all authors (OT prophets, wisdom, Gospels, epistles). Torment vocabulary for judgment appears only in Revelation's apocalyptic framework and in demonic speech.

Under the Tree 3 Subject Gate, all three subjects of Rev 20:10 automatically FAIL Gate 1 (not literal human beings). Under the Genre Gate, the passage automatically FAILS Gate 3 (apocalyptic vision per Rev 1:1 semaino). These gate failures do not automatically make the verse Neutral — the reclassification process (Tree 3 Step 3) determines the corrected positional classification.

Analysis completed: 2026-06-04

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Rev 20:10 -- named subjects (devil, beast, false prophet). Applied to humans or supernatural/symbolic entities? Basanizo (G928) usage. Apply Tree 3 subject gate.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G928-basanizo.md

Occurrences: 12

Verb from G931 basanos (touchstone for testing metals). 12 tokens in 12 verses across 6 books. Translation: 'torment' family 7/12 (58.3%); remaining 5 renderings (tossed, toiling, vexed, pained) reveal broader semantic range. Gospels: 6x (physical suffering, demonic encounters). Epistles: 1x (moral distress). Revelation: 5x (eschatological contexts). The 7 non-judgment uses (illness, waves, rowing, distress, childbirth) outnumber the 5 judgment uses. All 5 judgment uses are either in Revelation's apocalyptic framework or involve demons speaking of their own future. No epistle, no Gospel didactic section, and no OT passage uses basanizo for the final fate of generic human wicked.

Semantic categories: physical illness/suffering, physical distress/battering, moral distress, demonic anticipation of judgment, eschatological judgment (apocalyptic)

Key verses: Matt 8:29, Matt 14:24, 2 Pet 2:8, Rev 9:5, Rev 14:10, Rev 20:10, Rev 12:2

Relevance: THE core verb in Rev 20:10. basanisthesontai (V-FPI-3P) is the torment formula. The complete NT distribution shows the word's judgment uses are confined to Revelation's apocalyptic framework and demonic speech. The non-judgment uses demonstrate the word's broader semantic range, preventing the interpretive error of reading only the 'eternal torment' sense.

docs.title: G929 — basanismos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G929-basanismos.md

Occurrences: 6

Noun from G928. 6 occurrences, ALL in Revelation. Three semantic categories: demonic/supernatural torment (Rev 9:5, time-bounded at 5 months), eschatological judgment torment (Rev 14:11), commercial/imperial torment (Rev 18:7, 10, 15 — Babylon's fall, time-bounded at 'one hour'). Time-bounded in 4 of 6 occurrences. The word family's exclusive concentration in Revelation's apocalyptic framework is a key distributional observation.

Semantic categories: demonic/supernatural torment, eschatological judgment, commercial/imperial torment

Key verses: Rev 9:5, Rev 14:11, Rev 18:7, Rev 18:10, Rev 18:15

Relevance: Noun form of the basanizo word family. All 6 occurrences are in Revelation — the torment word family is genre-specific. Time-bounded in 4 of 6 uses (5 months in 9:5; 1 hour for Babylon in 18:7,10,15). The etc7-11 study documented this distribution.

docs.title: G931 — basanos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G931-basanos.md

Occurrences: 3

Root noun of the basanizo word family. Originally a touchstone (Lydian stone) used to test the purity of gold/silver. 3 occurrences: Matt 4:24 (physical diseases), Luke 16:23 (parabolic torment in Hades), Luke 16:28 (parabolic 'place of torment'). The etymological base reveals the word family's root meaning: testing/proving through pressure, extended to torture/torment.

Semantic categories: physical suffering/disease, parabolic afterlife torment, testing/examination (etymological)

Key verses: Matt 4:24, Luke 16:23, Luke 16:28

Relevance: The root noun reveals the word family's etymology: touchstone for testing metals. The metaphorical extension from 'testing by stone' to 'torment' is secondary. The Luke 16 uses are in a parabolic context (rich man and Lazarus), not didactic teaching about eschatological fate.

docs.title: G930 — basanistes
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G930-basanistes.md

Occurrences: 1

Agent noun 'tormentor.' Single occurrence: Matt 18:34 in the parable of the unforgiving servant — 'delivered him to the tormentors.' Parabolic context, not eschatological fate.

Semantic categories: parabolic tormentor

Key verses: Matt 18:34

Relevance: Completes the basanizo word family. The one occurrence is in a parable, not a description of eschatological fate. The 'tormentors' are jailers in a debtor's prison context — temporal, corrective, and parabolic.

docs.title: G2342 — therion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2342-therion.md

Occurrences: 46

Neuter noun, wild/dangerous animal. 46 NT occurrences: 38 in Revelation (84%), 8 outside (all literal animal sense). In Revelation, therion is ALWAYS the apocalyptic beast-entity — a symbolic political-religious power with seven heads, ten horns, composite body from Daniel 7 beasts. Outside Revelation: literal wild animals (Mark 1:13, Acts 28:4-5, Heb 12:20), generic animal class (Acts 10:12, 11:6, James 3:7), or metaphorical (Titus 1:12).

Semantic categories: literal wild animal, generic wild animals (class), metaphorical brutish character, apocalyptic beast (political-religious power), beast as object of false worship

Key verses: Rev 13:1, Rev 13:11, Rev 17:8, Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10

Relevance: Identifies one of the three subjects of Rev 20:10. The beast is NOT a human being but a symbolic entity: seven heads, ten horns, composite of Daniel 7 beasts, 'was and is not and shall ascend.' Tree 3 Gate 1 automatically FAILs: 'a symbolic entity (a figure in an apocalyptic vision).'

docs.title: G5578 — pseudoprophetes
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5578-pseudoprophetes.md

Occurrences: 11

Masculine noun, compound: false + prophet. 11 occurrences in 7 books. CRITICAL DISTINCTION: SINGULAR in Revelation (3x: Rev 16:13, 19:20, 20:10) = one specific apocalyptic entity (identified as the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17 via Rev 19:20's matching vocabulary). PLURAL elsewhere (7x: Matt 7:15, 24:11, 24:24, Mark 13:22, Luke 6:26, 2 Pet 2:1, 1 John 4:1) = a class of human deceivers. Acts 13:6 is singular with a personal name (Bar-Jesus) — human individual, distinct from the apocalyptic entity.

Semantic categories: warning against deceptive teachers, eschatological warning (signs and wonders), historical precedent, individual instance (Bar-Jesus), eschatological triad (dragon, beast, false prophet)

Key verses: Rev 16:13, Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Matt 7:15, Matt 24:11, Acts 13:6

Relevance: Identifies one of the three subjects of Rev 20:10. The singular/plural distinction is critical: the false prophet of Rev 20:10 is the specific apocalyptic entity (= earth beast of Rev 13:11-17), not a generic human false prophet. Rev 19:20 provides the identification key via matching vocabulary (poiesas ta semeia enopion autou). Tree 3 Gate 1 automatically FAILs: 'a symbolic entity.'

docs.title: G1228 — diabolos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1228-diabolos.md

Occurrences: 38

Adjective used substantively. 36 unique verses (38 tokens) across 14 books. Functions in two registers: (1) proper name/title of the chief adversary of God (always articular/singular), (2) adjective for human 'false accusers/slanderers' (1 Tim 3:11, 2 Tim 3:3, Tit 2:3). The personal-adversary uses establish the devil as: tempter (Matt 4:1-11), active adversary of believers (Eph 6:11, 1 Pet 5:8), origin of sin/murder (John 8:44, 1 John 3:8), subject of eschatological judgment (Rev 12:9, 20:2, 20:10, Matt 25:41).

Semantic categories: Satan as tempter, Satan as active adversary, Satan as origin of sin/murder, Satan in eschatological judgment, human slanderers (adjectival use)

Key verses: Rev 12:9, Rev 20:2, Rev 20:10, Matt 25:41, John 8:44, 1 John 3:8, Heb 2:14

Relevance: Identifies the first named subject of Rev 20:10. The devil (ho diabolos) is explicitly identified as the dragon/old serpent (Rev 12:9, 20:2), a spirit being (Eph 2:2), with angelic forces (Matt 25:41), predating humanity (Gen 3:1). Tree 3 Gate 1 automatically FAILs: 'a non-human spirit being.'

docs.title: G4567 — satanas
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4567-satanas.md

Occurrences: 36

Transliterated Hebrew title (from H7854 satan = adversary). 36 occurrences. Same referent as diabolos (G1228) but emphasizes different aspects: diabolos = slanderer/accuser (Greek semantic equivalent); satanas = adversary (Hebrew transliteration). Both refer to the same non-human supernatural being.

Semantic categories: personal adversary, tempter, cosmic adversary

Key verses: Rev 12:9, Rev 20:2, Rev 20:7

Relevance: Parallel identification for the devil in Rev 20:10. The identification chain (Rev 12:9, 20:2) links dragon = serpent = diabolos = satanas — all four titles refer to one non-human supernatural spirit being.

docs.title: G1404 — drakon
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1404-drakon.md

Occurrences: 13

All 13 NT occurrences in Revelation. The dragon is the primary symbolic representation of Satan in Revelation, explicitly identified as 'that old serpent, called the Devil and Satan' (Rev 12:9, 20:2). The dragon has seven heads, ten horns (Rev 12:3), leads angelic forces (Rev 12:7), gives authority to the beast (Rev 13:2).

Semantic categories: apocalyptic adversary figure

Key verses: Rev 12:3, Rev 12:7, Rev 12:9, Rev 13:2, Rev 20:2

Relevance: Part of the identification chain for the first subject of Rev 20:10: dragon = serpent = devil = Satan. All 13 occurrences are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework.

docs.title: G3041 — limne
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3041-limne.md

Occurrences: 10

Feminine noun, lake/pond. 10 occurrences: 5 in Luke (Lake of Gennesaret), 5 in Revelation (lake of fire). In Revelation, limne appears exclusively as 'lake of fire' (limne tou pyros) or 'lake of fire and brimstone.' Self-interpreted in Rev 20:14 as 'the second death' — a death concept, not a torment concept.

Semantic categories: natural body of water, eschatological place of punishment (lake of fire)

Key verses: Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14, Rev 20:15, Rev 21:8

Relevance: The destination of all three subjects in Rev 20:10. The lake of fire is self-defined as 'the second death' (Rev 20:14) via the X=Y symbol-decoding formula. Death and hades (personified entities) are also cast in (Rev 20:14), paralleling 1 Cor 15:26 (last enemy destroyed is death).

docs.title: G2303 — theion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2303-theion.md

Occurrences: 7

Noun, brimstone/sulfur. 7 occurrences: 6 in Revelation, 1 in Luke (17:29 Sodom). Fire-and-brimstone is the standard judgment pair. The Sodom paradigm (Gen 19:24) establishes the pattern: brimstone + fire = total, irreversible destruction. In Revelation, theion appears in lake of fire imagery (Rev 19:20, 20:10, 21:8), judgment torment (Rev 14:10), and demonic warfare (Rev 9:17-18).

Semantic categories: Sodom judgment archetype, eschatological torment, lake of fire imagery, demonic warfare imagery

Key verses: Luke 17:29, Rev 14:10, Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Rev 21:8

Relevance: Component of the 'lake of fire and brimstone' in Rev 20:10. The Sodom paradigm shows fire + brimstone produces total destruction (ashes, per 2 Pet 2:6), not ongoing torment. Every OT and NT use of fire-and-brimstone results in destruction.

docs.title: G2673 — katargeo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2673-katargeo.md

Occurrences: 32

27 NT occurrences. Semantic range includes: abolish, render powerless, nullify, destroy, do away with, make of no effect. Used in Heb 2:14 for Christ destroying the devil and in 1 Cor 15:26 for destroying death. The lexical ambiguity (render powerless vs. destroy utterly) means the exact outcome requires contextual determination.

Semantic categories: abolish/nullify, render powerless, destroy, do away with

Key verses: Heb 2:14, 1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10

Relevance: Applied to the destruction of the devil (Heb 2:14) and death (1 Cor 15:26). Even the supernatural entity (the devil) receives destruction vocabulary in a didactic epistle, not torment vocabulary.

docs.title: G2719 — katesthio
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2719-katesthio.md

Occurrences: 20

Compound verb: kata + esthio (eat down, devour, consume). Used in Rev 20:9 for fire 'devouring' the human nations — destruction vocabulary applied to human subjects at the same event where basanizo is applied to non-human/symbolic entities. The vocabulary differentiation is within the same literary unit.

Semantic categories: consume/devour, destruction by fire

Key verses: Rev 20:9

Relevance: The vocabulary applied to HUMAN subjects in Rev 20:9 — fire 'devoured' (katephagen) the nations. Different from basanizo applied to devil/beast/false prophet in v.10. This vocabulary differentiation within the same narrative is a key neutral observation.

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

119 tokens across 15 books. Encompasses physical death, death as sin's consequence (Rom 6:23), death as cosmic power (Rom 5:14), Christ's atoning death, spiritual death, and personified/second death (Rev 6:8, 20:14, 21:4). The 'second death' (ho thanatos ho deuteros) in Rev 20:14 and 21:8 is the term applied to human fate at the lake — death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

Semantic categories: physical/biological death, death as sin's consequence, death as cosmic power, Christ's atoning death, spiritual death, second death (personified/eschatological)

Key verses: Rom 6:23, 1 Cor 15:26, Rev 6:8, Rev 20:14, Rev 21:4, Rev 21:8

Relevance: The term used for HUMAN fate at the lake of fire: 'the second death.' When humans enter the lake (Rev 20:14-15, 21:8), the terminology is consistently thanatos (death), not basanizo (torment). This vocabulary differentiation is a key observation: non-human/symbolic entities receive torment language; humans receive death language.

docs.title: G165 — aion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G165-aion.md

Occurrences: 120

120 tokens across 22 books. Semantic range: age, era, perpetuity, world, universe. The doubled formula 'eis tous aionas ton aionon' (unto the ages of the ages) appears ~13x in Revelation: 9x for God's existence/reign (genuinely endless), 1x for saints' reign, 3x for judgment (14:11, 19:3, 20:10). The formula's meaning appears subject-determined: applied to the eternal God = genuinely eternal; applied to judgment on non-eternal subjects = permanent result. OT parallel: Isa 34:10 uses identical 'for ever' language for Edom — not still burning.

Semantic categories: duration/perpetuity, intensified perpetuity (ages of ages), this present age/world, the age to come, time-span/epochs, created order/universe, end of the age

Key verses: Rev 4:9-10, Rev 14:11, Rev 19:3, Rev 20:10, Rev 1:6

Relevance: Component of the 'for ever and ever' formula in Rev 20:10. The formula's meaning is demonstrably subject-determined: applied to God (genuinely eternal) vs. applied to judgment (Isa 34:10, Rev 19:3 — permanent result of completed destruction). The aion word study documents the full semantic range.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Adjective derived from aion (G165). Used in Matt 25:41 'everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels' and Matt 25:46 'everlasting punishment.' The Hebrews pattern (eternal redemption, eternal judgment, eternal salvation = single acts with permanent results) demonstrates aionios can describe the permanence of the result, not the duration of the process. Jude 1:7 + 2 Pet 2:6: Sodom suffered 'eternal fire' but is now 'ashes.'

Semantic categories: eternal/everlasting duration, permanent result (Hebrews pattern)

Key verses: Matt 25:41, Matt 25:46, Jude 1:7, Heb 6:2, Heb 9:12

Relevance: Related adjective form to aion. The 'eternal fire' of Matt 25:41 and Jude 1:7 produces ashes (2 Pet 2:6) and is 'prepared for the devil and his angels' — primary designation for non-human entities.

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

Destroy/perish — the primary NT verb for destruction. Jesus uses apollymi for the Sodom paradigm: 'destroyed them all' (Luke 17:29). Human fate vocabulary across all genres: destroy, perish. This destruction vocabulary spans Gospels, epistles, OT — unlike basanizo which is confined to Revelation's apocalyptic framework for judgment uses.

Semantic categories: physical destruction, eschatological destruction, spiritual perishing

Key verses: Luke 17:29, Matt 10:28, John 3:16

Relevance: Human fate vocabulary used by Jesus himself. The fire-and-brimstone paradigm is interpreted by Jesus as apollymi (destroy), not basanizo (torment). Cross-genre, cross-author destruction vocabulary for human wicked.

docs.title: G615 — apokteino
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G615-apokteino.md

Occurrences: 83

Slay/kill. Used in Rev 19:21 for human remnant 'slain' (apektanthesan, V-API-3P) with the sword. Different vocabulary from v.20 where beast/false prophet are cast 'alive' (zontes) into the lake. The vocabulary distinction is within the same verse pair.

Semantic categories: slay/kill (destruction vocabulary)

Key verses: Rev 19:21

Relevance: Human vocabulary in Rev 19:21 — humans are 'slain' (apokteino) while symbolic entities are cast 'alive' (zao) into the lake in v.20. The text maintains vocabulary differentiation between human and non-human/symbolic subjects.

docs.title: G4969 — sphazo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4969-sphazo.md

Occurrences: 10

Slay (violently). The beast counterfeits the Lamb through shared sphazo vocabulary: Rev 5:6 Lamb 'slain' (esphagmenon) and Rev 13:3 beast with deadly wound 'as it were wounded to death' (esphagmenen). The shared vocabulary establishes the counterfeit death-and-resurrection pattern — the beast mimics Christ.

Semantic categories: violent slaying, counterfeit death-resurrection pattern

Key verses: Rev 5:6, Rev 13:3

Relevance: Documents the beast's counterfeit relationship to the Lamb. The beast is a symbolic entity that mimics Christ's death/resurrection through shared vocabulary — further confirming its non-literal nature.

docs.title: G4442 — pyr
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4442-pyr.md

Occurrences: 74

74 tokens across 14 books. Primary word for fire. Revelation dominates (25/73 unique verses, 34%). Semantic categories: eschatological punishment (lake of fire, Gehenna), judgment parables, divine theophany, cosmic plagues, testing/refining, figurative/metaphorical. Fire collocates with ballo (cast, 19x), theion (brimstone, 7x), katakaiō (burn up, 7x). The fire-and-brimstone paradigm originates in Gen 19:24 (Sodom) and produces total destruction.

Semantic categories: eschatological punishment, judgment parables, divine theophany, cosmic plagues, testing/refining, figurative

Key verses: Matt 25:41, Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14-15, Luke 17:29, Jude 1:7

Relevance: Component of 'lake of fire' in Rev 20:10. The fire-and-brimstone paradigm consistently produces destruction and ashes (Gen 19:24 → 2 Pet 2:6 → Luke 17:29), not ongoing torment.

docs.title: H1966 — heylel
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1966-heylel.md

Occurrences: 1

Hapax legomenon in Isa 14:12. Noun from halal (H1984, to shine). Means 'shining one/morning star.' The full phrase 'heylel ben-shachar' (shining one, son of the dawn) uses astral imagery. Isaiah repurposes Canaanite mythic template as a taunt against the king of Babylon. The five 'I will' statements of self-exaltation (vv.13-14) followed by descent to sheol (v.15) became the template for understanding the origin of sin. The fate described is descent/humiliation, not ongoing torment.

Semantic categories: celestial epithet, pride and fall archetype, translation trajectory (epithet to proper name)

Key verses: Isa 14:12

Relevance: OT background for the Satan-figure. The fate described in Isa 14:12-15 is descent to sheol and the pit — humiliation and destruction language, not ongoing torment. The same entity whose Rev 20:10 fate is described as 'tormented for ever' is described in the OT with descent/destruction language.

docs.title: H3742 — kerub
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H3742-kruwb.md

Occurrences: 105

105 tokens across 12 OT books. Uncertain derivation. Cherubim appear as: Eden boundary guardians (Gen 3:24), ark/mercy seat figures (Exo 25), temple imagery, throne/presence language, Ezekiel visionary cherubim. Ezek 28:14 identifies the subject as 'the anointed cherub that covereth' — a non-human angelic being in God's presence.

Semantic categories: Eden guardians, ark/mercy seat figures, temple imagery, throne/presence language, Ezekiel visionary cherubim

Key verses: Gen 3:24, Ezek 28:14, Ezek 28:16

Relevance: Ezek 28:14 identifies the Satan-figure as a cherub — a non-human angelic being. This confirms the devil's ontological category as non-human for Tree 3 Gate 1 purposes. The same cherub becomes 'ashes upon the earth' (Ezek 28:18) and exists 'never any more' (Ezek 28:19).

docs.title: G4592 — semeion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4592-semeion.md

Occurrences: 77

Sign/miracle. Rev 19:20 uses 'ta semeia' (the signs/miracles) to identify the false prophet — 'the false prophet that wrought miracles before him.' This vocabulary matches Rev 13:13-14 exactly, confirming the false prophet IS the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17.

Semantic categories: miraculous signs, identification link

Key verses: Rev 19:20, Rev 13:13-14

Relevance: The identification link between the false prophet (Rev 19:20) and the earth beast (Rev 13:11-17). The matching vocabulary (semeia + enopion autou) confirms these are the same entity.

docs.title: Evidence Classification Audit Trail — etc7-12-tormented-forever
docs.text: Each item below received the full Tree 3/4/5 walkthrough per the ETC methodology. Parser-verified morphological data from raw-data/greek-parsing.md and raw-data/hebrew-parsing.md was used for Gate 2 assessments.

docs.title: E-Item Classifications
docs.text:
E8 (Rev 20:9) -- "fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "devoured" (katephagen, G2719) applied to human nations (Gog/Magog). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject of "devoured" is fire (pyr, N-NSN), acting upon human nations (autous, P-APM). The human nations are the objects receiving the destruction. The subject being described as experiencing the fate IS literal human beings (the deceived nations). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): katephagen (V-2AAI-3S from katesthio G2719) — second aorist active indicative 3rd singular. The verb unambiguously means "devoured/consumed." No alternative parsing available. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation is apocalyptic vision (Rev 1:1 semaino). FAIL — Genre is apocalyptic.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 3 failed).
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic vision. The devouring of nations occurs within a symbolic visionary narrative.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, fire from heaven devours the deceived nations — destruction vocabulary for human subjects within Revelation's symbolic framework."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: destruction vocabulary (devoured) still applies. However, genre qualification means this is an apocalyptic depiction, not didactic teaching. Both sides accept the text uses katephagen for these subjects.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails. Revised to Neutral (apocalyptic depiction using destruction vocabulary — both sides acknowledge the vocabulary choice without disputing the textual observation).

E9 (Rev 20:10) -- "shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "tormented" (basanisthesontai, G928) applied to devil, beast, false prophet. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subjects are: (1) ho diabolos (G1228, A-NSM) — the devil, a non-human spirit being per Rev 12:9, Eph 2:2; (2) to therion (G2342, N-NSN) — the beast, a symbolic composite entity per Rev 13:1-2, 17:8; (3) ho pseudoprophetes (G5578, N-NSM) — the false prophet, a symbolic entity per Rev 19:20 = Rev 13:11-17. FAIL — all three subjects are non-human spirit beings or symbolic entities in an apocalyptic vision.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Not reached (Gate 1 failed).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Not reached (Gate 1 failed).
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 1 failed).
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Gate 1 failure. Subject is (1) a non-human spirit being (the devil), (2) a symbolic entity (the beast), (3) a symbolic entity (the false prophet). None is a literal human being.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "Three non-human/symbolic entities — the devil (supernatural spirit being), the beast (symbolic political-religious system), and the false prophet (symbolic entity = earth beast) — are described as tormented in Revelation's apocalyptic vision."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1/V2: The corrected observation with the actual (symbolic/non-human) subjects — neither destruction vocabulary nor human-torment vocabulary applies as evidence about human fate. The statement is about non-human/symbolic entities.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails for all three subjects. Revised to Neutral (describes non-human/symbolic entities in an apocalyptic vision; does not constitute evidence about literal human fate in either direction).

E10 (Rev 20:14-15) -- "This is the second death" / humans cast into lake -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "second death" (ho thanatos ho deuteros, G2288) applied to the human fate at the lake. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The humans not found in the book of life are the subjects experiencing "the second death." Literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): eblethe (V-API-3S from ballo G906) — aorist passive indicative. "houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin he limne tou pyros" — predicate nominative construction identifying the lake as "the second death." Grammar is unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation is apocalyptic vision (Rev 1:1 semaino). FAIL — Genre is apocalyptic.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 3 failed).
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic vision.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In Revelation's apocalyptic framework, humans at the lake receive the designation 'the second death' — death vocabulary, not torment vocabulary."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: "death" is destruction/cessation vocabulary. However, genre qualification applies. Both sides accept the text says "second death" for humans at the lake.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails. Revised to Neutral (both sides accept the text uses death vocabulary for humans at the lake; the interpretation of "second death" is disputed).

E11 (Rev 21:8) -- Eight categories of human wicked: "which is the second death" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "second death" (ho thanatos ho deuteros) applied to eight human categories. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Eight categories of literal human wicked (fearful, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, whoremongers, sorcerers, idolaters, liars). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): The predicate nominative "which is the second death" (ho estin ho thanatos ho deuteros) is unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation is apocalyptic vision. FAIL — Genre is apocalyptic.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In Revelation's apocalyptic framework, eight human categories receive 'the second death' — death vocabulary without torment formula."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: death vocabulary applies but under genre qualification. Both sides accept the textual observation.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails. Revised to Neutral (textual observation about vocabulary usage in apocalyptic genre).

E17 (1 John 3:8) -- "that he might destroy the works of the devil" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destroy" (luse, from luo G3089) applied to the devil's works. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject of "destroy" is the Son of God; the object is "the works of the devil." The passage addresses the destruction of the devil's works, not the devil himself or human beings directly. PASS (the claim concerns destruction vocabulary applied to the adversary's domain).
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): luse (V-AAS-3S from luo G3089) — aorist active subjunctive, "might destroy/dissolve." The verb unambiguously means destroy/undo. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Johannine epistle — didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Heb 2:14 (katargeo for devil). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. Destruction vocabulary for the devil's works in a didactic epistle.

E18 (Ezek 28:18-19) -- "bring thee to ashes upon the earth... never shalt thou be any more" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "ashes" (epher H665), "devour" (akal), "never any more" (eneka ad olam) applied to the Satan-figure (anointed cherub). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subject is "the anointed cherub that covereth" (Ezek 28:14, kerub H3742) — a non-human angelic being. FAIL — subject is a non-human spirit being.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Not reached.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Not reached.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Gate 1 failure. Subject is a non-human spirit being (cherub), not a literal human.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "The Satan-figure (anointed cherub) is described with destruction/cessation vocabulary: fire devours, becomes ashes, exists never any more."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: Destruction vocabulary (ashes, devour, never any more) still applies to the non-human subject. The observation is that the same entity described in Rev 20:10 with torment vocabulary receives destruction vocabulary in the OT prophetic oracle. Both sides can acknowledge this textual fact.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails. Revised to Neutral (subject is non-human; the observation about destruction vocabulary for this entity is accepted by both sides as textual fact, though its implications are disputed).

Note: While the subject fails Gate 1 (non-human), the OT destruction language for the same entity referenced in Rev 20:10 remains a significant textual datum. The reclassification to Neutral reflects that the explicit statement is about a non-human being. The inference from this data is classified separately.

E19 (Dan 7:11) -- "the beast was slain, and his body destroyed, and given to the burning flame" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "slain," "destroyed," "burning flame" — destruction vocabulary applied to the fourth beast. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The fourth beast is a symbolic entity in a vision (Daniel 7). FAIL — symbolic entity in an apocalyptic vision.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Not reached.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Not reached.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Subject is a symbolic entity; genre is apocalyptic vision.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In Daniel's vision, a symbolic beast-entity is slain and destroyed with fire — destruction vocabulary for a symbolic entity."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: destruction vocabulary applies to a symbolic entity. Both sides accept the textual observation.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails. Revised to Neutral.

E28 (Rom 6:23) -- "The wages of sin is death" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "death" (thanatos, G2288) applied as the consequence of sin for humans. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The implicit subject is all sinners — literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): thanatos (N-NSM) — nominative singular masculine. The sentence structure is straightforward: "ta gar opsonia tes hamartias thanatos" — wages of sin is death. Unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Pauline epistle — didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with the death/destruction vocabulary pattern across OT and NT. No conflicting E-items at the E-tier. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. Didactic epistle states the wages of sin is death.

E29 (Luke 17:29) -- "destroyed them all" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destroyed" (apolesen, from apollymi G622) applied to Sodom's inhabitants. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects are Sodom's inhabitants — literal human beings in a historical event cited by Jesus. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): apolesen (V-AAI-3S from apollymi G622) — aorist active indicative, "destroyed." Unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Jesus' didactic saying within the Gospel — direct teaching. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with 2 Pet 2:6 (ashes), Jude 1:7 (eternal fire producing ashes). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. Jesus interprets the fire-and-brimstone paradigm as destruction.

E30 (2 Pet 2:6) -- "turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes... an ensample" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "ashes" (tephrosas, from tephroo G5077) — destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Sodom and Gomorrah (cities/inhabitants) — literal human beings in a historical event. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): tephrosas (V-AAP-NSM from tephroo G5077) — aorist active participle, "having turned to ashes." Unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Petrine epistle — didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Luke 17:29, Jude 1:7. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. Peter calls ashes-producing destruction "an ensample" for future judgment.

E32 (Mal 4:1) -- "shall be stubble... burn them up... neither root nor branch" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "burn up," "stubble," "neither root nor branch" — total consumption vocabulary applied to human wicked. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "All the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly" — literal human wicked. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hebrew: qash (H7179, stubble), lahat (Piel, "burn up"). "Neither root nor branch" — absolute destruction. Unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): OT prophetic eschatology — direct-speech prophecy ("saith the LORD of hosts"). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Obad 1:16, Psa 37:10, Luke 17:29. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E33 (Obad 1:16) -- "they shall be as though they had not been" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "as though they had not been" — cessation vocabulary applied to the heathen (human wicked). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "All the heathen" — literal human beings (nations). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): kelo hayu — "as though they had not been." Unambiguous cessation language. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): OT prophetic eschatology — direct prophecy. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:10, Mal 4:1. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E34 (Psa 37:10) -- "the wicked shall not be... his place shall not be" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "shall not be" (enenu) — cessation vocabulary applied to the wicked. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The wicked" — literal human wicked. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): enenu (ain + 3ms suffix) — "he is not/shall not be." Unambiguous negative existential. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom psalm. Wisdom literature is didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Obad 1:16, Mal 4:1. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: N-Item Classifications
docs.text:
N1 -- "The text uses different vocabulary for different subjects at the lake: humans receive destruction/death; non-human/symbolic entities receive torment" -- Based on: E8, E9, E10, E11, E12 -- Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree this follows? YES — the vocabulary distinction is observable from the text. Both ECT and conditionalist scholars can verify that katephagen is used for humans in v.9, basanisthesontai for devil/beast/false prophet in v.10, and "second death" for humans in vv.14-15. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? YES — the vocabulary difference is a grammatical/lexical fact, not an interpretation. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add nothing beyond the E-items? YES — it simply states the observable pattern from the E-items. PASS.
  • Gate 0 PASSES. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither V1 (destruction) nor V2 (conscious-ongoing) — this is a factual observation about vocabulary distribution, not itself a destruction or torment claim.
  • Result: Neutral — observable textual pattern both sides must accept.

N2 -- "Basanizo in judgment contexts appears exclusively in Revelation's apocalyptic framework or in demonic speech — never in epistles, Gospel didactic, or OT for human eschatological fate" -- Based on: E23, E24, E25, E26, E27, E9 and all 12 basanizo occurrences -- Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree? YES — the distributional fact is verifiable by counting occurrences. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? YES — one can mechanically classify each occurrence by genre and verify the distribution. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add nothing beyond the E-items? YES — it aggregates the observable distribution. PASS.
  • Gate 0 PASSES. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither V1 nor V2 — this is a distributional observation.
  • Result: Neutral — verifiable distributional fact.

N3 -- "The torment formula of Rev 20:10 (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) is applied only to non-human/symbolic entities, never to humans" -- Based on: E9, E37 -- Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree? YES — the formula appears once (Rev 20:10) and the subjects are verifiably the devil, beast, and false prophet. No other verse applies this exact formula to humans. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? YES — it is a simple search result. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): YES. PASS.
  • Gate 0 PASSES. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither V1 nor V2 — this is a distributional observation about where a formula appears.
  • Result: Neutral — verifiable textual fact about formula distribution.

docs.title: I-Item Classifications
docs.text:
I1 -- "Since devil/beast/false prophet and humans end up in the same lake, they experience the same outcome" -- Type: I-B -- Classified: ECT

  • Source test: All components from E/N? The claim that they are in the same lake comes from E-items (E9, E10). The inference that "same destination = same experience" is the added step. YES — text-derived components.
  • Direction test: Conflicts with E/N? YES — E12 shows the text uses DIFFERENT vocabulary for the entities and humans at the same lake; N1 confirms the vocabulary differentiation. The inference requires E/N statements to mean something other than their lexical value (different vocabulary must actually mean the same experience). → I-B.
  • FOR: E9 (all in same lake), E10 (humans also in lake), E16 (fire prepared for devil and his angels — humans sent there too)
  • AGAINST: E12 (different vocabulary in same narrative), N1 (vocabulary differentiation), E8/E10/E11 (humans consistently receive destruction/death vocabulary)
  • Result: Type I-B confirmed. Position: ECT. (Requires SIS resolution in CONCLUSION.md.)

I2 -- "Rev 20:10's torment formula describes the fate of non-human/symbolic entities, not the fate of human beings" -- Type: I-A -- Classified: Cond.

  • Source test: All components from E/N? YES — drawn from E2-E7 (subject identifications), E9 (formula), E37 (formula appears once, only these subjects), N1 (vocabulary differentiation), N3 (formula never applied to humans).
  • Direction test: Aligns with E/N? YES — does not require any E/N to mean something other than its lexical value. Simply systematizes the observations.

  • Source test: All components from E/N? YES — drawn from all 12 basanizo occurrences (E23-E27, E9, E25, E26), N2 (distributional observation).
  • Direction test: Aligns with E/N? YES — does not require any E/N statement to mean other than its lexical value.
  • Consistency check: Only requires criterion #5 (systematizing). PASS.
  • Result: Type I-A confirmed. Position: Cond.

I4 -- "The beast represents a system of human adherents; therefore the torment of the beast transfers to those humans" -- Type: I-C -- Classified: ECT

  • Source test: All components from E/N? NO — the claim that torment of a symbolic entity transfers to the humans within the system requires an external bridging concept (representative torment). The text does not state this transfer; it must be supplied by the interpreter.
  • Direction test: Does it override E/N? NO — it does not directly contradict any E/N statement. It adds an interpretive framework not stated in the text. → I-C.
  • Consistency check: Does not override an E/N statement (E12 shows different vocabulary, but I-C does not require overriding — it supplements). PASS.
  • Result: Type I-C confirmed. Position: ECT.

  • Source test: All components from E/N? YES — the formula appears in E-items (E9 for judgment, E20-E21 for Babylon/Edom).
  • Direction test: Conflicts with E/N? YES — E20 (Isa 34:10, Edom's "for ever" smoke, yet animals inhabit ruins) and E21 (Babylon's smoke "for ever" yet "found no more") show the formula can describe permanent results, not ongoing processes. The claim requires these E/N statements to mean something other than their face value. → I-B.
  • FOR: E9 (formula used in Rev 20:10), Rev 4:9-10 (formula applied to God = genuinely eternal)
  • AGAINST: E20 (Isa 34:10, identical formula for ended fire), E21 (Babylon: formula + fivefold cessation)

docs.title: CONCLUSION — Rev 20:10 Named Subjects, Basanizo Usage, and Tree 3 Subject Gate
Question
docs.text: Rev 20:10 names three subjects for the "tormented day and night for ever and ever" formula: the devil, the beast, and the false prophet. Are these literal human beings, or supernatural/symbolic entities? What does basanizo (G928) mean across its NT usage? What happens when Tree 3's Subject Gate is applied?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: All three named subjects of the "tormented for ever and ever" formula in Rev 20:10 are non-human or symbolic entities. The devil is a supernatural spirit being (Rev 12:9, 20:2, Eph 2:2). The beast is a symbolic political-religious system (Rev 13:1-2, 17:8-11). The false prophet is a symbolic entity identified as the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17 (Rev 19:20). Tree 3 Gate 1 (Subject Gate) fails for all three. The torment formula (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) appears once in Scripture, applied only to these three non-human/symbolic entities — never to any human being. Revelation consistently uses different vocabulary for humans at the lake of fire: devoured (Rev 20:9), slain (Rev 19:21), and the second death (Rev 20:14-15, 21:8).

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Four-Fold Identification Chain (Rev 12:9) And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.

Three Subjects Tormented (Rev 20:10) And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Humans Devoured (Rev 20:9) And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them.

The Lake Is the Second Death (Rev 20:14) And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Eight Human Categories Receive the Second Death (Rev 21:8) But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

Beast and False Prophet Cast Alive; Humans Slain (Rev 19:20-21) And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet that wrought miracles before him... These both were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone. And the remnant were slain with the sword of him that sat upon the horse.

Christ Destroys the Devil (Heb 2:14) Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil.

Satan-Figure Becomes Ashes (Ezek 28:18-19) Therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee... thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more.

Jesus Interprets Fire and Brimstone as Destruction (Luke 17:29) But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all.

Wages of Sin Is Death (Rom 6:23) For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

docs.title: 1. The Three Named Subjects — None Is a Literal Human Being
docs.text:
Rev 20:10 names three subjects for the torment formula: the devil (ho diabolos, G1228), the beast (to therion, G2342), and the false prophet (ho pseudoprophetes, G5578). The text itself identifies each as non-human or symbolic.

The Devil. Rev 12:9 provides the most comprehensive identification chain in Scripture: "the great dragon... that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world." Rev 20:2 restates this identification in the immediate context: "the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan." The four-fold articular apposition uses the naming-copula participle (ho kaloumenos) to link dragon, serpent, Devil, and Satan as one entity. Each title carries non-human content: drakon (G1404) appears exclusively in Revelation (all 13 occurrences); ophis (serpent) traces to Gen 3:1 (pre-human); Diabolos and Satanas are titles for a supernatural adversary. "His angels" (hoi aggeloi autou, Rev 12:9) confirms command over angelic forces — impossible for a human. Eph 2:2 identifies the devil as "the spirit" (to pneuma) — explicitly a spirit being. Gen 3:1 places the serpent before any human sin. Ezek 28:14 identifies the Satan-figure as "the anointed cherub that covereth" (kerub, H3742) — a non-human angelic being. The devil is a supernatural spirit entity, not a human.

The Beast. Rev 13:1-2 describes the beast rising from the sea with seven heads (kephalas hepta), ten horns (kerata deka), and a composite body from four Daniel 7 beasts in reverse order — leopard, bear, lion. No literal creature or human being has seven heads and ten horns. Rev 17:9-11 decodes the symbolism: the seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings. The beast's temporal description in Rev 17:8 — "was, and is not, and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit" — describes a multi-century political-religious system whose existence pattern no single human can fulfill. The beast counterfeits Christ through shared sphazo (G4969) vocabulary: Rev 13:3's "deadly wound" (esphagmenen) mirrors the Lamb "slain" (esphagmenon) in Rev 5:6. The word study for therion (G2342) confirms that 38 of its 46 NT occurrences are in Revelation, where it is always the apocalyptic beast-entity. The beast is a symbolic entity.

The False Prophet. Rev 19:20 identifies the false prophet by matching vocabulary from Rev 13:13-14: "the false prophet that wrought miracles (ta semeia) before him (enopion autou), with which he deceived them that had received the mark." This vocabulary match — poiesas ta semeia enopion autou — identifies the false prophet as the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17. The earth beast has entirely symbolic characteristics: two horns like a lamb, speaks as a dragon, exercises the first beast's delegated authority, gives breath (pneuma) to an image. No literal human has these features. The word study for pseudoprophetes (G5578) documents the critical singular/plural distinction: the singular form in Revelation (3 occurrences: Rev 16:13, 19:20, 20:10) always refers to one specific apocalyptic entity, while the plural form elsewhere (7 occurrences: Matt 7:15, 24:11, 24:24, Mark 13:22, Luke 6:26, 2 Pet 2:1, 1 John 4:1) refers to a class of human deceivers. Acts 13:6 is singular outside Revelation but with a personal name (Bar-Jesus). The false prophet of Rev 20:10 is a symbolic entity.

docs.title: 2. Tree 3 Subject Gate Application
docs.text:
The ETC methodology's Tree 3 requires every E-item with a positional candidate (Cond. or ECT) to pass four validation gates before the classification stands. Gate 1 is the Subject Gate: "Is the grammatical subject a literal human being?" Automatic FAIL conditions include "a non-human spirit being" and "a symbolic entity (a figure in an apocalyptic vision)."

For Rev 20:10's torment formula: - The devil: Non-human spirit being (Rev 12:9, Eph 2:2, Gen 3:1, Ezek 28:14). Gate 1 FAILS. - The beast: Symbolic entity in an apocalyptic vision (Rev 13:1-2, 17:8-11). Gate 1 FAILS. - The false prophet: Symbolic entity in an apocalyptic vision (Rev 19:20 = Rev 13:11-17). Gate 1 FAILS.

All three subjects fail the Subject Gate. The proposed ECT classification for E9 ("shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever") cannot stand because no literal human being is the subject of the torment formula. The reclassification check (Tree 3 Step 3) produces a corrected observation: "Three non-human/symbolic entities are described as tormented in Revelation's apocalyptic vision." This corrected observation does not pass V1 (destruction vocabulary) or V2 (human-torment vocabulary) as evidence about human fate. The item is reclassified as Neutral.

Additionally, Gate 3 (Genre Gate) would independently fail: Revelation is an apocalyptic vision per its own opening declaration (Rev 1:1, semaino G4591 — "communicated by signs/symbols").

docs.title: 3. Vocabulary Differentiation — The Text's Own Distinctions
docs.text:
The most striking internal evidence is that Revelation itself uses different vocabulary for different subjects at the lake of fire. This vocabulary differentiation appears in multiple passages:

Rev 20:9 vs. 20:10. In v.9, fire from heaven "devoured" (katephagen, V-2AAI-3S from katesthio G2719) the human nations. In v.10, the devil is cast into the lake and the three non-human/symbolic entities are "tormented" (basanisthesontai, V-FPI-3P from basanizo G928). Different verbs for different subjects in consecutive verses.

Rev 19:20 vs. 19:21. The beast and false prophet are cast "alive" (zontes, V-PAP-NPM from zao G2198) into the lake. The human remnant (hoi loipoi) is "slain" (apektanthesan, V-API-3P from apokteino G615). Different verbs for symbolic entities and humans in consecutive verses.

Rev 20:14-15 and 21:8. When humans enter the lake, the designation is "the second death" (ho thanatos ho deuteros). Rev 20:14 provides the self-interpreting formula: "This is the second death" — using the X=Y predicate nominative construction that functions throughout Daniel and Revelation as symbolic interpretation (cf. Rev 1:20, 17:9, 17:15, 17:18). Eight categories of human wicked in Rev 21:8 all receive "the second death" — not the torment formula.

The pattern is consistent: humans receive destruction/death vocabulary (devoured, slain, second death); non-human/symbolic entities receive torment vocabulary (basanisthesontai). The text maintains this distinction even when describing the same event.

docs.title: 4. Basanizo (G928) — Complete NT Semantic Range
docs.text:
The verb basanizo occurs 12 times in the NT across 6 books. The word derives from basanos (G931), a touchstone used for testing the purity of metals. The metaphorical extension to "torment/distress" is secondary. The KJV translators recognized the semantic breadth by using five different English words: tormented, tossed, toiling, vexed, pained.

Non-judgment uses (7 of 12): - Matt 4:24, Matt 8:6 — physical illness/paralysis - Matt 14:24 — a ship "tossed" by waves (inanimate object — the word does not require a conscious subject) - Mark 6:48 — disciples "toiling" in rowing (physical exertion) - 2 Pet 2:8 — Lot "vexed" his righteous soul at Sodom's wickedness (moral distress, the only epistle occurrence) - Rev 12:2 — woman "pained" in childbirth (within Revelation itself, a non-judgment use) - Rev 11:10 — two witnesses "tormented" earth-dwellers (prophetic ministry, not punishment)

Judgment uses (5 of 12): - Matt 8:29, Mark 5:7, Luke 8:28 — demons use basanizo for their own anticipated fate ("torment us/me not") - Rev 9:5 — basanizo with explicit five-month time limit (the word does not inherently carry eternal duration) - Rev 14:10 — beast-worshippers "tormented" in apocalyptic framework - Rev 20:10 — devil, beast, false prophet "tormented" in apocalyptic framework

The distribution is revealing. All 5 judgment uses are either in Revelation's apocalyptic framework or involve demons (non-human spirit beings) speaking of their own anticipated fate. No epistle, no Gospel didactic section, and no OT passage uses basanizo for the final fate of generic human wicked. Destruction/death vocabulary (apollymi, apokteino, thanatos, katesthio) for human fate spans all genres and all authors. Torment vocabulary for judgment is genre-specific to apocalyptic and demonic speech.

The word family reinforces this pattern. Basanismos (G929) has 6 occurrences, all in Revelation, time-bounded in 4 of 6 (five months in Rev 9:5; one hour for Babylon in Rev 18:7, 10, 15). Basanos (G931) has 3 occurrences: physical diseases (Matt 4:24) and parabolic context (Luke 16:23, 28). Basanistes (G930) has 1 occurrence in a parable (Matt 18:34).

docs.title: 5. OT Background — Destruction Language for the Same Entities
docs.text:
The OT describes the Satan-figure and symbolic beast-entities with destruction/cessation vocabulary — not torment.

Ezek 28:18-19. The "anointed cherub that covereth" (the Satan-figure behind the king of Tyre) receives this fate: "I will bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth... thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more." The Hebrew is absolute: akal (devour), epher (ashes), eneka ad olam (you are not unto eternity). This is the same entity described in Rev 20:10 with the torment formula. In the OT prophetic oracle — direct divine speech — the fate is ashes and cessation.

Isa 14:12-15. The "morning star" (heylel, H1966, hapax legomenon) is "fallen from heaven," "cut down to the ground," and "brought down to sheol, to the sides of the pit." Luke 10:18 applies this pattern to Satan. The fate is descent and humiliation, not ongoing torment.

Dan 7:11. The fourth beast (the conceptual predecessor of Revelation's beast) is "slain, and his body destroyed, and given to the burning flame." Aramaic destruction vocabulary (qetilat, slain; geshmah hoobad, body destroyed) for a symbolic beast-entity.

Under SIS principles, these passages carry significant weight. Ezek 28 is direct divine speech ("I will bring forth fire... I will bring thee to ashes") — a genre with higher interpretive clarity than apocalyptic vision. The OT consistently uses destruction, not torment, for these entities.

docs.title: 6. The "For Ever and Ever" Formula — Subject-Determined Meaning
docs.text:
The formula eis tous aionas ton aionon appears approximately 13 times in Revelation. Applied to God's existence and reign (9 occurrences: Rev 1:6, 4:9-10, 5:13, 7:12, 10:6, 11:15, 15:7, 22:5), it is genuinely eternal. Applied to saints' reign (Rev 22:5), it is genuinely eternal.

In judgment contexts (Rev 14:11, 19:3, 20:10), the OT parallel is decisive. Isa 34:9-10 uses identical language for Edom: smoke "shall go up for ever" (le-olam), "not quenched night nor day" — yet Isa 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the ruins. Edom is not still burning. Rev 19:3 says Babylon's smoke rises "for ever and ever" — yet Rev 18:21-23 describes Babylon with fivefold "found no more at all" cessation language. The same formula applied to Babylon describes a permanent result of completed destruction, not an ongoing process.

The formula's meaning is demonstrably subject-determined: applied to the eternal God, it is genuinely eternal; applied to judgment on non-eternal subjects, it communicates the total completeness and permanence of the judgment. Biblical "ascending" language consistently uses physical scale to communicate magnitude — smoke ascending to heaven means total destruction (Josh 8:20, Judg 20:40), sin reaching heaven means maximum accumulated magnitude (Rev 18:5, Gen 18:20). "Forever" applied to ascending smoke is the temporal equivalent: maximum magnitude of destruction. The escalation from le-olam (Isa 34:10, regional Edom) to eis tous aionas ton aionon (Rev 14:11, 20:10, final judgment) communicates that the final judgment is more total than any prior one.

In Rev 20:10, the formula "tormented day and night for ever and ever" does not use the smoke-ascending idiom — because the verse focuses on the torment process rather than the destruction result. The destruction is already stated on both sides: v.9 says fire "devoured" the human armies (katephagen, aorist — completed), and v.14 defines the lake of fire as "the second death." The torment of v.10 sits within this destruction framework. "Forever and ever" applied to the torment communicates its total completeness — the torment runs to full completion, and completed torment produces destruction, as the OT process→outcome pattern consistently shows (Isa 13:8-9, Nah 1:9-10, Zeph 1:15,18). (Examined in depth in etc7-11-smoke-ascending-forever and etc7-22-vengeance-and-justice.)

docs.title: 7. The "Beast-as-Representative" Counter-Argument
docs.text:
The strongest counter-argument holds that even if the beast is a symbolic system, it represents human adherents, and the torment of the symbol transfers to those humans. The text addresses this directly.

Rev 19:20-21 provides the clearest evidence: the beast and false prophet are cast "alive" (zontes) into the lake, while the human remnant is "slain" (apektanthesan). In the same two-verse narrative, the text deliberately uses different verbs for the symbolic entities and for their human followers. Rev 20:9 describes the post-millennium human followers of Satan as "devoured" (katephagen) by fire — destruction vocabulary. Rev 21:8 lists eight categories of human sinners and assigns them "the second death."

The text maintains the vocabulary distinction between what happens to the symbolic entities and what happens to the humans within those systems. The torment formula is not transferred from the symbol to the humans. The humans receive death vocabulary.

docs.title: 8. Cross-Genre Evidence Pattern
docs.text:
Destruction/death vocabulary for the fate of the wicked spans every genre and every major biblical author: - OT prophets: Mal 4:1 (burn up as stubble, neither root nor branch), Obad 1:16 (as though they had not been), Isa 34:9-10 (smoke ascending from ended fire) - Wisdom literature: Psa 37:10 (the wicked shall not be) - Pauline epistles: Rom 6:23 (wages of sin is death), 1 Cor 15:26 (death destroyed) - Johannine epistles: 1 John 3:8 (destroy the works of the devil) - Petrine epistles: 2 Pet 2:6 (turned to ashes, an ensample) - Jesus' own words: Luke 17:29 (destroyed them all), Matt 10:28 (destroy soul and body)

Torment vocabulary for judgment appears only in Revelation's apocalyptic framework and in demonic speech. This cross-genre distribution is a significant datum under SIS principles, where didactic passages have higher interpretive weight than apocalyptic vision.

docs.title: 9. The Sodom Paradigm — Fire and Brimstone Produces Ashes
docs.text:
The fire-and-brimstone imagery in Rev 20:10 traces directly to Gen 19:24 — the destruction of Sodom. Jesus interprets this paradigm: "destroyed them all" (Luke 17:29, apollymi G622). Peter interprets it: "turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes... an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly" (2 Pet 2:6). Jude calls it "the vengeance of eternal fire" (Jude 1:7) — yet the fire produced ashes, not ongoing burning. Peter explicitly calls this destruction paradigm an "ensample" (hupodeigma, G5262) for future judgment of the ungodly.

The inspired interpretation of the fire-and-brimstone paradigm is destruction producing ashes. "Eternal fire" describes the permanence of the result, not the duration of the process.

docs.title: 10. The Lake of Fire Self-Interpreted as the Second Death
docs.text:
Rev 20:14 provides an explicit self-interpretation: "This is the second death" (houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin he limne tou pyros). The predicate nominative construction uses the X=Y symbol-decoding formula attested throughout Daniel and Revelation. The lake of fire IS the second death — a death concept, not a torment concept.

When death and hades are cast into the lake (Rev 20:14), the result is the destruction of death itself — "there shall be no more death" (Rev 21:4), paralleling 1 Cor 15:26 ("The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death"). The lake functions as an instrument of destruction. (Examined in depth in etc6-13-lake-of-fire-second-death.)

Rom 6:23 states the wages of sin is thanatos (death) — the same word used for "second death." The didactic contrast is death vs. eternal life, not torment vs. eternal life.
