The OT prototypes: Gen 41:26-27 (kine ARE years), Dan 2:38 (thou ART head of gold). Every instance commits to full identity between symbol and referent. The predicate noun in the lake-of-fire identification is thanatos (death), not basanismos (torment).

docs.title: Pattern 3: The Death-of-Death Chain
docs.text:
A vocabulary chain traces the destruction of death from OT prophecy to Revelation fulfillment:

  1. Isa 25:8: God will swallow up (bala) death (maveth)
  2. Hos 13:14: O death, I will be thy destruction
  3. 1 Cor 15:26: Last enemy destroyed (katargeo) is death
  4. 1 Cor 15:54-55: Death swallowed up in victory (quoting Isa 25:8 + Hos 13:14)
  5. 2 Tim 1:10: Christ hath abolished (katargeo) death
  6. Heb 2:14: Christ to destroy (katargeo) the devil who had the power of death
  7. Rev 20:14: Death and hades cast into the lake of fire
  8. Rev 21:4: No more death

The verb katargeo (G2673) is applied to both death (1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10) and the devil (Heb 2:14). Both end up in the lake of fire. The chain is complete: OT promise → cross/resurrection inauguration → eschatological consummation.

docs.title: Pattern 4: The Fire-and-Brimstone Paradigm
docs.text:
Every OT fire-and-brimstone event produces destruction/ashes/cessation:

  • Gen 19:24-25: Sodom overthrown (haphak)
  • Luke 17:29: Jesus interprets: "destroyed them all" (apollymi)
  • 2 Pet 2:6: "Turned to ashes" (tephroo) as "an ensample"
  • Jude 1:7: "Suffering the vengeance of eternal fire" -- yet the fire ended
  • Mal 4:1-3: Wicked = stubble, burned up, become ashes
  • Isa 34:9-10: Edom's smoke ascending "forever" -- yet animals dwell in the ruins

The paradigm consistently produces cessation, not ongoing burning. The "smoke ascending forever" formula describes irreversibility of the outcome, not duration of the process.

docs.title: Pattern 5: The Perish-vs-Life Binary
docs.text:
Across four NT authors, the consistent binary is perish/death vs. life:

  • John 3:16: apollymi vs. zoe aionios
  • Matt 7:13-14: apoleia vs. zoe
  • Rom 6:23: thanatos vs. zoe aionios
  • Phil 3:19: apoleia as the "end"
  • Gal 6:8: phthora vs. zoe aionios

No author introduces a third category of eternal conscious torment. The penalty for sin is consistently identified as death/destruction/perishing, and the alternative is life.

docs.title: thanatos (G2288) — The Central Word
docs.text: Thanatos appears 119 times in 106 NT verses. It consistently means death -- cessation of life, not separation from God. The same word is used for physical death (Heb 9:27), the penalty for sin (Rom 6:23), death personified (Rev 6:8), and the "second death" (Rev 2:11, 20:6,14, 21:8). When the text identifies the lake of fire as the "second death" (deuteros thanatos), it uses the same word that means death everywhere else in Scripture.

docs.title: basanizo (G928) — Torment, Applied Only to Non-Human Entities at the Lake
docs.text: Basanizo appears 12 times. At the lake of fire, it is applied only to the devil, beast, and false prophet (Rev 20:10). No human is described with basanizo at the lake. The word never appears with aionios as a modifier anywhere in the NT.

docs.title: katargeo (G2673) — The Verb of Death's Destruction
docs.text: Katargeo appears 27 times, overwhelmingly Pauline. Applied to death (1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10) and the devil (Heb 2:14). Rev 20:14 fulfills 1 Cor 15:26 by showing death cast into the lake.

docs.title: katesthio (G2719) — Devour, Applied to Humans at the Lake
docs.text: Katesthio appears 20 times. In Rev 20:9, fire from heaven "devoured" (katephagen) human armies. This is consumption/destruction vocabulary -- one verse before basanisthesontai (torment) for the devil.

docs.title: adikeo (G91) — Hurt/Injure, the Effect of the Second Death
docs.text: Adikeo appears 35 times, meaning to wrong, injure, harm. In Rev 2:11, the overcomer will "not be hurt" (ou me adikethei) of the second death. The strongest Greek negation guarantees the overcomer's complete protection.

docs.title: exousia (G1849) — Authority/Jurisdiction of the Second Death
docs.text: Exousia appears 103 times, meaning delegated authority, jurisdiction. In Rev 20:6, the second death "hath no power/authority" (ouk echei exousian) over first resurrection participants. The second death's domain is jurisdictionally limited.

docs.title: apollymi (G622) — The Primary Destruction Verb
docs.text: Apollymi appears 102 times. Jesus uses it for the Sodom paradigm (Luke 17:29: "destroyed them all") and for gehenna (Matt 10:28: "destroy soul and body"). The apollymi/sozo binary is the NT's dominant framework for eternal outcomes.

docs.title: aionios (G166) — Eternal/Age-lasting
docs.text: Aionios appears 71 times. Dominant usage: "eternal life" (~43 of 69 verses). Also modifies: punishment (Matt 25:46), fire (Matt 25:41, Jude 1:7), destruction (2 Thess 1:9). Does NOT modify basanizo in any text. The "eternal fire" of Jude 1:7 refers to Sodom -- which is not still burning. Aionios describes the permanence of the result, not necessarily the duration of the process.

docs.title: athanasia (G110) — Immortality
docs.text: Athanasia appears 3 times. God alone has it (1 Tim 6:16). Humans must "put on" immortality at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54). If humans are not inherently immortal, they can be destroyed.

docs.title: Isaiah 25:8 → 1 Cor 15:54 → Rev 20:14 → Rev 21:4
docs.text: The death-of-death theme runs from Isaiah through Paul to Revelation. Isaiah prophesies death swallowed up; Paul quotes this at the climax of his resurrection argument; Revelation shows death cast into the lake; the result is "no more death" and "wipe away all tears" (echoing Isaiah's exact language).

docs.title: Hosea 13:14 → 1 Cor 15:55 → Rev 20:14
docs.text: Hosea's apostrophe to death and the grave is quoted by Paul and fulfilled in Revelation when both death and hades (= sheol/grave) are cast into the lake.

docs.title: Gen 19:24 → Luke 17:29 → 2 Pet 2:6 → Jude 1:7 → Rev 21:8
docs.text: The fire-and-brimstone paradigm runs from Genesis through the Gospels and epistles to Revelation. Every NT interpretation of the Sodom event uses destruction vocabulary (apollymi, tephroo). The paradigm consistently produces ashes and cessation.

docs.title: Ezek 28:18-19 → Rev 20:10
docs.text: The Satan-figure's fate in Ezekiel (devoured, ashes, never any more) provides the OT background for the same entity's treatment in Rev 20:10. The clearer OT passage (didactic oracle, destruction language) governs the reading of the less clear NT passage (apocalyptic vision, torment language).

docs.title: Dan 7:11 → Rev 19:20
docs.text: The fourth beast in Daniel (slain, body destroyed, given to fire) is the conceptual predecessor of Revelation's beast. Daniel uses destruction vocabulary; Revelation uses "cast alive" language.

docs.title: Ezek 18:4 → Rom 6:23 → Rev 20:14
docs.text: The OT "the soul that sins shall die" → Paul's "wages of sin is death" → Revelation's "second death." The same death vocabulary runs from OT law through Pauline theology to Revelation's eschatology.

docs.title: Rev 20:10 — The Torment Formula
docs.text:
Rev 20:10 is the passage most frequently cited in support of ECT. It states that the devil, beast, and false prophet "shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever." Three factors complicate a direct application of this verse to human subjects:

  1. Subject Gate: All three subjects are non-human/symbolic entities. The devil is a supernatural being (Rev 12:9, 20:2). The beast is a seven-headed, ten-horned composite entity (Rev 13:1-2). The false prophet is identified with the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17. None is a literal human being.

  2. Vocabulary differentiation: Torment vocabulary (basanizo) is used for these non-human entities; humans in the same passage sequence receive death/destruction vocabulary (katephagen in 20:9, thanatos in 20:14, 21:8).

  3. OT background: Ezek 28:18-19 describes the same Satan-figure using destruction language (ashes, never any more). Dan 7:11 describes the fourth beast (predecessor of Revelation's beast) as slain and destroyed. The OT didactic passages use destruction vocabulary for the same entities.

docs.title: Rev 14:10-11 — Smoke Ascending Forever
docs.text:
Rev 14:10-11 describes beast-worshippers "tormented with fire and brimstone" and their smoke ascending "for ever and ever." Two complications for applying this as ECT evidence:

  1. OT source: The "smoke ascending forever" formula derives from Isa 34:10, where it describes Edom -- and Isa 34:11-17 shows the fire ended (animals dwell in the ruins).

  2. Intra-Revelation parallel: Rev 19:3 applies the identical formula to Babylon, which Rev 18:21-23 documents as completely destroyed with fivefold "found no more at all."

docs.title: Matt 25:41, 46 — Everlasting Fire and Punishment
docs.text: Matt 25:41 states the fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" -- its primary designation is for non-human entities. Matt 25:46 uses "everlasting punishment" (kolasis aionion), where kolasis (only 2 NT uses) is etymologically distinct from basanismos (torment). The passage is parabolic in genre, introducing a complicating factor for direct application.

docs.title: Rev 21:4 and the ECT Tension
docs.text: If the ECT reading is correct and billions of humans are being consciously tormented forever in the lake of fire, Rev 21:4's declaration that there shall be "no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain" presents a difficulty. The ECT position must either restrict Rev 21:4 to the new earth alone while eternal torment continues elsewhere, or redefine "no more death" to exclude the second death. Both moves require adding a concept the text does not state.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The gathered evidence points in a consistent direction across multiple converging lines:

  1. The text's own identification: Both Rev 20:14 and 21:8 use the X=Y predicate nominative formula to identify the lake of fire as "the second death." The predicate noun is thanatos (death), not basanismos (torment) or kolasis (punishment). The text tells us what the lake does, and it calls the result death.

  2. Vocabulary differentiation: Torment vocabulary (basanizo) is applied only to non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet). Human subjects receive death/destruction vocabulary (slain, devoured, second death). This differentiation is observable across Rev 19:20-21:8.

  3. The death-of-death chain: The casting of death and hades into the lake fulfills the OT/NT death-of-death theme (Isa 25:8, Hos 13:14, 1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10, Heb 2:14), resulting in "no more death" (Rev 21:4).

  4. The fire-and-brimstone paradigm: Every OT fire-and-brimstone event produces ashes, ruins, and cessation. Every NT interpretation of these events uses destruction vocabulary. The paradigm consistently means irreversible destruction, not ongoing burning.

  5. The perish-vs-life binary: Across four NT authors, the penalty for sin is death/destruction/perishing, and the alternative is life. No author introduces a third category.

  6. Human mortality: God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16). Humans must receive immortality as a gift at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54). Without immortality, humans are destructible.

  7. Overcomer promises: The overcomer will "absolutely not be hurt" (ou me adikethei) by the second death (Rev 2:11). The second death has no "authority/jurisdiction" (exousia) over first resurrection participants (Rev 20:6). These formulations are consistent with the second death being actual death from which the righteous are exempt.

The weight of evidence -- across vocabulary analysis, grammatical structure, OT background, cross-testament parallels, and the text's own self-interpretation -- identifies the lake of fire as the instrument of the second death, which is the final, irreversible death of those not found in the book of life.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Lake of fire in Revelation. 'Second death' (Rev 2:11; 20:6,14; 21:8). Rev 20:14 ('lake of fire IS the second death'). Death/hell cast into lake (Rev 20:14). What is the lake of fire? What is the second death? What does it mean that Rev 20:14 identifies the lake of fire AS the second death? What does it mean that death and hades are cast into the lake of fire? Who are the subjects who enter the lake? What do Rev 2:11 and 20:6 say about overcomers and the second death? How does the 'second death' function as the text's own explanation of what the lake does?

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

Masculine noun from thnesko (to die). 119 tokens across 106 unique verses, 15 NT books. Primary meaning: death (physical, spiritual, eschatological). Semantic categories: physical/biological death, death as consequence of sin, death as cosmic power, Christ's atoning death, passage from death to life, death personified/second death, shadow of death. Central to this study: the 'second death' uses this word, NOT basanismos (torment) or kolasis (punishment). The text identifies the lake of fire's function using death vocabulary.

Semantic categories: physical death, death as sin's consequence, death as cosmic power, Christ's atoning death, spiritual death/passage to life, death personified/second death

Key verses: Rom 5:12, Rom 6:23, 1 Cor 15:26, Rev 6:8, Rev 20:14, Rev 21:4

Relevance: THE central word. The 'second death' (deuteros thanatos) is the text's own identification of what the lake of fire does. The predicate nominative in Rev 20:14 uses thanatos, not basanismos. Every identification formula in Rev 20:14 and 21:8 defines the lake's function as DEATH.

docs.title: G3041 — limne
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3041-limne.md

Occurrences: 10

Feminine noun. 10 occurrences: 5 in Luke (Sea of Galilee), 5 in Revelation (lake of fire). In Revelation, exclusively in the phrase 'lake of fire' (limne tou puros) or 'lake of fire and brimstone.' Identified as 'the second death' in Rev 20:14 and 21:8.

Semantic categories: natural body of water, eschatological lake of fire

Key verses: Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14, Rev 20:15, Rev 21:8

Relevance: The specific word for the 'lake' of fire. Unique to Revelation. All 5 Revelation occurrences refer to the eschatological place of judgment.

docs.title: G1208 — deuteros
docs.text:
Occurrences: 47

Ordinal adjective, 'second.' 47 occurrences across NT. Modifies thanatos in the phrase 'second death' (deuteros thanatos) in Rev 2:11, 20:6, 20:14, 21:8. The ordinal implies a first death and a second death -- the structural pairing of first resurrection/second death frames Revelation's eschatology.

Semantic categories: ordinal number, eschatological qualifier

Key verses: Rev 2:11, Rev 20:6, Rev 20:14, Rev 21:8, 1 Cor 15:47

Relevance: Modifies thanatos in 'second death.' Implies the existence of a first death (physical death) and a distinct second death (the lake of fire). The first resurrection exempts from the second death (Rev 20:6).

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G928-basanizo.md

Occurrences: 12

Verb from basanos (touchstone for testing metals). 12 occurrences across 6 books. Semantic range: physical illness (Matt 8:6), laborious struggle (Matt 14:24), moral anguish (2 Pet 2:8), eschatological punishment (Rev 14:10, 20:10). In Revelation's lake-of-fire context, used ONLY for non-human/symbolic entities: devil, beast, false prophet (Rev 20:10). Never applied to human subjects at the lake.

Semantic categories: physical suffering, demonic encounters, moral distress, eschatological torment

Key verses: Matt 8:29, Rev 14:10, Rev 20:10

Relevance: CRITICAL for vocabulary differentiation. In Rev 20:10, basanisthesontai (future passive, 'shall be tormented') is applied ONLY to the devil, beast, and false prophet -- non-human entities. No human is ever described with basanizo at the lake of fire. Humans receive thanatos (death) vocabulary.

docs.title: G929 — basanismos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G929-basanismos.md

Occurrences: 6

Masculine noun, 'torment.' All 6 NT occurrences in Revelation only. Used for: demonic locust torment (Rev 9:5), beast-worshipper torment smoke ascending (Rev 14:11), Babylon's commercial torment (Rev 18:7,10,15). Exclusively apocalyptic vocabulary.

Semantic categories: demonic torment, eschatological judgment torment, commercial/imperial torment

Key verses: Rev 9:5, Rev 14:11, Rev 18:7, Rev 18:10, Rev 18:15

Relevance: All 6 uses are in Revelation. The 'smoke of their basanismos' formula in Rev 14:11 uses the same 'ascending forever' language as Isa 34:10 (Edom, fire ended) and Rev 19:3 (Babylon, destroyed). The formula describes irreversible destruction, not eternal burning.

docs.title: G2673 — katargeo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2673-katargeo.md

Occurrences: 32

Verb from kata + argeo. 27 tokens, overwhelmingly Pauline (25/27). Primary senses: render idle/useless, abolish, do away with. Applied to DEATH in 1 Cor 15:26 ('last enemy destroyed is death'), 2 Tim 1:10 ('abolished death'), and the DEVIL in Heb 2:14 ('destroy him that had the power of death').

Semantic categories: render useless/idle, nullify/void, abolish powers/enemies of Christ, old covenant glory passing, cease/pass away

Key verses: 1 Cor 15:24, 1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10, Heb 2:14

Relevance: The verb of death's destruction. Applied to both death (1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10) and the devil (Heb 2:14). Rev 20:14 fulfills 1 Cor 15:26 by showing death being cast into the lake. In Louw-Nida domain 013003 (cease to exist, be abolished) alongside apollymi.

docs.title: G2719 — katesthio
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2719-katesthio.md

Occurrences: 20

Verb from kata + esthio. 20 occurrences. Means 'to eat down, devour utterly.' Semantic categories: literal consumption, fire consuming/destruction, figurative exploitation, consuming zeal, hostile intent to destroy. In Rev 20:9, fire from heaven 'devoured' (katephagen) human armies -- destruction vocabulary.

Semantic categories: literal eating, fire consuming/destruction, figurative exploitation, consuming zeal, hostile intent to destroy

Key verses: Rev 11:5, Rev 20:9, Rev 12:4

Relevance: Rev 20:9 uses katephagen (aorist active of katesthio) for fire devouring human armies. This is consumption/destruction vocabulary -- the humans are devoured/consumed, not tormented. ONE VERSE before basanisthesontai (torment) for the devil in v.10.

docs.title: G1849 — exousia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1849-exousia.md

Occurrences: 103

Feminine noun. 103 tokens across 93 verses, 16 books. Primary meaning: authority, delegated right, jurisdiction, power. Not raw force (dynamis) but vested right. In Rev 20:6, the second death has no exousia (authority/jurisdiction) over first resurrection participants.

Semantic categories: divine/delegated authority, personal capacity/right, governmental authority, cosmic authorities, apocalyptic beast authority

Key verses: Matt 28:18, Rev 13:2, Rev 20:6

Relevance: Rev 20:6 states the second death 'ouk echei exousian' (does not have authority/jurisdiction) over first resurrection participants. Exousia is a legal/jurisdictional word -- the second death's domain is limited.

docs.title: G3528 — nikao
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3528-nikao.md

Occurrences: 28

Verb, 'to overcome, conquer, prevail.' 28 NT occurrences, overwhelmingly in Johannine literature (86%). Dominant usage: overcomer promises in the seven churches (Rev 2-3). The overcomer (ho nikon) receives protection from the second death (Rev 2:11) and inherits all things (Rev 21:7).

Semantic categories: eschatological victory/overcomer promises, cosmic victory/Christ overcoming, moral victory, military/hostile conquest

Key verses: Rev 2:7, Rev 2:11, Rev 2:26, Rev 3:21, Rev 21:7

Relevance: The overcomer (ho nikon, present active participle) in Rev 2:11 is the one exempt from the second death. The overcomer vocabulary is paired with the second death vocabulary throughout Revelation.

docs.title: G91 — adikeo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G91-adikeo.md

Occurrences: 35

Verb from alpha-privative + dike. 35 tokens across 23 verses, 9 books. Means: to wrong, injure, harm. Revelation accounts for 38% of all occurrences (9/24 verses). In Rev 2:11, adikethei (aorist passive subjunctive) under ou me = the overcomer will ABSOLUTELY NOT be harmed by the second death.

Semantic categories: physical harm/injury, moral wrongdoing, legal context, relational injury, eschatological justice

Key verses: Rev 2:11, Rev 7:2-3, Rev 9:4, Rev 22:11

Relevance: Rev 2:11 uses ou me + adikethei (V-APS-3S) -- the strongest Greek negation with the verb 'to harm/injure.' The second death's effect is described as 'hurting/injuring' -- consistent with it being actual death rather than ongoing separation.

docs.title: G4442 — pyr
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4442-pyr.md

Occurrences: 74

Neuter noun, 'fire.' 74 tokens across 73 verses, 14 books. Revelation dominates (25/73 = 34%). Primary collocate in 'lake of fire' (limne tou puros). Semantic categories: eschatological punishment, judgment parables, divine theophany, cosmic plagues, testing/purifying.

Semantic categories: eschatological punishment, judgment parables, divine theophany, cosmic plagues, testing/refining

Key verses: Matt 25:41, Rev 20:14-15, Jude 1:7, Heb 12:29

Relevance: The fire element of the lake of fire. OT background (H784 esh) via LXX bridge (316 co-occurrences). In Revelation, fire functions both as instrument of judgment (Rev 20:9) and as component of the lake's designation.

docs.title: H1614 — gophriyth
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1614-gophriyth.md

Occurrences: 7

Feminine noun, 'brimstone/sulphur.' 7 OT occurrences across 6 books. Associated with divine judgment on cities (Gen 19:24, Deut 29:23), eschatological judgment (Ezek 38:22, Isa 34:9), individual retribution (Job 18:15, Psa 11:6), and prepared burning (Isa 30:33). Consistently collocates with esh (fire) and haphak (overthrow).

Semantic categories: divine judgment on cities, eschatological judgment, individual retribution, prepared burning

Key verses: Gen 19:24, Psa 11:6, Isa 30:33, Isa 34:9, Ezek 38:22

Relevance: The brimstone element of 'fire and brimstone.' Every OT fire-and-brimstone event produces destruction/ashes/cessation, not ongoing burning. The paradigm sets expectations for the lake 'burning with fire and brimstone' (Rev 21:8).

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

Verb, 'to destroy fully, perish, lose.' 102 tokens across 86 verses, 15 books. Active: to destroy, ruin, kill. Middle/passive: to perish, be lost. Primary antonym: sozo (save). The fundamental NT binary: perish (apollymi) vs. life (zoe). Used by Jesus to interpret Sodom (Luke 17:29 'destroyed them all') and for gehenna (Matt 10:28 'destroy soul and body').

Semantic categories: physical destruction/killing, divine judgment/eschatological ruin, perishing in eternal judgment, losing life/soul, losing/finding possession, decay/perishability

Key verses: John 3:16, Matt 10:28, Luke 17:29, 2 Pet 3:9

Relevance: The primary destruction verb. Jesus uses it for the Sodom paradigm (Luke 17:29) and for gehenna (Matt 10:28). The apollymi/sozo binary (perish vs. save) is the NT's dominant framework for eternal outcomes -- not torment vs. life.

docs.title: G684 — apoleia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G684-apoleia.md

Occurrences: 20

Feminine noun, 'destruction, perdition, waste.' 20 tokens across 19 verses, 11 books. Cognate noun of apollymi. Used for final eschatological ruin (Matt 7:13, Phil 3:19), 'son of perdition' (John 17:12, 2 Thess 2:3), the beast going into perdition (Rev 17:8,11). The NT's preferred eschatological-destiny word.

Semantic categories: final eschatological ruin, son of perdition, beast going to perdition, waste/squandering, false teachers' ruin

Key verses: Matt 7:13, Phil 3:19, 2 Pet 3:7, Rev 17:8

Relevance: The noun form of apollymi. 'Broad way leads to destruction' (Matt 7:13). The beast 'goes into perdition' (Rev 17:8,11) -- destruction vocabulary for the very entity that enters the lake.

docs.title: G2851 — kolasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2851-kolasis.md

Occurrences: 2

Feminine noun, 'punishment.' Only 2 NT occurrences: Matt 25:46 ('everlasting punishment') and 1 John 4:18 ('fear hath torment'). Root kolaz0 = to curtail/prune. The Aristotelian distinction: kolasis = corrective punishment; timoria = retributive punishment. Matt 25:46 uses kolasis, NOT basanismos, for human punishment.

Semantic categories: eschatological/judicial punishment, tormenting quality of fear

Key verses: Matt 25:46, 1 John 4:18

Relevance: Matt 25:46 uses kolasis (punishment) for humans, NOT basanismos (torment). Different vocabulary for humans vs. non-human entities. The etymological connection to 'curtailing' (kolazo = to prune) suggests limitation rather than endless extension.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Adjective from aion (age). 71 tokens across 69 verses, 19 books. Dominant usage: 'eternal life' (~43 of 69 verses). Also modifies: punishment (Matt 25:46), fire (Matt 25:41, Jude 1:7), destruction (2 Thess 1:9). Does NOT modify basanizo in any text -- aionios never directly modifies the torment verb.

Semantic categories: eternal life, eternal judgment/punishment, divine attributes, eternal realities, eternal purpose

Key verses: John 3:16, Matt 25:41, Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, Jude 1:7

Relevance: Modifies kolasis (punishment, Matt 25:46) and olethros (destruction, 2 Thess 1:9) but NEVER directly modifies basanizo (torment). The 'eternal fire' of Jude 1:7 refers to Sodom -- which is not still burning. Aionios describes the permanence of the result, not necessarily the duration of the process.

docs.title: G165 — aion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G165-aion.md

Occurrences: 120

Masculine noun, 'age, era, perpetuity.' 120 tokens across 95 verses, 22 books. The 'ages of the ages' formula (eis tous aionas ton aionon) appears in Rev 20:10 for the torment of the devil/beast/false prophet. This is a Semitic superlative-by-repetition idiom.

Semantic categories: duration/perpetuity, intensified perpetuity (ages of ages), this present age, age to come, created order/universe

Key verses: Rev 4:9-10, Rev 11:15, Rev 14:11, Rev 20:10

Relevance: The 'ages of ages' formula in Rev 20:10 is applied ONLY to the devil, beast, and false prophet -- non-human entities. The same formula is used in doxologies for God's eternal reign (Rev 11:15). Its application to non-human entities at the lake does not automatically extend to human subjects.

docs.title: G86 — hades
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G86-háidēs.md

Occurrences: 11

Proper locative noun, 'Hades.' 11 NT occurrences across 5 books. The unseen world, realm of the dead. Corresponds to Hebrew sheol (H7585). Paired with thanatos (death) 4 times in Revelation. Cast into the lake of fire in Rev 20:14 -- not a permanent state but a temporary condition abolished.

Semantic categories: realm of the dead/grave, judgment association, defeated power

Key verses: Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, Rev 1:18, Rev 6:8, Rev 20:13-14

Relevance: Hades is the intermediate state, not the final state. Its casting into the lake of fire (Rev 20:14) represents the abolition of the intermediate state of death. Hades delivers up its dead (Rev 20:13) and is then destroyed.

docs.title: G1067 — geenna
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1067-geenna.md

Occurrences: 12

Feminine noun, transliteration of Hebrew 'Valley of Hinnom.' 12 NT occurrences: 7 in Matthew, 3 in Mark, 1 in Luke, 1 in James. Almost exclusively on Jesus's lips (11/12). Associated with fire (6x collocate with pyr). Jesus uses apollymi (destroy) with gehenna (Matt 10:28), not basanizo (torment).

Semantic categories: fiery place of destruction, self-denial to escape it, destruction of soul and body, judicial judgment, moral corruption

Key verses: Matt 5:22, Matt 10:28, Mark 9:43, Luke 12:5

Relevance: Gehenna is Jesus's term for eschatological fire; 'lake of fire' is John's Revelation term. They occupy the same functional role but are never equated in the text. Jesus uses destruction vocabulary (apollymi) with gehenna, not torment vocabulary.

docs.title: G110 — athanasia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G110-athanasia.md

Occurrences: 3

Feminine noun, alpha-privative + thanatos = 'deathlessness, immortality.' Only 3 NT occurrences: 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54, 1 Tim 6:16. God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16 monos echon athanasian). Humans must 'put on' immortality at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54).

Semantic categories: eschatological transformation at resurrection, exclusive divine attribute

Key verses: 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54, 1 Tim 6:16

Relevance: If God alone has inherent immortality, humans are mortal. If immortality is a gift received at the resurrection, the wicked who do not receive it remain mortal -- and mortal beings can be destroyed. The ECT position requires inherent human immortality; athanasia suggests otherwise.

docs.title: G3639 — olethros
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3639-olethros.md

Occurrences: 4

Masculine noun from ollymi (to destroy). Only 4 NT occurrences, all Pauline. 'Everlasting destruction' (olethros aionios) in 2 Thess 1:9. Paired with apoleia in 1 Tim 6:9. Emphasizes catastrophic, violent ruin.

Semantic categories: disciplinary destruction, sudden eschatological destruction, everlasting destruction, destruction paired with perdition

Key verses: 1 Thess 5:3, 2 Thess 1:9, 1 Tim 6:9

Relevance: 2 Thess 1:9 uses olethros aionios (everlasting destruction) for the wicked's fate. Paul uses destruction vocabulary, not torment vocabulary, for eschatological punishment of humans.

docs.title: G2920 — krisis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2920-krisis.md

Occurrences: 47

Feminine noun from krino (to judge). 47 occurrences, concentrated in Matthew and John. Meaning: judgment (process), condemnation, tribunal, justice. The 'day of judgment' formula (hemera kriseos) is the most common usage.

Semantic categories: day of judgment, judicial process, present cosmic condemnation, righteous character of judgment

Key verses: Matt 10:15, Matt 12:36, John 5:22, Heb 9:27, Rev 19:2

Relevance: The judgment context for the lake of fire. Rev 20:12-13 describes the judgment process (ekritthesan, aorist passive of krino) that precedes the lake of fire casting.

docs.title: H4194 — maveth
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H4194-maveth.md

Occurrences: 170

Masculine noun from muth (to die). 170 tokens across 153 verses, 27 OT books. The OT's primary death noun. Near-perfect LXX bridge to thanatos (G2288) with PMI 5.98 (score 27.43). Semantic categories: physical death, legal penalty, death personified as cosmic power.

Semantic categories: physical death, legal penalty/judgment, death personified

Key verses: Isa 25:8, Hos 13:14, Ezek 18:4

Relevance: The Hebrew background for thanatos. Isa 25:8 (maveth swallowed up) → 1 Cor 15:54 (thanatos swallowed up) → Rev 20:14 (thanatos cast into lake). The maveth→thanatos→second death chain.

docs.title: H7585 — sheol
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H7585-showl.md

Occurrences: 68

Feminine noun. 68 tokens across 64 verses, 17 OT books. The unseen world of the dead, the grave. LXX renders sheol as hades (G86) with PMI 8.31 (score 33.87). Paired with maveth in synonymous parallelism 15 times. Hos 13:14: 'O grave (sheol), I will be thy destruction.'

Semantic categories: realm of the dead, descent language, sheol and death paired, fate of the wicked

Key verses: Gen 37:35, Num 16:33, Psa 89:48, Hos 13:14

Relevance: The OT equivalent of hades. Both sheol (OT) and hades (NT) are temporary intermediate states. Rev 20:14 fulfills Hos 13:14 by casting hades (= sheol) into the lake, abolishing the intermediate state.

docs.title: CLASSIFICATIONS.md — etc7-13 Lake of Fire / Second Death
docs.text: Per-item audit trail for all positional E-items (Cond. or ECT) and all N-items. Each entry runs the full Tree 3 or Tree 4 walkthrough using tool-verified parsing data.

docs.title: E-Item Classifications (Tree 3)
docs.text:
E4 (Rev 20:9) — "Fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "devoured" (katephagen, katesthio G2719) = destruction/consumption vocabulary applied to Gog/Magog armies. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject of katephagen is pyr (fire, G4442, N-NSN). The object (autous, P-APM) refers to the Gog/Magog armies — human beings. However, these are within an apocalyptic vision sequence (Rev 20:7-10). The armies represent "the nations in the four quarters of the earth" (v.8) — numberless as sand. PASS (literal humans are the object of the destruction).
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: katephagen (katesthio G2719, V-2AAI-3S, second aorist active indicative). The verb unambiguously means "devoured/consumed" with pyr as subject and autous as direct object. No alternative parsing exists. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation 20:7-10 is an apocalyptic vision (Rev 1:1 semaino — "signified"). The seer reports visionary scenes using symbolic imagery. FAIL — apocalyptic genre.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 3 fails).
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic vision. The verse depicts a visionary scene of fire consuming armies in an apocalyptic sequence.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, fire from God consumes human armies — the verb katesthio (devour) is used."
  • RC3: The corrected observation uses destruction vocabulary (V1: devour), but applied within apocalyptic genre. As a genre-qualified observation, it does not constitute direct didactic teaching about human fate. Neither V1 (destruction applied to humans as literal teaching) nor V2 applies in corrected form. Result: Neutral.

E6 (Rev 19:21) — "The remnant were slain with the sword" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "slain" (apektanthesan, apokteino G615) = death/killing vocabulary applied to human remnant. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): hoi loipoi (the remnant) — human armies/followers of the beast. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: apektanthesan (apokteino G615, V-API-3P, aorist passive indicative). Unambiguously "were killed." The instrument is en te romphaia (by the sword). No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation 19:19-21 is an apocalyptic vision (the Armageddon battle scene). The sword proceeds from Christ's mouth (v.15, 21) — symbolic imagery. FAIL — apocalyptic genre.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic vision. The sword from the mouth is symbolic (word-sword).
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, human followers are described as slain by the symbolic sword proceeding from the rider's mouth."
  • RC3: Genre-qualified: does not constitute direct didactic teaching. Result: Neutral.

E9 (Rev 21:4) — "There shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither pain" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "no more death" (ho thanatos ouk estai eti) = cessation vocabulary — death itself is abolished. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject is ho thanatos (death, G2288, N-NSM) — death as a category/condition, not a symbolic entity or allegory. The verse describes the new creation state. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: estai (eimi G1510, V-FDI-3S, future middle indicative) with negation ouk and adverb eti (anymore, G2089). "Death shall not be anymore." Grammar is unambiguous — future negation of death's existence. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Rev 21:1-8 is the new creation passage. While within Revelation, this section is descriptive/promissory — direct divine speech ("Behold, I make all things new," v.5). It functions as direct eschatological promise, not symbolic vision. The content echoes the didactic promise of Isa 25:8 (swallow up death, wipe away tears). PASS — promissory/didactic within Revelation.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E11 (1 Cor 15:26, last enemy destroyed is death), E12 (Isa 25:8, swallow up death), E1 (Rev 20:14, death cast into lake). No conflict with any E-item. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. The abolition of death is directly stated.

E10 (Rom 6:23) — "The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "death" (thanatos, G2288) = death vocabulary as the penalty for sin. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The statement is universal — about all humans who sin. Not symbolic or allegorical. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: thanatos (G2288, N-NSM) as predicate nominative in a verbless clause (ta gar opsonia tes hamartias thanatos). The predicate is unambiguously "death." The contrast is thanatos vs. zoe aionios (eternal life, G2222 + G166). No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Romans is a Pauline epistle — didactic prose, direct theological teaching. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E25 (Ezek 18:4, soul that sins shall die), E21 (John 3:16, perish vs. life), E26 (2 Thess 1:9, everlasting destruction). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E15 (Gen 19:24-25) — "The LORD rained brimstone and fire... he overthrew those cities" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "overthrew" (haphak H2015) = destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah — literal human beings and their cities. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Haphak (H2015) = to overthrow, overturn. Applied to the cities and "all the inhabitants" (et kol yoshvey ha-arim). Unambiguous destruction vocabulary. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Genesis 19 is historical narrative — reporting historical events. PASS — narrative (didactic weight).
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E16 (Luke 17:29, apollymi), E17 (2 Pet 2:6, tephroo/ashes), E18 (Mal 4:1-3, ashes). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E16 (Luke 17:29) — "It rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "destroyed" (apolesen, apollymi G622) = destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The people of Sodom — literal humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): apolesen (apollymi G622, V-AAI-3S, aorist active indicative). "Destroyed them all" (hapantas). Unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Jesus's eschatological discourse — direct teaching in didactic context. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E15, E17. No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E17 (2 Pet 2:6) — "Turning the cities of Sodom to ashes... an ensample unto the ungodly" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "ashes" (tephroo G5077) = destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Cities and inhabitants of Sodom — literal entities. The "ensample" (hupodeigma) explicitly extends the application to future "ungodly" (asebein) persons. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): tephrosas (tephroo G5077, aorist active participle). Means "having turned to ashes." Unique NT word. Unambiguous. katastrophe (G2692) = overthrow. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): 2 Peter is an epistle — didactic teaching. Peter explicitly makes this a type ("ensample") for the eschatological fate of the ungodly. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E15, E16, E18. No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. Peter explicitly makes the destruction-outcome a paradigm for the ungodly.

E18 (Mal 4:1-3) — "Shall be stubble... shall burn them up... they shall be ashes under your feet" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "stubble," "burn up," "ashes" (qash, lahat, epher H665) = destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "All the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly" — literal human wicked. Universal scope. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Three destruction terms: qash (stubble), lahat (burn up, set ablaze), epher (H665, ashes). Grammar is direct — the wicked ARE stubble, the day SHALL burn them up, they SHALL BE ashes. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Malachi 4 is direct-speech prophecy ("saith the LORD of hosts"). PASS — didactic/prophetic.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E15-E17. No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E20 (Matt 10:28) — "Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "destroy" (apolesai, apollymi G622) = destruction vocabulary applied to soul and body. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects to be destroyed are "soul and body" (psychen kai soma) of human beings. Universal application. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: apolesai — not directly in the parse window, but the verse text confirms apolesai (apollymi G622, aorist active infinitive). Applied to kai psychen kai soma (both soul and body). "The one being able (ton dynamenon) to destroy both soul and body in gehenna." Grammar is unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Matthew 10 is direct teaching of Jesus to his disciples — didactic discourse. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E25 (Ezek 18:4, soul can die), E10 (Rom 6:23, wages is death). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E21 (John 3:16) — "Should not perish, but have everlasting life" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "perish" (apoletai, apollymi G622) = destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "Whosoever believeth" / "whosoever does not believe" — universal human scope. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: apoletai would be V-2AMS-3S (aorist middle subjunctive of apollymi G622). In the hina clause: "in order that everyone believing in him might not perish (me apoletai) but have (eche) eternal life." The binary is apollymi vs. zoe aionios. Grammar is unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): John 3 is Jesus's direct teaching to Nicodemus — didactic discourse. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E10 (Rom 6:23, death vs. life), E20 (Matt 10:28, destroy), E27 (Phil 3:19, end is destruction). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E24 (1 Tim 6:16) — "Who only hath immortality" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "only hath immortality" implies others do NOT have immortality — cessation vocabulary by implication (humans are mortal/destructible). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subject is God (monos echon athanasian). The implication concerns humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): monos (G3441, alone/only) + echon (V-PAP-NSM, present active participle of echo) + athanasian (G110, N-ASF, immortality). "Alone having deathlessness." The word monos unambiguously means "alone/only." PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): 1 Timothy is a Pauline epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E35 (1 Cor 15:53, immortality as future gift), E25 (Ezek 18:4, soul can die). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E25 (Ezek 18:4) — "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "die" (muth H4191) = death vocabulary applied to the soul. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Nephesh (H5315, soul/person) — the literal human person. Universal statement: "all souls are mine." PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): hannephesh hachote't hi' tamuth — "the soul, the sinning one, it shall die." Muth (H4191) in Qal yiqtol (imperfect), expressing future certainty. Grammar is unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Ezekiel 18 is direct-speech divine oracle ("saith the Lord GOD"). PASS — didactic/prophetic.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E10 (Rom 6:23), E20 (Matt 10:28). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E26 (2 Thess 1:9) — "Punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "everlasting destruction" (olethron aionion) = destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "Those who know not God, and obey not the gospel" — literal human wicked. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): olethron (G3639, N-ASM, destruction) + aionion (G166, A-ASM, everlasting). Olethros means catastrophic ruin/destruction. Grammar is unambiguous — the penalty is destruction, qualified as everlasting. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): 2 Thessalonians is a Pauline epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E10, E20, E21, E27. No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E27 (Phil 3:19) — "Whose end is destruction" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "destruction" (apoleia G684) = destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "Enemies of the cross of Christ" — literal human persons. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): hon to telos apoleia — "of whom the end [is] destruction." Apoleia (G684) is the cognate noun of apollymi. Grammar is unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Philippians is a Pauline epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E10, E20, E21, E26. No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E28 (Ezek 28:18-19) — "I will bring thee to ashes... never shalt thou be any more" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "ashes" (epher H665), "devour" (akal H398), "never any more" (ayin H369) = destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The "anointed cherub" — identified as a supernatural being (the Satan-figure). Not a literal human being. However, unlike Revelation's symbolic beast, this is a non-human spirit being addressed directly by God in a prophetic oracle. FAIL — subject is a non-human spirit being.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Not reached.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Not reached.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Subject is a non-human spirit being (the anointed cherub / Satan-figure).
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "God's direct oracle describes the Satan-figure's fate as becoming ashes and existing never any more — destruction vocabulary applied to the same non-human entity tormented in Rev 20:10."
  • RC3: V1 (destruction vocabulary) applies, but to a non-human entity. As an observation about a non-human entity's fate, both sides can accept what the text says while disagreeing about its implications. Result: Neutral.

E31 (Psa 37:10,20) — "The wicked shall not be... shall consume into smoke" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "shall not be" (ayin H369), "perish" (abad H6), "consume" (kalah H3615) = non-existence/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The wicked" — literal human persons. Universal. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): ayin (H369) = non-existence; abad (H6, Qal yiqtol) = shall perish; kalah (H3615, Qal qatal) = consume/be finished. "Into smoke shall they consume away." All terms unambiguously denote cessation. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm 37 is wisdom poetry, functioning as didactic instruction. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E18 (Mal 4:1-3, ashes), E25 (Ezek 18:4, shall die), E32 (Obad 1:16, not been). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E32 (Obad 1:16) — "They shall be as though they had not been" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "as though they had not been" (kelo hayu) = non-existence vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "All the heathen" (kol-haggoyim) — literal human nations. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): kelo hayu — "as though they had not been." Perfect tense of hayah with negation and comparative. Unambiguous non-existence language. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Obadiah is direct-speech prophecy. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E31 (Psa 37:10, shall not be), E18 (Mal 4:1-3, ashes). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E33 (Rev 14:10-11) — "He shall be tormented with fire and brimstone... smoke ascendeth forever" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — "tormented" (basanisthesetai, basanizo G928), "no rest day nor night" = conscious-ongoing-existence vocabulary. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The same" (autos) — referring to "if any man worship the beast and his image" (v.9). Human beast-worshippers. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: basanisthesetai (basanizo G928, V-FPI-3S, future passive indicative). "He shall be tormented." Grammar supports ECT reading at surface level. However, the "smoke ascending forever" formula (kapnos anabainei eis aionas aionon) draws on Isa 34:10 (same formula for Edom — fire ended). The grammar itself does not resolve whether the formula describes duration of process or permanence of result. PASS (grammar supports the surface reading).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation 14 is an apocalyptic vision — the three angels' messages delivered within the visionary framework of Rev 1:1 (semaino, "signified"). FAIL — apocalyptic genre.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic vision. The passage uses the "smoke ascending forever" formula that derives from Isa 34:10 (Edom, where the fire ended — Isa 34:11-17).
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, the third angel uses the 'smoke ascending forever' formula — the same formula applied to Edom (Isa 34:10, fire ended) and Babylon (Rev 19:3, completely destroyed)."
  • RC3: The corrected observation is a genre-qualified statement about apocalyptic formula usage. Neither side's reading survives the genre gate without qualification. Result: Neutral.

E35 (1 Cor 15:53) — "This mortal must put on immortality" — Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "mortal" (thnetos) / "put on immortality" (athanasian endysasthai) = mortality vocabulary implying destructibility. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subject is the resurrected believer — literal humans. The implication extends to all humans (mortals by nature). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): endysasthai (endyo G1746, aorist middle infinitive) = "to put on." athanasian (G110, N-ASF) = immortality. The construction "must put on" (dei endysasthai) treats immortality as something external that is received, not inherent. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): 1 Corinthians is a Pauline epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E24 (1 Tim 6:16, God only has immortality). No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: N-Item Classifications (Tree 4)
docs.text:
N1 — "The text uses different vocabulary for different subject categories at the lake of fire" — Based on: E3, E4, E5, E6 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that the text uses different vocabulary for different subjects? YES — the vocabulary differentiation is observable: basanisthesontai for devil/beast/false prophet (E3), katephagen for human armies (E4), zontes for beast/false prophet (E5), apektanthesan for human remnant (E6). Both sides can verify this from the text. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? YES — the vocabulary IS different. This is an observable grammatical fact, not a choice between readings. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the E-items? NO — it simply observes that E3, E4, E5, E6 use different words. No concept added. PASS.
  • Gate 0 PASSES. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither V1 (destruction applied to wicked humans) nor V2 (torment applied to wicked humans). This is a grammatical/observational statement about vocabulary distribution. Both V1 and V2 fail. Result: Neutral. Stop.

N2 — "The casting of death and hades into the lake (Rev 20:14) fulfills the OT/NT death-of-death chain" — Based on: E1, E11, E12 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from either position agree that Rev 20:14 (death cast into lake) fulfills 1 Cor 15:26 (last enemy destroyed is death) and Isa 25:8 (death swallowed up)? YES — the vocabulary connections (katargeo/bala/eblethesan all applied to thanatos/maveth) and the intertextual quotation chain (Paul quoting Isaiah, Revelation echoing both) are verifiable. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion from the cited E-items? The E-items state: death will be swallowed up (E12), death is the last enemy destroyed (E11), death was cast into the lake (E1). That the casting IS the destruction/swallowing-up follows without alternative. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add any concept not in E1, E11, E12? NO — it merely observes that the same subject (death) receives the same treatment (destroyed/swallowed/cast-in) across the three passages. PASS.
  • Gate 0 PASSES. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — destruction of death. But death being destroyed is an observation both sides accept. Neither V1 nor V2 applies in a positional sense — both ECT and conditionalist scholars agree death is destroyed/abolished. Result: Neutral. Stop.

N3 — "The torment formula (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) appears once in Scripture (Rev 20:10), applied only to the devil, beast, and false prophet" — Based on: E3 — Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):

  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? YES — the formula either appears elsewhere or it does not. It does not. PASS.

docs.title: CONCLUSION — Lake of Fire and the Second Death
Question
docs.text: Lake of fire in Revelation. "Second death" (Rev 2:11; 20:6,14; 21:8). Rev 20:14 ("lake of fire IS the second death"). Death/hell cast into lake (Rev 20:14). What is the lake of fire? What is the second death? What does it mean that Rev 20:14 identifies the lake of fire AS the second death? What does it mean that death and hades are cast into the lake of fire? Who are the subjects who enter the lake? What do Rev 2:11 and 20:6 say about overcomers and the second death? How does the "second death" function as the text's own explanation of what the lake does?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The lake of fire is identified by the text itself as "the second death" (Rev 20:14; 21:8) using the same X=Y predicate nominative formula that Revelation uses throughout to equate symbols with their referents. The predicate noun in both identification formulas is thanatos (death), not basanismos (torment) or kolasis (punishment). Five categories of subjects enter the lake, and the text applies different vocabulary to each: torment language (basanizo) is used only for non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet), while human subjects receive death/destruction vocabulary (slain, devoured, second death). The casting of death and hades into the lake fulfills the OT/NT death-of-death chain (Isa 25:8, 1 Cor 15:26), resulting in "no more death" (Rev 21:4). Overcomers are exempt from the second death through the strongest Greek negation (ou me + aorist passive subjunctive, Rev 2:11) and jurisdictional exclusion (exousia, Rev 20:6).

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
The Text's Own Definition (Rev 20:14) And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

The Repeated Identification (Rev 21:8) But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

The Overcomer Promise (Rev 2:11) He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.

The Jurisdictional Statement (Rev 20:6) Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years.

Humans Devoured, Devil Tormented (Rev 20:9-10) And fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them. And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

The Wages of Sin (Rom 6:23) For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

The Last Enemy Destroyed (1 Cor 15:26) The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.

Death Abolished (Rev 21:4) And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

God Destroys Soul and Body (Matt 10:28) And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Sodom as Paradigm (2 Pet 2:6) And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly.

docs.title: 1. The Predicate Nominative Identification: "This IS the Second Death"
docs.text:
The linchpin of this study is Rev 20:14b: houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin, he limne tou puros -- "This, the second death, is the lake of fire." The construction is a predicate nominative identification formula. The subject (houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros) is maximally definite with triple determination: demonstrative pronoun (houtos), article on the noun (ho thanatos), and article on the ordinal adjective (ho deuteros). The copula is estin (V-PAI-3S, present active indicative of eimi). The predicate nominative (he limne tou puros) is articular and definite.

This is not an isolated grammatical construction. Revelation uses the identical formula throughout as a self-interpreting mechanism: Rev 1:20 ("the seven stars ARE the angels... the seven candlesticks ARE the seven churches"), Rev 17:9 ("the seven heads ARE seven mountains"), Rev 17:15 ("the waters ARE peoples"), Rev 17:18 ("the woman IS that great city"), Rev 5:8 ("odours which ARE the prayers of saints"). The OT prototypes include Gen 41:26-27 ("the seven good kine ARE seven years") and Dan 2:38 ("thou ART this head of gold"). In every case, the formula commits to full identity between the symbolic image and its referent.

The vocabulary choice in this identification is decisive. The predicate noun is thanatos (G2288, death) -- not basanismos (G929, torment) and not kolasis (G2851, punishment). The text had torment vocabulary available (basanizo appears in Rev 20:10, one verse earlier) and punishment vocabulary available (kolasis appears in Matt 25:46). The text chose neither. It chose death. Rev 21:8 repeats the formula: ho estin ho thanatos ho deuteros -- "which IS the second death." Both identification statements use the same word: thanatos.

The word thanatos appears 119 times across 106 NT verses in 15 books. Its consistent meaning throughout Scripture is death -- cessation of life, the reversal of the creative act of Gen 2:7. No verse defines thanatos as "separation from God" or "eternal conscious suffering." When the text identifies the lake of fire using this word, it draws on the entire biblical semantic range of thanatos.

docs.title: 2. Five Categories of Subjects: Vocabulary Differentiation
docs.text:
Five distinct categories of subjects enter the lake of fire, and the text applies different vocabulary to each:

Category 1: Beast and false prophet (Rev 19:20). Cast "alive" (zontes, V-PAP-NPM, present active participle of zao G2198) into the lake. These are symbolic entities -- the beast has seven heads, ten horns, and a composite Daniel 7 body (Rev 13:1-2). The false prophet is identified with the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17. Neither is a literal human being. The present active participle zontes encodes their ongoing state of being alive at the moment of casting -- they do not die first.

Category 2: Human remnant (Rev 19:21). "Slain" (apektanthesan, V-API-3P, aorist passive indicative of apokteino G615) with the sword from Christ's mouth. The fowls were filled with their flesh (echortasthesan ek ton sarkon). The vocabulary is death/killing: humans die, their bodies are consumed. No torment vocabulary. The contrast with v.20 is grammatically enforced: symbolic entities = cast alive; humans = killed.

Category 3: Human armies at Gog/Magog (Rev 20:9). "Devoured" (katephagen, V-2AAI-3S, second aorist active indicative of katesthio G2719). This is consumption/destruction vocabulary. Katesthio means to eat down, devour utterly. Fire from heaven devours them. ONE VERSE later, the devil receives torment vocabulary (basanisthesontai, Rev 20:10). The vocabulary switch between v.9 and v.10 is the most compact demonstration of the differentiation pattern.

Category 4: Devil (Rev 20:10). "Tormented" (basanisthesontai, V-FPI-3P, future passive indicative of basanizo G928) "day and night for ever and ever." The subject is explicitly the devil (ho diabolos), identified through a four-fold naming chain as the dragon, the old serpent, the Devil, and Satan (Rev 12:9; 20:2). The beast and false prophet are already present (hopou kai to therion kai ho pseudoprophetes). All three are non-human/symbolic entities. This is the only future-tense verb in the aorist narrative chain of vv.9-14, projecting the consequence beyond the vision's timeframe.

Category 5: Humans not in the book of life (Rev 20:15) and eight categories of wicked (Rev 21:8). Cast into the lake (eblethe, V-API-3S). No torment vocabulary is applied. Rev 21:8 specifies "their part" (to meros auton) in the lake "which is the second death." The identification is thanatos, not basanismos.

The torment formula (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) appears once in Scripture (Rev 20:10). It is applied only to three non-human/symbolic entities. No verse applies this formula to any human being at the lake of fire. When humans enter the lake, the text calls the experience "the second death."

docs.title: 3. The Death-of-Death Chain
docs.text:
The casting of death and hades into the lake of fire (Rev 20:14) is not an isolated event but the fulfillment of a vocabulary chain stretching from Isaiah through Paul to Revelation.

Isaiah 25:8 prophesied: "He will swallow up death (bala + maveth) in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Hosea 13:14 addressed death directly: "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction." Paul quoted both passages at the climax of his resurrection argument (1 Cor 15:54-55): "Death is swallowed up (katephothe, aorist passive of katapino G2666) in victory. O death, where is thy sting?" Paul also declared that Christ "hath abolished death" (katargesantos, aorist active participle of katargeo G2673, 2 Tim 1:10) and that "the last enemy that shall be destroyed (katargeitai, present passive of katargeo G2673) is death" (1 Cor 15:26).

The verb katargeo (G2673) is applied to both death (1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10) and the devil (Heb 2:14: "that through death he might destroy [katargese] him that had the power of death, that is, the devil"). Both death and the devil end up in the lake of fire (Rev 20:10, 14). The verb chain is consistent: death is to be swallowed up (Isa 25:8 / 1 Cor 15:54), abolished (2 Tim 1:10), destroyed (1 Cor 15:26), and cast into the lake (Rev 20:14). The result is stated in Rev 21:4: "there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." This verse echoes Isaiah 25:8's "wipe away tears from all faces."

In Rev 20:13, death and hades function as personified agents -- they "gave up" (edokan, V-AAI-3P) the dead that were in them. In v.14, the same entities become patients -- they "were cast" (eblethesan, V-API-3P, divine passive) into the lake. The active-to-passive voice reversal within two verses encodes the eschatological reversal: entities that held the dead are themselves consumed by the lake of fire. They are conditions/states being abolished, not persons being tormented.

docs.title: 4. The Fire-and-Brimstone Paradigm
docs.text:
The lake of fire "burning with fire and brimstone" (Rev 21:8) inherits a paradigm that begins in Genesis and runs through the entire canon. Every OT fire-and-brimstone event produces destruction, ashes, and cessation -- never ongoing burning.

Genesis 19:24-25: The LORD rained brimstone and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah. The outcome: "he overthrew" (haphak H2015) those cities -- total destruction. Luke 17:29: Jesus interpreted the event: "destroyed them all" (apolesen, aorist active of apollymi G622). 2 Peter 2:6: Peter identified the outcome as "turning to ashes" (tephrosas, aorist active participle of tephroo G5077, unique in the NT) and made it "an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly." Jude 1:7: Sodom suffered "the vengeance of eternal fire" (puros aioniou) -- yet the fire ended, the cities are destroyed, not still burning.

Malachi 4:1-3: The wicked are "stubble" (qash), "burned up" (lahat), and become "ashes under the soles of your feet" (epher H665). The outcome is complete consumption and cessation. Isaiah 34:9-10: Edom's "smoke thereof shall go up for ever" (le-olam) -- yet Isaiah 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the ruins. The fire ended. The "smoke ascending forever" formula describes the permanence and irreversibility of the destruction, not the duration of the burning.

This same "smoke ascending forever" formula appears in Rev 14:11 (beast-worshippers) and Rev 19:3 (Babylon). In the Babylon case, the formula is applied to an entity that Rev 18:21-23 documents as completely destroyed with fivefold "found no more at all" (ou me heurethe eti). The formula cannot mean ongoing burning when the text states the entity no longer exists.

docs.title: 5. The Overcomer Promises and the Second Death
docs.text:
Rev 2:11 uses the strongest possible Greek negation: ou me adikethei (V-APS-3S, aorist passive subjunctive of adikeo G91). The construction ou me + aorist subjunctive is the most emphatic way to deny a future possibility in Greek. The overcomer will ABSOLUTELY NOT be hurt/injured/wronged by the second death.

The verb adikeo (G91) means to wrong, injure, harm. It appears 35 times in the NT, with Revelation accounting for 38% of all occurrences. The second death's effect is described as "hurting" -- consistent with it being actual death (from which one is protected) rather than a state of ongoing torment (from which protection would mean something different).

Rev 20:6 uses exousia (G1849, authority/jurisdiction): "the second death hath no power (exousian)." Exousia is a delegated-authority word, not a force word. The second death's domain is jurisdictionally limited -- it has authority over some (those not in the book of life) but not over others (first resurrection participants). This framing treats the second death as a realm of authority, consistent with it being an event (death) that exercises jurisdiction.

The pairing of Rev 2:10-11 creates a first-death/second-death contrast: "be thou faithful unto death" (first death, martyrdom) in v.10, then "not hurt of the second death" in v.11. Those who endure the first death are exempt from the second. This structural pairing parallels Rev 20:5-6: the first resurrection exempts from the second death; the implied second resurrection (of "the rest of the dead," v.5) leads to the second death.

docs.title: 6. The Book of Life Mechanism
docs.text:
The criterion for the lake of fire is not a specific sin or category of offense but a single question: "whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire" (Rev 20:15). The construction is a first-class conditional (ei + indicative), presenting the condition as assumed true for the sake of the narrative.

The book of life concept begins in Exodus 32:32-33, where God tells Moses: "Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book." It continues through Psa 69:28 ("blotted out of the book of the living"), Dan 12:1 ("found written in the book"), and into Revelation (Rev 3:5, 13:8, 17:8, 20:12,15, 21:27). The overcomer promise of Rev 3:5 ("I will not blot out his name out of the book of life") and the overcomer promise of Rev 2:11 ("shall not be hurt of the second death") are two sides of the same coin: in the book = exempt from second death; not in the book = subject to second death.

docs.title: 7. The Wages-of-Sin-is-Death Theme
docs.text:
Romans 6:23 states the binary with maximum clarity: "the wages of sin is death (thanatos); but the gift of God is eternal life (zoe aionios)." The same word thanatos used for the penalty of sin is used in "second death" (deuteros thanatos). The binary is death vs. life, not torment vs. life.

This binary runs across four NT authors: John 3:16 (apollymi vs. zoe aionios -- John), Matt 7:13-14 (apoleia vs. zoe -- Matthew), Rom 6:23 (thanatos vs. zoe aionios -- Paul), Phil 3:19 (apoleia as "the end" -- Paul), Gal 6:8 (phthora vs. zoe aionios -- Paul). No author introduces a third category of eternal conscious torment. The consistent framework is perish/death/destruction vs. life.

docs.title: 8. Human Mortality and the Second Death
docs.text:
The ECT position requires that human souls are inherently immortal and therefore indestructible -- they must continue to exist forever, whether in bliss or torment. Two passages directly address this premise.

1 Timothy 6:16: God "only hath immortality" (monos echon athanasian). Athanasia (G110) appears only 3 times in the NT. God alone possesses inherent deathlessness. If humans possessed it, Paul's "only" (monos) would be false.

1 Corinthians 15:53-54: "This mortal must put on immortality." Immortality is not a present human possession but a future gift received at the resurrection. If only the righteous receive immortality at the resurrection, the wicked remain mortal. Mortal beings can be destroyed (Matt 10:28: "destroy both soul and body in hell"). The soul (nephesh/psyche) can die (Ezek 18:4: "the soul that sinneth, it shall die").

docs.title: 9. The "No More Death" Outcome
docs.text: Rev 21:4 declares the outcome of the lake of fire sequence: "there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain." This follows directly from the casting of death and hades into the lake (Rev 20:14). If death has been abolished, and "God may be all in all" (1 Cor 15:28, panta en pasin), a sector of reality in which eternal conscious torment prevails would contradict both statements.

docs.title: 10. Gehenna and the Lake of Fire
docs.text: Gehenna (G1067) is Jesus's term for eschatological fire; the "lake of fire" (limne tou puros) is John's Revelation term. They are never equated in the text but occupy the same functional role. Jesus uses destruction vocabulary with gehenna: "destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matt 10:28, apollymi G622). Revelation uses death vocabulary for the lake: "which is the second death" (Rev 21:8, thanatos G2288). Both terms involve fire; both involve the destruction of human subjects. The conceptual continuity lies in the shared destruction vocabulary, not in any torment vocabulary.

docs.title: Word Studies
docs.text:
thanatos (G2288): 119 occurrences. Means death throughout Scripture -- cessation of life. The "second death" uses this word, not basanismos. Both identification formulas (Rev 20:14, 21:8) define the lake's function using death vocabulary.

basanizo (G928): 12 occurrences. At the lake of fire, applied only to non-human/symbolic entities (Rev 20:10). Never applied to human subjects at the lake. The torment formula appears once (Rev 20:10) for three non-human entities.

katargeo (G2673): 27 occurrences. Applied to death (1 Cor 15:26, 2 Tim 1:10) and the devil (Heb 2:14). Rev 20:14 fulfills 1 Cor 15:26.

katesthio (G2719): 20 occurrences. Rev 20:9: fire "devoured" human armies -- consumption/destruction vocabulary, one verse before torment vocabulary for the devil.

apollymi (G622): 102 occurrences. Jesus uses it for the Sodom paradigm (Luke 17:29) and for gehenna (Matt 10:28). The apollymi/sozo binary is the NT's dominant framework for eternal outcomes.

aionios (G166): 71 occurrences. Never directly modifies basanizo. The "eternal fire" of Jude 1:7 refers to Sodom -- not still burning. Aionios describes the permanence of the result, not necessarily the duration of the process.

adikeo (G91): 35 occurrences. Rev 2:11: ou me adikethei -- the overcomer absolutely will not be harmed by the second death. The second death "hurts" -- consistent with actual death.

exousia (G1849): 103 occurrences. Rev 20:6: the second death "hath no power/authority" over first resurrection participants. Jurisdictional limitation.

athanasia (G110): 3 occurrences. God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16). Humans must receive it at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54).

docs.title: Rev 20:10 — The Torment Formula
docs.text:
Rev 20:10 states that the devil, beast, and false prophet "shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever." This is the primary text cited in support of ECT. Three factors qualify this verse:

(1) All three subjects fail the Subject Gate (Tree 3, Gate 1): the devil is a non-human spirit being; the beast is a seven-headed symbolic composite entity (Rev 13:1-2); the false prophet is a symbolic entity identified with the earth beast of Rev 13:11-17. The torment formula is never applied to any human being.

(2) The passage is apocalyptic genre (Tree 3, Gate 3 fails). Rev 1:1 states the book was "signified" (semaino), indicating symbolic communication. Apocalyptic imagery requires genre-appropriate reading.

(3) The OT didactic passages (clearer genre) describe the same Satan-figure using destruction vocabulary: Ezek 28:18-19 ("ashes upon the earth," "never shalt thou be any more"). Under SIS, the clearer passage governs.

docs.title: Rev 14:10-11 — Smoke Ascending Forever
docs.text:
Rev 14:10-11 uses basanizo vocabulary and the "smoke ascending forever" formula for beast-worshippers (humans). Two qualifications:

(1) The formula derives from Isa 34:10 (Edom's smoke ascending forever -- yet the fire ended, Isa 34:11-17). The same formula is applied to Babylon (Rev 19:3), which is completely destroyed (Rev 18:21-23).

(2) The passage is apocalyptic genre (Gate 3 fails).

docs.title: Matt 25:41, 46 — Everlasting Fire and Punishment
docs.text: Matt 25:41 designates the fire as "prepared for the devil and his angels" -- its primary purpose involves non-human entities. Matt 25:46 uses kolasis (G2851, punishment), not basanismos (torment), for human subjects. Kolasis appears only twice in the NT and etymologically connects to kolazo (to curtail/prune), distinct from the torment vocabulary. The passage is a judgment parable.

docs.title: The ECT Reading of Rev 21:4
docs.text: If the ECT reading is correct, Rev 21:4's "no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain" requires either restricting the verse to the new earth alone (while eternal torment continues elsewhere) or redefining "no more death" to exclude the second death. Both moves require adding a concept the text does not state.
