These words could describe temporary judgment leading to destruction, or they could describe a phase of the judgment process. The passage does not say the tribulation and anguish are eternal. But neither does it explicitly limit them. The resolution comes from context: v.7 (seeking immortality not yet possessed), v.12 (sinners perish), and v.5 (day of wrath = event).

docs.title: 4. The "Sorer Punishment" of Heb 10:29
docs.text: Timoria (G5098, 1 NT use) describes punishment "sorer" than death. The ECT reading takes this as punishment beyond death — ongoing torment worse than dying. The alternative reading: the second death (total, permanent, irreversible destruction) is worse than temporal death under Moses' law, which could be mitigated by mercy. The text does not specify which kind of "sorer" is meant; the surrounding vocabulary (devour, destruction vs saving) favors the destruction reading.

docs.title: 5. Rev 20:10 and Its Relationship to Human Fate
docs.text: The torment of the devil, beast, and false prophet in Rev 20:10 is in the same location (lake of fire) where humans are also sent (Rev 20:15). The ECT argument infers that same location = same experience. The text does not state this. The vocabulary differentiation (humans devoured/given second death, non-human entities tormented) contradicts the inference that same location means same experience. Additionally, all three tormented entities are non-human/symbolic — the inference requires extending what is said about non-human entities to humans, which the text does not do.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
Across all 8 major judgment passages:

What the passages say about human fate: - 4 of 8 use explicit destruction/death vocabulary (Rev 20, 2 Thess 1, Heb 10, Rom 2) - 2 of 8 use penalty/judgment vocabulary without specifying nature (Matt 25, John 5) - 2 of 8 describe corpses viewed with permanent abhorrence (Dan 12, Isa 66) - 0 of 8 use basanizo/basanismos (torment) for human wicked

The vocabulary pattern: When NT authors describe the final fate of human wicked in these judgment passages, they choose destruction words (olethros, apollymi, apoleia, katesthio), death words (thanatos — "the second death"), judgment words (krisis, kolasis, timoria), and abhorrence words (dera'on applied to corpses). They do not choose torment words (basanizo, basanismos) for human subjects. Torment vocabulary appears only for non-human/symbolic entities in Revelation's apocalyptic framework.

The anthropological prerequisite: Humans do not inherently possess immortality (1 Tim 6:16, Rom 2:7, 1 Cor 15:53-54). The soul can die (Ezek 18:4) and be destroyed (Matt 10:28). Without immortality, the wicked cannot be tormented forever.

The fire paradigm: Every OT fire-and-brimstone precedent (Sodom, Edom, Jerusalem, Malachi's day) produces destruction, ashes, and cessation. This paradigm provides the interpretive context for "everlasting fire" (Matt 25:41), "fiery indignation" (Heb 10:27), "flaming fire" (2 Thess 1:8), and the "lake of fire" (Rev 20:14-15).

The weight of evidence: The destruction/death vocabulary for human fate is didactic, repeated, multi-author, and cross-testamental. The torment vocabulary for human fate is confined to apocalyptic genre, applied to non-human subjects, and interpreted against the OT fire paradigm. The evidence at E-tier and N-tier points toward conditionalist direction. The ECT case relies on inferences from apocalyptic passages and from extending what is said about non-human entities to humans.

Analysis completed: 2026-06-04

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Major judgment passages: Rev 20:11-15, Matt 25:31-46, Dan 12:2, Isa 66:22-24, John 5:28-29, 2 Thess 1:7-10, Heb 10:26-31, Rom 2:5-11. Each analyzed for E/N/I tier.

docs.title: G2851 — kolasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2851-kolasis.md

Occurrences: 2

Feminine noun from kolazo (G2849, 'to curtail/prune'). Only 2 NT uses: Matt 25:46 ('everlasting punishment') and 1 John 4:18 ('fear hath torment'). Louw-Nida Domain 38 (Punish). The root meaning is penal infliction with judicial/deterrent sense, distinct from basanismos (experiential torment process). KJV translates as 'punishment' (1x) and 'torment' (1x).

Semantic categories: eschatological judicial punishment, tormenting quality of fear

Key verses: Matt 25:46, 1 John 4:18

Relevance: Core debate word in Matt 25:46. With only 2 NT uses, kolasis is too rare for extensive distributional analysis. Root kolazo means 'to curtail/prune' -- distinct from basanismos. Louw-Nida places it in the Punish domain alongside krisis, not in the Torture domain.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Adjective from aion (G165, 'an age'). 71 tokens in 69 unique verses across 19 books. Means 'pertaining to the age(s)' with actual duration determined by the nature of the subject. ~60% modify 'life'; ~10% modify judgment subjects. Three past-time uses prove it does not inherently mean 'endless' (Rom 16:25, 2 Tim 1:9, Tit 1:2). LXX translates olam (H5769) as aionios 100 times -- inheriting olam's context-dependent semantics.

Semantic categories: eternal life as gift, eternal judgment/punishment, eternal attributes of God, eternal realities, eternal purpose/pre-temporal

Key verses: Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, Jude 1:7, Heb 5:9, Heb 6:2, Heb 9:12, Tit 1:2

Relevance: Modifies 'punishment' (Matt 25:46), 'destruction' (2 Thess 1:9), 'fire' (Matt 25:41, Jude 1:7). The etc7-08 study falsified the symmetry argument (same adjective = same duration) via Tit 1:2. The Hebrews pattern (aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act) governs interpretation across judgment passages.

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

Verb from apo + ollymi ('to destroy fully'). 102 tokens in 86 unique verses across 15 books. Active voice: to destroy/kill. Middle/passive: to perish/be lost. Louw-Nida classifies in BOTH Violence/Destroy (20.003) AND Exist/Non-exist (13.003). The apollymi-sozo binary spans 14 verses. Primary LXX bridge: abad (H6) -> apollymi (141 co-occurrences, PMI 6.14).

Semantic categories: physical destruction/killing, divine judgment/eschatological ruin, perishing in eternal judgment, losing one's life/soul, losing a possession, decay/perishability

Key verses: John 3:16, Matt 10:28, Rom 2:12, Luke 17:29, 2 Pet 3:9

Relevance: The standard NT word for the wicked's final fate in the perish-vs-life binary. Used in Rom 2:12 for sinners 'perishing.' No lexicon defines apollymi as 'torment' -- the semantic core is ending/cessation. The etc7-06 study established this at E-tier.

docs.title: G684 — apoleia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G684-apoleia.md

Occurrences: 20

Feminine noun from apollymi (G622). 20 tokens in 19 unique verses across 11 books. Louw-Nida 20.031 (Violence/Destroy). Denotes ruin, loss, destruction. Binary with zoe in Matt 7:13 ('way to destruction' vs 'way to life'). Used in Heb 10:39 ('draw back unto perdition').

Semantic categories: final eschatological ruin, son of perdition destiny-genitive, beast goes into perdition, waste/squandering, heresy-induced ruin, apostasy drawing back

Key verses: Matt 7:13, Heb 10:39, Phil 3:19, 2 Pet 3:7, Rev 17:8

Relevance: Used in Heb 10:39 as the alternative to 'saving of the soul.' Appears in Matt 7:13 as the structurally decisive binary with zoe. The etc7-06 study confirmed: no lexicon defines apoleia as 'torment.'

docs.title: G3639 — olethros
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3639-olethros.md

Occurrences: 4

Masculine noun from ollymi ('to destroy'). ONLY 4 NT uses -- ALL mean destruction/ruin. (1) 1 Cor 5:5 disciplinary destruction (with explicit salvation-purpose clause); (2) 1 Thess 5:3 sudden destruction; (3) 2 Thess 1:9 everlasting destruction; (4) 1 Tim 6:9 destruction and perdition. All Pauline. KJV renders uniformly as 'destruction.'

Semantic categories: disciplinary destruction, sudden eschatological destruction, everlasting destruction from God's presence, destruction paired with perdition

Key verses: 2 Thess 1:9, 1 Thess 5:3, 1 Cor 5:5, 1 Tim 6:9

Relevance: Paul's word for final judgment in 2 Thess 1:9. With only 4 uses, all meaning destruction, Paul deliberately chose olethros over basanizo. The only 'remedial' use (1 Cor 5:5) has an explicit salvation clause absent from eschatological uses.

docs.title: G2920 — krisis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2920-krisis.md

Occurrences: 47

Feminine noun from krino (G2919, 'to judge'). 47 NT uses across 13 books. Means decision, tribunal, justice. Louw-Nida domains: Court of Justice (056.001), Judge/Condemn/Acquit (056.005), Punish (038.001). Primary Hebrew source: mishpat (H4941, 132 co-occurrences, PMI 5.38). KJV translates primarily as 'judgment' (80%).

Semantic categories: day of judgment eschatological, judicial process/legal setting, present cosmic condemnation, righteous character of judgment, prophetic fulfillment

Key verses: John 5:29, Matt 10:15, Heb 9:27, John 3:19, Rev 19:2

Relevance: Used in John 5:29 for 'resurrection of judgment/damnation.' Krisis describes a verdict-event (judicial process), not a mode of ongoing existence. No NT use of krisis implies ongoing torment -- all 47 uses are consistent with judgment-as-event.

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

Masculine noun from thnesko ('to die'). 119 tokens in 106 unique verses across 15 books. The standard NT word for death. Antonym: zoe (life, G2222). Used in Rev 20:14 for 'the second death' -- the identification word for the lake of fire.

Semantic categories: physical death, death as sin's consequence, death as cosmic power, Christ's atoning death, spiritual death/passage to life, death personified/second death, shadow of death OT allusion

Key verses: Rev 20:14, Rev 21:4, Rom 6:23, Rom 5:12, 1 Cor 15:26

Relevance: The identification word for the lake of fire in Rev 20:14 and 21:8. The text calls it 'the second death' (thanatos), not 'the second torment.' Death is consistently cessation of life throughout 119 NT uses.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G928-basanizo.md

Occurrences: 12

Verb from basanos (G931, 'touchstone for testing metals'). 12 NT uses across 6 books. 7 non-judgment uses (sickness, sea storms, moral distress); 5 judgment uses ALL in Revelation or demonic speech. Rev 20:10 is the ONLY verse with torment for final judgment -- and all three subjects are non-human/symbolic (devil, beast, false prophet).

Semantic categories: physical suffering/illness, demonic encounter torment, moral distress, eschatological judgment torment

Key verses: Rev 20:10, Rev 14:10, Matt 8:29, 2 Pet 2:8

Relevance: Critical distributional finding: 0 of 8 major judgment passages use basanizo for human wicked. Basanizo appears in judgment contexts only in Revelation's apocalyptic framework and demonic speech. Never used for generic human final fate in didactic genre.

docs.title: G929 — basanismos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G929-basanismos.md

Occurrences: 6

Masculine noun from basanizo (G928). ALL 6 NT uses in Revelation exclusively. 3 of 6 describe Babylon's completed destruction (Rev 18:7,10,15). Rev 9:5 has explicit 5-month limit. Rev 14:11 'smoke of their torment.' Antonym: anapausis (G372, 'rest').

Semantic categories: demonic/supernatural torment, eschatological judgment torment, commercial/imperial torment of Babylon

Key verses: Rev 14:11, Rev 18:7, Rev 18:10, Rev 18:15, Rev 9:5

Relevance: Exclusively Revelation vocabulary. 3 of 6 uses describe Babylon's COMPLETED destruction -- proving basanismos can describe a destruction-event, not necessarily ongoing torment. The antonym (anapausis/rest) uses the same construction as Rev 4:8 (living creatures' uninterrupted praise).

docs.title: H1860 — dera'on
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1860-draown.md

Occurrences: 2

Masculine noun from unused root meaning 'to repulse.' ONLY 2 OT occurrences (Dan 12:2, Isa 66:24). Denotes an object of visceral aversion/revulsion. In Isa 66:24, applied to peger (corpses/dead bodies). Describes what the transgressors BECOME (objects of abhorrence), not what they experience.

Semantic categories: object of horror -- eschatological corpses, everlasting contempt -- resurrection of the wicked

Key verses: Dan 12:2, Isa 66:24

Relevance: Links Dan 12:2 and Isa 66:24 through shared rare vocabulary. In Isa 66:24, the objects of dera'on are explicitly peger (corpses) -- the word describes how the living view the dead, not the conscious experience of the dead.

docs.title: H6297 — peger
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H6297-peger.md

Occurrences: 24

Masculine noun meaning carcass/corpse/dead body. 24 OT occurrences across 11 books. ALWAYS means dead body in every occurrence. Never refers to living persons. Used in battlefield dead, divine judgment on Israel, prophetic judgment imagery, and idolatrous contamination.

Semantic categories: battlefield dead, divine judgment on Israel, prophetic judgment imagery, idolatrous contamination

Key verses: Isa 66:24, Isa 14:19, Isa 34:3, Num 14:29

Relevance: Decisive E-tier fact: peger ALWAYS means dead body in all 24 OT uses. In Isa 66:24, the worm and fire act upon peger (corpses), not upon living, suffering persons.

docs.title: H5769 — olam
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5769-owlam.md

Occurrences: 432

Masculine noun from unused root related to 'concealment' -- 'the vanishing point.' 432 tokens in 406 unique verses across 34 books. Core image: time that recedes beyond the reach of perception. Duration is context-dependent, ranging from 3 days (Jonah 2:6) to genuinely eternal (Psa 90:2). 20+ ended institutions labeled olam. Fire/smoke judgments called olam historically ended.

Semantic categories: eternal duration of God, everlasting covenant/promises, perpetual cultic ordinances, immemorial past, eschatological age to come, permanent judgment/irreversible desolation

Key verses: Dan 12:2, Psa 90:2, Isa 34:10, Josh 8:28

Relevance: Modifies both outcomes in Dan 12:2 (chayyei olam, dera'on olam). The nature-of-subject principle: olam life for immortal beings = genuinely eternal; olam contempt for corpses = permanent result. Fire/smoke olam judgments that ended (Isa 34:10, Jer 17:4) prove olam does not always mean 'endless.'

docs.title: G3709 — orge
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3709-orge.md

Occurrences: 36

Feminine noun from orego ('to reach/stretch forth'). 36 NT uses. Dual Louw-Nida domains: Anger (88.024) and Punish (38.001). Denotes both emotional state (anger) and judicial action (punishment). Heavily concentrated in Romans (12/36) and Revelation (6/36).

Semantic categories: divine eschatological wrath, divine judicial wrath, wrath and the law, deliverance from wrath, human anger as vice

Key verses: Rom 2:5, Rom 2:8, Rev 6:16-17, Matt 3:7, 1 Thess 5:9

Relevance: Used in Rom 2:5 ('day of wrath') and Rom 2:8 ('indignation and wrath'). The 'day of wrath' (hemera orges) frames orge as an EVENT, not an eternal state. Orge describes God's settled judicial displeasure expressed at the day of judgment.

docs.title: G2372 — thumos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2372-thumos.md

Occurrences: 18

Masculine noun from thyo (G2380, 'to rush/breathe hard'). 18 NT uses. Heavily concentrated in Revelation (10/18, 56%). Root image: heated breathing, boiling fury. Distinguished from orge as the more passionate eruption vs settled judicial anger.

Semantic categories: divine eschatological fury, corrupting passion (Babylon's wine), satanic rage, human passionate outburst, vice/work of the flesh

Key verses: Rom 2:8, Rev 14:10, Rev 16:19, Rev 19:15

Relevance: Paired with orge in Rom 2:8 for the fate of the disobedient. In vice lists (Eph 4:31, Col 3:8), thumos names a distinct sin alongside orge. Neither thumos nor orge specifies eternal duration of the judgment.

docs.title: G2347 — thlipsis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2347-thlipsis.md

Occurrences: 45

Feminine noun from thlibo (G2346, 'to press/squeeze'). 45 tokens in 43 unique verses across 15 books. Core image: external pressure bearing down. Louw-Nida 022.001 (Trouble/Hardship). KJV: 'tribulation' (40%) and 'affliction' (40%).

Semantic categories: tribulation/affliction

Key verses: Rom 2:9, 2 Thess 1:4

Relevance: Used in Rom 2:9 ('tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil'). Describes suffering vocabulary but does not specify duration or eternality.

docs.title: G2719 — katesthio
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2719-katesthio.md

Occurrences: 20

Verb from kata (G2596) + esthio (G2068, 'to eat'). 20 NT uses across 7 books. Means 'to eat down/devour.' Concentrated in Revelation (7/20). Used for fire consuming (Rev 11:5, 20:9), literal eating (parable of sower), figurative exploitation, and consuming zeal.

Semantic categories: literal consumption, fire consuming/destruction, figurative exploitation, consuming zeal

Key verses: Rev 20:9, Rev 11:5

Relevance: Used in Rev 20:9 for fire devouring human armies. The verb conveys total, irreversible destruction by fire. In Rev 20:9, the HUMAN armies are devoured (katephagen) while in the very next verse (20:10) the DEVIL is tormented (basanisthesontai) -- vocabulary differentiation by subject.

docs.title: G4442 — pyr
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4442-pyr.md

Occurrences: 74

Neuter noun (primary word). 74 tokens in 73 unique verses across 14 books. Revelation dominates (25/73). Heaviest collocations: ballo ('cast,' 19x), theion ('brimstone,' 7x), katakaio ('burn up,' 7x), gehenna (6x). Primary LXX bridge: esh (H784, 316 co-occurrences).

Semantic categories: eschatological punishment (lake of fire/gehenna), judgment parables, divine theophany, cosmic/apocalyptic plagues, testing/refining, figurative/metaphorical

Key verses: Rev 20:14-15, Matt 25:41, Heb 10:27, 2 Thess 1:8, Mark 9:44-48

Relevance: Fire appears in all 8 judgment passages except John 5:28-29 and Rom 2:5-11 (which use wrath vocabulary instead). Every OT fire judgment paradigm produces destruction/ashes/cessation, never ongoing torment.

docs.title: G861 — aphtharsia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G861-aphtharsia.md

Occurrences: 8

Feminine noun, alpha-privative + phthartos ('corruptible'). 8 unique verses across 5 books. Exclusively Pauline. Means incorruptibility/immortality. Used in 1 Cor 15 resurrection chapter (4x) and Rom 2:7 ('seek for immortality').

Semantic categories: resurrection transformation, sought by believers, ethical sense (sincerity)

Key verses: Rom 2:7, 1 Cor 15:42, 1 Cor 15:53-54, 2 Tim 1:10

Relevance: Rom 2:7: believers SEEK (zetousin, present active participle) aphtharsia -- seeking what they do not possess. This is an anthropological prerequisite: if immortality must be sought, it is not inherent.

docs.title: G1341 — dikaiokrisia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1341-dikaiokrisia.md

Occurrences: 1

Feminine noun, compound of dikaios (G1342, 'righteous') + krisis (G2920, 'judgment'). ONLY 1 NT use (Rom 2:5). Means 'righteous judgment.' Frames divine judgment as inherently just.

Semantic categories: righteous judgment of God

Key verses: Rom 2:5

Relevance: Only 1 NT use -- a hapax legomenon created by Paul to emphasize the RIGHTEOUS character of God's judgment. Frames the judgment in Rom 2:5-11 as just, not capricious or disproportionate.

docs.title: G5098 — timoria
docs.text:
Occurrences: 1

Feminine noun. ONLY 1 NT use (Heb 10:29 'sorer punishment'). From lookup: 1 occurrence, translated 'punishment' (100%). Related to G5099 tino (verb 'to pay a penalty,' also 1 NT use in 2 Thess 1:9). Timoria = retributive penalty focused on what the offender deserves. Distinguished from kolasis (judicial/deterrent) and basanismos (experiential torment process).

Semantic categories: retributive penalty

Key verses: Heb 10:29

Relevance: The only NT use is in Heb 10:29 'of how much sorer punishment.' As a retributive penalty word (not a torment-process word), it describes what is deserved, not the mode of suffering. The comparison with v.28 ('died without mercy') sets death as the baseline.

docs.title: G5099 — tino
docs.text:
Occurrences: 1

Verb. ONLY 1 NT use (2 Thess 1:9 'shall be punished'). From lookup: 1 occurrence, translated 'shall be punished' (100%). Means 'to pay a penalty.' The verb behind timoria (G5098).

Semantic categories: paying a penalty

Key verses: 2 Thess 1:9

Relevance: Used in 2 Thess 1:9 -- the penalty paid is olethros (destruction), not basanismos (torment).

docs.title: G4663 — skolex
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4663-skṓlēx.md

Occurrences: 3

Masculine noun. Only 3 NT occurrences -- ALL in Mark 9:44, 46, 48, where Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24 ('their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched'). The skolex is the maggot/worm that feeds on corpses, symbolizing the unending decomposition and disgrace of those who have rebelled. The image is drawn from the Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna). KJV translates uniformly as 'worm.' Hebrew source: towla (H8438, PMI 8.57) and rimmah (H7415, PMI 10.2). Collocates: teleutao (G5053, 'dieth not') 3x, pyr (G4442, fire) 3x.

Semantic categories: decay and corruption of the unburied dead

Key verses: Mark 9:44, Mark 9:46, Mark 9:48

Relevance: The worm in Mark 9:43-48 quotes Isa 66:24, where the subjects are peger (corpses/dead bodies). The worm acts upon dead bodies, not upon living, conscious persons. In the source text (Isa 66:24), peger always means dead body in all 24 OT uses.

docs.title: G762 — asbestos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G762-ásbestos.md

Occurrences: 4

Adjective from alpha-privative + derivative of sbennymi (G4570, 'to extinguish'). Means unquenchable, inextinguishable. Only 4 NT uses: Matt 3:12 ('burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire'), Mark 9:43 and 9:45 ('the fire that never shall be quenched'), Luke 3:17 ('unquenchable fire'). All 4 modify pyr (G4442, fire) in eschatological judgment contexts. Describes fire that cannot be put out or suppressed -- fire that is irresistible, not necessarily fire that burns forever. Cf. Jer 17:27 where Jerusalem's gates 'shall not be quenched' but are not still burning.

Semantic categories: eschatological judgment fire

Key verses: Mark 9:43, Mark 9:45, Matt 3:12, Luke 3:17

Relevance: Key word in Mark 9:43 gehenna passage. 'Unquenchable' means fire that CANNOT BE PUT OUT (irresistible) -- it describes the certainty and thoroughness of divine judgment. It does not necessarily mean fire that burns for infinite duration, as shown by Jer 17:27 where the same concept is applied to Jerusalem's gates (a fire that historically ended). In Matt 3:12 and Luke 3:17, asbestos fire 'burns up' (katakaio, G2618) chaff -- the result is complete consumption, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: CLASSIFICATIONS.md — Tree 3/4 Walkthroughs for etc7-14
docs.text: All positional E-items (Cond. or ECT) and all N-items receive a full Tree 3 or Tree 4 walkthrough with tool-verified parsing data.

docs.title: E-Item Classifications
docs.text:
E1 (Rev 20:9) -- "fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "devoured" (katephagen, G2719) applied to human armies. Destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical object (autous, P-APM, "them") refers to the human armies of Gog/Magog described in vv.8-9a. Literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms katephagen (G2719, katesthio, V-2AAI-3S, Aorist Active Indicative). The verb means "to eat down/devour/consume." Aorist tense presents the devouring as a completed bounded event. No alternative parsing available. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Apocalyptic vision (Revelation). FAIL. Genre is apocalyptic.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 3 failed).
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic vision. The observation is within an apocalyptic framework.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, fire from heaven devours human armies (katephagen, destruction verb)."
  • RC3: Re-enter Step 1: The corrected observation still contains destruction vocabulary (devoured) applied to human subjects within the vision. V1 applies. However, the apocalyptic genre means this depicts what the seer saw, not didactic teaching. The destruction vocabulary remains.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails (apocalyptic). The vocabulary is destruction, but the genre qualifies the directness. Reclassified: Neutral (the text uses destruction vocabulary in an apocalyptic vision; the vocabulary choice is a factual observation both sides can acknowledge).

Note: The vocabulary differentiation between v.9 (devoured/humans) and v.10 (tormented/non-human) is itself a Neutral E-item (E3) — a factual observation about the text's word choices.

E2 (Rev 20:14) -- "This is the second death" (lake of fire identified as thanatos, not basanismos) -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "death" (thanatos, G2288) applied to the fate of humans cast into the lake of fire. Death/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The predicate nominative identifies the lake of fire (destination of human wicked per v.15) as "the second death." The subjects who receive this fate are humans not in the book of life. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms: houtos (D-NSM) ho thanatos (G2288, N-NSM) ho deuteros (G1208, A-NSM) estin (G1510, V-PAI-3S), he limne (G3041, N-NSF) tou pyros (G4442, N-GSN). Predicate nominative identification formula. The identification word is thanatos (death), confirmed by parser. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Apocalyptic vision (Revelation). FAIL. Genre is apocalyptic.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 3 failed).
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic. The identification formula is within a vision.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, the text identifies the lake of fire as 'the second death' (thanatos) using a predicate nominative formula."
  • RC3: The corrected observation notes the text's self-identification. The identification formula is Revelation's own self-interpreting mechanism (used in Rev 1:20, 5:8, 17:9, 17:15, 17:18). Both sides accept that the text calls it "the second death." The vocabulary choice (thanatos rather than basanismos) is a factual observation.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails (apocalyptic). Reclassified: Neutral (the text's self-identification of the lake of fire as "the second death" is a factual observation both sides acknowledge, even while disagreeing about what "the second death" entails).

E3 (Rev 20:9-10) -- "Rev 20:9 uses katephagen (devoured) for human armies; Rev 20:10 uses basanisthesontai (tormented) for devil/beast/false prophet" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Both V1 (devoured) and V2 (tormented) apply — but to different subjects. Neither vocabulary applies uniformly to the fate of human wicked. Both NO for a unified positional reading. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. This is a factual observation about the text's vocabulary choices that both sides must accept.

E4 (Rev 20:10) -- "The devil, beast, and false prophet shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "tormented" (basanisthesontai, G928) applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet. Conscious-ongoing-existence vocabulary. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subjects are: ho diabolos (the devil — supernatural spirit being), to therion (the beast — 7 heads, 10 horns, composite entity; Rev 17:8-11 decodes as political-religious system), ho pseudoprophetes (the false prophet — symbolic entity = earth beast of Rev 13:11-17). NONE is a literal human being. FAIL. Subject is symbolic/non-human for all three.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
  • RC1: All three subjects are non-human/symbolic entities (devil = supernatural spirit, beast = decoded as political system, false prophet = symbolic figure).
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "Three non-human/symbolic entities are described as tormented in the lake of fire."
  • RC3: The corrected observation describes torment applied to non-human entities. This does not constitute evidence about HUMAN fate. V2 vocabulary applies to non-human subjects — neither V1 nor V2 is relevant to human fate.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails (subjects are not literal human beings). Classification: Neutral (describes non-human entities; does not establish human experience in the lake of fire).

E5 (Isa 66:24) -- "They shall look upon the carcases (peger) of the men that have transgressed" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "carcases" (peger, H6297) = dead bodies/corpses. Death/cessation vocabulary (the subjects are dead). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject being viewed is pigrei (Noun.mp.Cst, corpses of) ha-anashim (Noun.mp.Abs, the men) ha-posh'im (Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs, the transgressing). The transgressors are literal human beings (men who transgressed). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms: pigrei (peger, Noun.mp.Cst, "corpses of") — construct state, plural. Peger means dead body/corpse in ALL 24 OT occurrences. The parser gives lemma peger with gloss "corpse." No alternative parsing for peger. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct-speech prophecy ("saith the LORD," v.23). Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with all other E-items — no E-item states that humans are alive and conscious after judgment. Other cessation E-items (Rom 2:12, 2 Thess 1:9, Heb 10:27) describe destruction. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E6 (Isa 66:16-17) -- "The slain of the LORD shall be many" / transgressors "consumed together, saith the LORD" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "slain" (chalalim, pierced/slain) and "consumed together" (yasufu from suph, "end/cease"). Destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects are human transgressors (those who sanctify themselves in the gardens, eat swine's flesh, etc.). Literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms v.17: yasufu (suph/soph, Verb.Qal.Impf.3mp, "end/cease") — the transgressors shall end/cease. Yachdaw (Adv., "together"). The verb means to come to an end. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct-speech prophecy ("saith the LORD" — ne'um YHWH, v.17). Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with other destruction E-items. No conflict with any E-item. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E7 (2 Thess 1:9) -- "Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction (olethron aionion)" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destruction" (olethron, G3639) = destruction/ruin. Death/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject (hoitines, R-NPM, "who") refers to "them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel" (v.8). Literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms: olethron (G3639, N-ASM, Acc Sg M, "destruction") aionion (G166, A-ASM, "everlasting"). Olethros (G3639) has only 4 NT uses, ALL meaning destruction/ruin. Tisousin (G5099, V-FAI-3P, "they shall pay") — future active indicative. The verb tino means "to pay a penalty." No alternative parsing for olethros. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Pauline epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with all destruction E-items. Paul had basanizo available and chose olethros. No conflict with any E-item. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E8 (Heb 10:27) -- Fire "shall devour (esthiein) the adversaries" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "devour" (esthiein, G2068, esthio) = to eat/consume/devour. Destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The object of the devouring is tous hupenantious (G5227, A-APM, "the adversaries"). Human adversaries of God. Literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms: esthiein (G2068, V-PAN, Pres Act Inf, "to eat/devour") mellontos (G3195, V-PAP-GSN, "being about to"). Esthio = to eat/consume. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Hebrews epistle — didactic warning. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with 2 Thess 1:9 (destruction), Rom 2:12 (perish), and other destruction E-items. No conflict. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E9 (Heb 10:39) -- "draw back unto perdition (apoleia)" vs "saving of the soul" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "perdition/destruction" (apoleian, G684, apoleia) = destruction/ruin. Cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects are humans — the audience of the Hebrews epistle ("we," hemeis). Literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms: apoleian (G684, N-ASF, "destruction/perdition") contrasted with peripoiesin (G4047, N-ASF, "preserving/saving") psyches (G5590, N-GSF, "of soul"). Binary: destruction vs saving. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Hebrews epistle — didactic warning. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Heb 10:27 (devour) and all other destruction E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E10 (Rom 2:12) -- "As many as have sinned without law shall also perish (apollymi)" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "perish" (apolountai, G622, apollymi) = perish/be destroyed. Destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects are sinners — "as many as have sinned without law." Literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser confirms: apolountai (G622, V-FMI-3P, Fut Mid Ind, "shall perish"). Apollymi = to destroy/perish. Future middle indicative = "they shall perish." No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Pauline epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with 2 Thess 1:9 (destruction), Heb 10:27/39, and all other destruction E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E11 (Rev 20:12-13) -- "the dead were judged according to their works" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO (no destruction vocabulary). V2 NO (no torment vocabulary). The text describes the judgment mechanism, not its nature. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

E12 (Rev 20:15) -- "whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO (no explicit destruction vocabulary in this verse alone). V2 NO (no torment vocabulary). The verse describes the criterion and destination but does not specify what happens there (the specification is in v.14: "the second death"). NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

E13 (Matt 25:46) -- "these shall go away into everlasting punishment (kolasin aionion)" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1: Kolasis (G2851) = punishment. Not unambiguously destruction vocabulary. V2: Kolasis is not torment vocabulary (basanismos). Kolasis is penalty/punishment — it does not specify the nature. Both V1 and V2 are NO for unambiguous positional vocabulary. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. The word kolasis denotes punishment without specifying whether the punishment is destruction or ongoing torment. Both sides dispute its meaning.

E14 (John 5:29) -- "resurrection of life" vs "resurrection of judgment (kriseos)" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO (krisis is not destruction vocabulary). V2 NO (krisis is not torment vocabulary). Krisis = judgment/verdict — a judicial event. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. Krisis describes the judgment event, not its outcome.

E15 (Dan 12:2) -- "some to shame and everlasting contempt (dera'on olam)" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1: Dera'on = abhorrence/contempt. Not unambiguously destruction vocabulary (it describes a state of being viewed, not destruction itself). V2: Not torment vocabulary. Both V1 and V2 are NO. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. Dera'on describes the state of being an object of revulsion. What makes the transgressors objects of revulsion (conscious shame or being dead corpses) is the disputed question. Both sides can accept the text says "everlasting contempt/abhorrence."

E16 (Matt 25:41) -- "fire prepared for the devil and his angels" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO (no destruction vocabulary in this statement). V2 NO (no torment vocabulary). The text identifies the fire's intended recipients, not its nature. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. This is a factual observation about the fire's designated recipients.

E17 (Rom 2:5) -- "day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment (dikaiokrisia) of God" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO. V2 NO. Wrath and judgment vocabulary without specifying nature. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

E18 (Rom 2:7) -- "seek for glory and honour and immortality (aphtharsia), eternal life" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO. V2 NO. This is about the positive outcome (seeking immortality). Neither destruction nor torment vocabulary. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. The anthropological observation (seeking what is not possessed) is a factual observation both sides can accept while disagreeing about its implications.

E19 (Rom 2:6) -- "Who will render to every man according to his deeds" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO. V2 NO. Proportionality principle without specifying outcome nature. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

E20 (Rom 2:8-9) -- "indignation and wrath... tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO (wrath and tribulation are not destruction vocabulary). V2: "tribulation" (thlipsis) and "anguish" (stenochoria) describe suffering but do not specify "torment" in the technical basanizo sense, nor do they specify eternal duration. Both V1 and V2 are NO for unambiguous positional vocabulary. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. Suffering vocabulary without duration specification.

E21 (Heb 10:28-29) -- "He that despised Moses' law died without mercy... how much sorer punishment" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1: "died" in v.28 is destruction vocabulary, but it's the baseline for comparison, not the penalty under discussion. V2 NO. The "sorer punishment" (timoria) is penalty vocabulary without specifying nature. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands. The escalation from death to "sorer punishment" does not specify whether that punishment is torment or permanent destruction.

E22 (Rev 20:6) -- "on such the second death hath no power" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 NO. V2 NO. Statement about who is exempt from the second death, not about its nature. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

E23 (Rev 21:8) -- "the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death" -- Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Same analysis as E2. The identification formula (lake of fire = second death) is a textual observation. Both sides accept the text calls it "the second death." NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

docs.title: N-Item Classifications
docs.text:
N1 -- "The 8 judgment passages collectively use destruction/death vocabulary for human wicked; none uses basanizo for humans" -- Based on: E1-E10 -- Classified: Neutral

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Major judgment passages: Rev 20:11-15, Matt 25:31-46, Dan 12:2, Isa 66:22-24, John 5:28-29, 2 Thess 1:7-10, Heb 10:26-31, Rom 2:5-11. Each analyzed for E/N/I tier.

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The eight major judgment passages collectively use destruction/death vocabulary for human wicked (4 of 8), penalty/judgment vocabulary without specifying nature (2 of 8), and dead-viewed-with-abhorrence vocabulary (2 of 8). None of the eight uses basanizo (torment) for human subjects. The explicit destruction vocabulary appears in didactic texts across multiple authors (Paul, Hebrews author, Isaiah). Torment vocabulary (basanizo/basanismos) for final judgment is confined to Revelation's apocalyptic framework and applied exclusively to non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet). The anthropological prerequisite — humans do not inherently possess immortality (1 Tim 6:16, Rom 2:7, 1 Cor 15:53-54) — is embedded within the Rom 2:5-11 judgment passage itself.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Everlasting Destruction from the Presence of the Lord (2 Thess 1:9) Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

Fire Shall Devour the Adversaries (Heb 10:27) But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.

Perdition vs Saving of the Soul (Heb 10:39) But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.

Sinners Shall Perish (Rom 2:12) For as many as have sinned without law shall also perish without law: and as many as have sinned in the law shall be judged by the law;

Carcases of the Transgressors (Isa 66:24) And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

Transgressors Consumed Together (Isa 66:16-17) For by fire and by his sword will the LORD plead with all flesh: and the slain of the LORD shall be many. They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD.

The Second Death (Rev 20:14) And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Everlasting Punishment vs Life Eternal (Matt 25:46) And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

Dual-Outcome Resurrection (Dan 12:2) And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

Seeking Immortality (Rom 2:7) To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life:

docs.title: The Vocabulary of Human Judgment: What the Eight Passages Say
docs.text:
The eight passages divide into four vocabulary categories when describing the fate of human wicked.

Category 1 — Explicit destruction/death vocabulary (4 of 8 passages):

2 Thessalonians 1:9 uses olethros (G3639, destruction) modified by aionios. Parser confirms: olethron (N-ASM) aionion (A-ASM). Olethros has only 4 NT uses, all meaning destruction/ruin. Paul chose this word deliberately — he had basanizo (torment) available in his Greek vocabulary and did not use it. The only remedial use of olethros (1 Cor 5:5) carries an explicit salvation-purpose clause ("that the spirit may be saved") that is absent from all eschatological uses. The apo prosopou phrase ("from the presence of the Lord") echoes Isa 2:10,19,21 LXX verbatim, where people hide from the glory of the LORD because the divine presence is itself the destructive agent. Psa 68:2 confirms the same concept: "as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God." The wicked perish AT the divine presence, not by banishment FROM it.

Hebrews 10:27 uses esthio (G2068, to eat/devour). Parser confirms: esthiein (V-PAN, Pres Act Inf). Fire "shall devour the adversaries" — devour is destruction vocabulary, a fire that consumes its fuel. The pyros zelos (fire of zeal) alludes to Isa 26:11 LXX. Hebrews 10:39 then provides the binary conclusion: apoleia (G684, destruction/perdition) vs peripoiesis psyches (preserving/saving of the soul). The Hebrews author frames the entire warning passage (vv.26-39) with destruction language at both ends — "devour" (v.27) and "destruction" (v.39).

Romans 2:12 uses apollymi (G622, perish/destroy). Parser confirms: apolountai (V-FMI-3P, Fut Mid Ind). Sinners "shall perish." Apollymi has 102 NT uses; Louw-Nida classifies it in both Violence/Destroy (20.003) and Exist/Non-exist (13.003). No lexicon defines apollymi as torment. Paul uses this word for the final outcome of sinners within the same passage where he discusses the day of wrath (v.5), proportional judgment (v.6), and seeking immortality (v.7).

Revelation 20:9 and 20:14 use katesthio (G2719, devour) for human armies (v.9) and thanatos (G2288, death) as the identification word for the lake of fire (v.14). Parser confirms: katephagen (V-2AAI-3S, "devoured") and thanatos (N-NSM, "death") in the predicate nominative formula. The text calls the fate of humans "the second death" — using the word for death, not the word for torment.

Category 2 — Penalty/judgment vocabulary without specifying nature (2 of 8 passages):

Matthew 25:46 uses kolasis (G2851, punishment). Kolasis has only 2 NT uses (Matt 25:46 and 1 John 4:18). Root kolazo means "to curtail/prune," distinct from basanismos (experiential torment). Louw-Nida places kolasis in the Punish domain (38), not in the Torture domain. The word denotes punishment without specifying whether the punishment is destruction or ongoing torment.

John 5:29 uses krisis (G2920, judgment). Krisis has 47 NT uses, meaning judgment/decision/verdict. It describes a judicial event — a verdict rendered — not a mode of ongoing existence. No NT use of krisis implies ongoing torment. The passage describes "resurrection of life" vs "resurrection of judgment" — two outcomes from the graves, one defined by the positive result (life), the other by the judicial process (judgment/verdict).

Category 3 — Dead viewed with abhorrence (2 of 8 passages):

Daniel 12:2 uses dera'on (H1860, contempt/abhorrence). Dera'on has only 2 OT occurrences: Dan 12:2 and Isa 66:24. The word describes what the transgressors BECOME — objects of visceral revulsion — not what they experience. In its only other occurrence (Isa 66:24), the objects of dera'on are explicitly peger (H6297, corpses/dead bodies). Peger means dead body in all 24 OT uses — never living persons.

Isaiah 66:24 uses peger (corpses) and dera'on (abhorrence). The living "go forth and look upon the carcases (peger) of the men that have transgressed." The worm and fire act upon corpses, not upon living, suffering persons. The context of vv.15-17 establishes that the transgressors are "slain of the LORD" and "consumed together" before the viewing in v.24. The chronological sequence is: slain/consumed (vv.16-17) → new creation (v.22) → corpse-viewing (v.24).

Category 4 — Torment vocabulary for human wicked (0 of 8 passages):

None of the eight judgment passages uses basanizo (G928, torment verb) or basanismos (G929, torment noun) for human wicked. Basanizo appears in the Rev 20 passage, but only in v.10, applied to the devil, beast, and false prophet — all non-human/symbolic entities. In consecutive verses, the text uses different verbs for different subjects: v.9 katephagen (devoured) for humans, v.10 basanisthesontai (tormented) for non-human entities. This vocabulary differentiation is a textual fact.

docs.title: The Aionios Question: Same Adjective, Different Subjects
docs.text:
The adjective aionios (G166) modifies punishment terms in two of the eight passages: kolasin aionion (Matt 25:46) and olethron aionion (2 Thess 1:9). The symmetry argument — that because aionios modifies both "punishment" (Matt 25:46) and "life" (Matt 25:46), both must have the same duration — is a real grammatical observation. The same adjective does modify both outcomes in the same construction.

The symmetry argument, however, does not necessitate identical duration. Tit 1:2 uses aionios for two different temporal scopes in the same verse (the etc7-08 study established this). The Hebrews pattern provides the governing framework: aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act. Eternal salvation (Heb 5:9) describes one act of saving with a permanent result. Eternal redemption (Heb 9:12) describes one act of redeeming with a permanent result. Eternal judgment (Heb 6:2) describes one act of judging with a permanent result. By this pattern, "eternal punishment" (Matt 25:46) describes one act of punishing with a permanent result, and "eternal destruction" (2 Thess 1:9) describes one act of destroying with a permanent result.

The LXX connection reinforces this: aionios renders the Hebrew olam in approximately a hundred LXX instances. Olam (H5769) has 432 OT occurrences with context-dependent duration. Fire/smoke judgments called olam historically ended (Isa 34:10 — Edom's fire, Jer 17:4 — Jerusalem's fire). Twenty-plus institutions labeled olam have ended (Passover, Day of Atonement, Aaronic priesthood, circumcision as covenant sign). Olam does not always mean "endless."

docs.title: The Fire-and-Brimstone Paradigm: What OT Fire Produces
docs.text:
The OT provides a consistent paradigm for divine fire judgments. Every recorded fire-and-brimstone event produces destruction, ashes, and cessation:

Sodom and Gomorrah: "destroyed them all" (Luke 17:29, apollymi), "turning to ashes" (2 Pet 2:6), set forth as "an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly" (2 Pet 2:6). Jesus uses Sodom as the paradigm for parousia judgment: "even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed" (Luke 17:30). If Sodom is the pattern, and Sodom was reduced to ashes, the pattern is destruction to ashes.

Edom: "The smoke thereof shall go up for ever" (Isa 34:10, olam). Edom is not still burning. The "smoke ascending forever" describes permanent evidence of completed destruction.

Malachi 4:1-3: The wicked become "stubble," the day "shall burn them up," they become "ashes under the soles of your feet." Every element describes total consumption and cessation.

Jerusalem's gates: "I will kindle a fire... and it shall not be quenched" (Jer 17:27). The gates of Jerusalem are not still burning. "Not quenched" means fire that cannot be extinguished while it burns — irresistible fire — not fire that burns for infinite duration.

This paradigm provides the interpretive context for "everlasting fire" (Matt 25:41), "fiery indignation" (Heb 10:27), "flaming fire" (2 Thess 1:8), and the "lake of fire" (Rev 20:14-15). The NT fire imagery draws on OT precedents that consistently produce cessation.

docs.title: The Anthropological Prerequisite: Can Humans Be Eternally Tormented?
docs.text:
The question of eternal torment depends on a prior question: do humans possess immortality? The biblical data, including evidence embedded within the judgment passages themselves:

God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16). Paul writes monos echon athanasian — "alone having immortality." The monos is unqualified.

Immortality is sought by believers (Rom 2:7). Within the Rom 2:5-11 judgment passage itself, Paul describes believers as those who "seek for... immortality" (zetousin, present active participle — seeking what they do not possess). If believers must seek immortality, they do not inherently have it. The wicked, who do not seek it, do not receive it.

Immortality is put on at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54). Endyo (G1746, "put on") describes acquiring something not previously possessed. The wicked never "put on" immortality.

The soul can die (Ezek 18:4) and be destroyed (Matt 10:28). Nephesh/psyche is not inherently immortal. The phrase "immortal soul" never appears in Scripture.

Without immortality, the wicked cannot be tormented forever. This is not an inference — it is a structural prerequisite. The data supporting it is at E-tier across prior studies (etc7-01, etc7-02).

docs.title: The Revelation Vocabulary Differentiation
docs.text:
The Rev 20 passage contains the clearest vocabulary differentiation in all eight passages. In consecutive verses:

Rev 20:9 — Human armies: katephagen (G2719, "devoured"). Destruction verb. Aorist active indicative — completed action.

Rev 20:10 — Devil, beast, false prophet: basanisthesontai (G928, "shall be tormented"). Torment verb. Future passive indicative — projected forward. All three subjects are non-human/symbolic entities.

Rev 20:14 — Lake of fire = "the second death" (thanatos, G2288). The identification word chosen by the text is death, not torment.

Rev 20:15 — Humans not in book of life: cast into lake of fire. No torment vocabulary applied. The fate is what v.14 identified: the second death.

This differentiation is encoded in the grammar. The passage uses active voice for human destruction (katephagen, active), passive voice for the devil being cast (eblethe, passive), and future tense for torment of non-human entities (basanisthesontai, future). The voice and tense shifts mark subject boundaries. The grammar reference analysis (rev-20-7-15.md) documents the progressive passivization and the tense-aspect map across the passage.

docs.title: The Proportionality Principle
docs.text:
Romans 2:6 states: "Who will render to every man according to his deeds." This principle appears in 11+ passages across 9 authors (Job 34:11, Psa 62:12, Jer 17:10, Matt 16:27, Rev 20:12-13). Jesus applies it in Luke 12:47-48 ("many stripes" vs "few stripes") and Matt 10:15 ("more tolerable for Sodom").

Proportional judgment — calibrated to knowledge, opportunity, and deeds — implies finite, measured punishment. "Few stripes" is incompatible with identical infinite punishment for all. If the punishment is proportional to deeds, and deeds are finite, the punishment is finite.

docs.title: The I-B Tension: Matt 25:46 and Dan 12:2
docs.text:
Two of the eight passages create I-B items (competing evidence from both sides).

Matt 25:46 presents the symmetry between kolasin aionion and zoen aionion. The grammatical parallelism is real (same adjective, same case, same construction). The ECT reading infers that the parallelism requires identical duration — punishment as long as life. The Cond. reading infers that aionios modifies the result (permanent punishment, permanent life) following the Hebrews pattern, and that kolasis (punishment, not torment) describes a completed judicial act.

Dan 12:2 presents dera'on olam. The ECT reading infers that "everlasting contempt" describes the conscious experience of shame. The Cond. reading notes that dera'on's only other occurrence (Isa 66:24) applies it to corpses, and that the parallel construct chains (chayyei olam / dera'on olam) are governed by the nature-of-subject principle — life for those who receive immortality is genuinely eternal; contempt for those who are dead is a permanent result.

Both I-B items are resolved below in the I-B Resolution section.

docs.title: Word Studies
docs.text:
Olethros (G3639): 4 NT uses, ALL meaning destruction/ruin. Paul's word for the wicked's fate in 2 Thess 1:9. The etc7-06 study established at E-tier that all destruction words (abad, shamad, kalah, shachath, apollymi, apoleia, olethros) share a common semantic core of ending/cessation. No lexicon defines any of them as torment.

Kolasis (G2851): 2 NT uses (Matt 25:46, 1 John 4:18). From kolazo "to curtail/prune." Louw-Nida Punish domain (38). Distinct from basanismos (experiential torment process). Denotes penal infliction without specifying whether the punishment is destruction or ongoing conscious suffering.

Krisis (G2920): 47 NT uses. Judgment/verdict/judicial decision. All 47 uses are consistent with judgment as an event or verdict, not as a mode of ongoing existence. No NT use implies ongoing torment.

Basanizo (G928): 12 NT uses. The majority are non-judgment contexts (sickness, sea storms, moral distress). The judgment uses are ALL in Revelation or demonic speech. Rev 20:10 is the only verse with torment for final judgment — and all three subjects are non-human/symbolic.

Dera'on (H1860): 2 OT uses only (Dan 12:2, Isa 66:24). Objects are peger (corpses) in Isa 66:24. Describes what the transgressors become (objects of revulsion), not what they experience.

Peger (H6297): 24 OT uses. ALWAYS means dead body/corpse. Never refers to living persons. Decisive for Isa 66:24 — the worm and fire act upon dead bodies.

Aionios (G166): 71 NT uses. Means "pertaining to the age(s)" with duration determined by subject. Three past-time uses. Hebrews pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act.

Timoria (G5098): 1 NT use (Heb 10:29). Retributive penalty — what the offender deserves. Not torment-process vocabulary. The comparison baseline is death (v.28).

docs.title: Matt 25:46 — Kolasin Aionion
docs.text: The strongest ECT-cited verse among the eight passages. The grammatical symmetry with zoen aionion is real and must be addressed. The Hebrews pattern (aionios + result-noun = permanent result) and the Tit 1:2 precedent (same adjective, different scopes) provide the alternative reading. The word used is kolasis (punishment), not basanismos (torment). The passage is parabolic genre. The fire is "prepared for the devil and his angels" (v.41), not originally for humans. The I-B resolution (below) addresses this directly.

docs.title: Rev 14:9-11 — Smoke of Torment Ascending
docs.text: Uses basanismos vocabulary for apparent human subjects (beast-worshippers). The passage is apocalyptic genre (Gate 3). The "smoke ascending forever" formula draws on Isa 34:10 (ended fire). Rev 19:3 uses the same formula for Babylon (five-fold "found no more at all"). The etc7-11 study established that the smoke-ascending formula describes permanent evidence of completed destruction. (Examined in depth in etc7-11-smoke-ascending-forever.)

docs.title: Heb 10:29 — Sorer Punishment
docs.text: The "sorer punishment" (timoria) could mean ongoing torment worse than death, or permanent irreversible destruction worse than temporal death. The surrounding vocabulary (v.27 devour, v.39 destruction vs saving) favors the destruction reading. The text does not specify which kind of "sorer" is meant.

docs.title: Rev 20:10 and Human Fate
docs.text: The devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented in the same location (lake of fire) where humans are also sent. The inference that same location = same experience is not stated by the text. The vocabulary differentiation (humans devoured/second death, non-human entities tormented) indicates different outcomes for different subjects in the same location.

FOR: Grammatical symmetry — same word = same scope. AGAINST: E7 (2 Thess 1:9): Paul defines the punishment as destruction (olethros), not torment. Tit 1:2 precedent: same adjective, different scopes. Requires interpreting kolasis as implying conscious process rather than completed act. FOR: Dera'on could describe subjective experience of shame. AGAINST: E5 (Isa 66:24): dera'on's only other occurrence applies to peger (corpses — always dead bodies). N2: dera'on-peger connection links the two passages. Requires reading dera'on as subjective experience when its only other occurrence applies to dead bodies. Must choose between "objects of contempt" and "experiencing contempt." #2, #4b I042 I5 Rev 20:10's torment of the devil/beast/false prophet establishes that humans in the same lake of fire also experience torment I-C ECT E4 (Rev 20:10): three entities tormented. E12 (Rev 20:15): humans cast into same lake. AGAINST: N4: Revelation differentiates vocabulary by subject. N5: torment formula applied only to non-human entities. E3: different verbs for different subjects in consecutive verses. Requires inferring that same destination = same experience. The text does not state this — it uses different vocabulary for different subjects. Introduces the concept of extending non-human experience to humans, which the text does not contain. #1, #4b I069 I6 The proportionality principle ("according to deeds") contradicts ECT because infinite punishment for finite sin is disproportionate I-A Cond. E19 (Rom 2:6): render according to deeds. Luke 12:47-48: many stripes vs few stripes. Matt 10:15: more tolerable for Sodom. Systematizes proportionality texts into a claim about what kind of punishment is just. Uses only biblical vocabulary/concepts. Inference because it draws a conclusion about what proportionality rules out. #5 I074 I7 The "sorer punishment" (Heb 10:29) means eternal conscious torment worse than physical death I-C ECT E21 (Heb 10:29): "sorer punishment" than death. Compatible with ECT reading. AGAINST: E8 (Heb 10:27): fire devours. E9 (Heb 10:39): destruction vs saving. Reads "sorer punishment" as a qualitatively different kind (torment vs death) rather than quantitatively worse (permanent vs temporary death). The text does not specify which reading is correct. Introduces an interpretation the text does not contain. #2 I075 I8 The anthropological data (humans lack inherent immortality) structurally precludes eternal conscious torment I-A Cond. E18 (Rom 2:7): seeking immortality not possessed. 1 Tim 6:16: God alone has immortality. 1 Cor 15:53-54: mortals put on immortality. Ezek 18:4: soul that sins dies. Matt 10:28: soul can be destroyed. Systematizes anthropological E-items into a structural argument. Uses only biblical vocabulary. Inference because it draws a doctrinal conclusion from multiple texts. #5 I076

docs.title: I-B Resolution: I1 — The Bible teaches that the punishment of the wicked is eternal conscious torment
docs.text:
Step 1 — Tension: - FOR (ECT): E13 (Matt 25:46, kolasin aionion), E4 (Rev 20:10, torment formula for non-human entities), E20 (Rom 2:8-9, wrath/tribulation/anguish), E21 (Heb 10:29, sorer punishment) - AGAINST (Cond.): E7 (2 Thess 1:9, olethron aionion), E8 (Heb 10:27, devour), E9 (Heb 10:39, apoleia vs saving), E10 (Rom 2:12, apollymi), E5 (Isa 66:24, peger/corpses), E6 (Isa 66:16-17, slain and consumed), N1 (0 of 8 use basanizo for humans), N4 (vocabulary differentiation by subject)

Step 2 — Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E7 (2 Thess 1:9, olethros) Plain Didactic epistle. Olethros means destruction in all 4 NT uses. Directly addresses the topic. E8 (Heb 10:27, devour) Plain Didactic epistle. Esthio means eat/devour. Directly states what fire does to adversaries. E9 (Heb 10:39, apoleia) Plain Didactic epistle. Binary: destruction vs saving. E10 (Rom 2:12, apollymi) Plain Didactic epistle. Apollymi means perish/destroy. E5 (Isa 66:24, peger) Plain Prophetic speech. Peger always means corpse. No interpretation needed. E6 (Isa 66:16-17, consumed) Plain Prophetic speech. "Consumed together" — cessation verb. E13 (Matt 25:46, kolasis) Ambiguous Parabolic genre. Kolasis could mean punishment-as-process or punishment-as-result. Only 2 NT uses prevent extensive distributional analysis. E4 (Rev 20:10, torment) Ambiguous Apocalyptic genre. Subjects are non-human. Cannot be directly applied to human fate without interpretation. E20 (Rom 2:8-9, wrath) Ambiguous Wrath/tribulation vocabulary without specified duration. Compatible with temporary or permanent. E21 (Heb 10:29, sorer) Ambiguous "Sorer punishment" without specified nature. Could be destruction or torment.

Step 3 — Weight: FOR (ECT): 0 Plain items, 4 Ambiguous items. AGAINST (Cond.): 6 Plain items, 0 Ambiguous items. Plus 2 N-items (N1, N4) supporting the vocabulary pattern.

Step 4 — SIS Application: Plain statements determine the reading of Ambiguous ones. The 6 Plain items (all using destruction/death/cessation vocabulary in didactic/prophetic genres) govern the reading of the 4 Ambiguous items: kolasis (Matt 25:46) is read as punishment-as-result (permanent punishment, not ongoing process); Rev 20:10 torment applies to non-human entities and does not establish human fate; wrath/tribulation (Rom 2:8-9) describes the judgment event, not an eternal state; "sorer punishment" (Heb 10:29) is read within its own context of devour (v.27) and destruction vs saving (v.39).

Step 5 — Resolution: Strong toward Cond. 6 Plain destruction/death items in didactic/prophetic genres on the Cond. side. 0 Plain items on the ECT side. All 4 ECT-supporting items are Ambiguous (parabolic, apocalyptic, or unspecified duration). The SIS principle governs: clear passages (didactic destruction vocabulary) interpret ambiguous ones (parabolic punishment, apocalyptic torment of non-human entities).

docs.title: I-B Resolution: I3 — Matt 25:46 "everlasting punishment" means ongoing conscious torment
docs.text:
Step 1 — Tension: - FOR (ECT): E13 (same adjective modifies both outcomes in same construction) - AGAINST (Cond.): E7 (Paul defines eschatological punishment as olethros/destruction). Tit 1:2 precedent. Hebrews pattern. Kolasis is not basanismos.

Step 2 — Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E7 (2 Thess 1:9) Plain Didactic. Olethros = destruction. Same topic (eschatological punishment). E13 (Matt 25:46) Ambiguous Parabolic genre. Kolasis has only 2 NT uses. The symmetry is real but does not dictate interpretation.

Step 3 — Weight: 1 Plain item (destruction vocabulary in didactic epistle) against 1 Ambiguous item (parabolic genre, rare word).

Step 4 — SIS Application: The didactic statement (2 Thess 1:9: the eschatological punishment IS destruction) governs the parabolic statement (Matt 25:46: the eschatological punishment is kolasis/punishment). Paul's use of olethros (destruction, not basanismos/torment) provides the clearer passage's definition: punishment = destruction.

Step 5 — Resolution: Strong toward Cond. The Plain didactic statement defines the nature of eschatological punishment as destruction. The parabolic statement uses a punishment word (kolasis) without specifying whether it means ongoing torment or completed destruction. SIS applies: the clear interprets the unclear.

docs.title: I-B Resolution: I4 — Dan 12:2 "everlasting contempt" describes conscious shame
docs.text:
Step 1 — Tension: - FOR (ECT): E15 (dera'on olam — could describe subjective experience of shame) - AGAINST (Cond.): E5 (Isa 66:24 — dera'on applied to peger/corpses). N2 (dera'on-peger connection).

Step 2 — Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E5 (Isa 66:24, peger + dera'on) Plain Prophetic speech. Peger always means corpse (24/24 OT uses). Dera'on describes how the living view the dead. No interpretation needed. E15 (Dan 12:2, dera'on olam) Ambiguous Could be read as conscious experience of shame or as the state of being an object of revulsion. Only 2 OT uses — the word is too rare for distributional resolution from Dan 12:2 alone.

Step 3 — Weight: 1 Plain item (Isa 66:24: dera'on applied to corpses) against 1 Ambiguous item (Dan 12:2: dera'on without specified subjects).

Step 4 — SIS Application: Dera'on has only 2 OT occurrences. In the passage where its objects are explicitly identified (Isa 66:24), they are peger (corpses). This is the only usage data available. The clear occurrence (objects identified as dead bodies) governs the ambiguous occurrence (objects not specified). Dera'on describes what the transgressors become (objects of revulsion), not what they experience.

Step 5 — Resolution: Strong toward Cond. The only occurrence with explicit objects (Isa 66:24 = corpses) governs the occurrence without specified objects (Dan 12:2). Both uses of this rare word are in judgment contexts; the clear usage (corpses viewed with revulsion) determines the reading.

docs.text:
Full Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for all positional E-items and all N-items are documented in CLASSIFICATIONS.md. Summary of results:

E-items reclassified by Tree 3: - E1 (Rev 20:9, devoured humans): Candidate Cond. → Reclassified Neutral (Gate 3 fail: apocalyptic genre) - E2 (Rev 20:14, second death): Candidate Cond. → Reclassified Neutral (Gate 3 fail: apocalyptic genre) - E4 (Rev 20:10, torment formula): Candidate ECT → Reclassified Neutral (Gate 1 fail: all subjects non-human/symbolic)

E-items that passed all four gates (classification confirmed): - E5 (Isa 66:24, peger/corpses): Cond. — all gates pass - E6 (Isa 66:16-17, slain/consumed): Cond. — all gates pass - E7 (2 Thess 1:9, olethros): Cond. — all gates pass - E8 (Heb 10:27, devour): Cond. — all gates pass - E9 (Heb 10:39, apoleia): Cond. — all gates pass - E10 (Rom 2:12, apollymi): Cond. — all gates pass

N-items: all passed Gate 0 (Foundation Gate), all classified Neutral.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies)
docs.text:
• Four of eight judgment passages use explicit destruction/death vocabulary for the fate of human wicked: olethros (2 Thess 1:9), esthio/devour (Heb 10:27), apoleia (Heb 10:39), apollymi (Rom 2:12)
  • The text identifies the lake of fire as "the second death" (thanatos), not as "the second torment" (Rev 20:14, 21:8)
  • None of the eight passages uses basanizo (torment) or basanismos (torment) for human wicked
  • Torment vocabulary in Rev 20:10 is applied exclusively to non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet)
  • Revelation uses different verbs for different subjects in consecutive verses: devoured for humans (Rev 20:9), tormented for non-human entities (Rev 20:10)
  • The objects of dera'on (contempt/abhorrence) in Isa 66:24 are peger (corpses/dead bodies) — dead bodies in all 24 OT uses of peger
  • The transgressors in Isa 66:15-17 are slain and consumed before the corpse-viewing in Isa 66:24
  • Believers "seek" immortality (present active participle, Rom 2:7) — seeking what they do not possess
  • God renders judgment "according to deeds" — the proportionality principle (Rom 2:6)
  • The fire of Matt 25:41 is "prepared for the devil and his angels," not originally for humans
  • Every OT fire-and-brimstone precedent produces destruction, ashes, and cessation

docs.title: What CANNOT Be Said (not explicitly stated or necessarily implied by Scripture)
docs.text:
• Scripture does not state that human wicked are tormented eternally — the torment formula is applied to non-human entities only
  • Scripture does not state that the same experience awaits humans and non-human entities in the lake of fire — different vocabulary is used for different subjects
  • Scripture does not state that kolasis (Matt 25:46) means ongoing conscious torment — the word means punishment without specifying nature
  • Scripture does not state that dera'on (Dan 12:2) describes conscious experience of shame — its only other occurrence applies it to corpses
  • Scripture does not state that the symmetry of aionios in Matt 25:46 requires identical duration — Tit 1:2 uses the same adjective for different scopes in one verse
  • Scripture does not state that "everlasting destruction" (2 Thess 1:9) means ongoing conscious torment — olethros means destruction in all 4 NT uses
  • Scripture does not state that the proportionality principle is limited to the judgment process rather than the outcome
  • Scripture does not state that humans possess inherent immortality enabling them to be tormented forever

docs.text:

  • Cond.: 6 (E5, E6, E7, E8, E9, E10)
  • ECT: 0
  • Neutral: 17 (E1, E2, E3, E4, E11, E12, E13, E14, E15, E16, E17, E18, E19, E20, E21, E22, E23)

  • I-C (Compatible External): 2 (I5 ECT, I7 ECT)
  • I-D (Counter-Evidence External): 0

Positional summary at E/N tier: 6 Cond., 0 ECT, 22 Neutral. The explicit destruction vocabulary for human fate appears in 4 didactic passages from 3 authors (Paul, Hebrews author, Isaiah). No E-item or N-item directly states or necessarily implies eternal conscious torment for human wicked. The ECT case rests entirely at the inference level — 3 I-B items (all resolved Strong toward Cond.), 2 I-C items.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The eight major judgment passages present a consistent vocabulary pattern for the fate of human wicked. When NT authors describe final punishment for humans, they select destruction words (olethros, apollymi, apoleia, katesthio/esthio) and death words (thanatos — "the second death"). They do not select torment words (basanizo, basanismos) for human subjects. Torment vocabulary appears exclusively for non-human/symbolic entities in Revelation's apocalyptic framework.

Six explicit statements use conditionalist-direction vocabulary — all verified by Tree 3 four-gate validation, all in didactic or prophetic genres, all using vocabulary that means destruction/cessation in every lexicon. No explicit statement uses ECT-direction vocabulary for human wicked. Three I-B items (the strongest ECT-cited texts among these passages) all resolve Strong toward conditionalist direction because the conditionalist-supporting evidence is Plain and didactic while the ECT-supporting evidence is Ambiguous and parabolic/apocalyptic.

The anthropological prerequisite, embedded within the Rom 2:5-11 passage itself (v.7: seeking immortality not yet possessed), reinforces the vocabulary data: humans do not possess inherent immortality. Without immortality, the wicked cannot be tormented forever. The fire-and-brimstone paradigm from OT precedents (Sodom, Edom, Malachi's day) consistently produces destruction, ashes, and cessation — not ongoing torment. This paradigm provides the interpretive context for every fire-judgment text among the eight passages.

The evidence tiers stand: 6 E-items (Cond.), 0 E-items (ECT), 17 E-items (Neutral), 5 N-items (all Neutral), 3 I-A (Cond.), 3 I-B (all resolved Strong toward Cond.), 2 I-C (ECT). The data speaks for itself.
