Context: Final verse of the sheep and goats judgment parable (Matt 25:31-46). The two outcomes are stated in parallel: everlasting punishment (kolasin aionion) vs life eternal (zoen aionion). The fire was 'prepared for the devil and his angels' (v.41).

Notes: Greek: kolasin (G2851, Acc Sg F) aionion (G166, Acc Sg F) // zoen (G2222, Acc Sg F) aionion (G166, Acc Sg F). Identical grammatical construction. ECT steelman: same adjective = same duration. Counter-evidence: kolasis means punishment (from kolazo 'to curtail'), NOT torment; Hebrews aionios + result-noun pattern; Tit 1:2 dual-scope; 2 Thess 1:9 defines punishment as olethros (destruction). Prior study etc7-14: classified Neutral — both readings grammatically possible.

docs.title: Unquenchable fire in OT usage — irresistible, not eternal
docs.text:
And say to the forest of the south, Hear the word of the LORD; Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will kindle a fire in thee, and it shall devour every green tree in thee, and every dry tree: the flaming flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north shall be burned therein.

Context: Ezekiel's prophecy against the southern forest. God will kindle a fire that 'shall not be quenched' — an unquenchable fire that historically ended. The forest is not still burning.

Notes: lo' tikbeh (H3808 + H3518) = 'shall not be quenched.' Same vocabulary as Isa 66:24, Mark 9:43-48, and Jer 17:27. 'Unquenchable' means irresistible (cannot be put out while it burns), not eternal (never stops burning). The fire devours (akal) — consumptive, not preservative.

docs.title: Identical 'certain rich man' formula — with explicit parable label
docs.text:
And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully:

Context: Jesus teaching about covetousness. The introduction uses the identical formula 'a certain rich man' (anthropos tis plousios) as Luke 16:19, but here Luke explicitly labels it 'a parable' (parabolen).

Notes: Luke 12:16 uses 'anthropos tis plousios' (a certain rich man) with an explicit parabole label. Luke 16:19 uses the identical formula without the label. Luke 16:1 also uses the same formula (universally recognized as parable). The 'certain rich man' formula is Luke's standard parable introduction.

docs.title: Single parabole label covering discourse unit Luke 15-16
docs.text:
And he spake this parable unto them, saying,

Context: Introduction to the lost sheep, lost coin, and prodigal son sequence. Luke provides a single 'parable' (parabolen) label that covers the discourse unit extending through chapters 15-16.

Notes: parabolen (G3850) — singular 'this parable.' Luke introduces the entire discourse unit (lost sheep, lost coin, prodigal son, unjust steward, rich man and Lazarus) with a single parable label. The rich man and Lazarus (16:19-31) falls within this parable-labeled discourse section.

docs.title: David NOT ascended into the heavens — same author as Luke 16
docs.text:
For David is not ascended into the heavens: but he saith himself, The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand,

Context: Peter's Pentecost sermon, recorded by Luke. Peter explicitly states that David has NOT ascended into the heavens — David is dead and buried (Acts 2:29), not consciously alive in heaven.

Notes: ou gar Daueid anebe eis tous ouranous — 'for David did NOT ascend into the heavens.' Same author (Luke) who records the rich man and Lazarus also records this statement about the dead not being in heaven. This is Luke's own theological position on the state of the dead.

docs.title: Babylon's destruction documented as total — fivefold 'found no more at all'
docs.text:
Therefore shall her plagues come in one day, death, and mourning, and famine; and she shall be utterly burned with fire: for strong [is] the Lord God who judgeth her. And the kings of the earth, who have committed fornication and lived deliciously with her, shall bewail her, and lament for her, when they shall see the smoke of her burning, Standing afar off for the fear of her torment, saying, Alas, alas, that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come. And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more: The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble, And cinnamon, and odours, and ointments, and frankincense, and wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, and beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men. And the fruits that thy soul lusted after are departed from thee, and all things which were dainty and goodly are departed from thee, and thou shalt find them no more at all. The merchants of these things, which were made rich by her, shall stand afar off for the fear of her torment, weeping and wailing, And saying, Alas, alas, that great city, that was clothed in fine linen, and purple, and scarlet, and decked with gold, and precious stones, and pearls! For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off, And cried when they saw the smoke of her burning, saying, What [city is] like unto this great city! And they cast dust on their heads, and cried, weeping and wailing, saying, Alas, alas, that great city, wherein were made rich all that had ships in the sea by reason of her costliness! for in one hour is she made desolate. Rejoice over her, [thou] heaven, and [ye] holy apostles and prophets; for God hath avenged you on her. And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast [it] into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all. And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft [he be], shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee; And the light of a candle shall shine no more at all in thee; and the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride shall be heard no more at all in thee: for thy merchants were the great men of the earth; for by thy sorceries were all nations deceived.

Context: The fall of Babylon the Great in Revelation 18. The passage documents Babylon's destruction as total and complete with a fivefold 'found no more at all' formula. Rev 19:3 then says 'her smoke rose up for ever and ever' — the same smoke formula as Rev 14:11.

Notes: Fivefold 'no more at all' (ou me heurethē eti): (1) v.21 Babylon found no more; (2) v.22 music heard no more; (3) v.22 craftsmen found no more; (4) v.22 millstone heard no more; (5) v.23 light/voice no more. Then Rev 19:3: 'her smoke rose up for ever and ever.' The smoke formula marks total, completed destruction — not ongoing torment. This controls interpretation of the identical formula in Rev 14:11.

docs.title: Sphazō vocabulary chain — Abel slain, same word as Rev martyrs
docs.text:
Not as Cain, [who] was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous.

Context: John's teaching on love and righteousness. Cain 'slew' (esphaxen) Abel — using sphazō (G4969), the same slaughter vocabulary used for the Lamb (Rev 5:6) and the martyrs (Rev 6:9).

Notes: esphaxen (G4969, sphazō, Aor Act Ind 3S) — slew/slaughtered. The sphazō vocabulary chain links Abel (1 John 3:12), the Lamb (Rev 5:6), and the martyrs under the altar (Rev 6:9). All three are slaughter victims — the Rev 6:9 souls are identified by their manner of death, not by ongoing conscious existence.

docs.title: Sphazō — Lamb as though slain, vocabulary link to Rev 6:9
docs.text:
And I beheld, and, lo, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent forth into all the earth.

Context: Throne room vision. The Lamb stands 'as it had been slain' (hōs esphagmenon) — using the same sphazō vocabulary as the martyrs in Rev 6:9 and Abel in 1 John 3:12.

Notes: esphagmenon (G4969, sphazō, Perf Pass Ptcp Acc Sg N) — as having been slain. The perfect participle indicates a past completed action with ongoing visible results. The Lamb bears the marks of slaughter. The same participle form (esphagmenon) describes the martyrs in Rev 6:9. Both Lamb and martyrs are identified as slaughter victims — linking sacrificial death imagery.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: 8 key ECT arguments evaluated at E/N/I tier: Rev 14:9-11, Rev 20:10, Matt 25:46, Mark 9:43-48, Luke 16:19-31, Rev 6:9-11, 2 Thess 1:9, Dan 12:2.

docs.title: ECT Argument #1 — Rev 14:9-11: Smoke of Torment Ascending Forever
docs.text:
Context: Third angel's message in Revelation 14. Apocalyptic genre. Part of the three angels' messages sequence (vv.6-12). The beast-worshippers are warned of divine wrath.

Direct statement: The text says: (1) those who worship the beast will drink God's wrath unmixed; (2) they will be tormented (basanisthesetai, G928) with fire and brimstone in the presence of angels and the Lamb; (3) the smoke of their torment (basanismou, G929) ascends unto the ages of the ages; (4) they have no rest (anapausin, G372) day and night.

ECT steelman: The plain language describes ongoing conscious torment with smoke ascending forever and no rest. This is the strongest ECT passage because it names human subjects (beast-worshippers) and uses duration language ("for ever and ever") with explicit denial of cessation ("no rest day and night").

Original language: basanismos (G929) appears 6 times in the NT, all in Revelation. 4 of 6 occurrences are time-bounded (Rev 9:5 — five months; Rev 18:7,10,15 — Babylon's fall). The genitive chain "smoke of their torment" (kapnos tou basanismou auton) — the smoke ascends, not necessarily the torment itself. anapausis (G372) in "no rest day and night" uses the identical construction as Rev 4:8, where the living creatures "have no rest day and night" in their ceaseless praise — a quality-of-activity marker, not a guaranteed eternal duration claim.

Cross-references: The smoke-ascending formula (eis aionas aionon) draws directly on Isa 34:10, where Edom's smoke "shall go up for ever" (le'olam ya'aleh ashannah). Isa 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the ruins — the fire ended, the smoke ceased, animals nest there. Rev 19:3 uses the identical smoke formula for Babylon, whose destruction is documented as total in Rev 18:8-23 with a fivefold "found no more at all."

Relationship to other evidence: The passage is apocalyptic genre (Tree 3 Gate 3 fail). Prior study etc7-11 classified E1 as Neutral. The I-B resolution found 9+ Plain didactic items from 5 authors using destruction vocabulary governing 1 Ambiguous apocalyptic item. Resolution: Strong toward Cond.

docs.title: ECT Argument #2 — Rev 20:10: Tormented Day and Night Forever
docs.text:
Context: Post-millennium judgment in Revelation 20. The devil is cast into the lake of fire where the beast and false prophet already are.

Direct statement: The text says: (1) the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire; (2) the beast and false prophet are already there; (3) they shall be tormented (basanisthesontai, G928) day and night unto the ages of the ages.

ECT steelman: This is the only verse with the full "tormented day and night for ever and ever" formula. The ECT argument extends this fate to humans who are cast into the same lake (vv.14-15): same destination, same experience.

Original language: basanisthesontai (G928, Fut Pass Ind 3P) — the torment-for-ever formula appears once in all of Scripture. The three subjects are: the devil (diabolos — supernatural being, Rev 12:9 four-fold identification chain), the beast (therion — 7 heads, 10 horns, Rev 13:1 — symbolic political-religious system), and the false prophet (pseudoprophetes — earth beast of Rev 13:11-17). All three are non-human or symbolic entities.

Cross-references: Vocabulary differentiation in consecutive verses by the same author: Rev 20:9 — humans are devoured (katephagen, G2719); Rev 20:10 — devil/beast/false prophet are tormented (basanisthesontai); Rev 20:14-15 — the lake is the second death (thanatos, G2288). Ezek 28:18-19 describes the same being (Satan-figure) with cessation vocabulary: fire devours, becomes ashes, "never shalt thou be any more" (ayin + ad-olam).

Relationship to other evidence: Tree 3 Gate 1 fails (non-human/symbolic subjects). Gate 3 fails (apocalyptic genre). Prior study etc7-12 classified E9 as Neutral. The extension of the torment formula to humans (I-B) was resolved Strong against — the text's own vocabulary differentiation (devoured vs. tormented for different subjects in consecutive verses) governs.

docs.title: Rev 20:9: Humans Devoured by Fire
docs.text:
Context: One verse before the torment formula. The human armies are the direct subject.

Direct statement: Fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them (katephagen, G2719 katesthio, Aor Act Ind 3S).

Original language: katesthio means to devour, eat up, consume. Different verb from basanizo. Same author (John), same passage, different vocabulary for different subjects.

Relationship to other evidence: This is the vocabulary differentiation datum — the single most important piece of evidence from Rev 20. Humans get "devoured." The devil gets "tormented." The text differentiates.

docs.title: Rev 20:14-15: Lake of Fire IS the Second Death
docs.text:
Context: Conclusion of the white throne judgment.

Direct statement: "This is the second death" (houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin). Death and hades are cast into the lake. Whoever was not found in the book of life was cast into the lake.

Original language: The predicate nominative formula (X = Y) identifies the lake of fire as death (thanatos, G2288), not as torment (basanismos, G929). The lake destroys death and hades — resulting in "no more death" (Rev 21:4).

Relationship to other evidence: The self-interpretation of the lake as "the second death" controls its meaning. Death is the last enemy destroyed (1 Cor 15:26). If the lake is death, those cast into it die — they are not tormented.

docs.title: Rev 21:8: Second Death Applied to Human Sinners
docs.text:
Context: New Jerusalem vision listing human sinners.

Direct statement: The fearful, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, whoremongers, sorcerers, idolaters, and liars have their part in the lake burning with fire and brimstone — "which is the second death."

Original language: Again thanatos (G2288), not basanismos (G929). Human sinners receive the second death.

Relationship to other evidence: Confirms the pattern: humans at the lake receive death, not torment.

docs.title: Rev 19:20-21: Vocabulary Differentiation at Armageddon
docs.text:
Context: Battle of Armageddon conclusion.

Direct statement: Beast and false prophet cast alive into the lake (v.20). The remnant (humans) were slain (apektanthesan, G615 apokteino) with the sword (v.21).

Original language: apokteino means to kill. Humans are killed. Non-human entities enter the lake alive. Different vocabulary, different fate, consecutive verses.

Relationship to other evidence: The same vocabulary differentiation pattern as Rev 20:9-10. Every time humans and non-human entities appear in the same context at the lake of fire, humans receive destruction/death vocabulary while non-human entities receive torment vocabulary.

docs.title: Rev 19:3: Smoke Formula Applied to Babylon
docs.text:
Context: Heavenly response to Babylon's fall.

Direct statement: "Her smoke rose up for ever and ever" (ho kapnos autes anabainei eis tous aionas ton aionon).

Original language: Identical smoke formula as Rev 14:11. But Babylon's destruction is documented as total in Rev 18:8-23 — fivefold "found no more at all" (music, craftsmen, millstone, light, voice of bridegroom).

Relationship to other evidence: Controls interpretation of Rev 14:11. If the identical formula applied to Babylon describes total destruction (not ongoing torment), the same formula in Rev 14:11 carries the same meaning.

docs.title: Rev 4:8: Identical "Day and Night" Construction
docs.text:
Context: Throne room vision. The four living creatures praise God.

Direct statement: "They rest not day and night" (anapausin ouk echousin hemeras kai nuktos) saying "Holy, holy, holy."

Original language: anapausis (G372) + "day and night" — structurally identical to Rev 14:11. The construction characterizes uninterrupted activity quality: the living creatures praise without intermission. It does not guarantee this specific activity continues eternally without change.

Relationship to other evidence: The identical construction in Rev 4:8 demonstrates that "no rest day and night" is a quality marker — describing what happens while it happens — not a duration guarantee.

docs.title: ECT Argument #3 — Matt 25:46: Everlasting Punishment
docs.text:
Context: Sheep and goats judgment parable. The parabolic framework is established by v.32 ("as a shepherd divideth").

Direct statement: "These shall go away into everlasting punishment (kolasin aionion): but the righteous into life eternal (zoen aionion)."

ECT steelman: The same adjective (aionios, G166) modifies both outcomes with identical grammatical construction (Acc Sg F). If eternal life is genuinely endless, everlasting punishment must be genuinely endless. The parallel demands equal duration.

Original language: kolasis (G2851, Acc Sg F) means punishment/penalty, from kolazo (G2849, "to curtail/prune"). Only 2 NT occurrences: Matt 25:46 and 1 John 4:18. Jesus chose kolasis, not basanismos (G929). The word means penalty — not experiential torment. The Hebrews pattern shows aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act: eternal redemption (Heb 9:12) obtained once, eternal judgment (Heb 6:2) rendered once, eternal salvation (Heb 5:9) authored once. The punishment is inflicted once and the result is permanent. Tit 1:2 uses aionios twice in one verse with different temporal scopes (zoes aioniou = eternal life; chronon aionion = "eternal times" that ended), falsifying the claim that the same adjective always demands the same duration.

Cross-references: 2 Thess 1:9 defines eschatological punishment as olethron aionion (everlasting destruction) — didactic epistle, all Tree 3 gates pass. Matt 25:41 specifies the fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" — primary non-human designation.

Relationship to other evidence: Prior study etc7-14 classified E13 as Neutral — both readings are grammatically possible. I-B resolved Strong toward Cond. because the Plain didactic statement (2 Thess 1:9: olethros = destruction) governs the Ambiguous parabolic statement (Matt 25:46: kolasis = punishment, reading uncertain).

docs.title: Matt 25:41: Fire Prepared for Non-Human Entities
docs.text:
Context: Same judgment parable, five verses before v.46.

Direct statement: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

Original language: The fire's primary designation is for the devil and his angels — non-human entities. Humans are sent there secondarily.

Relationship to other evidence: This verse specifies that the fire was not originally prepared for humans. Its original purpose is the destruction of supernatural/symbolic entities.

docs.title: ECT Argument #4 — Mark 9:43-48: Unquenchable Fire, Worm Dieth Not
docs.text:
Context: Jesus' teaching on radical discipleship. Threefold repetition of the worm/fire formula.

Direct statement: Mark 9:48 quotes Isa 66:24 directly: "Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched."

ECT steelman: Jesus warns of a place where the fire is never quenched and the worm never dies — implying ongoing, never-ending suffering. The language of ceaseless destruction agents (fire, worm) acting continuously suggests the subjects are alive and experiencing it.

Original language: skolex (G4663) — worm; teleutao (G5053) — dies; pyr (G4442) — fire; sbennymi (G4570) — is quenched. This is a direct quotation of Isaiah 66:24. The OT source text identifies the subjects as peger (H6297) — corpses. Peger means dead body in ALL 24 OT occurrences, never a living person. The worm (tola, H8438) is a biological organism (maggot) feeding on dead flesh. Isa 66:16-17 establishes the transgressors were "slain of the LORD" and "consumed together" before the viewing in v.24.

Cross-references: "Unquenchable fire" in OT usage: Jer 17:27 — fire on Jerusalem's gates "shall not be quenched" (lo' tikbeh, same vocabulary) — Jerusalem's gates are not still burning. Ezek 20:47 — unquenchable fire in a forest — the forest is not still burning. "Unquenchable" means irresistible (cannot be extinguished while burning), not eternal (never stops burning).

Relationship to other evidence: The ECT reading requires adding consciousness to subjects the OT source text identifies as corpses (I-C — Compatible External inference). Prior study etc7-21 classified as I-C at the ECT level with three I-D items. katakaio (G2618), Jesus' verb for the fate of tares in Matthew's parables, means "burn completely/consume."

docs.title: Isa 66:24: OT Source Text — Subjects Are Corpses
docs.text:
Context: Final verse of Isaiah. The redeemed view the aftermath of judgment.

Direct statement: "They shall go forth, and look upon the carcases (peger) of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring (dera'on) unto all flesh."

Original language: peger (H6297, Noun mp Cst) — always means dead body (24/24 OT uses). tola'at (H8438) — worm acting on corpses. dera'on (H1860) — abhorrence/revulsion. The subjects of viewing are dead bodies, not conscious living beings.

Relationship to other evidence: This is the source text that Jesus quotes in Mark 9:48. The worm and fire act on corpses. The dera'on is what the corpses evoke in observers — passive, not experienced.

docs.title: Isa 66:16-17: Transgressors Slain Before Viewing
docs.text:
Context: Two verses before Isa 66:24.

Direct statement: "By fire and by his sword will the LORD plead with all flesh: and the slain of the LORD shall be many. They... shall be consumed together."

Original language: chalal (H2491) — slain. suph (H5486) — consumed together. The sequence: transgressors are killed and consumed, then their corpses are viewed in v.24. Death precedes the dera'on.

Relationship to other evidence: Establishes that the objects of viewing in Isa 66:24 are already dead. The worm and fire act on dead bodies after slaughter.

docs.title: ECT Argument #5 — Luke 16:19-31: Rich Man and Lazarus
docs.text:
Context: Part of Luke's discourse unit beginning at 15:3 with a single parabole label. The "certain rich man" (anthropos tis plousios) formula appears at Luke 12:16 (explicit parable label) and 16:1 (universally recognized parable).

Direct statement: The rich man in hades (G86, not gehenna) is "in torments" (basanois, G931 basanos — grief vocabulary, NOT basanismos G929). He says "I am tormented" (odunomai, G3600 odunao — "I am grieved/pained," NOT basanizo G928). Abraham's bosom as post-mortem destination appears only here. The climactic teaching point is the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets (vv.29,31).

ECT steelman: Jesus names a specific person (Lazarus) — unique among parables — suggesting literal narrative. The rich man's conscious suffering in flame is presented as factual post-mortem reality. If Jesus describes a real person in a real afterlife scenario, this teaches conscious post-mortem existence and suffering.

Original language: basanos (G931) — torment/touchstone/pain — different vocabulary register from basanismos (G929). odunao (G3600) — grief, emotional pain — different from basanizo (G928). chasma (G5490) — chasm — hapax legomenon. The passage uses grief vocabulary, not eschatological torment vocabulary.

Cross-references: Luke 12:16 uses the identical "certain rich man" formula with an explicit parabole label. Luke 16:1 uses the same formula — universally recognized as parable. Luke 15:3 provides a single parabole label covering the discourse unit. Same author (Luke) records David is dead and NOT ascended into the heavens (Acts 2:29,34). Paul's logic in 1 Cor 15:18 requires the dead NOT to be in conscious bliss. 7 didactic death-state passages from 6 authors describe the dead as unconscious (Ecc 9:5, Ps 146:4, Ps 6:5, Ps 115:17).

Relationship to other evidence: Genre classified as parabolic via I-B resolution (Strong) in etc7-09 — 15+ Plain items from 8 independent lines against 1 Contextually Clear item (naming of Lazarus). Even ECT scholars acknowledge this describes hades (intermediate state), not the final hell/lake of fire.

docs.title: ECT Argument #6 — Rev 6:9-11: Souls Under the Altar
docs.text:
Context: Fifth seal in Revelation's seal sequence. Apocalyptic vision — "I saw" (eidon) introduces the scene.

Direct statement: John sees souls under the altar who were slain (esphagmenon, G4969 sphazo) for the word of God. They cry "How long?" and are told to rest (anapauomai, G373) for a little season.

ECT steelman: These souls are conscious, speaking, and aware of time passing — proving the soul survives death in a conscious state. If souls are conscious between death and resurrection, they could be conscious in hell.

Original language: sphazo (G4969) links these martyrs to Abel (1 John 3:12 — esphaxen) and the Lamb (Rev 5:6 — esphagmenon). The souls occupy the typological position of sacrificial blood poured at the base of the altar (Lev 4:7). Their "cry" follows the forensic personification pattern: Abel's blood cries (Gen 4:10), wages cry (Jas 5:4), the altar itself speaks (Rev 16:7).

Cross-references: Rev 20:4-5 identifies the same group (five-link verbal parallel) and locates their "living" (ezesan, G2198) at the first resurrection. The "rest" (anapauo G373) parallels Rev 14:13 (blessed dead rest) and Dan 12:13 (Daniel rests, then stands at the end).

Relationship to other evidence: Tree 3 Gate 1 fails — symbolic vision-figures, not literal humans. Gate 3 fails — apocalyptic genre, not didactic. Prior study etc7-10 classified all E-items as Neutral or Cond. ECT claims require treating apocalyptic vision as literal anthropological teaching (I-C).

docs.title: ECT Argument #7 — 2 Thess 1:7-10: Everlasting Destruction
docs.text:
Context: Didactic epistle — Paul writing to the Thessalonians. Doctrinal statement about eschatological punishment.

Direct statement: The disobedient "shall be punished with everlasting destruction (olethron aionion) from the presence of the Lord (apo prosopou tou kyriou), and from the glory of his power."

ECT steelman: "Everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord" means ongoing ruin or separation from God, not cessation of existence. "Destruction" can mean an ongoing ruinous state, and "from the presence" means banishment, not annihilation by the presence.

Original language: olethros (G3639, Acc Sg M) — destruction/ruin. All 4 NT occurrences are in Pauline epistles. No lexicon defines olethros as torment. From ollymi (to destroy) — same root as apollymi. Paul chose olethros (destruction), not basanizo (torment). The "apo prosopou" (G575 + G4383) phrase echoes Isa 2:10,19,21 LXX, where the divine presence is the destructive agent — people hide FROM the destroying presence, not are banished from a location. Psa 68:2 confirms: "as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God."

Cross-references: The Isa 2:10 LXX parallel establishes the "from the presence" construction as source-of-destruction, not banishment-from-presence. The wax metaphor in Psa 68:2 — wax melts and ceases to be wax; it does not exist in a perpetual state of melting.

Relationship to other evidence: Prior study etc7-14 classified E7/E15 as Cond. — all four Tree 3 gates passed. This is the only E-tier Cond. classification among the 8 ECT passages. The ECT reading (ongoing ruin, not cessation) requires redefining olethros from its lexical meaning — classified I-D because it overrides the word's established meaning.

docs.title: ECT Argument #8 — Dan 12:2: Everlasting Contempt
docs.text:
Context: The only OT text explicitly naming two resurrection outcomes.

Direct statement: "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life (chayyei olam), and some to shame (cherpah) and everlasting contempt (dera'on olam)."

ECT steelman: "Everlasting life" and "everlasting contempt" use identical olam modification in parallel grammatical construction. If life is genuinely eternal, contempt must be genuinely eternal conscious experience — the parallelism demands equal duration.

Original language: chayyei olam (H2416 + H5769) — everlasting life. dera'on olam (H1860 + H5769) — everlasting contempt. Dera'on has only 2 OT occurrences: Dan 12:2 and Isa 66:24. In Isa 66:24, the objects of dera'on are peger (corpses — dead bodies). Dera'on describes what transgressors become (objects of visceral revulsion), not what they experience. Olam duration is governed by nature-of-subject principle: olam spans from 3 days (Jonah 2:6) to genuinely eternal (Psa 90:2).

Cross-references: Isa 66:24 provides the only other occurrence of dera'on — applied to corpses being viewed by the redeemed. Dan 12:13 — Daniel himself will rest (nuwach) and stand (qum) at the end — rest = death, standing = resurrection.

Relationship to other evidence: Prior study etc7-14 classified E15/E17 as Neutral — ambiguous between experienced shame and observed contempt. The I-B resolution found the only occurrence with specified objects (Isa 66:24 = corpses) governs the occurrence without specified objects (Dan 12:2). Resolution: Strong toward Cond.

docs.title: Rom 6:23: Wages of Sin Is Death
docs.text:
Context: Didactic epistle — Paul's summary statement.

Direct statement: "The wages of sin is death (thanatos, G2288); but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Original language: thanatos — death. The binary is death vs. eternal life. Not torment vs. eternal life.

Relationship to other evidence: E-tier Cond. All Tree 3 gates pass. Didactic genre, universal scope.

docs.title: 1 Tim 6:16: God Alone Has Immortality
docs.text:
Context: Paul's doxology. Didactic epistle.

Direct statement: "Who only hath immortality" (monos echon athanasian).

Original language: monos (G3441) — only/alone. athanasia (G110) — immortality. Only 3 NT occurrences of athanasia: here, 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54. God alone possesses immortality inherently. Humans do not.

Relationship to other evidence: Undermines the ECT foundational assumption that human souls cannot cease to exist. If God alone has immortality, humans are mortal and can die permanently.

docs.title: Matt 10:28: God Able to Destroy Soul and Body in Gehenna
docs.text:
Context: Jesus' teaching to the twelve. Didactic instruction.

Direct statement: "Fear him which is able to destroy (apollymi, G622) both soul (psyche, G5590) and body in hell (gehenna, G1067)."

Original language: apollymi with divine/authority subject in Matthew consistently means actual destruction (Matt 2:13; 12:14; 21:41; 22:7). God is able to destroy both soul and body.

Relationship to other evidence: E-tier Cond. All Tree 3 gates pass. If the soul can be destroyed, it is not inherently immortal.

docs.title: Ezek 18:4: The Soul That Sins Shall Die
docs.text:
Context: Ezekiel's theodicy. Didactic prophetic teaching.

Direct statement: "The soul (nephesh, H5315) that sinneth, it shall die (muwth, H4191)."

Original language: nephesh — soul/living being (mortal). muwth — to die. The soul dies. E-tier Cond.

docs.title: Mal 4:1-3: Wicked Become Ashes
docs.text:
Context: Malachi's eschatological prophecy. Didactic prophetic teaching.

Direct statement: The wicked become stubble (qash), are burned up with neither root nor branch remaining, and become ashes (epher, H665) under the feet of the righteous.

Original language: saraph (H8313) — burn up; epher — ashes. Complete consumption vocabulary. E-tier Cond.

docs.title: John 3:16: Perish vs. Eternal Life
docs.text:
Context: Jesus' discourse with Nicodemus. The foundational Gospel statement.

Direct statement: "Whosoever believeth in him should not perish (apollymi, G622), but have everlasting life (zoe aionios)."

Original language: apollymi (Aor Mid Subj 3S) — perish. The Gospel binary: perishing vs. eternal life.

docs.title: 2 Pet 2:6: Sodom Turned to Ashes as Example
docs.text:
Context: Peter's argument from historical precedent.

Direct statement: Sodom and Gomorrah turned to ashes (tephroo — hapax legomenon) as an example (hupodeigma) for the ungodly.

Original language: tephroo — to reduce to ashes. If Sodom is the example of what happens to the ungodly, the ungodly's fate is destruction, not ECT.

docs.title: Ezek 28:18-19: Satan-Figure Consumed — Cessation Vocabulary
docs.text:
Context: Lamentation over the king of Tyre — addressing the supernatural being behind the earthly king.

Direct statement: "I will bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee (akal, H398), and I will bring thee to ashes (epher, H665)... thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more" (ayin + ad-olam — permanent non-existence).

Original language: The "ayin + ad-olam" formula describes permanent cessation: "you are nothing unto forever." This describes the same being (Satan-figure) who receives the torment formula in Rev 20:10. The OT describes his end as consumption to ashes and permanent non-existence.

Relationship to other evidence: Ezek 28:18-19 (cessation) and Rev 20:10 (torment) describe the same entity's fate in competing ways. The OT passage is prophetic didactic; Rev 20:10 is apocalyptic vision. SIS clarity criteria: didactic > apocalyptic.

docs.title: Isa 34:9-10: OT Source of Ages-of-Ages Smoke Formula
docs.text:
Context: Prophecy against Edom.

Direct statement: "The smoke thereof shall go up for ever (le'olam): from generation to generation it shall lie waste."

Original language: le'olam ya'aleh ashannah — "forever ascends its smoke." Identical formula to Rev 14:11.

Relationship to other evidence: Isa 34:11-17 proves the fire and smoke ended — animals dwell in the ruins. The olam smoke formula describes permanent destruction, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Isa 34:11-17: Animals Dwell in Edom's Ruins
docs.text:
Context: Immediately follows the "smoke ascending forever" passage.

Direct statement: Cormorant, bittern, owl, raven, wild beasts, vultures possess and dwell in the ruins "for ever" (olam). They nest, hatch, and gather there.

Relationship to other evidence: Animals dwelling in the ruins proves the fire ended. The olam fire produced permanent desolation — the result is eternal, not the process.

docs.title: Tit 1:2: Aionios Used Twice with Different Temporal Scopes
docs.text:
Context: Paul's letter to Titus.

Direct statement: "In hope of eternal life (zoes aioniou), which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began (pro chronon aionion)."

Original language: zoes aioniou (G2222 + G166, Gen Sg F) — eternal life. chronon aionion (G5550 + G166, Gen Pl M) — "eternal times" (that ended — we are past them). Same adjective, different temporal scope, same verse. Falsifies "same adjective = same duration."

docs.title: Heb 9:12: Eternal Redemption Obtained Once
docs.text:
Context: Christ's superior priesthood.

Direct statement: Christ entered the holy place "having obtained eternal redemption (aionion lytrosis) for us."

Original language: The adjective modifies the result (permanent), not the process (ongoing). Christ redeemed once; the result is eternal.

docs.title: Heb 6:2: Eternal Judgment Rendered Once
docs.text: Direct statement: "Eternal judgment" (krimatos aioniou) — judged once, result permanent.

docs.title: Heb 5:9: Eternal Salvation Authored Once
docs.text: Direct statement: Christ "became the author of eternal salvation" — saved once, result permanent.

docs.title: Ecc 9:5: The Dead Know Not Anything
docs.text: Direct statement: "The dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward."

docs.title: Ps 146:4: Thoughts Perish at Death
docs.text: Direct statement: "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish (abad, H6)."

docs.title: Ps 6:5: No Remembrance in Death
docs.text: Direct statement: "In death there is no remembrance of thee."

docs.title: Ps 115:17: The Dead Praise Not the LORD
docs.text: Direct statement: "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence (dumah)."

docs.title: Acts 2:29,34: David Dead, Not Ascended
docs.text:
Direct statement: "David... is both dead and buried" (v.29). "David is not ascended into the heavens" (v.34).

Relationship to other evidence: Same author (Luke) who records the rich man and Lazarus parable also records Peter's statement that the dead patriarch David is dead and not in heaven. This reflects Luke's theological position on the state of the dead.

docs.title: 1 Cor 15:18: Paul's Logic Requires Dead Not Conscious
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished (apollymi)."

Relationship to other evidence: Paul argues: if Christ is not raised, the dead are perished. This only works if the dead are not already in conscious bliss. If they were, the resurrection's failure would be irrelevant.

docs.title: Psa 37:10: Wicked Shall Not Be
docs.text: Direct statement: "Yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be."

docs.title: Psa 37:20: Consume into Smoke
docs.text: Direct statement: "The wicked shall perish (abad, H6)... they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away."

docs.title: Psa 68:2: Wicked Perish at God's Presence
docs.text: Direct statement: "As wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish (abad) at the presence (mippanei) of God."

docs.title: Rev 21:4: No More Death
docs.text:
Direct statement: "There shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain."

Relationship to other evidence: If death ceases to exist in the new creation, the concept of eternal dying/torment is inconsistent.

docs.title: Heb 10:27: Fire Devours Adversaries
docs.text: Direct statement: "A certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour (esthio, G2068) the adversaries."

docs.title: Jer 17:27: Unquenchable Fire on Jerusalem
docs.text: Direct statement: God will kindle fire in Jerusalem's gates "and it shall not be quenched." Jerusalem's gates are not still burning.

docs.title: Ezek 20:47: Unquenchable Fire — Historically Ended
docs.text: Direct statement: "The flaming flame shall not be quenched" — describing fire in a forest that historically ended.

docs.title: Jonah 2:6: Olam = 3 Days
docs.text: Direct statement: "The earth with her bars was about me for ever (olam)" — Jonah was in the fish 3 days.

docs.title: 1 Sam 2:30: Olam Promise Revoked
docs.text: Direct statement: "I said indeed that thy house... should walk before me for ever (ad-olam): but now the LORD saith, Be it far from me."

docs.title: Gen 4:10: Abel's Blood Cries — Forensic Personification
docs.text: Direct statement: "The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground."

docs.title: Jas 5:4: Wages Cry Out — Forensic Personification
docs.text: Direct statement: "The hire of the labourers... crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."

docs.title: Rev 16:7: Altar Speaks — Apocalyptic Personification
docs.text: Direct statement: "I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty."

docs.title: Rev 20:4-5: Martyrs Live at First Resurrection
docs.text:
Direct statement: "I saw the souls of them that were beheaded... and they lived (ezesan) and reigned with Christ a thousand years... This is the first resurrection."

Relationship to other evidence: The same martyrs from Rev 6:9-11 are shown living at the first resurrection — their conscious existence is located at resurrection, not at death.

docs.title: Rev 14:13: Blessed Dead Rest
docs.text: Direct statement: "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord... that they may rest (anapauo, G373) from their labours."

docs.title: Dan 12:13: Daniel Rests Then Stands
docs.text: Direct statement: "Thou shalt rest (nuwach), and stand (qum) in thy lot at the end of the days."

docs.title: Jude 1:7: Eternal Fire — Fire Ended, Result Permanent
docs.text:
Direct statement: Sodom and Gomorrah "are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire (pyr aionion)."

Relationship to other evidence: Sodom's fire is called "eternal" (aionios) — but Peter says Sodom was "turned to ashes" (2 Pet 2:6). The fire is eternal in result, not in duration.

docs.title: Gen 19:24-28: Sodom Destroyed — OT Fire Paradigm
docs.text: Direct statement: "The LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven; and he overthrew those cities."

docs.title: Luke 17:29: Jesus Cites Sodom as Destruction
docs.text: Direct statement: "It rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed (apollymi) them all."

docs.title: Phil 3:19: End Is Destruction
docs.text: Direct statement: "Whose end is destruction (apoleia, G684)."

docs.title: Matt 8:29: Demons Use Basanizo
docs.text:
Direct statement: Demons ask: "Art thou come hither to torment (basanizo, G928) us before the time?"

Relationship to other evidence: The only Gospel use of basanizo in an eschatological context is demonic speech, not Jesus' teaching about human fate.

docs.title: Rom 2:7: Seeking Immortality
docs.text:
Direct statement: "To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality (aphtharsia, G861), eternal life."

Relationship to other evidence: You do not seek what you already possess. If humans had inherent immortality, seeking it would be meaningless.

docs.title: 1 Cor 15:53-54: Mortal Puts On Immortality
docs.text:
Direct statement: "This mortal (thnetos, G2349) must put on (endyo) immortality (athanasia, G110)."

Relationship to other evidence: Humans are mortal. Immortality is a future gift at resurrection. The wicked do not receive it.

docs.title: Obad 1:16: As Though They Had Not Been
docs.text: Direct statement: "They shall be as though they had not been" — complete cessation of existence.

docs.title: Nah 1:9: Utter End — Affliction Does Not Rise Again
docs.text: Direct statement: "He will make an utter end (kalah): affliction shall not rise up the second time."

docs.title: 1 John 3:12 / Rev 5:6: Sphazo Vocabulary Chain
docs.text: Direct statement: Cain "slew (esphaxen) his brother" (1 John 3:12). The Lamb stood "as it had been slain (esphagmenon)" (Rev 5:6). Same sphazo vocabulary as Rev 6:9 martyrs — all slaughter victims.

docs.title: Lev 4:7: Blood Poured at Base of Altar
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Shall pour all the blood of the bullock at the bottom of the altar."

Relationship to other evidence: The Rev 6:9 souls occupy the position of poured-out sacrificial blood at the altar's base — a typological, not anthropological, datum.

docs.title: Rev 12:9: Four-Fold Devil Identification
docs.text:
Direct statement: "The great dragon... that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan."

Relationship to other evidence: The devil of Rev 20:10 is identified as a supernatural being, not human.

docs.title: Rev 13:1: Beast Is Symbolic
docs.text:
Direct statement: "A beast rise up out of the sea, having seven heads and ten horns."

Relationship to other evidence: A multi-headed creature is not a literal human — it is a symbolic entity.

docs.title: Pattern 1: Torment Vocabulary Confined to Apocalyptic Genre
docs.text: basanizo (G928) and basanismos (G929) for human eschatological fate appear in zero epistles, zero Gospel teachings, zero OT passages. All eschatological judgment uses are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework. The only Gospel eschatological use (Matt 8:29) is demonic speech, not Jesus' teaching. Luke 16 uses basanos/odunao (grief vocabulary), not basanizo/basanismos. Matt 25:46 uses kolasis (punishment), not basanismos (torment).

docs.title: Pattern 2: Destruction Vocabulary Spans All Genres and Authors
docs.text: Destruction/death vocabulary for the fate of the wicked spans: - Jesus: apollymi (Matt 10:28, John 3:16), katakaio (Matt 13:30,40) - Paul: thanatos (Rom 6:23), olethros (2 Thess 1:9), apoleia (Phil 3:19) - Peter: tephroo (2 Pet 2:6) - Hebrews: esthio (Heb 10:27) - Psalms: abad, kalah, ayin (Psa 37:10,20; 68:2) - Isaiah: chalal, suph (Isa 66:16-17), epher (Isa 34; Ezek 28:18) - Malachi: epher, saraph (Mal 4:1-3) - Ezekiel: muwth + nephesh (Ezek 18:4)

docs.title: Pattern 3: Vocabulary Differentiation at the Lake of Fire
docs.text: In every passage where humans and non-human entities appear together at the lake of fire, different verbs are used for different subjects: - Rev 19:20-21: Beast/false prophet cast alive into lake; humans slain (apektanthesan) - Rev 20:9-10: Humans devoured (katephagen); devil tormented (basanisthesontai) - Rev 20:14-15: Lake = second death (thanatos); humans cast into = receive death

docs.title: Pattern 4: Duration Vocabulary (Olam/Aionios) Subject-Determined
docs.text: olam spans from 3 days (Jonah 2:6) to genuinely eternal (Psa 90:2). Ended institutions labeled olam. Explicitly revoked olam promises (1 Sam 2:30). Fire/smoke called olam that historically ended (Isa 34:10, Jer 17:27). aionios used for past time that ended (Tit 1:2 dual-scope). Hebrews pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act. aidios (G126) exists as the strict "everduring" word — the NT authors did not use it for eschatological punishment.

docs.title: Pattern 5: All OT Comparisons Describe Cessation
docs.text: Nave's "WICKED — COMPARED WITH" entry lists comparisons: chaff (blown away), stubble (burned), ashes (consumed residue), wax (melted), smoke (vanishes), grass (withers), tares (burned). Every comparison describes something that ceases to exist.

docs.title: Pattern 6: The "Ages of Ages" Formula Distribution
docs.text: The formula "eis tous aionas ton aionon" appears 21 times in the NT: 19 doxological (praise to God), 2 judgment uses (Rev 14:11 smoke, Rev 20:10 torment). Both judgment uses are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework for non-human/symbolic entities.

docs.title: Word Study Integration
docs.text:
The vocabulary data transforms the English reading of every ECT passage:

  • Rev 14:11: basanismos (G929) — 6 NT occurrences, all in Revelation, 4 of 6 time-bounded. The word never appears in any didactic genre.
  • Rev 20:10: basanizo (G928) — the torment-for-ever formula appears once, applied to non-human entities.
  • Matt 25:46: kolasis (G2851) — punishment/penalty from kolazo "to curtail." 2 NT occurrences. Not torment.
  • Mark 9:48: peger (H6297) — corpse, dead body. 24/24 OT uses = dead body. The subjects are corpses.
  • Luke 16: basanos (G931) / odunao (G3600) — grief vocabulary, not eschatological torment vocabulary.
  • Rev 6:9-11: sphazo (G4969) — slaughter vocabulary linking to sacrificial blood.
  • 2 Thess 1:9: olethros (G3639) — destruction. 4 NT occurrences, all Pauline. No lexicon defines it as torment.
  • Dan 12:2: dera'on (H1860) — abhorrence/contempt applied to corpses in its only other occurrence (Isa 66:24).

docs.title: Cross-Testament Connections
docs.text:
1. Rev 14:11 ← Isa 34:10: The smoke-ascending formula is an OT allusion. Edom's fire ended; animals dwell in the ruins.
  2. Mark 9:48 ← Isa 66:24: Direct quotation. The subjects are peger (corpses).
  3. 2 Thess 1:9 ← Isa 2:10/Psa 68:2: "From the presence" = source of destruction, not banishment.
  4. Rev 20:10 ← Ezek 28:18-19: Same entity (Satan-figure) described with cessation vocabulary in OT.
  5. Jude 1:7 / 2 Pet 2:6 ← Gen 19:24-28: Sodom's "eternal fire" ended — turned to ashes as example.
  6. Rev 6:9 ← Gen 4:10 / Lev 4:7: Forensic personification and altar-blood typology.
  7. Matt 25:46 ← Dan 12:2 ← Isa 66:24: The dera'on chain linking all three passages to corpses.

docs.title: Rev 14:9-11: Human Subjects with Torment Language
docs.text:
This is the most difficult passage for the conditionalist position because it applies torment vocabulary to beast-worshippers (human subjects), not just to the devil/beast/false prophet. The text says "he shall be tormented" (basanisthesetai) and "they have no rest day and night." The passage names human subjects experiencing torment.

The complication is addressed by: (1) the genre gate (apocalyptic, not didactic); (2) the identical smoke formula in Isa 34:10 describing an ended fire; (3) the identical "no rest day and night" construction in Rev 4:8 characterizing quality, not guaranteed duration; (4) Rev 19:3 applying the identical formula to Babylon's total destruction. But the difficulty remains real: this is the one passage where torment language is applied to human subjects in an eschatological context.

docs.title: Matt 25:46: The Parallel Construction
docs.text:
The parallel "everlasting punishment / life eternal" with the same adjective in identical grammatical construction is a genuine difficulty. If the adjective means "endless" when modifying life, the parallel seems to demand the same for punishment.

The complication is addressed by: (1) the Hebrews pattern showing aionios + result-noun = permanent result; (2) Tit 1:2 showing the same adjective with different temporal scopes in one verse; (3) the nature-of-subject principle from olam evidence. But the surface-level parallel reading is natural and must be acknowledged as a genuine exegetical consideration.

docs.title: Rev 20:10: Extension to Humans
docs.text:
The extension argument (same lake = same experience) has surface plausibility. If the devil is tormented in the lake, and humans are thrown into the same lake, the inference that both groups experience the same thing is natural.

The complication is addressed by the text's own vocabulary differentiation: humans get different verbs (devoured, slain, second death) from non-human entities (tormented) in consecutive verses by the same author. The text itself distinguishes the experiences.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The 8 ECT arguments follow a consistent pattern when evaluated at the E/N/I tier:

  1. E-tier ECT items: 0 across all 8 passages. Not one passage produces an explicit statement that, after passing all four Tree 3 gates, classifies as ECT-direction evidence.

  2. E-tier Cond. items: 62 from prior studies, drawn from didactic passages across multiple authors and genres (Jesus, Paul, Peter, Isaiah, Malachi, Ezekiel, Psalms, Hebrews).

  3. Every ECT claim exists at the inference level:

  4. Rev 14:9-11: I-B (resolved Strong toward Cond.)
  5. Rev 20:10: I-B (resolved Strong toward Cond.)
  6. Matt 25:46: I-B (resolved Strong/Moderate toward Cond.)
  7. Mark 9:43-48: I-C (requires adding consciousness to corpses)
  8. Luke 16:19-31: I-C (parabolic genre, grief vocabulary)
  9. Rev 6:9-11: I-C (apocalyptic vision-figures)
  10. 2 Thess 1:9: ECT reading is I-D (requires redefining olethros)

  11. Dan 12:2: I-B (resolved Strong toward Cond.)

  12. The evidence hierarchy (E > N > I) governs: The ECT position has no evidence above the inference level. The conditionalist position has 62 E-items and multiple N-items from didactic sources across the entire biblical canon. By the evidence hierarchy, lower-tier inferences cannot override higher-tier explicit statements and necessary implications.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: 8 key ECT arguments evaluated at E/N/I tier: Rev 14:9-11, Rev 20:10, Matt 25:46, Mark 9:43-48, Luke 16:19-31, Rev 6:9-11, 2 Thess 1:9, Dan 12:2.

docs.title: G929 — basanismos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G929-basanismos.md

Occurrences: 6

Basanismos (torment) — 6 NT occurrences, ALL in Revelation. Distribution: demonic/supernatural torment (Rev 9:5, time-bounded 5 months), eschatological judgment (Rev 14:11), commercial/imperial grief-torment (Rev 18:7,10,15, time-bounded — Babylon's fall). 4 of 6 occurrences are time-bounded. Zero epistles, zero Gospel teachings, zero OT passages. Never used by Jesus, Paul, Peter, or any didactic author for human eschatological fate.

Semantic categories: demonic torment, eschatological judgment, commercial grief

Key verses: Rev 9:5, Rev 14:11, Rev 18:7, Rev 18:10, Rev 18:15

Relevance: Core ECT vocabulary word. Its exclusive confinement to Revelation's apocalyptic framework (zero occurrences in any other genre) is the single most important vocabulary datum in the debate. If torment vocabulary for human eschatological fate existed in epistles, Gospels, or OT, it would be E-tier evidence for ECT. Its absence is decisive.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G928-basanizo.md

Occurrences: 12

Basanizo (to torment/torture/vex) — 12 NT occurrences across 6 books. Distribution: Gospels physical suffering and demonic encounters (6x: Matt 8:6,29; 14:24; Mark 5:7; 6:48; Luke 8:28), epistles moral distress (1x: 2 Pet 2:8), Revelation eschatological torment (5x: Rev 9:5; 11:10; 12:2; 14:10; 20:10). The 'torment-for-ever' formula (basanisthesontai eis tous aionas ton aionon) appears ONCE — Rev 20:10 — applied only to devil/beast/false prophet (all non-human).

Semantic categories: physical suffering, demonic encounter, moral anguish, eschatological torment

Key verses: Matt 8:29, 2 Pet 2:8, Rev 14:10, Rev 20:10

Relevance: Root verb of the basanizo word family. Its distribution across genres is critical: the only eschatological uses are in Revelation. Matt 8:29 (demons) is the only Gospel eschatological use — and it is demonic speech, not Jesus' teaching. Paul never uses basanizo for eschatological punishment.

docs.title: G931 — basanos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G931-basanos.md

Occurrences: 3

Basanos (touchstone, torment, grief) — 3 NT occurrences: Matt 4:24 (physical sickness), Luke 16:23 (rich man 'in torments'), Luke 16:28 ('place of torment'). Luke 16 uses basanos, NOT basanizo/basanismos. Different vocabulary register from Revelation's eschatological torment. basanos connotes grief/painful testing, not the eschatological torment of basanismos.

Semantic categories: physical pain, grief, testing

Key verses: Luke 16:23, Luke 16:28

Relevance: Critical for Luke 16 analysis: the parable uses basanos (grief vocabulary), NOT the eschatological torment vocabulary of Revelation (basanizo/basanismos). Different word family register.

docs.title: G2851 — kolasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2851-kolasis.md

Occurrences: 2

Kolasis (punishment/penalty) — only 2 NT occurrences: Matt 25:46 ('everlasting punishment') and 1 John 4:18 ('fear hath torment/punishment'). Etymology from kolazo (G2849, 'to curtail/prune') — original sense of cutting short, deterrent penalty. Distinct from basanismos (experiential torment) and timoria (retributive penalty). Jesus chose kolasis, not basanismos — a deliberate vocabulary choice.

Semantic categories: judicial punishment, penalty, fear's punishing quality

Key verses: Matt 25:46, 1 John 4:18

Relevance: The key word in Matt 25:46. ECT reads this as 'everlasting conscious torment,' but the word means punishment/penalty, not torment. Jesus had basanismos available and chose a different word. The kolazo root ('to curtail') suggests ending/cutting off, not perpetuating.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Aionios (eternal/everlasting/age-lasting) — 71 NT occurrences across 19 books. Dominant usage: ~43 of 69 unique verses modify 'life' (zoe). Three past-time uses prove aionios does not inherently mean 'endless': Rom 16:25, 2 Tim 1:9, Tit 1:2. Tit 1:2 uses aionios twice with different temporal scopes in the same verse. The Hebrews pattern (aionios + result-noun = permanent result) controls Matt 25:46 interpretation. aidios (G126) exists as the strict 'everduring' word, distinct from aionios.

Semantic categories: eternal life, divine attributes, judgment/punishment, pre-temporal reference, eschatological realities

Key verses: Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, Tit 1:2, Heb 9:12, Jude 1:7

Relevance: Central to the ECT duration argument. ECT claims same adjective = same duration in Matt 25:46. The evidence shows aionios duration is governed by subject, not by the word itself. The Hebrews pattern and Tit 1:2 datum are decisive counter-evidence.

docs.title: G126 — aidios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G126-aidios.md

Occurrences: 2

Aidios (everduring, strictly eternal) — only 2 NT occurrences: Rom 1:20 (God's 'eternal power') and Jude 1:6 (angels kept in 'everlasting chains'). Derived from aei ('always'), emphasizing continuous unbroken duration. Distinct from aionios which derives from aion ('age'). The existence of aidios as a separate word for strict eternality demonstrates that aionios does not inherently carry the same meaning.

Semantic categories: strictly eternal, divine attribute, permanent binding

Key verses: Rom 1:20, Jude 1:6

Relevance: The existence of aidios as a distinct word for strict eternality is evidence that Greek had the vocabulary to express 'genuinely endless' — and the NT authors chose NOT to use aidios for eschatological punishment.

docs.title: G3639 — olethros
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3639-olethros.md

Occurrences: 4

Olethros (destruction/ruin) — 4 NT occurrences, ALL in Pauline epistles: 1 Cor 5:5 (disciplinary destruction of flesh), 1 Thess 5:3 (sudden destruction), 2 Thess 1:9 (everlasting destruction), 1 Tim 6:9 (destruction and perdition). KJV renders uniformly as 'destruction.' No lexicon defines olethros as torment. From ollymi (to destroy) — the same root as apollymi.

Semantic categories: disciplinary destruction, sudden eschatological destruction, everlasting destruction, catastrophic ruin

Key verses: 2 Thess 1:9, 1 Thess 5:3, 1 Tim 6:9

Relevance: Paul's chosen word for eschatological punishment in 2 Thess 1:9. He had basanizo available and chose olethros (destruction). This is the single E-tier Cond. classification among the 8 passages — all four Tree 3 gates pass.

docs.title: G622 — apollymi
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G622-apollymi.md

Occurrences: 102

Apollymi (to destroy/perish/lose) — 86 unique verses across 15 NT books. Active: to destroy, put to death. Middle/passive: to perish, be ruined. Jesus' primary eschatological verb: 'fear him which is able to destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in hell' (Matt 10:28). Core Gospel binary: 'should not perish (apollymi) but have everlasting life' (John 3:16). Heaviest in Synoptics (Luke 25x, Matthew 18x). Absent from Revelation. LXX equivalent of Hebrew abad (H6).

Semantic categories: physical destruction, divine judgment, eschatological perishing, losing life/soul, losing possessions, decay

Key verses: Matt 10:28, John 3:16, Luke 17:29, 2 Pet 3:9

Relevance: Jesus' chosen word for what God does to the wicked in gehenna. With divine subject in Matthew, apollymi consistently means actual destruction. The perish/eternal-life antithesis (John 3:16) is the core Gospel binary — perishing is the opposite of eternal life.

docs.title: G684 — apoleia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G684-apoleia.md

Occurrences: 20

Apoleia (destruction/perdition) — cognate noun of apollymi. Used for eschatological destruction: 'son of perdition' (John 17:12), 'whose end is destruction' (Phil 3:19), 'vessels of wrath fitted to destruction' (Rom 9:22). Paired with olethros in 1 Tim 6:9 ('destruction and perdition'). Part of the broad NT destruction vocabulary for final punishment.

Semantic categories: eschatological destruction, perdition, waste

Key verses: Phil 3:19, 2 Pet 2:1, Rev 17:8

Relevance: NT destruction noun used across multiple authors (Paul, Peter, John) for eschatological punishment. Spans multiple genres. Part of the destruction vocabulary pattern that contrasts with Revelation's exclusive torment vocabulary.

docs.title: H5769 — owlam
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5769-owlam.md

Occurrences: 432

Olam (forever/everlasting/perpetual) — 432 tokens across 406 OT verses in 34 books. From root alam (H5956, 'to conceal') — 'the vanishing point,' time that recedes beyond perception. Spans from 3 days (Jonah 2:6) to genuinely eternal (Psa 90:2). Applied to ended institutions: circumcision, Levitical priesthood, Sabbath, land promises. Explicitly revoked olam promise in 1 Sam 2:30. Fire/smoke judgments called olam that historically ended (Isa 34:10, Jer 17:27). Duration determined by nature of subject.

Semantic categories: divine eternity, covenant permanence, cultic ordinances, judgment duration, past time

Key verses: Psa 90:2, Isa 34:10, Dan 12:2, Jonah 2:6, 1 Sam 2:30

Relevance: Hebrew equivalent of aionios. The extensive OT evidence that olam duration is subject-determined (not word-determined) controls interpretation of Dan 12:2 'dera'on olam' and all aionios judgment passages.

docs.title: H1860 — dera'on
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1860-draown.md

Occurrences: 2

Dera'on (contempt/abhorrence) — only 2 OT occurrences: Dan 12:2 ('everlasting contempt') and Isa 66:24 ('an abhorring unto all flesh'). From unused root meaning 'to repulse.' Denotes an object that provokes active recoil/revulsion. In Isa 66:24, the objects of dera'on are peger (corpses). Dera'on describes what transgressors BECOME (objects of visceral revulsion), not what they EXPERIENCE.

Semantic categories: eschatological revulsion, observed abhorrence

Key verses: Dan 12:2, Isa 66:24

Relevance: Critical for Dan 12:2 analysis. The only occurrence with specified objects (Isa 66:24 = corpses) must govern the occurrence without specified objects (Dan 12:2). If dera'on is observed revulsion at corpses, then 'everlasting contempt' is a permanent state of the objects (being abhorrent), not a conscious experience.

docs.title: H6297 — peger
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H6297-peger.md

Occurrences: 24

Peger (corpse/dead body) — always means dead body in ALL 24 OT occurrences. Never refers to a living person. The subjects being viewed in Isa 66:24 are peger — corpses. The worm (tola) acts on corpses. The fire burns corpses. The dera'on is observed on corpses. This is the decisive datum for Mark 9:43-48 and Dan 12:2.

Semantic categories: dead body, corpse, carcass

Key verses: Isa 66:24, Isa 14:19, Isa 34:3

Relevance: Every ECT reading of Mark 9:43-48 must add consciousness to subjects the OT source text identifies as corpses. Peger never means a living person in any of its 24 OT uses.

docs.title: G5590 — psyche
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5590-psyche.md

Occurrences: 105

Psyche (soul/life) — 105 NT occurrences. Semantic range: inner self/emotions (Matt 26:38), physical life-force (Matt 10:28), person/individual (Acts 2:41), destroyed in gehenna (Matt 10:28). NOT inherently immortal — can be destroyed. NT equivalent of Hebrew nephesh (H5315). Heaviest in Gospels + Acts (82%).

Semantic categories: inner self, physical life, person, mortal entity

Key verses: Matt 10:28, Matt 22:37, Rev 6:9

Relevance: Central to the immortality question. If psyche can be 'destroyed' in gehenna (Matt 10:28, apollymi), then the soul is not inherently immortal. ECT requires inherent soul immortality — the biblical data contradicts this.

docs.title: G110 — athanasia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G110-athanasia.md

Occurrences: 3

Athanasia (immortality/deathlessness) — only 3 NT occurrences: 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54, 1 Tim 6:16. Alpha-privative + thanatos = 'deathlessness.' In 1 Tim 6:16: God ALONE (monos) has immortality. In 1 Cor 15:53-54: mortal MUST PUT ON immortality (at resurrection). Never applied to inherent human nature. Absent from Gospels, Revelation, and all other NT writings.

Semantic categories: divine attribute, resurrection transformation

Key verses: 1 Tim 6:16, 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54

Relevance: The ECT framework assumes inherent human immortality. The NT teaches the opposite: God alone has immortality, and believers receive it at resurrection. If the wicked never receive immortality, they cannot exist forever.

docs.title: G2288 — thanatos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2288-thanatos.md

Occurrences: 119

Thanatos (death) — 119 tokens across 106 unique verses in 15 NT books. Dominant in Romans (20x) and Revelation (15x). Semantic range: physical death, death as consequence of sin (Rom 5:12; 6:23), spiritual death, second death (Rev 20:14; 21:8). 'Wages of sin is death' (Rom 6:23) — Paul's definitive statement uses thanatos, not basanismos.

Semantic categories: physical death, sin's consequence, second death, personified death

Key verses: Rom 6:23, Rev 20:14, Rev 21:8, 1 Cor 15:26

Relevance: The lake of fire is called 'the second death' (thanatos) — not 'the second torment.' Death is the final enemy destroyed (1 Cor 15:26). The consistent NT vocabulary for sin's ultimate consequence is death/destruction, not torment.

docs.title: G372 — anapausis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G372-anapausis.md

Occurrences: 5

Anapausis (rest/intermission/cessation) — 5 NT occurrences: Matt 11:29 (soul rest from Christ), Matt 12:43/Luke 11:24 (demon seeking rest), Rev 4:8 (living creatures 'have no rest' in ceaseless praise), Rev 14:11 (beast-worshippers 'have no rest'). Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11 share identical construction: 'ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos.' In Rev 4:8, 'no rest day and night' characterizes quality of ceaseless activity, not guaranteed eternal duration.

Semantic categories: spiritual rest, demonic restlessness, ceaseless activity

Key verses: Rev 14:11, Rev 4:8, Matt 11:29

Relevance: The 'no rest day and night' phrase in Rev 14:11 is central to the ECT reading. But the identical construction in Rev 4:8 (ceaseless praise of living creatures) shows this phrase characterizes uninterrupted quality, not a duration guarantee. The living creatures' praise will not literally continue forever in the new creation.

docs.title: G4969 — sphazo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4969-sphazo.md

Occurrences: 10

Sphazo (to slay/slaughter) — NT occurrences linking Abel, the Lamb, and the martyrs. 1 John 3:12: Cain 'slew' (esphaxen) Abel. Rev 5:6: Lamb 'as it had been slain' (esphagmenon). Rev 6:9: 'souls of them that were slain' (esphagmenon). The sphazō vocabulary chain connects the Rev 6:9 martyrs to sacrificial death imagery, not to conscious survival.

Semantic categories: sacrificial slaughter, martyrdom, violent death

Key verses: Rev 6:9, Rev 5:6, 1 John 3:12

Relevance: The Rev 6:9 souls are 'slain' (sphazō) — slaughter victims. Their position under the altar and their sphazō identification link them to sacrificial blood (Lev 4:7), not to conscious survival of death.

docs.title: G2618 — katakaio
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2618-katakaio.md

Occurrences: 12

Katakaio (to burn completely/consume) — Jesus' verb for the fate of the tares in Matthew's parables. 'Burn completely' — complete consumption, not preservation in fire. Used for chaff, tares, fruitless branches.

Semantic categories: complete burning, consumptive fire

Key verses: Matt 13:30, Matt 13:40

Relevance: Jesus' own vocabulary for what happens to the wicked in fire is 'burn completely' (katakaio), not 'torment' (basanizo). His parabolic teaching consistently uses destruction vocabulary.

docs.title: G3600 — odunao
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3600-odynao.md

Occurrences: 4

Odunao (to grieve/be in pain) — Luke 16:24,25 vocabulary. The rich man says 'I am grieved/pained' (odunomai) in this flame. This is grief vocabulary, NOT the eschatological torment vocabulary of Revelation (basanizo/basanismos). Different word family, different register.

Semantic categories: grief, emotional pain, sorrow

Key verses: Luke 16:24, Luke 16:25

Relevance: Luke 16 uses odunao (grief), not basanizo (torment). This vocabulary distinction separates Luke 16 from Revelation's eschatological torment passages. The parable uses grief/sorrow vocabulary appropriate to its literary genre.

docs.title: G165 — aion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G165-aion.md

Occurrences: 120

Aion (age/eon/era) — root noun from which aionios derives. 128 NT occurrences. Means 'an age' — a bounded period of time. The plural formula 'eis tous aionas ton aionon' (ages of ages) appears 21 times in the NT: 19 doxological (praise to God), 2 judgment uses (Rev 14:11 smoke, Rev 20:10 torment). Both judgment uses are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework for non-human entities.

Semantic categories: age, era, eternity formula

Key verses: Rev 14:11, Rev 20:10, Gal 1:5

Relevance: The 'ages of ages' formula's distribution is critical: 19 of 21 uses are doxological (praise to God). Only 2 are for judgment — both in Revelation's apocalyptic framework. The formula is overwhelmingly a doxological expression.

docs.title: G1067 — geenna
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1067-geenna.md

Occurrences: 12

Geenna (Gehenna/Valley of Hinnom) — used by Jesus for the place of final punishment. Background: the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, site of child sacrifice (Jer 7:31-32), later became a garbage dump. Connotes destruction in its Valley of Hinnom background — a place where things are destroyed and consumed, not preserved.

Semantic categories: final punishment, destruction, Valley of Hinnom

Key verses: Matt 10:28, Mark 9:43, Matt 5:22

Relevance: The Valley of Hinnom background connotes destruction (fire consuming refuse), not eternal preservation. No hell-word inherently requires eternal conscious torment.

docs.title: G86 — hades
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G86-háidēs.md

Occurrences: 11

Hades (the grave/unseen realm) — temporary holding place destroyed in Rev 20:14 when death and hades are cast into the lake of fire. Luke 16 is set in hades (intermediate state), not the final lake of fire. ECT scholars themselves acknowledge Luke 16 describes hades, not final hell.

Semantic categories: intermediate state, the grave, temporary realm

Key verses: Rev 20:13, Rev 20:14, Luke 16:23

Relevance: Hades is temporary — it is destroyed in Rev 20:14. Luke 16 is set in hades (not final hell), which even ECT scholars acknowledge. The passage therefore cannot teach about the final state of the wicked.

docs.title: G2719 — katesthio
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2719-katesthio.md

Occurrences: 20

Katesthio (to devour/eat up/consume) — the verb used for what happens to humans at the lake of fire in Rev 20:9 ('fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them'). Different from basanizo (torment) used for the devil in Rev 20:10. The vocabulary differentiation between consecutive verses by the same author is critical.

Semantic categories: consuming, devouring, total destruction

Key verses: Rev 20:9

Relevance: The verb used for human fate at the lake of fire is 'devoured' (katephagen), not 'tormented' (basanisthesontai). Same author, same passage, different vocabulary for different subjects.

docs.title: G373 — anapauo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G373-anapauo.md

Occurrences: 13

Anapauo (to rest/refresh) — cognate verb of anapausis (G372). Used for the rest of the blessed dead (Rev 14:13), the rest commanded to the souls under the altar (Rev 6:11), and Daniel's rest until the end (Dan 12:13 via LXX). Rest = death; standing/resurrection = the next event.

Semantic categories: rest, refreshment, death-rest

Key verses: Rev 6:11, Rev 14:13

Relevance: The 'rest' vocabulary connects Rev 6:11, Rev 14:13, and Dan 12:13 — in all three, rest refers to the state of death before resurrection.

docs.title: H5956 — alam
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5956-alam.md

Occurrences: 33

Alam (to conceal/hide) — root of olam (H5769). The verb means 'to conceal, hide from sight.' Olam derives from this root, meaning 'time whose endpoint is hidden/concealed from view' — not 'time without an endpoint.' The etymological evidence supports subject-determined duration.

Semantic categories: concealment, hiddenness

Relevance: Etymological root of olam. The root meaning 'to conceal' indicates olam refers to time whose end is hidden — not time that has no end. This is the linguistic foundation for the nature-of-subject principle.

docs.title: H8438 — tola
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H8438-tôwlâʻ.md

Occurrences: 44

Tola (worm/maggot) — biological organism that acts on dead bodies. In Isa 66:24 and Mark 9:48, the worm acts on corpses (peger), not on living conscious beings. Maggots feed on dead flesh — they do not torment living people.

Semantic categories: biological organism, decomposition agent

Key verses: Isa 66:24

Relevance: The 'worm that dieth not' in Mark 9:48/Isa 66:24 is a biological organism feeding on corpses. This imagery describes post-mortem decomposition, not conscious torment.

docs.title: G2349 — thnetos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2349-thnetos.md

Occurrences: 6

Thnetos (mortal) — 6 NT occurrences. Describes the current state of human beings: mortal, subject to death. In 1 Cor 15:53, 'this mortal must put on immortality' — establishing that humans are currently mortal and need a transformation to become immortal.

Semantic categories: mortality, human condition

Key verses: 1 Cor 15:53, Rom 6:12

Relevance: Humans are described as thnetos (mortal). If mortal, they cannot exist forever unless given immortality. ECT requires inherent immortality the Bible does not teach.

docs.title: Classification Audit Trail
docs.text: This study is a synthesis compiling and cross-referencing classifications from 13 prior etc7 studies. The Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for each individual item were performed in the source studies by classifier subagents with actual parser tool output. This document compiles the verified results organized by the 8 ECT passages.

docs.title: E-items from the 8 ECT Passages
docs.text:
E1 (Rev 14:11) — "The smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night" — Classified: Neutral

Source: etc7-11-smoke-ascending-forever

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — basanismos (G929), torment vocabulary applied to beast-worshippers. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Beast-worshippers are human subjects described within an apocalyptic vision. PASS (borderline — subjects are human but within visionary framework).
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): basanismou (G929, Gen Sg M) in genitive chain "smoke of their torment" — smoke ascends, not necessarily the torment itself. anapausis (G372) "no rest day and night" — identical construction to Rev 4:8 (ceaseless praise). Grammar permits multiple readings. PASS (no single grammar issue forces failure, but ambiguity noted).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Apocalyptic vision — third angel's message within Revelation's seal/trumpet/bowl framework. FAIL.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 3 fail).
  • Step 3 Reclassification: Gate 3 fail — apocalyptic genre, not didactic. RC2: "An apocalyptic vision describes smoke ascending from tormented beast-worshippers." RC3: Apocalyptic depiction does not constitute didactic teaching about human fate. Neither V1 nor V2 applies at the didactic level.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails. Classification revised to Neutral.

E2 (Rev 20:10) — "And shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever" — Classified: Neutral

Source: etc7-12-tormented-forever

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — basanisthesontai (G928), torment vocabulary. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Three subjects: diabolos (devil — supernatural being, Rev 12:9), therion (beast — 7 heads/10 horns, Rev 13:1 — symbolic system), pseudoprophetes (false prophet — earth beast, Rev 13:11-17). None is a literal human being. FAIL.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Not reached (Gate 1 fail).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Apocalyptic vision. FAIL.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification: Gate 1 fail — all three subjects are non-human/symbolic. RC2: "An apocalyptic vision describes three non-human/symbolic entities tormented." RC3: Non-human entities' torment does not establish what happens to literal humans. Neither V1 nor V2 applies to human fate.
  • Result: Gate 1 and Gate 3 fail. Classification revised to Neutral.

E3 (Matt 25:46) — "And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal" — Classified: Neutral

Source: etc7-14-judgment-passages

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — kolasis (G2851) "punishment" — from kolazo "to curtail." Could be read as destruction-result. V2 — "everlasting punishment" could imply ongoing conscious experience. Both V1 and V2 potentially triggered.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Human subjects (goats in judgment parable). PASS (subjects are human within parabolic framework).
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): kolasin aionion (G2851 + G166, Acc Sg F) // zoen aionion (G2222 + G166, Acc Sg F) — identical grammatical construction. kolasis means punishment/penalty, NOT torment. Grammar permits both "everlasting punishment-as-process" and "everlasting punishment-as-result." FAIL — alternative parsing valid (both readings grammatically possible).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Parabolic — sheep/goats imagery (v.32 "as a shepherd divideth"). FAIL.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification: Gate 2 and Gate 3 fail. Both readings grammatically valid; parabolic genre. RC2: "A judgment parable states two outcomes: everlasting punishment and life eternal, using the same adjective." RC3: Neither V1 nor V2 exclusively applies — the observation is factual without position.
  • Result: Gates 2 and 3 fail. Classification: Neutral — the grammatical parallel is an observable fact both sides accept.

E4 (Mark 9:48 / Isa 66:24) — "Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched" — Classified: Neutral

Source: etc7-21-judgment-parables-imagery

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — fire and worm imagery applied to judgment subjects. Candidate: ECT (if subjects are conscious).
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Jesus quotes Isa 66:24. The OT source identifies subjects as peger (H6297) — corpses/dead bodies in ALL 24 OT uses. Isa 66:16-17 establishes the transgressors were slain and consumed BEFORE the viewing. Subjects are corpses. FAIL — subjects are dead, not living conscious beings.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Not reached for ECT classification (Gate 1 fail).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Jesus' direct teaching — didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification: Gate 1 fail — subjects are corpses per OT source text. RC2: "Undying worm and unquenchable fire act on corpses (peger) of transgressors who were already slain."
