Earnest, down payment, pledge. 3 NT occurrences: 2 Cor 1:22, 5:5, Eph 1:14. Loanword from Hebrew H6162. A commercial first installment guaranteeing full payment later. The Spirit IS the arrabon — a present foretaste guaranteeing the full inheritance (resurrection body).

Semantic categories: Spirit as God's pledge of completed redemption, OT background: material pledge

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:5, 2 Cor 1:22, Eph 1:14

Relevance: The arrabon metaphor in 2 Cor 5:5 confirms the eschatological framework: the Spirit is a present guarantee of a FUTURE completion. The full payment (resurrection body) has not yet been received.

docs.title: G360 — analyo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G360-analyo.md

Occurrences: 2

To break up, to loosen back, to depart. 2 NT uses: Luke 12:36 (master returning from a wedding) and Phil 1:23 (Paul's desire to depart). Military/nautical background: loosing from moorings, striking camp. The cognate noun analusis (G359) appears in 2 Tim 4:6.

Semantic categories: physical return/departure, departure from life (euphemism for death)

Key verses: Phil 1:23, Luke 12:36

Relevance: The departure verb in Phil 1:23. The metaphor pictures death as striking camp or unmooring — an unloosing. The aorist infinitive analysai presents departure as a complete event; the kai syn Christo einai that follows does not specify temporal relationship.

docs.title: G2349 — thnetos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2349-thnetos.md

Occurrences: 6

Mortal, subject to death. 6 NT occurrences, all Pauline. Used substantivally in 1 Cor 15:53-54 and 2 Cor 5:4 ('this mortal,' 'mortality'). Paired with athanasia as direct antonym. The shared vocabulary confirms both passages describe the same resurrection event.

Semantic categories: mortal body under sin, mortal body awaiting resurrection, mortal-to-immortal transformation, life manifested in mortal flesh

Key verses: 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54, 2 Cor 5:4, Rom 8:11

Relevance: Links 2 Cor 5:4 to 1 Cor 15:53-54. The substantival use 'this mortal' in both passages identifies the same transformation event.

docs.title: G110 — athanasia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G110-athanasia.md

Occurrences: 3

Immortality, deathlessness. Alpha-privative + thanatos. 3 NT uses: 1 Cor 15:53,54 (put on at resurrection), 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has it). Immortality is not inherently possessed by humans — it must be 'put on' (endyo) at the resurrection.

Semantic categories: eschatological transformation at resurrection, exclusive divine attribute

Key verses: 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54, 1 Tim 6:16

Relevance: The endyo+athanasia construction in 1 Cor 15:53-54 proves immortality is received at resurrection, not inherently possessed. God ALONE has immortality (1 Tim 6:16). If humans had immortal souls, this verse would be false.

docs.title: G3619 — oikodome
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3619-oikodomē.md

Occurrences: 18

Building, edification. 18 NT occurrences. In 2 Cor 5:1: the permanent 'building from God' contrasted with the temporary 'tent.' Physical structure + spiritual edification.

Semantic categories: physical structure, spiritual edification, church as building, apostolic authority for building up

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:1, 1 Cor 3:9, Eph 2:21

Relevance: The 'building of God' in 2 Cor 5:1 = the permanent resurrection body. The tent/building contrast captures the temporary/permanent, dissoluble/eternal duality.

docs.title: G3613 — oiketerion
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3613-oiketerion.md

Occurrences: 2

Dwelling-place, habitation. Only 2 NT uses: 2 Cor 5:2 (heavenly dwelling = resurrection body) and Jude 1:6 (angels' proper habitation). From oikeo (to dwell) + -terion (place suffix). Both uses describe a divinely assigned proper dwelling.

Semantic categories: heavenly/resurrection body, assigned spiritual domain

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:2, Jude 1:6

Relevance: The rare oiketerion in 2 Cor 5:2 identifies what believers groan to receive — their heavenly dwelling/habitation (the resurrection body). Its only parallel (Jude 1:6) confirms the 'proper dwelling' sense.

docs.title: G886 — acheiropoietos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G886-acheiropoietos.md

Occurrences: 3

Not made with hands. Alpha-privative + cheiropoietos. 3 NT uses: Mark 14:58 (temple Jesus would build), 2 Cor 5:1 (building from God), Col 2:11 (circumcision of Christ). All three describe divine vs. human origin.

Semantic categories: divine-origin structure, spiritual transformation

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:1, Mark 14:58, Col 2:11

Relevance: In 2 Cor 5:1, acheiropoieton characterizes the resurrection body as divine workmanship — not of human making. The Mark 14:58 parallel links the 'body-as-temple' to the 'body-as-building' in 2 Cor 5:1.

docs.title: G2106 — eudokeo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2106-eudokeo.md

Occurrences: 25

To think well of, to be pleased, to be willing. 25 NT occurrences. In 2 Cor 5:8: eudokoumen (V-PAI-1P, present active indicative) = 'we are willing/pleased.' Present tense expresses ongoing disposition, not a decisive act. Distinguished from thelo (general will) by its element of considered satisfaction.

Semantic categories: divine approval, divine sovereign pleasure, human willing/readiness, human pleasure/delight

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:8, Mat 3:17, 1 Thess 2:8

Relevance: In 2 Cor 5:8, eudokoumen is weaker than thelo — it means 'we are willing/content with' rather than 'we desire.' Paul is expressing willingness to accept death (if necessary) with confidence in resurrection, not eagerness for death.

docs.title: G2309 — thelo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2309-thelo.md

Occurrences: 211

To will, wish, desire, prefer. 211 NT occurrences. In 2 Cor 5:4: ou thelomen (V-PAI-1P, negated present active indicative) = 'we do NOT wish/want.' Paul explicitly negates the desire for ekdysasthai (being unclothed/death).

Semantic categories: personal desire, settled resolve, refusal (negated), divine sovereign choice

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:4

Relevance: The negated thelo in 2 Cor 5:4 is Paul's explicit statement of non-preference for death. If ou thelomen ekdysasthai means 'we do NOT want to be unclothed,' then Paul is NOT expressing a desire for death/disembodiment.

docs.title: G2837 — koimao
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2837-koimao.md

Occurrences: 19

To put to sleep, to fall asleep. 19 NT occurrences. Dominant as a euphemism for death: Acts 7:60, Acts 13:36, 1 Cor 15:6,18,20,51, 1 Thess 4:13-15. The sleep metaphor implies: (a) unconsciousness, (b) temporary state, (c) expected awakening/resurrection.

Semantic categories: literal sleep, death as sleep (euphemism), resurrection context

Key verses: 1 Thess 4:13-14, 1 Cor 15:6, 1 Cor 15:18, 1 Cor 15:51, Acts 7:60

Relevance: Paul's consistent vocabulary for death is 'sleep' (koimao). Sleep implies unconsciousness. When Paul describes the dead as 'asleep,' this determines how 'absent from the body' in 2 Cor 5:8 should be understood.

docs.title: G5590 — psyche
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5590-psyche.md

Occurrences: 105

Soul, life, self, person. From psycho (to breathe). 105 NT occurrences. LXX equivalent of nephesh (H5315). Semantically wide: inner self, physical life, person (counting), living creature, mind/will. Can die (Matt 10:28), be destroyed — NOT inherently immortal.

Semantic categories: inner self/emotions, physical life, person/individual, living creature, mind/will

Key verses: Matt 10:28, Rev 6:9

Relevance: The souls 'under the altar' in Rev 6:9 uses psyche in the 'person/life' sense, not as a detachable immortal substance. Matt 10:28 says God can DESTROY psyche — incompatible with inherent immortality.

docs.title: G4151 — pneuma
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4151-pneuma.md

Occurrences: 385

Spirit, breath, wind. From pneo (to blow). 385 NT occurrences. In 2 Cor 5:5, pneuma appears as the content of the arrabon — the Spirit IS the down payment. Pneuma in 'receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59) parallels Ecc 12:7 (spirit returns to God).

Semantic categories: Holy Spirit, human spirit, wind/breath, demonic spirits

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:5, Acts 7:59, 1 Thess 5:23

Relevance: The Spirit as arrabon in 2 Cor 5:5 is the guarantee of future bodily resurrection. The spirit returning to God at death (Ecc 12:7, Acts 7:59, Luke 23:46) does not prove conscious survival.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Eternal, everlasting, pertaining to the age(s). In 2 Cor 5:1: aionion qualifies the building from God as 'eternal in the heavens' — permanent, divine quality contrasted with the temporary earthly tent.

Semantic categories: eternal life, eternal punishment, eternal God/Spirit

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:1

Relevance: The 'eternal in the heavens' describes the resurrection body's permanence, contrasted with the dissoluble tent.

docs.title: G4983 — soma
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4983-soma.md

Occurrences: 146

Body. 146 NT occurrences. Paul's primary term for the physical frame. In 2 Cor 5:6,8,10: the soma is the current dwelling from which believers are 'absent from the Lord.' In Phil 3:21: the soma tes tapeinoseos (body of humiliation) will be changed.

Semantic categories: physical body, dead body, Christ's body, body under sin, body as temple, church as body, resurrection body

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:6, 2 Cor 5:8, 2 Cor 5:10, Phil 3:21, 1 Cor 15:35-44

Relevance: Paul does not view the body as a prison from which the soul escapes. The body is the arena of moral action (2 Cor 5:10) and the object of resurrection transformation (Phil 3:21).

docs.title: G861 — aphtharsia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G861-aphtharsia.md

Occurrences: 8

Incorruption, imperishability. Alpha-privative + phtheiro. 8 NT uses, all Pauline. Paired with athanasia in 1 Cor 15:53-54. Something 'put on' at resurrection, not presently possessed.

Semantic categories: resurrection transformation, object of aspiration, ethical purity

Key verses: 1 Cor 15:42, 1 Cor 15:50, 1 Cor 15:53, 1 Cor 15:54

Relevance: Parallel to athanasia — incorruption is received at resurrection. The corruptible/incorruptible pair in 1 Cor 15 uses the same conceptual framework as the tent/building pair in 2 Cor 5.

docs.title: G386 — anastasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G386-anastasis.md

Occurrences: 40

Resurrection, a standing up again. 40 unique verses. Paul's consistent hope — Phil 3:11 uses the compound exanastasis (G1815) for the resurrection of the dead.

Semantic categories: bodily resurrection, first/second resurrection

Key verses: Phil 3:11, 1 Cor 15:12-13, Acts 24:15

Relevance: Resurrection is Paul's stated hope. If conscious intermediate existence were the norm, resurrection would be anti-climactic — merely adding a body to an already-conscious spirit.

docs.title: G2222 — zoe
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2222-zoe.md

Occurrences: 134

Life. 134 NT occurrences. In 2 Cor 5:4: 'that mortality might be swallowed up of life (zoe).' Life is the agent that absorbs mortality — the resurrection life.

Semantic categories: eternal life, present spiritual life, physical life

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:4, John 11:25

Relevance: In 2 Cor 5:4, zoe is the force that swallows mortality — pointing to resurrection life, not a disembodied spirit-existence.

docs.title: G1131 — gymnos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1131-gymnos.md

Occurrences: 15

Naked, bare. 15 NT occurrences across 9 books. Physical nakedness (Matt 25:36, Acts 19:16), partially unclothed (Mark 14:51-52, John 21:7), bare/unadorned (1 Cor 15:37 'bare grain'), exposed before God (Heb 4:13), spiritual exposure/shame (2 Cor 5:3, Rev 3:17, Rev 16:15). In 2 Cor 5:3 the 'naked' state is what Paul hopes NOT to be found in — the death-state without a resurrection body.

Semantic categories: physical nakedness, partially unclothed, bare/unadorned, exposed before God, spiritual exposure/shame

Key verses: 2 Cor 5:3, 1 Cor 15:37, Rev 3:17, Rev 16:15

Relevance: In 2 Cor 5:3, gymnoi ('naked') is the undesirable state — being found without the resurrection body. In 1 Cor 15:37, gymnon ('bare') grain describes the seed sown before receiving its new body. Both uses identify the death-state-without-resurrection-body as the 'naked' condition Paul wants to avoid.

docs.title: Study: etc7-19 — 2 Corinthians 5: Intermediate State
docs.text: This document contains the full Tree 3/4 classification walkthroughs for every E-item classified as Cond. or ECT and every N-item. Each walkthrough was run mechanically using parser-verified grammatical data.

docs.title: E6 (Ecc 9:5) — "The dead know not any thing" — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — cessation vocabulary: "know not any thing" applied to the dead. The dead lack knowledge — a cessation-of-consciousness statement. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The dead" (hammethim, Qal participle of muth H4191) — literal dead human beings, not symbolic entities. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hebrew parsing: hammethim einam yodeim meumah — "the dead are-not knowing anything." yada H3045, Qal participle with negative particle ein. Plain negation — no alternative parsing. The statement is syntactically unambiguous: the dead do not know anything. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature — observational/didactic prose. Not parable, apocalyptic, or typological. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E7 (thoughts perish, Psa 146:4), E8 (no remembrance, Psa 6:5), E9 (dead go to silence, Psa 115:17), E22 (no knowledge in sheol, Ecc 9:10), E25 (grave cannot praise, Isa 38:18-19). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E7 (Psa 146:4) — "In that very day his thoughts perish" — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — cessation vocabulary: "thoughts perish" (abad H6). Applied to a dying person. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dying person whose spirit departs — a literal human being ("princes," mortal men, v.3). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hebrew parsing: eshtonotav (eshtonot H6250, hapax, "his thoughts/plans") abdu (abad H6, Qal perfect 3p, "perish"). bayyom hahu ("in that very day") — temporal marker. The subject (thoughts) perishes on the day of death. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of praise — poetic but didactic in its observational claim about death. The statement about thoughts perishing is presented as factual observation, not as apocalyptic symbolism or parable. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E6 (dead know nothing), E8 (no remembrance), E9 (silence), E22 (no knowledge in sheol). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E8 (Psa 6:5) — "In death there is no remembrance of thee" — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — cessation vocabulary: "no remembrance" applied to the dead. Cessation of memory/consciousness. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead in general — literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hebrew: ein zeker (H2143, "remembrance/memory") — plain negation of remembrance in death. bisheol ("in sheol/the grave"). No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of lament — David's prayer. The statement about death is presented as a factual basis for his appeal to God. Didactic/observational. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E6, E7, E9, E22, E25. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E9 (Psa 115:17) — "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — cessation vocabulary: "praise not," "silence" (dumah H1745). The dead are described as going into silence — cessation of activity. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "The dead" — literal dead human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hebrew: lo hamethim yehalelu-yah — "not the-dead praise-Yah." Plain negation of praise activity. dumah ("silence") — the destination of the dead. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Psalm of trust — observational/didactic statement about the dead. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E6, E7, E8, E22, E25. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E10 (1 Cor 15:18) — "They also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished" (conditional on no resurrection) — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — cessation/destruction vocabulary: "perished" (apolonto, from apollymi G622). Applied to deceased believers if there is no resurrection. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Believers who have died ("fallen asleep in Christ") — literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Greek: apolonto (V-2AMI-3P, aorist middle indicative of apollymi G622) = "they perished." The statement is conditional (part of Paul's hypothetical: "if Christ be not raised," v.17), but within that conditional, the assertion is plain — without resurrection, the dead have perished. The grammar is unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Epistle — direct theological argument. Didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E6-E9, E22, E25. The statement that without resurrection the dead have perished is consistent with death as cessation of existence. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E22 (Ecc 9:10) — "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave" — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — cessation vocabulary: "no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom" — four categories of conscious activity negated in sheol. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The dead in sheol — literal dead human beings ("whither thou goest"). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hebrew: ein maaseh wecheshbon wedaat wechokmah bisheol — plain negation of four types of activity in sheol. No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom literature — didactic/observational prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E6, E7, E8, E9, E25. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: E25 (Isa 38:18-19) — "The grave cannot praise thee, death can not celebrate thee" — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — cessation vocabulary: "cannot praise," "cannot celebrate," "cannot hope." Cessation of conscious activity in death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Those who go down to the pit / the dead — literal human beings. Hezekiah speaks of himself and all who die. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Hebrew: lo sheol todeka maveth tehalaleka — "not sheol praises-you, death celebrates-you." Plain negation. Hezekiah then contrasts: "the living, the living, he shall praise thee." No alternative parsing. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct speech by Hezekiah — prayer/testimony. Didactic content within narrative. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E6-E9, E22. No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: N1 — "Since Paul uses identical vocabulary (katapino G2666, thnetos G2349) in 2 Cor 5:4 and 1 Cor 15:54, both passages describe the same resurrection event" — Based on: E1 (2 Cor 5:4), E3 (1 Cor 15:53), E4 (1 Cor 15:54) — Candidate: Neutral
docs.text:
• Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree that katapothE (2 Cor 5:4) and KatepothE (1 Cor 15:54) are the same verb (katapino G2666), and thneton appears in both passages? YES — this is a verifiable grammatical fact. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion from the shared vocabulary? The shared vocabulary is a fact; whether it means both passages describe "the same event" or "similar but different events" could be debated. However, same author, same verb, same adjective, same conceptual framework — the conclusion that the same event is in view requires no interpretation beyond recognizing the vocabulary match. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the E-items? The E-items state what each verse says. The N-item identifies the vocabulary overlap and draws the connection. The "same event" conclusion follows directly from the vocabulary identity. PASS.
  • Gate 0 passes. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither destruction/cessation vocabulary (V1) nor conscious-ongoing-existence vocabulary (V2). This is a factual observation about vocabulary overlap. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

docs.title: N2 — "Paul's stated preference is transformation without death (ependysasthai), not death as a positive transition (ekdysasthai)" — Based on: E1 (2 Cor 5:4) — Candidate: Neutral
docs.text:
• Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree that ou thelomen ekdysasthai means Paul does not want to be unclothed, and all' ependysasthai means he wants to be clothed upon? YES — the lexical meanings are plain. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? Some ECT scholars argue Paul's non-preference for death in v.4 is qualified by his willingness in v.8, making death merely "second-best" rather than "not desired." However, the N-item states what v.4 says: Paul's stated preference is ependysasthai. This is lexically forced. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): The N-item restates the three-part preference structure of v.4 as a conclusion. No concept is added. PASS.
  • Gate 0 passes. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither V1 nor V2. This is about Paul's preference (transformation vs. death), not about destruction or conscious torment. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

docs.title: N3 — "The groaning in 2 Cor 5:2,4 is for bodily redemption, since the identical verb form (stenazomen) in Rom 8:23 groans for 'the redemption of our body'" — Based on: E5 (Rom 8:23), E1 (2 Cor 5:4) — Candidate: Neutral
docs.text:
• Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree that stenazomen in Rom 8:23 is for "the redemption of our body" and that the same verb form appears in 2 Cor 5:2,4? YES — grammatical fact. Would they agree the groaning in 2 Cor 5 is for the same object? An ECT scholar might argue the groaning in 2 Cor 5 has a different object (escape from the body, not bodily redemption). This is a borderline case — the conclusion requires accepting that same verb + same author + same topic = same object. A reasonable scholar might dispute this. BORDERLINE.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Choosing between "groaning for bodily redemption" and "groaning for release from the body" involves interpreting the object of the groaning in 2 Cor 5. The Romans passage is explicit; applying it to 2 Corinthians requires cross-referencing. This is #4a SIS (verified textual connection: same verb, same form, same author), not an arbitrary bridge. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): The connection is based on the shared vocabulary (stenazomen) between two passages by the same author. No external concept is added. PASS.
  • Gate 0: N-Test 1 is borderline. The universal agreement test is not clearly met — an ECT scholar could argue the groaning in 2 Cor 5 has a different object. However, the same verb, same form, same author, and same contextual topic (bodily transformation) make this a very strong connection. I will classify this as N with a note, since the connection is SIS-verified (#4a).
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither V1 nor V2. Factual observation about the object of groaning. NEUTRAL. Stop.
  • Result: Classification: Neutral stands.

docs.title: N4 — "Paul places being with the Lord at the parousia/resurrection, not at death" — Based on: E11 (1 Thess 4:17), E12 (2 Tim 4:8) — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree that 1 Thess 4:17 places being "ever with the Lord" at the resurrection/catching-up, and that 2 Tim 4:8 places the crown "at that day" (the parousia)? YES — these are textual facts. Would they agree that this means Paul places being with the Lord ONLY at the parousia? NO — an ECT scholar would say Paul teaches BOTH immediate post-death presence AND final eschatological presence, and these texts address the latter without excluding the former. FAIL.
  • N-Test 2: Since N-Test 1 fails, the item does not pass Gate 0.
  • N-Test 3: Not reached.
  • Gate 0 FAILS. N4 is reclassified as I-tier.
  • Reclassification: The claim that Paul places being with the Lord ONLY at the parousia requires the inference that 1 Thess 4:17 and 2 Tim 4:8 exhaust Paul's eschatological timeline. This is criterion #5 (systematizing) — an I-A inference if all components are from E/N tables.
  • Result: Reclassified to I-A, Cond. (systematizes E11 and E12 into a comprehensive timeline claim).

docs.title: N5 — "Death without resurrection means the end — deceased believers are not conscious anywhere" — Based on: E10 (1 Cor 15:18) — Candidate: Cond.
docs.text:
• Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would a scholar from the opposite position agree that "perished" (apolonto) in 1 Cor 15:18 means the dead have ceased to exist if there is no resurrection? An ECT scholar would argue that "perished" means "lost their hope" or "are in a state of spiritual ruin," not "ceased to exist." The meaning of apolonto is the point of dispute between the positions. FAIL.
  • N-Test 2: Since N-Test 1 fails, the item does not pass Gate 0.
  • N-Test 3: Not reached.
  • Gate 0 FAILS. N5 is reclassified as I-tier.
  • Reclassification: The claim requires choosing between two possible meanings of apolonto (G622) — "have ceased to exist" vs. "have been lost/ruined." This is criterion #2 (choosing between possible readings). The inference is text-derived (based on E10) but involves interpretation of the key verb. Both sides have textual support: the Cond. reading draws on the destruction sense of apollymi, while the ECT reading draws on the "lost" sense. This is I-B (competing evidence).
  • Result: Reclassified to I-B, Cond. (requires choosing between two meanings of apolonto; both sides can cite textual support).

docs.title: Conclusion: 2 Corinthians 5:1-8 and the Intermediate State
Question
docs.text: What does 2 Corinthians 5:1-8 teach about the intermediate state? Does "unclothed" (ekdysasthai) mean disembodied? What is Paul's actual preference and what does the clothing metaphor mean? Does this passage support conscious existence between death and resurrection, or is Paul expressing preference for resurrection without dying?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: 2 Corinthians 5:1-8 teaches about the resurrection body, not a conscious intermediate state. Paul's clothing metaphor contrasts the mortal body (tent) with the resurrection body (building from God), and his stated preference is transformation without death (ependysasthai, "to be clothed upon") rather than death (ekdysasthai, "to be unclothed"). The vocabulary of 2 Cor 5:4 (katapothE, thneton) is drawn from 1 Cor 15:54, linking both passages to the same resurrection event. The phrase "absent from the body and present with the Lord" (2 Cor 5:8) uses aorist infinitives connected by kai, which the grammar does not encode as temporally immediate — the temporal relationship must be determined from context. Paul's own clearer statements (1 Thess 4:17, 1 Cor 15:23, 2 Tim 4:8) consistently place being with the Lord at the resurrection/parousia.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Paul's Three-Part Preference (2 Corinthians 5:4) For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.

Mortality Swallowed at Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53-54) For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

Absent from Body, Present with Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8) We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.

Groaning for Bodily Redemption (Romans 8:23) And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.

Being with the Lord Placed at Resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17) For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.

The Dead Know Nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:5) For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.

Thoughts Perish at Death (Psalms 146:4) His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

Without Resurrection the Dead Have Perished (1 Corinthians 15:18) Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished.

Crown Given at the Parousia (2 Timothy 4:8) Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.

Resurrection Hope in the Same Chapter (2 Corinthians 4:14) Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you.

docs.title: The Literary Unit: 2 Corinthians 4:7-5:10
docs.text:
The clothing metaphor of 2 Corinthians 5 does not begin at the chapter boundary. The argument runs continuously from 2 Cor 4:7 through 5:10. Paul's flow of thought proceeds through a series of connected contrasts:

  • Treasure in earthen vessels (4:7) — the mortal body as a fragile container
  • Bearing the dying of Jesus in the body (4:10-11) — present suffering in mortal flesh (thnete sarki, using the same thnetos adjective that appears in 5:4)
  • Resurrection as the explicit hope (4:14) — "he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also" — stated before the clothing metaphor begins
  • Outward man perishing, inward man renewed (4:16) — the perishing outward man IS the tent being dissolved in 5:1
  • Temporal affliction vs. eternal glory (4:17-18) — the temporal/eternal contrast that flows directly into the tent/building contrast of 5:1
  • Earthly tent vs. heavenly building (5:1) — the same temporal/eternal dualism applied to bodies
  • Groaning, clothing metaphor, purpose clause (5:2-4) — the desire for transformation
  • Spirit as guarantee (5:5) — the arrabon ensuring future completion
  • Confidence despite present arrangement (5:6-8) — willingness to accept either outcome
  • Judgment seat of Christ (5:9-10) — final accountability at the future judgment

The resurrection framework established in 4:14 governs everything that follows. Paul does not shift from resurrection hope to intermediate-state teaching at the chapter boundary. The same argument continues.

docs.title: The Vocabulary Link Between 2 Corinthians 5:4 and 1 Corinthians 15:54
docs.text:
The shared vocabulary between these two passages is the single most important piece of evidence for understanding 2 Cor 5:4. Paul uses:

  • katapino (G2666): In 2 Cor 5:4 as katapothE (aorist passive subjunctive, "might be swallowed up") and in 1 Cor 15:54 as KatepothE (aorist passive indicative, "was swallowed up"). Same verb, same voice, same person/number — differing only in mood. The subjunctive appears in a purpose clause; the indicative appears in a quotation from Isa 25:8.
  • thnetos (G2349): In 2 Cor 5:4 as thneton ("mortality/the mortal") and in 1 Cor 15:53 as thneton ("this mortal"). The identical substantival form in both passages.
  • endyo/ependyomai (G1746/G1902): In 1 Cor 15:53-54, endysasthai ("to put on") describes putting on immortality. In 2 Cor 5:2,4, the intensified compound ependysasthai ("to be clothed upon") describes the same acquisition but with the epi- prefix indicating superimposition — putting the new body on top of the old.

The Isa 25:8 source text ("He will swallow up death in victory") is quoted in 1 Cor 15:54 and alluded to in 2 Cor 5:4. Both passages look to the same eschatological event. The purpose clause of 2 Cor 5:4 ("that mortality might be swallowed up of life") is Paul's restatement of the Isaianic prophecy he explicitly quotes in 1 Cor 15:54.

docs.title: Paul's Three-Part Preference Structure
docs.text:
2 Corinthians 5:4 contains Paul's explicit statement of his preference, structured in three parts:

  1. What Paul does NOT want: ou thelomen ekdysasthai — "we do not wish to be unclothed." The negated present active indicative of thelo (G2309, 211 NT occurrences, expressing personal desire) paired with the aorist middle infinitive of ekdyo (G1562, "to strip/unclothe"). Every other NT use of ekdyo involves violent stripping: soldiers stripping Jesus (Matt 27:28,31; Mark 15:20), thieves stripping a traveler (Luke 10:30). Paul explicitly rejects this state.

  2. What Paul DOES want: all' ependysasthai — "but to be clothed upon." The adversative alla establishes the contrast. Ependyomai (G1902) is Paul's unique compound verb, appearing only here and 2 Cor 5:2 in the NT. The epi- prefix means "upon/over," indicating the resurrection body placed ON TOP of the mortal body — transformation without passing through death. This is the exact equivalent of "we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed" (1 Cor 15:51).

  3. The purpose: hina katapothE to thneton hypo tes zoes — "that mortality might be swallowed up by life." The purpose clause uses the vocabulary from 1 Cor 15:54 and Isa 25:8. The goal is the defeat of mortality through the reception of resurrection life.

This three-part structure means Paul's first preference is transformation at the parousia (being alive when Christ returns), not death. His willingness to accept death (expressed in v.8 with eudokoumen, G2106, a weaker term than thelo) is a secondary acceptance — he is willing to accept death because he is confident in the resurrection outcome, not because death itself is desirable.

docs.title: The Clothing Verb Grid
docs.text:
Three verbs form a deliberate grid in 2 Corinthians 5:

  • endyo (G1746, 31 NT occurrences): the base clothing verb. Every Pauline use describes acquisition — putting on something not previously possessed. Put on Christ (Rom 13:14, Gal 3:27), put on the new man (Eph 4:24), put on the armor of God (Eph 6:11), put on immortality (1 Cor 15:53-54). The endyo metaphor demands that immortality is received at resurrection, not revealed as something already present.
  • ekdyo (G1562, 5 NT verses): to strip, unclothe. Every Synoptic use involves violent stripping. Paul's sole use (2 Cor 5:4) is negated — he does NOT want this.
  • ependyomai (G1902, 2 NT occurrences): Paul's unique compound (epi + endyo). Only in 2 Cor 5:2,4. The epi- prefix indicates superimposition — the new on top of the old. Paul's stated preference.

The clothing metaphor throughout Paul's letters consistently describes acquisition: something received from outside, not something uncovered from within. Immortality is "put on" (endyo, 1 Cor 15:53-54), not released. This is inconsistent with the view that the soul is inherently immortal and merely freed from the body at death.

docs.title: The Tent/Building Architectural Contrast
docs.text:
The architectural metaphors in 2 Cor 5:1-2 describe two types of embodiment:

  • skenos (G4636, 2 NT occurrences): the tent — temporary, collapsible, earthly. Used only in 2 Cor 5:1,4. The cognate skenoma (G4638) appears in 2 Pet 1:13-14 for Peter's body. The OT background includes Hezekiah's lament: "mine age is removed from me as a shepherd's tent" (Isa 38:12).
  • oikodome (G3619): the building — permanent, constructed by God, eternal in the heavens.
  • acheiropoietos (G886, 3 NT occurrences): "not made with hands" — divine origin vs. human handiwork. Also in Mark 14:58 for the temple Jesus would rebuild (his resurrection body, John 2:21).
  • oiketerion (G3613, 2 NT occurrences): "dwelling/habitation." Only here and Jude 1:6. In Jude, the proper habitation that fallen angels abandoned. Here, the heavenly dwelling believers desire — their resurrection body.

These metaphors describe two bodies (mortal and resurrection), not two states of existence (embodied and disembodied). The passage does not describe what happens between the dissolution of the tent and the reception of the building. It describes the contrast between the two, and Paul's desire to transition directly from one to the other (ependysasthai) without an interval.

docs.title: The Aorist Infinitives in 2 Corinthians 5:8
docs.text:
The key construction in v.8 is: ekdemesai ek tou somatos kai endemesai pros ton Kyrion — "to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord." Both ekdemesai (G1553, V-AAN) and endemesai (G1736, V-AAN) are aorist active infinitives connected by kai.

The grammar reference on aorist infinitive temporal relationships, generated from NT-wide parser data, confirms that kai between two aorist infinitives does NOT encode temporal sequence. The construction is compatible with: - Sequential actions (e.g., Matt 8:21 "to go and bury") - Simultaneous actions (e.g., 1 Thess 3:2 "to establish and to comfort") - Comprehensive pairing (e.g., Jas 4:12 "to save and to destroy")

Greek marks explicit temporal sequence with constructions like meta to + infinitive ("after") or pro tou + infinitive ("before"). When these markers are absent and bare kai connects two aorist infinitives, temporal sequence must be inferred from context, not from the grammar.

The claim that 2 Cor 5:8 teaches immediate temporal sequence between departure from the body and presence with the Lord requires importing temporal immediacy from outside the grammar. The grammar itself is neutral on timing.

docs.title: The Philippians 1:23 Parallel
docs.text:
Phil 1:23 presents the same structure: eis to analysai kai syn Christo einai — "unto the departing and being with Christ." The construction pairs an aorist active infinitive (analysai, G360, "to depart") with a present active infinitive (einai, G1510, "to be"). The mixed tense pattern is noteworthy: the departure is perfective (complete event), the being-with-Christ is imperfective (ongoing state).

The same-letter context interprets this verse: - Phil 3:11: Paul hopes to "attain unto the resurrection of the dead" (exanastasin, G1815). If Paul already expected conscious presence with Christ immediately at death, why would resurrection be something he hopes to "attain"? - Phil 3:20-21: "We look for the Saviour... who shall change (metaschEmatisei, G3345) our vile body." The mechanism is bodily transformation — the same concept as ependysasthai in 2 Cor 5:4.

docs.title: The Subjective-Instantaneity Model
docs.text:
The model that reconciles 2 Cor 5:8 and Phil 1:23 with the rest of Paul's eschatology: if death is unconsciousness (as the OT consistently states — Ecc 9:5, Psa 146:4, Psa 6:5, Psa 115:17, Ecc 9:10), then from the dead person's subjective perspective, the next conscious moment after death IS the resurrection and being with Christ. There is no subjective interval. Paul can speak of departure from the body and presence with the Lord as a single complex event because from the experiential standpoint of the person who dies, they are. The objective time between death and resurrection (which may span millennia) is subjectively instantaneous because the dead person experiences no passage of time.

This model does not require adding anything to the text. It requires only the OT teaching on unconscious death (which Paul, educated in the Hebrew Scriptures, would have known) combined with the NT teaching on future resurrection (which Paul explicitly affirms in 1 Cor 15, 1 Thess 4, Phil 3, 2 Tim 4).

docs.title: The Spirit as Guarantee (Arrabon)
docs.text:
The arrabon (G728, "earnest/deposit") of the Spirit in 2 Cor 5:5 is a commercial metaphor: a first installment that legally obligates the full payment. The full payment is the resurrection body. Three NT occurrences establish the eschatological function: - 2 Cor 1:22: God sealed believers and gave the arrabon of the Spirit - 2 Cor 5:5: God prepared believers for transformation and gave the arrabon of the Spirit - Eph 1:14: the Spirit is arrabon of the inheritance "until the redemption of the purchased possession" — the "until" (eis) marks a future terminus

The parallel metaphor aparche ("firstfruits," G536) in Rom 8:23 functions identically: the Spirit is the firstfruits of the full harvest (bodily redemption). The object of the groaning in Rom 8:23 is explicitly stated: "the redemption of our body" (ten apolutrosin tou somatos). Since the same verb form (stenazomen, G4727) appears in 2 Cor 5:2,4, the object of groaning in 2 Cor 5 is defined by the same-author parallel in Romans: bodily redemption, not death or disembodiment.

docs.title: Paul's Eschatological Timing
docs.text:
Paul's clearer statements about WHEN believers will be with the Lord are consistent across his letters:

  • 1 Thess 4:16-17 (earliest letter): The dead rise first, the living are caught up, "and so (houtos) shall we ever be with the Lord." The houtos ("in this way") specifies the mechanism: being with the Lord comes through resurrection and catching-up, not through death.
  • 1 Cor 15:23 (mid-career): Resurrection occurs "at his coming" (en te parousia autou).
  • 2 Tim 4:8 (final letter): Paul's crown of righteousness given "at that day" (en ekeine te hemera) — the day of Christ's epiphaneia. Even facing imminent death, Paul locates the reward at the parousia.
  • Phil 3:11,20-21 (same letter as Phil 1:23): Paul aspires to "the resurrection of the dead" and looks for the Saviour who will transform his body.

Not one of these clear, contextually unambiguous statements places being with the Lord at the moment of death. Every one places it at the resurrection/parousia. The hermeneutical principle of Scripture interpreting Scripture (SIS) requires that these plain statements govern the reading of the ambiguous ones (2 Cor 5:8, Phil 1:23).

docs.title: The OT Framework: Death as Unconsciousness
docs.text:
Paul was educated within the OT framework where death means the cessation of consciousness. The OT testimony spans multiple authors, genres, and centuries:

  • Solomon (Ecc 9:5): "The dead know not any thing." (Ecc 9:10): No work, device, knowledge, or wisdom in sheol.
  • David (Psa 6:5): No remembrance in death. (Psa 115:17): The dead go to silence. (Psa 88:10-12): Sheol is "the land of forgetfulness."
  • Hezekiah (Isa 38:18-19): The grave cannot praise; death cannot celebrate. Only the living praise.
  • Job (14:12-14): The dead lie down, do not rise till the heavens are no more. Job waits for his "change" (resurrection).
  • Daniel (12:2): The dead "sleep in the dust" and will "awake."

This cross-author, cross-genre, cross-century consistency establishes the interpretive context within which Paul writes. His "absent from the body" language should be read within this framework, not against it.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence Passages
docs.text:
Several passages are cited in support of a conscious intermediate state. Each requires genre, grammar, or context analysis:

Revelation 6:9-11 (souls under the altar): Apocalyptic genre using symbolism. The "souls" are under the altar — the location where sacrificial blood was poured (Lev 4:7). Abel's blood "cries out" from the ground (Gen 4:10) without implying Abel is conscious. The altar itself speaks in Rev 16:7. The souls are told to "rest" — consistent with the sleep metaphor.

Luke 23:43 (today in paradise): Greek has no punctuation. The placement of "today" (semeron) is grammatically ambiguous. Jesus had not ascended to the Father by Sunday (John 20:17), making the standard punctuation ("today you will be with me in paradise") problematic for its proponents. The Semitic pattern "I say unto you today" is well-attested in Deuteronomy.

Luke 20:38 (God of the living): The context is about resurrection (vv.35-36), not the intermediate state. Jesus argues that God's covenant faithfulness guarantees future resurrection. "All live unto him" means "all are alive in his purpose/plan," not "all are currently conscious."

Acts 2:34 and Heb 11:39-40: These are not counter-evidence — they explicitly support the position that the dead are not in heaven. David has not ascended. The OT faithful have not received the promise. These texts directly contradict the claim of conscious heavenly existence between death and resurrection.

docs.title: The Spirit-Commitment Pattern
docs.text:
Three instances of committing one's spirit at death establish a pattern: 1. Jesus committed his spirit to the Father on Friday (Luke 23:46) but had "not yet ascended" by Sunday (John 20:17). 2. Stephen committed his spirit to Jesus (Acts 7:59) and then "fell asleep" (Acts 7:60, ekoimEthE, G2837). 3. Ecc 12:7: The spirit returns to God who gave it — reversing the Gen 2:7 creation formula.

Since committing one's spirit to God did not result in immediate conscious presence even for Jesus himself, it cannot be used as proof of conscious intermediate existence for believers.

docs.title: Key Findings That Affect Interpretation
docs.text:
ependyomai (G1902): 2 occurrences, both in 2 Cor 5:2,4. Paul's unique compound verb: epi (upon) + endyo (clothe). The epi- prefix means superimposition — putting the new body on top of the old without removing the old first. This is Paul's stated preference: transformation without death. The word itself eliminates the ECT reading that Paul views death as a desirable transition.

ekdyo (G1562): 5 NT verses. Every Synoptic use involves violent stripping. Paul says he does NOT want this.

endyo (G1746): 31 NT occurrences. Every Pauline use describes acquisition of something not previously possessed. Immortality is "put on" at resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54), not revealed.

katapino (G2666): 7 NT occurrences. Links 2 Cor 5:4 (katapothE, subjunctive) to 1 Cor 15:54 (KatepothE, indicative) and Isa 25:8 (bala H1104). Same verb, same event — the eschatological defeat of death.

stenazo (G4727): 6 NT occurrences. Identical form (stenazomen, V-PAI-1P) in 2 Cor 5:2,4 and Rom 8:23. In Romans, the groaning is explicitly for "the redemption of our body."

arrabon (G728): 3 NT occurrences. Commercial down-payment guaranteeing full payment. The Spirit is the present guarantee of the future resurrection body.

eudokeo (G2106): 25 NT occurrences. In 2 Cor 5:8: "we are willing/pleased" — weaker than thelo (G2309). Expresses settled willingness, not eager desire. Paul is willing to accept death, not eager for it.

koimao (G2837): 19 NT occurrences. Paul's consistent vocabulary for death is "sleep," implying unconsciousness and expected awakening.

docs.title: 2 Corinthians 5:8
docs.text: The natural English reading suggests temporal immediacy between departure from the body and presence with the Lord. Three factors qualify this reading: (1) the grammar (kai between aorist infinitives) does not encode temporal sequence; (2) Paul's own clearer statements consistently place being with the Lord at the resurrection; (3) the subjective-instantaneity model explains the language without requiring a conscious intermediate state.

docs.title: Philippians 1:23
docs.text: The same structure as 2 Cor 5:8. The same-letter context (Phil 3:11, 3:20-21) points to resurrection as Paul's ultimate hope. The mixed tense pattern (aorist analysai + present einai) does not require temporal immediacy.

docs.title: 2 Corinthians 5:6 — "At Home in the Body, Absent from the Lord"
docs.text: The present-tense participles describe the current state of embodied life. The "absence" is epistemological (faith vs. sight, v.7), not spatial. This does not describe a conscious disembodied state.

docs.title: Necessary Implications
docs.text: # Necessary Implication Based on Why it is unavoidable Position Master ID N1 The vocabulary overlap (katapino, thnetos) between 2 Cor 5:4 and 1 Cor 15:54 identifies both passages as referring to the same resurrection event E1, E3, E4 Same author, same verb, same adjective, same conceptual framework — the vocabulary match is verifiable and both sides must acknowledge it Neutral N063 N2 Paul's stated preference is transformation without death (ependysasthai), not death as a positive transition E1 The three-part structure of 2 Cor 5:4 (NOT X / BUT Y / PURPOSE Z) is syntactically plain — negation, adversative, purpose clause Neutral N064 N3 The groaning in 2 Cor 5:2,4 (stenazomen) is for bodily redemption, since the identical form in Rom 8:23 groans for "the redemption of our body" E5, E1 Same verb, same form, same author, same topic — SIS-verified connection (#4a: shared vocabulary) Neutral N065

docs.title: Inferences
docs.text: # Claim Type Position What the Bible actually says Why this is an inference Criteria Master ID I1 Paul places being with the Lord exclusively at the parousia/resurrection, not at death I-A Cond. E11: "so shall we ever be with the Lord" at the resurrection sequence (1 Thess 4:17). E12: crown given "at that day" (2 Tim 4:8). E17: Paul aspires to "the resurrection of the dead" (Phil 3:11). All Pauline passages that specify timing place the event at the parousia. No single verse says being with the Lord occurs ONLY at the parousia. The claim systematizes multiple texts into a comprehensive timeline. #5 (systematizing) I077 I2 The "absent from the body / present with the Lord" in 2 Cor 5:8 refers to the resurrection, not to a conscious intermediate state I-B Cond. E15: Paul is willing to be absent from body and present with Lord (2 Cor 5:8). E11: Being with the Lord placed at resurrection (1 Thess 4:17). E12: Crown at the parousia (2 Tim 4:8). E6-E9, E22, E25: OT death = unconsciousness. AGAINST: E15 and E16 express preference for departure, and the natural English reading implies immediacy. Both sides can cite Paul's own words. The Cond. side appeals to the clearer resurrection statements and OT death-state testimony. The ECT side appeals to the surface reading of 2 Cor 5:8 and Phil 1:23. The grammar (aorist inf. + kai + aorist inf.) does not determine the temporal relationship. #2 (choosing between readings), #4b (cross-referencing without proved connection between timing and mechanism) I078 I3 Paul teaches that death is unconsciousness, and the dead person's next conscious experience is the resurrection I-A Cond. E6: dead know nothing (Ecc 9:5). E7: thoughts perish (Psa 146:4). E8: no remembrance in death (Psa 6:5). E9: dead go to silence (Psa 115:17). E22: no knowledge in sheol (Ecc 9:10). E21: "we shall not all sleep" — death as sleep (1 Cor 15:51). E24: Stephen "fell asleep" (Acts 7:60). E10: without resurrection the dead have perished (1 Cor 15:18). The claim systematizes these into a comprehensive doctrine. No single verse states "the dead person's next conscious experience is the resurrection." This combines the OT unconsciousness testimony with the NT resurrection timing to produce the subjective-instantaneity model. #5 (systematizing) I020 I4 2 Cor 5:8 and Phil 1:23 teach immediate conscious presence with Christ at death I-B ECT E15: Paul is willing to be absent from body and present with Lord (2 Cor 5:8). E16: Paul desires to depart and be with Christ (Phil 1:23). The surface reading of both texts implies temporal immediacy. AGAINST: E6-E9, E22, E25: OT unconsciousness. E11, E12: timing at parousia. Grammar: kai between aorist infinitives does not encode temporal sequence. Both sides cite Paul's own words. The ECT side appeals to the natural reading of the text. The Cond. side appeals to grammar (aorist infinitives + kai = temporally neutral), clearer same-author statements, and the OT framework. The grammar allows both readings, so choosing between them requires interpretation. #2 (choosing between readings) I004 I5 The "souls under the altar" in Rev 6:9-11 prove conscious existence of the dead I-D ECT Rev 6:9-11 depicts souls under the altar crying out. The passage is apocalyptic genre. Gen 4:10: Abel's blood cries out without implying consciousness. Rev 16:7: the altar itself speaks. Taking the apocalyptic symbolism as literal teaching about the intermediate state requires overriding the genre classification and ignoring the OT precedent (Gen 4:10). The E-items on OT unconsciousness (E6-E9, E22, E25) must be qualified or limited for this reading to stand. #3 (external framework — literal reading of apocalyptic imagery), overrides E6-E9 I062 I6 Luke 23:43 proves the thief was consciously in paradise with Jesus on the day of crucifixion I-D ECT Luke 23:43: "Verily I say unto thee, Today shalt thou be with me in paradise." The placement of "today" depends on editorial punctuation (Greek has none). E23: Jesus had not ascended to the Father by Sunday (John 20:17). The Semitic "I say unto you today" pattern is attested (Deut 4:26, 6:6, 8:19, 30:18). The reading requires editorial punctuation not present in the Greek, and it conflicts with E23 (Jesus not yet ascended). The alternative reading ("I say unto you today, you will be with me in paradise") is grammatically valid and consistent with E23. #2 (choosing punctuation placement), overrides E23 I079 I7 The dead are unconscious, therefore 2 Cor 5:8 describes the subjective experience of the dead person for whom the next moment of consciousness after death is the resurrection I-A Cond. E6-E9, E22, E25: OT texts on death as unconsciousness. E11: being with Lord at resurrection (1 Thess 4:17). E15: willing to be absent from body and present with Lord (2 Cor 5:8). The subjective-instantaneity model combines these: if death = no consciousness, then the dead person's next experience = resurrection. No verse explicitly states "the dead person's next conscious experience is the resurrection." The model systematizes the OT unconsciousness data with the NT resurrection timeline to explain 2 Cor 5:8. All components are from E/N tables. #5 (systematizing) I080

docs.title: I-B Resolution: I2 — Does "absent from body / present with Lord" (2 Cor 5:8) refer to resurrection or to a conscious intermediate state?
docs.text:
Step 1 — Tension: - FOR (Cond. — refers to resurrection): E11 (1 Thess 4:17: being with Lord at resurrection), E12 (2 Tim 4:8: crown at parousia), E17 (Phil 3:11: aspires to resurrection), E6-E9, E22, E25 (OT unconsciousness), N1 (vocabulary link to 1 Cor 15:54), N2 (Paul's preference is transformation not death), N3 (groaning is for bodily redemption) - AGAINST (ECT — refers to immediate post-death presence): E15 (2 Cor 5:8: willing to be absent from body and present with Lord), E16 (Phil 1:23: depart and be with Christ)

Step 2 — Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E11 (1 Thess 4:17) Plain Directly addresses WHEN being with the Lord occurs — at the resurrection. Uses houtos ("in this way") to specify the mechanism. E12 (2 Tim 4:8) Plain Directly states the crown is given "at that day" — the parousia. Even facing death, Paul's timing is future. E17 (Phil 3:11) Contextually Clear Same letter as Phil 1:23. Paul's hope is "the resurrection of the dead." Requires recognizing same-letter context. E6 (Ecc 9:5) Plain "The dead know not any thing." Direct statement about the state of the dead. E7 (Psa 146:4) Plain "In that very day his thoughts perish." Direct statement about cessation of consciousness at death. E15 (2 Cor 5:8) Ambiguous Paul expresses willingness to be absent from body and present with Lord. The temporal relationship between the two is not specified by the grammar (aorist inf. + kai + aorist inf. = temporally neutral). Could be read as immediate or as ultimate outcome. E16 (Phil 1:23) Ambiguous Paul desires to depart and be with Christ. Same grammatical pattern (aorist inf. + kai + present inf.). Same-letter context (Phil 3:11, 3:20-21) points to resurrection, but the verse itself does not specify timing. N1 Plain Vocabulary overlap between 2 Cor 5:4 and 1 Cor 15:54 is verifiable. N2 Plain The three-part preference structure of 2 Cor 5:4 is syntactically unambiguous.

Step 3 — Weight: The FOR side has multiple Plain statements (E11, E12, E6, E7, N1, N2) plus Contextually Clear (E17). The AGAINST side has two Ambiguous statements (E15, E16). Plain statements outweigh Ambiguous ones.

Step 4 — SIS Application: Plain statements determine the reading of ambiguous ones. E11 (being with the Lord at resurrection, Plain) and E12 (crown at parousia, Plain) govern the reading of E15 (absent from body / present with Lord, Ambiguous) and E16 (depart and be with Christ, Ambiguous). The clear passages specify the timing; the ambiguous ones do not contradict this timing but are compatible with it when read through the subjective-instantaneity model.

Step 5 — Resolution: Strong toward Cond. Multiple Plain statements on the Cond. side (E11, E12, E6, E7, N1, N2), including same-author statements that directly address timing. Only Ambiguous statements on the ECT side (E15, E16). The plain passages govern the ambiguous.

docs.title: I-B Resolution: I4 — Do 2 Cor 5:8 and Phil 1:23 teach immediate conscious presence with Christ at death?
docs.text:
Step 1 — Tension: - FOR (ECT — immediate presence): E15 (2 Cor 5:8: willing to be absent and present), E16 (Phil 1:23: depart and be with Christ) - AGAINST (Cond. — not immediate): E11 (being with Lord at resurrection), E12 (crown at parousia), E6-E9 (OT unconsciousness), E22, E25, E23 (Jesus not yet ascended), Grammar reference (aorist inf. + kai = temporally neutral)

Step 2 — Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E15 (2 Cor 5:8) Ambiguous The grammar does not encode temporal immediacy. The verse expresses willingness; timing is unspecified. E16 (Phil 1:23) Ambiguous Same grammatical indeterminacy. Same-letter context points to resurrection. E11 (1 Thess 4:17) Plain Directly addresses timing. E12 (2 Tim 4:8) Plain Directly addresses timing. E6 (Ecc 9:5) Plain Direct statement on the state of the dead. E23 (Luke 23:46 + John 20:17) Contextually Clear Requires connecting two verses by the same author (Luke) about the same person (Jesus).

Step 3 — Weight: FOR (ECT): Two Ambiguous items. AGAINST (Cond.): Multiple Plain items, plus Contextually Clear items.

Step 4 — SIS Application: Plain statements govern ambiguous ones. The same principle as I2 applies.

Step 5 — Resolution: Strong toward Cond. Same analysis as I2. The ECT reading of 2 Cor 5:8 and Phil 1:23 requires importing temporal immediacy that the grammar does not contain, against the weight of Paul's own clearer statements.

docs.title: I-B Resolution: Former N5 (reclassified) — Does "perished" (apolonto) in 1 Cor 15:18 mean the dead ceased to exist or merely "were lost/ruined"?
docs.text:
Step 1 — Tension: - FOR (Cond. — ceased to exist): E10 (1 Cor 15:18: "perished"), E6-E9 (OT unconsciousness testimony), E10 in context of 1 Cor 15:19 ("if in this life only we have hope, we are most miserable") - AGAINST (ECT — spiritual ruin, not cessation): The verb apollymi (G622) has a range from "destroy" to "lose/ruin" — the "lost sheep" sense (Luke 15:4) vs. the "destroy soul and body" sense (Matt 10:28)

Step 2 — Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E10 (1 Cor 15:18) Contextually Clear The argument's logic requires that without resurrection, the dead are in a hopeless state — Paul's conclusion is "most miserable" (v.19). Whether "perished" means cessation or spiritual loss, the logic requires that resurrection is the decisive factor, not intermediate consciousness. E6 (Ecc 9:5) Plain Direct statement: dead know nothing.

Step 3 — Weight: The FOR side has the contextual argument (resurrection-or-nothing logic) plus the OT unconsciousness data. The AGAINST side has the lexical range of apollymi but no E/N statement supporting the "spiritual ruin" reading in this specific context.

Step 4 — SIS Application: The contextual logic of 1 Cor 15:17-19 governs: "if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain... then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished... if in this life only we have hope, we are most miserable." The argument requires that without resurrection, hope is limited to this life. If the dead were already consciously with Christ, Paul could not say hope is limited to this life even without resurrection.

Step 5 — Resolution: Moderate toward Cond. The contextual logic favors the Cond. reading but the lexical range of apollymi prevents a Strong resolution.

docs.title: Classification Audit Trail
docs.text: Full Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for every positional E-item and every N-item are documented in CLASSIFICATIONS.md. Two N-items (former N4 and N5) were reclassified during Gate 0 testing: N4 became I1 (I-A, Cond.) and N5 was absorbed into the I-B resolution analysis.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies)
docs.text:
• The dead do not know anything (Ecc 9:5), their thoughts perish (Psa 146:4), there is no remembrance or praise in death (Psa 6:5, 115:17, Isa 38:18-19), and there is no work, knowledge, or wisdom in sheol (Ecc 9:10).
  • Paul's stated preference in 2 Cor 5:4 is transformation without death (ependysasthai), not death/disembodiment (ekdysasthai).
  • The vocabulary of 2 Cor 5:4 (katapino, thnetos) matches 1 Cor 15:54, linking both passages to the same resurrection event.
  • The groaning in 2 Cor 5:2,4 uses the identical verb form (stenazomen) as Rom 8:23, where the groaning is explicitly for "the redemption of our body."
  • Paul's crown is given "at that day" (2 Tim 4:8) — the parousia.
  • Being "ever with the Lord" follows the resurrection/catching-up sequence (1 Thess 4:17).
  • David has not ascended to heaven (Acts 2:34). The OT faithful have not received the promise (Heb 11:39-40).
  • Immortality is "put on" at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54), not inherently possessed. God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16).
  • The grammar of 2 Cor 5:8 (aorist infinitive + kai + aorist infinitive) does not encode temporal immediacy between departure from the body and presence with the Lord.

docs.title: What CANNOT Be Said (not explicitly stated or necessarily implied by Scripture)
docs.text:
• Scripture does not explicitly state that 2 Cor 5:8 describes temporal immediacy between death and being with the Lord. The grammar is neutral on timing.
  • Scripture does not explicitly state that 2 Cor 5:8 describes the resurrection. This is an inference (I-B) supported by vocabulary links and clearer same-author statements, but no verse says "absent from the body means the resurrection."
  • Scripture does not explicitly define the intermediate state as either conscious or unconscious using a single unambiguous didactic statement. The OT unconsciousness testimony is explicit; the NT "depart and be with Christ" language is grammatically ambiguous.
  • Scripture does not explicitly state the subjective-instantaneity model. It is an inference (I-A) that systematizes the OT unconsciousness data with the NT resurrection timeline.
  • Neither side can claim that Paul definitively settled the intermediate state question in 2 Cor 5:1-8. The passage is about the resurrection body, not the intermediate state.

docs.title: Tally Summary
docs.text:
• Explicit statements: 26
  • Cond.: 7 (E6, E7, E8, E9, E10, E22, E25)
  • ECT: 0
  • Neutral: 19 (E1, E2, E3, E4, E5, E11, E12, E13, E14, E15, E16, E17, E18, E19, E20, E21, E23, E24, E26)
  • Necessary implications: 3
  • Cond.: 0
  • ECT: 0
  • Neutral: 3 (N1, N2, N3)
  • Inferences: 7
  • I-A (Evidence-Extending): 3 (I1 Cond., I3 Cond., I7 Cond.)
  • I-B (Competing-Evidence): 2 (I2 Cond. — resolved Strong, I4 ECT — resolved Strong toward Cond.)
  • I-C (Compatible External): 0
  • I-D (Counter-Evidence External): 2 (I5 ECT, I6 ECT)

Both I-B items resolved Strong toward Cond. direction. The former N5 (reclassified to I-B during classification) resolved Moderate toward Cond.

The two ECT-direction claims (I5, I6) are both I-D (Counter-Evidence External) — they require overriding E-tier statements (OT unconsciousness, Jesus' non-ascension) to be maintained.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The evidence from 2 Corinthians 5:1-8 and its parallel passages distributes across tiers as follows:

At the E-tier, 7 explicit statements use cessation/unconsciousness vocabulary for the state of the dead, all classified Cond. after Tree 3 gate testing. Zero explicit statements in this study's scope use conscious-ongoing-existence vocabulary applied to literal human dead in didactic prose. The 19 Neutral E-items establish factual observations both sides must accept: Paul's stated preference for transformation, the vocabulary link to 1 Cor 15:54, the placement of being with the Lord at the resurrection, the grammatical neutrality of the aorist infinitive construction in 2 Cor 5:8.

At the N-tier, 3 necessary implications are Neutral — factual observations about vocabulary overlap, Paul's preference structure, and the object of groaning. Two candidate N-items (N4, N5) failed Gate 0 and were reclassified to I-tier.

At the I-tier, the conditionalist inferences (I1, I3, I7) are all I-A (evidence-extending) — they systematize E/N items using only the text's own vocabulary and concepts. The ECT inferences (I4, I5, I6) are either I-B (resolved Strong toward Cond.) or I-D (requiring override of E-tier statements). The ECT reading of 2 Cor 5:8 (I4) has only Ambiguous-level textual support (E15, E16), while the Cond. reading has multiple Plain-level same-author statements governing interpretation (E11, E12, E6, E7).

The passage teaches about the resurrection body (the building from God that replaces the tent), Paul's preference for transformation at the parousia over death, and the Spirit's guarantee of future bodily redemption. The "absent from the body / present with the Lord" language in 2 Cor 5:8 is grammatically compatible with both immediate and non-immediate readings, but Paul's own clearer statements consistently place being with the Lord at the resurrection/parousia.

Study completed: 2026-06-05 Evidence items tracked in etc6-master-evidence.md

docs.title: Prior Research Summary
docs.text: Eleven prior studies were consulted (see 00-references.md). The prior 2-corinthians-5-unclothed-intermediate-state study (2026-02-20) established that Paul's stated preference is ependysasthai (transformation) not ekdysasthai (death/disembodiment), and that the katapothE/thnEton vocabulary links to 1 Cor 15:54. The etc7-04-state-of-the-dead study (2026-06-03) classified E43 (2 Cor 5:8) and E44 (Phil 1:23) as Neutral after Tree 3 gate tests. The etc7-01-what-is-man study established holistic anthropology (man IS a nephesh, not HAS a soul). The etc7-02-who-has-immortality study showed endyo vocabulary demands that immortality is received at resurrection. The etc7-03-biblical-death study defined death as reversal of creation, not separation of soul from body. All prior studies agree on the subjective-instantaneity model for explaining 2 Cor 5:8. Gaps identified: deeper study of analysai (G360) in Phil 1:23, the oikia/oikodome contrast in 2 Cor 5:1, the proleptic present echomen, the textual variant in 5:3, the arrabon metaphor in 5:5, and the broader 2 Cor 4:7-5:10 literary unit.

The epi-prefix determines whether Paul envisions transformation or exchange yes G1562 ekdyo core verb — 'unclothe/strip,' what Paul explicitly does NOT want. Every NT use involves violent stripping (missing) G1746 endyo base clothing verb — 'put on.' Same verb in 1 Cor 15:53-54 for putting on immortality. Only in 2 Cor 5:6,8,9. Counterpart to ekdemeo yes G4636 skenos core noun — 'tent.' Only in 2 Cor 5:1,4. The temporary body metaphor yes G2666 katapino core verb — 'swallow up.' Links 2 Cor 5:4 to 1 Cor 15:54 (same resurrection event) (missing) G4727 stenazo core verb — 'groan.' Links 2 Cor 5:2,4 to Rom 8:23 (groaning for redemption of the body) (missing) G728 arrabon core noun — 'earnest/deposit/guarantee.' 3x NT (2 Cor 1:22, 5:5, Eph 1:14). The undesirable state. Also 1 Cor 15:37 for bare grain (missing) G2349 thnetos 2 Cor 5:4 — 'mortal/mortality.' Same word in 1 Cor 15:53.
