docs.title: Primary Verses (35 — full analysis required)
docs.text:
Core passage: 2 Corinthians 5:1-10: The primary passage under study. Retrieve with full chapter context for both chapters 4 and 5 - 2 Cor 5:1 — Core passage v.1 — earthly tent-house vs. building from God, 'eternal in the heavens' (aionios), oikia/oikodome contrast - 2 Cor 5:2 — Core passage v.2 — groaning (stenazomen), desiring to be 'clothed upon' (ependysasthai) with dwelling from heaven (oiketerion) - 2 Cor 5:3 — Core passage v.3 — 'if so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked' — textual variant endysamenoi vs. ekdysamenoi - 2 Cor 5:4 — Core passage v.4 — three-part preference: ou thelomen ekdysasthai / all ependysasthai / hina katapothE to thnEton hypo tEs zOEs — resurrection vocabulary from 1 Cor 15:54 - 2 Cor 5:5 — Core passage v.5 — God prepared us (katergasamenos), gave earnest (arrabon) of the Spirit — guarantee of future resurrection body - 2 Cor 5:6 — Core passage v.6 — confidence language, endemoumen/ekdemoumen pair — 'at home in the body, absent from the Lord' - 2 Cor 5:7 — Core passage v.7 — 'we walk by faith not by sight' — parenthetical explaining present condition - 2 Cor 5:8 — Core passage v.8 — eudokoumen/tharrountes — 'willing rather to be absent from the body and present with the Lord' — key verse for intermediate state debate, aorist infinitives - 2 Cor 5:9-10 — Immediate following context — judgment seat of Christ, 'whether present or absent we aim to please him'

Immediate preceding context: The argument leading into the clothing metaphor — suffering, resurrection hope, temporal/eternal contrast - 2 Cor 4:14 — Immediate preceding context — 'He which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus' — resurrection as the explicit hope - 2 Cor 4:16 — Immediate preceding context — 'outward man perish, inward man renewed day by day' — what perishing/renewal means - 2 Cor 4:17-18 — Immediate context — 'eternal weight of glory' vs. 'light affliction' — temporal/eternal contrast leading into ch.5

Same-author resurrection vocabulary: Passages where Paul uses the identical vocabulary found in 2 Cor 5:1-8 — katapino, thnetos, endyo, stenazo - 1 Cor 15:35-44 — Same-author — natural body vs spiritual body, sown in corruption raised in incorruption — the clothing metaphor's conceptual framework - 1 Cor 15:51-54 — Same-author parallel — 'this mortal must put on (endysasthai) immortality,' 'death is swallowed up (katepothE) in victory' — identical vocabulary to 2 Cor 5:4 - Rom 8:10-11 — Same-author — Spirit as guarantee of bodily resurrection: 'shall also quicken your mortal (thneta) bodies' - Rom 8:23 — Same-author parallel — groaning (stenazomen, same verb as 2 Cor 5:2,4), waiting for 'the redemption of our body' (apolutrosin tou somatos)

Parallel 'depart/be with Christ' passages: Other Pauline statements about death and being with Christ, with their immediate contexts - Phil 1:21-24 — Same-author parallel — 'to depart (analysai) and be with Christ, which is far better' — parallel preference expression for being with Christ after death - Phil 3:11 — Same-letter context for Phil 1:23 — Paul's hope is 'the resurrection of the dead' (exanastasin), not immediate post-death presence - Phil 3:20-21 — Same-letter context — Saviour who 'shall change our vile body' (metaschEmatisei) — transformation, not soul-release - 2 Tim 4:6-8 — Same-author — Paul's departure language: 'crown of righteousness at that day' — future reception at parousia, not at death - 1 Thess 4:13-17 — Same-author — the dead in Christ rise first, then caught up together, 'so shall we ever be with the Lord' — being with Lord placed at parousia/resurrection - 1 Thess 5:10 — Same-author — 'whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him' — Paul envisions both possibilities (alive or dead at parousia)

OT death-state testimony: Explicit OT statements about the unconsciousness of the dead - Ecc 9:5-6 — OT death-state — 'the dead know not any thing' — explicit statement on unconsciousness in death - Psa 146:4 — OT death-state — 'his breath goeth forth, he returneth to earth; in that very day his thoughts perish' - Psa 6:5 — OT death-state — 'in death there is no remembrance of thee' - Psa 115:17 — OT death-state — 'the dead praise not the LORD' — going down into silence - Isa 38:18-19 — OT death-state — Hezekiah: 'the grave cannot praise thee, death cannot celebrate thee' — the dead do not praise God - Job 14:12-14 — OT death-state — 'man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more' — death as sleep until resurrection - Ecc 12:7 — OT death-state — 'the spirit shall return unto God who gave it' — reversal of Gen 2:7 creation, parallel to Stephen's prayer

Counter-evidence passages: Passages cited in favor of conscious intermediate state — require genre/context analysis - Rev 6:9-11 — Comparison passage — 'souls under the altar' crying out — ECT-direction text for conscious dead, requires genre analysis (apocalyptic symbol) - Luke 23:43 — Comparison passage — 'today shalt thou be with me in paradise' — punctuation debate, temporal question - Acts 2:34 — NT — 'David is not ascended into the heavens' — explicit that OT saint is not in heaven consciously - Heb 11:39-40 — NT — OT faithful 'received not the promise' — they await resurrection, not already in heaven

Additional Primary Verses: - 1 Cor 15:18 — Same-author — 'they which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished' — incompatible with conscious intermediate state (if they are already consciously with Christ, how perished?) - 1 Cor 15:19-20 — Same-author — if only in this life we have hope, 'most miserable' — resurrection as THE hope, not intermediate conscious existence

docs.title: Supporting Verses (26 — retrieve for context, no individual analysis)
docs.text:
• 2 Cor 1:22 — Same-letter — God 'gave the earnest (arrabon) of the Spirit in our hearts' — same metaphor as 2 Cor 5:5
  • Eph 1:13-14 — Same-author — Holy Spirit as arrabon of our inheritance 'until the redemption of the purchased possession'
  • Gen 2:7 — OT creation formula — dust + breath = living soul — foundational anthropology for understanding Paul's body/clothing language
  • Acts 7:59-60 — Stephen: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' then 'he fell asleep' — spirit-commitment + sleep language pattern
  • Luke 23:46 — Jesus: 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit' — parallel to Stephen, but Jesus 'not yet ascended' on Sunday (John 20:17)
  • John 20:17 — Jesus had 'not yet ascended to my Father' — committing spirit did NOT mean immediate conscious presence
  • Ecc 3:19-21 — OT — same ruach for man and beast, both return to dust
  • Ecc 9:10 — OT — 'there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave (sheol)'
  • Psa 88:10-12 — OT — 'Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee?'
  • Isa 25:8 — OT prophecy — 'He will swallow up death in victory' — source text for 1 Cor 15:54 and 2 Cor 5:4 katapino vocabulary
  • Isa 26:19 — OT resurrection hope — 'Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise'
  • Dan 12:2 — OT — 'many that sleep in the dust shall awake' — sleep vocabulary for death, resurrection at end
  • Job 19:25-27 — OT resurrection hope — 'in my flesh shall I see God' — bodily resurrection, not disembodied existence
  • 1 Cor 15:6 — Same-author — 'some are fallen asleep' — death-as-sleep vocabulary in resurrection chapter
  • 1 Cor 15:23-26 — Same-author — resurrection order: Christ, then those who are his 'at his coming' — timing specified
  • Luke 20:35-38 — Jesus on resurrection — 'in the resurrection' they are like angels — the eschatological event, not intermediate state
  • Matt 10:28 — Jesus — 'fear him which is able to destroy (apolesai) both soul and body in gehenna' — soul is not inherently immortal
  • Isa 61:10 — OT clothing metaphor — 'He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation' — righteousness as garment
  • 2 Cor 12:2-4 — Same-letter — Paul caught up to paradise, 'whether in the body or out of the body I cannot tell' — Paul does not equate being out of body with consciousness
  • 2 Pet 1:13-14 — Peter — 'as long as I am in this tabernacle (skenomati)' — tent/tabernacle metaphor for the body, linked to 2 Cor 5:1
  • Rom 13:14 — Same-author — 'put on (endysasthe) the Lord Jesus Christ' — endyo metaphor for acquisition, not revelation
  • Gal 3:27 — Same-author — 'have put on (enedysasthe) Christ' — clothing metaphor as acquisition of new identity
  • 1 Cor 15:37 — Same-author — 'bare (gymnon) grain' — gymnos (naked) applied to the seed sown before receiving its body, parallel to 2 Cor 5:3
  • Ezek 37:1-14 — OT resurrection vision — valley of dry bones — bodily resurrection prophesied
  • Hos 13:14 — OT — 'I will ransom them from the power of the grave' — victory over death at future point, cited by Paul in 1 Cor 15:55
  • Isa 38:10-13 — OT — Hezekiah's lament about death — 'I said in the cutting off of my days' — death as ending, not transition

docs.title: Focus Areas
docs.text:
1. The three-part preference structure of 2 Cor 5:4: This is THE decisive verse for understanding the passage. Run greek_parser.py --verse on 2 Cor 5:4 and verify the three elements: (1) ou thelomen ekdysasthai — 'we do not wish to be unclothed' — Paul explicitly rejects the state ECT interpreters argue he desires; (2) all' ependysasthai — 'but [we wish] to be clothed upon' — the epen- prefix means 'upon/over,' indicating the resurrection body placed ON TOP of the mortal body without passing through death; (3) hina katapothE to thnEton hypo tEs zOEs — the purpose clause uses identical vocabulary to 1 Cor 15:54 (katapothE from katapino G2666, thnEton from thnetos G2349). READ the library entries for G2349-thnetos.md and G110-athanasia.md. Run greek_parser.py --verse on 1 Cor 15:54 and compare the verb forms. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py --hybrid-ot on 2 Cor 5:4 to check for OT source texts (Isa 25:8 'He will swallow up death in victory'). The research agent should verify whether katapothE and katepothE are the same or different forms and what the semantic overlap means. Verses: 2 Cor 5:4, 1 Cor 15:54, Isa 25:8, 1 Cor 15:53 Strong's: G2666, G2349, G1902, G1562

  2. The ependyomai (G1902) and ekdyo (G1562) verb contrast: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G1902-ependyomai.md for the canonical word study. Run search_strongs.py --verses G1902 to verify it appears ONLY in 2 Cor 5:2,4 (2x total in NT — Paul's unique coinage). Then run search_strongs.py --verses G1562 to check every NT use of ekdyo — prior study found every other use involves violent stripping (soldiers stripping Jesus: Matt 27:28,31; Mark 15:20; Luke 10:30). READ $WORD_STUDIES/G1746-endyo.md for the base verb. The three-verb grid is: endyo (G1746, 'clothe') = standard clothing, used in 1 Cor 15:53-54 for 'put on immortality'; ekdyo (G1562, 'unclothe') = what Paul does NOT want; ependyomai (G1902, 'clothe upon/over') = what Paul DOES want — transformation without death. Run greek_parser.py on all occurrences to verify morphology. The epi- compound prefix semantics need analysis — does epi- always imply 'upon what is already there'? Verses: 2 Cor 5:2, 2 Cor 5:4, 1 Cor 15:53, Matt 27:28, Matt 27:31, Gal 3:27, Rom 13:14 Strong's: G1902, G1562, G1746

  3. The aorist infinitives in 2 Cor 5:8 and temporal relationship: Run greek_parser.py --verse on 2 Cor 5:8 and verify the morphological forms ekdEmEsai (V-AAN from G1553 ekdemeo) and endEmEsai (V-AAN from G1736 endemeo). READ $WORD_STUDIES/G1553-ekdemeo.md and $WORD_STUDIES/G1736-endemeo.md — these words occur ONLY in 2 Cor 5:6,8,9 (3x each). The research question: does kai between two aorist infinitives require temporal immediacy? Search for parallel constructions in the NT where two aorist infinitives are connected by kai — do they always imply immediate temporal sequence? The subjective-instantaneity model from prior studies argues that from the dead person's perspective (if death is unconsciousness), the next conscious moment IS being with Christ, even if millennia intervene objectively. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py on 2 Cor 5:8 to find structural parallels. Verses: 2 Cor 5:8, 2 Cor 5:6, 2 Cor 5:9 Strong's: G1553, G1736, G2106

  4. The oikia/oikodome and skenos/oiketerion architectural metaphors in 2 Cor 5:1: Run greek_parser.py --verse on 2 Cor 5:1. The verse has a first-class conditional (ean + subjunctive — or is it ean katalythe? check mood). The proleptic present echomen ('we HAVE a building from God') is significant — Paul uses present tense for a future reality, expressing certainty. Search search_strongs.py --verses G4636 to verify skenos appears ONLY in 2 Cor 5:1,4. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G3619-oikodomē.md and $WORD_STUDIES/G4638-skenoma.md. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G4633-skene.md for the related noun. The contrast is deliberate: skenous (tent, temporary, collapsible) vs. oikodome (building, permanent, constructed). The phrase acheiropoieton ('not made with hands') in v.1 is used in Mark 14:58 for the temple Jesus said he would rebuild — run search_strongs.py --verses G886 to check. Compare with 2 Pet 1:13-14 where Peter uses skenoma (G4638) for his body. The oiketerion (G3613) in v.2 occurs only here and Jude 1:6 — run search_strongs.py --verses G3613 to verify. Verses: 2 Cor 5:1, 2 Cor 5:2, 2 Pet 1:13-14, Mark 14:58, Jude 1:6 Strong's: G4636, G3619, G3624, G3613, G886

  5. The arrabon (G728) of the Spirit and its eschatological guarantee function: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G728-arrabon.md for the canonical word study. Run search_strongs.py --verses G728 to verify all 3 NT occurrences (2 Cor 1:22, 2 Cor 5:5, Eph 1:14). The arrabon was a commercial term — a down-payment guaranteeing full payment later. In 2 Cor 5:5 the 'full payment' is the resurrection body. Compare with Rom 8:23 where Paul uses aparche ('firstfruits') for the Spirit with the same future-guarantee function — 'groaning (stenazomen, same verb as 2 Cor 5:2!) within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body.' Run greek_parser.py --verse on 2 Cor 5:5 to analyze katergasamenos (the aorist middle participle 'having prepared') and the phrase eis auto touto ('for this very purpose'). Cross-reference Eph 1:13-14 where the Spirit is arrabon 'until the redemption of the purchased possession' — the 'until' (eis) marks the still-future completion point. Verses: 2 Cor 5:5, 2 Cor 1:22, Eph 1:13-14, Rom 8:23 Strong's: G728, G4727, G536

  6. The Philippians 1:21-24 parallel and analysai (G360): READ $WORD_STUDIES/G360-analyo.md for the canonical word study. Run greek_parser.py --verse on Phil 1:23 — the key construction is eis to analysai kai syn Christō einai ('unto the departing and being with Christ'). The question is whether kai syn Christō einai is simultaneous with, or consequent to, analysai. The verb analysai has military/nautical background (loosing from moorings, striking camp) — check LXX uses. Now read the same-letter context: Phil 3:11 — Paul's hope is exanastasin tēn ek nekrōn ('the resurrection from the dead'), not immediate post-death consciousness. Phil 3:20-21 — 'we look for the Saviour... who shall change (metaschEmatisei) our vile body (to sōma tēs tapeinōseōs)' — transformation of the body, same concept as 2 Cor 5:4. The same-author/same-letter hermeneutical principle: if Paul's clear statements about his hope are consistently eschatological (resurrection, parousia, crown 'at that day'), his ambiguous statements (2 Cor 5:8, Phil 1:23) should be read in light of the clear ones. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py on Phil 1:23. Verses: Phil 1:21-24, Phil 3:11, Phil 3:20-21, 2 Tim 4:6-8 Strong's: G360, G1815, G3345

  7. The textual variant in 2 Cor 5:3 — endysamenoi vs. ekdysamenoi: Run greek_parser.py --verse on 2 Cor 5:3 to get the parsed form. The variant centers on the aorist middle participle: endysamenoi (from endyo G1746, 'having clothed ourselves') vs. ekdysamenoi (from ekdyo G1562, 'having unclothed ourselves'). The conditional eige ('if so be that,' 'if indeed' — G1489 or G1487 + G1065) introduces a condition. With endysamenoi: 'if indeed having been clothed, we shall not be found gymnoi (naked/bare).' With ekdysamenoi: 'if indeed having been unclothed, we shall not be found gymnoi.' The gymnos (G1131) concept is key — Paul uses it in 1 Cor 15:37 for the 'bare grain' that is sown. Being found 'naked' is the undesirable state — whether that is death-without-resurrection-hope or standing before God without the resurrection body. Research agent should retrieve manuscript evidence from standard apparatus notes and document which MSS support each reading. Verses: 2 Cor 5:3, 1 Cor 15:37, 2 Cor 5:2, 2 Cor 5:4 Strong's: G1746, G1562, G1131

  8. OT death-state testimony — the explicit unconsciousness passages: The OT death-state passages span multiple authors and genres. Run hebrew_parser.py --verse on Psa 146:4 — 'his thoughts (eshtonoth) perish' — the word for 'thoughts' is H6250, a hapax form related to H6245 (to think). Run on Ecc 9:5-6 — 'the dead know (yodeim from yada H3045) not anything.' Run on Psa 6:5 — 'in death there is no remembrance (zeker H2143) of thee.' Run on Psa 115:17 — 'the dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence (dumah H1745).' READ $WORD_STUDIES/H4194-maveth.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H7585-showl.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H7901-shakab.md. These OT passages establish the interpretive context for Paul. Job 14:12-14 is especially relevant: 'man lieth down and riseth not: till the heavens be no more... if a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change (chaliphah H2487) come.' The 'change' Job awaits is resurrection — same concept as Paul's clothing metaphor. Verses: Ecc 9:5-6, Psa 146:4, Psa 6:5, Psa 115:17, Isa 38:18-19, Job 14:12-14, Ecc 12:7, Psa 88:10-12 Strong's: H3045, H4194, H7585, H7901, H2143

  9. The broader literary unit: 2 Cor 4:7-5:10: The research agent should retrieve the full chapter context for 2 Cor 4:7-5:10. Key markers in the argument: 4:7 'treasure in earthen vessels' — the earthen vessel IS the skenos of 5:1; 4:10-11 'bearing about in the body the dying of Jesus... delivered unto death for Jesus' sake' — suffering vocabulary; 4:14 'knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you' — EXPLICIT resurrection hope preceding the clothing metaphor; 4:16 'outward man perish, inward man renewed' — the perishing outward man is the tent being dissolved in 5:1; 4:17-18 'light affliction...eternal weight of glory... things not seen are eternal' — the eternal/temporal contrast that opens into 5:1's tent/building contrast. The logical flow is continuous: suffering (4:7-12) → resurrection hope (4:14) → temporal vs eternal (4:17-18) → tent vs building (5:1) → groaning for transformation (5:2-4) → Spirit as guarantee (5:5) → confidence (5:6-8) → judgment seat (5:9-10). Run greek_parser.py on key transitional words: gar (G1063) in 5:1 'for we know,' eidotes (from oida G1492) in 5:6, tharrountes (from tharreo G2292) in 5:8. Verses: 2 Cor 4:7-11, 2 Cor 4:14, 2 Cor 4:16-18, 2 Cor 5:1-10 Strong's: G1063, G1492, G2292

  10. The sleep vocabulary chain across authors: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G2837-koimao.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H7901-shakab.md for the canonical word studies. The sleep metaphor for death is used by: Moses (Deut 31:16 'thou shalt sleep with thy fathers'), Job (Job 14:12), David (Psa 13:3), Solomon (Ecc 9:5-10), Daniel (Dan 12:2 'sleep in the dust'), Jesus (John 11:11 'our friend Lazarus sleepeth'), Paul (1 Thess 4:14 'them which sleep in Jesus'; 1 Cor 15:6,18,51), Stephen's death narrated with ekoimEthE (Acts 7:60). The consistent implication of sleep is: (a) unconsciousness, (b) temporary state, (c) expected awakening (resurrection). When Paul uses katheudomen ('we sleep') in 1 Thess 5:10, he pairs it with grEgoromen ('we wake') — the binary options for his audience at the parousia. This vocabulary framework governs how 2 Cor 5:8 should be read: being 'absent from the body' is entering sleep, and the next conscious experience (from the sleeper's perspective) is 'present with the Lord.' Run search_strongs.py --verses G2837 to get the full occurrence list. Verses: 1 Thess 4:13-14, 1 Cor 15:6, 1 Cor 15:18, 1 Cor 15:51, Acts 7:60, John 11:11-12, Dan 12:2, Job 14:12 Strong's: G2837, H7901, G2518

  11. Counter-evidence: passages that potentially support conscious intermediate state: For Rev 6:9-11 — the 'souls under the altar' cry out. Run greek_parser.py --verse on Rev 6:9-10. Note that Revelation is apocalyptic genre using symbolism throughout. Abel's blood 'cries out' (Gen 4:10) without implying Abel is conscious. Compare with Rev 16:7 where the altar itself speaks. For Luke 23:43 — the punctuation issue: 'Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise' vs. 'Truly I say to you today, you will be with me in paradise.' Jesus himself had not ascended to the Father by Sunday (John 20:17). For Luke 16:19-31 — a parable, not a doctrinal description of the afterlife. Note that Abraham's bosom is not heaven, and the rich man has a tongue and requests water — is this literal? For Luke 20:38 — 'He is not a God of the dead, but of the living, for all live unto him' — is this about present consciousness or about God's faithfulness to resurrect? The research agent should retrieve and parse each passage, but remember: the ETC methodology classifies evidence by tier (E/N/I) and position (Cond./ECT/Neutral). Apply Tree 3 gate tests to each. Verses: Rev 6:9-11, Luke 23:43, Luke 16:22-26, Luke 9:30-31, Luke 20:38, Gen 4:10 Strong's: G5590, G3857, G86

  12. Paul's eschatological timing: did he expect to be alive at the parousia?: Paul's eschatological expectation shifted over his career. In 1 Thess 4:15 'we which are alive and remain' — the first person plural includes himself among those potentially alive at the parousia. In 1 Cor 15:51 'we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed' — same hope. This is EXACTLY the ependysasthai of 2 Cor 5:4 — transformation without passing through death. 1 Cor 15:51-52 describes the mechanics: 'in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump... the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.' By 2 Tim 4:6-8, Paul has accepted that he will die before the parousia: 'the time of my departure (analusis, cognate of analysai in Phil 1:23) is at hand.' But even then, his hope is 'a crown of righteousness, which the Lord... shall give me AT THAT DAY' — future, at the parousia, not at death. Run search_strongs.py --verses G359 (analusis) to verify it appears only in 2 Tim 4:6. Parse 2 Tim 4:8 to verify 'at that day' (en ekeinE tE hEmera). Verses: 1 Thess 4:15-17, 1 Cor 15:51-52, 2 Cor 5:4, 2 Tim 4:6-8, 1 Thess 5:10 Strong's: G359, G236, G4983

docs.title: What Does 2 Corinthians 5:1-8 Teach About Death and the Afterlife?
The Big Picture
docs.text: This passage is often quoted to prove that Christians go straight to heaven when they die. But a closer look at the Greek vocabulary, Paul's own stated preferences, and his clearer writings elsewhere tells a different story. Paul is writing about the resurrection body -- not a conscious disembodied existence between death and resurrection.

docs.title: Paul's Tent and Building Metaphor
docs.text: Paul compares our current mortal body to a tent -- temporary and fragile -- and the future resurrection body to a permanent building made by God. The contrast is between two kinds of bodies, not between having a body and floating free without one.

docs.title: What Paul Actually Wanted
docs.text:
In 2 Corinthians 5:4, Paul spells out his preference in three parts:

  1. What he did NOT want: to be "unclothed" -- stripped of his body through death.
  2. What he DID want: to be "clothed upon" -- to receive the resurrection body on top of his mortal one, skipping death entirely.
  3. Why: so that "mortality might be swallowed up of life."

His first choice was to be alive when Christ returns and be transformed without dying. Death was not the goal; resurrection was.

docs.title: "Absent from the Body, Present with the Lord"
docs.text: This phrase (2 Cor 5:8) sounds like it means the instant you die, you are with the Lord. But the Greek grammar does not actually say that. The two actions are connected by "and" (kai) without any word marking immediate timing. The construction is neutral -- it could mean "right away" or it could describe the ultimate outcome without specifying when.

docs.title: How Paul's Other Letters Clarify This
docs.text:
When Paul speaks clearly about when believers will be with the Lord, he always points to the resurrection:

  • 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 -- The dead rise first, the living are caught up, "and so shall we ever be with the Lord."
  • 2 Timothy 4:8 -- Paul's crown of righteousness is given "at that day" -- the day Christ appears.
  • Philippians 3:11 -- Paul hopes to "attain unto the resurrection of the dead."

Not one of these clear statements places being with the Lord at the moment of death. Every one places it at Christ's return.

docs.title: What the Old Testament Says About Death
docs.text:
The Old Testament consistently describes death as unconsciousness:

  • "The dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
  • "In that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalm 146:4)
  • "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)

Paul, trained in these Scriptures, would have written within this framework.

docs.title: How It All Fits Together
docs.text: If death is unconsciousness, then from the dead person's perspective there is no waiting. The next thing they experience after closing their eyes in death is the resurrection and being with Christ. Objectively, centuries may pass. Subjectively, it is instant. This explains why Paul can speak of departing and being with Christ as though they go together -- for the person who dies, they do.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
2 Corinthians 5:1-8 is a passage about the hope of resurrection, not a description of life after death before the resurrection. Paul's preference was transformation at Christ's return. His willingness to accept death reflected confidence in the resurrection outcome, not a belief that death itself would bring him into Christ's presence.

  • Phil 1:23 → Phil 3:11 (nt, same-letter context — Paul's hope is resurrection of the dead)
  • Phil 1:23 → Phil 3:20-21 (nt, same-letter — bodily transformation by Saviour from heaven)

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Matthew 10:28 -- "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." What does this verse teach about the fate of the wicked? Same-author usage analysis of psyche (G5590), apollymi (G622), gehenna (G1067), and phobeo (G5399) in Matthew's Gospel.

docs.title: Full pericope: fear hierarchy, sparrow analogy, 'fear not' repetitions
docs.text:
Matthew 10:26 Fear them not therefore: for there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known. Matthew 10:27 What I tell you in darkness, [that] speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, [that] preach ye upon the housetops. Matthew 10:28 And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. Matthew 10:29 Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. Matthew 10:30 But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Matthew 10:31 Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows.

Context: Part of Jesus' commissioning discourse to the twelve apostles (Matt 10:1-42). Jesus warns of persecution (v.16-23), then transitions to three 'fear not' commands (v.26, v.28, v.31), building an a fortiori argument: men can only kill the body; God can destroy both soul and body in gehenna. The sparrow analogy (v.29-31) reassures the disciples of God's providential care.

Notes: Matt 10:28 is the crux text. The verb shift from apokteino (kill, v.28a) to apollymi (destroy, v.28b) signals a qualitative difference: human killing is limited to the body; divine destroying encompasses both soul and body. The kai...kai correlative construction emphasizes totality. The location is gehenna (G1067), not hades (G86).

docs.title: Same discourse, same word-pair psyche+apollymi = 'lose one's life'
docs.text:
Matthew 10:39 He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it.

Context: Just 11 verses after 10:28, in the same commissioning discourse. Jesus uses the identical word-pair psyche + apollymi, but here it clearly means 'lose one's life' — not 'destroy an immaterial soul.' This same-author, same-discourse usage provides the most immediate contextual control for interpreting psyche and apollymi in 10:28.

  • ὁ (G3588) — T-NSM — Nom Sg M
  • εὑρὼν (G2147) — V-2AAP-NSM — Aor Act Ptcp Nom Sg M
  • ψυχὴν (G5590) — N-ASF — Acc Sg F
  • αὐτοῦ (G846) — P-GSM — Gen Sg M
  • ἀπολέσει (G622) — V-FAI-3S — Fut Act Ind Sg thirdPers
  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — ὁ ὁ G3588 [T-NSM] Nom Sg M
  • ἕνεκεν (G1752) — PREP — ἐμοῦ ἐγώ G1473 [P-1GS] Gen Sg

Notes: Parser confirms: apollymi here is V-FAI-3S (future active indicative) and V-AAP-NSM (aorist active participle). Psyche is N-ASF (accusative singular feminine) — identical form to 10:28. The semantic shift between 10:28 (divine judgment destruction) and 10:39 (losing one's life for Christ's sake) shows Matthew's flexibility with the word pair while maintaining the core sense of loss/cessation.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — Herod seeks to destroy the child
docs.text:
Matthew 2:13 And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.

Context: Herod's intent to kill Jesus. Apollymi used for literal physical destruction — killing the child. First occurrence of apollymi in Matthew.

Notes: Apollymi here = literal physical destruction (killing). Active voice, articular infinitive (tou apolesai). Matthew's first use of apollymi is in the context of murderous intent.

docs.title: Matthean psyche — 'they are dead which sought the young child's life'
docs.text:
Matthew 2:20 Saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child's life.

Context: Angel's message to Joseph after Herod's death. Psyche = physical life that was sought/threatened. First occurrence of psyche in Matthew.

Notes: Psyche used for physical life. Matthew's first use of psyche — establishing the word's basic meaning in his vocabulary.

docs.title: Matthean psyche — 'Take no thought for your life (psyche)'
docs.text:
Matthew 6:25 Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

Context: Sermon on the Mount. Jesus distinguishes psyche (life — what you eat/drink) from soma (body — what you wear). Both are physical concerns.

Notes: Psyche here = physical life requiring sustenance. The psyche/soma pairing in 6:25 (life vs. body as parallel physical concerns) contrasts with the psyche/soma pairing in 10:28 (soul vs. body as objects of destruction in gehenna).

docs.title: Matthean gehenna — 'danger of hell fire' — first gehenna reference in Matthew
docs.text:
Matthew 5:22 But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

Context: Sermon on the Mount. Jesus introduces gehenna in an escalating series of judgments: judgment → council → gehenna fire. First use of gehenna in Matthew.

Notes: First of Matthew's 7 gehenna occurrences. Gehenna is paired with fire (pyr) — the dominant collocation pattern.

docs.title: Matthean gehenna — 'whole body cast into hell' — body-in-gehenna parallel to 10:28
docs.text:
Matthew 5:29 And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast [it] from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not [that] thy whole body should be cast into hell. Matthew 5:30 And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast [it] from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not [that] thy whole body should be cast into hell.

Context: Sermon on the Mount, immediately following 5:22. The body-in-gehenna language directly parallels 10:28. Uses apollymi (V-2AMS-3S, apoletai — aorist middle subjunctive) for the member 'perishing' and ballo (V-APS-3S, blethe — aorist passive subjunctive) for the body being 'cast into' gehenna.

Notes: Parser confirms apollymi appears in these verses (apoletai). The pattern is: it is better to lose (apollymi) a part than for the whole body to be cast into gehenna. This pairs apollymi with gehenna, as does 10:28.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — 'Lord, save us: we perish' — physical death fear
docs.text:
Matthew 8:25 And his disciples came to [him], and awoke him, saying, Lord, save us: we perish.

Context: Storm on the sea. Disciples fear drowning. Apollymi = facing physical death. Sozo (save) and apollymi (perish) used as antonyms.

Notes: Apollymi in the middle voice = perishing (physical death by drowning). The sozo-apollymi antithesis appears here: save us from perishing.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — wineskins perish — apollymi for inanimate ruin/destruction
docs.text:
Matthew 9:17 Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.

Context: New wine and old wineskins parable. Apollymi used for the ruin of inanimate objects (wineskins) — demonstrating the word's broad semantic range.

Notes: Apollymi can describe inanimate objects being ruined/destroyed. This shows the 'ruin' end of the semantic range — the wineskins cease to function as vessels.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — 'lost sheep of the house of Israel' — apollymi as 'lost/straying'
docs.text:
Matthew 10:6 But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

Context: Same commissioning discourse as 10:28. 'Lost' (apollymi, perfect middle participle) sheep — recoverable loss, not destruction. Shows the 'lost/straying' sense.

Notes: Apollymi here = 'lost/straying' (recoverable condition). This is the middle-voice 'lost' sense, distinct from the active-voice 'destroy' sense used in 10:28. Same discourse but different semantic category.

docs.title: Matthean psyche — 'find rest unto your souls' — psyche as inner person
docs.text:
Matthew 11:29 Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

Context: Jesus' invitation to the weary. Psyche = the inner self that experiences rest or turmoil.

Notes: Psyche as the inner person/self — the seat of weariness and rest. Not a statement about immortality.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — Pharisees conspire to destroy Jesus — human destructive intent
docs.text:
Matthew 12:14 Then the Pharisees went out, and held a council against him, how they might destroy him.

Context: After Jesus heals on the Sabbath. The Pharisees plot to apollymi (destroy/kill) Jesus. Active voice, subjunctive mood — deliberate planning of lethal action.

Notes: Apollymi = plot to kill. Human agents using apollymi for murderous intent. Same verb used of God's action in 10:28 — but there God's scope extends beyond mere killing to destroying soul AND body.

docs.title: Matthean psyche — 'in whom my soul is well pleased' — God's psyche (OT quotation)
docs.text:
Matthew 12:18 Behold my servant, whom I have chosen; my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my spirit upon him, and he shall shew judgment to the Gentiles.

Context: Matthew quoting Isa 42:1. God's psyche is 'well pleased' with the Servant. OT quotation preserving the anthropomorphic nephesh-language of Isaiah.

Notes: Psyche applied to God — reflecting the OT nephesh usage where God speaks of 'my nephesh.' Not a statement about the immortality or immateriality of psyche.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — 'lost sheep of the house of Israel' — second 'lost' usage
docs.text:
Matthew 15:24 But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

Context: Jesus' response to the Canaanite woman. Same 'lost sheep' formula as 10:6.

Notes: Second use of apollymi as 'lost' (perfect middle participle). The straying/lost sense, not destruction.

docs.title: Matthean psyche+apollymi — save/lose life; what profit to gain world and lose soul
docs.text:
Matthew 16:25 For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. Matthew 16:26 For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?

Context: Following Peter's confession and first passion prediction. The psyche+apollymi word pair reappears (as in 10:28, 10:39). In v.25, psyche = 'life' (save/lose paradox). In v.26, KJV translates psyche as 'soul' — but the meaning is the same: one's whole self/life is at stake.

Notes: The same word psyche is translated 'life' (v.25) and 'soul' (v.26) in the same two-verse passage. This demonstrates that the life/soul distinction is a translation artifact, not a conceptual difference in Greek. Apollymi appears in v.25.

docs.title: Matthean gehenna — 'cast into hell fire' — enter life vs. gehenna contrast
docs.text:
Matthew 18:9 And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast [it] from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire.

Context: Discourse on stumbling blocks. The life-vs-gehenna contrast: 'enter into life' is the alternative to 'cast into gehenna fire.' Echoes Matt 5:29-30.

Notes: The life/gehenna antithesis: life (zoe) vs. gehenna. Not life vs. torment, but life vs. fiery destruction. Same body-in-gehenna language as 5:29-30 and 10:28.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — 'to save that which was lost' — apollymi as lost, paired with sozo
docs.text:
Matthew 18:11 For the Son of man is come to save that which was lost.

Context: Following the lost sheep parable. Sozo (save) and apollymi (lost) as antonyms. What sozo rescues from is what apollymi describes.

Notes: The sozo-apollymi antithesis at its clearest. If sozo = 'give/preserve life,' then apollymi = 'remove/end life.' James 4:12 applies this same antonym pair to God.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — 'not the will of your Father that one should perish'
docs.text:
Matthew 18:14 Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.

Context: Following the lost sheep parable. God does not will that any should apollymi (perish). This passage links to 2 Pet 3:9 ('not willing that any should perish').

Notes: Apollymi = perish (complete loss). The Father's will is set against apollymi, not for eternal preservation in torment.

docs.title: Matthean psyche — 'give his life (psyche) a ransom for many'
docs.text:
Matthew 20:28 Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.

Context: Jesus describes his mission — giving his psyche (life) as a ransom. Psyche = physical life given up in death.

Notes: Psyche = physical life laid down in death. Jesus' psyche is mortal — he gives it up. This is incompatible with a naturally immortal psyche.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — judgment: 'miserably destroy those wicked men'
docs.text:
Matthew 21:41 They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out [his] vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons.

Context: Parable of the wicked husbandmen. The vineyard owner (representing God) apollymi (destroys) the wicked tenants. Active voice, future indicative (apolesei). Actual destruction by authority.

Notes: Parser: apolesei = V-FAI-3S (future active indicative). Judgment apollymi = actual destruction by authority. When Matthew records God/authority figures using apollymi on the wicked, it consistently means actual destruction.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — judgment: king 'destroyed those murderers and burned up their city'
docs.text:
Matthew 22:7 But when the king heard [thereof], he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city.

Context: Parable of the marriage feast. The king (representing God) apollymi (destroyed) the murderers AND burned their city. Active voice, aorist indicative (apolesen). Apollymi + fire vocabulary together.

Notes: Parser: apolesen = V-AAI-3S (aorist active indicative). Destruction + burning. Apollymi is paired with empiprhmi (to burn/set on fire). This echoes 10:28 where apollymi is paired with gehenna (fire). When God/king destroys the wicked, the result is actual destruction, not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Matthean psyche — 'love the Lord with all thy soul' — Shema quotation
docs.text:
Matthew 22:37 Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.

Context: Jesus quoting the Shema (Deut 6:5). Psyche = the whole self/devotion — standard OT nephesh usage in the covenant formula.

Notes: Psyche in the Shema quotation = whole-person devotion, reflecting nephesh in Deut 6:5. Not a statement about the soul as an immortal entity.

docs.title: Matthean gehenna — 'twofold more the child of hell (gehenna)'
docs.text:
Matthew 23:15 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.

Context: Jesus' woes against the Pharisees. 'Child of gehenna' = one destined for gehenna. Gehenna as destination/destiny descriptor.

Notes: 'Son of gehenna' (huios geennEs) — Semitic idiom of destiny (cf. 'son of perdition'). Gehenna is the destiny, not a location of ongoing conscious experience.

docs.title: Matthean gehenna — 'how can ye escape the damnation of hell (gehenna)?'
docs.text:
Matthew 23:33 [Ye] serpents, [ye] generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?

Context: Jesus' strongest denunciation of the Pharisees. 'Damnation of gehenna' = krisis (judgment/condemnation) + gehenna. Gehenna paired with krisis (judgment vocabulary), not basanizo (torment vocabulary).

Notes: Gehenna + krisis (judgment), not gehenna + basanizo (torment). Consistent with the pattern: gehenna collocates with destruction/judgment vocabulary, never torment vocabulary.

docs.title: Matthean psyche — 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death' — Jesus' psyche is mortal
docs.text:
Matthew 26:38 Then saith he unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.

Context: Gethsemane. Jesus says his psyche is sorrowful 'unto death' (heos thanatou). His psyche can experience death — it is mortal.

Notes: Jesus' own psyche is subject to death. If even Jesus' psyche can experience sorrow 'unto death,' then psyche is not inherently immortal. This is Matthew's own usage of psyche in the most personal context.

docs.title: Matthean apollymi — crowd persuaded to 'destroy Jesus'
docs.text:
Matthew 27:20 But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus.

Context: Before Pilate. The crowd is persuaded to apollymi (destroy/kill) Jesus. Human agents seeking to execute Jesus.

Notes: Apollymi = kill/execute. Active voice. Another instance of human destructive intent. Same verb as 10:28 but limited to physical killing — humans cannot apollymi the psyche.

docs.title: Matthean phobeo — Jesus says 'be not afraid' on the water
docs.text:
Matthew 14:27 But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.

Context: Jesus walking on the water. 'Be not afraid' = me phobeisthe. Present imperative prohibition — stop the ongoing fear.

Notes: Phobeo in 'fear not' command — same construction as 10:28. Physical fear being addressed.

docs.title: Matthean phobeo — Peter afraid of wind and waves
docs.text:
Matthew 14:30 But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.

Context: Peter walking on the water, then fearing. Phobeo = physical fear/terror. Followed by cry for sozo (save).

Notes: Phobeo for physical terror at natural danger. The phobeo-sozo pairing: Peter fears and cries 'save me.'

docs.title: Matthean phobeo — disciples 'sore afraid' at transfiguration; Jesus says 'be not afraid'
docs.text:
Matthew 17:6 And when the disciples heard [it], they fell on their face, and were sore afraid. Matthew 17:7 And Jesus came and touched them, and said, Arise, and be not afraid.

Context: Transfiguration. Disciples fall in terror before the divine theophany. Jesus commands: 'me phobeisthe' — do not keep fearing.

Notes: Phobeo for numinous dread — terror before the supernatural. Same 'fear not' command form as 10:28.

docs.title: Matthean phobeo — guards shake for fear; angel says 'Fear not ye'
docs.text:
Matthew 28:4 And for fear of him the keepers did shake, and became as dead [men]. Matthew 28:5 And the angel answered and said unto the women, Fear not ye: for I know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified.

Context: Resurrection morning. Guards shake with phobos (fear noun). Angel says 'me phobeisthe' (present imperative — stop fearing) to the women.

Notes: Phobeo/phobos in the resurrection context. The guards fear the supernatural manifestation. The women are told to stop fearing — same form as 10:28.

docs.title: Matthean phobeo — Jesus says 'Be not afraid' to women at empty tomb
docs.text:
Matthew 28:10 Then said Jesus unto them, Be not afraid: go tell my brethren that they go into Galilee, and there shall they see me.

Context: Post-resurrection appearance. Another 'me phobeisthe' command. Jesus' characteristic response to human fear.

Notes: Final phobeo occurrence in Matthew. The 'fear not' pattern bookends the Gospel: 1:20 (Joseph), 10:26,28,31 (disciples), 14:27 (sea), 17:7 (transfiguration), 28:5,10 (resurrection).

docs.title: Synoptic parallel — Luke's version omits psyche, uses apokteino for God's action
docs.text:
Luke 12:4 And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. Luke 12:5 But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him.

Context: Luke's parallel to Matt 10:28. Three key differences: (1) Luke uses aorist passive imperative phobethete (decisive act of fearing) vs. Matthew's present imperative phobeisthe (ongoing posture); (2) Luke uses apokteino (kill) for BOTH human and divine action, while Matthew escalates to apollymi (destroy); (3) Luke omits psyche entirely, adding a temporal sequence: 'after he hath killed, hath power to cast into gehenna.'

Notes: Parser confirms: Luke 12:4 phobethete = V-AOM-2P (aorist passive imperative); Luke 12:5 phobethete = V-AOM-2P (same form, repeated for emphasis with nai). Luke uses apokteino (V-AAN, aorist active infinitive) for God's action, whereas Matthew uses apollymi (V-AAN, aorist active infinitive). Matthew's verb shift from apokteino to apollymi signals something MORE than killing — destruction of both soul and body.

docs.title: OT — Valley of Hinnom: child sacrifice site renamed 'Valley of Slaughter'
docs.text:
Jeremiah 7:31 And they have built the high places of Tophet, which [is] in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I commanded [them] not, neither came it into my heart. Jeremiah 7:32 Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that it shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter: for they shall bury in Tophet, till there be no place.

Context: Jeremiah prophesying against the Valley of Hinnom (ge-Hinnom = gehenna). The site of child sacrifice will be renamed 'Valley of Slaughter' — death and burial, not ongoing torment. The OT background establishes gehenna as a place of death, slaughter, and corpse disposal.

Notes: Critical OT background for gehenna. The valley of Hinnom will be used for burial (corpse disposal) — 'they shall bury in Tophet, till there be no place.' Slaughter + burial = death, not eternal conscious torment.

docs.title: OT — 'worm shall not die, fire not quenched' — subjects are peger (carcasses/corpses)
docs.text:
Isaiah 66:24 And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

Context: Final verse of Isaiah. The righteous look upon the peger (carcasses/corpses) of the wicked. The subjects of the undying worm and unquenchable fire are DEAD BODIES, not living persons. Mark 9:43-48 alludes to this passage.

Notes: Parser confirms: peger (H6297, corpse) is Noun.mp.Cst — plural construct state. The subjects being consumed by worm and fire are already dead. The word peger is NEVER used for a living person in the OT — it exclusively means 'corpse/carcass.' The 'unquenchable' fire is fire that cannot be extinguished before completing its work.

docs.title: OT — 'man became a living soul (nephesh)' — creation formula
docs.text:
Genesis 2:7 And the LORD God formed man [of] the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

Context: The creation of man. The verb wayehi (hayah, H1961) is a transformation verb: man BECAME a living nephesh. Man did not receive a soul as a separate component — the composite entity of dust + breath IS the living nephesh.

Notes: Parser confirms: wayehi = Verb.Qal.Wayq.3ms of hayah (H1961, 'be/become'). nephesh = Noun.fs.Abs (H5315). chayah = Adj.fs.Abs (H2416, 'alive'). Man BECAME (wayehi) a living nephesh — the same phrase (nephesh chayyah) applied to animals in Gen 1:20,24.

docs.title: OT — 'the soul (nephesh) that sinneth, it shall die' — nephesh is mortal
docs.text:
Ezekiel 18:4 Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

Context: God declares all nepheshoth (souls) belong to Him. The nephesh that sins will muwth (die). Nephesh + muwth = the soul can die. This directly contradicts the doctrine of innate soul immortality.

Notes: Parser confirms: nephesh = Noun.fs.Abs (H5315). tamuwth = Verb.Qal.Impf.3fs of muwth (H4191, 'die'). The sinning nephesh dies — not 'is separated' or 'is tormented forever.' The nephesh co-occurs with muwth 47 times in the OT.

docs.title: OT — 'the soul (nephesh) that sinneth, it shall die' — repeated for emphasis
docs.text:
Ezekiel 18:20 The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

Context: Repeated declaration from Ezek 18:4. Individual responsibility: each nephesh that sins will die.

Notes: Repetition of the same formula: nephesh + muwth. The emphatic repetition in a single chapter establishes this as a settled principle, not an isolated statement.

docs.title: Counter-evidence — 'everlasting punishment' vs. 'life eternal' — kolasis not basanizo
docs.text:
Matthew 25:46 And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

Context: Sheep and goats judgment. The word for 'punishment' is kolasis (G2851), NOT basanismos (torment). Kolasis = penal infliction, from kolazo (to curtail/prune). The punishment is 'everlasting' (aionios) — the question is whether this describes everlasting duration of punishing or everlasting finality of the punishment.

Notes: Parser confirms: kolasin = N-ASF (accusative singular feminine) of kolasis G2851. aionion = A-ASF of aionios G166. The parallel structure ('everlasting punishment' // 'life eternal') uses the same adjective aionios for both, but the noun is kolasis (punishment), not basanismos (torment). Kolasis has only 2 NT occurrences (Matt 25:46 and 1 John 4:18).

docs.title: OT — wicked burned to ashes, stubble consumed — OT eschatological fire produces cessation
docs.text:
Malachi 4:1 For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. Malachi 4:2 But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. Malachi 4:3 And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do [this], saith the LORD of hosts.

Context: Last OT prophet's eschatological vision. The wicked become stubble, are burned up leaving 'neither root nor branch,' and become 'ashes under the soles of your feet.' Total consumption — not eternal preservation in flame.

Notes: The wicked become ashes (epher). They are trodden underfoot. The fire consumes completely — leaving nothing (neither root nor branch). This is the OT eschatological fire paradigm: total destruction, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Vocabulary differentiation — 'devoured' (humans) vs. 'tormented' (devil/beast/false prophet)
docs.text:
Revelation 20:9 And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them. Revelation 20:10 And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet [are], and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Context: Post-millennium judgment. In consecutive verses, John uses DIFFERENT verbs for different subjects: katephagen (devoured, G2719) for human armies (v.9); basanisthesontai (shall be tormented, G928) for the devil, beast, and false prophet (v.10).

Notes: Parser confirms: Rev 20:9 katephagen = V-2AAI-3S of katesthio (G2719), aorist active indicative — 'devoured' (a destruction verb). Rev 20:10 basanisthesontai = V-FPI-3P of basanizo (G928), future passive indicative — 'shall be tormented.' Different verbs for different subjects in consecutive verses. Humans are devoured (destroyed); non-human symbolic entities are tormented.

docs.title: Sozo/apollymi antonym pair — God 'able to save and to destroy'
docs.text:
James 4:12 There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?

Context: James declares that ONE lawgiver is 'able to save (sozo) and to destroy (apollymi).' The same verb pair as Matt 10:28's implicit structure. If sozo means 'give eternal life,' then apollymi means 'remove eternal life' — cessation.

Notes: Parser confirms: sosai = V-AAN of sozo (G4982, aorist active infinitive — 'to save'). apolesai = V-AAN of apollymi (G622, aorist active infinitive — 'to destroy'). Both complementary infinitives completing dynamenos (able). Identical grammatical structure to Matt 10:28: dynamenos + aorist active infinitive of apollymi. God's ability to destroy is presented as the counterpart of His ability to save.

docs.title: Only God has immortality (athanasia)
docs.text:
1 Timothy 6:16 Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom [be] honour and power everlasting. Amen.

Context: Paul's doxology. God ALONE (monos) has immortality (athanasia, G110). If only God possesses immortality, then humans do not inherently possess it — and the wicked cannot be tormented forever if they lack immortality.

Notes: Monos echon athanasian — 'alone having immortality.' The alpha-privative athanasia (a- + thanatos) = 'deathlessness.' Only God has it. Humans must 'put it on' (1 Cor 15:53-54) or 'seek' it (Rom 2:7).

docs.title: Mortals 'put on' immortality at resurrection — not inherently possessed
docs.text:
1 Corinthians 15:53 For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal [must] put on immortality. 1 Corinthians 15:54 So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

Context: Paul's resurrection argument. Immortality is something mortals 'put on' (enduo) at the resurrection — it is not presently possessed. If immortality must be acquired, the wicked (who do not receive it) cannot exist forever to be tormented.

Notes: Endysasthai athanasian — 'to put on immortality.' The clothing metaphor implies the mortal does not currently possess immortality. The righteous receive it at the resurrection; the wicked do not.

docs.title: Believers 'seek for immortality' — seeking what they do not have
docs.text:
Romans 2:7 To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life:

Context: Paul describing the judgment. Those who seek (zeteo, present active participle) immortality receive eternal life. You do not seek what you already possess.

Notes: Aphtharsia (G861, incorruption/immortality) is the object of seeking. The present active participle zetousin describes ongoing seeking — they do not yet have immortality.

docs.title: Wages of sin is death — thanatos as punishment
docs.text:
Romans 6:23 For the wages of sin [is] death; but the gift of God [is] eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Context: Paul's definitive statement: the wages of sin is thanatos (death, G2288), not endless torment. Death is contrasted with eternal life — they are mutually exclusive outcomes.

Notes: Thanatos (death) vs. zoe aionios (eternal life). If the punishment is death and the reward is life, then the punishment is the absence of life — not ongoing conscious existence in torment.

docs.title: Apollymi/life antithesis — 'not perish but have everlasting life'
docs.text:
John 3:16 For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

Context: The apollymi/zoe antithesis at its most famous. Those who believe receive eternal life; those who do not, perish (apollymi). Perishing is the alternative to life — not an alternative form of life.

Notes: Apolletai (V-2AMS-3S, aorist middle subjunctive) vs. zoen aionion. Perishing and everlasting life are mutually exclusive outcomes — you get one or the other.

docs.title: Everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord
docs.text:
2 Thessalonians 1:9 Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

Context: Paul describes the fate of the wicked: 'everlasting destruction' (olethros aionios). The word is olethros (G3639, destruction/ruin), not basanismos (torment). Modified by aionios — the destruction is permanent/irrevocable.

Notes: Olethros aionion — everlasting destruction. Not everlasting torment (basanismos aionios, which never appears in the NT). The destruction is from (apo) the presence of the Lord — the result of being separated from the source of all life.

docs.title: OT — Tree of life barred — immortality not inherent
docs.text:
Genesis 3:22 And the LORD God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever: Genesis 3:23 Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken. Genesis 3:24 So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

Context: After the fall, God bars access to the tree of life to prevent man from living forever. If humans already had an immortal soul, barring the tree would serve no purpose.

Notes: God explicitly prevents the sinful human from living forever. Immortality must be accessed through the tree of life — it is not inherent in human nature.

docs.title: Matthean judgment — 'burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire' — katakaio = consume
docs.text:
Matthew 3:12 Whose fan [is] in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

Context: John the Baptist's judgment imagery. The verb is katakaio (G2618, burn up/consume — 12 NT occurrences). Chaff is burned UP — consumed — not preserved in fire forever. The 'unquenchable' fire is fire that cannot be extinguished (it completes its work), not fire that burns forever.

Notes: Katakaio (G2618) = burn down/consume. The prefix kata- intensifies: burn COMPLETELY. All 12 NT occurrences describe total consumption. The chaff does not survive the burning.

docs.title: Matthean judgment — 'broad way that leads to destruction (apoleia)'
docs.text:
Matthew 7:13 Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide [is] the gate, and broad [is] the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:

Context: Sermon on the Mount. The broad way leads to apoleia (G684, destruction/perdition) — the noun cognate of apollymi. The destination is destruction, not torment.

Notes: Apoleia (G684) = the noun of apollymi. 20 NT occurrences. KJV translates as 'destruction' (5x) and 'perdition' (5x). Louw-Nida classifies it in domain 20.031 (Violence, Harm, Destroy) — the destruction domain, not a torment domain.

docs.title: Lake of fire = second death (thanatos, not basanismos)
docs.text:
Revelation 20:14 And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Context: The lake of fire is identified as 'the second death' (ho thanatos ho deuteros). The identifying word is thanatos (death), not basanismos (torment). When humans encounter the lake of fire, the text uses death vocabulary.

Notes: The lake of fire IS the second death. Death (thanatos) is the category, not torment (basanismos). The same lake produces different outcomes: death for humans, torment for the devil/beast/false prophet (v.10).

docs.title: Matthean judgment — tares burned, furnace of fire — katakaio destruction
docs.text:
Matthew 13:40 As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world. Matthew 13:41 The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity; Matthew 13:42 And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Parable of the tares. The tares are burned (katakaio) — consumed. The 'furnace of fire' is the same OT image from Mal 4:1. Wailing and gnashing describe the response to the judgment, not an ongoing state.

Notes: Katakaio (G2618) appears here for the burning of the tares. Same verb as Matt 3:12. The simile requires correspondence: as tares are consumed by fire, so the wicked are consumed. No torment vocabulary used.

docs.title: Everlasting fire 'prepared for the devil and his angels'
docs.text:
Matthew 25:41 Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

Context: Sheep and goats judgment. The 'everlasting fire' was prepared for the devil and his angels — not originally for humans. The fire is aionios (everlasting) — but as Sodom's 'eternal fire' produced ashes (Jude 1:7; 2 Pet 2:6), the adjective may describe the permanence of the result, not the duration of burning.

Notes: Aionios fire — same adjective used for 'eternal life' in v.46. The fire was prepared for non-human entities. Humans are sent there, but the vocabulary for what happens to them (v.46: kolasis, punishment) differs from the vocabulary for what happens to the devil (Rev 20:10: basanismos, torment).

docs.title: Markan parallel — gehenna + 'worm dieth not and fire is not quenched'
docs.text:
Mark 9:43 And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Mark 9:44 Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. Mark 9:45 And if thy foot offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter halt into life, than having two feet to be cast into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Mark 9:46 Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. Mark 9:47 And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out: it is better for thee to enter into the kingdom of God with one eye, than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire: Mark 9:48 Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.

Context: Mark's gehenna passage. The 'worm dieth not' allusion is to Isa 66:24, where the subjects are peger (carcasses/corpses). The worm is a decomposition agent feeding on dead bodies. 'Unquenchable' fire = fire that cannot be put out before completing its work.

Notes: The allusion to Isa 66:24 establishes the referent: the worm and fire act on corpses (peger), not living persons. The 'unquenchable' fire in the OT (Jer 17:27; Amos 5:6; Ezek 20:47-48) burned to completion — Jerusalem's fire was unquenchable but is not still burning.

docs.title: Counter-evidence — Rich man and Lazarus — basanizo in hades, not gehenna
docs.text:
Luke 16:23 And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom. Luke 16:24 And he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame. Luke 16:25 But Abraham said, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented. Luke 16:26 And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that [would come] from thence. Luke 16:27 Then he said, I pray thee therefore, father, that thou wouldest send him to my father's house: Luke 16:28 For I have five brethren; that he may testify unto them, lest they also come into this place of torment.

Context: Rich man and Lazarus parable. Uses basanizo (torment) in hades (G86, NOT gehenna G1067). The parabolic context, the pre-judgment timing (the rich man's brothers are still alive), and the use of hades rather than gehenna all raise questions about whether this passage describes the final state of the wicked or is a parabolic illustration using Second Temple imagery.

Notes: Basanizo (G928) appears here in hades (G86). NOT gehenna. The parable is set before the final judgment (the rich man's brothers are alive). Even if taken as descriptive, it describes an intermediate state in hades, not the final fate in gehenna. Gehenna and basanizo never co-occur in any NT passage.

docs.title: Counter-evidence — 'tormented with fire and brimstone...smoke ascends forever'
docs.text:
Revelation 14:10 The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: Revolution 14:11 And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

Context: Angel's warning about beast-worshippers. Uses basanizo (torment). The subjects are specifically those who worship the beast. The smoke 'ascending forever' echoes Isa 34:10 (Edom's smoke ascends forever — yet Edom is not still burning). The 'no rest day nor night' may refer to the period of torment, not to eternal duration.

Notes: Basanizo appears here for beast-worshippers specifically. The smoke-ascending-forever language echoes Isa 34:10 where Edom's smoke 'shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever' — yet Edom is a physical location that is not still burning. The formula expresses the irrevocable, irreversible nature of the judgment, not necessarily its infinite duration.

docs.title: Sodom as example of 'eternal fire' yet 'turned to ashes' (2 Pet 2:6)
docs.text:
Jude 1:7 Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

Context: Sodom suffered 'eternal fire' — yet 2 Pet 2:6 says Sodom was 'turned to ashes.' The 'eternal fire' produced complete destruction (ashes), not ongoing burning.

Notes: Aionios fire produced ashes. The fire is 'eternal' in its effect (the destruction is permanent and irreversible), not in its duration. Sodom is not still burning.

docs.title: Sodom 'turned to ashes' — 'eternal fire' produced complete destruction
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:6 And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned [them] with an overthrow, making [them] an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

Context: Peter's example: Sodom's 'eternal fire' (Jude 1:7) turned the cities to ashes. The result of the eschatological fire is ashes — complete destruction — not ongoing burning.

Notes: Tephrosas — 'turning to ashes.' The verb explicitly describes the result: ashes. This is the interpretive key for 'eternal fire' — it produces permanent destruction, not eternal burning.

docs.title: OT — Valley of Hinnom as geographic boundary — earliest ge-Hinnom reference
docs.text:
Joshua 15:8 And the border went up by the valley of the son of Hinnom unto the south side of the Jebusite; the same [is] Jerusalem: and the border went up to the top of the mountain that [lieth] before the valley of Hinnom westward, which [is] at the end of the valley of the giants northward:

Context: Earliest OT reference to the Valley of Hinnom (ge-Hinnom). A neutral geographic boundary marker — the valley had no negative associations yet.

Notes: The valley of Hinnom begins as a geographic term. Its associations with child sacrifice, cursing, and eschatological judgment developed later.

docs.title: OT — Ahaz burns children in Valley of Hinnom — ge-Hinnom + child sacrifice
docs.text:
2 Chronicles 28:3 Moreover he burnt incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and burnt his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen whom the LORD had cast out before the children of Israel.

Context: King Ahaz practices child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom. This begins the valley's association with fire and death.

Notes: The valley of Hinnom becomes associated with fire + death through child sacrifice — the very associations Jesus invokes when he uses 'gehenna.'

docs.title: OT — Manasseh burns children in Valley of Hinnom
docs.text:
2 Chronicles 33:6 And he caused his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom: also he observed times, and used enchantments, and used witchcraft, and dealt with a familiar spirit, and with wizards: he wrought much evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.

Context: King Manasseh continues the child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom.

Notes: Second king using the valley for child sacrifice. The fire in the Valley of Hinnom consumed its victims — they did not survive the fire.

docs.title: OT — Topheth prepared for the king, fire and wood
docs.text:
Isaiah 30:33 For Tophet [is] ordained of old; yea, for the king it is prepared; he hath made [it] deep [and] large: the pile thereof [is] fire and much wood; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of brimstone, doth kindle it.

Context: Isaiah uses Topheth (in the Valley of Hinnom) as a judgment metaphor. Prepared by YHWH for the king (the Assyrian). Fire, wood, and brimstone — destruction imagery, not ongoing torment.

Notes: Topheth in the valley of Hinnom prepared by God as a burning place. The breath of the LORD kindles it — divine judgment imagery. Fire + brimstone = total consumption.

docs.title: OT — Josiah defiles Topheth in Valley of Hinnom
docs.text:
2 Kings 23:10 And he defiled Topheth, which [is] in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.

Context: Josiah's reform. He defiles Topheth to end child sacrifice. This action contributes to the valley's cursed status.

Notes: Josiah defiles the valley — making it permanently unclean. This contributes to its use as a refuse dump and later as a metaphor for eschatological judgment.

docs.title: OT — 'his thoughts perish' at death — unconsciousness at death
docs.text:
Psalms 146:4 His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

Context: At death, the person's thoughts perish (abad, H6). Same verb used throughout the OT for destruction/cessation.

Notes: Thoughts perish (abad) at death. The dead have no conscious activity — their machshebah (thoughts/plans) cease. This is inconsistent with conscious experience after death.

docs.title: OT — Valley renamed 'Valley of Slaughter'
docs.text:
Jeremiah 19:6 Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that this place shall no more be called Tophet, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of slaughter.

Context: Jeremiah's prophecy. The Valley of Hinnom is renamed 'Valley of Slaughter' — death and killing vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

Notes: Slaughter (haregah) = killing/death. The valley's prophetic name describes death and killing, not ongoing torture.

docs.title: Crux text — God destroys both soul and body in gehenna; apokteino vs apollymi verb shift
docs.text:
Matthew 10:28 And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: Jesus' commissioning discourse to the twelve apostles. The central verse of this study. Jesus contrasts what humans can do (kill the body only) with what God can do (destroy both soul and body in gehenna). The verb shifts from apokteino (kill) to apollymi (destroy), signaling a qualitative escalation. The kai...kai correlative construction ('both soul and body') emphasizes totality. The location is gehenna (G1067), where destruction occurs.

  • καὶ (G2532) — CONJ — μὴ μή G3361 [PRT-N]
  • φοβεῖσθε (G5399) — V-PNM-2P — Pres M/P Impv Pl secondPers
  • ἀπὸ (G575) — PREP — τῶν ὁ G3588 [T-GPM] Gen Pl M
  • ἀποκτεννόντων (G615) — V-PAP-GPM — Pres Act Ptcp Gen Pl M
  • τὸ (G3588) — T-ASN — Acc Sg N
  • σῶμα, (G4983) — N-ASN — Acc Sg N
  • δὲ (G1161) — CONJ — ψυχὴν ψυχή G5590 [N-ASF] Acc Sg F
  • μὴ (G3361) — PRT-N — δυναμένων δύναμαι G1410 [V-PNP-GPM] Pres M/P Ptcp Gen Pl M
  • δυνάμενον (G1410) — V-PNP-ASM — Pres M/P Ptcp Acc Sg M
  • ἀπολέσαι (G622) — V-AAN — Aor Act Inf
  • ἐν (G1722) — PREP — γεέννῃ. γέεννα G1067 [N-DSF] Dat Sg F

Notes: Parser verified: phobeisthe = V-PNM-2P (present middle/passive imperative — 'stop fearing'); apokteino = V-AAN (aorist active infinitive — 'to kill'); apollymi = V-AAN (aorist active infinitive — 'to destroy'); geenne = N-DSF (dative singular feminine — 'in gehenna'). Both infinitives complement participial forms of dynamai (being able). The kai...kai correlative binds psyche and soma into a single object of apolesai.

docs.title: Matthean phobeo — angel says 'Fear not ye' — phobeo negated as reassurance
docs.text:
Matthew 28:5 And the angel answered and said unto the women, Fear not ye: for I know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified.

Context: Resurrection morning. The angel at the empty tomb tells the women 'me phobeisthe' — present imperative prohibition, same construction as Matt 10:28. The 'fear not' pattern bookends Matthew's Gospel.

Notes: Phobeo in 'fear not' command — me phobeisthe (V-PNM-2P). Same morphological form as 10:28a. Part of Matthew's pattern of 'fear not' commands (1:20, 10:26, 10:28, 10:31, 14:27, 17:7, 28:5, 28:10).

docs.title: Matthean phobeo context (1:20) — sozo from sins — fear/salvation frame
docs.text:
Matthew 1:21 And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.

Context: Angel's announcement to Joseph, immediately following the first 'fear not' command in Matthew (1:20 — me phobethes, aorist subjunctive). Jesus' mission is defined by sozo (save) — the antonym of apollymi. The fear/salvation frame established here carries through the Gospel.

Notes: First occurrence of sozo (G4982) in Matthew, paired with the first phobeo 'fear not' command (1:20). The sozo-apollymi antithesis established at the beginning of Matthew's Gospel.

docs.title: Matthean phobeo — 'Fear not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows'
docs.text:
Matthew 10:31 Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows.

Context: Third 'fear not' command in the pericope (10:26, 10:28, 10:31). Following the sparrow analogy (10:29-30), Jesus concludes the fear hierarchy argument with reassurance: if God watches sparrows, He values His disciples far more. The implicit a fortiori argument: if God cares for sparrows, how much more for you?

Notes: Me phobeisthe (V-PNM-2P) — same form as 10:28. This is the third and final 'fear not' in the pericope, shifting from warning (10:28) to reassurance (10:31).

docs.title: Matthean judgment — wicked severed, furnace of fire — parallel judgment vocabulary
docs.text:
Matthew 13:49 So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just, Matthew 13:50 And shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Parable of the net. Parallels the wheat-and-tares parable (13:40-42). The wicked are severed from the just and cast into the 'furnace of fire' (kaminos tou pyros). Same judgment vocabulary as 13:42. No torment vocabulary used — the furnace imagery describes destruction, not ongoing preservation in fire.

Notes: Parallel to Matt 13:40-42. The wicked are cast into the furnace — same OT furnace imagery from Mal 4:1. 'Wailing and gnashing of teeth' describes the response to the judgment, not an ongoing state of torment.

docs.title: Matthean judgment — Sodom/Gomorrah comparison — proportionality of judgment
docs.text:
Matthew 10:15 Verily I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.

Context: Same commissioning discourse as 10:28. Jesus compares the judgment on cities that reject the apostles with the judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah. The 'more tolerable' language implies proportionality — degrees of judgment, not one-size-fits-all eternal torment.

Notes: Proportional judgment language: 'more tolerable' (anektoteron) for Sodom than for the rejecting city. Proportionality implies finite, measured judgment. Sodom's 'eternal fire' (Jude 1:7) produced ashes (2 Pet 2:6) — the fire's result was destruction, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Matthean judgment — Capernaum/Sodom comparison — degree of judgment
docs.text:
