Fear noun — companion to phobeo (G5399) verb. The fear of God concept runs through both testaments. In Matt 28:4, phobos is used of the guards' terror at the resurrection angel.

Semantic categories: terror, reverence, fear of God

Key verses: Matt 28:4, Rev 14:7, 1 Pet 2:17

Relevance: Noun form of phobeo. The 'fear of God' concept in Matt 10:28 uses phobeo (verb), while Matt 28:4 uses phobos (noun) for terror. Both forms participate in Matthew's fear vocabulary.

docs.title: H3372 — yare
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H3372-yare.md

Occurrences: 414

Primary Hebrew fear/revere verb. LXX maps yare to phobeo 241 times (PMI 5.75, score 31.55) — the dominant Hebrew equivalent. Three Hebrew fear words (yare = reverence, eimah = terror, pachad = dread) collapse into Greek phobos/phobeo, requiring context to determine meaning.

Semantic categories: reverence for God, terror before danger, awe before the divine

Key verses: Deut 6:13, Ps 111:10, Isa 8:13

Relevance: OT background for phobeo in Matt 10:28. The LXX yare→phobeo bridge (241x) establishes semantic continuity between OT 'fear of God' and Jesus' 'fear him who can destroy' command.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Eternal/everlasting adjective. Key qualifier in Matt 25:46 ('everlasting punishment'), Rev 14:11. The Hebrews aionios pattern (eternal redemption Heb 9:12, eternal judgment Heb 6:2, eternal salvation Heb 5:9) shows aionios can describe the permanent RESULTS of completed acts — not necessarily infinite duration of process.

Semantic categories: eternal, everlasting, age-lasting

Key verses: Matt 25:46, John 3:16, Heb 9:12

Relevance: Key adjective in Matt 25:46. Whether 'everlasting punishment' means everlasting duration of punishing or everlasting finality of the punishment depends on whether kolasis (punishment) describes a process or a result.

docs.title: G4442 — pyr
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4442-pyr.md

Occurrences: 74

Fire — gehenna's dominant collocate. Gehenna + fire appears 6 times in the NT. Fire vocabulary in Matthew's judgment passages: gehenna fire (5:22, 18:9), unquenchable fire (3:12), everlasting fire (18:8, 25:41), furnace of fire (13:42,50).

Semantic categories: literal fire, judgment fire, purifying fire, divine presence

Key verses: Matt 5:22, Matt 3:12, Matt 25:41, Rev 20:14

Relevance: Fire is the dominant collocate of gehenna. The fire imagery throughout Matthew's judgment passages consistently describes consumption/destruction, not ongoing preservation.

docs.title: G110 — athanasia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G110-athanasia.md

Occurrences: 3

Immortality (alpha-privative: a- + thanatos = deathlessness). Only 3 NT occurrences: 1 Tim 6:16 (God alone has it), 1 Cor 15:53-54 (mortals put it on at resurrection). If only God possesses immortality, humans do not inherently have it. The wicked, who do not receive it at the resurrection, cannot be tormented forever.

Semantic categories: divine attribute, eschatological gift to the redeemed

Key verses: 1 Tim 6:16, 1 Cor 15:53-54

Relevance: Anthropological prerequisite for interpreting Matt 10:28. If humans do not inherently possess immortality, the wicked cannot experience endless torment — they would simply cease to exist when destroyed.

docs.title: G2618 — katakaio
docs.text:
Occurrences: 12

Verb from kata (down) + kaio (burn). 12 NT occurrences. Definition: to burn down (to the ground), to consume. KJV: 'burn/burned/burn up/burned up/utterly burned' — all forms describe complete consumption. Key judgment passages: Matt 3:12 (burn up chaff), Matt 13:30,40 (burn tares), Rev 17:16, 18:8, Heb 13:11. All 12 occurrences describe total consumption — nothing survives the burning.

Semantic categories: total consumption by fire, judgment parable vocabulary

Key verses: Matt 3:12, Matt 13:40, Rev 17:16, Rev 18:8

Relevance: Key judgment parable verb in Matthew. The prefix kata- intensifies: burn COMPLETELY/DOWN. When Matthew uses katakaio for the fate of the wicked (tares burned, chaff burned up), the verb inherently means total consumption.

docs.title: G2719 — katesthio
docs.text:
Occurrences: 20

Verb from kata + esthio (to eat). 15 NT occurrences. Definition: to eat down, devour. Used in Rev 20:9 for what happens to human armies: fire 'devoured' (katephagen, V-2AAI-3S) them. A destruction verb — devouring produces cessation, not preservation.

Semantic categories: complete consumption / devouring, metaphorical consumption

Key verses: Rev 20:9, Rev 11:5, Gal 5:15

Relevance: Rev 20:9 uses katesthio (devoured) for human armies, while the very next verse (20:10) uses basanizo (tormented) for the devil, beast, and false prophet. This vocabulary differentiation by subject is theologically critical: humans are devoured (destroyed), non-human entities are tormented.

docs.title: H1516 — gay/ge
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H1516-gayʼ.md

Occurrences: 67

Valley (ge) — the geographic term underlying gehenna. Valley of Hinnom (ge-Hinnom) = gehenna. OT trajectory: geographic boundary (Josh 15:8) → child sacrifice site (2 Chr 28:3, 33:6) → prophetically cursed 'Valley of Slaughter' (Jer 7:31-32, 19:6) → eschatological metaphor.

Semantic categories: geographic term, judgment site

Key verses: Josh 15:8, Jer 7:31-32, 2 Ki 23:10

Relevance: OT geographic background for gehenna (G1067). The Valley of Hinnom was a real location associated with fire, death, and divine curse — not with ongoing torment.

docs.title: G86 — hades
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G86-háidēs.md

Occurrences: 11

Realm of the dead. 10 NT occurrences. KJV: 'hell.' Equivalent to Hebrew sheol (H7585). Morally neutral — the state/place of all the dead. DISTINCT from gehenna: hades = temporary holding place before judgment; gehenna = place of final judgment/destruction. Luke 16:23 places the rich man in hades (not gehenna). This distinction is critical for interpreting counter-evidence texts.

Semantic categories: realm of the dead, unseen world

Key verses: Luke 16:23, Rev 20:13-14, Acts 2:27

Relevance: The hades/gehenna distinction is critical. Luke 16:23 (rich man) is set in hades, NOT gehenna. Basanizo appears with hades (Luke 16) but NEVER with gehenna. The two 'hell' words have different referents.

docs.title: G2222 — zoe
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2222-zoe.md

Occurrences: 134

Life — particularly eternal/spiritual life. The primary antonym of thanatos (death). In the life-vs-gehenna contrast (Matt 18:9; Mark 9:43,45,47), zoe is the alternative to gehenna — life vs. destruction, not happiness vs. suffering.

Semantic categories: eternal life, spiritual life, biological vitality

Key verses: John 3:16, Matt 18:9, Matt 25:46, Rom 6:23

Relevance: The life/gehenna antithesis in Matt 18:9 frames the alternatives: 'enter into life' vs. 'cast into gehenna.' Life and gehenna are mutually exclusive outcomes. Similarly, John 3:16: 'not perish but have everlasting life.'

docs.title: G2920 — krisis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2920-krisis.md

Occurrences: 48

Judgment — the judicial process/verdict. Paired with gehenna in Matt 23:33 ('damnation of hell'). Gehenna is associated with krisis (judgment vocabulary), not basanismos (torment vocabulary).

Semantic categories: judicial process, divine judgment, condemnation

Key verses: Matt 23:33, John 5:24, Heb 9:27

Relevance: Gehenna collocates with krisis (judgment), not basanizo (torment). Matt 23:33: 'how can ye escape the krisis (damnation/judgment) of gehenna?'

docs.title: G2919 — krino
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2919-krino.md

Occurrences: 132

To judge — the verb form of krisis. Judgment vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

Semantic categories: to judge, to condemn, to assess

Key verses: Matt 7:1, John 12:48, Acts 17:31

Relevance: Verb form of krisis. Judgment vocabulary associated with gehenna passages.

docs.title: Evidence Classifications — etc7-20-matthew-10-28
docs.text: Per-item Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for all positional E-items and N-items.

docs.title: E-Item Classifications (Tree 3)
docs.text:
E1 (Matt 10:28) -- "God is able to destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destroy" (apollymi, G622) applied to "both soul and body" (human persons). Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject of the destruction is "both soul and body" -- the complete human person. The one who destroys is God ("him which is able"). Subject is a literal human being (the human whose soul and body are destroyed). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: apolesai = V-AAN (aorist active infinitive of apollymi, G622). Complementary infinitive completing dynamenon (V-PNP-ASM, present middle/passive participle of dynamai). The kai...kai correlative (G2532...G2532) binds psychen (N-ASF) and soma (N-ASN) into a single direct object. No editorial punctuation issue. No ambiguous particle. The verb apollymi means "destroy fully" (apo + ollymi); no alternative parsing yields a torment reading. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct speech of Jesus in a commissioning discourse (Matt 10:1-42). Didactic -- direct teaching to the twelve apostles about what to fear and why. Not parabolic, not apocalyptic, not typological. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E11 (Matt 21:41, apollymi = destroy wicked tenants), E12 (Matt 22:7, apollymi = destroy murderers + burn city), E6 (Ezek 18:4, nephesh that sins shall die), E10 (Rom 6:23, wages of sin is death), E15 (Mal 4:1,3, wicked become ashes). No E-item states that the soul survives destruction in gehenna. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E6 (Ezek 18:4) -- "The soul (nephesh) that sinneth, it shall die (muwth)" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "die" (muwth, H4191) applied to "the soul" (nephesh, H5315). Death/cessation vocabulary applied to the soul. Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject is "the soul (nephesh) that sinneth" -- a human being described as a nephesh. Literal human subject. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): Parser output: tamuwth = Verb.Qal.Impf.3fs of muwth (H4191, "die"). nephesh = Noun.fs.Abs (H5315). The Qal imperfect of muwth is unambiguous: "shall die." No alternative parsing exists. The nephesh co-occurs with muwth 47 times in the OT. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Prophetic oracle -- direct divine speech ("Behold, all souls are mine...the soul that sinneth, it shall die"). This is direct-speech prophecy ("Thus says the Lord" type). Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1 (Matt 10:28, God destroys soul and body), E10 (Rom 6:23, wages of sin is death), E15 (Mal 4:1,3, wicked become ashes). Repeated verbatim in Ezek 18:20. No E-item contradicts that the sinning nephesh dies. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E9 (1 Tim 6:16) -- "God alone (monos) has immortality (athanasia)" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- The verse denies immortality to all beings except God. By stating God "alone" has immortality, it implicitly states that humans do not possess inherent immortality. The wicked, lacking immortality, cannot be sustained in eternal torment. This is destruction-direction vocabulary (denying the prerequisite for ECT). Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject is God ("who only hath immortality"). The statement is about God's unique attribute. The implication concerns humans (they lack what God alone has). Subject is God -- but the evidence claim is about what this means for humans. The subject of the E-statement itself is God, not a symbolic entity. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): monos echon athanasian -- "alone having immortality." Monos (A-NSM) modifies the implied subject (God). Echon (V-PAP-NSM) = present active participle of echo. Athanasian (N-ASF) = alpha-privative noun (a- + thanatos = "deathlessness"). The grammar is unambiguous: "alone having deathlessness." PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Pauline epistle -- direct didactic teaching in a doxological passage. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with 1 Cor 15:53-54 (mortals "put on" immortality -- they do not have it inherently) and Rom 2:7 (believers "seek for" immortality -- you do not seek what you have). No E-item states that humans inherently possess immortality. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E10 (Rom 6:23) -- "The wages of sin is death (thanatos)" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "death" (thanatos, G2288) as the penalty for sin. Death/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject is "the wages of sin" -- the penalty received by sinning humans. Subject is human sinners (implied). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): opsonia tes hamartias thanatos -- "the wages of sin [is] death." Thanatos (N-NSM) is the predicate nominative. No ambiguity in parsing: death is the stated wage. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Pauline epistle -- direct didactic teaching. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1 (Matt 10:28, destruction), E6 (Ezek 18:4, nephesh dies), E15 (Mal 4:1,3, ashes). Contrasted with "eternal life" in the same verse, establishing death and life as mutually exclusive. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E11 (Matt 21:41) -- "He will miserably destroy (apollymi) those wicked men" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destroy" (apollymi, G622) applied to "those wicked men." Destruction vocabulary applied to the wicked. Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects being destroyed are "those wicked men" (kakous kakos apolesei autous). Within the parable, these are the wicked tenants. However, the answer is given by the audience (the chief priests and Pharisees, Matt 21:45), describing what a vineyard lord would do. The parable's tenants are figurative, but the answer states a general principle about what happens to the wicked. FAIL -- subject is an allegorical character in a parable (the wicked tenants are narrative figures illustrating a point).
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
    • RC1: Gate 1 fails -- subject is a parabolic character (wicked tenant), not a literal human facing eschatological judgment.
    • RC2: Corrected observation: "In a parable, a vineyard lord destroys wicked tenants -- illustrating judgment by authority."
    • RC3: Re-enter Step 1. The corrected observation still contains destruction vocabulary ("destroy") but the parabolic context prevents it from being direct evidence about human eschatological fate. Neither V1 nor V2 apply to parabolic characters as evidence about literal human fate.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails. Classification revised to Neutral.

E12 (Matt 22:7) -- "King destroyed (apollymi) those murderers and burned up their city" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destroyed" (apollymi) + "burned up" (empiprhmi). Destruction + fire vocabulary applied to "those murderers." Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects are "those murderers" -- characters within the parable of the marriage feast. The king represents God, the murderers represent those who reject the invitation. FAIL -- subject is an allegorical character in a parable.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
    • RC1: Gate 1 fails -- subject is a parabolic character.
    • RC2: Corrected observation: "In a parable, a king destroys murderers and burns their city -- illustrating judgment by authority using destruction + fire vocabulary."
    • RC3: Re-enter Step 1. Parabolic context prevents direct application to human eschatological fate. Neither V1 nor V2 apply.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails. Classification revised to Neutral.

E15 (Mal 4:1,3) -- "Wicked shall be stubble...burned up...shall be ashes under the soles of your feet" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "burned up" + "ashes" + "stubble" -- destruction/cessation vocabulary applied to "all that do wickedly." Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subjects are "all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly" -- literal wicked humans in an eschatological oracle. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): saraph (H8313, "burn") in Piel = "burn up." epher (H665) = "ashes." qash (H7179) = "stubble." The grammar is unambiguous: the wicked become ashes. The simile vocabulary (stubble, root, branch, ashes) all denote complete consumption. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Prophetic oracle -- direct eschatological prophecy from Malachi. "Behold, the day cometh, saith the LORD of hosts." Direct-speech prophecy. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1 (destroy soul and body), E6 (nephesh dies), E10 (wages of sin is death). No E-item contradicts that the wicked become ashes. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E17 (Rev 14:10-11) -- "He shall be tormented with fire and brimstone...smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever" -- Classified: ECT

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 -- "tormented" (basanizo, G928), "no rest day nor night" -- conscious-ongoing-existence vocabulary applied to "whosoever receiveth the mark." Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects are "whosoever receiveth the mark of his name" and "whosoever worshippeth the beast and his image." These are human beings within the apocalyptic beast-worship scenario. The subjects are described as humans who worship the beast. PASS (with note: the subjects are human, though the context is apocalyptic).
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): basanisthesetai = V-FPI-3S of basanizo (G928), future passive indicative. "Shall be tormented." The grammar is unambiguous for the verb. However, the "smoke ascending forever" phrase uses eis aionas aionon -- this is a formulaic expression whose meaning is debated (does it denote infinite duration, or is it a judgment-finality formula as in Isa 34:10?). The grammar itself does not resolve this -- it is a legitimate reading either way. The "no rest day nor night" phrase hemera kai nuktos is a temporal phrase that could describe the period of torment or an eternal state. PASS (the grammar supports the ECT reading, though alternatives exist at the semantic level).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Apocalyptic vision -- the passage occurs in the angel's proclamation within the Revelation judgment sequence. FAIL -- apocalyptic genre. The passage is part of the apocalyptic vision of Revelation, not didactic prose.
  • Step 3 Reclassification:
    • RC1: Gate 3 fails -- genre is apocalyptic.
    • RC2: Corrected observation: "In an apocalyptic vision, an angel declares that beast-worshippers will be tormented with fire and their smoke ascends forever."
    • RC3: Re-enter Step 1. The corrected observation still contains torment vocabulary (basanizo) -- V2 applies. But the apocalyptic genre means this observation does not constitute didactic teaching about human fate. Apocalyptic imagery requires genre-appropriate interpretation.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails. Classification revised to Neutral.

Note: The reclassification to Neutral does not mean the passage says nothing about the fate of the wicked. It means that as an apocalyptic text, its vocabulary does not carry the same evidentiary weight as didactic passages for establishing doctrine about human fate. The passage remains relevant as an I-tier item.

E19 (John 3:16) -- "Whosoever believeth in him should not perish (apollymi) but have everlasting life" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "perish" (apollymi, G622) -- destruction/cessation vocabulary for those who do not believe. Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subject is "whosoever believeth" / the implied counter-group "whosoever does not believe." Literal humans. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): apolletai = V-2AMS-3S (aorist middle subjunctive of apollymi). "Should not perish" -- the hina me clause gives the purpose: so that the believer does not perish. The apollymi/zoe antithesis is grammatically clear: perish and everlasting life are mutually exclusive. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Johannine discourse -- direct teaching of Jesus (or narrator's comment). Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1 (destroy in gehenna), E6 (nephesh dies), E10 (wages of sin is death), E15 (ashes). The perish/life antithesis matches the gehenna/life antithesis in Matt 18:9. PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E20 (2 Thess 1:9) -- "Punished with everlasting destruction (olethros aionios)" -- Classified: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 -- "destruction" (olethros, G3639) -- destruction vocabulary applied to the wicked. Candidate: CONDITIONALIST.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The subjects are "them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel" (v.8) -- literal human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): olethron aionion = "everlasting destruction." Olethros (N-ASM) = destruction/ruin. Aionios (A-ASM) = everlasting. The grammar is unambiguous: the punishment is described as destruction, not torment. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Pauline epistle -- direct didactic teaching about the second coming. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with E1, E6, E10, E15. "Everlasting destruction" parallels Matt 10:28's "destroy in gehenna." PASS.
  • Result: All gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

docs.title: N-Item Classifications (Tree 4)
docs.text:
N1 -- "Same-discourse word pair psyche+apollymi means 'lose one's life' (10:39), governing the interpretation of psyche+apollymi in 10:28" -- Based on: E1, E3 -- Classified: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that 10:39 uses psyche+apollymi to mean "lose one's life"? Yes -- both sides agree that 10:39 means "lose one's life." However, would an ECT scholar agree this GOVERNS the meaning in 10:28? Not necessarily -- an ECT scholar would argue that the different context (eschatological judgment vs. discipleship paradox) produces a different sense. FAIL.
  • Result: N-Test 1 fails. The observation that the word pair appears in both verses is E-tier (both sides agree). The claim that 10:39 GOVERNS 10:28's meaning requires choosing between two hermeneutical approaches (same-discourse semantics vs. context-dependent semantics). Reclassified as I-A (evidence-extending inference, Cond. direction).

N2 -- "When Matthew records authority figures using apollymi on the wicked (10:28, 21:41, 22:7), the meaning is actual destruction in all cases" -- Based on: E1, E11, E12 -- Classified: Cond.

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would an ECT scholar agree that apollymi means actual destruction in all three passages? For 10:28, an ECT scholar would argue apollymi can mean "ruin" (ongoing state of ruin/loss) rather than cessation. The meaning of apollymi in 10:28 is precisely what is disputed. FAIL.
  • Result: N-Test 1 fails. The claim that apollymi means "actual destruction" in judgment contexts requires choosing between the "destroy/cease" and "ruin/ongoing loss" senses of apollymi. Reclassified as I-A (evidence-extending inference, Cond. direction).

Note: E11 and E12 were reclassified to Neutral (parabolic subjects), which weakens the pattern claim. The remaining foundation is E1 alone (Matt 10:28 itself). The inference that apollymi = cessation in 10:28 remains I-A because it extends E1's destruction vocabulary using the lexical data (apollymi's Louw-Nida classification in Destroy/Non-exist domains, the abad→apollymi LXX bridge).

N3 -- "No gehenna passage in any NT uses basanizo for human subjects" -- Based on: E5 -- Classified: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):
  • N-Test 1 (Universal agreement): Would both sides agree that gehenna and basanizo never co-occur for human subjects? Yes -- this is a verifiable textual fact. Both sides can cross-reference the 12 gehenna and 12 basanizo occurrences and confirm zero overlap. PASS.
  • N-Test 2 (No interpretation): Is this the only possible conclusion? Yes -- it is a factual observation about vocabulary distribution, not an interpretation. PASS.
  • N-Test 3 (Zero added concepts): Does this add anything beyond the source E-item? No -- E5 states the collocation data; N3 states the implication of zero overlap. PASS.
  • Gate 0 passes. Proceed to Tree 3.
  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: Neither V1 (destruction vocabulary) nor V2 (torment vocabulary). This is a factual observation about vocabulary distribution. Neither side's vocabulary applies.
  • Result: Neutral stands. This is a shared factual observation both sides must accept.

docs.title: CONCLUSION — Matthew 10:28: Same-Author Usage and the Fate of the Wicked
Question
docs.text: Matthew 10:28 -- "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." What does this verse teach about the fate of the wicked? Same-author usage analysis of psyche (G5590), apollymi (G622), gehenna (G1067), and phobeo (G5399) in Matthew's Gospel.

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: Matthew 10:28 teaches that God possesses the ability to destroy the complete person -- both soul and body -- in gehenna. The verb Jesus uses for God's action is apollymi (G622, "destroy"), not basanizo (G928, "torment"). Same-author analysis of Matthew's Gospel shows that apollymi in judgment contexts describes actual destruction, that psyche denotes physical life or the whole person (not an immortal soul-component), that gehenna consistently collocates with destruction vocabulary and never with torment vocabulary, and that the fear hierarchy commands ongoing reverential fear toward a God whose power encompasses total destruction.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
God Destroys Soul and Body in Gehenna (Matthew 10:28) And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Same-Discourse Word Pair (Matthew 10:39) He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it.

The Soul That Sins Dies (Ezekiel 18:4) Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

Wages of Sin Is Death (Romans 6:23) For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

God Alone Has Immortality (1 Timothy 6:16) Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen.

Perish or Everlasting Life (John 3:16) For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

Wicked Become Ashes (Malachi 4:1,3) For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. ... And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do this, saith the LORD of hosts.

Everlasting Destruction (2 Thessalonians 1:9) Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power.

docs.title: The Verb Shift: Apokteino to Apollymi
docs.text:
The grammatical center of Matt 10:28 is the verb shift from apokteino (G615, "kill") to apollymi (G622, "destroy"). Both verbs appear as aorist active infinitives (V-AAN) complementing participial forms of dynamai ("to be able"). The first half of the verse describes what human persecutors can do: they are able to kill (apokteino) the body, but they are not able to kill the soul. The second half describes what God can do: He is able to destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna.

The shift from apokteino to apollymi is not stylistic variation. If Jesus intended to say that God merely "kills" the soul in the same way humans kill the body, he could have repeated apokteino. Instead he escalated to apollymi -- a stronger verb meaning "to destroy fully," from the compound apo ("away from, completely") + ollymi ("destroy"). The lexical data confirms this: Louw-Nida classifies apollymi in the Violence/Destroy domain (20.003) and the Exist/Non-exist domain (13.003). No lexicon places apollymi in a torment domain. The LXX maps Hebrew abad (H6, "perish/destroy") to apollymi 141 times (PMI 6.14), making apollymi the canonical NT heir to the OT's primary destruction verb. When the OT says the wicked "perish" (abad, Ps 37:20; Ps 146:4), the Greek translation uses apollymi -- the same verb Jesus uses in Matt 10:28 for what God does to soul and body in gehenna.

The aorist aspect of both infinitives (apokteinai and apolesai) presents these actions as complete events -- bounded acts of killing and destroying, not ongoing processes. The grammar describes what agents are able to accomplish as completed actions, not states they maintain indefinitely.

docs.title: Same-Author Usage: Psyche in Matthew's Gospel
docs.text:
Psyche (G5590, 105 NT occurrences) appears sixteen times across Matthew's Gospel. The distribution falls into two semantic categories. Eight occurrences denote physical life: Matt 2:20 (those who sought the child's "life" are dead), 6:25 (take no thought for your "life" regarding food and drink, twice), 10:39 (lose one's "life" for Christ's sake, twice), 16:25 (save/lose one's "life," twice), and 20:28 (give his "life" a ransom). Eight denote the whole person or inner self: Matt 10:28 (soul and body destroyed in gehenna, twice), 11:29 (rest for your "souls"), 12:18 (God's "soul" well pleased), 16:26 (what profit to lose one's own "soul," twice), 22:37 (love God with all your "soul"), and 26:38 ("my soul" is sorrowful unto death).

The most significant datum for interpreting 10:28 is Matt 10:39. In the same commissioning discourse, just 11 verses later, Matthew uses the identical word pair psyche + apollymi to mean "lose one's life" -- not "destroy an immaterial soul." The parser confirms morphological identity: psyche appears as N-ASF (accusative singular feminine) in both verses. The word pair that in 10:28 describes divine judgment (God destroys both soul and body) in 10:39 describes the discipleship paradox (whoever loses his life finds it). The same-discourse proximity makes 10:39 the closest contextual control for the meaning of psyche in 10:28.

Matt 26:38 adds another datum: Jesus says "my psyche is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death (heos thanatou)." Jesus describes his own psyche as approaching death. If psyche were inherently immortal, the phrase would be incoherent -- an immortal entity cannot approach death. Matthew records Jesus treating his own psyche as mortal.

The OT background reinforces this reading. The LXX maps nephesh (H5315, 788 OT occurrences) to psyche in approximately six hundred instances (87% mapping rate). Man became (wayehi, transformation verb) a living nephesh (Gen 2:7) -- man IS a nephesh, not a body that has a nephesh. The same phrase "nephesh chayyah" (living soul/creature) applies to animals (Gen 1:20, 24). Nephesh can die: "the soul (nephesh) that sinneth, it shall die (muwth)" appears in both Ezek 18:4 and 18:20. Nephesh can refer to corpses (nephesh meth, Lev 21:11; Num 6:6). The LXX nephesh-psyche bridge means NT psyche inherits the full semantic range of OT nephesh -- including mortality.

docs.title: Same-Author Usage: Apollymi in Matthew's Gospel
docs.text:
Apollymi (G622, 102 NT occurrences) appears eighteen times in Matthew. The occurrences fall into five semantic categories:

(a) Judgment/authority destruction (active voice, actual destruction): Matt 10:28 -- God destroys soul and body in gehenna. Matt 21:41 -- the vineyard lord "will miserably destroy those wicked men" (apolesei, V-FAI-3S, future active indicative). Matt 22:7 -- the king "destroyed those murderers and burned up their city" (apolesen, V-AAI-3S, aorist active indicative, paired with fire vocabulary).

(b) Lost/straying (middle voice, recoverable condition): Matt 10:6, 15:24 -- "lost sheep of the house of Israel" (perfect middle participle). Matt 18:11 -- "to save that which was lost."

(c) Physical peril (middle voice, facing death): Matt 8:25 -- "Lord, save us: we perish." Sozo and apollymi as antonyms.

(d) Human destructive intent (active voice, plotting to kill): Matt 2:13 -- Herod seeks to destroy the child. Matt 12:14 -- Pharisees conspire to destroy Jesus. Matt 27:20 -- crowd persuaded to destroy Jesus.

(e) Ruin of inanimate objects: Matt 9:17 -- wineskins perish.

(f) Loss of life paradox: Matt 10:39, 16:25 -- "he that loseth (apollymi) his life (psyche) shall find it."

The pattern reveals a voice-dependent semantic distinction. Active voice apollymi with a divine or authority-figure subject consistently describes actual destruction: the child is killed (2:13), wicked tenants are destroyed (21:41), murderers are destroyed and their city burned (22:7), and God destroys soul and body in gehenna (10:28). Middle voice apollymi describes being lost (10:6, 15:24, 18:11) or perishing/facing death (8:25, 18:14). The "lost sheep" usage (middle voice, recoverable loss) does not govern the meaning of the judgment usage (active voice, actual destruction by authority).

Matt 18:14 provides a distinctive angle: "It is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish (apollymi)." God does not will that any should apollymi. The Father's will opposes apollymi -- perishing. If apollymi in judgment contexts described eternal conscious torment rather than cessation, the Father's will against apollymi would mean God opposes eternal torment for the wicked rather than opposes their destruction.

docs.title: Same-Author Usage: Gehenna in Matthew's Gospel
docs.text:
Matthew contains seven of the twelve total NT gehenna (G1067) occurrences. Every Matthean gehenna passage follows a consistent vocabulary pattern:

  • Matt 5:22: gehenna + fire (pur)
  • Matt 5:29-30: gehenna + apollymi (member perishing) + ballo (body cast into)
  • Matt 10:28: gehenna + apollymi (destroy soul and body)
  • Matt 18:9: gehenna + fire (pur) + zoe (life as antithesis)
  • Matt 23:15: gehenna as destiny-idiom ("son of gehenna")
  • Matt 23:33: gehenna + krisis (judgment/condemnation)

The collocates are: fire (5:22, 18:9), apollymi/destroy (5:29-30, 10:28), ballo/cast (5:29-30), zoe/life as antithesis (18:9), krisis/judgment (23:33), destiny-idiom (23:15). At no point does Matthew -- or any other NT author -- pair gehenna with basanizo (torment) for human subjects. This zero-overlap between gehenna vocabulary and basanizo vocabulary is a verifiable textual fact confirmed by cross-referencing all 12 gehenna occurrences with all 12 basanizo occurrences.

The OT background of gehenna (ge-Hinnom, Valley of the son of Hinnom) reinforces the destruction reading. The Valley of Hinnom progressed from a geographic boundary marker (Josh 15:8) through its association with child sacrifice (2 Chr 28:3; 33:6; 2 Ki 23:10), to prophetic renaming as the "Valley of Slaughter" (Jer 7:31-32; 19:6), to an eschatological judgment metaphor (Isa 30:33). At every stage, the associations are fire, death, slaughter, and corpse disposal -- not ongoing torment. When Jesus uses "gehenna" in Matt 10:28, his audience would understand it against this OT background.

The life-vs-gehenna contrast in Matt 18:9 (and parallels in Mark 9:43, 45, 47) is instructive: "enter into life" vs. "be cast into gehenna fire." The alternatives are life and gehenna. If gehenna were a place of ongoing conscious existence (even tormented existence), the contrast would be life vs. alternative-life, not life vs. destruction. The antithesis between zoe (life) and gehenna frames gehenna as the place where life does not continue.

docs.title: Same-Author Usage: Phobeo in Matthew's Gospel
docs.text:
Phobeo (G5399, 110 NT occurrences) appears sixteen times in Matthew. The pattern is distinctive: 8 of these are "fear not" commands (me + phobeo in various forms): Matt 1:20, 10:26, 10:28, 10:31, 14:27, 17:7, 28:5, 28:10. Jesus' characteristic response to human fear throughout the Gospel is "fear not."

The singular exception is Matt 10:28b, where phobeo is positively commanded: "phobeisthe de mallon ton dynamenon..." -- "rather fear the one who is able..." This is the only place in Matthew where Jesus tells his audience TO fear. The positive command to fear marks God's destructive power as the one thing worthy of ongoing reverential fear.

The tense distinction is significant. Matt 10:28 uses the present imperative phobeisthe (V-PNM-2P), which in prohibition (with me) means "stop fearing" and in positive command means "continue to fear / maintain a posture of fear." Luke's parallel (12:5) uses the aorist imperative phobethete (V-AOM-2P), which commands a decisive act of fearing. Matthew's present imperative indicates an ongoing disposition of reverential fear toward God, while Luke's aorist imperative commands a specific, decisive act.

The phobeo pattern bookends Matthew's Gospel: the first occurrence is the angel's "fear not" to Joseph (1:20); the last is Jesus' "fear not" to the women at the empty tomb (28:10). At the center of the narrative, the pivotal 10:28 redirects fear from human persecutors to God. The literary structure emphasizes that the proper response to God's power is not terror (which Jesus repeatedly tells people to stop) but reverential fear grounded in the recognition that God can destroy the complete person.

docs.title: The Kai...Kai Construction and Totality
docs.text:
The correlative kai...kai in Matt 10:28 binds psyche and soma into a single object of apolesai: "to destroy both (kai) soul and (kai) body in gehenna." This construction emphasizes totality -- God destroys the complete person, not merely one component. The correlative kai...kai functions differently from the simple copulative kai ("and"): it pairs two elements into a conceptual unit, asserting that both are equally included in the predicate.

The theological significance is direct. If God destroys BOTH soul and body, then neither component survives the destruction. If the soul survived destruction in gehenna (continuing in conscious torment while the body was destroyed), Jesus' assertion that God destroys "both soul and body" would be misleading -- He would actually destroy only the body while preserving the soul. The kai...kai construction asserts the totality of destruction: the complete person ceases.

docs.title: The Sozo-Apollymi Antithesis
docs.text:
Fourteen NT verses set sozo (G4982, "save") and apollymi (G622, "destroy/perish") in direct opposition. The antonym relationship constrains apollymi's meaning in judgment contexts: what sozo rescues from is what apollymi inflicts. If sozo = "preserve life / give eternal life," then apollymi = "end life / remove from life."

James 4:12 provides the clearest parallel to Matt 10:28's implicit structure: "There is one lawgiver, who is able to save (sosai, V-AAN, aorist active infinitive of sozo) and to destroy (apolesai, V-AAN, aorist active infinitive of apollymi)." The grammatical structure is identical: dynamenos + aorist active infinitive of apollymi (and sozo). God's two abilities are save and destroy -- not save and torment. The antonym pair defines apollymi by its contrast with sozo: destruction as the opposite of salvation.

Matt 8:25 applies the same antithesis in a physical context: "Lord, save (sozo) us: we perish (apollymi)." The disciples face physical death by drowning. Sozo rescues from perishing. The antonym relationship is consistent across physical and eschatological contexts.

docs.title: The Anthropological Foundation
docs.text:
The destructibility of the psyche in Matt 10:28 is grounded in the broader biblical anthropology. Four data points establish that humans do not inherently possess immortality:

  1. God alone has athanasia (1 Tim 6:16 -- monos echon athanasian). The alpha-privative athanasia (a- + thanatos) means "deathlessness." Only God has it.

  2. Mortals "put on" (enduo) immortality at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54). The clothing metaphor indicates the mortal does not currently possess immortality -- it must be acquired.

  3. Believers "seek for" (zeteo, present active participle) immortality (Rom 2:7). One does not seek what one already has.

  4. God barred the tree of life after the fall (Gen 3:22-24). If humans already had immortal souls, barring the tree would serve no purpose -- they would live forever regardless.

If the wicked never receive immortality (they do not "put it on" at the resurrection, they do not "seek" it), they cannot be tormented forever. Without immortality, the wicked simply cease to exist when destroyed. God's ability to "destroy both soul and body in gehenna" (Matt 10:28) is coherent only if the soul is destructible.

docs.title: The Synoptic Parallel: Luke 12:4-5
docs.text:
Luke's version of the same logion differs from Matthew's in three ways:

  1. Tense of phobeo: Luke uses the aorist imperative phobethete (decisive act); Matthew uses the present imperative phobeisthe (ongoing posture).

  2. Verb for God's action: Luke uses apokteino (kill) for BOTH human and divine action; Matthew escalates from apokteino (human action) to apollymi (divine action).

  3. Psyche: Luke omits psyche entirely, adding a temporal sequence: "after he hath killed, hath power to cast into gehenna."

Matthew's distinctive contribution is the verb shift from apokteino to apollymi. Luke maintains apokteino throughout, emphasizing the sequence (kill, then cast). Matthew changes the verb to emphasize the nature of God's action (destroy, not merely kill). Both versions agree on the location (gehenna), the reason for fear (God's ultimate authority), and the absence of torment vocabulary. Neither version uses basanizo.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence: Passages Used for ECT
docs.text:
Matt 25:46 ("everlasting punishment"): The word is kolasis (G2851, punishment from kolazo "to curtail/prune"), not basanismos (ongoing torment). The parallel structure with "everlasting life" uses the same adjective aionios, but the Hebrews aionios pattern (eternal redemption Heb 9:12, eternal judgment Heb 6:2, eternal salvation Heb 5:9) shows aionios can describe the permanent results of completed acts. "Everlasting punishment" is consistent with a punishment whose result is permanent (irreversible destruction), not necessarily with a punishing process that continues forever.

Luke 16:23-28 (Rich Man and Lazarus): This parable uses basanizo (torment) in hades (G86), not gehenna (G1067). The passage is parabolic (genre), set in hades (not the final judgment location), and describes a pre-judgment state (the rich man's brothers are still alive). Even if the parable describes a real intermediate state, it does not address the final fate of the wicked in gehenna, which is the subject of Matt 10:28.

Rev 14:10-11 ("tormented with fire and brimstone"): This passage uses basanizo for beast-worshippers in an apocalyptic context. The "smoke ascending forever" formula echoes Isa 34:10, where Edom's smoke "shall go up for ever" -- yet Edom is not still burning. The OT formula expresses irrevocable judgment, not necessarily infinite duration. The apocalyptic genre requires genre-appropriate interpretation, and this passage carries less evidentiary weight than didactic passages per the clarity criteria.

Mark 9:43-48 ("worm dieth not, fire is not quenched"): The allusion is to Isa 66:24, where the subjects are peger (H6297, corpses/carcasses) -- a word never used for a living person in the OT. The worm is a decomposition agent acting on dead bodies. "Unquenchable" fire in the OT (Jer 17:27; Amos 5:6; Ezek 20:47-48) burned to completion -- Jerusalem's fire was unquenchable but is not still burning.

docs.title: Word Studies
docs.text:
Psyche (G5590): 105 NT occurrences. Feminine noun from psycho ("to breathe"). KJV: "soul/souls" (58%), "life/lives" (33%). LXX maps nephesh (H5315) to psyche 599 times (87%). Matthew has 16 occurrences split evenly: 8 as "life," 8 as "soul." The translation split is an English artifact -- the Greek word is the same. Same-discourse usage in Matt 10:39 (psyche + apollymi = "lose one's life") provides the nearest contextual control for 10:28. Applied to animals (nephesh chayyah, Gen 1:20; psyche in Rev 16:3). Can die (Ezek 18:4,20). Can be destroyed (Matt 10:28). Can refer to corpses (nephesh meth, Lev 21:11). Not a technical term for an immortal soul.

Apollymi (G622): 102 NT occurrences. Verb from apo + ollymi ("destroy fully"). Active = destroy; Middle/Passive = perish, be lost. KJV: "perish" (36%), "destroy" (30%), "lose/lost" (27%). LXX maps abad (H6) to apollymi 141 times (PMI 6.14). Louw-Nida: Violence/Destroy (20.003) + Exist/Non-exist (13.003). No lexicon places apollymi in a torment domain. Matthew's judgment-context apollymi (10:28, 21:41, 22:7) consistently means actual destruction.

Gehenna (G1067): 12 NT occurrences. Transliteration of ge-Hinnom (Valley of Hinnom). Matthew has 7 (58%). Collocates: fire (6x), apollymi (3x), ballo (5x), zoe as antithesis (3x). Never collocates with basanizo for human subjects. OT background: geographic boundary → child sacrifice site → "Valley of Slaughter" → eschatological judgment metaphor. Associations at every stage: fire, death, destruction.

Phobeo (G5399): 110 NT occurrences. Deponent verb from phobos (G5401). Matthew has 16 occurrences, 8 in "fear not" commands. Matt 10:28 contains the only positive fear-command in Matthew (phobeisthe de mallon -- "rather fear"). Present imperative = ongoing posture of reverential fear. LXX maps yare (H3372) to phobeo 241 times (PMI 5.75).

docs.title: Difficult Passages
docs.text:
Matt 25:46 -- The aionios parallel: The most frequently cited passage against a conditionalist reading of Matt 10:28. The same adjective aionios modifies both "punishment" (kolasis) and "life" (zoe). Both sides agree that the adjective is the same. The question is whether aionios describes the duration of a process (everlasting punishing) or the permanence of a result (everlasting punishment-as-completed-act). The word for "punishment" is kolasis (G2851, penal infliction from kolazo "to curtail"), not basanismos (ongoing torment). The Hebrews aionios pattern shows the adjective can describe permanent results. The aionios parallel does not resolve the question on its own -- it is compatible with both readings.

Rev 14:10-11 -- Torment with fire and brimstone: Uses basanizo (torment) for beast-worshippers. This is the strongest ECT-direction text using torment vocabulary applied to human subjects. However, it is apocalyptic (not didactic), uses the Isa 34:10 "smoke ascending forever" formula (which described Edom's completed destruction), and specifically addresses beast-worshippers within the Revelation judgment sequence. The apocalyptic genre means this text does not carry the same evidentiary weight as didactic passages.

The fear hierarchy argument: Does the fear hierarchy require the threat to be "worse than death" in a way that only eternal conscious torment satisfies? The text does not state that duration is the distinguishing factor. The distinguishing factor is scope: humans can only kill the body; God can destroy BOTH soul and body. The totality of divine destruction (the complete person, not just the physical body) is what makes God more fearsome, regardless of whether the destruction is permanent cessation or ongoing torment. The kai...kai construction emphasizes the scope of God's power, not the duration of its effect.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Matt 10:28 states that God is able to destroy (apollymi) both soul (psyche) and body (soma) in gehenna. Same-author analysis of Matthew's four key words produces a consistent pattern: psyche denotes the whole person or physical life, apollymi in judgment contexts means actual destruction, gehenna pairs with destruction/judgment vocabulary but never with torment vocabulary, and phobeo establishes an ongoing posture of reverential fear toward a God whose power encompasses total destruction. The OT background (nephesh mortality, ge-Hinnom as "Valley of Slaughter," the abad-apollymi LXX bridge) and the broader NT framework (God alone has immortality, wages of sin is death, perish-vs-life antithesis) reinforce the same reading. The counter-evidence texts use different vocabulary (basanizo, kolasis), operate in different genres (parabolic, apocalyptic), or address different subjects (hades vs. gehenna, non-human entities vs. humans).

docs.title: Inferences
docs.text: # Claim Type Position What the Bible actually says Why this is an inference Criteria I1 God's destruction of both soul and body in gehenna results in the complete cessation of the wicked's existence I-A Cond. E1: God can destroy both soul and body in gehenna (Matt 10:28). E6: The soul that sins shall die (Ezek 18:4). E9: God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16). E10: Wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23). E15: Wicked become ashes (Mal 4:1,3). E19: Perish vs. everlasting life (John 3:16). E20: Everlasting destruction (2 Thess 1:9). Systematizes multiple E-items (destruction of soul, soul can die, no human immortality, wages = death, wicked = ashes, perish/life antithesis) into a single doctrinal claim. All components from E/N tables. Only #5 (systematizing). I081 I2 Same-discourse word pair psyche+apollymi in 10:39 ("lose one's life") governs the meaning of psyche+apollymi in 10:28 ("destroy soul and body") I-A Cond. E1: God destroys psyche+soma in gehenna (Matt 10:28). E3: In the same discourse (10:39), psyche+apollymi = "lose one's life." The observation that the word pair appears in both verses with the same morphology is E-tier. The interpretive claim that 10:39 governs 10:28 requires applying same-discourse hermeneutics -- choosing this approach over context-dependent semantics. I082 I3 Matthew's judgment-apollymi pattern (10:28, 21:41, 22:7) shows apollymi means actual destruction when God/authority acts on the wicked I-A Cond. E1: God destroys soul and body in gehenna (Matt 10:28). E11: Vineyard lord destroys wicked tenants (Matt 21:41, parabolic). E12: King destroys murderers and burns city (Matt 22:7, parabolic). E11 and E12 are parabolic (reclassified to Neutral by Gate 1). The pattern claim systematizes E1 with parabolic data and lexical evidence (Louw-Nida classification, LXX abad→apollymi bridge). Requires criterion #5 (systematizing) and #4b (cross-referencing parabolic data with didactic). I083 I4 The soul survives bodily death and exists consciously in gehenna, experiencing ongoing torment I-B ECT E17 (reclassified Neutral): In apocalyptic vision, beast-worshippers tormented (Rev 14:10-11). E8: "everlasting punishment" (Matt 25:46). Luke 16:23-28: Rich man in torment (parabolic, hades not gehenna). AGAINST: E1 (destroy both soul and body), E6 (soul dies), E9 (God alone has immortality), E10 (wages = death), E15 (ashes), E19 (perish vs. life), E20 (everlasting destruction). FOR: E17 (reclassified Neutral, apocalyptic), E8 (kolasis not basanismos, Neutral). The claim requires: (a) reading apollymi as "ruin" rather than "destroy" (#2); (b) importing innate soul immortality, which no E-item states (#1); (c) treating apocalyptic texts as governing didactic texts (reversing genre hierarchy) (#3). I084 I5 The "everlasting punishment" of Matt 25:46 describes an everlasting process of punishing (ongoing conscious torment) rather than an everlasting result of punishment (permanent destruction) I-B ECT E8: "everlasting punishment" (kolasis aionios) vs. "life eternal" (zoe aionios) (Matt 25:46). E16: The word is kolasis (punishment), not basanismos (torment). FOR ECT: E8 (aionios parallel structure). AGAINST ECT: E16 (kolasis not basanismos), E1 (destroy not torment), E10 (death not torment), Hebrews aionios pattern (permanent results of completed acts). Requires choosing between two readings of aionios + kolasis: process-duration ("ongoing punishing") vs. result-permanence ("permanent punishment"). Neither reading is forced by the grammar alone. I033 I6 The fear hierarchy in Matt 10:28 requires the threat to be worse than physical death, which only eternal conscious torment (not cessation) satisfies I-C ECT E1: God destroys both soul and body in gehenna (Matt 10:28). E2: Humans can kill the body but not the soul. The text does not state that the duration of the consequence is the distinguishing factor. The text states that the scope is different: humans kill only the body; God destroys both soul AND body. The claim that "worse" requires "longer" is an external framework (philosophical reasoning about what constitutes a "worse" fate). The text itself distinguishes scope (body-only vs. body+soul), not duration. I038 I7 Proportional judgment language ("more tolerable," "many/few stripes") implies finite, measured punishment incompatible with identical eternal torment for all I-A Cond. E-items from Matt 10:15 (more tolerable for Sodom), Matt 11:23-24 (more tolerable for Sodom than Capernaum), Luke 12:47-48 (many stripes vs. few stripes). These passages state proportional judgment as a textual fact. The inference systematizes them into the claim that proportional judgment excludes uniform infinite punishment. Requires only #5 (systematizing). I074

docs.title: I-B Resolution: I4 -- Soul survives and experiences ongoing conscious torment in gehenna
docs.text:
Step 1 -- Tension: - FOR (ECT): E17 (Rev 14:10-11, reclassified Neutral -- apocalyptic genre), E8 (Matt 25:46, Neutral -- "everlasting punishment" uses kolasis not basanismos), Luke 16:23-28 (parabolic, hades not gehenna) - AGAINST (Cond.): E1 (God destroys soul and body in gehenna, Cond.), E6 (soul dies, Cond.), E9 (God alone has immortality, Cond.), E10 (wages = death, Cond.), E15 (wicked become ashes, Cond.), E19 (perish vs. life, Cond.), E20 (everlasting destruction, Cond.)

Step 2 -- Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E1 (Matt 10:28) Plain Didactic discourse, direct speech of Jesus, destruction vocabulary applied to humans, no interpretive framework needed E6 (Ezek 18:4) Plain Direct divine speech, "the soul dies" is the plain lexical meaning of the words E9 (1 Tim 6:16) Plain Didactic epistle, "alone having immortality" -- plain meaning of monos E10 (Rom 6:23) Plain Didactic epistle, "wages of sin is death" -- direct statement E15 (Mal 4:1,3) Plain Prophetic oracle, "ashes" is the stated result of eschatological fire E19 (John 3:16) Plain Didactic discourse, "perish" vs. "everlasting life" as antithesis E20 (2 Thess 1:9) Plain Didactic epistle, "everlasting destruction" -- destruction vocabulary E17 (Rev 14:10-11) Ambiguous Apocalyptic vision, "smoke ascending forever" formula also used for completed destruction (Isa 34:10) E8 (Matt 25:46) Ambiguous Uses kolasis (punishment), not basanismos (torment); aionios can describe permanent results Luke 16:23-28 Ambiguous Parabolic genre, hades not gehenna, pre-judgment setting

Step 3 -- Weight: AGAINST ECT (Cond. direction): 7 E-items at Plain level (E1, E6, E9, E10, E15, E19, E20), all using destruction/death vocabulary in didactic genres. FOR ECT: 0 E-items at Plain level. E17 is Ambiguous (apocalyptic genre). E8 is Ambiguous (kolasis not basanismos, aionios interpretation debated). Luke 16:23-28 is Ambiguous (parabolic, hades not gehenna).

Step 4 -- SIS Application: The plain, didactic statements (God destroys soul and body; the soul dies; wages of sin is death; perish vs. life; everlasting destruction; wicked become ashes; God alone has immortality) determine the reading of the ambiguous, apocalyptic/parabolic passages. "Tormented with fire and brimstone, smoke ascending forever" (Rev 14:10-11) is read in light of the plain statements that use destruction/death vocabulary. The OT parallel (Isa 34:10 -- Edom's smoke ascending "forever" after being turned to ashes) confirms the formula describes completed destruction. The rich man parable (Luke 16:23-28) is set in hades (not gehenna) and is parabolic (not didactic).

Step 5 -- Resolution: Strong toward Cond. All Plain-level E-items use destruction/death vocabulary in didactic genres and point in the Cond. direction. All ECT-direction evidence is at the Ambiguous level, requiring apocalyptic genre interpretation, choosing between word senses, or accepting parabolic imagery as didactic teaching. Plain statements govern the reading of ambiguous ones: the soul is destroyed (Matt 10:28), the soul dies (Ezek 18:4), the wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23), the wicked become ashes (Mal 4:1,3).

docs.title: I-B Resolution: I5 -- "Everlasting punishment" describes ongoing process vs. permanent result
docs.text:
Step 1 -- Tension: - FOR (process-reading, ECT): E8 (Matt 25:46 -- aionios parallel: same adjective for "everlasting punishment" and "life eternal") - AGAINST (result-reading, Cond.): E16 (kolasis not basanismos), E1 (destroy not torment), E10 (wages = death), Hebrews aionios pattern (eternal redemption/judgment/salvation = permanent results)

Step 2 -- Clarity Assessment:

Item Level Rationale E8 (Matt 25:46) Ambiguous Aionios parallel is observable, but whether it forces identical duration-type for both nouns is debated; kolasis (not basanismos) used E16 (kolasis vocabulary) Contextually Clear The word choice is a textual fact; its interpretive significance requires awareness of the kolasis/basanismos distinction E1 (Matt 10:28) Plain Same author uses apollymi (destroy) for fate of wicked E10 (Rom 6:23) Plain Wages of sin is death (thanatos), not torment Heb 9:12, 6:2, 5:9 Contextually Clear Aionios + result-noun pattern established in same corpus

Step 3 -- Weight: The process-reading rests on the aionios parallel (Ambiguous -- both readings are grammatically possible). The result-reading rests on the kolasis word choice (Contextually Clear), the Hebrews aionios pattern (Contextually Clear), and the broader NT destruction vocabulary (Plain -- E1, E10).

Step 4 -- SIS Application: The same author (Matthew) uses apollymi (destroy) for God's action on the wicked in 10:28. When Matthew describes "everlasting punishment" in 25:46, the verb-noun combination kolasis aionios should be read in light of the same author's destruction vocabulary. The Hebrews aionios pattern provides a verified cross-reference (#4a -- shared vocabulary within the same corpus) showing aionios can describe permanent results.

Step 5 -- Resolution: Moderate toward Cond. The result-reading has Contextually Clear and Plain support. The process-reading rests on the aionios parallel alone (Ambiguous). The resolution is Moderate rather than Strong because the aionios parallel, while not decisive, is a legitimate textual observation that both sides must reckon with.

docs.title: What CAN Be Said (Scripture explicitly states or necessarily implies)
docs.text:
• God is able to destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in gehenna (Matt 10:28).
  • The soul (nephesh) that sins shall die (Ezek 18:4, 20).
  • God alone possesses immortality (1 Tim 6:16).
  • The wages of sin is death, not eternal life in torment (Rom 6:23).
  • The wicked become ashes, leaving neither root nor branch (Mal 4:1, 3).
  • Perishing and everlasting life are mutually exclusive outcomes (John 3:16).
  • The punishment of the wicked is described as "everlasting destruction" (2 Thess 1:9).
  • Gehenna vocabulary and basanizo (torment) vocabulary never overlap for human subjects in any NT passage.
  • Matt 25:46 uses kolasis (punishment), not basanismos (torment).
  • The subjects of worm and fire in Isa 66:24 are corpses (peger), not living persons.
  • Humans are "devoured" (katesthio) in Rev 20:9; the devil/beast/false prophet are "tormented" (basanizo) in Rev 20:10 -- different verbs for different subjects.

docs.title: What CANNOT Be Said (not explicitly stated or necessarily implied by Scripture)
docs.text:
• That the soul is inherently immortal -- no verse states this; Scripture says God alone has immortality.
  • That gehenna is a place of eternal conscious torment -- no gehenna passage uses torment vocabulary for humans.
  • That basanizo (torment) applies to human beings in gehenna -- basanizo and gehenna never co-occur.
  • That apollymi in Matt 10:28 means "ruin" rather than "destroy" -- no judgment-context apollymi in Matthew uses the "ruin" sense; the "ruin" sense (9:17, wineskins) applies to inanimate objects.
  • That the fear hierarchy requires ongoing torment -- the text distinguishes scope (body vs. soul+body), not duration.
  • That "everlasting punishment" in Matt 25:46 necessarily means "everlasting punishing" -- the word is kolasis (judicial penalty), and aionios can describe permanent results.
  • That Luke 16:23-28 describes the final fate of the wicked in gehenna -- the passage is parabolic, set in hades, and pre-judgment.
  • That Rev 14:10-11 establishes the duration of punishment for all the wicked -- the passage is apocalyptic, addresses beast-worshippers specifically, and uses the Isa 34:10 completed-destruction formula.

docs.title: Prior Research Summary
docs.text: Nine prior studies directly address Matt 10:28 or its key terms. etc6-19-matthew-10-28 (exact predecessor) found: psyche 16x in Matthew (8 'life', 8 'soul'), apollymi ~18x (judgment uses = actual destruction), gehenna 7/12 NT occurrences in Matthew (never paired with basanizo), and the same word-pair psyche+apollymi in 10:39 = 'lose one's life'. etc7-01-what-is-man established nephesh/psyche as destructible composite-entity terms. etc7-05-four-hell-words confirmed gehenna collocates with apollymi 3x and fire 6x but never basanizo. etc7-06-destruction-vocabulary confirmed apollymi (102 NT occ.) as canonical heir to abad via LXX (141 mappings, PMI 6.14). etc7-14-judgment-passages found 0/8 major judgment passages use basanizo for humans. 3am-05-fear-god analyzed phobeo broadly but did not map all Matthean occurrences. Key gaps: (1) complete parser-verified Matthean distribution of all four words, (2) phobeo distribution in Matthew specifically, (3) etc7 methodology with per-item classifier agents.

All Matthean psyche (G5590) occurrences: Every occurrence of psyche in Matthew for same-author analysis - Matt 2:20 — Matthean psyche — 'they are dead which sought the young child's life (psyche)' - Matt 6:25 — Matthean psyche — 'Take no thought for your life (psyche)' — psyche as physical life - Matt 10:28 — Crux text — God destroys both soul and body in gehenna; apokteino vs apollymi verb shift - Matt 10:39 — Same discourse, same word-pair psyche+apollymi = 'lose one's life' — 11 verses later - Matt 11:29 — Matthean psyche — 'find rest unto your souls' — psyche as inner person - Matt 12:18 — Matthean psyche — 'in whom my soul is well pleased' — God's psyche (OT quotation) - Matt 16:25-26 — Matthean psyche+apollymi — save/lose life (psyche); what profit to gain world and lose soul (psyche) - Matt 20:28 — Matthean psyche — 'give his life (psyche) a ransom for many' — psyche as physical life given up - Matt 22:37 — Matthean psyche — 'love the Lord with all thy soul (psyche)' — Shema quotation - Matt 26:38 — Matthean psyche — 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death' — Jesus' psyche as mortal

All Matthean apollymi (G622) occurrences: Every occurrence of apollymi in Matthew for same-author analysis - Matt 2:13 — Matthean apollymi — Herod seeks to destroy the child (literal destruction intent) - Matt 5:29-30 — Matthean gehenna — 'whole body cast into hell' — body-in-gehenna language parallel to 10:28 - Matt 8:25 — Matthean apollymi — 'Lord, save us: we perish' — disciples' fear of physical death - Matt 9:17 — Matthean apollymi — 'wineskins perish' — apollymi for inanimate ruin/destruction - Matt 10:6 — Matthean apollymi — 'lost sheep of the house of Israel' — apollymi as 'lost/straying' - Matt 10:28 — Crux text — God destroys both soul and body in gehenna; apokteino vs apollymi verb shift - Matt 10:39 — Same discourse, same word-pair psyche+apollymi = 'lose one's life' — 11 verses later - Matt 12:14 — Matthean apollymi — Pharisees conspire to destroy Jesus — human destructive intent - Matt 15:24 — Matthean apollymi — 'lost sheep of the house of Israel' — second 'lost' usage - Matt 18:11 — Matthean apollymi — 'to save that which was lost' — apollymi as lost/straying, paired with sozo - Matt 18:14 — Matthean apollymi — 'not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish' - Matt 21:41 — Matthean apollymi — 'miserably destroy those wicked men' — judgment apollymi = actual destruction by authority - Matt 22:7 — Matthean apollymi — king 'destroyed those murderers and burned up their city' — judgment apollymi + fire - Matt 27:20 — Matthean apollymi — crowd persuaded to 'destroy Jesus' — apollymi for killing/execution

All Matthean gehenna (G1067) occurrences: Every occurrence of gehenna in Matthew for same-author analysis - Matt 5:22 — Matthean gehenna — 'danger of hell fire' — first gehenna reference in Matthew - Matt 10:28 — Crux text — God destroys both soul and body in gehenna; apokteino vs apollymi verb shift - Matt 18:9 — Matthean gehenna — 'cast into hell fire' — enter life vs. gehenna contrast - Matt 23:15 — Matthean gehenna — 'twofold more the child of hell (gehenna)' — gehenna as destination metaphor - Matt 23:33 — Matthean gehenna — 'how can ye escape the damnation of hell (gehenna)?'

Key Matthean phobeo (G5399) occurrences: Representative phobeo uses in Matthew for same-author analysis - Matt 10:28 — Crux text — God destroys both soul and body in gehenna; apokteino vs apollymi verb shift - Matt 14:27 — Matthean phobeo — Jesus says 'be not afraid' to disciples on the water - Matt 14:30 — Matthean phobeo — Peter afraid of wind and waves; phobeo for physical fear - Matt 17:6-7 — Matthean phobeo — disciples fall on face 'sore afraid' at transfiguration; Jesus says 'be not afraid' - Matt 28:10 — Matthean phobeo — Jesus says 'Be not afraid' to women at empty tomb

Synoptic parallel: Luke's version of the same logion for comparison - Luke 12:4-5 — Synoptic parallel — Luke omits psyche, uses apokteino instead of apollymi for God's action

OT gehenna background: Valley of Hinnom / Topheth passages establishing OT background - Jer 7:31-32 — OT — Valley of Hinnom background: child sacrifice site renamed 'Valley of Slaughter' - Isa 66:24 — OT — 'worm shall not die, fire not quenched' — subjects are peger (carcasses/corpses), not living persons

OT nephesh mortality: Passages establishing that the soul (nephesh) can die - Gen 2:7 — OT — 'man became a living soul (nephesh)' — creation formula, nephesh as whole being - Ezek 18:4 — OT — 'the soul (nephesh) that sinneth, it shall die' — nephesh is mortal - Ezek 18:20 — OT — 'the soul (nephesh) that sinneth, it shall die' — repeated for emphasis

Counter-evidence texts: Passages most commonly cited for eternal conscious torment - Matt 25:46 — Matthean judgment vocabulary — 'everlasting punishment' vs. 'life eternal' — kolasis not basanizo

Additional Primary Verses: - Matt 28:4 — Matthean phobeo — guards at the tomb 'did shake and became as dead men' for fear - Matt 28:5 — Matthean phobeo — angel says 'Fear not ye' — phobeo negated as reassurance - Mal 4:1-3 — OT — wicked burned to ashes, stubble consumed — OT eschatological fire produces cessation

  • 2 Chr 33:6 — OT — Manasseh burns children in Valley of Hinnom — ge-Hinnom + fire
