  • James 4:12 — NT — 'able to save and to destroy' — sozo/apollymi antonym pair applied to God
  • Mark 9:43-48 — Markan parallel — gehenna + 'where their worm dieth not and the fire is not quenched'
  • Jude 1:7 — Sodom as example of 'eternal fire' yet 'turned to ashes' (2 Pet 2:6)
  • 2 Pet 2:6 — Sodom 'turned to ashes' — 'eternal fire' produced complete destruction, not ongoing burning
  • Matt 10:15 — Matthean judgment — Sodom/Gomorrah comparison — proportionality of judgment
  • Matt 11:23-24 — Matthean judgment — Capernaum/Sodom comparison — degree of judgment
  • Gen 3:22-24 — OT — Tree of life barred — immortality not inherent, must be accessed
  • Luke 12:47-48 — Proportional judgment — many stripes vs. few stripes — finite, measured punishment

docs.title: Focus Areas
docs.text:
1. Psyche (G5590) distribution in Matthew — same-author usage analysis: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G5590-psyche.md and $WORD_STUDIES/TR-nephesh-psyche.md for the canonical word study and LXX translation relationship. The research agent should run greek_parser.py --search G5590 filtered to Matthew to verify the distribution. Prior study etc6-19 found 16 occurrences across 11 verses: 8 translated 'life' (2:20; 6:25 2x; 10:39 2x; 16:25 2x; 20:28) and 8 translated 'soul(s)' (10:28 2x; 11:29; 12:18; 16:26 2x; 22:37; 26:38). The critical datum is Matt 10:39 — just 11 verses after 10:28, in the SAME discourse, Matthew uses the identical word-pair psyche + apollymi meaning 'lose one's life,' NOT 'destroy an immaterial soul.' Run greek_parser.py --verse on Matt 10:28 and 10:39 to compare morphology. Also check Matt 26:38 where Jesus says 'my psyche is exceeding sorrowful even unto death' — psyche is mortal in Jesus' own usage. Compare with OT background: read $WORD_STUDIES/H5315-nephesh.md for nephesh semantics (788 occ., can die per Ezek 18:4,20, refers to corpses in Lev 21:11/Num 6:6). Verses: Matt 10:28, Matt 10:39, Matt 2:20, Matt 6:25, Matt 11:29, Matt 12:18, Matt 16:25-26, Matt 20:28, Matt 22:37, Matt 26:38 Strong's: G5590, H5315

  2. Apollymi (G622) distribution in Matthew — same-author usage analysis: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G622-apollymi.md and $WORD_STUDIES/TR-abad-apollymi.md for the canonical word study and the critical LXX connection (abad->apollymi 141 mappings, PMI 6.14). The research agent should run greek_parser.py --search G622 filtered to Matthew to get all ~18 occurrences. Prior study etc6-19 classified them into semantic categories: (a) judgment/authority destruction — 10:28, 21:41, 22:7 (actual destruction by divine/royal authority); (b) lost/straying — 10:6, 15:24, 18:11 (recoverable loss); (c) physical peril — 8:25 (disciples fear drowning); (d) human destructive intent — 2:13, 12:14, 27:20 (plot to kill); (e) ruin — 9:17 (wineskins perish). The critical observation: when Matthew records God or authority figures acting on the wicked with apollymi, the meaning is ALWAYS actual destruction (10:28, 21:41, 22:7), never 'make lost' or 'ruin.' Also read $WORD_STUDIES/H6-abad.md for the Hebrew root. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py --hybrid-nt on Matt 10:28 to find OT parallels. Verses: Matt 10:28, Matt 2:13, Matt 8:25, Matt 9:17, Matt 10:6, Matt 10:39, Matt 12:14, Matt 15:24, Matt 16:25, Matt 18:11, Matt 18:14, Matt 21:41, Matt 22:7, Matt 27:20 Strong's: G622, H6, G684

  3. Gehenna (G1067) distribution in Matthew — same-author usage analysis: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G1067-geenna.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H1516-gayʼ.md for the canonical word studies covering gehenna and its OT geographic origin in the Valley of Hinnom. The research agent should run greek_parser.py --search G1067 filtered to Matthew to verify all 7 occurrences: 5:22, 5:29, 5:30, 10:28, 18:9, 23:15, 23:33. For each, retrieve full verse context and note the COLLOCATING vocabulary — what other words appear in the same verse or pericope. Prior studies found: gehenna collocates with fire 6x and apollymi 3x across the NT; it NEVER collocates with basanizo (G928) for human subjects. This is a verifiable textual fact. The research agent should also run search_strongs.py --verses G928 to confirm that basanizo never appears in any gehenna passage. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G928-basanizo.md for the torment word study. Run greek_parser.py --verse on Matt 5:22, 5:29-30, 18:9 to check the life-vs-gehenna contrast pattern ('enter into life' vs. 'cast into gehenna'). Also trace OT background: retrieve Jer 7:31-32, 19:6, 2 Chr 28:3, 33:6, Josh 15:8, 2 Ki 23:10, Isa 30:33 for the Valley of Hinnom as child sacrifice site and prophetically cursed location. Verses: Matt 5:22, Matt 5:29-30, Matt 10:28, Matt 18:9, Matt 23:15, Matt 23:33, Jer 7:31-32, Jer 19:6, Josh 15:8, 2 Ki 23:10, Isa 30:33 Strong's: G1067, H1516, G928, G4442

  4. Phobeo (G5399) distribution in Matthew — same-author usage analysis: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G5399-phobeo.md, $WORD_STUDIES/G5401-phobos.md, $WORD_STUDIES/TR-yare-phobeo.md, and $WORD_STUDIES/H3372-yare.md for the fear vocabulary chain. The research agent should run greek_parser.py --search G5399 filtered to Matthew to get all occurrences. Prior study 3am-05 covered phobeo broadly but did NOT provide a complete Matthean distribution. Key observations to verify: (a) Matt 10:28 uses present imperative phobeisthe (ongoing posture of fear/reverence toward God) vs. aorist passive imperative phobethete in Rev 14:7; (b) Matthew frequently uses phobeo in 'fear not' commands (1:20, 10:26, 10:28, 10:31, 14:27, 17:7, 28:5, 28:10); (c) the 'fear not' pattern in Matthew frames the fear of God as categorically different from human fear. Run greek_parser.py --verse on Matt 10:28 to parse the exact morphology of both phobeo forms. Also check whether Matthew uses phobos (G5401) noun alongside phobeo verb. The LXX bridge is critical: yare (H3372) collapses three Hebrew fear words into one Greek family — the research agent should note that context determines whether phobeo means terror or reverence in each Matthean occurrence. Verses: Matt 10:26, Matt 10:28, Matt 10:31, Matt 14:27, Matt 14:30, Matt 17:6-7, Matt 21:26, Matt 21:46, Matt 25:25, Matt 27:54, Matt 28:4-5, Matt 28:10 Strong's: G5399, G5401, H3372, H6343

  5. The apokteino-apollymi verb shift in Matt 10:28: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G615-apokteino.md for the 'kill' word study. The research agent should run greek_parser.py --verse on Matt 10:28 to verify that both apokteino and apollymi appear as aorist active infinitives — the punctiliar aspect describes completed actions. The verb shift from apokteino (human killing, limited to the body) to apollymi (divine destroying, encompassing BOTH soul and body) signals a qualitative difference. Apokteino means straightforward physical killing; apollymi means utter destruction/ruin. If Jesus meant to say God merely 'kills' the soul in the same way humans kill the body, he could have repeated apokteino. Instead, he escalated to apollymi. The research agent should also run greek_parser.py --verse on Luke 12:4-5 to compare: Luke uses apokteino for BOTH human and divine action, but adds a temporal sequence ('after he hath killed, hath power to cast into gehenna'). This synoptic comparison reveals Matthew's distinctive emphasis on the NATURE of God's action (destroy, not just kill) while Luke emphasizes the SEQUENCE (kill, then cast into gehenna). Also read $WORD_STUDIES/TR-harag-apokteino.md for the OT-NT translation relationship. Verses: Matt 10:28, Luke 12:4-5 Strong's: G615, G622

  6. The kai...kai construction and totality of destruction: The research agent should run greek_parser.py --verse on Matt 10:28 and analyze the kai...kai (both...and) construction. In Greek, kai...kai is a correlative conjunction emphasizing that BOTH elements are included — it is a completeness marker. The phrase 'apollesai kai psychen kai soma en geenne' asserts that God can destroy the COMPLETE person in gehenna. This totality language is theologically significant: if the soul survives destruction (as ECT requires), then Jesus' statement that God can destroy BOTH soul and body is misleading, since God would only destroy the body while preserving the soul for torment. The research agent should check grammar reference $GRAMMAR_REF/greek/emphatic-double-negation-ou-me.md for the negation pattern in 10:28a ('fear NOT'), and also look at the a fortiori argument structure in $GRAMMAR_REF/greek/a-fortiori-poso-mallon.md since Matt 10:28 uses an implicit a fortiori ('how MUCH MORE should you fear God'). Also parse the accusative case of psychen and soma — both are direct objects of the aorist active infinitive apolesai. Verses: Matt 10:28 Strong's: G5590, G4983, G622

  7. The apollymi-sozo antonym pair in Matthew: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G4982-sozo.md and $WORD_STUDIES/WG-perish-save.md for the save/perish antonym word group. The research agent should run search_strongs.py --co-occurrence G622 G4982 to find all passages where apollymi and sozo appear together. Prior study etc7-06 found 14 verses setting 'destroy/perish' and 'save' in direct opposition (Matt 16:25; Luke 9:24; 19:10; Jam 4:12; 1 Cor 1:18; 2 Cor 2:15). In Matthew specifically: Matt 16:25 uses psyche + apollymi + sozo in the same verse, and Matt 18:11 pairs apollymi with sozo ('to save that which was lost'). James 4:12 is particularly striking: God is 'able to save (sozo) and to destroy (apollymi)' — the same verb pair as Matt 10:28's implicit structure. If sozo means 'give eternal life,' then apollymi means 'remove eternal life' = cessation. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py --hybrid-nt on James 4:12 and Matt 16:25. Verses: Matt 16:25, Matt 18:11, James 4:12, 1 Cor 1:18, 2 Cor 2:15, John 3:16 Strong's: G622, G4982

  8. Gehenna vocabulary vs. basanizo vocabulary — the non-overlap: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G928-basanizo.md and $WORD_STUDIES/G2851-kolasis.md for the torment/punishment word studies. The research agent should run search_strongs.py --verses G928 to get all basanizo occurrences and search_strongs.py --verses G1067 to get all gehenna occurrences, then cross-reference. Prior studies found: gehenna appears in Matt 5:22, 5:29, 5:30, 10:28, 18:9, 23:15, 23:33, Mark 9:43, 9:45, 9:47, Luke 12:5, James 3:6. Basanizo appears in Matt 8:6, 8:29, 14:24, Mark 5:7, 6:48, Luke 8:28, 16:23, 16:28, 2 Pet 2:8, Rev 9:5, 11:10, 12:2, 14:10, 20:10. The ZERO overlap is a verifiable datum. Furthermore, in Rev 20:9-10, John uses 'devoured' (katephagen, G2719 — a destruction verb) for human armies but 'tormented' (basanisthesontai) for the devil, beast, and false prophet — different verbs for different subjects in consecutive verses. The research agent should verify this vocabulary differentiation by parsing Rev 20:9 and 20:10. Verses: Rev 20:9-10, Rev 14:10-11, Luke 16:23-28, Matt 8:29, Matt 25:46 Strong's: G928, G1067, G2851, G2719

  9. OT background: nephesh mortality and ge-Hinnom as judgment site: READ $WORD_STUDIES/H5315-nephesh.md for the full nephesh word study (788 OT occurrences, 214 unique KJV translations). Key findings: nephesh can die (Ezek 18:4,20 uses muwth H4191), can refer to corpses (nephesh meth, Lev 21:11; Num 6:6), and is shared with animals (Gen 1:20-25). Man did NOT receive a nephesh — man BECAME a living nephesh (Gen 2:7, wayehi transformation verb). READ $WORD_STUDIES/H1516-gayʼ.md for the Valley of Hinnom word study. The research agent should run hebrew_parser.py --verse on Ezek 18:4, Gen 2:7, and Jer 7:31-32 to verify the parsing. For ge-Hinnom background: Josh 15:8 (geographic boundary), 2 Chr 28:3 and 33:6 (child sacrifice site), Jer 7:31-32 and 19:6 (renamed 'Valley of Slaughter'), 2 Ki 23:10 (Josiah defiles it), Isa 30:33 (Topheth prepared by YHWH). Also read $WORD_STUDIES/H6297-peger.md for Isa 66:24 — the subjects of the worm and fire are peger (H6297, carcasses/corpses), a word NEVER used for a living person. Run hebrew_parser.py --verse on Isa 66:24. Verses: Ezek 18:4, Ezek 18:20, Gen 2:7, Jer 7:31-32, Jer 19:6, Josh 15:8, 2 Chr 28:3, 2 Chr 33:6, 2 Ki 23:10, Isa 30:33, Isa 66:24 Strong's: H5315, H1516, H4191, H6297

  10. Counter-evidence: passages used to support eternal conscious torment: The research agent should retrieve Luke 16:23-28, Rev 14:10-11, Matt 25:46, and Mark 9:43-48 with full context. For Luke 16:23-28: this is the Rich Man and Lazarus parable. It uses basanizo (G928) in hades (G86, NOT gehenna G1067) — check whether parabolic context governs interpretation. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G86-háidēs.md for the hades/gehenna distinction. For Rev 14:10-11: check the subjects — 'if any man worship the beast.' The smoke ascending 'forever' (eis aionas aionon) uses the same phrase applied to God's attributes. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G166-aionios.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H5769-owlam.md for the aionios/olam word studies. For Matt 25:46: the word is kolasis (G2851, punishment), NOT basanismos (torment). READ $WORD_STUDIES/G2851-kolasis.md. For Mark 9:43-48: the 'worm dieth not' allusion is to Isa 66:24 where the subjects are carcasses. The research agent should run greek_parser.py --verse on each passage to verify the exact vocabulary used. Verses: Luke 16:23-28, Rev 14:10-11, Matt 25:46, Mark 9:43-48, Isa 66:24 Strong's: G928, G86, G166, G2851, H5769

  11. Anthropological prerequisite: human mortality and conditional immortality: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G110-athanasia.md for the immortality (athanasia) word study. The research agent should retrieve 1 Tim 6:16 ('who alone has immortality'), 1 Cor 15:53-54 ('this mortal must put on immortality' — at the resurrection, not inherently possessed), Rom 2:7 ('seek for immortality' — seeking what one does not have), and Gen 3:22-24 (tree of life barred after the fall — if humans were already immortal, barring the tree would be unnecessary). Also read $WORD_STUDIES/G2222-zoe.md for the life/zoe word study and $WORD_STUDIES/G2288-thanatos.md for the death word study. The prior study etc7-01-what-is-man established: 'God alone has athanasia (1 Tim 6:16 — monos echon). Mortals put on immortality at the resurrection (1 Cor 15:53-54). Immortality is something to seek (Rom 2:7), not presently possessed.' If the wicked never receive immortality, they cannot be tormented forever — they would simply cease to exist when destroyed. Verses: 1 Tim 6:16, 1 Cor 15:53-54, Rom 2:7, Gen 3:22-24 Strong's: G110, G861, G862, G2222, G2288

docs.title: Research Instructions
docs.text:
You are the Research Agent. Execute this study by:

  1. Read the SKILL.md for full tool documentation and principles
  2. Read your agent instructions at agents/research-agent.md
  3. Read ALL library entries listed in "Available Library Entries" above
  4. Follow the workflow from the skill
  5. Write research files to this folder:
  6. 01-topics.md — Nave's topics and full entries (retrieve full entries for: SOUL, BODY, DEATH, HELL, GEHENNA, HADES, FEAR, IMMORTALITY, WICKED (PEOPLE), SECOND DEATH, TORMENTS, TOPHET, JUDGMENT, PUNISHMENT, ETERNAL PUNISHMENT, EVERLASTING FIRE, FURNACE, LOST SHEEP, TARES, SPIRIT)
  7. 02-verses.md — All verse texts retrieved with context for:
    • Matt 10:28 crux text and immediate context (Matt 10:26-31, Matt 10:28, Matt 10:39) — retrieve with FULL chapter context
    • All Matthean psyche (G5590) occurrences (Matt 2:20, Matt 6:25, Matt 10:28, Matt 10:39, Matt 11:29...)
    • All Matthean apollymi (G622) occurrences (Matt 2:13, Matt 5:29-30, Matt 8:25, Matt 9:17, Matt 10:6...)
    • All Matthean gehenna (G1067) occurrences (Matt 5:22, Matt 5:29, Matt 5:30, Matt 10:28, Matt 18:9...)
    • Key Matthean phobeo (G5399) occurrences (Matt 10:26, Matt 10:28, Matt 10:31, Matt 14:27, Matt 14:30...)
    • Synoptic parallel (Luke 12:4-5) — retrieve with FULL chapter context
    • OT gehenna background (Josh 15:8, 2 Chr 28:3, 2 Chr 33:6, Jer 7:31-32, Jer 19:6...)
    • OT nephesh mortality (Gen 2:7, Ezek 18:4, Ezek 18:20)
    • Counter-evidence texts (Luke 16:23-28, Rev 14:10-11, Matt 25:46, Mark 9:43-48) — retrieve with FULL chapter context
    • Anthropological prerequisite (1 Tim 6:16, 1 Cor 15:53-54, Rom 2:7, Gen 3:22-24)

  8. 04-word-studies.md — Strong's research:
    • FROM LIBRARY (read, don't re-derive): G5590 (psyche), G622 (apollymi), G1067 (geenna), G5399 (phobeo), G615 (apokteino), H5315 (nephesh), H1516 (gay/ge), G928 (basanizo), G4982 (sozo), G684 (apoleia), G2851 (kolasis), G2288 (thanatos), G4983 (soma), G5401 (phobos), H3372 (yare), G166 (aionios), G4442 (pyr), G110 (athanasia)

docs.title: What Does Matthew 10:28 Teach About the Fate of the Wicked?
docs.text: "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." -- Matthew 10:28

docs.title: The Core Teaching
docs.text: Jesus tells his disciples not to fear human persecutors who can only kill the body. Instead, they should fear God, who can destroy both soul and body in gehenna (hell). The word Jesus chooses for what God does is "destroy" (Greek apollymi), not "torment" (Greek basanizo). That word choice matters.

docs.title: What "Destroy" Means in Matthew
docs.text:
When Matthew records Jesus using apollymi in judgment settings, it consistently means actual destruction:

  • Matt 10:28 -- God destroys both soul and body in gehenna.
  • Matt 21:41 -- The vineyard owner "will miserably destroy" the wicked tenants.
  • Matt 22:7 -- The king "destroyed" the murderers and burned their city.

No judgment passage in Matthew uses apollymi to mean "torment" or "keep alive in suffering." It means what it sounds like: destroy.

docs.title: What "Soul" Means in This Passage
docs.text:
Eleven verses later, in the same speech, Jesus uses the exact same Greek words -- psyche (soul) and apollymi (destroy/lose) -- to say: "He that findeth his life shall lose it" (Matt 10:39). Here "soul" clearly means "life," not an immortal spirit-component.

The Old Testament background confirms this. In Genesis 2:7, man became a living soul -- he did not receive one as a separate part. And Ezekiel 18:4 states plainly: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die."

docs.title: Gehenna: Destruction, Not Torment
docs.text: Matthew mentions gehenna seven times -- more than any other Gospel writer. Every time, the surrounding language involves fire, destruction, judgment, or the loss of life. Not once does Matthew -- or any New Testament author -- pair gehenna with the word for "torment" (basanizo) when talking about human beings.

docs.title: What About "Everlasting Punishment"?
docs.text: Matthew 25:46 speaks of "everlasting punishment." The Greek word for "punishment" here is kolasis (a judicial penalty), not basanismos (ongoing torment). The adjective "everlasting" can describe a permanent result -- the way "eternal redemption" (Hebrews 9:12) means a redemption accomplished once with permanent effect, not an ongoing process of redeeming.

docs.title: The Bigger Biblical Picture
docs.text:
Several plain statements across Scripture reinforce the same conclusion:

  • God alone has immortality (1 Timothy 6:16). Humans do not inherently possess it.
  • The wages of sin is death -- not eternal life in torment (Romans 6:23).
  • The wicked become ashes, leaving "neither root nor branch" (Malachi 4:1, 3).
  • Perishing and everlasting life are opposites -- not two forms of living forever (John 3:16).
  • The wicked face everlasting destruction (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Jesus chose his words carefully. He said God destroys both soul and body -- not that God torments them forever. The same author's usage of every key word in this verse points in one direction: the final punishment of the wicked is real, total, and permanent destruction -- not an existence of endless suffering.

docs.title: Parable of the Wheat and Tares - primary judgment parable
docs.text:
Matthew 13:24 Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field: Matthew 13:25 But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way. Matthew 13:26 But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also. Matthew 13:27 So the servants of the householder came and said unto him, Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares? Matthew 13:28 He said unto them, An enemy hath done this. The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up? Matthew 13:29 But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Matthew 13:30 Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.

Context: Jesus teaching in parables by the sea (Matt 13:1-3). Seventh kingdom-of-heaven parable. The householder sows good seed; an enemy sows tares. At harvest, tares are gathered, bound, and burned (katakaio). Wheat goes into the barn. Jesus later interprets this parable privately to his disciples (vv.36-43).

Notes: katakaio (G2618) appears in v.30 as aorist active infinitive (katakausai) — 'to burn them.' The purpose clause (pros to katakausai auta) uses the articular infinitive construction specifying the PURPOSE of gathering the tares: total consumption. The wheat/barn contrast (saved vs. consumed) mirrors the save/destroy antithesis (sozo/apollymi).

docs.title: Jesus' self-interpretation of the tares parable - semi-didactic with copular identification formulas
docs.text:
Matthew 13:36 Then Jesus sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field. Matthew 13:37 He answered and said unto them, He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man; Matthew 13:38 The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked [one]; Matthew 13:39 The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels. Matthew 13:40 As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world. Matthew 13:41 The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity; Matthew 13:42 And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. Matthew 13:43 Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.

Context: Private session in a house after the public parables. Disciples request explanation. Jesus provides systematic symbol-to-referent decoding using copular identification (X estin/eisin Y) in vv.37-39, then describes the eschatological judgment in vv.40-43. This self-interpretation pattern (per grammar reference: self-interpretation-literal-correction.md) elevates the passage from purely parabolic to semi-didactic.

Notes: Critical genre datum: Matt 13:38-39 contains five copular identification formulas (ho agros estin ho kosmos; to kalon sperma outoi eisin hoi huioi tes basileias; ta zizania eisin hoi huioi tou ponerou; ho echthros ho speiras auta estin ho diabolos; ho therismos synteleia aionos estin; hoi theristai angeloi eisin). After this decoding, v.40 uses katakaio (present passive indicative: katakaietal = 'is consumed') with decoded referents. V.42: ballo + kaminos tou pyros + klauthmos kai brygmos ton odonton formula. V.43: the righteous shine as the sun — contrast between consumption and radiance.

docs.title: Parable of the Dragnet - second furnace-of-fire passage with identical judgment vocabulary
docs.text:
Matthew 13:47 Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind: Matthew 13:48 Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away. Matthew 13:49 So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just, Matthew 13:50 And shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Seventh parable in the Matt 13 discourse, immediately following the tares parable and interpretation. Same separation-then-destruction pattern. Same furnace formula. Same gnashing formula. Identical Greek in v.50 and v.42.

Notes: The Greek text of v.50 is verbatim identical to v.42: kai balousin autous eis ten kaminon tou pyros; ekei estai ho klauthmos kai ho brygmos ton odonton. The repetition within the same chapter reinforces the formulaic nature. V.49 explicitly states 'so shall it be at the end of the world' (en te synteleia tou aionos) — identical phrase to 13:39.

docs.title: Centurion's faith and first 'outer darkness' occurrence - sons of the kingdom cast out
docs.text:
Matthew 8:5 And when Jesus was entered into Capernaum, there came unto him a centurion, beseeching him, Matthew 8:6 And saying, Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented. Matthew 8:7 And Jesus saith unto him, I will come and heal him. Matthew 8:8 The centurion answered and said, Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed. Matthew 8:9 For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this [man], Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth [it]. Matthew 8:10 When Jesus heard [it], he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel. Matthew 8:11 And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven. Matthew 8:12 But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Matthew 8:13 And Jesus said unto the centurion, Go thy way; and as thou hast believed, [so] be it done unto thee. And his servant was healed in the selfsame hour.

Context: Non-parabolic narrative context. The centurion's faith prompts Jesus' declaration about Gentile inclusion and Jewish exclusion. The feast imagery (sitting down with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) frames the outer darkness as exclusion FROM a lit banquet, not a separate punishment location. First of three outer-darkness occurrences.

Notes: Key grammatical features: ekblethesontai (future passive indicative 3P of ekballo G1544) — 'shall be cast out.' to skotos to exoteron — double article construction (T-ASN + N-ASN + T-ASN + A-ASN-C). The comparative adjective exoteros [A-ASN-C] with the repeated article marks 'THE outer darkness' as a definite, particular destination. This is NOT parabolic (no 'the kingdom of heaven is like...' formula) — Jesus is making a direct prophetic statement.

docs.title: Wedding feast parable - second outer darkness with binding + destruction + burning
docs.text:
Matthew 22:1 And Jesus answered and spake unto them again by parables, and said, Matthew 22:2 The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son, Matthew 22:3 And sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come. Matthew 22:4 Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and [my] fatlings [are] killed, and all things [are] ready: come unto the marriage. Matthew 22:5 But they made light of [it], and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise: Matthew 22:6 And the remnant took his servants, and entreated [them] spitefully, and slew [them]. Matthew 22:7 But when the king heard [thereof], he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city. Matthew 22:8 Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy. Matthew 22:9 Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage. Matthew 22:10 So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests. Matthew 22:11 And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: Matthew 22:12 And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless. Matthew 22:13 Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast [him] into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Matthew 22:14 For many are called, but few [are] chosen.

Context: Parable of the wedding feast, addressed to chief priests and Pharisees. Two judgment phases: (1) v.7 — apollymi + empretho (destroyed murderers and burned their city); (2) v.13 — binding + casting into outer darkness. Same-author use of apollymi and empretho for destruction. The outer darkness is where the improperly dressed guest is expelled.

Notes: V.7 pairs apollymi (G622 — destroyed) with empretho (G1714 — burned up, hapax). V.13: desantes (aorist active participle of deo G1210 — having bound) + ekbalete (aorist active imperative of ekballo G1544 — cast out). The binding imagery (hand and foot) adds helplessness to the exclusion — the expelled cannot return. The darkness/fire tension: this parable uses darkness (v.13), while the tares parable uses furnace of fire (13:42). Both describe the fate of the excluded within the SAME author and SAME eschatological framework.

docs.title: Parable of the talents - third outer darkness occurrence with unprofitable servant
docs.text:
Matthew 25:14 For [the kingdom of heaven is] as a man travelling into a far country, [who] called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods. Matthew 25:15 And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey. Matthew 25:16 Then he that had received the five talents went and traded with the same, and made [them] other five talents. Matthew 25:17 And likewise he that [had received] two, he also gained other two. Matthew 25:18 But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money. Matthew 25:19 After a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them. Matthew 25:20 And so he that had received five talents came and brought other five talents, saying, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents: behold, I have gained beside them five talents more. Matthew 25:21 His lord said unto him, Well done, [thou] good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord. Matthew 25:22 He also that had received two talents came and said, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me two talents: behold, I have gained two other talents beside them. Matthew 25:23 His lord said unto him, Well done, good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord. Matthew 25:24 Then he which had received the one talent came and said, Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed: Matthew 25:25 And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, [there] thou hast [that is] thine. Matthew 25:26 His lord answered and said unto him, [Thou] wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed: Matthew 25:27 Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and [then] at my coming I should have received mine own with usury. Matthew 25:28 Take therefore the talent from him, and give [it] unto him which hath ten talents. Matthew 25:29 For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. Matthew 25:30 And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Third and final outer-darkness occurrence. Same Olivet Discourse as the unfaithful servant parable (24:45-51) and the sheep/goats (25:31-46). The contrast is 'enter into the joy of thy lord' (vv.21,23) vs. 'cast into outer darkness' (v.30) — inside/outside, light/dark, joy/grief.

Notes: V.30 Greek: ton achreion doulon ekbalete eis to skotos to exoteron. achreios (G888) = 'unprofitable, useless.' Same ekballo + eis to skotos to exoteron formula as 8:12 and 22:13. The pattern across all three outer-darkness passages: a feast/celebration context, an exclusion verb (ekballo), the definite location (to skotos to exoteron), the consequence formula (klauthmos kai brygmos ton odonton).

docs.title: Unfaithful servant - dichotomeo (cut asunder) + gnashing formula
docs.text:
Matthew 24:45 Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season? Matthew 24:46 Blessed [is] that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing. Matthew 24:47 Verily I say unto you, That he shall make him ruler over all his goods. Matthew 24:48 But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; Matthew 24:49 And shall begin to smite [his] fellowservants, and to eat and drink with the drunken; Matthew 24:50 The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for [him], and in an hour that he is not aware of, Matthew 24:51 And shall cut him asunder, and appoint [him] his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Olivet Discourse. The unfaithful servant abuses fellow servants and indulges. The master returns unexpectedly. Judgment: dichotomeo (cut asunder) + appointed portion with hypocrites + gnashing formula. This is the only gnashing occurrence that uses neither furnace nor outer-darkness imagery.

Notes: V.51: dichotomosei (G1371 — future active indicative 3S) — 'shall cut him asunder.' Unique judgment verb. Literally 'to cut in two.' The gnashing formula follows as the consequence. The verb tithemi (G5087 — thesei, future active indicative 3S) = 'shall appoint/place' his portion (meros G3313) with the hypocrites (hypokritai G5273). Luke's parallel (12:46) has 'unbelievers' (apistoi G571) instead of 'hypocrites.'

docs.title: Luke's gnashing passage - interpretive key identifying the trigger of gnashing
docs.text:
Luke 13:22 And he went through the cities and villages, teaching, and journeying toward Jerusalem. Luke 13:23 Then said one unto him, Lord, are there few that be saved? And he said unto them, Luke 13:24 Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able. Luke 13:25 When once the master of the house is risen up, and hath shut to the door, and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are: Luke 13:26 Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. Luke 13:27 But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all [ye] workers of iniquity. Luke 13:28 There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you [yourselves] thrust out. Luke 13:29 And they shall come from the east, and [from] the west, and from the north, and [from] the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. Luke 13:30 And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last.

Context: Non-Matthean version of the gnashing formula. Crucial because Luke identifies the TRIGGER: 'when ye shall see (hotan opsesthe) Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets IN the kingdom, and you yourselves thrust out (ekballomenous exo).' The gnashing occurs AT THE MOMENT of seeing exclusion — others inside, you outside.

Notes: V.28: hotan (G3752 — 'when/whenever') + opsesthe (aorist middle subjunctive 2P of horao G3708 — 'ye shall see'). The temporal clause identifies gnashing as a response TO SEEING exclusion, not an ongoing state. ekballomenous (present passive participle APM of ekballo G1544) + exo (G1854 — 'outside'). The participial form shows the thrust-out as simultaneous with the seeing/gnashing — a judgment-event snapshot.

docs.title: OT gnashing - charaq: enemy gnashes in hostile rage against righteous sufferer
docs.text:
He teareth [me] in his wrath, who hateth me: he gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me.

Context: Job's complaint about his adversary. Hostile actions: tearing (taraph), hating (satam), gnashing (charaq), sharpening eyes (latash). All express rage and animosity DIRECTED AT Job.

Notes: charaq (H2786) Qal Perfect 3ms. Paired with aph (H639 'wrath/nose'), satam (H7852 'bear grudge'), and latash (H3913 'sharpen'). The subject is an enemy (tsar H6862) who directs gnashing AT (al + 1cs suffix) Job. This is the prototype for gnashing = hostile rage.

docs.title: OT gnashing - charaq: mockers gnash teeth at David in malice
docs.text:
With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth.

Context: David's lament against enemies. The mockers gnash their teeth AT (al + 1cs suffix) him. Paired with 'hypocritical mockers' (chaneph laagey).

  • חַנְפֵי () — Adj.mp.Cst — alienated
  • לַעֲֲגֵ֣י () — Noun.mp.Cst — stammering
  • מָעֹבוג () — Noun.ms.Abs — venue
  • חָרֹזק () — Verb.Qal.InfAbs — grind
  • עָלַ֣י () — Prep.+1us — upon
  • שִׁנֵּֽימֹו () — Noun.fd.Abs.+3mp — tooth

Notes: charaq (H2786) Qal Infinitive Absolute. The infinitive absolute intensifies the action — emphatic gnashing. The laagey maowg ('mockers at a feast/cake') suggests contemptuous, derisive hostility.

docs.title: OT gnashing - charaq: wicked gnashes at the righteous, paired with plotting
docs.text:
The wicked plotteth against the just, and gnasheth upon him with his teeth.

Context: Wisdom psalm. The wicked (rasha) plots (zamam) against the righteous (tsaddiq) and gnashes (charaq) at him. Hostile intent clearly established — plotting + gnashing as compound hostile action.

  • זֹמֵ֣ם () — Verb.Qal.Ptcp.ms.Abs — ponder
  • רָ֭שָׁע () — Adj.ms.Abs — guilty
  • צַּדִּבק () — Adj.ms.Abs — just
  • וְ () — Conj.+NAN — and
  • חֹרֵזק () — Verb.Qal.Ptcp.ms.Abs — grind
  • עָלָ֣יו () — Prep.+3ms — upon
  • שִׁנָּֽיו () — Noun.fd.Abs.+3ms — tooth

Notes: charaq (H2786) Qal Participle ms. The participial form indicates habitual, characteristic action — the wicked characteristically gnashes at the righteous. Subject: rasha (H7563 'the wicked'). Object: tsaddiq (H6662 'the just'). Verb zamam (H2161 'to plot/plan evil').

docs.title: OT gnashing + cessation simile - charaq + masas (melt away): gnashing linked to destruction
docs.text:
The wicked shall see [it], and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish.

Context: Acrostic wisdom psalm. The wicked sees the righteous prospering and responds with grief (kaas), gnashing (charaq), and then MELTS AWAY (masas, Niphal). The final clause: the desire (taavah) of the wicked shall PERISH (abad). This verse uniquely combines gnashing (rage) with a cessation simile (melting) and destruction verb (perish).

  • רָטשָׁ֤ע () — Adj.ms.Abs — guilty
  • יִרְאֶ֨ה () — Verb.Qal.Impf.3ms — see
  • וְ () — Conj.+NAN — and
  • כָעָחחח () — Verb.Qal.Perf.3ms — be discontent
  • שִׁנָּ֣יו () — Noun.fd.Abs.+3ms — tooth
  • יַחֲרֹ֣ק () — Verb.Qal.Impf.3ms — grind
  • וְ () — Conj.+NAN — and
  • נָמָבס () — Verb.Niphal.Perf.3ms — melt
  • תַּאֲוַזת () — Noun.fs.Cst — desire
  • רְשָׁעִ֣ים () — Adj.mp.Abs — guilty
  • תֹּאבֵֽד () — Verb.Qal.Impf.3fs — perish

Notes: Three-step sequence: (1) kaas (H3707) Qal Perfect 3ms 'be discontent/angry'; (2) charaq (H2786) Qal Imperfect 3ms 'shall gnash'; (3) masas (H4549/masas) Niphal Perfect 3ms 'melt away.' The Niphal of masas indicates the subject dissolves/wastes away — a cessation verb. Then abad (H6) Qal Imperfect 3fs — 'shall perish.' This is THE critical OT verse linking gnashing (rage) to cessation (melting away, perishing).

docs.title: OT gnashing - charaq: enemies gnash in triumph over Jerusalem's destruction
docs.text:
All thine enemies have opened their mouth against thee: they hiss and gnash the teeth: they say, We have swallowed [her] up: certainly this [is] the day that we looked for; we have found, we have seen [it].

Context: Lament over Jerusalem's destruction. Enemies perform three hostile actions: opening mouths against (patsah), hissing (sharaq), gnashing teeth (charaq). They claim to have 'swallowed her up' (bala, Piel). Hostile triumph, not pain.

  • כָּל () — Noun.ms.Cst — whole
  • אֹ֣ויְבַהיִךְ () — Verb.Qal.Ptcp.mp.Abs.+2fs — be hostile
  • שָֽׁרְקוּי () — Verb.Qal.Perf.3p — whistle
  • וַ () — Conj.+NAN — and
  • יַּֽחַרְקוּ () — Verb.Qal.Wayq.3mp — grind

Notes: charaq (H2786) Qal Wayyiqtol 3mp — 'and they gnashed.' Paired with sharaq (H8319) Qal Perfect 3mp — 'they hissed/whistled.' Both are sounds of contempt and hostility. The subject: kol oybayik ('all thine enemies'). Conclusive: gnashing is RAGE/HOSTILITY in all 5 OT passages.

docs.title: NT gnashing (brycho) - Sanhedrin gnashes at Stephen in murderous fury
docs.text:
When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with [their] teeth.

Context: Stephen's martyrdom. The Sanhedrin hears Stephen's prophetic accusation and responds with fury: diaprio (cut to the heart, i.e., enraged) + brycho (gnash teeth). They then stone him. This is NOT pain but murderous rage.

Notes: ebruchon (G1031 brycho — Imperfect Active Indicative 3P) — 'they were gnashing' — continuous hostile action. The imperfect aspect shows sustained rage, not a momentary response. Paired with diepriento (G1282 diaprio — Imperfect Passive Indicative 3P) — 'they were being cut to the heart.' brycho is the Greek equivalent of charaq (H2786), with 5/5 LXX co-occurrences confirming the mapping. ep' auton — 'upon/against him' — directional hostility.

docs.title: Same-author destruction vocabulary - apollymi both soul and body in gehenna
docs.text:
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Context: Jesus' commissioning discourse. The one to fear can apollymi (destroy) BOTH soul AND body in gehenna. The kai...kai construction binds psyche and soma as a single compound object of destruction.

Notes: apolesai (G622 — Aorist Active Infinitive) — 'to destroy.' The active infinitive with divine subject (ton dynamenon — 'the one being able') in a non-parabolic didactic context. Same author as the furnace/darkness parables. Same verb (apollymi) used for judgment in Matt 21:41 ('miserably destroy') and 22:7 ('destroyed those murderers'). gehenna (G1067) — Dative of place.

docs.title: Same-author judgment - apollymi for destruction of wicked tenants
docs.text:
They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out [his] vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons.

Context: Parable of the wicked tenants. The audience themselves pronounce the judgment: 'He will miserably destroy those wicked men.' Same-author use of apollymi for judgment destruction.

Notes: kakous kakos apolesei autous — 'wicked [men] he will wickedly/miserably destroy them.' Double use of kakos (adverb + adjective) for intensification. apollymi (G622) in future active indicative 3S. Same verb as Matt 10:28.

docs.title: Same-author judgment - apollymi + empretho (destroyed murderers, burned city)
docs.text:
But when the king heard [thereof], he was wroth: and he sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city.

Context: Wedding feast parable, v.7. The king's response to those who killed his servants: apollymi (destroyed) the murderers + empretho (burned up) their city. Two destruction verbs in one verse — one for people, one for property.

Notes: apollymi (G622) aorist active indicative 3S for 'destroyed.' empretho/empipremi (G1714) aorist active indicative 3S (enepresen) for 'burned up' — hapax legomenon in NT. This verse is in the same parable that ends with outer darkness (v.13), creating the darkness-after-destruction sequence.

docs.title: John the Baptist's winnowing imagery - katakaio for burning chaff
docs.text:
Whose fan [is] in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

Context: John the Baptist's preaching. Same verb (katakaio) as the tares parable. Same winnowing imagery. Same wheat/chaff separation. The chaff is burned up (katakausei — future active indicative 3S of katakaio G2618) with unquenchable (asbestos G762) fire.

Notes: katakausei (G2618 — Future Active Indicative 3S). The kata- prefix intensifies to completion: not merely 'burn' but 'burn up completely.' Combined with asbestos (G762 — 'unquenchable') — the fire cannot be extinguished UNTIL it completes its work, not that the burning is endless. Same verb + same imagery in Jesus' mouth (Matt 13:30,40) — cross-speaker consistency within the same Gospel.

docs.title: OT furnace/oven judgment - tannuwr: wicked become stubble, burned to ashes under feet
docs.text:
Malachi 4:1 For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. Malachi 4:2 But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. Malachi 4:3 And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do [this], saith the LORD of hosts.

Context: Final OT fire-judgment prophecy. The day burns as a tannuwr (oven/furnace). The wicked become qash (stubble). They are burned up (lahat, Piel) with neither root nor branch remaining. Result: ashes (epher) under the soles of the righteous' feet. This is THE definitive OT passage for fire-as-consumption.

Notes: V.1: baar (H1197 — Qal Participle 'burning') + katannuwr (ke + ha + tannuwr H8574 — 'as the oven/furnace'). Wicked = qash (H7179 'stubble'). lahat (H3857 — Piel Perfect 3ms 'shall devour/burn up'). Result: lo ya'azob lahem shoresh va'anaph ('shall leave them neither root nor branch') — total consumption. V.3: epher (H665 'ashes') — the wicked's final state. They are trodden UNDERFOOT — they are no longer standing, conscious entities but residue.

docs.title: OT chaff simile - wicked like chaff driven by wind
docs.text:
The ungodly [are] not so: but [are] like the chaff which the wind driveth away.

Context: Opening psalm of the Psalter. Sharp contrast between the righteous (tree planted by waters, v.3) and the wicked (chaff driven by wind, v.4). Chaff = lightweight residue that ceases to exist as a substance when the wind takes it.

  • לֹא () — Neg.+NAN — not
  • כֵ֥ן () — Adv.+NAN — thus
  • הָ () — Art.+NAN — the
  • רְשָׁעִבים () — Adj.mp.Abs — guilty
  • כִּי () — Conj.+NAN — that
  • אִם () — Conj.+NAN — if
  • מֹּחחח () — Noun.ms.Abs — chaff
  • אֲֽשֶׁר () — Conj.+NAN —
  • תִּדְּפֶ֥נּוּ () — Verb.Qal.Impf.3fs.+3ms — scatter
  • רֽוּחַ () — Noun.s.Abs — wind

    • Notes: mots (H4671 'chaff') — the light husk separated from grain in winnowing. ruach (H7463/H7307 'wind/spirit') — the agent of removal. nadaph (H5086 — Qal Imperfect 3fs + 3ms suffix 'driveth away') — the chaff is expelled/scattered. Same imagery Jesus uses in Matt 3:12 with katakaio.

docs.title: OT fire/chaff cessation simile - flame consumes chaff, root rots, blossom goes up as dust
docs.text:
Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, [so] their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.

Context: Isaiah's woe oracle against Israel. Multi-part cessation simile: fire devours stubble (qash), flame consumes dry grass (chashash), root becomes rottenness (maq), blossom goes up as dust (abaq). Four cessation images in one verse.

Notes: akal (H398 — 'devour/eat') qash (H7179 'stubble'). leshon esh = 'tongue of fire.' chashash (H2842 'dry grass') — lehabhah (H3852 'flame') yirpeh (H7503 'goes slack/sinks'). Both root and blossom — the complete plant — are destroyed. The reason: rejection of Torah.

docs.title: Sheep and goats separation - same discourse as parables, judgment framework
docs.text:
Matthew 25:31 When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory: Matthew 25:32 And before him shall be gathered all nations: and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth [his] sheep from the goats: Matthew 25:33 And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.

Context: Same Olivet Discourse as the parables. The Son of Man sits on his throne (v.31) — same authority figure as the one who sends angels in Matt 13:41. Separation of sheep/goats parallels the separation of wheat/tares and good/bad fish.

Notes: This is the immediate context for Matt 25:41 (everlasting fire) and 25:46 (everlasting punishment). The separation imagery (aphorizei G873 — 'separate') corresponds to the collection/separation of 13:49.

docs.title: Everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels - not originally for humans
docs.text:
Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

Context: The sentence pronounced on the goats. The fire is 'prepared for' (hetoimasmenon) the devil and his angels — humans are sent there but it was not designed for them. This echoes the furnace of fire (kaminos tou pyros) in the parables.

Notes: pur aionion (G4442 + G166) — 'everlasting fire.' hetoimasmenon (G2090 — Perfect Passive Participle ASN) — 'having been prepared' — the fire's original purpose was for non-human entities. The Hebrews pattern (per etc7-08): aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed action. Cf. Heb 9:12 'eternal redemption' (obtained once, result permanent), Heb 6:2 'eternal judgment' (rendered once, verdict permanent).

docs.title: Everlasting punishment vs. everlasting life - kolasin aionion // zoen aionion
docs.text:
And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

Context: Climactic verse of the sheep/goats judgment. Grammatical parallel between kolasin aionion and zoen aionion. Both use aionios (G166) in accusative singular feminine. Both governed by the same verb (aperchomai G565) and preposition (eis).

Notes: kolasin (G2851 — Accusative Singular Feminine of kolasis) — 'punishment.' From kolazo (G2849) meaning 'to curtail, dock, prune.' Only 2 NT occurrences: here and 1 John 4:18. This is PUNISHMENT vocabulary, not TORMENT vocabulary (which would be basanismos G929). aionion (G166 — Accusative Singular Feminine) — identical form for both punishment and life. The symmetry is real but does not determine nature: the Hebrews pattern shows aionios qualifies results differently based on the noun it modifies.

docs.title: OT furnace (attuwn) - execution furnace that kills by default, survival requires divine intervention
docs.text:
Daniel 3:6 And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. Daniel 3:17 If it be [so], our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver [us] out of thine hand, O king. Daniel 3:20 And he commanded the most mighty men that [were] in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, [and] to cast [them] into the burning fiery furnace. Daniel 3:21 Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their [other] garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. Daniel 3:22 Therefore because the king's commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Daniel 3:23 And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell down bound into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. Daniel 3:25 He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God. Daniel 3:26 Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace, [and] spake, and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, ye servants of the most high God, come forth, and come [hither]. Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, came forth of the midst of the fire.

Context: Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace in Daniel 3. The Aramaic word attuwn (H861) is the primary LXX source for kaminos (G2575). Default outcome: death (v.22 — soldiers killed by proximity). Survival: only through divine intervention (fourth figure in fire). The furnace's function is EXECUTION, not confinement.

Notes: V.22: 'the flame of the fire slew those men' — shebiyba di nuwra qetal (Aramaic: the flame of fire killed). The soldiers who merely APPROACHED the furnace were killed. The three Hebrews survived ONLY because of divine intervention (v.25 — the fourth figure). This establishes the furnace as an instrument of death-by-default. When Jesus uses kaminos (the LXX translation of attuwn), the OT background is execution, not preservation-in-suffering.

docs.title: Vocabulary differentiation at the lake of fire - humans devoured vs. non-human tormented
docs.text:
Revelation 20:9 And they went up on the breadth of the earth, and compassed the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city: and fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them. Revelation 20:10 And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet [are], and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Context: Post-millennium judgment. Two consecutive verses use DIFFERENT verbs for DIFFERENT subjects. V.9: humans (Gog/Magog forces) — katephagen (devoured, aorist of katesthio G2719). V.10: the devil — basanisthesontai (shall be tormented, future passive of basanizo G928). The vocabulary differentiation is in consecutive verses by the same author.

Notes: V.9: katephagen (G2719 katesthio — 2nd Aorist Active Indicative 3S) — 'devoured.' The kata- prefix = complete consumption (same prefix pattern as katakaio). Object: autous (them = the human armies). V.10: basanisthesontai (G928 basanizo — Future Passive Indicative 3P) — 'shall be tormented.' Subject: the devil, beast, false prophet (non-human/symbolic entities). The vocabulary split is systematic: destruction words for humans, torment words for non-human.

docs.title: Sodom turned to ashes (tephroo) - paradigm case of 'eternal fire' producing ashes
docs.text:
And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned [them] with an overthrow, making [them] an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

Context: Peter's paradigm case. The 'eternal fire' of Jude 1:7 produced ASHES (tephroo G5077). Sodom is set as an 'example' (hupodeigma G5262) for the ungodly. If the paradigm case of 'eternal fire' reduced cities to ashes, 'eternal fire' describes permanent results, not endless burning.

Notes: tephrosas (G5077 — Aorist Active Participle NSM of tephroo) — 'having turned to ashes.' Hapax legomenon. The participle is circumstantial, describing the manner of condemnation. katastrophe (G2692 — Dative Singular Feminine) — 'with an overthrow/destruction.' hupodeigma (G5262 — Accusative Singular Neuter) — 'example/pattern.' The word tetheikos (G5087 — Perfect Active Participle NSM of tithemi) — 'having set/placed' — the example is ESTABLISHED and ongoing (perfect aspect).

docs.title: Edom judgment - smoke ascending le-olam yet land becomes ruins with animals dwelling
docs.text:
Isaiah 34:9 And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. Isaiah 34:10 It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever.

Context: Edom judgment oracle. The smoke 'goes up le-olam' (forever). Yet Isa 34:11-17 describes animals dwelling in the ruins — owls, ravens, cormorants inhabiting the desolate land. The 'forever' smoke formula describes the permanent memorial of COMPLETED destruction, not ongoing burning.

Notes: le-olam (H5769) — 'for concealed time/forever.' This is the OT source text for Rev 14:11 ('the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever'). But the same land where smoke 'goes up forever' is inhabited by animals (34:11-17) — proving the smoke formula cannot mean the subject is still burning. It means: the destruction is permanent, the memorial is perpetual.

docs.title: OT background for unquenchable fire - subjects are peger (corpses), not living persons
docs.text:
And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

Context: Final verse of Isaiah. The objects of the fire and worm are peger (H6297 — corpses/carcasses). Peger is NEVER used for living persons in the OT (24 uses, all = dead bodies). The worm feeds on dead bodies; the fire consumes dead bodies. The result is dera'on (H1860 — 'abhorrence/contempt') — onlookers view the aftermath with revulsion.

Notes: peger (H6297) — always 'corpse/carcass' in OT usage. tola'ah (H8438) — 'worm' — feeds on dead organic matter. esh (H784) — 'fire' — the unquenchable fire acts on corpses. This is the source text for Mark 9:44,46,48. Jesus quotes Isaiah's imagery — the subjects are already dead.

docs.title: Everlasting fire in same Gospel as furnace passages
docs.text:
Wherefore if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off, and cast [them] from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life halt or maimed, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into everlasting fire.

Context: Same-author usage of pur aionion (everlasting fire) in the same Gospel that has kaminos tou pyros (furnace of fire). The enter-life vs. cast-into-fire contrast parallels the life vs. gehenna contrast of Mark 9:43-48.

Notes: pur aionion (G4442 + G166) — same phrase as Matt 25:41. The contrast is 'enter into life' (eiselthein eis ten zoen) vs. 'be cast into everlasting fire' (blethenal eis to pur to aionion). Life vs. fire — not life vs. alternative-life.

docs.title: Teeth-grinding (trizo) in demonic seizure - involuntary physical event, not judgment
docs.text:
And wheresoever he taketh him, he teareth him: and he foameth, and gnasheth with his teeth, and pineth away: and I spake to thy disciples that they should cast him out; and they could not.

Context: The boy with the unclean spirit. The teeth-grinding (trizo G5149) is an involuntary physical symptom alongside foaming and wasting away. This shows teeth-grinding can describe a temporary, physical event that ends when the cause is removed.

Notes: trizei (G5149 — Present Active Indicative 3S) — 'gnashes/grinds.' Distinct from brygmos (judgment formula) and brycho (hostile rage). Trizo is involuntary, physical, and temporary — it stopped when Jesus cast out the demon.

docs.title: Basanistais (tormentors) in unforgiving servant parable - non-eschatological parabolic detail
docs.text:
And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him.

Context: Parable of the unforgiving servant. The 'tormentors' (basanistais G930) appear in a debt parable, NOT an eschatological judgment parable. The 'till he should pay all' implies a finite, measurable process. This is the ONLY basanizo-family word in any Matthean parable.

Notes: basanistais (G930 — Dative Plural Masculine) — 'tormentors/jailers.' This is a parabolic detail about debt imprisonment, not eschatological judgment. The 'till he should pay' (heos hou apodo) implies an end-point. Contrast with the judgment parables (tares, dragnet, sheep/goats, talents, wedding feast) which use ZERO basanizo-family words.

docs.title: OT smelting furnace (kuwr) - Israel as dross consumed in divine fury
docs.text:
Ezekiel 22:18 Son of man, the house of Israel is to me become dross: all they [are] brass, and tin, and iron, and lead, in the midst of the furnace; they are [even] the dross of silver. Ezekiel 22:19 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because ye are all become dross, behold, therefore I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem. Ezekiel 22:20 [As] they gather silver, and brass, and iron, and lead, and tin, into the midst of the furnace, to blow the fire upon it, to melt [it]; so will I gather [you] in mine anger and in my fury, and I will leave [you there], and melt you. Ezekiel 22:21 Yea, I will gather you, and blow upon you in the fire of my wrath, and ye shall be melted in the midst thereof. Ezekiel 22:22 As silver is melted in the midst of the furnace, so shall ye be melted in the midst thereof; and ye shall know that I the LORD have poured out my fury upon you.

Context: Ezekiel's furnace metaphor using kuwr (H3564). Israel = dross (sig H5509). The smelting furnace CONSUMES the dross — it does not preserve it. The verb nathak (H5413 'melt/pour') appears throughout. The melting is driven by divine fury (chemah H2534).

Notes: kuwr (H3564) = smelting furnace. sig (H5509) = dross — the waste product that is consumed in smelting. nathak (H5413) = melt — repeated 4x in vv.20-22. chemah (H2534) = fury/wrath — the driving force. The LXX translates kuwr as kaminos (G2575) — the same word Jesus uses for the furnace of fire.

docs.title: Sodom suffering vengeance of eternal fire - paradigm with 2 Pet 2:6
docs.text:
Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

Context: Jude's Sodom reference. The cities 'suffer the vengeance of eternal fire' (pur aionion). But 2 Pet 2:6 says the same cities were 'turned to ashes' (tephroo). The 'eternal fire' produced ashes — fire whose results are permanent.

Notes: puros aioniou (G4442 + G166 — Genitive Singular Neuter) — 'of eternal fire.' deigma (G1164 — Accusative Singular Neuter) — 'example.' The word is different from Peter's hupodeigma but the function is identical: Sodom as THE paradigm for fire judgment. Note: Jude uses aidios (G126 'everduring') in v.6 for the chains of rebellious angels, then aionios (G166) in v.7 for the fire — different duration words in adjacent verses.

docs.title: Wicked perish and consume away into smoke - cessation simile
docs.text:
But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD [shall be] as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away.

Context: Wisdom psalm. The wicked 'perish' (abad H6) and 'consume away into smoke' (kala H3615 + ashan H6227). Smoke is a cessation simile — it rises and disappears.

Notes: abad (H6) Qal Imperfect 3P — 'shall perish.' kala (H3615) Qal Perfect 3P — 'they shall consume/end.' ashan (H6227) — 'smoke.' The wicked are compared to 'the fat of lambs' (yaqar karim) — which is consumed on the altar, leaving nothing. The smoke rises as evidence of completed consumption.

docs.title: Wicked perish like wax melting before fire - cessation simile
docs.text:
As smoke is driven away, [so] drive [them] away: as wax melteth before the fire, [so] let the wicked perish at the presence of God.

Context: David's psalm of God's majesty. Two cessation similes: (1) smoke driven away (nadaph H5086), (2) wax melting (masas H4549) before fire. Both substances cease to exist. The wicked 'perish' (abad H6) at God's presence.

Notes: donag (H1749) — 'wax.' masas (H4549) — 'melt.' Same verb as Psa 112:10 where the gnashing wicked 'melts away.' abad (H6) — 'perish.' The combination of melting wax + perishing at God's presence perfectly parallels the furnace imagery: what fire does to wax is what divine judgment does to the wicked.

docs.title: Four cessation similes - morning cloud, early dew, chaff, chimney smoke
docs.text:
Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff [that] is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.

Context: Hosea's judgment oracle against Ephraim. Four cessation similes in one verse: morning cloud (disappears), early dew (evaporates), chaff driven by whirlwind (blown away), smoke from chimney (dissipates). All four substances cease to exist.

Notes: Four similes: (1) anan-boqer (morning cloud), (2) tal mashkim (early dew), (3) mots (chaff) + suphah (whirlwind), (4) ashan (smoke) + arubbah (chimney/opening). Every biblical cessation simile describes a substance that CEASES TO EXIST. No biblical simile for the wicked depicts something continuing in a ruined state.

docs.title: Jesus on Sodom - apollymi 'destroyed them all'
docs.text:
But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed [them] all.

Context: Jesus' own interpretation of the Sodom event. He uses apollymi (G622) — 'destroyed them all.' Jesus treats the fire-and-brimstone event as DESTRUCTION, not ongoing torment.

Notes: apolesen (G622 — Aorist Active Indicative 3S) — 'destroyed.' hapantas (G537 — Accusative Plural Masculine) — 'all of them.' The aorist tense treats the destruction as a completed, one-time event. Jesus + Peter (2 Pet 2:6) + Jude (1:7) all interpret the Sodom fire the same way: destruction/ashes, not ongoing burning.

docs.title: Same-author fire judgment - every tree not producing good fruit cast into fire
docs.text:
Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

Context: Sermon on the Mount. Same-author judgment fire imagery. The unfruitful tree is 'hewn down' (ekkopto G1581) and 'cast into the fire' (ballo eis to pur). Same verb pattern as the furnace casting (ballo eis ten kaminon tou pyros).

Notes: Same imagery as Matt 3:10 (John the Baptist) and Luke 3:9. Matthew uses the tree/fire metaphor in both the Baptist's preaching and Jesus' Sermon on the Mount, establishing fire-as-destruction as a consistent framework across speakers within the same Gospel.

docs.title: Same-author gehenna reference - hell fire in Sermon on the Mount
docs.text:
But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

Context: Jesus' first gehenna reference in Matthew. Three-tiered warning: judgment (krisis), council (synedrion), gehenna of fire (geennan tou pyros). gehenna is the ultimate sanction, associated with fire, not darkness or torment.

Notes: geennan tou pyros — 'gehenna of fire.' The genitive tou pyros specifies gehenna's character: it is defined by fire. Same fire vocabulary as kaminos tou pyros (furnace of fire). Zero basanizo vocabulary in any Matthean gehenna reference.

docs.title: Second NT occurrence of kolasis - fear has punishment/correction
docs.text:
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.

Context: John's teaching on love and fear. kolasis here = the corrective/punitive dimension of fear. KJV translates as 'torment' but the Greek word is kolasis (G2851), not basanismos (G929). This is the only other NT use besides Matt 25:46.

Notes: kolasin (G2851 — Accusative Singular Feminine) — same form as Matt 25:46. echei (G2192 — Present Active Indicative 3S) — 'has/involves.' The KJV translation 'torment' for kolasis here is misleading — kolasis means 'punishment/correction,' from kolazo 'to curtail/prune.' The verb basanizo does NOT appear.

docs.title: Eternal redemption - Hebrews aionios pattern: permanent result of completed act
docs.text:
Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption [for us].

Context: Hebrews' theological use of aionios. 'Eternal redemption' (aionian lutrosis) = redemption obtained ONCE, with PERMANENT result. The act of redeeming is not ongoing — Christ entered 'once' (hapax/ephapax). The result is permanent.

Notes: aionian lutrosin — 'eternal redemption.' This is the Hebrews pattern: aionios + result-noun = the result is permanent, not the act. If 'eternal redemption' means 'a once-completed act with permanent result,' then 'eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion, Matt 25:46) may follow the same pattern: punishment rendered once, result permanent.

docs.title: Eternal judgment - Hebrews aionios pattern: verdict rendered once, permanent
docs.text:
Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.

Context: Foundational doctrines listed. 'Eternal judgment' (krimatos aioniou) = judgment rendered ONCE, verdict PERMANENT. The judging is not ongoing — it is a completed act with an enduring result.

Notes: krimatos aioniou — 'eternal judgment.' Same pattern as aionian lutrosin. The judgment is not eternally in process; it is rendered once and its verdict stands forever.

docs.title: Aionios used twice with different scopes in one verse
docs.text:
In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began;

Context: Paul uses aionios twice: 'eternal life' (zoes aioniou) and 'before the world began' (pro chronon aionion — 'before ages-long times'). The same adjective describes (1) the promised life (eternal/future) and (2) past time periods (ages ago, not eternal). Same adjective, different temporal scopes in ONE verse.

Notes: Two aionios uses: (1) zoes aioniou — 'eternal life'; (2) pro chronon aionion — 'before age-long times' (the times are PAST and FINISHED). This falsifies the claim that 'aionios always means exactly the same duration.' If aionios meant strictly 'eternal' in both uses, the second would be incoherent — 'before eternal times' implies times that are no longer running.

docs.title: Everlasting destruction - olethros aionios, destruction vocabulary with aionios qualifier
docs.text:
Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

Context: Paul's judgment prophecy. The punishment is olethros aionios — 'everlasting DESTRUCTION.' olethros (G3639) is in the destruction word family, not the torment word family. Combined with aionios, it means: destruction whose result is permanent.

Notes: olethron aionion — 'everlasting destruction.' olethros (G3639) = destruction/ruin. This is the only NT passage combining a destruction word directly with aionios. If this means 'permanent destruction' (Hebrews pattern), it confirms that the eschatological fate of the wicked is destructive, not tormenting.

docs.title: Lake of fire = second death - identification formula using thanatos not basanismos
docs.text:
And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.

Context: The identification formula: houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin, he limne tou puros. The lake of fire IS 'the second death' — thanatos (G2288), not basanismos (G929). The predicate noun defining the lake's nature is DEATH.

Notes: thanatos (G2288) — 'death.' The identification uses the same X=Y copular formula as Matt 13:38-39 (X eisin Y). If Jesus' self-interpretation formula is authoritative, Revelation's self-interpretation formula is equally authoritative: the lake of fire = DEATH.

docs.title: Fiery indignation to devour adversaries - destruction verb for fire judgment
docs.text:
But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.

Context: Warning against willful sin after receiving knowledge. The fire (puros zelos — 'fiery zeal/indignation') shall 'devour' (esthio G2068) the adversaries. esthio = to eat/consume — destruction vocabulary.

Notes: esthiein (G2068 — Present Active Infinitive) — 'to devour/eat.' Same semantic field as katesthio (G2719) used in Rev 20:9. Fire devours — it does not preserve. The adversaries (hypenantious G5227) are consumed.

docs.title: Every plant not planted by the Father uprooted - destruction vocabulary
docs.text:
But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.

Context: Jesus' statement about the Pharisees. Plants not planted by God will be 'rooted up' (ekrizoo G1610). Same agricultural imagery as the tares parable — plants removed and destroyed.

Notes: ekrizothsetai (G1610 — Future Passive Indicative 3S) — 'shall be rooted up.' Agricultural destruction vocabulary consistent with the tares parable's burning and the Mal 4:1 'neither root nor branch.'

docs.title: First outer darkness + gnashing formula — sons of the kingdom cast out
docs.text:
But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Jesus contrasts centurion's faith with unbelieving Israel. Those expected at the kingdom feast are cast into outer darkness instead.

Notes: Individual gnashing occurrence #1. ekblethesontai (G1544 Fut Pass Ind 3P). to skotos to exoteron — double article + comparative adjective.

docs.title: Second outer darkness — wedding feast, binding + casting out
docs.text:
Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast [him] into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Wedding feast parable. Guest without garment bound and expelled.

Notes: Individual gnashing occurrence #4. desantes (G1210 AAP) + ekbalete (G1544 AAM). Binding adds helplessness to exclusion.

docs.title: Third outer darkness — unprofitable servant cast out from joy
docs.text:
And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Talents parable conclusion. Contrast: enter joy (v.21,23) vs. cast into outer darkness.

Notes: Individual gnashing occurrence #6. achreion (G888 'unprofitable'). Same formula as 8:12 and 22:13.

docs.title: First furnace formula — furnace of fire + wailing and gnashing
docs.text:
And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Tares parable interpretation conclusion. Angels cast the wicked into the furnace.

Notes: Individual gnashing occurrence #2. balousin (G906 FAI 3P) + kaminon tou pyros (G2575 + G4442).

docs.title: Second furnace formula — identical wording in dragnet context
docs.text:
And shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Dragnet parable conclusion. Verbatim identical Greek to Matt 13:42.

Notes: Individual gnashing occurrence #3. Verbatim identical to 13:42.

docs.title: Fifth gnashing — dichotomeo (cut asunder) + portion with hypocrites
docs.text:
And shall cut him asunder, and appoint [him] his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Context: Unfaithful servant parable. Unique judgment verb dichotomeo.

Notes: Individual gnashing occurrence #5. dichotomosei (G1371 FAI 3S). Only gnashing occurrence with neither furnace nor darkness.

docs.title: Key interpretive verse — gnashing triggered by seeing exclusion
docs.text:
There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you [yourselves] thrust out.

Context: Luke's non-parabolic teaching. Identifies the trigger: seeing patriarchs inside, being thrust outside.

Notes: Individual gnashing occurrence #7. hotan opsesthe (G3752 + G3708) — temporal clause identifying gnashing as response to seeing exclusion.

docs.title: Luke's parallel to Matt 3:12 — chaff burned with unquenchable fire
docs.text:
Whose fan [is] in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.

Context: John the Baptist's winnowing prophecy in Luke's Gospel. Synoptic parallel to Matt 3:12.

Notes: Same katakaio verb as Matt 3:12. Cross-Gospel consistency of chaff/fire/consumption imagery.

docs.title: Gehenna fire passages — parallel fire imagery in Mark's Gospel
docs.text:
Mark 9:43 And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Mark 9:44 Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. Mark 9:45 And if thy foot offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter halt into life, than having two feet to be cast into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Mark 9:46 Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. Mark 9:47 And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out: it is better for thee to enter into the kingdom of God with one eye, than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire: Mark 9:48 Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.

Context: Mark's gehenna passages. Life/gehenna contrast repeated three times. Quotes Isa 66:24 where subjects are peger (corpses).

Notes: Three-fold repetition of life vs. gehenna contrast. The worm/fire imagery from Isa 66:24 acts on dead bodies (peger), not living persons.

docs.title: Daniel's judgment scene — fiery stream from Ancient of Days, books opened
docs.text:
Daniel 7:9 I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment [was] white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne [was like] the fiery flame, [and] his wheels [as] burning fire. Daniel 7:10 A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.

Context: Daniel's vision of the heavenly court. The fiery throne and fiery stream establish fire as the medium of divine judgment. Books opened for judicial review.

Notes: Fire imagery in judicial/courtroom setting — fire as instrument of divine authority, not preservation of the condemned.

docs.title: Everlasting contempt — dera'on subjects are dead/risen, parallel with Isa 66:24
docs.text:
And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame [and] everlasting contempt.

Context: Resurrection prophecy. Two outcomes: everlasting life vs. shame and everlasting contempt. dera'on (H1860) has only 2 OT uses: here and Isa 66:24.

Notes: dera'on (H1860 'contempt/abhorrence') — only 2 uses. In Isa 66:24 the objects are peger (corpses). 'Everlasting contempt' = permanent abhorrence directed at dead bodies, not ongoing experience of living subjects.

docs.title: Wicked shall not be (ayin) — non-existence language
docs.text:
For yet a little while, and the wicked [shall] not [be]: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it [shall] not [be].

Context: Wisdom psalm. ayin (H369) non-existence language: the wicked 'shall not be' and their place 'shall not be.' Complete cessation.
