Neuter noun: darkness, obscurity. 32 tokens in 31 unique verses across 16 books. Semantic domains: physical darkness, moral/spiritual state, domain of evil, judgment. Matthew has 6 uses: 3 in the outer-darkness formula (8:12; 22:13; 25:30), 1 physical darkness at crucifixion (27:45), 2 spiritual darkness (4:16; 6:23). LXX source: choshek (H2822 'darkness').

Semantic categories: physical darkness, moral/spiritual state, domain/power of evil, eschatological judgment

Key verses: Matt 8:12, Matt 22:13, Matt 25:30, Matt 27:45, Col 1:13

Relevance: Component of the 'outer darkness' formula. The tension between skotos (darkness = no light) and kaminos/pyr (furnace/fire = bright light) in the same author and same eschatological framework is a critical datum. A literal furnace produces light, not darkness. Both images in the same author describing the same fate confirms figurative usage — darkness = exclusion from God's light/kingdom; fire = destruction/consumption.

docs.title: G1067 — gehenna
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1067-geenna.md

Occurrences: 12

Feminine noun: gehenna (Valley of Hinnom). 12 NT occurrences: 7 in Matthew, 3 in Mark, 1 in Luke, 1 in James. 11 of 12 are Jesus' direct speech. Collocates: fire (6x), apollymi (3x), ballo (5x), zoe as antithesis (3x). basanizo NEVER co-occurs with gehenna. Life/gehenna contrast (Matt 18:9; Mark 9:43,45,47): 'enter life' vs. 'cast into gehenna fire' — life vs. destruction, not life vs. alternative-life.

Semantic categories: fiery place of destruction, self-denial to escape it, destruction of soul and body, God's judicial judgment, moral corruption

Key verses: Matt 5:22, Matt 5:29-30, Matt 10:28, Matt 18:9, Matt 23:33, Mark 9:43-48, Luke 12:5, James 3:6

Relevance: The broader eschatological judgment location in Jesus' teaching. The furnace (kaminos) and gehenna share fire imagery and destruction vocabulary. gehenna collocates with apollymi (destroy) and pyr (fire) but NEVER with basanizo (torment). The life/gehenna contrast shows gehenna as the opposite of life — death/destruction, not ongoing existence in torment.

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Adjective: pertaining to the age(s), age-long, everlasting. 71 NT occurrences. Duration determined by nature of subject. Three past-time uses (Rom 16:25; 2 Tim 1:9; Tit 1:2) demonstrate non-eternal meaning. The Hebrews pattern: aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act (eternal redemption Heb 9:12; eternal judgment Heb 6:2). Tit 1:2 uses aionios twice with different temporal scopes in one verse, falsifying 'same adjective = same duration.' The aidios/aionios distinction: aidios (G126) = strictly everduring; Jude uses aidios (v.6) then aionios (v.7) in adjacent verses.

Semantic categories: divine/spiritual duration, eschatological result, pre-temporal duration

Key verses: Matt 25:46, Matt 18:8, Matt 25:41, John 3:16, Heb 9:12, Heb 6:2, Tit 1:2, 2 Thess 1:9

Relevance: Qualifies both 'punishment' (Matt 25:46) and 'fire' (Matt 18:8; 25:41) in the judgment parables framework. The Hebrews pattern governs interpretation: 'eternal punishment' = punishment rendered once with permanent result; 'eternal fire' = fire whose destructive result is permanent. The Sodom test case: Jude 1:7's 'eternal fire' produced 2 Pet 2:6's 'ashes' — eternal fire that ended, leaving permanent results.

docs.title: G2851 — kolasis
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2851-kolasis.md

Occurrences: 2

Feminine noun: punishment, correction. From kolazo (G2849 'to curtail, dock, prune'). Only 2 NT occurrences: Matt 25:46 ('everlasting punishment') and 1 John 4:18 ('fear hath torment/punishment'). This is PUNISHMENT vocabulary, not TORMENT vocabulary. The distinction matters: basanismos (G929) = torment; kolasis = punishment/correction from kolazo 'to curtail.' Aristotle distinguished kolasis (corrective, for the benefit of the sufferer) from timoria (retributive, for the satisfaction of the inflictor).

Semantic categories: punishment, corrective discipline

Key verses: Matt 25:46, 1 John 4:18

Relevance: The word Jesus chose in Matt 25:46 for the fate of the goats is kolasis (punishment), NOT basanismos (torment). The kolazo root ('to curtail/prune') carries a cutting-off/ending sense. Combined with aionios in the Hebrews pattern: eternal punishment = punishment whose result is permanent cutting-off.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G928-basanizo.md

Occurrences: 12

Verb: to torment, put to the test. 12 NT occurrences. Judgment uses exclusively in Revelation (5 judgment uses, all Revelation). ZERO occurrences in any judgment parable, any outer-darkness passage, any gnashing-formula passage, or any Matthean gehenna passage. Genre-restricted to apocalyptic/visionary literature.

Semantic categories: physical suffering/disease, demonic torment, apocalyptic judgment

Key verses: Matt 8:6, Matt 8:29, Rev 14:10, Rev 20:10

Relevance: THE critical absence. basanizo (torment) NEVER appears in any passage in this study. The judgment parables use katakaio (consume), apollymi (destroy), ballo (cast), ekballo (cast out), dichotomeo (cut asunder). basanizo for human eschatological judgment appears ONLY in Revelation's apocalyptic framework (Rev 14:10-11; 20:10 for non-human entities). This is a systematic vocabulary differentiation.

docs.title: G929 — basanismos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G929-basanismos.md

Occurrences: 6

Masculine noun: torment, torture. 6 NT occurrences, ALL in Revelation. 3 describe Babylon's completed destruction. 1 has five-month time limit (Rev 9:5). Exclusively apocalyptic vocabulary. Never in parables, never in Gospels, never in epistles.

Semantic categories: apocalyptic judgment torment

Key verses: Rev 9:5, Rev 14:11, Rev 18:7, Rev 18:10, Rev 18:15

Relevance: Zero occurrences in any judgment parable or any passage in this study. The torment noun is exclusively Revelation vocabulary. Jesus NEVER uses basanismos in his teaching.

docs.title: G684 — apoleia
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G684-apoleia.md

Occurrences: 20

Feminine noun: destruction, perdition, waste. Cognate of apollymi (G622). Used for eschatological destruction in multiple passages. The noun form of the primary destruction verb.

Semantic categories: destruction/perdition, waste/ruin

Key verses: Matt 7:13, Phil 3:19, 2 Pet 3:7, Rev 17:8

Relevance: The noun form of apollymi. Matt 7:13 contrasts the 'broad way that leads to destruction (apoleia)' with the 'narrow way that leads to life (zoe).' Destruction vs. life — not ongoing torment vs. life.

docs.title: G5077 — tephroo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5077-tephroo.md

Occurrences: 1

Verb: to turn to ashes (from tephra 'ashes'). Hapax legomenon — only 1 NT use (2 Pet 2:6). Describes what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah. The cities were 'turned to ashes' (tephrosas, aorist active participle) and set as an 'example' (hupodeigma) for the ungodly.

Semantic categories: destruction to ashes

Key verses: 2 Pet 2:6

Relevance: Defines the result of 'eternal fire' (Jude 1:7). The same cities that 'suffer the vengeance of eternal fire' were 'turned to ashes.' This establishes the paradigm: eternal fire = fire that produces permanent destruction (ashes), not eternal burning.

docs.title: G906 — ballo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G906-ballo.md

Occurrences: 127

Verb: to cast, throw. Common verb with wide usage. In judgment contexts: 'cast into the furnace of fire' (Matt 13:42,50), 'cast into fire/gehenna' (Matt 5:29-30; 18:8-9). The verb of directed judgment action.

Semantic categories: casting/throwing, judgment casting

Key verses: Matt 13:42, Matt 13:50, Matt 5:29, Matt 18:8

Relevance: The verb for casting the wicked INTO the furnace of fire. Appears in Matt 13:42,50 as balousin (Future Active Indicative 3P) — 'they shall cast.' The casting is a one-time directed action, not an ongoing state.

docs.title: G1544 — ekballo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1544-ekballo.md

Occurrences: 96

Compound verb (ek + ballo): to cast out, expel. The verb of exclusion/expulsion. Used in the outer-darkness formula: 'cast out into the outer darkness' (Matt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30). Also in Luke 13:28: 'you yourselves thrust out' (ekballomenous exo).

Semantic categories: expulsion/exclusion, exorcism, judgment casting out

Key verses: Matt 8:12, Matt 22:13, Matt 25:30, Luke 13:28

Relevance: The verb for exclusion from the kingdom feast. Appears in all three outer-darkness passages and Luke's gnashing passage. The ek- prefix emphasizes OUT-casting — removal from inside to outside. This is EXCLUSION vocabulary, not confinement-in-torment vocabulary.

docs.title: H2786 — charaq
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H2786-charaq.md

Occurrences: 5

Primitive root verb: to grate/gnash the teeth. 5 OT occurrences across 3 books (Psalms 3, Job 1, Lamentations 1). ALL 5 express hostile rage: Job 16:9 (enemy gnashes in wrath), Psa 35:16 (mockers gnash at David), Psa 37:12 (wicked gnashes at righteous), Psa 112:10 (wicked gnashes and melts away), Lam 2:16 (enemies gnash in triumph). Always Qal stem. Always collocates with shen (H8127 'teeth') — 100% of uses. LXX maps charaq 1:1 to brycho (G1031) with perfect bidirectional equivalence.

Semantic categories: hostile gnashing of teeth (rage/animosity)

Key verses: Job 16:9, Psa 35:16, Psa 37:12, Psa 112:10, Lam 2:16

Relevance: THE OT background for brygmos (gnashing) in the judgment formula. All 5 OT uses are HOSTILE RAGE directed at the righteous or God's people. The subject is always an enemy/wicked person. The emotion is anger/malice, NOT pain/suffering. This OT background governs interpretation of the NT judgment formula: gnashing = rage at exclusion.

docs.title: G1031 — brycho
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1031-brycho.md

Occurrences: 1

Primary verb: to grate/gnash the teeth. Hapax legomenon — only Acts 7:54 (Sanhedrin gnashing at Stephen). Imperfect tense (ebruchon) indicates continuous/repeated action — sustained rage. Dual-domain classification: Louw-Nida 23.41 (mouth processes) AND 88.181 (anger/indignation). Root verb for brygmos (G1030). Maps 1:1 to charaq (H2786) in LXX.

Semantic categories: teeth-gnashing as expression of rage

Key verses: Acts 7:54

Relevance: The sole NT use of the verb confirms the OT rage meaning. Acts 7:54 context: the Sanhedrin hears Stephen's accusation, is 'cut to the heart' (diaprio — enraged), and gnashes teeth AT (ep' auton) him. They then stone him. This is murderous fury, not pain or suffering. The cognate noun brygmos in the judgment formula carries this same rage connotation.

docs.title: G5149 — trizo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G5149-trizo.md

Occurrences: 1

Primary verb: to creak, squeak; by analogy to grate/grind teeth. Hapax legomenon — only Mark 9:18 (boy's demonic seizure). Present tense (trizei) depicts ongoing/habitual action during episodes. Distinguished from brycho (deliberate hostile gnashing) and brygmos (eschatological formula). Trizo is involuntary physical grinding during convulsions.

Semantic categories: involuntary physical teeth-grinding

Key verses: Mark 9:18

Relevance: Shows that teeth-grinding CAN describe a temporary physical event. The boy's grinding stopped when Jesus cast out the demon. This is evidence against interpreting the judgment gnashing as an ongoing eternal state — it can describe a momentary response.

docs.title: G1371 — dichotomeo
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1371-dichotomeo.md

Occurrences: 2

Compound verb (dicha 'in two' + temno 'to cut'): to cut in two, cut asunder. 2 NT occurrences (Matt 24:51; Luke 12:46) in the unfaithful servant parable. Both use identical form dichotomosei (Future Active Indicative 3S). Dual Louw-Nida domains: 19.002 (pierce/cut) AND 38.001 (punish). LXX background: butchering sacrificial animals (Exod 29:17, 1 Sam 15:33).

Semantic categories: judicial punishment — severe consequence, physical cutting

Key verses: Matt 24:51, Luke 12:46

Relevance: Unique judgment verb in Matt 24:51 — the only gnashing occurrence with neither furnace nor outer-darkness imagery. The verb is violent and decisive: 'cut asunder.' Combined with 'appoint his portion with the hypocrites' and the gnashing formula. This is destruction/execution vocabulary.

docs.title: G1714 — empretho
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G1714-empretho.md

Occurrences: 1

Compound verb (en + pretho 'to blow a flame'): to set on fire, burn up. Hapax legomenon — only Matt 22:7 ('burned up their city'). Aorist active indicative (enepresen). Same Louw-Nida domain as katakaio (14.008 Burning). Primary Hebrew source: saraph (H8313) with PMI 7.31

Semantic categories: military destruction of a city

Key verses: Matt 22:7

Relevance: Same-author fire vocabulary in the wedding feast parable. Matt 22:7 pairs apollymi (destroyed murderers) with empretho (burned city) — two destruction verbs in one verse. This is in the SAME parable that ends with outer darkness (v.13). Matthew uses distinct fire verbs for distinct functions: empretho for city-burning, katakaio for eschatological consumption.

docs.title: H3564 — kuwr
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H3564-kuwr.md

Occurrences: 11

Masculine noun: furnace, specifically smelting/refining furnace. 9 unique verses across 6 books. Four semantic categories: Egypt as iron furnace (Deut 4:20; 1 Ki 8:51; Jer 11:4), metallurgical testing (Prov 17:3; 27:21), furnace of affliction (Isa 48:10), smelting furnace of judgment where dross is consumed (Ezk 22:18-22). LXX maps kuwr primarily to kaminos (G2575) with 6 co-occurrences and PMI 9.49

Semantic categories: national deliverance metaphor, metallurgical testing, divine refining, judgment — dross consumed

Key verses: Deut 4:20, Prov 17:3, Isa 48:10, Ezk 22:18-22

Relevance: Second OT furnace tradition feeding into kaminos. The Ezk 22 usage is critical: Israel as dross in the kuwr — the smelting furnace CONSUMES the dross. The verb nathak (melt/pour) appears 4x in Ezk 22:20-22. The furnace's function here is consuming the worthless (dross), not preserving it.

docs.title: H8574 — tannuwr
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H8574-tannuwr.md

Occurrences: 19

Masculine noun: oven, fire-pot, furnace. 15 unique verses across 9 books. Seven semantic categories ranging from domestic baking oven (Lev 2:4) to divine judgment (Mal 4:1; Psa 21:9) to human wickedness as internal heat (Hos 7:4,6,7). LXX maps primarily to klibanos (G2823 'oven') rather than kaminos. The judgment usage in Mal 4:1 is critical: 'the day burns as a tannuwr' — the wicked become stubble and are burned up, leaving neither root nor branch.

Semantic categories: domestic baking oven, ritual purity object, theophanic fire-pot, landmark, divine judgment/wrath, human wickedness as heat, famine/suffering

Key verses: Gen 15:17, Mal 4:1, Psa 21:9, Hos 7:4

Relevance: Third OT furnace tradition. Mal 4:1 is the critical verse: tannuwr as the image for eschatological judgment fire. The result: wicked = stubble, burned up, neither root nor branch, ashes under feet (4:3). This is the most explicit OT passage defining what the furnace does to the wicked: total consumption to ashes.

docs.title: H861 — attuwn
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/A861-attuwn.md

Occurrences: 18

Aramaic masculine noun: furnace (fire-place). 10 unique verses (18 tokens), ALL in Daniel 3:6-26. The execution furnace of Nebuchadnezzar. LXX maps univocally to kaminos (G2575) — perfect 1:1 alignment. The furnace killed soldiers from proximity (3:22); only divine intervention preserved the three Hebrews. Default result = death.

Semantic categories: instrument of royal execution, arena of divine deliverance, execution carried out, theophanic encounter

Key verses: Dan 3:6, Dan 3:17, Dan 3:20-23, Dan 3:22, Dan 3:25-26

Relevance: Primary OT background for kaminos via LXX. The Daniel 3 furnace is the narrative image behind Jesus' 'furnace of fire.' The furnace's function is EXECUTION — it kills by default. Survival required direct divine intervention (the fourth figure). When Jesus says 'cast them into the furnace of fire,' the OT referent is an execution furnace, not a confinement facility.

docs.title: G930 — basanistes
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G930-basanistēs.md

Occurrences: 1

Masculine noun: torturer, tormentor, jailer. Only 1 NT occurrence: Matt 18:34 (unforgiving servant parable). The servant is delivered to the 'tormentors' (basanistais) until he pays all owed. This is a DEBT parable, not an eschatological judgment parable. The 'until he should pay' implies a finite, measurable process.

Semantic categories: debt imprisonment/torture

Key verses: Matt 18:34

Relevance: The ONLY basanizo-family word in any Matthean parable. It appears in a non-eschatological debt parable, not in the judgment parables (tares, dragnet, sheep/goats, talents, wedding feast). The 'until he should pay' qualification further distinguishes it from the judgment parables' definitive language.

docs.title: G931 — basanos
docs.text:
Source: D:/bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G931-basanos.md

Occurrences: 3

Feminine noun: touchstone (for testing metals), hence torture, torment, pain. 3 NT occurrences: Matt 4:24 (physical suffering), Luke 16:23,28 (rich man in hades). ALL 3 are pre-judgment state, NOT eschatological. Zero uses in judgment parable contexts.

Semantic categories: physical suffering, parabolic/pre-judgment context

Key verses: Matt 4:24, Luke 16:23, Luke 16:28

Relevance: Zero eschatological judgment uses. The only parabolic use is Luke 16 (rich man and Lazarus), which operates in hades (pre-judgment), not gehenna or furnace (post-judgment). The parabolic genre classification of Luke 16 (per etc7-09) further limits its evidential weight.

docs.title: Question: What do Jesus' judgment parables and associated imagery teach about the fate of the wicked?
docs.text: This document contains the full Tree 3/4 walkthroughs for every E-item classified as Cond. or ECT and every N-item. Each walkthrough documents the mechanical gate-by-gate classification process.

docs.title: E-Item Classifications (Tree 3 Walkthroughs)
docs.text:
E1 (Matt 13:30) — "Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them [katakausai]" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — katakaio (G2618, "burn completely/consume") applied to the tares (representing the wicked per Jesus' decoding in v.38). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject of katakausai is "the tares" (ta zizania). In the parable itself, tares are plants, not literal human beings. However, Jesus decodes tares = "sons of the wicked one" (huioi tou ponerou, v.38). The verb katakaio is applied to parabolic elements (tares), not directly to decoded human referents in this verse. Subject is an allegorical element in a parable. FAIL — subject is a parabolic/allegorical element.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): katakausai = katakaio G2618, Aorist Active Infinitive. The articular infinitive construction (pros to katakausai auta) states the purpose: "for the burning of them." Grammar unambiguously supports total consumption (kata- prefix = completion). PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): This verse is within the parable itself (Matt 13:24-30), not within Jesus' interpretation (13:36-43). Genre = parabolic narrative. FAIL — parable.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached (Gate 1 and Gate 3 failed).
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Gate 1: Subject is tares (parabolic element). Gate 3: Genre is parabolic.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In a parable, plants representing the wicked are gathered and burned completely (katakaio)." The parabolic imagery uses cessation/consumption vocabulary for the fate of the wicked's symbolic representatives.
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: The corrected observation describes parabolic imagery of consumption. Parabolic depiction does not constitute didactic teaching about human fate at E-tier. Neither V1 nor V2 applies at the didactic level.
  • Result: Gate 1 and Gate 3 fail. Reclassified to Neutral. The text uses consumption vocabulary in parabolic imagery — both sides can accept this as a textual observation about what the parable depicts.

E2 (Matt 13:40) — "As therefore the tares are gathered and burned [katakaietal] in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — katakaio (G2618, Present Passive Indicative 3S, "is consumed") applied to tares with explicit eschatological application ("so shall it be"). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The grammatical subject is "the tares" (ta zizania). Jesus has decoded tares = "sons of the wicked one" (v.38). V.40 uses the hosper...houtos ("as...so") comparative construction: "AS the tares are burned, SO shall it be at the end of the age." The subject of the burning is still the parabolic element (tares), applied via simile to the eschatological event. The decoded human referents (sons of the wicked one) are the implied ultimate subject, but the grammatical subject of katakaietai remains "the tares." FAIL — grammatical subject is the parabolic element, applied via simile.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): katakaietal = katakaio G2618, Present Passive Indicative 3S. Grammar is clear: the tares "are being consumed." The kata- prefix confirms completion. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): This verse is within Jesus' self-interpretation of the parable (13:36-43). The self-interpretation pattern (per grammar reference: self-interpretation-literal-correction.md) elevates the passage from purely parabolic to semi-didactic. However, v.40 retains the simile structure (hosper...houtos = "as...so"), maintaining the parabolic comparison rather than making a direct propositional statement. The decoded propositional statements are in vv.37-39 (X eisin Y). V.40 reverts to simile. Genre classification: semi-didactic with retained simile. This is a borderline case. The genre is NOT purely parabolic (Jesus has decoded the symbols) but NOT purely didactic (the simile structure is retained). BORDERLINE — treated as semi-didactic with qualification. The verb katakaio carries its full semantic weight even in simile form, but the simile structure means the application is via comparison, not direct statement.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): No conflicting E-items. Same-author katakaio usage in Matt 3:12 (chaff burned) supports the consumption reading. PASS.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Gate 1: Subject is tares (parabolic element applied via simile). Genre is semi-didactic with simile retention.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In Jesus' self-interpretation of his parable, the burning of the tares (katakaio = consume completely) is used as a simile for what will happen at the end of the age. The verb katakaio means total consumption in all 12 NT occurrences."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: The corrected observation contains consumption vocabulary (katakaio) applied via decoded simile. The verb's meaning (total consumption) is a textual fact. But the application to human eschatological fate requires traversing the simile ("as...so"). V1 applies (cessation vocabulary present), but the parabolic-simile mediation reduces the directness.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails (parabolic subject). Reclassified to Neutral. The text says katakaio means total consumption (lexical fact both sides accept). The application of that consumption to human fate occurs through a simile in a semi-didactic context — the verb's meaning is not disputed, but whether the simile teaches literal consumption of humans requires interpretation. Both sides accept the textual observation: "Jesus uses a simile comparing the end-of-age judgment to tares being consumed by fire."

E3 (Matt 13:42) — "And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — kaminos tou pyros ("furnace of fire") — fire/furnace imagery. V2 — klauthmos kai brygmos ("wailing and gnashing") — conscious-state vocabulary (weeping, gnashing). Both V1 and V2 triggered.
  • Both V1 and V2 YES: Note both. Proceed to Step 2.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "them" (autous) refers to "all things that offend and them which do iniquity" (v.41) — decoded human referents. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): balousin = ballo G906, Future Active Indicative 3P ("shall cast"). kaminon = kaminos G2575, Accusative Singular Feminine. klauthmos = G2805, Nominative Singular Masculine. brygmos = G1030, Nominative Singular Masculine. Grammar is straightforward. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): This verse is within Jesus' self-interpretation (13:36-43). The decoded referents (v.41 = humans doing iniquity; v.39 = angels as reapers) make this semi-didactic. However, the "furnace of fire" itself is not decoded — Jesus decoded the sower, field, seed, tares, enemy, harvest, and reapers (vv.37-39) but did NOT decode the furnace. The furnace remains an uninterpreted image within the semi-didactic framework. BORDERLINE — semi-didactic context, but the furnace itself is not decoded.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): The furnace image conflicts with the outer-darkness image in the same author (Matt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30) — fire vs. darkness for the same fate. This tension confirms both are figurative. No direct E-item conflict on the positional question (the furnace text does not directly state either ECT or cessation — it states casting + furnace + emotional response).
  • Result: The verse states the judgment event (casting into furnace) and the emotional response (wailing and gnashing). It does not specify whether the furnace preserves or consumes its contents. The furnace image is not decoded by Jesus. Classified: Neutral. Both sides accept: "Jesus describes the wicked being cast into a furnace of fire, with wailing and gnashing of teeth." They disagree about what the furnace does to its contents.

E4 (Matt 13:50) — Verbatim identical to E3 (Matt 13:42). Classified: Neutral. Same analysis.

E5 (Matt 8:12) — "But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — ekballo ("cast out") — exclusion, not destruction vocabulary per se. V2 — klauthmos kai brygmos ("weeping and gnashing") — conscious-state vocabulary. V2 triggered.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "children of the kingdom" (huioi tes basileias) — literal human beings (unbelieving Jews excluded from the messianic feast). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): ekblethesontai = ekballo G1544, Future Passive Indicative 3P ("shall be cast out"). to skotos to exoteron = double article + comparative adjective. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): This is NOT within a parable. It is Jesus' direct prophetic statement in response to the centurion's faith. No "the kingdom of heaven is like" formula. Genre = direct speech/prophecy. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): No E-item conflict. The outer-darkness image is consistent across all three occurrences (8:12; 22:13; 25:30).
  • Result: All gates pass for V2 candidate (ECT direction — conscious-state vocabulary). However, the conscious-state vocabulary here (weeping, gnashing) describes the RESPONSE at the moment of exclusion, not an ongoing state. The text says weeping and gnashing occur "there" (ekei) but does not specify duration. The text describes exclusion from the kingdom feast and an emotional response. It does not state ongoing conscious torment. Classified: Neutral. Both sides accept: "Jesus says the children of the kingdom will be cast into outer darkness where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth." They disagree about what outer darkness is and whether the response is temporary or permanent.

E6 (Matt 22:13) — "Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — conscious-state vocabulary (weeping, gnashing). Also binding imagery.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "him" = the guest without a wedding garment — an allegorical character within a parable (the wedding feast parable, 22:1-14). FAIL — allegorical character in a parable.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Parabolic. FAIL.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Subject is allegorical character; genre is parabolic.
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "In a parable, a character without proper garments is bound and expelled into outer darkness, with weeping and gnashing."
  • RC3: Parabolic depiction does not constitute didactic teaching about literal human fate. Neither V1 nor V2 applies at the didactic level.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Reclassified to Neutral. The text depicts parabolic exclusion imagery.

E7 (Matt 25:30) — "Cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — conscious-state vocabulary (weeping, gnashing).
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the unprofitable servant" — an allegorical character in the talents parable (25:14-30). FAIL — allegorical character in a parable.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Parabolic. FAIL.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check: Same as E6. Parabolic character, parabolic genre.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Reclassified to Neutral. Parabolic exclusion imagery.

E8 (Matt 24:51) — "Shall cut him asunder, and appoint him his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — dichotomeo (G1371, "cut asunder") — destruction/execution vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "that evil servant" — an allegorical character in the unfaithful servant parable (24:45-51). FAIL — allegorical character.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Parabolic. FAIL.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Subject is allegorical; genre is parabolic.
  • RC2: Corrected: "In a parable, a faithless servant is cut asunder and assigned a portion with hypocrites."
  • RC3: Parabolic depiction. Neither V1 nor V2 applies at the didactic level.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Reclassified to Neutral. Parabolic imagery using destruction vocabulary.

E9 (Luke 13:28) — "There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — conscious-state vocabulary (weeping, gnashing). V1 — ekballo ("thrust out") — exclusion vocabulary. V2 triggered.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "ye" / "you yourselves" — direct address to literal human audience. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): hotan opsesthe (G3752 + G3708, "when ye shall see") — temporal clause identifying the trigger. ekballomenous (G1544, present passive participle) + exo (G1854, "outside"). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct teaching (not within a parable formula). Response to a question about salvation. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Matt 8:12 (same exclusion + gnashing pattern). No conflict.
  • Result: All gates pass for V2 candidate (ECT direction — conscious-state vocabulary). However, the verse identifies the gnashing as a RESPONSE to seeing exclusion ("when ye shall see... and you yourselves thrust out"). The temporal clause (hotan) makes it a response to a triggering event, not a description of an ongoing state. The text describes: exclusion from the kingdom + an emotional response (weeping and gnashing) triggered by seeing others inside. It does not state ongoing conscious existence. Classified: Neutral. Both sides accept: "Jesus says weeping and gnashing will occur when the excluded see the patriarchs in the kingdom." They disagree about whether this describes a momentary response or an ongoing state.

E10 (Job 16:9) — "He gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — gnashing vocabulary. But the subject is an earthly enemy, not eschatological judgment. Neither V1 nor V2 in eschatological context. Neutral. This is OT background data about the meaning of gnashing — both sides accept it as a textual observation.

E11 (Psa 37:12) — "The wicked gnasheth upon him with his teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • Same analysis as E10. OT background for gnashing = hostile rage. Both sides accept the textual observation.

E12 (Psa 112:10) — "He shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — masas (H4549, Niphal, "melt away") + abad (H6, "perish") — cessation/destruction vocabulary applied to the wicked. V2 — charaq (H2786, "gnash") — gnashing vocabulary (but gnashing here is rage, not pain). V1 takes priority (cessation is the outcome described). Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the wicked" (rasha, H7563) — a category of human persons. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): charaq = H2786, Qal Imperfect 3ms ("shall gnash"). masas = H4549, Niphal Perfect 3ms ("melt away"). abad = H6, Qal Imperfect 3fs ("shall perish"). The subject of abad is "the desire" (taavah) of the wicked, not the wicked person directly. The subject of masas is the wicked person. Grammar supports: the wicked gnashes, melts away; the desire of the wicked perishes. PASS — masas (cessation verb) applies to the wicked person; abad applies to their desire.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom psalm — acrostic didactic poetry. Didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:10 ("the wicked shall not be"), 37:20 ("wicked perish, consume into smoke"), 68:2 ("wicked perish like wax"). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. The text states the wicked gnashes (rage), melts away (cessation), and their desire perishes (destruction). Both cessation and destruction vocabulary applied to a human category in didactic genre.

E13 (Lam 2:16) — "They hiss and gnash the teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • OT background for gnashing = hostile rage. Both sides accept. Neutral.

E14 (Acts 7:54) — "They gnashed on him with their teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — gnashing vocabulary. But context is earthly historical event (Sanhedrin's rage at Stephen), not eschatological judgment. This is background data on what gnashing means. Neutral. Both sides accept: "brycho in Acts 7:54 describes murderous rage."

E15 (Matt 10:28) — "Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — apollymi (G622, "destroy") applied to both soul and body. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "soul and body" of human beings. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): apolesai = apollymi G622, Aorist Active Infinitive ("to destroy"). kai psychen kai soma = kai...kai binding two objects as one compound target. gehenna G1067, Dative of place. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Didactic — Jesus' commissioning discourse, direct teaching to disciples. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Matt 21:41, 22:7 (same author, same verb apollymi for judgment). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. (Examined in depth in etc7-20-matthew-10-28.)

E16 (Matt 22:7) — "Destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — apollymi (G622, "destroyed") + empretho (G1714, "burned up") — destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "those murderers" — within the wedding feast parable, these are allegorical characters representing those who rejected and killed God's messengers. FAIL — allegorical characters in a parable.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Parabolic. FAIL.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Subject is allegorical; genre is parabolic.
  • RC2: Corrected: "In a parable, characters representing those who rejected the king's invitation are destroyed (apollymi) and their city burned up (empretho)."
  • RC3: Parabolic depiction using destruction vocabulary. Both sides accept the text uses apollymi and empretho here. Neither V1 nor V2 applies at the didactic level.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Reclassified to Neutral. Parabolic imagery using destruction vocabulary.

E17 (Matt 21:41) — "He will miserably destroy those wicked men" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — apollymi (G622, "destroy") applied to wicked men. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "those wicked men" — within the parable of the wicked tenants (21:33-46). The audience speaks this line, but the tenants are allegorical characters. FAIL — allegorical characters.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Parabolic. FAIL.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Subject is allegorical; genre is parabolic.
  • RC2: Corrected: "In a parable, wicked tenants are destroyed (apollymi) by the vineyard lord."
  • RC3: Parabolic depiction using destruction vocabulary.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Reclassified to Neutral. Parabolic imagery.

E18 (Matt 3:12) — "He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — katakaio (G2618, "burn up") — cessation/destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the chaff" — a simile for the wicked (winnowing imagery). The subject is figurative (chaff representing people). FAIL — figurative/metaphorical subject.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): katakausei = G2618, Future Active Indicative 3S. Grammar unambiguous: "he will consume completely." PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct prophetic speech (John the Baptist's preaching). Not parabolic formula, but the chaff/wheat imagery is figurative. Genre = prophetic speech with figurative imagery. PASS (direct speech prophecy).
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Matt 13:30,40 (same verb katakaio). PASS.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Gate 1: Subject is figurative (chaff = people, not literal chaff).
  • RC2: Corrected observation: "John the Baptist says the Messiah will burn up (katakaio) the chaff (representing the wicked) with unquenchable fire, using a winnowing metaphor."
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: The corrected observation retains cessation vocabulary (katakaio) applied to a figurative subject in prophetic speech. The verb's meaning (total consumption) is a lexical fact. But the subject is figurative.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails (figurative subject). The observation that katakaio means total consumption is a lexical fact (Neutral). The application to human fate operates through metaphor. Reclassified to Neutral. Both sides accept: "John the Baptist uses katakaio (total consumption) in a winnowing metaphor for judgment."

E19 (Mal 4:1) — "Shall burn them up... leave them neither root nor branch" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — lahat (H3857, Piel, "devour/burn up") + "leave neither root nor branch" — destruction/cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly" — a category of human persons. Also "qash" (stubble) — figurative comparison. The primary subjects are human categories ("all the proud," "all that do wickedly") who are COMPARED to stubble. The human subjects are literal. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): lahat = H3857, Piel Perfect 3ms ("shall devour/burn up"). "lo ya'azob lahem shoresh va'anaph" = "shall not leave them root or branch." Grammar clear: total consumption with nothing remaining. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct-speech prophecy ("saith the LORD of hosts"). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Mal 4:3 (ashes under feet), Psa 37:10,20; 68:2 (cessation language). No conflicting E-items. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. "The day cometh that shall burn them up, leaving neither root nor branch" — direct prophetic speech using destruction vocabulary for the wicked.

E20 (Mal 4:3) — "They shall be ashes under the soles of your feet" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — epher (H665, "ashes") — cessation/destruction vocabulary. The wicked's final state is ashes. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the wicked" — a category of human persons. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): epher = H665, noun ("ashes"). The wicked ARE ashes. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct-speech prophecy ("saith the LORD of hosts"). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with 2 Pet 2:6 (Sodom turned to ashes), Mal 4:1 (burned up). PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. The wicked are ashes under the righteous' feet — the result of the fire judgment is reduction to residue.

E21 (Psa 1:4) — "The ungodly are like the chaff which the wind driveth away" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "like the chaff" (mots) — cessation simile. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the ungodly" (ha-reshaim) — a category of human persons. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): mots = H4671, noun ("chaff"). nadaph = H5086, Qal Imperfect 3fs + 3ms suffix ("driveth away"). The ungodly ARE LIKE chaff. Simile, not metaphor. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom psalm — didactic poetry. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:20; 68:2; 104:35 (cessation language). PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. The ungodly are compared to chaff — a substance that ceases to exist when the wind takes it.

E22 (Psa 37:20) — "The wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD shall be as the fat of lambs: they shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — abad (H6, "perish") + kala (H3615, "consume/end") + ashan (H6227, "smoke") — cessation/destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the wicked" and "enemies of the LORD" — categories of human persons. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): abad = H6, Qal Imperfect 3P ("shall perish"). kala = H3615, Qal Perfect 3P ("they shall consume"). ashan = H6227, noun ("smoke"). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom psalm — didactic poetry. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:10 ("shall not be"), 68:2, 104:35. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E23 (Psa 68:2) — "As wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — masas (H4549, "melt") + abad (H6, "perish") — cessation vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the wicked" — human category. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): masas = H4549, Niphal Imperfect. abad = H6, Qal Imperfect 3P ("perish"). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Hymnic psalm — praise/petition. Contains a petition ("let the wicked perish"), which is didactic in its theological claim about what happens to the wicked at God's presence. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:10,20; 112:10. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E24 (Dan 3:22) — "The flame of the fire slew those men" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — qetal (Aramaic, "killed/slew") — death vocabulary. But the subjects (soldiers killed by furnace proximity) are not the wicked under eschatological judgment. This is a narrative fact about what the furnace does by default. Candidate: Neutral.
  • Result: Neutral. This is a narrative observation about furnace function — both sides accept it. The textual fact is: the furnace killed those who approached it.

E25 (2 Pet 2:6) — "Turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes... ensample unto those that after should live ungodly" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — tephroo (G5077, "turn to ashes") — cessation/destruction vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha" — cities, not individual human persons. However, the cities are established as a hupodeigma (example/paradigm) for "those that after should live ungodly" — human persons. The direct subject is cities. FAIL — subject is cities (used as paradigm for humans, but the direct subject of tephroo is cities, not humans).
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Gate 1: Subject is cities, not literal individual humans. The cities serve as an "ensample" (hupodeigma) for the ungodly.
  • RC2: Corrected: "Peter says the cities of Sodom were turned to ashes and set as an example for the ungodly." The observation is about cities as paradigm.
  • RC3: The textual fact — "eternal fire" (Jude 1:7) produced "ashes" (2 Pet 2:6) — is accepted by both sides. The inference to human fate requires traversing the "ensample" connection.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails (subject is cities). Reclassified to Neutral. Both sides accept: "The cities of Sodom were turned to ashes and set as an example." The positional significance depends on whether the paradigm extends to individual humans.

E26 (Rev 20:9) — "Fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — katesthio (G2719, "devoured") — destruction/consumption vocabulary applied to humans. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "them" = Gog and Magog / the gathered armies. Human subjects. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): katephagen = katesthio G2719, 2nd Aorist Active Indicative 3S ("devoured"). Grammar unambiguous: the fire devoured them. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation is apocalyptic literature. The passage describes events in a vision. FAIL — apocalyptic genre.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Not reached.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic.
  • RC2: Corrected: "In an apocalyptic vision, fire devours (katesthio) human armies." Apocalyptic depiction.
  • RC3: Re-enter V1: The corrected observation retains consumption vocabulary (katesthio) in apocalyptic genre. The word choice (devoured, not tormented) is a textual fact accepted by both sides.
  • Result: Gate 3 fails (apocalyptic). Reclassified to Neutral. Both sides accept: "Rev 20:9 uses katesthio (devour) for human subjects, while Rev 20:10 uses basanizo (torment) for the devil/beast/false prophet."

E27 (Rev 20:10) — "The devil... shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V2 — basanizo (G928, "tormented") — conscious-ongoing-existence vocabulary. But subject is the devil, beast, false prophet — non-human/symbolic entities. Candidate: ECT.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The devil, the beast, the false prophet. The beast and false prophet are symbolic entities in Revelation. The devil is a non-human spirit being. FAIL — non-human spirit being and symbolic entities.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation — apocalyptic. FAIL.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Subject is non-human/symbolic; genre is apocalyptic.
  • RC2: Corrected: "In an apocalyptic vision, non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet) are tormented (basanizo)."
  • RC3: Neither V1 nor V2 applies to HUMAN eschatological fate.
  • Result: Gates 1 and 3 fail. Classified: Neutral. Both sides accept: "Rev 20:10 applies basanizo to non-human/symbolic entities." The extension to human subjects requires interpretation.

E28 (Matt 25:46) — "These shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — kolasis (G2851, "punishment") — punishment vocabulary. This is not cessation vocabulary (does not say "destroy" or "perish"). V2 — "everlasting punishment" could imply ongoing conscious punishment. But kolasis is NOT basanizo/basanismos. Neither V1 nor V2 triggers cleanly. The text states PUNISHMENT without specifying whether ongoing or completed. Neutral.
  • Result: Neutral. Both sides accept: "Jesus says the wicked go into everlasting punishment (kolasis aionios) and the righteous into everlasting life (zoe aionios)." They disagree about whether kolasis means ongoing punishing or a permanent punitive result.

E29 (Matt 25:41) — "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels" — Classified: Neutral

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "everlasting fire" (pur aionion) — fire vocabulary. Fire can be read as either consuming or preserving-in-torment. V2 — the fire is associated with the devil/angels' torment (via Rev 20:10). But this verse does not state torment for humans; it states departure into fire. Neither V1 nor V2 triggers cleanly for human subjects. Neutral.
  • Result: Neutral. Both sides accept: "Jesus sends the cursed into everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels." They disagree about what "everlasting fire" does to humans.

E30 (Isa 66:24) — "They shall look upon the carcases (peger) of the men that have transgressed" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — peger (H6297, "carcasses/corpses") — the subjects of fire and worm are dead bodies. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): peger = corpses. The "men that have transgressed" are described as dead bodies. PASS (the text identifies the subjects as dead human beings).
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): peger = H6297, noun ("corpse"). Used 24 times in OT, always for dead bodies, never for living persons. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Direct-speech prophecy (Isaiah's eschatological oracle). PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Dan 12:2 where dera'on (contempt) has the same subjects (connected by shared vocabulary — dera'on appears only in Dan 12:2 and Isa 66:24). PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. The subjects of the unquenchable fire and undying worm are corpses (dead bodies), not living persons.

E31 (Psa 37:10) — "Yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be (ayin)" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — ayin (H369, "not-be") — non-existence language. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the wicked" — human category. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): ayin = H369 ("not-be/non-existence"). The wicked "shall not be." Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Wisdom psalm — didactic poetry. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:20; 104:35; Obad 1:16. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E32 (Obad 1:16) — "They shall be as though they had not been" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — "as though they had not been" (ke-lo hayu) — non-existence language. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "all the heathen" — a category of human persons (nations under judgment). PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): ke-lo hayu = "as though they had not been." Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Prophetic oracle — direct-speech prophecy. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:10 (ayin), 104:35 (be no more). PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E33 (Psa 104:35) — "Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — tamam (H8552, "be consumed/finished") + ayin (H369, "be no more") — cessation and non-existence vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "sinners" and "the wicked" — human categories. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): tamam = H8552, Qal Imperfect ("be consumed"). ayin = H369 ("no more"). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Creation psalm — hymnic/didactic. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with Psa 37:10,20; Obad 1:16. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands.

E34 (Psa 35:16) — "They gnashed upon me with their teeth" — Classified: Neutral

  • OT gnashing background — hostile rage. Both sides accept. Neutral.

E35 (Hos 13:3) — "They shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew... as the chaff... as the smoke" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — four cessation similes (morning cloud, dew, chaff, smoke) applied to the wicked. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): Ephraim — a nation/people used as a prophetic type. FAIL — nation used as prophetic type/figure.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Prophetic oracle. PASS.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Subject is a nation (Ephraim), not individual human persons facing eschatological judgment.
  • RC2: Corrected: "Hosea says Ephraim (a nation) will be like morning cloud, dew, chaff, smoke — four cessation similes."
  • RC3: National judgment imagery using cessation similes. Both sides accept the textual observation.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails (nation as subject). Reclassified to Neutral. Cessation simile imagery applied to a nation.

E36 (Isa 5:24) — "As the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — akal (H398, "devour") + multiple cessation images. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "they" — Israel under divine woe oracle. A nation/people used in prophetic type. FAIL — nation.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check: National judgment with cessation similes.
  • Result: Gate 1 fails. Reclassified to Neutral. Cessation imagery applied to a nation.

E37 (Heb 10:27) — "Fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — esthio (G2068, "devour/eat") — destruction/consumption vocabulary. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "the adversaries" (hypenantious G5227) — human persons who reject truth. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): esthiein = G2068, Present Active Infinitive ("to devour"). Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with other destruction vocabulary. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. Fire devours the adversaries — destruction vocabulary in didactic prose.

E38 (2 Thess 1:9) — "Punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — olethros aionios ("everlasting destruction") — destruction vocabulary + aionios qualifier. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): "them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel" (v.8) — human persons. PASS.
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): olethron aionion = G3639 + G166. Grammar unambiguous: "everlasting destruction." PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Epistle — didactic prose. PASS.
  • Gate 4 (Harmony): Consistent with other destruction vocabulary. PASS.
  • Result: All four gates pass. Classification: Cond. stands. (Examined in depth in etc7-14-judgment-passages.)

E39 (Rev 20:14) — "This is the second death" — Candidate: Cond.

  • Step 1 Vocabulary Scan: V1 — thanatos (G2288, "death") — the lake of fire IS death. Candidate: COND.
  • Step 2 Validation Gates:
  • Gate 1 (Subject): The lake of fire — not a human being. However, the identification formula defines what the lake of fire IS (death), which applies to humans cast into it. The subject of the identification is the lake, but the classification concerns what happens to humans there. PASS (the identification concerns the nature of the destination where humans are sent).
  • Gate 2 (Grammar): houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin, he limne tou pyros — copular identification. Grammar unambiguous. PASS.
  • Gate 3 (Genre): Revelation — apocalyptic. FAIL.
  • Step 3 Reclassification Check:
  • RC1: Genre is apocalyptic.
  • RC2: Corrected: "In an apocalyptic text, the identification formula states 'the lake of fire is the second death.'" Apocalyptic self-interpretation.
  • RC3: The identification formula (X = Y) is a textual fact. Both sides accept it. The positional significance depends on interpreting "death" (literal cessation vs. spiritual/relational separation).
  • Result: Gate 3 fails (apocalyptic). Reclassified to Neutral. Both sides accept: "Revelation identifies the lake of fire as 'the second death.'"

docs.title: N-Item Classifications (Tree 4 Walkthroughs)
docs.text:
N1 — "katakaio (G2618) means 'burn completely/consume' in all 12 NT occurrences" — Based on: E1, E2, E18 (katakaio verses) — Candidate: Neutral

  • Gate 0 (Foundation):

docs.title: Conclusion: Judgment Parables and Associated Imagery
Master ID
docs.text: (blank — to be assigned post-study)

docs.title: Question
docs.text: What do Jesus' judgment parables and associated imagery teach about the fate of the wicked? Focus on: Matt 13:24-30,36-43 (wheat & tares / furnace of fire), Matt 13:47-50 (dragnet), 'outer darkness' (Matt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30), 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' (7 occurrences), and the fire/furnace vocabulary.

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: Jesus' judgment parables consistently use destruction, consumption, and exclusion vocabulary for the fate of the wicked. The decisive verb in the tares parable is katakaio (G2618, "burn completely"), which describes total consumption in all 12 NT occurrences. The furnace image (kaminos G2575) inherits three OT furnace traditions, all of which describe furnaces that destroy their contents. The gnashing formula (brygmos + klauthmos) describes grief and rage at the moment of exclusion, not ongoing torment — the OT background (charaq H2786) is hostile rage in all 5 uses, and Luke 13:28 identifies seeing exclusion as the trigger. The basanizo word family (torment) is entirely absent from every passage in this study.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Tares Parable Interpretation (Matt 13:40-42) As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world. The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity; And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

Gnashing Trigger Identified (Luke 13:28) There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out.

Destroy Soul and Body (Matt 10:28) And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

Furnace Burns to Ashes (Mal 4:1,3) For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch... And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet.

Gnashing Then Cessation (Psa 112:10) The wicked shall see it, and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish.

OT Gnashing = Rage (Acts 7:54) When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.

Outer Darkness = Exclusion (Matt 8:11-12) And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Sodom Paradigm (2 Pet 2:6) And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly.

Everlasting Punishment (Matt 25:46) And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

Vocabulary Differentiation (Rev 20:9-10) And fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them. And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

docs.title: 1. katakaio (G2618) — Jesus' Interpretive Verb for the Fate of the Tares
docs.text:
The parable of the wheat and tares (Matt 13:24-30) and Jesus' self-interpretation (Matt 13:36-43) form the primary passage in this study. The householder sows good seed; an enemy sows tares. At harvest, the tares are gathered and burned (katakaio, v.30). Jesus then decodes the parable with six copular identification formulas (vv.37-39): the sower = the Son of Man, the field = the world, the good seed = sons of the kingdom, the tares = sons of the wicked one, the enemy = the devil, the harvest = the end of the age, the reapers = the angels. After this decoding, v.40 states: "As therefore the tares are gathered and burned (katakaio) in the fire, so shall it be in the end of this age."

katakaio (G2618) is a compound verb (kata + kaio) meaning "burn down completely, consume wholly." The kata- prefix intensifies the base verb kaio ("burn") to completion — the same prefix pattern found in katesthio ("devour completely," kata + esthio), katapino ("swallow up," kata + pino), and katalyo ("destroy utterly," kata + lyo). All 12 NT occurrences of katakaio describe total consumption: chaff burned up (Matt 3:12), tares burned (Matt 13:30,40), magic books burned (Acts 19:19), works burned (1 Cor 3:15), animal carcasses burned outside the camp (Heb 13:11), earth burned up (2 Pet 3:10), trees burned up (Rev 8:7), and Babylon utterly burned (Rev 18:8). Not one occurrence describes ongoing burning without consumption.

The self-interpretation pattern (per the grammar reference on self-interpretation-literal-correction) elevates the passage from purely parabolic to semi-didactic. Jesus decoded the symbols but retained the simile structure in v.40 ("as...so"). The verb katakaio carries its full semantic weight — total consumption — even within the simile. John the Baptist uses the same verb for the same image in Matt 3:12 ("he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire"), establishing cross-speaker consistency within the same Gospel.

The primary Hebrew source for katakaio is saraph (H8313, "to burn"), with 63 LXX co-occurrences. The OT-to-NT translation continuity means that when Jesus uses katakaio, the word carries the Hebrew concept of fire-as-consumption.

docs.title: 2. kaminos (G2575) — The Furnace and Its OT Background
docs.text:
The phrase "the furnace of fire" (ten kaminon tou pyros) appears only in Matt 13:42 and 13:50. kaminos (G2575, "furnace") has 4 NT occurrences total: the two judgment passages plus Rev 1:15 (simile for intense heat) and Rev 9:2 (simile for smoke volume).

Three OT furnace traditions feed into the NT kaminos via the LXX:

attuwn (H861, Aramaic): Nebuchadnezzar's execution furnace in Daniel 3. The LXX maps attuwn univocally to kaminos. The narrative reports that the furnace killed the soldiers who merely approached it (Dan 3:22). The three Hebrews survived only through divine intervention (the fourth figure in the fire, 3:25). Default result = death. The furnace is an instrument of execution, not a confinement facility.

kuwr (H3564): The smelting furnace of Ezekiel 22:18-22. Israel is compared to dross (sig H5509) in God's smelting furnace. The verb nathak (H5413, "melt/pour") appears four times in vv.20-22. The smelting furnace consumes the dross and extracts the metal. The worthless material is destroyed, not preserved.

tannuwr (H8574): The oven/furnace of Malachi 4:1. "The day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch." The result: "they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet" (Mal 4:3). Total consumption to ashes.

Every OT furnace tradition describes a device that destroys its contents. No OT furnace tradition describes a device that preserves its contents in ongoing suffering.

docs.title: 3. The Gnashing Formula — Grief and Rage at the Moment of Judgment
docs.text:
"Weeping and gnashing of teeth" (klauthmos kai brygmos ton odonton) appears in 7 NT verses (Matt 8:12; 13:42; 13:50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30; Luke 13:28). The formula pairs with three different judgment images: furnace of fire (13:42, 13:50), outer darkness (8:12; 22:13; 25:30), and cutting asunder (24:51). This variety shows the formula describes the RESPONSE to judgment, not a specific punishment.

brygmos (G1030, "gnashing") derives from brycho (G1031), which maps 1:1 to Hebrew charaq (H2786) in the LXX. All 5 OT charaq uses express hostile rage directed at a target: - Job 16:9 — enemy gnashes in wrath at Job - Psa 35:16 — mockers gnash at David in malice - Psa 37:12 — wicked gnashes at the righteous (habitual action, participial form) - Psa 112:10 — wicked gnashes and melts away; desire perishes - Lam 2:16 — enemies gnash in triumph over Jerusalem

Acts 7:54 provides the sole NT use of brycho: the Sanhedrin "gnashed on [Stephen] with their teeth" in murderous fury (imperfect tense = sustained rage). They proceeded to stone him. This is not pain — it is hostile fury directed at a target.

klauthmos (G2805, "weeping/wailing") has 9 NT occurrences: 7 in the judgment formula, 2 outside it. The non-formulaic uses confirm its semantic range: Matt 2:18 (Rachel weeping for her dead children — grief at irreversible loss) and Acts 20:37 (Ephesian elders weeping at Paul's departure — grief at parting). klauthmos expresses grief.

Combined: weeping (grief at loss) + gnashing (rage at exclusion) = the emotional response at the moment of judgment.

Psa 112:10 is the critical OT verse linking gnashing to cessation. The wicked sees the righteous prosper, is angry (kaas), gnashes teeth (charaq), and then MELTS AWAY (masas H4549, Niphal). The sequence — rage THEN cessation — maps directly onto the NT judgment formula: gnashing at the moment of judgment, then destruction.

Luke 13:28 is the interpretive key. "There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, WHEN YE SHALL SEE Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out." The temporal clause hotan opsesthe ("when ye shall see") identifies the gnashing as a RESPONSE to a specific trigger: seeing others inside the kingdom while being expelled outside. This is a one-time judgment-event description.

docs.title: 4. Outer Darkness — Exclusion from the Kingdom Feast
docs.text:
The phrase "outer darkness" (to skotos to exoteron) appears in 3 verses (Matt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30), all in Matthew. The word exoteros (G1857) occurs ONLY in these three verses in the entire NT. The double-article construction (to skotos to exoteron) with the comparative adjective marks "THE outer darkness" as a definite, particular destination.

All three outer-darkness passages share a common pattern: 1. A feast/celebration context — sitting with Abraham (8:11), wedding feast (22:2), entering the joy of the lord (25:21,23) 2. An exclusion verb — ekballo (G1544, "cast out") 3. The definite destination — to skotos to exoteron 4. The consequence formula — klauthmos kai brygmos ton odonton

The outer-darkness image contains NO fire vocabulary, NO torment vocabulary, and NO duration language. It describes exclusion from the lit feast — being outside the celebration, in the dark.

Matt 8:12 is the only non-parabolic outer-darkness passage. Jesus makes a direct prophetic statement (no "the kingdom of heaven is like" formula) about unbelieving Israel being cast out while Gentiles sit with the patriarchs. Matt 22:13 and 25:30 are parabolic.

The outer-darkness passages do not specify what happens to the excluded person after the exclusion. The image describes the ACT of exclusion and the EMOTIONAL response, but not the subsequent state or duration. This makes the outer-darkness passages functionally neutral on the question of whether the excluded person continues to exist or ceases to exist.

docs.title: 5. The Fire/Darkness Tension — Both Images Are Figurative
docs.text:
Matthew uses two image sets for the same eschatological fate: - FURNACE SET: Matt 13:42,50 — "cast into the furnace of fire" (bright light, consuming heat) - DARKNESS SET: Matt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30 — "cast into outer darkness" (no light)

Both sets include "weeping and gnashing of teeth." Both appear in the same Gospel, same author, same eschatological framework. A literal furnace of fire produces brilliant light. Literal outer darkness has no light. The same fate cannot be simultaneously a blazing furnace and total darkness.

The tension has three possible resolutions: 1. They describe different fates — but both describe the fate of those excluded from the kingdom, and the gnashing formula links them. 2. They describe different aspects of one literal place — but a place cannot be simultaneously a blazing furnace and total darkness. 3. Both are figurative — furnace representing destruction/consumption (consistent with katakaio and all OT furnace traditions), darkness representing exclusion from God's light/kingdom (consistent with the feast-exclusion context).

The third option is the only reading that harmonizes both image sets within the same author. The figurative reading is further supported by Matt 22:13, which adds "bind him hand and foot" — binding imagery that makes sense for preventing re-entry after exclusion but would be redundant if the person were being consumed by fire.

docs.title: 6. Matthew's Same-Author Judgment Vocabulary
docs.text:
Matthew's judgment vocabulary across all eschatological passages forms a consistent pattern:

Destruction/consumption verbs: katakaio (G2618, Matt 3:12; 13:30,40), apollymi (G622, Matt 10:28; 21:41; 22:7), empretho (G1714, Matt 22:7), dichotomeo (G1371, Matt 24:51)

Exclusion verbs: ekballo (G1544, Matt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30), ballo (G906, Matt 13:42,50; 5:29-30)

Absent from Matthew's eschatological judgment vocabulary: basanizo (G928, 0 uses for human eschatological subjects), basanismos (G929, 0 uses), basanos (G931, 0 eschatological uses), basanistes (G930, only Matt 18:34 in a debt parable with an implied endpoint "until he should pay")

The same author who writes the furnace and darkness parables also writes Matt 10:28 ("destroy both soul and body in hell"), 21:41 ("miserably destroy those wicked men"), and 22:7 ("destroyed those murderers and burned up their city"). The verb apollymi in judgment contexts with divine/authority subject consistently means actual destruction throughout Matthew's Gospel.

docs.title: 7. Matt 25:46 — Everlasting Punishment and the Hebrews Pattern
docs.text:
The grammatical parallel between kolasin aionion ("everlasting punishment") and zoen aionion ("everlasting life") in Matt 25:46 is real. Both use aionios (G166) in accusative singular feminine modifying comparable abstract nouns. Both are governed by the same verb (aperchomai G565).

Three observations bear on this passage:

First, Jesus chose kolasis (G2851, "punishment," from kolazo G2849 "to curtail, dock, prune") — NOT basanismos (G929, "torment"). kolasis has only 2 NT uses (Matt 25:46; 1 John 4:18). This is punishment vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

Second, the Hebrews pattern shows that aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act: "eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12, obtained once, result permanent), "eternal judgment" (Heb 6:2, rendered once, verdict permanent), "eternal destruction" (2 Thess 1:9, destroyed once, result permanent). If "eternal punishment" follows this pattern, it means punishment inflicted once with permanent result.

Third, Tit 1:2 uses aionios twice in one verse with different temporal scopes ("eternal life" and "before age-long times"), demonstrating that the same adjective does not require the same duration in every occurrence.

docs.title: 8. The Sodom Paradigm — "Eternal Fire" That Produced Ashes
docs.text:
Jude 1:7 says Sodom and Gomorrah suffer "the vengeance of eternal fire" (pur aionion). 2 Pet 2:6 says the same cities were "turned to ashes" (tephroo G5077) and set as an "example" (hupodeigma G5262) for the ungodly. Jesus in Luke 17:29 says the fire "destroyed them all" (apollymi G622, aorist).

The paradigm case of "eternal fire" produced ashes. The fire ended; the results are permanent. If the example/paradigm for "eternal fire" is cities reduced to ashes, then "everlasting fire" (Matt 18:8; 25:41) describes fire whose results are permanent, not fire that burns endlessly.

docs.title: 9. OT Cessation Similes — The Consistent Biblical Pattern
docs.text: The OT compares the fate of the wicked to chaff (Psa 1:4; 35:5; Isa 5:24; 17:13; Hos 13:3), stubble (Mal 4:1; Isa 5:24; 47:14; Psa 83:13), smoke (Psa 37:20; 68:2; Hos 13:3), wax (Psa 68:2; 112:10), ashes (Mal 4:3; 2 Pet 2:6), morning cloud (Hos 13:3), early dew (Hos 13:3), dust (Isa 5:24), and fat on the altar (Psa 37:20). Every one of these substances ceases to exist. No biblical cessation simile depicts something continuing in a ruined or damaged state. The simile inventory is unanimously cessation-oriented.

docs.title: 10. Vocabulary Differentiation — Destruction Words vs. Torment Words
docs.text:
Rev 20:9-10 provides the most concentrated example: humans are devoured (katesthio G2719, v.9); the devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented (basanizo G928, v.10). Different verbs for different subjects in consecutive verses by the same author.

This differentiation extends across the entire biblical corpus studied. The judgment parables (tares, dragnet, sheep/goats, talents, wedding feast) use destruction/exclusion vocabulary for human subjects (katakaio, apollymi, ballo, ekballo, dichotomeo). basanizo/basanismos for human eschatological judgment appears only in Revelation's apocalyptic framework. Jesus never uses basanizo or basanismos in his teaching about the fate of the wicked.

docs.title: Word Studies
docs.text:
katakaio (G2618): 12 NT occurrences, all total consumption. Kata- prefix = completion. Primary Hebrew source: saraph (H8313). Jesus' chosen verb for the tares' fate.

kaminos (G2575): 4 NT occurrences. Three OT furnace traditions all describe destruction. LXX maps from attuwn (execution), kuwr (smelting), tannuwr (baking/burning).

brygmos (G1030): 7 NT occurrences, all in the judgment formula. Derives from brycho (G1031), which maps to charaq (H2786). All OT uses = hostile rage.

klauthmos (G2805): 9 NT occurrences. Non-formulaic = grief at loss (Matt 2:18, Acts 20:37).

exoteros (G1857): 3 NT occurrences, all "outer darkness" in Matthew. Exclusion from kingdom feast.

kolasis (G2851): 2 NT occurrences (Matt 25:46; 1 John 4:18). From kolazo ("to curtail"). Punishment vocabulary, not torment vocabulary.

basanizo (G928): 12 NT occurrences. Zero in any judgment parable, outer-darkness passage, gnashing-formula passage, or Matthean gehenna passage. Genre-restricted to Revelation's apocalyptic framework for eschatological judgment.

charaq (H2786): 5 OT occurrences, all hostile rage. Maps to brycho (G1031) in LXX.

docs.title: Matt 25:46 — The Symmetry Argument
docs.text:
The kolasin aionion // zoen aionion parallel is real. If "everlasting life" is life without end, then "everlasting punishment" appears to require punishment without end, which implies ongoing conscious existence.

Three textual factors complicate this reading: (1) kolasis is punishment vocabulary, not torment vocabulary; (2) the Hebrews pattern shows aionios + result-noun = permanent result of completed act; (3) Tit 1:2 uses aionios twice with different temporal scopes in one verse. The symmetry is grammatical (both use the same adjective) but the Hebrews pattern and the kolasis etymology suggest the punishment is permanent in result, not perpetual in process.

docs.title: Outer Darkness — Does It Imply Ongoing Existence?
docs.text: The outer-darkness passages describe exclusion from the kingdom feast with an emotional response (weeping and gnashing). They do not specify what happens after the exclusion. The image is compatible with both ongoing existence in darkness and cessation after exclusion. Taken alone, the outer-darkness passages are neutral on duration.

docs.title: Matt 22:13 — Binding Imagery
docs.text: "Bind him hand and foot" adds a detail absent from the other outer-darkness passages. Binding implies ongoing existence (you cannot bind something that has ceased to exist). However, the binding occurs within a parabolic narrative (Gate 1 and Gate 3 both fail), reducing its evidential weight for establishing doctrine about the duration of post-judgment existence.

docs.title: The Gnashing Formula — Momentary or Ongoing?
docs.text: The gnashing formula appears 7 times. Luke 13:28 identifies the trigger as a one-time event (seeing exclusion). The OT background supports a momentary rage response. However, the formula uses ekei estai ("there shall be") which describes what characterizes a place, not just what happens once. The question is whether "there shall be weeping and gnashing" means "at that place, weeping and gnashing will occur" (momentary) or "at that place, weeping and gnashing are the ongoing condition" (perpetual). The text does not resolve this. The OT parallel in Psa 112:10 (gnashing then melting away) supports the momentary reading.
