The verb is future passive indicative — different from the present active indicative in Rev 4:8 and 14:11. The subject (ὁ διάβολος) is cast (ἐβλήθη, V-API-3S, aorist passive) into the lake. Humans in v.9 are 'devoured' (κατέφαγεν, aorist) — different verb entirely.

docs.title: Eschatological dissolution of night — 'there shall be no night there'
docs.text:
Revelation 22:5 And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever.

Context: The abolition of the day/night framework. νὺξ οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι — 'night shall not be any more.' If 'day and night' is the temporal framework within which activities occur, then the dissolution of this framework in the new creation proves that 'day and night' is a quality-marker for the present age, not an assertion about eternal states.

Notes: νὺξ (N-NSF, nominative singular of νύξ G3571) οὐκ ἔσται (V-FDI-3S, future middle/deponent indicative of εἰμί) ἔτι (ADV, 'any more'). The saints βασιλεύσουσιν (V-FAI-3P, future active indicative, 'shall reign') εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων — 'for ever and ever.' The saints reign forever, but without night. The day/night framework is gone. Rev 7:15's 'day and night' service continues — but in a reality without night. The formula must be qualitative.

docs.title: Eschatological dissolution — Gates never shut because no night
docs.text:
Revelation 21:25 And the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there.

Context: Parallel to Rev 22:5. No night in the new Jerusalem. Confirms the abolition of the day/night cycle.

Notes: νὺξ γὰρ οὐκ ἔσται ἐκεῖ — 'for night shall not be there.' Second affirmation of night's abolition.

docs.title: Fire-and-brimstone judgment — Context for 14:11
docs.text:
Revelation 14:10 The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb:

Context: Immediately precedes 14:11. The beast-worshipper 'shall be tormented' (basanisthesetai, future passive indicative 3S) with fire and brimstone. The fire-and-brimstone imagery echoes Gen 19:24 (Sodom) and Isa 34:9 (Edom).

Notes: βασανισθήσεται (V-FPI-3S, future passive indicative 3S of βασανίζω G928). Same verb as Rev 20:10 but singular — the individual beast-worshipper is subject here.

docs.title: OT source for Rev 4:8 — Seraphim trishagion
docs.text:
Isaiah 6:2 Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. Isaiah 6:3 And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, [is] the LORD of hosts: the whole earth [is] full of his glory.

Context: The OT source for Rev 4:8's living creatures. Six-winged creatures, triple 'holy', throne room setting, divine title. John's 'rest not day and night saying Holy, holy, holy' echoes this continuous worship.

Notes: The seraphim's continuous praise in Isaiah provides the template for Rev 4:8's 'rest not day and night.' Neither Isaiah nor anyone reads the seraphim's praise as torment.

docs.title: OT source for Rev 14:11 — Edom's fire 'not quenched night nor day' with aftermath
docs.text:
Isaiah 34:9 And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. Isaiah 34:10 It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever. Isaiah 34:11 But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness. Isaiah 34:12 They shall call the nobles thereof to the kingdom, but none [shall be] there, and all her princes shall be nothing. Isaiah 34:13 And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of dragons, [and] a court for owls. Isaiah 34:14 The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest. Isaiah 34:15 There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow: there shall the vultures also be gathered, every one with her mate.

Context: The direct OT source for Rev 14:11's smoke-ascending formula. Edom's fire is 'not quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever.' But vv.11-15 show that animals dwell in the ruins — the fire is OUT, the land is desolate but habitable by creatures. The 'night nor day' and 'for ever' language describes completed, irreversible destruction, not ongoing burning.

Notes: Hebrew parsing: לַיְלָה (layil, noun ms Abs, 'night') וְיֹומָם (yowmam, adverb, 'by day') לֹא תִכְבֶּה (lo tikhbeh, Qal imperfect 3fs of כבה, 'go out'). The imperfect expresses the fire's character during its burning phase. לְעוֹלָם (le-owlam, 'for ever') יַעֲלֶה (ya'aleh, Qal imperfect 3ms of עלה, 'ascend') עֲשָׁנָהּ (ashana, 'its smoke'). The smoke ascends 'for ever' — but the aftermath (vv.11-17) shows animals nesting in the ruins. The fire has done its work.

docs.title: Sodom paradigm — Fire, brimstone, smoke ascending
docs.text:
Genesis 19:24 Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven; Genesis 19:25 And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground. Genesis 19:26 But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt. Genesis 19:27 And Abraham gat up early in the morning to the place where he stood before the LORD: Genesis 19:28 And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace.

Context: The paradigmatic fire-and-brimstone judgment. God rains fire and brimstone; the cities are overthrown; Abraham sees smoke ascending. The three stages: fire falls (v.24) → cities overthrown (v.25) → smoke ascends (v.28). This is Rev 14:11's source imagery.

Notes: 2 Pet 2:6 interprets this event: Sodom and Gomorrah were 'turned to ashes.' The fire produced destruction and ashes, not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Sodom 'turned to ashes' — Interpretive key for fire-and-brimstone outcome
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:6 And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned [them] with an overthrow, making [them] an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly;

Context: Peter interprets the Sodom fire-and-brimstone event: the cities were 'turned to ashes' (tephrosas). They are an 'ensample' (hupodeigma) of what happens to the ungodly. The fire produced ashes, not eternal burning.

Notes: The Greek τεφρώσας (tephrosas) means 'having reduced to ashes' — the outcome of fire-and-brimstone is complete destruction, not preservation in torment.

docs.title: OT merism — 'day and night shall not cease' as creation order
docs.text:
Genesis 8:22 While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.

Context: God's post-flood promise. The day/night cycle is paired with other merisms (seedtime/harvest, cold/heat, summer/winter) to express totality and continuity of the created order.

Notes: Hebrew: וְיֹום (ve-yom, conjunction + noun ms Abs, 'and day') וָלַיְלָה (va-laylah, conjunction + noun ms Abs, 'and night') לֹא יִשְׁבֹּתוּ (lo yishbotu, 'shall not cease,' Qal imperfect 3mp of שׁבת H7673). The verb שׁבת ('to cease/sabbath') is the same root behind the Sabbath. Day and night are presented as a continuous created order — a merism for the totality of time.

docs.title: OT merism — 'meditate therein day and night'
docs.text:
Joshua 1:8 This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.

Context: 'Day and night' meditation — the OT paradigm for the merism as quality-marker. No one reads this as requiring literal 24-hour non-stop meditation. It means devotional completeness.

Notes: The 'day and night' merism here indisputably means 'constantly, thoroughly' — not 'without any break for 24 hours.' This is the interpretive baseline for the formula.

docs.title: OT merism — 'in his law doth he meditate day and night'
docs.text:
Psalm 1:2 But his delight [is] in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.

Context: Parallel to Josh 1:8. The blessed man meditates 'day and night' — continuous devotion, not literal non-stop meditation.

Notes: Same merism as Josh 1:8, same meaning: quality of devotion, not duration claim.

docs.title: OT merism — 'day and night thy hand was heavy upon me'
docs.text:
Psalm 32:4 For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah.

Context: David describes divine conviction. 'Day and night' here characterizes the thoroughness of God's discipline — the quality and completeness of the pressure, not a claim that it never paused for a moment.

Notes: Hebrew: יֹומָם (yomam, adverb, 'by day') וָלַיְלָה (va-laylah, conjunction + noun ms Abs, 'and night') תִּכְבַּד (tikhbad, Qal imperfect 3fs of כבד, 'be heavy') עָלַי (alai, 'upon me') יָדֶךָ (yadkha, 'your hand'). The 'day and night' pressure is qualitative — thoroughgoing divine discipline.

docs.title: OT source — 'not quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever'
docs.text:
Isaiah 34:10 It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever.

Context: The direct OT source for Rev 14:11. Both formulas — 'night nor day' and 'smoke shall go up for ever' — appear here. But vv.11-17 prove the fire is out (animals inhabit the ruins). The formula describes irreversible completed destruction.

Notes: Already covered in Isa 34:9-15 entry. This standalone reference ensures the verse is not missed.

docs.title: OT merism — Watchmen 'shall never hold their peace day nor night'
docs.text:
Isaiah 62:6 I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, [which] shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence,

Context: 'Day nor night' used for watchmen who never hold their peace — continuous vigilance, not literal non-stop shouting.

Notes: Same merism pattern as the Revelation passages. No one reads this as literal 24-hour non-stop speaking.

docs.title: NT 'day and night' — Twelve tribes 'instantly serving God day and night'
docs.text:
Acts 26:7 Unto which [promise] our twelve tribes, instantly serving [God] day and night, hope to come. For which hope's sake, king Agrippa, I am accused of the Jews.

Context: Paul describes the twelve tribes' devotion. They serve God 'day and night' — wholehearted, constant devotion.

Notes: CRITICAL CASE CONTRAST: νύκτα (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE Sg F) καὶ ἡμέραν (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE Sg F). This is ACCUSATIVE, not genitive — measuring extent of time, not characterizing the period. Paul uses the accusative of extent here (like Luke 2:37), emphasizing the duration of their service. Compare Rev 4:8 etc. which use the GENITIVE (ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός), characterizing the temporal framework.

docs.title: NT 'night and day' — Paul 'labouring night and day'
docs.text:
1 Thessalonians 2:9 For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God.

Context: Paul's labor described as 'night and day' — working intensely, not literally without stopping.

Notes: νυκτὸς (N-GSF, GENITIVE Sg F) καὶ ἡμέρας (N-GSF, GENITIVE Sg F). GENITIVE of time — same construction as all 5 Revelation passages. Paul did not literally labor without rest. The formula characterizes the quality/intensity of his work ethic.

docs.title: NT 'night and day' — Paul working 'night and day'
docs.text:
2 Thessalonians 3:8 Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:

Context: Parallel to 1 Thess 2:9. Paul's self-supporting labor described with the 'night and day' merism.

Notes: Same genitive construction as 1 Thess 2:9. Quality-marker, not duration claim.

docs.title: NT 'night and day' — Widow 'continueth in supplications and prayers night and day'
docs.text:
1 Timothy 5:5 Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.

Context: The true widow's devotion described as 'night and day' prayers — habitual, characteristic devotion.

Notes: Genitive of time: νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας. Same pattern. No one claims the widow literally prays without stopping.

docs.title: NT 'night and day' — Paul remembering Timothy 'in my prayers night and day'
docs.text:
2 Timothy 1:3 I thank God, whom I serve from [my] forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day;

Context: Paul's prayer life described with 'night and day' — faithful, regular, devoted remembrance.

Notes: Genitive of time. Same formula, same qualitative function.

docs.title: NT 'night and day' — Anna serving God 'night and day' (ACCUSATIVE contrast)
docs.text:
Luke 2:37 And she [was] a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served [God] with fastings and prayers night and day.

Context: Anna served God 'night and day' — but Luke uses the ACCUSATIVE case (nykta kai hemeran), not the genitive used in Revelation. The accusative measures extent/duration; the genitive characterizes the time-frame. This diagnostic contrast is key.

Notes: CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC: νύκτα (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE Sg F) καὶ ἡμέραν (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE Sg F). Luke uses the ACCUSATIVE of extent of time, measuring the duration of Anna's service. This contrasts with the GENITIVE used in all 5 Revelation 'day and night' passages (and in 1 Thess 2:9, Mark 5:5, etc.). The same words (νύξ, ἡμέρα) change grammatical function by case: accusative = how long; genitive = during what kind of time. The Revelation passages use the genitive — characterizing the temporal backdrop, not measuring duration.

docs.title: NT 'day and night' — God's elect 'cry day and night unto him'
docs.text:
Luke 18:7 And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them?

Context: The elect cry to God 'day and night' — persistent prayer, not literal non-stop crying.

Notes: ἡμέρας (N-GSF) καὶ νυκτός (N-GSF) — GENITIVE of time, same construction as Revelation passages. Quality-marker for persistent prayer.

docs.title: NT 'night and day' — Demoniac 'always, night and day, crying'
docs.text:
Mark 5:5 And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones.

Context: The demoniac's activity described as 'always, night and day' — the one negative 'day and night' outside Revelation. Even here, it describes the quality/character of continuous distressed behavior, not a literal claim of unbroken activity.

Notes: διὰ παντὸς νυκτὸς (N-GSF) καὶ ἡμέρας (N-GSF) — GENITIVE of time, reinforced by διὰ παντός ('continually'). Even this strongest possible 'day and night' is qualitative — the demoniac did sleep, eat, and pause. The formula describes the relentless, pervasive character of his torment.

docs.title: NT 'day and night' — Enemies 'watched the gates day and night'
docs.text:
Acts 9:24 But their laying await was known of Saul. And they watched the gates day and night to kill him.

Context: Surveillance intensity — the enemies watched 'day and night,' meaning thoroughly and persistently, not that they literally never blinked.

Notes: ἡμέρας τε καὶ νυκτὸς — genitive of time with τε particle. Same qualitative function.

docs.title: NT 'night and day' — Paul warning 'night and day with tears'
docs.text:
Acts 20:31 Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.

Context: Paul's pastoral ministry described as 'night and day' warning — devoted, persistent, not literal non-stop.

Notes: Genitive of time. Same qualitative function as all other NT uses.

docs.title: Creation of day/night distinction
docs.text:
Genesis 1:5 And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.

Context: The creation of the day/night framework. What God named in Gen 1:5, He abolishes in Rev 22:5. The dissolution of 'night' at the end of Revelation consummates what began at creation.

Notes: The bookend: Gen 1:5 names the night; Rev 22:5 abolishes it.

docs.title: Christ's offer of rest (anapausis)
docs.text:
Matthew 11:28 Come unto me, all [ye] that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Matthew 11:29 Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

Context: Jesus offers anapausis (G372) — rest for the soul. The same word used in Rev 4:8 and 14:11. If Christ's 'rest' is spiritual refreshment and cessation of burden, then the denial of 'rest' in Rev 14:11 is the absence of this relief.

Notes: ἀνάπαυσιν (N-ASF, G372) — same word as Rev 4:8 and 14:11. Only positive use in the NT.

docs.title: Rest (katapausis) theology — Entering God's rest
docs.text:
Hebrews 4:1 Let us therefore fear, lest, a promise being left [us] of entering into his rest, any of you should seem to come short of it. Hebrews 4:9 There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. Hebrews 4:10 For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God [did] from his. Hebrews 4:11 Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.

Context: Hebrews' 'rest' theology uses katapausis (G2663), a synonym of anapausis (G372). The concept of entering God's rest vs. failing to enter provides the theological backdrop for Rev 14:11's 'no rest' vs. 14:13's 'rest from their labours.'

Notes: Different Greek word (katapausis G2663 vs. anapausis G372) but same rest concept. The theological structure is: rest is the reward of faith; absence of rest is the consequence of unbelief/rebellion.

docs.title: Everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels
docs.text:
Matthew 25:41 Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

Context: The fire was prepared for the devil and his angels — not originally for humans. Rev 20:10 shows the devil actually entering this fire. Humans are secondary recipients.

Notes: The 'everlasting fire' (πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον) was prepared (ἡτοιμασμένον) for the devil and his angels — the primary subjects of Rev 20:10.

docs.title: Wicked become ashes — Final fire produces destruction
docs.text:
Malachi 4:1 For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. Malachi 4:2 But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. Malachi 4:3 And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do [this], saith the LORD of hosts.

Context: The wicked become 'ashes under the soles of your feet' — complete destruction. Fire burns them up (v.1), leaves neither root nor branch (v.1), produces ashes (v.3). Cf. 2 Pet 2:6 (Sodom turned to ashes).

Notes: The outcome of divine fire: ashes, not ongoing torment. 'Shall leave them neither root nor branch' — nothing remains.

docs.title: Satan-figure becomes ashes — 'never shalt thou be any more'
docs.text:
Ezekiel 28:18 Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee. Ezekiel 28:19 All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never [shalt] thou [be] any more.

Context: The same being described in Rev 20:10 (the devil) is here described as becoming 'ashes upon the earth' and ceasing to exist: 'never shalt thou be any more' (ayin + owlam). This provides the didactic framework for interpreting Rev 20:10's apocalyptic imagery.

Notes: The didactic oracle (Ezek 28) describes the ultimate end of the Satan-figure: fire from within, reduced to ashes, 'never any more.' This governs the apocalyptic vision of Rev 20:10.

docs.title: The second death — What happens to humans at the lake of fire
docs.text:
Revelation 20:14 And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. Revelation 20:15 And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.

Context: Humans who are not in the book of life are 'cast into the lake of fire.' This is called 'the second death' — not 'the second life in torment.' The vocabulary for humans is death, not torment.

Notes: The lake of fire = 'the second death' (ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερος). Death is the absence of life, not the continuation of conscious experience in torment.

docs.title: Eschatological endpoint — No more death, sorrow, crying, pain
docs.text:
Revelation 21:4 And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

Context: The eschatological endpoint: no death, no sorrow, no crying, no pain. If the wicked were being eternally tormented, there would be ongoing pain and sorrow in the universe forever. This verse envisions complete resolution.

Notes: If eternal conscious torment exists, 'no more pain' is not universally true. The eschatological vision requires that pain ceases everywhere.

docs.title: Worship smoke ascending — Same verb as judgment smoke
docs.text:
Revelation 8:4 And the smoke of the incense, [which came] with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand.

Context: Worship smoke uses the same verb ἀναβαίνω (G305) as judgment smoke in Rev 14:11. The symmetry: incense smoke carries prayer upward; judgment smoke carries testimony upward.

Notes: Both Rev 8:4 and Rev 14:11 use ἀναβαίνω for smoke ascending before God. Same verb, different contexts — worship vs. judgment.

docs.title: Revelation's self-interpretation pattern
docs.text:
Revelation 1:20 The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.

Context: Revelation interprets its own symbols: stars = angels, candlesticks = churches. The same book that uses 'day and night' also provides interpretive keys for its own symbolic language.

Notes: Establishes that Revelation is a book of symbols with built-in interpretive guides.

docs.title: OT 'day and night' prayer — Intensity of intercession
docs.text:
Nehemiah 1:6 Let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open, that thou mayest hear the prayer of thy servant, which I pray before thee now, day and night, for the children of Israel thy servants, and confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against thee: both I and my father's house have sinned.

Context: Nehemiah prays 'day and night' — intensity of intercession, not literal 24-hour continuous prayer.

Notes: OT merism: quality-marker for devout, persistent prayer.

docs.title: OT 'night and day' — Unceasing grief expressed through tears
docs.text:
Jeremiah 14:17 Therefore thou shalt say this word unto them; Let mine eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease: for the virgin daughter of my people is broken with a great breach, with a very grievous blow.

Context: 'Night and day' tears — thoroughness of grief, not literal non-stop weeping.

Notes: OT merism: characterizes the completeness of Jeremiah's grief.

docs.title: OT 'night and day' — God's eyes open toward the temple
docs.text:
1 Kings 8:29 That thine eyes may be open toward this house night and day, [even] toward the place of which thou hast said, My name shall be there: that thou mayest hearken unto the prayer which thy servant shall make toward this place.

Context: God's eyes 'open night and day' — continuous divine attention toward the temple.

Notes: OT merism: God's continuous, unwavering attention.

docs.title: Satan's heavenly access — Background for Rev 12:10
docs.text:
Job 1:6 Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them. Job 1:7 And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it. Job 1:8 And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that [there is] none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? Job 1:9 Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought?

Context: Satan's heavenly access — he comes before God and accuses. This is the OT background for Rev 12:10's 'accuser of our brethren... which accused them before our God day and night.' Satan's access to God's presence was eventually terminated (Rev 12:9-10).

Notes: OT background for Rev 12:10. Satan's accusatory role before God — the 'day and night' activity that was terminated at Christ's victory.

docs.title: Satan the accuser — Standing to accuse Joshua
docs.text:
Zechariah 3:1 And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him. Zechariah 3:2 And the LORD said unto Satan, The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: [is] not this a brand plucked out of the fire?

Context: Satan as prosecutor in the heavenly court — standing at the right hand to accuse (the customary position of the prosecutor). This is the courtroom imagery behind Rev 12:10.

Notes: OT courtroom imagery. Satan functions as a legal accuser (cf. G2725 kategoros in Rev 12:10).

docs.title: Second Revelation 'day and night' — Great multitude serves God day and night in his temple
docs.text:
Revelation 7:15 Therefore are they before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple: and he that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them.

Context: The second positive 'day and night' in Revelation. The great multitude who came out of great tribulation serve God hemeras kai nuktos in his naos. This occurs in a reality where Rev 22:5 says 'there shall be no night there' — the formula is qualitative, not literal temporal.

Notes: λατρεύουσιν (V-PAI-3P, present active indicative 3P of λατρεύω G3000) αὐτῷ ἡμέρας (N-GSF) καὶ νυκτὸς (N-GSF) — genitive of time, identical construction to Rev 4:8. See also Rev 7:13-17 entry for full context.

docs.title: Third Revelation 'day and night' — Satan's terminated accusation
docs.text:
Revelation 12:10 And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night.

Context: Satan 'accused them before our God day and night' — but this 'day and night' activity is explicitly TERMINATED. The heavenly voice declares 'NOW (Ἄρτι, G737) is come salvation... for the accuser is cast down (ἐβλήθη, aorist passive).' This proves 'day and night' describes the character of an activity during its occurrence, not its guaranteed eternal continuation.

Notes: κατηγορῶν (V-PAP-NSM, present active participle) αὐτοὺς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν ἡμέρας (N-GSF) καὶ νυκτός (N-GSF). The participle is present tense but the activity is terminated by ἐβλήθη (V-API-3S, aorist passive). See also Rev 12:7-12 entry for full context.

docs.title: Fourth Revelation 'day and night' — 'no rest day nor night' for beast-worshippers
docs.text:
Revelation 14:11 And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

Context: The crux text. The 'no rest day nor night' formula uses the IDENTICAL construction as Rev 4:8 — ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos. Same verb, same noun, same genitive of time, same book, same author.

Notes: οὐκ ἔχουσιν (V-PAI-3P) ἀνάπαυσιν (N-ASF, G372) ἡμέρας (N-GSF, G2250) καὶ νυκτός (N-GSF, G3571). IDENTICAL to Rev 4:8 in every grammatical element. Also: ἀναβαίνει (V-PAI-3S, gnomic present of G305). See also Rev 14:9-12 entry for full context.

docs.title: Fifth Revelation 'day and night' — Non-human subjects 'tormented day and night for ever and ever'
docs.text:
Revelation 20:10 And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet [are], and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

Context: The fifth and final 'day and night' in Revelation. Three subjects: devil, beast, false prophet — all non-human/symbolic. The torment formula applies ONLY to these three. Humans in the same passage are 'devoured' (v.9) and receive 'the second death' (v.14-15).

Notes: βασανισθήσονται (V-FPI-3P, future passive indicative 3P of βασανίζω G928) ἡμέρας (N-GSF) καὶ νυκτὸς (N-GSF) εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Same genitive of time construction. See also Rev 20:9-15 entry for full context.

docs.title: Aftermath of Isa 34:10 — Animals dwell in the ruins, proving fire is out
docs.text:
Isaiah 34:11 But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness. Isaiah 34:12 They shall call the nobles thereof to the kingdom, but none [shall be] there, and all her princes shall be nothing. Isaiah 34:13 And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of dragons, [and] a court for owls. Isaiah 34:14 The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest. Isaiah 34:15 There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow: there shall the vultures also be gathered, every one with her mate.

Context: Immediately follows Isa 34:10 ('not quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever'). These verses describe animals dwelling in the ruins — cormorants, bitterns, owls, ravens, wild beasts, vultures nesting and hatching. Animals cannot inhabit a place that is still on fire. The fire that was 'not quenched night nor day' is demonstrably OUT. This proves the 'night nor day' and 'for ever' formula describes completed, irreversible destruction, not ongoing burning.

Notes: The decisive proof that Isa 34:10's 'night nor day' fire has ended: v.11 cormorant and bittern 'possess it,' owls and ravens 'dwell in it'; v.13 thorns grow in palaces; v.14 wild beasts meet, screech owl 'rests there'; v.15 owls 'make her nest, and lay, and hatch.' Living creatures inhabiting the ruins = fire is extinguished.

docs.title: Night worship — 'ye that by night stand in the house of the LORD'
docs.text:
Psalm 134:1 A Song of degrees. Behold, bless ye the LORD, all [ye] servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD.

Context: Night worship in the temple. The servants of the LORD 'by night stand in the house of the LORD.' Night is the setting for devoted worship, paralleling the 'day and night' worship of Rev 4:8 and Rev 7:15.

Notes: OT night-worship background for the Revelation 'day and night' service passages.

docs.title: Night meditation — 'mine eyes prevent the night watches'
docs.text:
Psalm 119:148 Mine eyes prevent the [night] watches, that I might meditate in thy word.

Context: The psalmist's eyes anticipate the night watches — he wakes before the watch to meditate in God's word. Night as the setting for intense devotion to Scripture, paralleling the 'day and night' meditation of Josh 1:8 and Psa 1:2.

Notes: Night meditation tradition. The psalmist is so devoted to God's word that he rises before the night watches — not because he is tormented but because he is devoted.

docs.title: Thematic Analysis: The "Day and Night" Formula in Revelation
Question
docs.text: What does the "day and night" (hemeras kai nuktos) formula mean in Revelation? Does "no rest day nor night" (Rev 14:11) describe eternal conscious experience, or the thoroughgoing nature of a judgment during its execution?

docs.title: Focus Area 1: The Genitive of Time Construction (hemeras kai nuktos)
docs.text:
The grammatical backbone of this study is the case form of hemeras kai nuktos. In all five Revelation "day and night" passages, the Greek parser confirms the identical construction:

  • Rev 4:8: hemeras (N-GSF, Gen Sg F) kai nuktos (N-GSF, Gen Sg F)
  • Rev 7:15: hemeras (N-GSF) kai nuktos (N-GSF)
  • Rev 12:10: hemeras (N-GSF) kai nuktos (N-GSF)
  • Rev 14:11: hemeras (N-GSF) kai nuktos (N-GSF)
  • Rev 20:10: hemeras (N-GSF) kai nuktos (N-GSF)

All five use the genitive case for both nouns. The genitive of time in Greek expresses "time within which" or "time during which" -- it characterizes the temporal backdrop of an action. It tells the reader what kind of time-frame the activity fills. It does not measure how long the activity lasts.

The critical diagnostic contrast is Luke 2:37, where Anna serves God nykta (N-ASF, Acc Sg F) kai hemeran (N-ASF, Acc Sg F). Luke uses the accusative case -- the accusative of extent, which measures duration ("for how long?"). Acts 26:7 also uses the accusative: nykta (N-ASF) kai hemeran (N-ASF) for the twelve tribes "instantly serving God day and night."

The distinction matters. When a Greek author wants to say "for the entire span of day and night" (measuring duration), the accusative is available. When the author wants to say "during the day-and-night period" (characterizing the activity as filling that framework), the genitive is the right tool. John uses the genitive in all five Revelation passages. He is characterizing the nature of these activities -- they are continuous, uninterrupted, thoroughgoing within their temporal framework -- not measuring how long they last.

Outside Revelation, the same genitive construction appears in 1 Thess 2:9 (nuktos kai hemeras, both GSF -- Paul "labouring night and day"), 2 Thess 3:8, 1 Tim 5:5, 2 Tim 1:3, Luke 18:7 (hemeras kai nuktos, both GSF -- God's elect "cry day and night"), and Mark 5:5 (nuktos kai hemeras, both GSF -- the demoniac "always, night and day, crying"). In every case, the genitive of time characterizes the quality of the activity, not the literal unbroken span.

docs.title: Focus Area 2: All 5 Revelation "Day and Night" Occurrences Mapped Side by Side
docs.text:
John uses the hemeras kai nuktos formula exactly five times in Revelation. Mapped together, a clear pattern emerges:

# Reference Subject Activity Tone Status 1 Rev 4:8 Living creatures Worship ("Holy, holy, holy") Positive Ongoing 2 Rev 7:15 Great multitude Temple service (latreuo) Positive Eschatological 3 Rev 12:10 Satan (the accuser) Accusation before God Negative Terminated 4 Rev 14:11 Beast-worshippers No rest (anapausis) Negative Judgment 5 Rev 20:10 Devil, beast, false prophet Torment (basanizo) Negative Judgment

Three of the five are positive (worship, service, and the removal of accusation). Two are negative-judgment uses. But the single most significant observation is occurrence #3: the "day and night" accusation that has explicitly ended.

The formula appears across the entire span of Revelation -- chapter 4, 7, 12, 14, 20. It is not a localized expression but a structural literary device that John deploys across the book's major sections: the throne room vision, the sealed multitude, the cosmic war, the three angels, and the final judgment.

docs.title: Focus Area 3: Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11 -- Identical Construction, Opposite Contexts
Rev 4:8
docs.text:
Context: The throne room of heaven. John sees four living creatures, each with six wings, full of eyes, surrounding God's throne. They worship without ceasing.

Direct statement: "They rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come."

Original language: anapausin (G372, N-ASF, Acc Sg F) ouk echousin (V-PAI-3P, Pres Act Ind 3P) hemeras (N-GSF) kai nuktos (N-GSF). The verb echousin is present active indicative third person plural. The noun anapausin is accusative singular -- the direct object of echousin. The genitive pair hemeras kai nuktos modifies the whole clause as a temporal characterizer.

Cross-references: Isaiah 6:2-3 provides the OT source -- seraphim with six wings crying "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts." The trishagion (triple "holy") is carried directly into Revelation's throne room. The creatures' continuous praise echoes and expands Isaiah's vision.

Relationship to other evidence: No interpreter reads Rev 4:8 as a statement about the living creatures being in eternal conscious distress. The "no rest" here is positive -- it describes the quality of their worship as uninterrupted, perpetual, filling every part of the day-and-night cycle. This is the interpretive baseline for the formula.

docs.title: Rev 14:11
docs.text:
Context: The third angel's message. Beast-worshippers are warned of fire-and-brimstone judgment.

Direct statement: "And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name."

Original language: ouk echousin (V-PAI-3P) anapausin (N-ASF, G372) hemeras (N-GSF, G2250) kai nuktos (N-GSF, G3571). Additionally, ho kapnos (G2586, N-NSM) tou basanismou (G929, N-GSM) auton eis aionas aionon anabainei (G305, V-PAI-3S, gnomic present).

The parallel: The Greek construction is identical element by element: - Same verb: echousin (PAI-3P) - Same noun: anapausin (ASF) - Same negation: ouk - Same genitive of time: hemeras kai nuktos (both GSF) - Same book, same author

The only difference is context. In Rev 4:8, "no rest" describes worship. In Rev 14:11, "no rest" describes judgment. The grammar is identical. If the formula in 4:8 describes the quality of the creatures' activity (uninterrupted, thoroughgoing) rather than asserting their eternal conscious existence, then the same formula in 14:11 describes the quality of the judgment (thoroughgoing, without relief) rather than asserting its eternal conscious duration.

Cross-references: The smoke-ascending formula echoes Isaiah 34:10 ("the smoke thereof shall go up for ever") and the gnomic present anabainei matches the timeless present tense used for the creatures' worship in 4:8.

docs.title: Rev 14:9-12 (Full Third Angel Context)
docs.text:
Context: The third angel's message, Rev 14:9-12, is the warning framework surrounding the crux text. Verse 9 identifies the sin (worshipping the beast and receiving his mark). Verse 10 names the punishment (fire and brimstone, in the presence of the holy angels and the Lamb). Verse 11 describes the smoke ascending and the "no rest day nor night." Verse 12 draws the practical conclusion: "Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus."

Direct statement: The passage is a warning -- prospective, not retrospective. It describes what will happen to beast-worshippers, using language drawn from OT judgment imagery (Isa 34:9-10, Gen 19:24-28).

Original language: In verse 10, basanisthesetai (V-FPI-3S, future passive indicative 3S of basanizo G928) -- the individual beast-worshipper "shall be tormented." The future tense places this judgment in the eschatological future. In verse 11, the verbs shift to the present tense (anabainei, echousin) -- the gnomic present, expressing timeless truths about the nature of this judgment.

docs.title: Rev 14:10 (Fire-and-Brimstone Judgment)
docs.text:
Context: "The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb."

Direct statement: The beast-worshipper faces fire-and-brimstone judgment. The imagery draws on Gen 19:24 (Sodom) and Isa 34:9 (Edom).

Original language: basanisthesetai (V-FPI-3S of basanizo G928). Same verb root as Rev 20:10 (basanisthesontai, FPI-3P), but singular here -- the individual is subject, not the symbolic triad.

docs.title: Focus Area 4: Rev 12:10 -- The "Day and Night" Activity That Ended
Rev 12:10
docs.text:
Context: War in heaven. Michael and his angels fight the dragon. The dragon and his angels are defeated and cast out. A loud voice in heaven declares the victory.

Direct statement: "Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night."

Original language: Three elements converge: 1. kategoron (G2723, V-PAP-NSM, present active participle) -- "the one accusing." The present participle describes the ongoing, continuous character of Satan's accusation during the period it was happening. 2. hemeras kai nuktos (both N-GSF) -- the genitive of time characterizing the accusation as thoroughgoing, filling the day-night framework. 3. eblethe (G906, V-API-3S, aorist passive indicative) -- "was cast." The aorist marks the completed, decisive action of casting Satan down. 4. Arti (G737, ADV) -- "Now, at this very moment." The temporal boundary marker declares the turning point.

Why this verse is decisive: Satan's "day and night" accusation was not paused -- it was terminated. The heavenly voice announces "NOW is come salvation... for the accuser is cast down." The present participle (kategoron) describes what Satan was doing continuously. The aorist (eblethe) ends it. The adverb arti marks the exact point of termination.

This proves that hemeras kai nuktos can describe an activity that is continuous, uninterrupted, and thoroughgoing during its occurrence -- and yet has a definite endpoint. The formula characterizes the quality of the activity within its period, not its guaranteed eternal continuation. If "day and night" meant "forever without end," Satan would still be accusing. He is not. The formula describes the character of the accusation (relentless, unceasing, filling the entire temporal framework), not its infinite duration.

Cross-references: Job 1:6-12 and Zech 3:1-2 provide the OT background. Satan comes before God and accuses. In Job, he accuses Job's motives. In Zechariah, he stands as prosecutor against Joshua the high priest. Rev 12:10 declares this entire accusatory ministry terminated.

docs.title: Rev 12:7-12 (Full War in Heaven Context)
docs.text:
Context: The full passage traces the arc: war in heaven (v.7), dragon defeated (v.8), cast out with his angels (v.9), heavenly proclamation of victory (v.10), the means of overcoming (v.11), and the warning to earth (v.12 -- "Woe to the inhabiters of the earth... for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time").

Relationship to other evidence: The phrase "he hath but a short time" (v.12) further confirms the bounded nature of the devil's activities. Even after being cast down, his activity is time-limited. "Day and night" described his accusatory work; "a short time" describes his remaining earthly activity. Both are bounded.

docs.title: Focus Area 5: Rev 7:15 -- Positive "Day and Night" Service
Rev 7:15
docs.text:
Context: The great multitude who came out of great tribulation. They have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.

Direct statement: "Therefore are they before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple: and he that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them."

Original language: latreuousin (G3000, V-PAI-3P, present active indicative 3P) auto hemeras (N-GSF) kai nuktos (N-GSF) en to nao (G3485, N-DSM) autou. The verb latreuo designates sacral, whole-life religious service -- the exclusive devotion of worship.

Cross-references: This parallels Rev 4:8 as the second positive "day and night" in Revelation. The living creatures worship "day and night"; the great multitude serves "day and night." Both are positive, both use the genitive of time, both describe the character of the devotion as uninterrupted.

The logical tension with Rev 22:5: Rev 7:15 says the great multitude serves "day and night" in God's temple. Rev 22:5 says "there shall be no night there" and Rev 21:25 confirms "there shall be no night there." If the great multitude's service is "day and night" but there is no night in eternity, then "day and night" cannot be a literal temporal description. It must be a quality-marker -- expressing the character of their service as perpetual, uninterrupted, complete. The service continues; the temporal framework does not.

docs.title: Rev 7:13-17 (Full Context)
docs.text: Context: One of the elders asks John who the white-robed multitude is. John defers. The elder explains: these are the ones from great tribulation, washed in the Lamb's blood. Therefore they serve before God's throne day and night. The passage concludes with the promise of no more hunger, thirst, or tears (vv.16-17) -- anticipating the eschatological resolution of Rev 21:4.

docs.title: Focus Area 6: The Eschatological Dissolution of Day/Night (Rev 22:5, 21:25)
Rev 22:5
docs.text:
Context: The final chapter of Revelation. The new Jerusalem. The river of life, the tree of life, and the ultimate state of the redeemed.

Direct statement: "And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever."

Original language: nyx (G3571, N-NSF, nominative singular) ouk estai (V-FDI-3S, future middle indicative) eti (ADV, "any more"). The saints basileuousin (G936, V-FAI-3P, future active indicative) eis tous aionas ton aionon -- "shall reign for ever and ever."

What this means for the formula: If "night" (nyx) no longer exists in the new creation, then the "day and night" framework within which all five Revelation occurrences operate has been dissolved. The saints' "day and night" service (Rev 7:15) continues, but not because night continues -- because their service is perpetual in character. The beast-worshippers' "day and night" torment (Rev 14:11) operates within a framework that is itself temporary. The formula describes activity within the present-age temporal framework, not within eternity.

The bookend with Gen 1:5: God named the darkness "Night" in Gen 1:5. In Rev 22:5, night ceases to exist. What began at creation ends at consummation. The day/night cycle is a feature of the present created order, not of the eternal state.

docs.title: Rev 21:25
docs.text:
Direct statement: "And the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there."

Original language: nyx gar ouk estai ekei -- "for night shall not be there." Second affirmation of night's abolition, linked here to the gates of the new Jerusalem never shutting.

docs.title: Rev 21:4
docs.text:
Context: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."

Relationship to the formula: If the "former things" have passed away, and these include death, sorrow, crying, and pain, then the ongoing conscious torment of any beings would contradict the promise. The eschatological vision envisions complete resolution -- no remaining suffering anywhere in the universe. This governs how we read the judgment passages: the judgment is real and thoroughgoing, but it reaches an endpoint.

docs.title: Gen 1:5 (Creation of the Day/Night Distinction)
docs.text:
Context: "And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day."

Relationship: The origin point of the framework. God establishes day and night as created realities. Rev 22:5 abolishes one half of this pair, dissolving the framework itself.

docs.title: Gen 8:22 (Day and Night as Creation Order)
docs.text:
Context: "While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease."

Original language: Hebrew: ve-yom (conjunction + noun ms Abs, "and day") va-laylah (conjunction + noun ms Abs, "and night") lo yishbotu (Qal imperfect 3mp of shavat H7673, "shall not cease"). The verb shavat is the root behind "Sabbath."

Relationship: Day and night are paired with other merisms (seedtime/harvest, cold/heat, summer/winter) expressing the totality of the created order. They are features of "while the earth remaineth" -- the present age. When the earth is made new (Rev 21:1), this promise reaches its natural boundary.

docs.title: Focus Area 7: The Anapausis Antithesis -- Rev 14:11 vs. Rev 14:13
Rev 14:13
docs.text:
Context: Two verses after the "no rest day nor night" of 14:11. A voice from heaven commands John to write a beatitude.

Direct statement: "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them."

Original language: anapahsontai (G373, V-2FPI-3P, future passive indicative 3P of anapauo) ek ton kopon (G2873, N-GPM) auton -- "they shall rest from their labours." The verb is the cognate of the noun anapausis (G372) used in 14:11.

The antithesis: John constructs a deliberate contrast: - 14:11: The beast-worshippers ouk echousin anapausin (G372) hemeras kai nuktos -- "they have no rest (noun) day nor night." - 14:13: The blessed dead anapahsontai (G373) ek ton kopon auton -- "they shall rest (verb) from their labours."

Same word family (ana + pauo = to cease, stop). Noun in 14:11, cognate verb in 14:13. Two verses apart. Opposite groups receiving opposite outcomes. This is not coincidence -- it is a literary structure. John places the two side by side so that each defines the other.

If the blessed dead's "rest" means cessation of labor and entry into reward -- the end of struggle and the beginning of peace -- then the beast-worshippers' "no rest" means the absence of relief during their judgment. They find no intermission, no pause, no relief from the fire that consumes them. This defines the quality of the judgment (thoroughgoing, without respite) rather than its duration (eternal).

docs.title: Matt 11:28-29 (Christ's Offer of Anapausis)
docs.text:
Context: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

Original language: anapausin (N-ASF, G372) -- the same word as Rev 4:8 and 14:11. Jesus offers anapausis as spiritual refreshment, cessation of burden, soul-rest.

Relationship: The only positive non-Revelation use of the noun anapausis. If Christ's "rest" is the positive -- relief, peace, cessation of striving -- then the denial of this rest in Rev 14:11 is the negative: no relief, no peace, no cessation of the judgment's pressure.

docs.title: Heb 4:1-11 (Rest Theology)
docs.text:
Context: Hebrews develops a theology of entering God's rest (katapausis, G2663 -- a synonym of anapausis, G372). Those who believe enter rest; those who disobey fail to enter.

Direct statement: "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his" (Heb 4:9-10).

Relationship: The theological structure is: rest is the reward of faith and obedience; absence of rest is the consequence of rebellion. Rev 14:11-13 maps this same structure onto eschatological outcomes: beast-worshippers receive no rest; the faithful dead receive rest.

docs.title: Focus Area 8: Broader NT "Day and Night" Pattern
docs.text: Outside Revelation, the NT uses the "day and night" / "night and day" formula in at least ten passages. Every single one describes the quality or intensity of an activity rather than making a literal claim about 24-hour unbroken performance.

docs.title: Acts 26:7
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Unto which promise our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come."

Original language: nykta (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE) kai hemeran (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE). Paul uses the accusative of extent here, not the genitive. This emphasizes the span of their service. Even so, no one claims the twelve tribes literally served God without a single pause.

Relationship: Though accusative rather than genitive, the phrase still functions as a quality-marker for devoted, wholehearted service.

docs.title: 1 Thess 2:9
docs.text:
Direct statement: "For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God."

Original language: nuktos (N-GSF, GENITIVE) kai hemeras (N-GSF, GENITIVE). Identical genitive construction to all five Revelation passages. Paul labored "night and day" -- characterizing the quality and intensity of his work ethic. He did not literally labor without sleeping.

docs.title: 2 Thess 3:8
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you."

Relationship: Parallel to 1 Thess 2:9. Same genitive construction, same qualitative function.

docs.title: 1 Tim 5:5
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day."

Original language: nuktos kai hemeras -- genitive of time. The true widow's prayer life is characterized as continuous and devoted. No one reads this as literal non-stop prayer.

docs.title: 2 Tim 1:3
docs.text:
Direct statement: "I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day."

Relationship: Same genitive formula, same qualitative function. Paul remembers Timothy "night and day" in prayer -- regularly, faithfully, devotedly.

docs.title: Luke 2:37 (ACCUSATIVE -- The Diagnostic Contrast)
docs.text:
Direct statement: "And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day."

Original language: nykta (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE) kai hemeran (N-ASF, ACCUSATIVE). Luke uses the accusative of extent -- measuring the duration of Anna's service. This contrasts with the genitive used in all five Revelation passages.

Relationship: This is the key diagnostic. The same words (nyx, hemera) change grammatical function by case. Accusative = measuring how long. Genitive = characterizing what kind of time. Revelation uses the genitive every time -- characterizing the temporal backdrop, not measuring duration.

docs.title: Luke 18:7
docs.text:
Direct statement: "And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them?"

Original language: hemeras (N-GSF) kai nuktos (N-GSF) -- genitive of time. The elect's persistent prayer is characterized as "day and night" -- continuous, fervent, devoted. Not literal non-stop crying.

docs.title: Mark 5:5 (The Strongest Possible "Day and Night")
docs.text:
Direct statement: "And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones."

Original language: dia pantos (continually) nuktos (N-GSF) kai hemeras (N-GSF). The genitive of time is reinforced by dia pantos ("continually"). Even this strongest possible "day and night" -- continuous, relentless, negative activity -- is qualitative. The demoniac did sleep. He did eat. He did pause. The formula describes the pervasive, relentless character of his torment, not a literal claim of unbroken activity.

Relationship: If the demoniac's "always, night and day" crying is qualitative (and it must be -- no human maintains unbroken activity), then Rev 14:11's "no rest day nor night" can also describe the quality and thoroughness of judgment without requiring literal unbroken conscious experience.

docs.title: Acts 9:24
docs.text:
Direct statement: "But their laying await was known of Saul. And they watched the gates day and night to kill him."

Original language: hemeras te kai nuktos -- genitive of time with te particle. The enemies' surveillance is described as "day and night" -- thorough, persistent. They did not literally stare at the gates without blinking.

docs.title: Acts 20:31
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears."

Relationship: Genitive of time. Paul's pastoral vigilance over three years is characterized as "night and day" -- devoted, persistent, thorough. Not literal non-stop warning.

The pattern is uniform: In every NT occurrence outside Revelation, "day and night" describes the quality, intensity, or thoroughgoing character of an activity. Not once does it make a literal claim of unbroken 24-hour performance. This is the established NT usage that John inherits when he uses the formula in Revelation.

docs.title: Focus Area 9: The OT Yom V'laylah Merism
docs.text: The Hebrew "day and night" merism (yom v'laylah / yomam va-laylah) provides the OT foundation for the NT formula. The word studies for yowm (H3117) and layil (H3915) confirm that these are the Hebrew words behind hemera (G2250) and nyx (G3571), with the LXX mapping as one of the most stable available (layil-nyx: PMI 6.64, 189 co-occurrences).

docs.title: Josh 1:8 / Psa 1:2 (Devotional Completeness)
docs.text:
Direct statement: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night" (Josh 1:8). "In his law doth he meditate day and night" (Psa 1:2).

Relationship: The baseline for the OT merism. No interpreter claims Joshua or the blessed man meditates literally without pause for 24 hours. "Day and night" means continuously, thoroughly, as a characteristic practice. This is the interpretive foundation.

docs.title: Psa 32:4 (Bounded "Day and Night" Pressure)
docs.text:
Direct statement: "For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer."

Original language: yomam (adverb, "by day") va-laylah (conjunction + noun ms Abs, "and night") tikhbad (Qal imperfect 3fs of kavad, "be heavy") alai (upon me) yadkha (your hand).

Relationship: David describes divine conviction pressing on him "day and night." The pressure was thoroughgoing -- it characterized every part of his experience. But it ended. Psalm 32:5 says "I acknowledged my sin unto thee... and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." The "day and night" pressure terminated when David confessed. This is the same pattern as Rev 12:10: continuous "day and night" activity that reaches an endpoint.

docs.title: Isa 34:10 (The Direct OT Source for Rev 14:11)
docs.text:
Direct statement: "It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever."

Original language: laylah (noun ms Abs, "night") ve-yomam (adverb, "by day") lo tikhbeh (Qal imperfect 3fs of kavah, "go out") -- "night nor day it shall not be quenched." Le-owlam (to eternity) ya'aleh (Qal imperfect 3ms of alah, "ascend") ashana (its smoke) -- "forever its smoke shall ascend."

The aftermath (Isa 34:11-15): The verses immediately following describe animals dwelling in the ruins. Cormorants and bitterns possess the land (v.11). Thorns grow in the palaces (v.13). Wild beasts meet there (v.14). The screech owl "rests there" (v.14 -- note the irony: the owl finds rest in the place whose fire was "not quenched night nor day"). Owls make nests, lay eggs, hatch young (v.15). Vultures gather with their mates (v.15).

Animals cannot inhabit a place that is still on fire. The fire that was "not quenched night nor day" is out. The smoke that "shall go up for ever" is testimony to completed destruction, not ongoing burning. This is the OT source imagery for Rev 14:11 -- and in the OT source, the fire has done its work and the ruins are cold enough for nesting birds.

docs.title: Isa 62:6 (Watchmen "Day nor Night")
docs.text:
Direct statement: "I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night."

Relationship: Continuous vigilance expressed through the "day nor night" formula. No one reads this as literal non-stop shouting.

docs.title: Neh 1:6 (Prayer "Day and Night")
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open, that thou mayest hear the prayer of thy servant, which I pray before thee now, day and night."

Relationship: Nehemiah's intercessory intensity -- "day and night" prayer meaning devoted, persistent, fervent.

docs.title: Jer 14:17 (Tears "Night and Day")
docs.text:
Direct statement: "Let mine eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease."

Relationship: The thoroughness of prophetic grief. "Night and day" with "let them not cease" expresses completeness and depth of sorrow.

docs.title: 1 Ki 8:29 (God's Eyes "Night and Day")
docs.text:
Direct statement: "That thine eyes may be open toward this house night and day."

Relationship: God's continuous, unwavering attention toward the temple. The merism expresses quality of divine attentiveness, not a temporal measurement.

The OT pattern is consistent: "Day and night" (in any order) expresses the completeness, thoroughness, and pervasive quality of an activity. It is a merism -- a figure of speech that names two poles (day/night, heaven/earth, old/young) to express totality. In no OT passage does "day and night" require literal 24-hour non-stop performance.

docs.title: Focus Area 10: Quality vs. Duration -- The Governing Principle
docs.text:
The evidence converges from eight independent lines:

  1. The genitive of time construction characterizes the temporal backdrop, not the extent. All five Revelation occurrences use the genitive, not the accusative of duration.

  2. Rev 4:8's identical formula is universally read as describing quality (ceaseless worship), not eternal conscious existence without rest. The same construction in Rev 14:11 should carry the same function.

  3. Rev 12:10 proves "day and night" can describe a terminated activity. Satan's accusation was "day and night" -- and it ended when he was cast down. The formula characterized the thoroughness of the accusation during its period, not its eternal continuation.

  4. Rev 7:15's "day and night" service occurs in a reality where "there shall be no night" (Rev 22:5). The formula must be qualitative -- the service continues, but not because night continues.

  5. Every NT "day and night" outside Revelation is qualitative. Paul's laboring, the widow's prayers, Timothy's remembrance, the demoniac's crying, the enemies' surveillance -- all describe quality and intensity, never literal unbroken performance.

  6. Every OT yom v'laylah is qualitative. Joshua's meditation, David's conviction, Nehemiah's prayer, Jeremiah's tears, Solomon's prayer about God's attention -- all describe completeness and thoroughness, not literal 24-hour activity.

  7. Isa 34:10 uses the same formula for a fire that is demonstrably out. Animals nest in the ruins. The "night nor day" fire has completed its work.

  8. The anapausis antithesis (14:11 vs. 14:13) defines "no rest" as absence of relief during judgment, not eternal conscious experience. The blessed dead's "rest" is cessation of labor; the beast-worshippers' "no rest" is absence of relief.

The hermeneutical principle: "day and night" in biblical usage -- Old Testament and New, Hebrew and Greek, positive and negative contexts -- is a quality-marker describing the thoroughgoing, uninterrupted nature of an activity during its occurrence. It does not function as a duration-guarantee. When applied to the judgment of Rev 14:11, the formula tells us that the judgment is thoroughgoing, complete, without relief or intermission -- not that it continues eternally.

docs.title: Rev 19:3 (Babylon's Smoke)
docs.text:
Context: "And again they said, Alleluia. And her smoke rose up for ever and ever."

Direct statement: Babylon's smoke rises "for ever and ever." But Babylon is destroyed. Rev 18:21 says she is "found no more at all" -- repeated six times in 18:21-24 ("shall be found no more at all," "shall be heard no more at all," "shall shine no more at all," "shall be heard no more at all," "shall be found no more at all"). The smoke is memorial testimony of completed destruction, not ongoing burning of a surviving entity.

Relationship: Parallel to Rev 14:11's smoke formula. Same verb (anabaino), same "for ever and ever" phrase. Applied to an entity that is unambiguously and totally destroyed.

docs.title: Rev 8:4 (Worship Smoke)
docs.text:
Context: "And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand."

Relationship: Both worship smoke (Rev 8:4) and judgment smoke (Rev 14:11) use the same verb anabaino (G305). Incense smoke carries prayer upward; judgment smoke carries testimony upward. The symmetry shows that smoke ascending is about the message carried, not about the fire still burning.

docs.title: Rev 20:9-15 (Lake of Fire Context)
docs.text:
Context: The final judgment sequence. Gog and Magog surround the beloved city. Fire from heaven devours them (v.9, katephagen -- "devoured," aorist active). The devil is cast into the lake of fire (v.10) where the beast and false prophet already are. The great white throne judgment follows (vv.11-13). Death and hell are cast into the lake of fire (v.14). Anyone not in the book of life is cast into the lake of fire (v.15).

Key observation: The vocabulary diverges by subject. Non-human/symbolic entities (devil, beast, false prophet) receive basanizo vocabulary (tormented day and night for ever and ever, v.10). Humans receive destruction vocabulary: "devoured" (v.9, katephagen), "cast into the lake of fire" (v.15), "the second death" (v.14). Different verbs for different subjects in consecutive verses.

docs.title: Rev 20:14-15 (The Second Death)
docs.text:
Context: "And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire."

Direct statement: The lake of fire is called "the second death" -- not "the second life in torment." Death is the absence of life, not the continuation of conscious experience. The name the text gives the lake of fire is itself the definition of what happens there: death.

docs.title: Gen 19:24-28 (The Sodom Paradigm)
docs.text:
Context: The paradigmatic fire-and-brimstone judgment. Three stages: fire falls from heaven (v.24), cities are overthrown (v.25), Abraham sees smoke ascending (v.28). This is the source imagery for Rev 14:11.

Relationship: 2 Pet 2:6 interprets the result: Sodom and Gomorrah were "turned to ashes" (tephrosas). The fire-and-brimstone sequence produces ashes, not eternal burning. The cities are an "ensample" (hupodeigma) of what happens to the ungodly. If the ensample produced ashes, the thing it foreshadows should produce the same.

docs.title: 2 Pet 2:6 (Sodom Turned to Ashes)
docs.text:
Context: Peter interprets the Sodom event as a didactic example.

Direct statement: "And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly."

Relationship: The interpretive key for the fire-and-brimstone imagery. The outcome is ashes -- complete destruction, not ongoing torment.

docs.title: Isa 6:2-3 (OT Source for Rev 4:8)
docs.text:
Context: Isaiah's throne room vision. Six-winged seraphim crying "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts."

Relationship: The direct OT source for Rev 4:8's living creatures. Six wings, triple "holy," throne room, divine title. John's "rest not day and night, saying Holy, holy, holy" is an expansion of Isaiah's vision. The continuous praise of the seraphim establishes the pattern that "no rest" can describe positive, ceaseless worship.

docs.title: Matt 25:41 (Everlasting Fire)
docs.text:
Context: "Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

Relationship: The fire was "prepared for the devil and his angels" -- the primary subjects of Rev 20:10. Humans are secondary recipients of a judgment designed for supernatural entities. The "everlasting" (aionios) fire describes fire whose result is permanent (cf. Hebrews' aionios + result-noun pattern: eternal redemption obtained once, eternal judgment rendered once).

docs.title: Mal 4:1-3 (Wicked Become Ashes)
docs.text:
Context: "The day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch... they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet."

Relationship: The outcome of divine fire: ashes. Not preservation in torment. "Neither root nor branch" -- nothing remains. The wicked become ashes under the feet of the righteous. This is the didactic, prophetic description of what fire does to the wicked.

docs.title: Ezek 28:18-19 (Satan-Figure Becomes Ashes)
docs.text:
Context: "I will bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth... thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more."

Relationship: The same being described in Rev 20:10 (the devil) is described here as reduced to ashes and ceasing to exist: "never shalt thou be any more" (ayin + owlam). The didactic oracle (Ezekiel) governs the apocalyptic vision (Revelation). The prophecy describes the ultimate end: fire, ashes, cessation of existence.

docs.title: Rev 1:20 (Revelation's Self-Interpretation Pattern)
docs.text:
Context: Revelation interprets its own symbols: stars = angels, candlesticks = churches.

Relationship: Revelation is a book of symbols with built-in interpretive guides. The "day and night" formula, the smoke imagery, and the fire-and-brimstone language are all symbolic elements that should be interpreted through the OT source material and Revelation's own interpretive patterns.

docs.title: Psa 134:1 (Night Worship)
docs.text:
Context: "Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD."

Relationship: Night as a setting for devoted worship. The tradition of night-time temple service provides background for Rev 4:8 and Rev 7:15 -- "day and night" worship encompassing the night watches.

docs.title: Psa 119:148 (Night Meditation)
docs.text:
Context: "Mine eyes prevent the night watches, that I might meditate in thy word."

Relationship: The psalmist's devotion extends into the night -- not because he is tormented but because he is devoted. Night meditation is a positive expression of commitment to God's word, paralleling the "day and night" meditation of Josh 1:8 and Psa 1:2.

docs.title: Job 1:6-12 (Satan's Heavenly Access)
docs.text:
Context: "There was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them."

Relationship: OT background for Rev 12:10. Satan has access to God's presence and functions as an accuser. This access -- the "day and night" accusation -- was terminated when Satan was cast down.

docs.title: Zech 3:1-2 (Satan as Prosecutor)
docs.text:
Context: "And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him."

Relationship: The courtroom imagery behind Rev 12:10. Satan functions as a legal prosecutor (the right-hand position was the accuser's place in ancient courts). The verb kategoreo (G2723) in Rev 12:10 carries this legal-prosecution meaning.

docs.title: Pattern 1: The Formula as Quality-Marker Across Testaments
docs.text: In every biblical occurrence examined -- OT Hebrew, LXX Greek, NT Greek -- "day and night" functions as a merism expressing thoroughness, completeness, and uninterrupted character. Not once does it require literal, unbroken 24-hour performance.

docs.title: Pattern 2: Positive and Negative Uses Follow the Same Grammar
docs.text: The positive uses (worship, service, prayer, meditation) and the negative uses (accusation, torment, surveillance, weeping) all use the same genitive of time construction and all function the same way: characterizing quality, not guaranteeing duration.

docs.title: Pattern 3: The Formula Can Describe Bounded Activity
docs.text: Rev 12:10 (terminated accusation), Psa 32:4 (ended when David confessed), and Isa 34:10 (fire out, animals in ruins) all demonstrate that "day and night" describes activity with definite endpoints.

docs.title: Pattern 4: Identical Constructions Demand Identical Functional Readings
docs.text: Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11 share the exact Greek construction: ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos. The same grammar in the same book by the same author cannot mean "ceaseless worship" in one place and "eternal conscious torment" in another without compelling contextual reason. No such reason exists.

docs.title: Pattern 5: The Dissolution of Night Dissolves the Framework
docs.text: Rev 22:5 and 21:25 abolish night itself. Activities described as occurring "day and night" must therefore be qualitative descriptions that outlast the framework they reference. The service continues (Rev 7:15) in a nightless eternity. The judgment reaches its conclusion within the framework.

docs.title: Word Study Integration
docs.text:
The word studies confirm the analysis at every point:

  • Anapausis (G372): 5 NT occurrences. The identical construction in Rev 4:8 (positive) and Rev 14:11 (negative) is the central evidence. The word means "rest, intermission, cessation" -- its denial means "no intermission, no pause, no relief."

  • Anapauo (G373): 12 NT occurrences. The cognate verb in Rev 14:13 creates the deliberate antithesis with the noun in 14:11. Same word family, opposite outcomes.

  • Hemera (G2250): 388 NT tokens. Paired with nyx in the "day and night" merism across both testaments. The collocation is a fixed expression for continuous activity.

  • Nyx (G3571): 65 NT occurrences. The abolition of nyx in Rev 22:5 is the eschatological endpoint of the entire "day and night" framework.

  • Basanizo (G928): 12 NT occurrences. Seven are non-judgment (illness, waves, rowing, moral distress). Five are in Revelation's apocalyptic framework. The word does not inherently require eternal duration -- Rev 9:5 limits it to five months.

  • Basanismos (G929): 6 occurrences, all in Revelation. Four of six are time-bounded or applied to destroyed entities. The word is genre-specific to apocalyptic.

  • Kapnos (G2586): 13 tokens, 91% in Revelation. Smoke is testimony -- the visible trace of completed transformation.

  • Ashan (H6227): 25 OT occurrences. Smoke in the Hebrew mind is evidence that fire has done its work -- the witness, not the process.

  • Owlam (H5769): 432 OT tokens. Subject-determined: applied to God = genuinely eternal; applied to Edom's smoke (Isa 34:10) = permanent result of completed destruction.

  • Kategoros (G2725): 7 NT occurrences. Rev 12:10 is the theological climax: the accuser's "day and night" role is terminated.

  • Arti (G737): 36 NT occurrences. In Rev 12:10, it marks the temporal boundary where the "day and night" accusation ends.

  • Latreuo (G3000): 21 NT occurrences. The sacral service verb in Rev 7:15 describes the great multitude's "day and night" temple service -- positive, perpetual, qualitative.

docs.title: Cross-Testament Connections
docs.text:
The OT provides the interpretive key for the NT at every level:

  1. Isa 34:10 → Rev 14:11: "Not quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever" is the direct source for "the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever." In the OT source, the fire is out and animals inhabit the ruins.

  2. Gen 19:24-28 → Rev 14:10-11: Fire and brimstone from the LORD; smoke ascending. 2 Pet 2:6 interprets: "turned to ashes." The trajectory is fire → destruction → ashes → smoke as memorial.

  3. Isa 6:2-3 → Rev 4:8: Six-winged creatures, triple "holy," throne room. The continuous praise of the seraphim is the template for the living creatures' "rest not day and night."

  4. Josh 1:8 / Psa 1:2 → NT "day and night": The OT merism for devotional completeness crosses into the NT as the hemeras kai nuktos formula via the LXX bridge (yowm→hemera, layil→nyx).

  5. Gen 1:5 → Rev 22:5: God named the darkness "Night" at creation. In the new creation, night ceases to exist. The bookend dissolves the entire framework within which "day and night" operates.

  6. Ezek 28:18-19 → Rev 20:10: The Satan-figure becomes "ashes upon the earth" and "never shalt thou be any more." The didactic prophecy governs the apocalyptic vision.

docs.title: Rev 20:10 -- "Tormented Day and Night For Ever and Ever"
docs.text:
This is the passage most often cited against the quality-reading of the formula. It says the devil, beast, and false prophet "shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever." The combination of "day and night" AND "for ever and ever" seems to press toward eternal duration.

Response: (1) All three subjects are non-human/symbolic -- the devil (supernatural spirit being), the beast (seven-headed composite entity), and the false prophet (two-horned earth beast). None is a literal human being. (2) The "for ever and ever" (eis tous aionas ton aionon) formula is subject-determined -- applied to God it means genuinely eternal; applied to Edom's smoke (Isa 34:10) it means permanent aftermath. (3) Ezek 28:18-19 describes the same Satan-figure as becoming "ashes upon the earth" and ceasing to exist: "never shalt thou be any more." (4) Humans in the same passage receive different vocabulary: "devoured" (v.9), "second death" (v.14-15). (5) The genitive of time (hemeras kai nuktos) still characterizes the quality of the judgment. The passage describes the total, thoroughgoing nature of the judgment on these three symbolic entities, using the strongest available language. It does not override the grammatical evidence, the Rev 12:10 counter-example, or the eschatological dissolution of night.

docs.title: Matt 25:41 -- "Everlasting Fire"
docs.text:
