The fire is "everlasting" (aionios). Does this require eternal burning of conscious subjects?

Response: The Hebrews pattern governs aionios + result-noun: "eternal redemption" (obtained once, result permanent), "eternal judgment" (rendered once, result permanent). "Everlasting fire" is fire whose result is permanent -- everlasting destruction, not everlasting burning. 2 Pet 2:6 confirms: the paradigmatic fire-and-brimstone event (Sodom) produced ashes.

docs.title: Matt 25:46 -- "Everlasting Punishment"
docs.text:
Though not a "day and night" passage, this verse is often connected. "These shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal."

Response: "Everlasting punishment" follows the Hebrews pattern -- punishment whose result is permanent. The righteous receive everlasting life (they live forever). The wicked receive everlasting punishment (they are punished with a result that lasts forever -- death, the second death). The symmetry is in the permanence of the result, not in the duration of the conscious experience.

docs.title: Mark 5:5 -- Negative "Day and Night" Activity
docs.text:
The demoniac cries "always, night and day" -- the strongest possible phrasing (dia pantos reinforcing the genitive merism). Does this show "day and night" can describe literal ongoing distress?

Response: Even this strongest phrasing is qualitative. The demoniac was not literally awake and crying 24 hours a day without any pause. He slept, he paused, he had moments of quiet. The formula describes the relentless, pervasive character of his distress, not a literal claim of unbroken activity. And crucially, his "day and night" torment ended when Jesus delivered him.

docs.title: Preliminary Synthesis
docs.text:
The weight of evidence points clearly in one direction. The hemeras kai nuktos formula in Revelation -- and across the entire Bible -- is a quality-marker describing the thoroughgoing, uninterrupted nature of an activity during its occurrence. It does not function as a duration-guarantee.

The most powerful evidence:

  1. Rev 4:8 = Rev 14:11 in grammar -- identical construction, universally read as quality in 4:8, which demands the same reading in 14:11.
  2. Rev 12:10 -- bounded activity -- the "day and night" accusation that ended proves the formula can describe terminated activity.
  3. Rev 22:5 -- no night in eternity -- the dissolution of the temporal framework makes all "day and night" language qualitative by definition.
  4. Rev 14:11 vs. 14:13 -- the anapausis antithesis -- "no rest" is defined by contrast with "rest from labours," not by duration claims.
  5. Isa 34:10-15 -- the OT source -- the same formula describes a fire that is demonstrably out.

The "day and night" formula in Rev 14:11 describes the thoroughgoing nature of a judgment during its execution -- complete, without relief, filling every part of the temporal framework -- not eternal conscious experience.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: What does the 'day and night' (hemeras kai nuktos) formula mean in Revelation? Does 'no rest day nor night' (Rev 14:11) describe eternal conscious experience, or the thoroughgoing nature of a judgment during its execution?

docs.title: G372 — anapausis
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G372-anapausis.md

Occurrences: 5

Rest, intermission, cessation — from anapauo (G373). All 5 NT occurrences in accusative singular (anapausin). Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11 share the identical construction: ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos. In Rev 4:8 the absence of rest is positive (ceaseless worship); in Rev 14:11 it is negative (no relief during judgment). The identical grammatical construction in the same book by the same author demands the same functional reading.

Semantic categories: spiritual rest offered by Christ, rest sought by unclean spirits, ceaseless activity (absence of rest), absence of rest as punishment

Key verses: Matt 11:29, Matt 12:43, Luke 11:24, Rev 4:8, Rev 14:11

Relevance: Core word — the 'no rest' formula in Rev 4:8 and 14:11. The identical construction in opposite contexts (worship vs. judgment) is the central evidence that 'no rest day nor night' describes quality of activity, not eternal duration.

docs.title: G373 — anapauo
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G373-anapauo.md

Occurrences: 12

Cognate verb of anapausis (G372) — to cause to rest, give rest, refresh. Rev 14:13 uses anapahsontai (future passive indicative 3P) — 'they shall rest from their labours.' This is the deliberate antithesis to Rev 14:11's 'no anapausis': same word family, adjacent verses, opposite outcomes.

Semantic categories: rest given by Christ, physical rest/sleep, refreshment by believers, eschatological rest of the dead

Key verses: Matt 11:28, Rev 6:11, Rev 14:13

Relevance: The verb form of the 'rest' concept. Rev 14:13 (blessed dead rest) vs. 14:11 (beast-worshippers have no rest) creates the anapausis antithesis — the sharpest evidence for what 'no rest' means.

docs.title: G2250 — hemera
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2250-hemera.md

Occurrences: 388

Day — 365 unique verses, 388 tokens. Critical collocation: nyx (G3571) co-occurs 28 times in 'day and night' merism expressing continuous action. Hebrew source: H3117 yowm with 1,485 LXX co-occurrences (score 25.24, PMI 3.46), the highest-confidence Hebrew-to-Greek bridge in day/time vocabulary.

Semantic categories: calendar/literal day, daylight hours vs night, eschatological day, last days, historical epoch

docs.title: G3571 — nyx
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3571-nyx.md

Occurrences: 65

Night — 65 NT occurrences across 13 books. The 'day-and-night merism in Revelation' is identified as a distinct semantic category: hemera kai nyx functioning as a merism for ceaseless, uninterrupted activity. Used for worship (4:8), service (7:15), accusation (12:10), torment (14:11, 20:10). The abolition of night in 21:25 and 22:5 signals the end of the present order. Hebrew source: H3915 layil with score 34.83 (PMI 6.64) — one of the most stable LXX mappings.

Semantic categories: literal temporal night, spiritual vigilance/devotion, spiritual darkness metaphor, day-and-night merism in Revelation, night watches

Key verses: Rev 4:8, Rev 7:15, Rev 12:10, Rev 14:11, Rev 20:10, Rev 21:25, Rev 22:5

Relevance: Core word — 'night' in the hemeras kai nuktos formula. The genitive singular form nuktos appears in all 5 Revelation passages. The abolition of nyx in Rev 22:5 is the eschatological endpoint.

docs.title: G305 — anabaino
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G305-anabaínō.md

To go up, ascend — from ana (up) + baino (to walk). 13 Revelation occurrences including Rev 14:11 (smoke of torment ascending) and Rev 19:3 (Babylon's smoke ascending). Rev 14:11 uses present tense anabainei — gnomic present, timeless assertion, same kind of present as Rev 4:8.

docs.title: G928 — basanizo
docs.text:

To torment, test, vex — from basanos (touchstone). 12 NT occurrences: 7 non-judgment (illness, waves tossing a ship, toiling at rowing, moral distress), 5 in Revelation's apocalyptic framework. docs.title: G2586 — kapnos

docs.title: G2725 — kategoros
docs.text:

Occurrences: 7

Accuser, formal legal prosecutor — from kata (against) + agora (assembly). 7 NT occurrences: 5 in Acts (Roman judicial accusers), 1 in Revelation (Satan as cosmic accuser, Rev 12:10), 1 in John 8:10 (disputed text). docs.title: G2723 — kategoreo
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G2723-katēgoréō.md

Occurrences: 24

To accuse, bring formal charges — the verb cognate of kategoros (G2725). 24 NT occurrences. In Rev 12:10, the present active participle kategoron describes the ongoing character of Satan's accusation 'day and night.' The participle is present tense (continuous aspect) but the activity is terminated by the aorist eblethe (was cast down).

Semantic categories: legal/judicial accusation, hostile surveillance, spiritual/cosmic accusation

Key verses: Rev 12:10, Matt 27:12, Acts 24:2

docs.title: G737 — arti
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G737-árti.md

Occurrences: 36

Now, at this moment, this instant — adverb marking the present moment with emphasis on immediacy. In Rev 12:10, arti marks the cosmic turning point: 'NOW is come salvation... for the accuser is cast down.' Functions as a temporal boundary marker declaring that the 'day and night' accusation has ended at this very instant.

Semantic categories: punctiliar present, now-then contrast, epoch-marking transition, forward-looking present

Key verses: Rev 12:10, Matt 3:15, 1 Cor 13:12

docs.title: G166 — aionios
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G166-aionios.md

Occurrences: 71

Eternal, everlasting — adjective from aion (G165). 71 NT occurrences. ~43 for 'eternal life.' Applied to God's attributes (genuinely eternal), to believers' inheritance (genuinely eternal), and to judgment (3 uses in Revelation — Rev 14:6,11; subject-determined meaning). Hebrew source: owlam (H5769) with PMI 26.16.

Semantic categories: eternal life, eternal judgment, divine attributes, eternal realities, eternal purpose

Key verses: John 3:16, Matt 25:41, Matt 25:46, Rev 14:6

Relevance: The 'ages of ages' formula co-occurs with 'day and night' in Rev 14:11 and 20:10. Subject-determined meaning: applied to eternal God = genuinely eternal; applied to judgment on non-eternal subjects = permanent result.

docs.title: G4352 — proskyneo
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G4352-proskyneo.md

Occurrences: 65

To worship, prostrate — 54 unique verses, 65 tokens. Revelation dominates with 22 occurrences (41%). Includes both proper worship (throne room) and false worship (beast/dragon). Rev 14:11's 'who worship the beast' identifies the subjects of the 'no rest day nor night' formula.

Semantic categories: prostration before Jesus, recognition of divine sonship, true worship discourse, exclusive worship command, heavenly throne room worship, eschatological false worship

docs.title: H5769 — owlam
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H5769-owlam.md

Occurrences: 432

Forever, eternity, perpetual — 406 unique verses (432 tokens) across 34 books. Core meaning: 'the vanishing point' — time that recedes beyond the reach of human perception. Subject-determined: applied to God = genuinely eternal; applied to slave's lifetime = 'for ever' (bounded); applied to Ai's destruction = permanent desolation. Isa 34:10 uses owlam for Edom's smoke — but Edom is not burning today.

Semantic categories: eternal duration of God, everlasting covenant, perpetual cultic ordinances, immemorial past, eschatological age to come, permanent judgment/desolation

Key verses: Psa 90:2, Isa 34:10, Josh 8:28, Dan 12:2

Relevance: The Hebrew 'forever' behind Rev 14:11's 'for ever and ever.' Subject-determined: Isa 34:10's 'for ever' smoke comes from a fire that is demonstrably out (animals inhabit the ruins, Isa 34:11-17).

docs.title: H3117 — yowm

docs.title: H3915 — layil
docs.text:

Occurrences: 241

Night — 223 unique verses (241 tokens) across 30 books. First occurrence: Gen 1:5. Nearly all renderings contain 'night.' Forms the OT half of the yom v'laylah merism. LXX bridge to nyx (G3571) with 189 co-occurrences (score 34.83, PMI 6.64) — one of the most stable in the LXX.

Relevance: The Hebrew 'night' behind the OT yom v'laylah merism. The same pattern crosses into the NT via the LXX bridge layil → nyx.

docs.title: H6227 — ashan
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/H6227-ashan.md

Occurrences: 25

Smoke — 25 occurrences across 13 OT books. Five semantic categories: theophanic smoke (Gen 15:17, Exo 19:18), divine wrath/judgment (Isa 34:10, 2 Sam 22:9), transience/vanishing (Psa 37:20, Psa 102:3), military signal (Josh 8:20), and eschatological sign (Joel 2:30). docs.title: G3000 — latreuo
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G3000-latreuo.md

Occurrences: 21

To serve/worship (God) — from latris (hired menial). 21 NT occurrences across 8 books. In Rev 7:15, the great multitude latreuousin (PAI-3P, 'serve') God hemeras kai nuktos ('day and night') en to nao autou ('in his temple'). The verb designates exclusive, whole-life religious service. Distinguished from proskyneo (reverence act) in Matt 4:10. Acts 26:7 uses latreuo for the twelve tribes 'instantly serving God day and night.'

docs.title: G930 — basanistes
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G930-basanistēs.md

Occurrences: 1

Tormentor/torturer — agent noun from basanizo (G928). Hapax legomenon: only Matt 18:34. The master delivers the unforgiving servant 'to the tormentors' until the debt is paid. The basanistes is the agent who carries out punishment.

Semantic categories: punitive authority/judicial torment

docs.title: G931 — basanos
docs.text:
Source: D:/Bible/bible-studies/word-studies/G931-basanos.md

Touchstone, then torture/torment — 3 NT occurrences. Matt 4:24 (physical suffering), Luke 16:23,28 (torment in Hades parable). Root of the basanizo word family. Originally a stone for testing metal purity, extended to testing by torture, then to torment generally.

docs.title: Conclusion: The "Day and Night" Formula in Revelation
Question
docs.text: What does the "day and night" (hemeras kai nuktos) formula mean in Revelation? Does "no rest day nor night" (Rev 14:11) describe eternal conscious experience, or the thoroughgoing nature of a judgment during its execution?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The hemeras kai nuktos ("day and night") formula in Revelation is a genitive-of-time construction that characterizes the thoroughgoing, uninterrupted quality of an activity during its occurrence -- not its eternal duration. All five Revelation occurrences use the identical genitive case, the same construction appears in Rev 4:8 where no one reads it as eternal conscious torment of the living creatures, Rev 12:10 proves the formula can describe activity that has definitively ended, and Rev 22:5 dissolves the day/night temporal framework entirely in the new creation. The "no rest day nor night" of Rev 14:11 describes the thoroughgoing nature of a judgment during its execution -- complete, without relief or intermission -- not eternal conscious experience.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
The Ceaseless Worship Formula (Revelation 4:8) And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come.

The Perpetual Temple Service (Revelation 7:15) Therefore are they before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple: and he that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them.

The Terminated Accusation (Revelation 12:10) And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night.

The Crux Text (Revelation 14:11) And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

The Anapausis Antithesis (Revelation 14:13) And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.

The Lake of Fire Formula (Revelation 20:10) And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

The Dissolution of Night (Revelation 22:5) And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever.

docs.title: 1. The Greek Grammar: Genitive of Time, Not Accusative of Extent
docs.text:
The grammatical foundation of this study is the case form used in all five Revelation "day and night" passages. The Greek parser confirms that every occurrence uses hemeras (G2250, N-GSF, genitive singular feminine) kai nuktos (G3571, N-GSF, genitive singular feminine). The genitive of time in Greek expresses "time within which" or "time during which." It characterizes the temporal backdrop of an action -- what kind of time-frame the activity fills. It answers the question "during what kind of time?" rather than "for how long?"

Greek has a different tool for measuring duration: the accusative of extent of time, which answers "for how long?" Luke demonstrates this distinction in Luke 2:37, where Anna serves God nykta (N-ASF, accusative singular) kai hemeran (N-ASF, accusative singular). Luke uses the accusative to measure the extent of Anna's service. Acts 26:7 similarly uses the accusative (nykta kai hemeran) for the twelve tribes serving God "instantly day and night."

The diagnostic contrast is exact. The same words -- nyx and hemera -- change grammatical function by case. Accusative = how long. Genitive = what kind of time. John uses the genitive in all five Revelation passages, consistently characterizing the quality of the activity rather than measuring its duration. This is not an incidental detail. It is a grammatical choice available to a Greek author who wants to express either quality or duration, and John consistently chooses the quality-characterizing construction.

docs.title: 2. The Five Occurrences as a Unified Pattern
docs.text:
Revelation contains exactly five hemeras kai nuktos passages. Mapped together, they form a coherent literary pattern:

Rev 4:8 -- the living creatures worship God "day and night" with the trishagion ("Holy, holy, holy"). This is positive, continuous praise. No interpreter reads this as the creatures being consciously tormented by their worship. The "no rest" (ouk echousin anapausin) describes the thoroughgoing quality of their devotion -- they fill every part of the day-night cycle with worship.

Rev 7:15 -- the great multitude serves God "day and night in his temple" (latreuousin auto hemeras kai nuktos en to nao autou). This is the second positive use. The verb latreuo (G3000) designates sacral, whole-life worship. The setting is God's inner temple (naos, G3485). The "day and night" describes the quality of their access -- perpetual, uninterrupted, complete.

Rev 12:10 -- Satan "accused them before our God day and night" (kategoron autous... hemeras kai nuktos). This is the negative use that resolves the entire question. The present participle kategoron (G2723) describes the continuous character of Satan's accusation during the period it was occurring. But the aorist eblethe (G906, "was cast," aorist passive indicative) marks the decisive end of that activity. The adverb arti (G737, "now, at this very moment") declares the turning point: "NOW is come salvation... for the accuser is cast down."

Satan's "day and night" accusation was not paused, rescheduled, or reduced in intensity. It was permanently terminated. The heavenly court has changed. The accuser has been removed. The "day and night" activity is over. This single verse proves that hemeras kai nuktos can describe an activity that is continuous and thoroughgoing during its occurrence and yet has a definite, final endpoint. If "day and night" meant "forever without end," Satan would still be accusing. He is not.

Rev 14:11 -- the beast-worshippers "have no rest day nor night" (ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos). The crux text, using the identical construction as Rev 4:8.

Rev 20:10 -- the devil, beast, and false prophet "shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever" (basanisthesontai hemeras kai nuktos eis tous aionas ton aionon). All three subjects are non-human or symbolic: the devil (a supernatural spirit being), the beast (a seven-headed composite entity), and the false prophet (the two-horned earth beast of Rev 13:11-17). Humans in the same passage receive different vocabulary -- "devoured" (Rev 20:9, katephagen, aorist active), "cast into the lake of fire" (Rev 20:15), and "the second death" (Rev 20:14). Revelation maintains a consistent vocabulary distinction between non-human/symbolic entities (torment language) and human beings (death/destruction language).

docs.title: 3. The Rev 4:8 / Rev 14:11 Parallel -- The Same Grammar Demands the Same Reading
docs.text:
The identical grammatical construction in Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11 is the most direct evidence available. The word study for anapausis (G372) confirms that the word appears only 5 times in the NT, and the two Revelation uses share exact grammatical form:

  • Rev 4:8: anapausin ouk echousin hemeras kai nuktos
  • Rev 14:11: ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos

Same verb (echousin, present active indicative 3P). Same noun (anapausin, accusative singular feminine). Same negation (ouk). Same genitive of time (hemeras kai nuktos, both genitive singular feminine). Same book. Same author.

In 4:8, the absence of rest is positive -- the creatures worship without pause. In 14:11, the absence of rest is negative -- the beast-worshippers have no relief from judgment. The function of the formula is the same in both: it describes the quality and completeness of the activity. The creatures' worship fills the entire day-night cycle without interruption. The beast-worshippers' judgment fills the entire day-night cycle without relief.

If someone insists that "no rest day nor night" in 14:11 means eternal conscious experience, they must explain why the identical phrase in 4:8 does not mean eternal conscious existence of the living creatures in a state of restless distress. The grammar is the same. The meaning must be the same unless compelling contextual evidence overrides the parallel -- and no such evidence exists.

docs.title: 4. Rev 12:10 -- The Decisive Counter-Example
docs.text:
Revelation 12:10 is the single most powerful argument in this study. Satan "accused them before our God day and night." The participle kategoron is present tense, describing the ongoing character of the accusation. The genitive hemeras kai nuktos characterizes the accusation as continuous and relentless. And then -- arti egeneto he soteria -- "NOW is come salvation." The aorist eblethe ("was cast down") marks the completed, irreversible expulsion of the accuser.

This is not a pause. It is not an interruption. The accusatory ministry is permanently ended. The OT background (Job 1:6-12, Zech 3:1-2) shows Satan in the role of courtroom prosecutor, standing before God and bringing charges against the saints. Rev 12:10 declares that this "day and night" prosecutorial activity has been terminated at Christ's victory.

The implications are straightforward: if hemeras kai nuktos described the eternal nature of an activity, Satan would still be accusing. The formula describes the character of the activity during its occurrence (unceasing, relentless, thoroughgoing) and says nothing about its guaranteed eternal continuation. The "day and night" accusing was absolute -- without pause, without exception, filling the entire temporal framework -- and it ended.

docs.title: 5. Rev 22:5 and 21:25 -- The Temporal Framework Dissolves
docs.text:
Rev 22:5 declares: nyx ouk estai eti -- "night shall not be any more." Rev 21:25 confirms: nyx gar ouk estai ekei -- "for night shall not be there." The day/night framework that God established in Gen 1:5 ("God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night") is abolished in the new creation.

This dissolution has direct consequences for the "day and night" formula. If "night" no longer exists in the eternal state, then activities described as occurring "day and night" cannot be literal temporal descriptions of eternal realities. The saints' "day and night" service (Rev 7:15) continues in eternity -- but not because night continues. The service is perpetual in character, described using the "day and night" merism because that is the present-age framework within which John writes. The judgment activities described as "day and night" (Rev 14:11, 20:10) operate within a framework that is itself temporary.

The bookend is complete: Gen 1:5 creates the day/night distinction. Rev 22:5 abolishes it. Everything described as "day and night" within Revelation operates inside this created framework that has a beginning and an end.

docs.title: 6. The Anapausis Antithesis -- Rev 14:11 vs. Rev 14:13
docs.text:
John places the sharpest possible contrast two verses apart. In 14:11, the beast-worshippers have no anapausis (G372, rest/intermission/cessation). In 14:13, the blessed dead anapahsontai (G373, future passive of anapauo, the cognate verb) ek ton kopon auton -- "they shall rest from their labours."

Same word family: ana (up, again) + pauo (to cease, stop). Noun in 14:11, cognate verb in 14:13. Adjacent verses. Opposite groups. Opposite outcomes. This is a deliberate literary antithesis -- John places the two side by side so that each defines the other.

If the blessed dead's "rest" means cessation of labor, the end of struggle, entry into reward -- and it does, since their "works follow them" -- then the beast-worshippers' "no rest" means the absence of this relief. They receive no intermission, no pause, no cessation from the judgment's pressure. The antithesis defines "no rest" as the opposite of "rest from labours" -- not as eternal conscious existence, but as thoroughgoing judgment without relief.

Jesus himself offers anapausis in Matt 11:28-29: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (anapausin). Take my yoke upon you... and ye shall find rest (anapausin) unto your souls." If Christ's rest is spiritual refreshment and the cessation of burden, then the denial of rest in Rev 14:11 is the absence of this refreshment -- no relief from the judgment that is coming.

docs.title: 7. The Broader NT Pattern -- Every "Day and Night" Is Qualitative
docs.text:
Outside Revelation, the NT uses the "day and night" / "night and day" formula in at least ten passages. Every one describes the quality or intensity of an activity:

Paul labored "night and day" (nuktos kai hemeras, genitive, 1 Thess 2:9; 2 Thess 3:8) -- working hard, not literally without sleeping. The widow "continueth in supplications and prayers night and day" (1 Tim 5:5, genitive) -- devout, not literally non-stop prayer. Paul remembers Timothy "in my prayers night and day" (2 Tim 1:3, genitive) -- faithful, persistent remembrance. God's elect "cry day and night unto him" (Luke 18:7, genitive) -- fervent, persistent prayer. The enemies "watched the gates day and night to kill" Paul (Acts 9:24, genitive) -- thorough surveillance. Paul "ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears" over three years (Acts 20:31, genitive) -- devoted pastoral vigilance.

Even the strongest possible case -- Mark 5:5, where the demoniac is "always, night and day" (dia pantos nuktos kai hemeras) crying and cutting himself -- is qualitative. The demoniac did sleep, eat, and pause. The formula describes the relentless, pervasive character of his torment. And his "day and night" torment ended when Jesus delivered him.

Luke 2:37 and Acts 26:7 use the accusative (measuring extent) rather than the genitive (characterizing quality). Even these accusative uses do not claim literal unbroken activity -- Anna did not pray without a single pause for 84 years. The accusative measures the span; the genitive characterizes the quality. Revelation uses the genitive every time.

docs.title: 8. The OT Merism -- The Foundation John Inherited
docs.text:
The Hebrew yom v'laylah / yomam va-laylah merism provides the OT foundation:

Gen 8:22: "Day and night shall not cease" -- the created order expressed as merism. Josh 1:8 / Psa 1:2: "Meditate therein day and night" -- devotional completeness, not literal 24-hour meditation. Psa 32:4: "Day and night thy hand was heavy upon me" -- thoroughgoing divine conviction that ended when David confessed (Psa 32:5). Isa 62:6: Watchmen who "shall never hold their peace day nor night" -- continuous vigilance. Neh 1:6: Praying "day and night" -- intensity of intercession. Jer 14:17: Tears "night and day" -- depth of grief. 1 Ki 8:29: God's eyes "open toward this house night and day" -- continuous divine attention.

The OT pattern is uniform: "day and night" expresses completeness, thoroughness, and pervasive quality. It is a merism -- a figure naming two poles to express totality, like "heaven and earth" meaning "everything" or "searched high and low" meaning "searched everywhere." The formula crosses into the NT via the LXX bridge (yowm H3117 to hemera G2250, PMI 3.46; layil H3915 to nyx G3571, PMI 6.64 -- among the most stable mappings in the LXX).

docs.title: 9. Isaiah 34:10-15 -- The OT Source That Resolves the Question
docs.text:
The most telling OT evidence is Isa 34:10, the direct source for Rev 14:11. Both share the same three elements: (1) fire not quenched "night nor day," (2) smoke ascending "for ever," (3) permanent desolation. The Hebrew reads: laylah ve-yomam lo tikhbeh ("night nor day it shall not be quenched"); le-owlam ya'aleh ashana ("forever its smoke shall ascend").

But Isaiah 34:11-15 describes the aftermath. Cormorants and bitterns possess the land. Owls and ravens dwell in it. Thorns grow in the palaces. Wild beasts meet in the ruins. The screech owl rests there and finds a place of rest. Owls make nests, lay eggs, hatch young. Vultures gather with their mates.

Animals cannot inhabit a place that is still on fire. Nesting birds cannot raise young in burning ruins. Thorns cannot grow in active flames. The fire that was "not quenched night nor day" is demonstrably out. The smoke that "shall go up for ever" (le-owlam) is the permanent testimony of completed destruction, not ongoing burning. The subject of owlam (H5769) determines its scope: applied to God, it means genuinely eternal; applied to Edom's fire, it means a permanent result -- destruction that cannot be reversed, not fire that burns without end.

This is the imagery John draws on in Rev 14:11. If the OT source describes a fire that has completed its work, the NT passage that echoes it should be read the same way.

docs.title: 10. The Convergence of Evidence
docs.text:
Eight independent lines of evidence converge on the same conclusion:

(1) The genitive of time characterizes quality, not extent. (2) Rev 4:8's identical formula is read as quality by everyone. (3) Rev 12:10 proves "day and night" can describe terminated activity. (4) Rev 7:15's "day and night" service occurs where "there shall be no night." (5) Every NT "day and night" outside Revelation is qualitative. (6) Every OT yom v'laylah is qualitative. (7) Isa 34:10's same formula describes a fire that is out. (8) The anapausis antithesis (14:11 vs. 14:13) defines "no rest" as absence of relief, not eternal duration.

No single argument is decisive in isolation. Together, they form an overwhelming case. The formula means the same thing everywhere it appears: thoroughgoing, uninterrupted activity filling the entire day-night framework. It describes the character of the action, not its guaranteed eternal continuation.

docs.title: Word Studies
docs.text:
Anapausis (G372): Rest, intermission, cessation. 5 NT occurrences. The identical construction ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos in Rev 4:8 and 14:11 is the central grammatical parallel. In 4:8 it describes positive ceaseless worship; in 14:11 it describes negative judgment without relief. Same grammar, same function.

Anapauo (G373): To cause to rest, give rest. 12 NT occurrences. The cognate verb creates the antithesis in Rev 14:13 -- the blessed dead "rest from their labours," directly contrasting the beast-worshippers' "no rest" two verses earlier.

Hemera (G2250) and Nyx (G3571): Day (388 tokens) and night (65 occurrences). The paired merism appears 28 times in the NT, expressing continuous activity. The genitive forms hemeras and nuktos appear in all five Revelation passages. The abolition of nyx in Rev 22:5 dissolves the framework.

Basanizo (G928): To torment. 12 NT occurrences. Seven non-judgment uses (illness, waves, rowing, moral distress). Five judgment uses, all in Revelation's apocalyptic framework. The word does not inherently require eternal duration -- Rev 9:5 limits it to five months.

Basanismos (G929): Torment (noun). 6 occurrences, exclusively in Revelation. Four are time-bounded or applied to destroyed entities.

Kapnos (G2586) and Ashan (H6227): Greek smoke (13 tokens) and Hebrew smoke (25 occurrences). Smoke in biblical thought is the visible trace of completed transformation -- evidence that fire has done its work. The verb anabaino (G305) is used for both worship smoke (Rev 8:4) and judgment smoke (Rev 14:11) ascending before God.

Owlam (H5769): Forever, eternity. 432 OT tokens. Subject-determined: applied to God = genuinely eternal; applied to Edom's smoke = permanent result of completed destruction.

Kategoreo (G2723): To accuse, 24 occurrences. The related noun kategoros (G2725, accuser) appears in Rev 12:10 alongside the verb. Rev 12:10 is the theological climax: the accuser's "day and night" prosecutorial role is permanently terminated by Christ's victory.

Arti (G737): Now, at this moment. 36 occurrences. In Rev 12:10, it marks the temporal boundary where "day and night" accusation ends -- the cosmic turning point.

Latreuo (G3000): To serve, worship. 21 occurrences. The sacral service verb in Rev 7:15 describes positive "day and night" temple worship, paralleling Rev 4:8.

docs.title: Rev 20:10 -- "Tormented Day and Night For Ever and Ever"
docs.text:
The combination of hemeras kai nuktos with eis tous aionas ton aionon ("for ever and ever") appears to press toward eternal duration. This is the strongest passage for the eternal-conscious-torment reading.

However, several factors qualify this: (1) All three subjects (devil, beast, false prophet) are non-human/symbolic. No literal human being is the subject of this formula. (2) The "ages of ages" formula is subject-determined -- applied to God it means genuinely eternal; applied to judgment on non-eternal subjects it means permanent result (cf. Isa 34:10). (3) Ezek 28:18-19 describes the same Satan-figure as becoming "ashes upon the earth" and ceasing to exist: "never shalt thou be any more." The didactic oracle governs the apocalyptic vision. (4) Humans in the same passage receive different vocabulary: "devoured" (v.9), "second death" (vv.14-15). (5) The genitive of time still functions as a quality-characterizer, and the Rev 12:10 counter-example still proves the formula can describe terminated activity.

docs.title: Matt 25:41, 46 -- "Everlasting Fire" and "Everlasting Punishment"
docs.text: Though not "day and night" passages, these are frequently connected to Rev 14:11 in theological discussion. "Everlasting fire" and "everlasting punishment" use aionios (G166), the adjective form. The Hebrews pattern governs: "eternal redemption" is redemption obtained once with a permanent result, "eternal judgment" is judgment rendered once with a permanent result. "Everlasting punishment" is punishment with a permanent result -- not punishment that is consciously experienced forever. The result (death, the second death) is what is everlasting, not the process.

docs.title: Mark 5:5 -- The Strongest Negative "Day and Night"
docs.text: The demoniac's "always, night and day" (dia pantos nuktos kai hemeras) crying and self-harm is the most intense "day and night" formula outside Revelation, reinforced by dia pantos. Even this is qualitative -- the demoniac was not literally awake and active every second. He slept. He paused. The formula describes the pervasive, relentless character of his distress. And his "day and night" torment ended when Jesus cast out the demons. The activity was thoroughgoing during its occurrence and reached a definite endpoint.

docs.title: Rev 21:4 -- "No More Pain" in the Eschatological State
docs.text: If the wicked are consciously tormented forever, then "there shall be no more pain" (Rev 21:4) is not universally true -- pain exists eternally somewhere in the universe. The eschatological vision of Revelation envisions complete resolution: no death, no sorrow, no crying, no pain. "The former things are passed away." If eternal conscious torment continues, the former things have not fully passed away. The eschatological endpoint requires that judgment reaches completion and pain ceases everywhere.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The "day and night" formula in Revelation is a genitive-of-time construction inherited from the OT yom v'laylah merism, carried through the LXX into the NT, and deployed by John as a quality-marker for continuous, uninterrupted activity. It appears five times in Revelation, always in the genitive case, always characterizing the thoroughgoing nature of the activity it describes rather than measuring its duration.

The evidence converges from grammar, internal Revelation parallels, broader NT usage, OT source imagery, and literary structure. The genitive of time characterizes quality, not extent (Rev 4:8, 7:15, 12:10, 14:11, 20:10 all use the genitive; Luke 2:37 and Acts 26:7 use the accusative for duration). Rev 4:8's identical construction is universally read as describing the quality of worship. Rev 12:10 proves the formula can describe an activity that has been permanently terminated. Rev 22:5 dissolves the day/night temporal framework itself. The anapausis antithesis (Rev 14:11 vs. 14:13) defines "no rest" by contrast with "rest from labours." Isa 34:10-15 uses the same formula for a fire that is demonstrably out, with animals nesting in the cold ruins. Every NT "day and night" outside Revelation is qualitative. Every OT yom v'laylah is qualitative.

"No rest day nor night" (Rev 14:11) describes the thoroughgoing nature of a judgment during its execution -- complete, without relief, without intermission, filling the entire day-night cycle -- not eternal conscious experience. The judgment is real, severe, and without respite while it lasts. But the formula tells us about the quality of the judgment, not its infinite duration.

This study builds on the foundations established in prior studies: the anapausis parallel (etc7-11), the smoke-ascending formula (smoke-imagery-hebrew-mind), the basanizo genre restriction (etc7-11, etc7-12), the non-human subjects of Rev 20:10 (etc7-12), the "ages of ages" subject-determination (for-ever-and-ever-revelation, etc7-08), and the bounded "day and night" accusation of Rev 12:10 (hist-11, revelation-12-timing). Its unique contribution is the systematic mapping of all five Revelation "day and night" occurrences as a unified literary pattern, the genitive-of-time grammatical analysis, the anapausis antithesis as deliberate literary structure, the broader NT and OT "day and night" evidence, and the eschatological dissolution of the day/night framework in Rev 22:5.

docs.title: Focus Areas
docs.text:
1. The Genitive of Time Construction (hemeras kai nuktos): READ $GRAMMAR_REF/greek/genitive-of-time.md — this entry specifically covers the hemeras kai nuktos pattern including all 5 Revelation occurrences. The genitive of time expresses 'time within which' or 'during which,' characterizing the temporal backdrop of an action rather than measuring its extent. The paired merism hemeras kai nuktos is a special subtype expressing continuous uninterrupted activity spanning the full day-night cycle. The critical diagnostic contrast is Luke 2:37, which uses the ACCUSATIVE nykta kai hemeran (measuring extent of Anna's service) vs. the GENITIVE in Rev 4:8 etc. (characterizing the activity as filling the day-night framework). Run greek_parser.py --verse on Rev 4:8, Rev 7:15, Rev 12:10, Rev 14:11, Rev 20:10, Luke 2:37, and Matt 24:20 to verify case forms. Also run semantic_grammar.py 'genitive of time' --greek for Wallace/BDF textbook citations beyond what the library entry provides. Verses: Rev 4:8, Rev 7:15, Rev 12:10, Rev 14:11, Rev 20:10, Luke 2:37, Matt 24:20 Strong's: G2250, G3571

  2. All 5 Revelation 'Day and Night' Occurrences Mapped as a Unified Pattern: Retrieve KJV text with full chapter context for all 5 occurrences: Rev 4:8 (living creatures, positive worship, ongoing), Rev 7:15 (great multitude, positive service, eschatological), Rev 12:10 (Satan, negative accusation, terminated), Rev 14:11 (beast-worshippers, negative torment, judgment), Rev 20:10 (devil/beast/false prophet, negative torment, judgment). Run greek_parser.py --verse on each to verify the exact Greek construction — particularly whether the formula is identical or varies. Map the pattern: THREE positive uses (4:8, 7:15, and arguably 12:10 as positive-by-removal) vs. TWO negative-judgment uses (14:11, 20:10). Note that Rev 12:10's 'day and night' activity was TERMINATED by a historical event — the only 'day and night' in Revelation that has explicitly ended. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py --hybrid-ot and --hybrid-nt on Rev 4:8, Rev 14:11, and Rev 20:10 to find parallels. Verses: Rev 4:8, Rev 7:15, Rev 12:10, Rev 14:11, Rev 20:10 Strong's: G2250, G3571, G372, G928

  3. The Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11 Parallel — Identical Construction, Opposite Contexts: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G372-anapausis.md — the canonical entry documents the identical construction ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos in both Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11. Both are present active indicative (echousin) + accusative noun (anapausin) + genitive of time (hemeras kai nuktos). In Rev 4:8, no interpreter reads 'they rest not day and night' as a statement about the creatures being in perpetual conscious distress — it describes the QUALITY of their worship as uninterrupted. The same construction in Rev 14:11 should carry the same function: describing the quality of the judgment as thoroughgoing during its execution, not guaranteeing its eternal duration. Run greek_parser.py --verse on both Rev 4:8 and Rev 14:11. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py on both. The research agent should note whether any grammatical difference exists between the two uses. Verses: Rev 4:8, Rev 14:11, Isa 6:2-3 Strong's: G372, G373, G2250, G3571

  4. Rev 12:10 — The 'Day and Night' Activity That Ended: Prior studies (hist-11, revelation-12-timing) establish that Satan's 'day and night' accusation was terminated at Christ's victory. READ the relevant sections of those studies (referenced in 00-references.md). The key verb is kategoreō (G2723) — the accuser 'accused them before our God day and night.' The heavenly voice says 'NOW (arti, G737) is come salvation... for the accuser is cast down.' The 'day and night' activity is not merely paused — it is permanently ended by the casting down. This demonstrates conclusively that hemeras kai nuktos describes the CHARACTER of an activity during its occurrence (unceasing, thoroughgoing), not its guaranteed eternal continuation. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G2725-kategoros.md for the accuser terminology. Run greek_parser.py --verse on Rev 12:10 and retrieve Rev 12:7-12 with full context. Verses: Rev 12:10, Rev 12:7-12, Job 1:6-12, Zech 3:1-2 Strong's: G2725, G2723, G737

  5. Rev 7:15 — Positive 'Day and Night' Service in God's Temple: Rev 7:15 says the great multitude 'serve him day and night in his temple.' This is the second positive use of the formula in Revelation, paralleling Rev 4:8. The verb is latreuō (G3000, serve/worship) — a sacral service term. The setting is God's naos (inner temple), not just the broader hieron. The 'day and night' here describes the quality of their access — perpetual, uninterrupted temple service — not a statement about the literal passage of time (especially since Rev 21:25 and 22:5 declare there will be no night). Run greek_parser.py --verse on Rev 7:15. Retrieve Rev 7:13-17 full context. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G4352-proskyneo.md for worship vocabulary context. Note the logical tension: if the great multitude serves 'day and night' but Rev 22:5 says 'there shall be no night,' the formula must describe quality, not literal temporal framework. Verses: Rev 7:15, Rev 7:13-17, Rev 22:5, Rev 21:25 Strong's: G3000, G3485, G4352

  6. The Eschatological Dissolution of Day/Night (Rev 21:25, 22:5): READ $WORD_STUDIES/TR-layil-nyx.md — the translation relationship entry documents the eschatological reversal: 'there shall be no night there' (Rev 21:25, 22:5) echoes and consummates Gen 1:5 where God first named the night. Rev 22:5 declares nyx ouk estai eti — 'night shall not be any more.' If the 'day and night' framework itself is dissolved in the new creation, then 'day and night' in Revelation functions as a temporal-quality marker for the present age, not an assertion about eternal states. The saints' 'day and night' service (Rev 7:15) continues eternally because the saints continue — but without the night/day distinction. The beast-worshippers' 'day and night' torment (Rev 14:11) describes their judgment within the temporal framework that is itself abolished. READ $WORD_STUDIES/H3915-layil.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H3117-yowm.md for the OT creation vocabulary. Run greek_parser.py --verse on Rev 22:5 and Rev 21:25. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py on Rev 22:5. Verses: Rev 22:5, Rev 21:25, Gen 1:5, Gen 8:22 Strong's: G3571, G2250, H3915, H3117

  7. The Anapausis Antithesis: Rev 14:11 vs. Rev 14:13: READ $WORD_STUDIES/G372-anapausis.md and $WORD_STUDIES/G373-anapauo.md. Rev 14:11 uses the noun anapausis (G372, rest/intermission) — the beast-worshippers 'have no rest (anapausin) day nor night.' Rev 14:13 uses the cognate verb anapauo (G373, to rest/cease) — the blessed dead 'rest (anapauontai or anapausontai) from their labours.' Same root, two verses apart, opposite outcomes. The beast-worshippers receive NO anapausis; the faithful dead receive FULL anapauo. This is a deliberate literary structure — John places the antithesis in adjacent verses to define 'no rest' by contrast with 'rest.' If the faithful's 'rest' is the cessation of labor and the beginning of reward, then the beast-worshippers' 'no rest' is the absence of relief during their judgment. Run greek_parser.py --verse on both Rev 14:11 and Rev 14:13. Verses: Rev 14:11, Rev 14:13, Matt 11:28-29, Heb 4:1-11 Strong's: G372, G373

  8. Broader NT 'Day and Night' Pattern — The Merism as Quality-Marker: The NT uses hemeras kai nuktos / nuktos kai hemeras in at least 10 passages outside Revelation: Acts 9:24 (enemies watching gates), Acts 20:31 (Paul warning), Acts 26:7 (twelve tribes serving), 1 Thess 2:9 (Paul laboring), 2 Thess 3:8 (Paul working), 1 Tim 5:5 (widow praying), 2 Tim 1:3 (Paul remembering), Luke 2:37 (Anna serving — but ACCUSATIVE, not genitive), Luke 18:7 (elect crying), Mark 5:5 (demoniac crying). In EVERY case, 'day and night' describes the QUALITY or INTENSITY of the activity — its thoroughgoing, uninterrupted nature — not a literal claim that the person never stopped for 24 continuous hours. Paul did not literally labor without a single second of rest. Anna did not literally pray without interruption for 84 years. The twelve tribes did not literally serve God every conscious second. The formula is a quality-marker, not a duration-guarantee. Run greek_parser.py --verse on Acts 26:7, 1 Thess 2:9, Luke 2:37, Luke 18:7, and Mark 5:5. Note the case variation (genitive vs. accusative in Luke 2:37). Verses: Acts 26:7, 1 Thess 2:9, 2 Thess 3:8, 1 Tim 5:5, 2 Tim 1:3, Luke 2:37, Luke 18:7, Mark 5:5, Acts 9:24, Acts 20:31 Strong's: G2250, G3571

  9. The OT Yom V'laylah Merism — Day and Night as Totality Expression: READ $WORD_STUDIES/H3117-yowm.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H3915-layil.md for the OT temporal vocabulary. READ $WORD_STUDIES/TR-layil-nyx.md for the cross-testament bridge. Key OT 'day and night' passages: Gen 8:22 (creation order — 'day and night shall not cease,' totality of time), Josh 1:8 / Psa 1:2 (meditate 'day and night' — devotional completeness, not literal non-stop meditation), Psa 32:4 ('day and night thy hand was heavy upon me' — thoroughness of divine discipline), Isa 34:10 ('not quenched night nor day' — the direct OT source for Rev 14:11, describing a fire that is OUT by v.11-15), Isa 62:6 (watchmen 'shall never hold their peace day nor night' — continuous vigilance), Neh 1:6 (praying 'day and night' — intensity of intercession), Jer 14:17 (tears 'night and day' — unceasing grief). Run hebrew_parser.py --verse on Isa 34:10, Josh 1:8, Psa 1:2, Psa 32:4, and Gen 8:22. The OT pattern is consistent: 'day and night' describes COMPLETENESS or THOROUGHNESS of an activity, not its literal uninterrupted 24-hour performance. Verses: Gen 8:22, Josh 1:8, Psa 1:2, Psa 32:4, Isa 34:10, Isa 62:6, Neh 1:6, Jer 14:17, 1 Ki 8:29 Strong's: H3117, H3915

  10. Quality vs. Duration — The Governing Principle: The convergence of evidence should be evaluated: (1) The genitive of time construction characterizes the temporal backdrop, not the extent. (2) Rev 4:8's identical formula is universally read as quality, not eternal-conscious-torment of the living creatures. (3) Rev 12:10 proves 'day and night' can describe a terminated activity. (4) Rev 7:15's 'day and night' service occurs in a reality where 'there shall be no night' (Rev 22:5), proving the formula is qualitative. (5) Every NT 'day and night' outside Revelation is qualitative. (6) Every OT yom v'laylah is qualitative. (7) Isa 34:10 uses the same formula for a fire that is demonstrably out. (8) The anapausis antithesis (14:11 vs. 14:13) defines 'no rest' as absence of relief during judgment, not eternal conscious experience. The research agent should retrieve the smoke-formula data from prior studies (smoke-imagery-hebrew-mind, etc7-11) and the basanizo data from etc7-12 to integrate with the 'day and night' analysis. Run cross_testament_parallels_v2.py --hybrid-ot and --hybrid-nt on Isa 34:10. READ $WORD_STUDIES/G166-aionios.md and $WORD_STUDIES/H5769-owlam.md for the 'forever' vocabulary that co-occurs with 'day and night' in judgment contexts. Verses: Rev 4:8, Rev 14:11, Rev 12:10, Rev 7:15, Rev 22:5, Isa 34:10, Gen 8:22 Strong's: G372, G2250, G3571, G166, H5769

docs.text:
לַ֤יְלָה וְיֹומָם֙ לֹ֣א תִכְבֶּ֔ה לְעֹולָ֖ם יַעֲלֶ֣ה עֲשָׁנָ֑הּ מִדֹּ֤ור לָדֹור֙ תֶּחֱרָ֔ב לְנֵ֣צַח נְצָחִ֔ים אֵ֥ין עֹבֵ֖ר בָּֽהּ׃

Key parsing: לַיְלָה - לילה Noun.ms.Abs 'night' וְיֹומָם - יומם Adv 'by day' לֹא - לא Neg 'not' תִכְבֶּה - כבה Verb.Qal.Impf.3fs 'go out/be quenched' לְעוֹלָם - עולם Noun.ms.Abs 'eternity/forever' יַעֲלֶה - עלה Verb.Qal.Impf.3ms 'ascend' עֲשָׁנָהּ - עשׁן Noun.ms.Abs+3fs 'its smoke' מִדֹּור לָדֹור - 'from generation to generation' תֶּחֱרָב - חרב Verb.Qal.Impf.3fs 'be dry/lie waste' לְנֵצַח נְצָחִים - 'for ever and ever' אֵין עֹבֵר בָּהּ - 'none passes through it'

docs.text:
כִּ֤י׀ יֹומָ֣ם וָלַיְלָה֮ תִּכְבַּ֥ד עָלַ֗י יָ֫דֶ֥ךָ נֶהְפַּ֥ךְ לְשַׁדִּ֑י בְּחַרְבֹ֖נֵי קַ֣יִץ סֶֽלָה׃

Key parsing: יֹומָם - יומם Adv 'by day' וָלַיְלָה - לילה Noun.ms.Abs 'and night' תִּכְבַּד - כבד Verb.Qal.Impf.3fs 'be heavy' עָלַי - על Prep+1us 'upon me' יָדֶךָ - יד Noun.s.Abs+2ms 'your hand'

docs.title: Cross-Testament Parallels
docs.text:
• Rev 4:8 → Isa 6:2 (ot, vocabulary + structural — six-winged creatures, triple 'holy', throne room worship)
  • Rev 14:11 → Isa 34:10 (ot, vocabulary + structural + theological — 'night nor day,' 'smoke shall go up for ever,' burn/age language. Top OT parallel (hybrid score 0.401, theological match 0.30))
  • Rev 14:11 → Rev 20:10 (nt, vocabulary + structural + theological — age, beast, burn, torment, 'day and night for ever and ever.' Top NT parallel (hybrid score 0.498))
  • Rev 14:11 → Rev 19:3 (nt, vocabulary + theological — 'smoke rose up for ever and ever,' age, burn language)
  • Rev 14:11 → Rev 14:9 (nt, vocabulary — beast, image, mark, anyone (immediate context))
  • Rev 20:10 → Rev 19:20 (nt, vocabulary — beast, burn, cast, deceive. Top NT parallel (hybrid score 0.641))
  • Rev 20:10 → Matt 25:41 (nt, vocabulary + structural — age, burn, devil, 'everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels')
  • Rev 20:10 → Isa 34:10 (ot, vocabulary + theological — age, burn, 'continual/forever' language)
  • Rev 22:5 → Isa 60:19 (ot, vocabulary — age, light, sun. Top OT parallel (hybrid score 0.433). 'The sun shall be no more thy light... the LORD shall be unto thee an everlasting light')
  • Rev 22:5 → Rev 21:23 (nt, vocabulary — enlighten, lamp, need, sun. Top NT parallel (hybrid score 0.471))
  • Rev 4:8 → Rev 15:7 (nt, vocabulary — creature, four, full. Top NT parallel (hybrid score 0.452))
